Holy crap this was a good book. 
 Review here [CONTAINS SPOILERS!]: http://www.renaemcbrianbooks.com/2014...

I liked it; I didn't love it. I'm still thinking about the ending and how weird it was (in my opinion). It was a very straightforward detective novel. It felt slow for me at times - not suspenseful enough - and the characters felt a bit cookie-cutter/cliche. I still wanted to know what happened though, and spent most of yesterday reading the entire second half. And Rowling's descriptions are just fantastic. All in all, probably worth reading but not earth-shattering.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I loved the back and forth format. The unreliable narrators- but maybe not how you first think! A stay up all night because you have to see how it ends! kind of book. And then it just ends. That's fine, I hate them both and don't care about how miserable they will be for the rest of their lives. At least I hope so. Still, I'd have liked to have seen justice done. I don't think Amy behaved very true to herself in the third part where she wants to take Nick back, what happened to all the righteous fury that she maintained for a whole year? 
 A real page turner!

It's pretty wonderful to read serious science fiction that's so well written and that (especially) has such a great focus on deep and evolving characters. 
 The science fiction is also quite good. It's inventive, it's interesting, it's modern, and it's innovative. 
 Finally, the authors do a great job of creating real mysteries that aren't answered while still presenting a book with solid closure. 
 All around, a spectacular debut.

This was a great tragic love story, one that ended up with a happy ending. Yes Granted a very weird ending, but I good one. This book showed that one who has been through so much could find love as great as this, and that even with the loss sacrifices were made, and redemptions unfolded. It was great I loved it!

I was reluctant to read this one at first because High School Romance really has NEVER been my thing. After a very strong suggestion from a colleague I trust, a number of gushing reviews and the fact that music (the really good new wavy 80's music that was my soundtrack through my high school years - and sort of now too), I decided to pick it up. I'm really glad I did. First of all, Eleanor and Park are two realistic, often confused, misfits who eventually find each other. I was really able to relate to them. 
 Eleanor lives with her mother, completely abusive drunk step-father, and her 4 little siblings. She had already been kicked out of the house by her step-father once before. They are broke (or more likely, the step-dad controls all the money). Mom has to sneak the kids new used clothes, food, toothbrushes, etc. She is chubby, has curly red hair and freckles, and is bullied badly. 
 Park is the only Asian kid in Omaha - or at least he thinks he is. He sometimes wonders if he is gay because of his almost blanket disinterest in the girls (and boys) around him. 
 It has the feeling of a John Hughes movie, with great music, kids that don't fit in with the accepted crowds, and hope without the obligatory fairy tale ending. I'm curious about her new book too.

Received for free through Goodreads First Reads. 
 I really want to give this book 2.5 stars, but as goodreads doesn't have a half star option yet, I'll rate high because I'm generous that way. Craig Larsen has a decent-enough story here, and he does a fantastic job creating an atmosphere of disorientation and dread. I was literally a little sick to my stomach while reading this, because the feelings are so well developed. Ultimately, though, the characters are a little one-dimensional, and the conspiracy-theory finish is kind of overwrought. Another reviewer wrote "less is more", although she was referencing Larsen's use of adjectives. I would quote her, only on plot points--not everything has to tie together into a neat even bow, and not everyone has to show up in here. 
 I like Larsen's style, plus he seems to like The Killers, so props to him. I'd be interested in reading his next novel.
A decent Picoult read, although not my favorite. The reason why I gave it so few stars was because I really disliked the ending.

Part of the enjoyment of reading is discovering the magic of a new author. I'm so glad I staring reading this novella after remembering that a lot of Goodreads friends loved it. What a refreshing change to have an average looking hero who you can't help falling a little in love with because of his actions. Hugo Marshall nicknamed The Wolf of Clermont" is one such hero, the fourteenth son of a coalminer whose quick brain has brought him into service to the dissolute Duke of Clermont. When the impoverished but brave Selena Barton challenges the Duke's reputation(and is completely in her rights to do so) it is Hugo's job to rectify the situation by whatever means possible. What follows is a meeting of wit and minds as what started as an impossible situation leads to a passionate love. 
 What a beautifully written and involving story. My only criticism is that I would have loved a full length novel and more of the witty interchanges between Selena and Hugo. Great characters. This novella sets up the story for Courtney Milan's new series The Brothers Sinister which if this novella is anything to go by promises to be a refreshing new historical series.
The blood in this book bothered me a lot. I guess that's why I didn't like it quite as well as the others. A lot of interesting plot twists that kept me wondering what would happen next.

3.5 Stars, Completed March 9, 2017 
 I was currently reading a wide array of books as I read Pachinko, but, surprisingly, it was the one I found myself reaching for the most. (Seeing as my most highly anticipated release of 2017, 
 A Conjuring of Light 
 was also vying for my attention at the time, this is saying quite a lot.) 
 Essentially, it's a story that follows an ethnic Korean family for four generations. First, with their beginnings in a Japanese-occupied Korea then later in Japan. The book is divided into three parts. The first being written the strongest and most compelling to read, in my opinion, since it tells the tale of the kind and wise but disfigured Hoonie and then his daughter, Sunja, as she faces a judgmental society when she becomes pregnant out of wedlock. The middle being more of a filler but much needed segment all the same. And, lastly, the third that is about the fourth generation with characters such as Solomon; this also happened to be my least favorite because the supporting subplots felt like random, unnecessary tangents at times. However what I thought to be inconsistent storytelling with part three was the only criticism I had. And this one reservation doesn't change that I found this multigenerational family saga extremely fascinating and gripping as a whole. 
 And, curiously, throughout reading I was reminded of two of my all time favorite books: 
 A Little Life 
 by Hanya Yanagihara and 
 East of Eden 
 by John Steinbeck. I think the relentless suffering that the fictional characters undergo was what made it reminiscent of A Little Life for me. And probably the biblical references and multigenerational aspect of it reminded me of the latter. However Pachinko resembles both beloved tomes the most for the way the story is presented in a span of decades. And, more importantly, they way it encourages readers to ponder over ideas such as identity, loyalty, and forgiveness. 
 Anyway, those are my initial thoughts after finishing the novel for now. 
 Full review to come!

I couldn't even make it past the 10% mark on this book. I am not now nor have I ever been a kindergarten mom. I'm not a fan of Chic-Lit. I don't like caricatures for characters. I don't like pretension parading as cleverness. And most of all, I do not like being 'written down to'. 
 In short, I did not like this book.

When I read the introduction of this book, I was convinced I would be blown away by it. Vance made some very interesting points about the cultural impact of changes in our society and how it's impacted the hillbilly lifestyle. There were several issues that he mentioned, things like "welfare queens" and changes in the message/support offered by churches. I was looking forward to a memoir that had some really strong messages in it related to social, political and economical impacts of the modern world on this group. 
 Unfortunately I felt like the book fell short on both accounts. 
 In a lot of ways it wasn't much of a memoir. Much of the beginning of the book was about his extended family and family history. But after introducing all of his uncles, he hardly mentioned them again in the book. He talks about the profound influence they had on his life, but then doesn't really talk about any of them again. In the beginning he talks about how much of his time he spent in Kentucky with his Mamaw and her extended family, but in the rest of the book he hardly ever talked about Kentucky again. Many of the chapters in the story talked about global things--the history of Middletown, the area in which he lived, etc. But then he wouldn't share many stories related to those things. I really felt like he didn't have enough of a memoir to write an entire book, so he padded it with a lot of facts and figures. 
 Likewise, I felt like the commentary that he seemed to want to share fell short. Maybe it's because his background is in law and not sociology or psychology. But I felt as though there was a message that he was trying to share that was important. In our current political climate, there's a lot of back and forth about "black lives matter" versus "all lives matter" and liberals not understanding how Trump could have been elected. I feel as though Vance had some answers to the whys and wherefores of much of the conflict that is going on in our country right now. But he never really committed to saying anything. 
 I wanted a book that I could share with friends to say "This. You have to read this. It explains a lot of what is wrong and why people are so angry and upset." I wanted a book that would better express the things I haven't been able to find the words for. I truly believe that there is a large portion of our population that is feeling disenfranchised and lost and angry about the status quo, and that too often we are ignoring them because we want to lock them in a box that says "these people are too ignorant to know better" instead of actually understanding their own needs and struggle and trying to find answers for them, too. 
 I think there's a lot good in this book, and I would overall recommend that it be read. But I didn't feel like in the end it was a complete book and that it really fell short of what it could have been.

~6 Phenomenal Can I Have You Stars~ 
 This is my first read by Tillie Cole. And for sure it will not be my last. Everything about this book was phenomenal. Completely captured by the writing, the story, the characters. Every detail captured to be put through your mind very vividly. 
 **Please be advise on the violence, domestic abuse and rape situations in this book.** 
 A simply beautiful story of "Two hearts split into two" Two separate souls shattered through circumstances that neither were both ready to face. 
 Kisa Volkov is reeling in from a past that she cannot let go. Living under the possessive man that is her fiance, Alik Durov. And trying her best to be the perfect Bratva wife. In her life she is no longer living in a world that made her safe, fearful of the path she has been on since that one faithful day where her life changed forever. Loving a dead man is never easy to forget and move past from. Only to slowly kill you inside day by day. 
 "I know I was made for you too... We matched... you were part of my heart..." 
 818. Raze. Where to start with Raze? I felt so much for him. Sadness, pain, anger, and just so many other emotions, but I came to love the Stone cold killer! He was the story of it all. A lost boy thrown into a world where no one would ever expect fighting for a life that was no longer his. Fighting by any means necessary, including killing for the name of survival. 
 "You'll become addicted you know. You'll live for the kill... live to see the life force drain from your opponents eye." 
 But what happens when your heart starts to beat again from being dead for so long? 
 What do you do when you're no longer more than a number? 
 You never give up. And you Raze through it all!
So. Many. Feelings. An absolute game changer of a book! Can't wait to see the movie with a box of tissues...

This was an okay book, but it was only okay. 
 You Know Me Well is a book about two people who sit next to each other in maths for a year without really getting to know each other until a crazy night out in San Francisco. 
 The plot moves really quickly and manages to cram an awful lot into what is only a medium-sized book. Which is good, because the book was never boring. However, the friendship between Mark and Kate felt rushed. Like they'd only known each other a day and they were already BFFs. 
 I found their alternate viewpoints both good and bad. Good because both the MCs were interesting people, but bad because in an already packed plot it just made things even more fast-paced and I didn't feel like I got to know Mark and Kate as much as I wanted to. 
 I liked that this wasn't a coming-out book (not for the MCs anyway), but was more about already being out and trying to find who you are and where you fit into the world. And I liked the depiction of San Francisco Pride. It sounded like a hoot and a half. 
 This actually had a lot in common with Nina Lacour's other book, Everything Leads To You, in that inboth books the MC is an amazingly talented teenager. Like, seriously talented. In Everything Leads To You, the MC is barely eighteen but she has already been employed by a film studio to be a set designer. A set designer. For a film studio. In You Know Me Well, the MC is an amazingly talented artist, whose pictures raise thousands of dollars for charity when they are sold. It's just ... It makes the MCs seem older than they're supposed to be. Like they're thirty-something. When I was eighteen, I could barely find my arse with both hands. There's no effin' way I'd have had the talent or chutzpah to achieve the things Lacour's MCs do. No effin' way. And while this makes the MCs interesting, it doesn't make them real or relatable for the 99.9% of teenagers who don't achieve such greatness. 
 Not sure who I'd recommend this to because it didn't grab me as much as I'd hoped but it was still an okay read.

I don't know if it's just because this book appealed so very, very well to my geeky side (so many references to beloved fantasy novels of youth, etc.) or my love to NJ (hey, don't knock it, it's a cool state), but I was grinning ear-to-ear while reading almost all of this novel (except for some of the worse parts, of course). I think it also spoke partly to the deep sadness I feel about human loneliness, and those people who just can't seem to connect with the rest of the world. Amazingly written in a rather colloquial-but-very-intelligent style, using a narrator who is himself a peripheral part of the story. I don't know why it was important to tell the story of Oscar Wao; I'm still working that one out. But I have to say that, pointless or no, I enjoyed the book immensely. (To say nothing of the amazing Dominican Republic history lesson I received during the reading! I love learning through novels; history lessons told through prose tend to stick with me much more then those told in non-fiction; I think it might have to do with how my mind connects things on a personal level, and thus I'm more likely to remember stories about a specific person than stories about a large group.) In any case, I highly, highly, highly recommend this book. But I can promise that not everyone is going to like it, so my apologies in advance!

The Sea Keepers Daughters is the third book in the Carolina series and it's the first one I have read. The book can be read as a stand-alone, at least, I think so since I found this one to be perfectly fine to read even though I haven't read the previous two books. 
 Here is the blurb from the book: From modern-day Roanoke Island to the sweeping backdrop of North Carolina's Blue Ridge Mountains and Roosevelt's WPA folklore writers, past and present intertwine to create an unexpected destiny... 
 I found it so beautifully written that I just had to add it to my review even though I ordinarily don't do that, but it summarizes the book so well. I was quite captivated both by the blurb and the cover of the book, and I'm happy to say that the book was just as good as I hoped it to be. 
 I have found that I prefer romance book when the romance is incorporated into the story and not romance as the main genre. As long as the romance part doesn't take the central stage is it fine and this book manages to convey an interesting story and integrate the romance part without making me mentally roll my eyes. 
 Whitney trying to save her restaurant and at the same time finding letters from her grandmother's sister. Whitney never knew her grandmother had a sister so she is very surprised to learn that fact. As the story progress, we get to follow Whitney trying to find something among all the family heirlooms that will save her business, but we also get to know her grandmother's sister Alice through the letters she discovers. She learns that Alice traveled the Blue Ridge Mountains as part of the Federal Writers' Folklore Project. 
 I admit that I was taken by surprise how engaged in the story I would become and how the ending would make me feel. This was just a truly beautiful written story and I'm quite eager to get my hands on the two previous books in this series.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I loved this book conceptually from the time it came out, but didn't get a chance to read it until recently. The book centers around the Peter Pan story that we all know and love, but centers around the character of Tiger Lily, and is told from the perspective of Tinkerbell. 
 Pros: 
 The ending of this book is what saved it for me. If I ever have a daughter, I will make sure that she reads this book early and often. Tiger Lily is a strong character, and the ending of the book is much closer to what romantic love is than most of the young adult novels that I read. In the end, you can love someone and not get to have them. I say that, but the novel was also able to avoid becoming preachy. A tough line to walk, and one that I feel earns the author quite a bit of credit in my eyes. 
 Tik Tok's character and relationship with Tiger Lily is also phenomenal. Every exchange between the two of them was emotional and even handed. 
 Cons: 
 Action sequences have a tendency to get muddy and convoluted. 
 Narrating a book about Tiger Lily through the perspective of Tinkerbell gets messy in some places. There are clearly places where the author wanted to include thoughts and feelings, but had to go through the narrator instead, removing us from them by a strange narrative degree. 
 Overall: Would recommend. Especially to actual teenagers. Probably won't read again, but will be on the lookout for other books from this author.

Well. I know what book I'll be recommending to everyone for a while. 
 I avoided this book for a long time despite its outstanding reputation because on its surface, it is a book about baseball. Not only do I hate sports novels (truly, desperately...) but out of all sports I find baseball the least entertaining (Hockey and Rugby are tied in first for most entertaining), yet this novel was devoured with zeal. The kind of zeal I usually reserve for the last book in a long series whose characters I already know and love and am committed to. That was maybe the most incredible part. 
 The passion and connection I felt for a group of deeply flawed characters, and how quickly I felt it. 
 Also for my Virginia Tech friends, if you pay close attention I'm pretty sure there is a clever jab at ol' VT in the first couple hundred pages, so be on the lookout ;) .

 You know, there's only so much repeating of the last two books that I can really take, mostly because no one needs a reminder or 2000000 from histrionic, psycho Nan. I'm so over it, I don't even want to read Grant's books because she'll probably be in them, even though I really like Harlow and want to see her and Grant's HEA. I'm not so sure I'll read Woods' story either because Angelina, the girl he was supposed to marry seems like Nan part 2. I don't need that. We get it, the heroine is perfect and angelic, heavenly and kind even in the face of all the horribleness of the world, but do we really need the ridiculous side by side comparison of good girls and bad girls? No thanks. Still, I really enjoy the books, just wish the Nan's of the stories didn't exist. They take away from the plot in my opinion.

It's very weird how negative reviews are easier for me to write and very positive ones are the hardest because I always have the urge to only write "Read it!" and leave it at that, but today I will try to review this properly. 
 This book was amazing! It broke my heart in the best (and worst) ways possible. When I picked up Orbiting Jupiter I had a already read many positive reviews and expected great things from it (It surpassed those predictions). I also knew the ending (because of a review with NO spoiler warning). Nevertheless when the "things" 
 happened I cried. Overall, It's a very compelling story who I think anyone can benefit from.

Don't Even Think About It is a quirky high school story with a paranormal twist. 
 A bad batch of the flu shot, gives a group of high school students the ability to hear everyone's thoughts. It starts out as a funny, wacky turn of events with lots of humorous situations. With the progression of the story, it takes a sadder and darker turn. 
 The story is highly original, written with multiple perspectives, taking us deep inside these fictional teen psyches. I can see the attraction of this story but for some reason it didn't grab me...although it might be very popular with a teen audience. They do delve into some racier topics and openly discuss sexual situations (not explicitly but implied). 
 In the end I found, Don't Even Think About It a paranormal drama with many humorous situations and lots of teen angst. It is an easy, entertaining story.

It felt normal. The fact that the love interest wasn't white actually excited me because it was so different from what I usually read but it was like every other love story at the same time.

 I felt like I was living Samantha's life ( or death?), it was so frustrating to begin with ( I mean waking up in the same freaking day everyday!) But then it was such a beautiful story and a painful one too. It takes courage to figure out what life is all about but it takes more than courage to figure out what death is all about and how to go through it... 
 And now I am just gonna call my friends and tell them that I love them before it's to late! :')

OMG, I loved this one so much! 
 The entire story was essentially a love letter to all things P&P-related (especially 
 Bridget Jones's Diary 
 , of course!), with a few other fun references (Mean Girls) thrown in. So. Much. Fun! So many highlights! 
 There's a wet shirt scene. Excuse me-- 
 two 
 . And kissing in the rain. 
 Sigh... :) 
 I adored Lady Bridget's endearing clumsiness, her quick humor, her earnest attempts to fit in to London society, and how much she loved her family. And of course, her diary entries:Lessons in proper etiquette avoided: 27 
 Lessons I should not have avoided: 27 
 Reception in English society: dreadfuland:Times I have thought about Darcy in his wet shirt: 27 
 Times I have felt something resembling lust when I think about Darcy in his wet shirt: 27 
 Times I have written "Rupert and Bridget" in my diary since Lady Winterbourne's garden party: 0 
 I am dreadfully confused."Looord" Darcy was absolutely delightful--even when he's being an a**, as any self-respecting Darcy must be; since we saw his side of the story, we understood better why he was doing and/or saying things that seemed less-than heroic on the outside. Plus, his first name is Colin. Obviously, I'm going to love him, even when he's--well--being a Darcy.Lord Darcy knew that there was only one thing to do when one's equilibrium was disturbed, and that was to stand very still and patiently wait for the world to right itself.(That one made me want to just go over and give him a consoling hug. Though of course that would have horrified the poor man, it would have made me feel better.)Didn't she realize that he couldn't, just physically could not, say such thoughts aloud? He was English, for God's sake.LOL!God, he'd given her the wrong idea. He was terrible at proposing and at not-proposing. And people thought he was perfect. Ha.Seriously, just OMG. It's really not safe to try and ingest liquids while reading approximately 2/3 of this book. 
 Their romance is simply lovely, with just the right amounts of misunderstanding, pride, prejudice, lust, and yearning from afar in there, with a healthy dose of smoldering glances thrown in just because. Darcy even says my all-time favorite BJD quote! And then when they're finally together? Le. Sigh. 
 All of the "American Cavendishes" are fantastic characters--such a fun and delightfully quirky family; even the dreaded duchess (AKA Aunt Josephine, but don't call her Josie!) becomes likable by the end--I can't wait until they all have their own books. Amelia's story is next--a good chunk of it is going on during Bridget's, though we get hardly any details--and it just cannot come out soon enough. Fortunately, Ms. Rodale has quite the backlist to keep me occupied in the meantime, and yay! some of them are even on audio so I can more easily squeeze them in during the semester :) 
 (I do have to admit there were several bits that were even less historically-accurate than in your typical Regency romance--there's a pretty big one near the end, when Bridget says something I'm fairly certain no one in that period would "get" let alone say--I just couldn't let it really bother me. But if you're a stickler for that kind of thing, consider yourself warned...) 
 Rating: 4 1/2 stars / A

Good god, this was so drippy... without actually being all that angsty. While the H is rather mean and cutting in the beginning, he loses that very quickly. And yes, he's very blind and stupid to not see what's going on, or to realize (earlier, or at all!) that  his parents were manipulating him by tampering with his letters-- this is why tampering with letters is such a big deal, and yes, it used to be a lot easier to get away with it than it is now-- but he really is quite innocent in all of this, so not so distressing to the reader, or the h, except that for 3 years she thought he was ignoring her.  
 And it was a happy ending- people with weak hearts can still manage to live quite well and long. Also, I really liked the last few chapters. Wish there were some more to show their reconciliation, but their getting back together is not just a footnote. I also liked the fact that the H said that his career was also on the list of things that were important, and he felt guilty for that, but that he has come to terms with it. That just cemented it in reality, which I really prefer, over a H throwing his hard won career into the dust for the love of his wife (which he did, except with more rationale). 
 I'm glad I stuck through with the woe-is-me first half. If it had been even a tad bit lighter, I'd rate it 5 stars. But with the last few chapters, the author changed the tone completely and does manage to redeem the novel- 4 stars.

4.5 sizzling hot stars 
 Mother of god, where the hell do I start! This book was so hot! I am not a usual customer of the MM side, but Ella Frank, she can make anything amazing. I fell in love with her writing when I read her for the first time in Veiled Innocence, and then when I came across this, I couldn't let the chance to read her again pass me by. When I started Alasdair, I expected it to be a bit like Lover at Last by J.R. Ward, which has the same things going for it- vampire, and MM. But man is it so much better. 
 Leo, Alasdair and Vasilios made one hell of a trio, one of the hottest I have ever come across. Leo is a historian who very coincidentally studies the the same Greece era when Alasdair lived, and was working on recreating the same bath area where Alasdair was turned. Big coincidence there, but as we see, there were a lot of higher powers at work. 
 So I am not going to say much, and ruin the fun for anyone, but Alasdair was attracted to Leo big time, and Vasilios had his moments with the green monster.

 I am a huge fan of the post-apocalyptic genre, so when I saw The Book of The Unnamed Midwife on NetGalley I was intrigued. A novel that follows a nurse the initial days after an apocalyptic event that kills a large portion of the female gender. In the days following the apocalypse women become property to men and it is revealed that no pregnancies render living children. As humanity struggles to overcome the loss of civilization, they also now must face a future without the ability to have children. 
 I appreciated what this novel tried to do by bringing feminism to the apocalypse. The supreme maltreatment of women and the moral ambiguity of a society without civilization was an interesting addition to a traditional tale of survival that has saturated the literary market. 
 The Book of the Unnamed Midwife is a tale about an average woman in an extraordinary world. Although a short novel of only 190 pages, the midwife goes through many different experiences: discovering her own weaknesses, saving women from horrific situations and realizing that helping others is more important than making herself happy. 
 This is a novel about self discovery as much as it is about feminism and the fall of civilization. 
 I did not love how sexual the book became approximately half way through, with some behaviours by the main character that she doesn't seem to really feel all that bad about. She hurts others, including women, but then continues on her crusade to save people. Some of the events in the novel were unbelievable, but served the purpose of creating a world that is very much unlike our own. 
 Personally, I found this book to be a satisfactory read. I loved that the author tried to make this book more than just a typical apocalyptic novel and inject some deeper meaning into the main character's experiences. The Book of the Unnamed Midwife is about individuality as much as it is about the human condition. 
 This book will appeal to readers who enjoy post-apocalyptic novels, feminist literature, tales about self-discovery and flawed female leads. I would not recommend this to readers who are sensitive to rape literature or literature with an uncomfortable level of description of abuse scenes.

Vivian Carter is sick of the toxic sexism and systemic misogyny at her high in East Rockport, Texas. She's sick of girls being targeted by the administration's sexist dress code. She's sick of the harassment from the football team boys and their cronies who get away with everything. But she isn't sure what she can do about it when even the thought of making waves is terrifying. 
 That changes when Viv finds her mom's box of mementos from her misspent youth. In the 90's Viv's mom was part of the Riot Grrrl movement known for their music, their feminist manifesto, and the zines they used to share ideas and find each other. Suddenly Vivian has a plan to help her speak out and Moxie, her own zine, is born. 
 Viv doesn't know what to expect when she distributes the first issue of Moxie in secret to her classmates. In the pages of her zine she calls out sexist jokes, harassment, and unfair dress codes and asks girls at the school to join her in protests that quickly gain momentum and help the Moxie movement take on a life of its own. As the stakes rise for what the zine and the Moxie girls are fighting for, Vivian has to decide how far she's willing to go for what she believes in Moxie (2017) by Jen Mathieu. 
 Vivian's no nonsense narration brings East Rockport to life--complete with its small town charm and stifling atmosphere. Mathieu does a great job of showing Viv's love of her home and family alongside her frustration with the town's dated, sexist culture as well as her desire to do more and be more than she might ever manage if she stays. 
 Moxie shows a grassroots movement at its finest as the Moxie girls' ranks swell and girls in East Rockport learn that they can (and should) speak up for themselves. Frank and nuanced discussions of feminism showcase a variety of perspectives from self-proclaimed feminists like Viv's new friend Lucy to those more reluctant to label themselves (like Vivian's best friend Claudia). Mathieu works to make sure Moxie is an inclusive movement with many girls taking the lead while acknowledging the school's previous stratification along racial and social lines. 
 The growing sense of community among the Moxie girls and the feel good girl power vibes are balanced with the push and pull between Viv and a sympathetic (but not always understanding) boy. Their romance subplot adds a touch of sweetness to this edgy story while reminding readers that being a feminist doesn't have to preclude love. 
 This powerful book proves that the pen can be mightier than the sword and that girls are always stronger when they're united. Moxie is a must read for everyone but especially young women who have had to apologize on behalf of boys, girls whose ideas only gain validity when a boy shares them, and anyone who's had the moment of realization that some people will never understand what it's like to walk down a dark street alone. 
 In the first issue of Moxie, Vivian asks readers to draw hearts and stars on their hands so likeminded students can find each other at school. After you read and love Moxie (and I'm sure you will) don't forget to add stars and hearts to your own hands. And always remember: Moxie Girls Fight Back! 
 Possible Pairings: In a Perfect World by Trish Doller, The Careful Undressing of Love by Corey Ann Haydu, The Outsiders by S. E. Hinton, Here We Are: Feminism for the Real World edited by Kelly Jensen, The Last Time We Were Us by Leah Konen, Wonder Women: 25 Innovators, Inventors, and Trailblazers Who Changed History by Sam Maggs, Saving Francesca by Melina Marchetta, The Nowhere Girls by Amy Reed, Wild Swans by Jessica Spotswood

[This comment is long overdue - the author kindly sent me a copy when I won it during one of her giveaways, which I received and read months ago. Recently, I rediscovered my almost-finished review of this book and polished it up a bit.] 
 I thought this book presented an interesting perspective on how a person lives through wars and conflicts. It follows the life of a young boy, as he struggles and perseveres through his depressingly difficult live, until he's a successful adult. Most of the book is sad, but inspiring. 
 To me, a reader of minimal knowledge of Middle Eastern conflicts, this book gave me much more personal and interesting perspective on it. I thought the details seemed genuine and well-researched - I enjoyed experiencing the different world-views (despite some of the black-and-white-ness) and the little traditions that we encounter throughout this book. 
 While I understand that it is no easy feat to compress 60+ years of one's life in one novel, I thought some events were disappointingly (and oddly) under-explored. Take, for example, the death of Nora . It came out of nowhere, and it was told retrospectively and to me seemed to be rather lacking emotion. The flow of the story was also a bit choppy at times, where the time skips just didn't really fit, but they weren't too disruptive overall. It does, however, tell about Ichmad's life as if it's one continuous period of misery - as we experience it from suffering to suffering, while the periods in between may have been much more peaceful. Of course, I understand that the real lives of many Palestinians are one continuous struggle, but this book could do with some levity. Most supportive characters were also rather one-dimensional and underdeveloped, and ultimately, difficult to relate to. 
 Kudos for the author for tackling such a difficult subject matter - I thought it quite impressive and thought-provoking.

 Now that I've re-read the book, it's time to get into what gave this book 3.5 stars. I'm going to start with what I loved about this book. I loved Katniss's character, like genuinely loved it. This is a 16 year old girl who has known survival all her life, and the way the author portrays her in risky situations help me understand that she isn't all cold and calculating but instinctual. Her character development is beyond amazing, especially since the end of the Quarter Quell. I don't know how accurately Katniss's PTSD is portrayed, but I take joy in the fact that it doesn't disappear when it's convenient, unlike most books where PTSD and depression just 'go away' when the author finds it an obstacle. I also loved the author's ability to put us in Katniss's shoes (Yes, I know its first person perspective). 
 Another thing I loved about this book was Peeta. What happened to him was the most heart-breaking thing ever, but you get to see the boy with the bread just as much as you see his struggle. Yes, I hated the way Katniss treated him half-way through the book, but it became painfully obvious that it was a just a way for her to keep herself away from feeling anything that would take her away from her goal, even if it was just for a moment. 
 I also loved how Prim died, and no, i'm not a maniac for thinking so. The concept of taking away from Katniss the reason all of it even started for her (i.e., her volunteering) and Katniss still not losing herself completely was just so fascinating. And when she did eventually let herself break down over all that has happened, you get that she isn't hardcore, she's just a teenager who has had to deal with the death of those she loved and hundreds more who she didn't even know. 
 What I hated about this book was Gale. I get he's useful in the field and when he's with Beetee and all, but god, I swear he existed in this book just to make things harder for Katniss (I openly cringed when he was talking with Peeta) and the reader. I would understand his love for Katniss, but only it doesn't make any sense, and thankfully, Katniss does too, even if it is towards the very end of this book. 
 Another thing I didn't like about this book was all the wasted potential. The entire concept of Coin could have been explored much more. All the book did was paint out obviously that Coin and Snow are both manipulative, one just secretive about it and the other proud of it. We don't even know that much about Coin other than a few lines of her back-story, and that in turn made her death less compelling, less exciting. The same goes for Haymitch. He doesn't get more than a page of back-story at best. Think of all the amazing things that could've happened if this book explored his character more. Another thing that didn't get me was how Katniss shot Coin in the end instead of Snow. I mean, I understand why she did it, but it felt so sudden and random even. 
 But because I love the story and all the characters, I wish this book would've been longer. I don't mind an extra 100 pages, as long as it doesn't feel as hasty as it does. This book does get 4 stars though; mostly because it's the closest I've come to a happy ending in a dystopian novel.

 I dive into The Bear and The Nightingale without really knowing anything about it beside everyone recommending it and it revolves around Russian folklore. I've been wanting to read more on Russian Folklore since I've read Deathless by Catherynne Valente. And to the tell the truth, The Bear and The Nightingale did not disappoint with its whimsical, but also rather dark ways. 
 The Bear and The Nightingale should be read by taking your time and slowly taking everything in for its beauty. Katherine Arden has a way of writing that makes you feel like you're listening to a story around a campfire. 
 The story starts out slow as we learn about our characters and everything that will lead to the main event. Vasya is our protagonist that was "gifted?" with having a sense of seeing spirits and demons, which I thought was really cool, but at the same time... NOPE! That's spooky. Vasya lives in the town of Lesnaya Zemlya where many still practice the old ways, worshipping the old deities, and leaving food to the house spirits. But soon, Konstantin, a priest comes into their town evangelizing the people to Christianity and to get rid of their old ways. However this backfire as the people of Lesnaya Zemlya learn to fear the old demons/spirits and forget about them, a monster starts to rise. With their fears, a monster; the bear, the one-eyed demon, the brother of the Winter Demon starts to wake up and regain his power, he will be able to escape his forest/confinement the more fear he feeds on and then darkness will prevail. Only Vasya seem to notice what is truly happening and tries to save the spirits/demons before something inevitable happens. 
 I honestly thought this story was going to be all whimsical, I did not think that at certain point of the story, it will feel like watching a horror movie. The walking dead/Upyrs, the crying outside Vasya's house, and the one eyes man creeped me out. I grew up in a really superstitious culture and a family that practiced Shaman (Of course I no longer practice that), so you can guess how creeped out I was. 
 But don't worry, it doesn't stay that way for long. Thank goodness. 
 But what's up with all of the slapping though? *giggle* 
 THE CHARACTERS 
 I will said that Vasya is one of the best female heroine I have read about in a long time. I adore Vasya character, she is strong, independent, courageous, and just like her failed bethrothed described her: MAGNIFICIENT. I love Vasya's quirkiness and woodsprite ways. I love the relationship she has with her family, her witty comments at time, her relationship with her brothers Alyosha, her wild and curious spirit, and for caring so much for the spirits. 
 I did not see the dark, twisted characters coming; Vasya's step mother Anna and the priest Konstantin. I honestly thought that these characters will be more for Vasya. I thought Anna would learn to care for her Vasya and her siblings. Konstantin and the way he was tempted and deceive was just honestly so twisted. 
 Morozko, I feel like we didn't get much of him. But no worry, there's a sequel! I don't know if Morozko will be a love interest, but there was some kissing. ;) 
 I love Vasya's father Pyotr and his love for his children and his belated wife Marina. 
 I love Vasya's brother Alyosha and him just always trusting Vasya when everyone see her as a crazy witch. And Vasya's sister Irina who loves Vasya wholeheartedly. 
 Dunya, do I need to said more? 
 I recommend this to anyone wanting to read something set in a different culture and looking for a dark atmosphere story. I'm not comparing this to Uprooted or Deathless, for this beat both of them, but if you enjoyed those book, you will surely enjoy this. 
 And there's a sequel? YES!

Well, I finally finished this today. I say "finally," because for some reason, it took me a span of weeks to finish wading through the second half of this book. Upon finishing it, I'm left with a really strange and uneasy feeling about it because while this book is far from terrible - there are certain things about it that really, really bring it down. Lets quickly visit the aspects of the story I took issue with: 
 - Kvothe: the mystery that is Kvothe and his innkeeper alter ego as Kote presented in the first book is certainly intriguing upon it's surface, but I can't help but feel like the more we learn about his story, the less interesting it has all actually become. I think part of the problem here is in the fact that Rothfuss attempts to give Kvothe too much notoriety, far too quickly. It makes Kvothe come off as a poorly developed Marty Sue. Think about it for a second: how much have we seen Kvothe go through in the last two books (most of which took place over the last year of his life.) He's got the typical tragic background necessary for a fantasy-trope MC, coupled with the fact that he joined a magical university, killed a draccus; worked in the employ of a very powerful political figure for some time; killed a bunch of other bad guys; lost his virginity to a magical fairy; and then saved some more people.  It's all a bit hard to swallow. 
 And if I had to listen to Kvothe remind the reader what a wonderful lute player, singer, magician, or lover he was for much longer I was going to throw the book out the window. 
 The Plot: Never have I really encountered a book where so little actually happens that advances the plot. Yes, things happen in this book, and it's all generally interesting stuff but there were points in it that I couldn't help but wonder how exactly it was adding to the story at all. Suddenly it hit me: a lot of it really wasn't. There is so much page-filler (especially in the second half of this book) that it becomes a journey in an of itself to slog through some of it. 
 I know that Rothfuss has insisted that this is meant to be a trilogy, but I absolutely cannot see how he can neatly reconcile what has happened thus far in the book with what we know of Kote the innkeeper from the interludes in the story. Who knows, maybe the third book will turn out to be absolutely action-packed in order to get there, but I can't help but expect to hear an announcement any day now that the series has been extended in order to reach its conclusion more naturally. 
 Denna: Good lord, Denna. This is a character that Kvothe is madly, wildly in love with, and basically has been since the first book - but he can't tell her because of reasons and as such he spends a fair majority of this book basically obsessing over her. There are whole chapters dedicated to Kvothe searching the streets for her in whatever city he happens to be in at the time, and then when he does find her they both inevitably say something that annoys the other and the game begins anew. I'm not going to sugarcoat it: it was exasperating. 
 A *lot* of those scenes (and many others in the novel) seem to be included only to increase the page length. Rothfuss has stated in interviews that he had had the entire series written before the first book was published, which makes me wonder if his publisher or a beta reader or someone in his life strongly encouraged him to go back and lengthen the books in order to reach more "epic fantasy proportions." This book certainly seems to have a case of attempting to do way too much and likely would have been far more enjoyable if the excess fat had been trimmed prior to publishing. 
 The Prose: Patrick Rothfuss is a BEAUTIFUL writer. Seriously. He has such a command of words and adjectives and he can craft lines that in and of themselves are exceptionally beautiful. However, I feel like with a book series so long, it has begun to work against him here. When he finds certain methods to describing someone, or something, he tends to repeat it over and over and over again. I can't note any specific examples at this time, but the problem was frequent enough that there were moments when I was reading that I desperately wanted someone to hand Rothfuss a thesaurus during his editing stages in order to find some new ways of describing certain sounds, sights or characters. 
 Characters: Okay, am I the only one who notices that the only character who really seems to have undergone any change at all in this story is Kvothe himself? To be fair, Bast seems to be undergoing change as well, but it's far vague at this point to completely extend that credit to Rothfuss. Otherwise, the side characters in this novel all seem to exist simply to bolster young Kvothe's ego. It's actually a little bit frustrating. Take Kvothe's arch enemy at University: Ambrose Jakis. Ambrose is a character that we literally know nothing about, besides that he has a rich father and is a womanizing jerk. Otherwise, he's just another faceless baddie in the story. So many of the supporting characters read in that way, which is really unfortunate. 
 I feel like I'm giving the impression that I hated this book, which I don't want to do. This book isn't terrible. In fact, a lot of it is great, and entertaining! It's a wonderful read for anyone who loves fantasy. However, I can't give it anything more than 3 stars due to what I feel like is a heavily disorganized story that was in desperate need for another round of editing before publishing.

It manages to do so many things at once: it works as a time travel tale (and an unusual one at that), it works as a vision of a scarily plausible near-future (and sneakily comments on our own time in the process), and as a (former) physicist I thought it was spot on about the social (and gender/race) dynamics of science academia.

[EDIT] So glad I gave this book another chance! I really enjoyed the stream of consciousness feel that this novel has, and I can absolutely relate to this character in retrospect. The youth and bluntness of the character's narrative is refreshing and insightful, and I admire the sense of mystery about who the letters are being sent to and the unspoken incident towards the end of the novel. If you didn't appreciate this novel on the first read, I'd recommend putting it down and coming back to it in a few years for a retry. It was worth it for me. 
 [EDIT] Giving this novel another chance! I keep hearing lovely things about the book, and I imagine I'll have a different perspective on it four years later. Fingers crossed? 
 This novel felt unrealistic to me. I never knew a freshman in high school who thought or wrote like this young character, but perhaps one could argue that that is what signifies the idea of "being a wallflower". The letters felt awkward and the sentence structure was too choppy for me to read comfortably. 
 However 
 , one of the things I liked about the book were the small revelations and thoughts revealed by Charlie in his letters. Those moments when you think to yourself, "Kids say the darndest things, don't they?" One thought I am particularly fond of is Charlie describing Paul as a popular kid until Sam introduced him to good music. I found the novel humorous at times but overall, a struggle to get through.

This was a fun, fast read with lovely characters and an interesting post-war universe. Or galaxy. Empire? The main character, Alisa, was a captain in what seems to have been an insurgency to overthrow an abusive empire. A successful one, so there's that. Only now that the dominant source of order (however corrupt) has been blown to bits, there's a lot of anarchy and bad things are happening. Which sucks for Alisa as she emerges from medical discharge with no way off the planet she's stranded on. 
 Alisa's goals are simple: get off planet, get to the former capital planet, reunite with the daughter she hasn't seen in years (who is living with an aunt since Alisa's husband died in the war). That doesn't mean the goals easy. Along the way, she finds herself leading a group of people desperate for direction and/or leadership and embroiled in pirates and mafias and a string of frying pan/fire situations. 
 I really liked her and the crew she pulls together--including some who fought on the other side of the recent conflict. Learning to overcome prejudices and recover from war-time hatreds is a emotional dimension of a story that is an otherwise straight-forward sci-fi romp. It helps that Buroker excels at giving even her side-characters full dimensions and personalities (along with the frictions that can crop up to complicate matters as a result). I loved the banter and the characters and the pacing is top-notch. 
 The story has two weaknesses that put this at four stars rather than five. The first is that this isn't a complete story so much as it's an episode along the way; which means it stops kind of abruptly after what seemed like a minor victory (however hard-won). The problem second is spoilery so I'll tag it. There are some truly despicable folks roaming around using might-makes-right to commit slavery, rape, and murder. At some point in the story, these people capture Alisa and her crew. Which means imminent rape and eventual slavery. That's tense enough, but there's a big difference between threatened rape and actual rape (emotion-wise) and Buroker pulls some convenient rabbits out of her hat to keep from crossing that line. Not that it was easy so much as it relied rather a lot on stupidity and circumstance coming up to turn the tables in the moment. Which is good because I was enjoying the light-ish tone for so serious a milieu and didn't want that to change. At the same time, I can't help feeling like Buroker used the illusion of the possibility of rape as an emotional manipulation. And, in the process, cheapened the seriousness/gravity of rape in its horrific reality.  
 So yeah, it's a dark universe, but I enjoyed Alisa and her crew being light spots within it and I look forward to further stories there. I do hope the central goal of finding her daughter isn't dragged out too much longer. I can see that getting old fast.

 NEW BOOK BOYFRIEND ALERT 
 : Drew frigging Evans 
 Why it took me so long to read this book is beyond me. If there's a guilty-pleasure New Adult book that is worth your attention, it's Tangled by Emma Chase. It's funny as hell and so addictive. Emma's writing was also so delicious you just can't get enough of it! 
 The story centers around Drew Evans. It's told in his POV. Yes, guys. His and his POV alone. I don't normally encounter a romance book where the only one that speaks is the guy. It's fun and refreshing in a way. It's nice to know Drew's thoughts-- including the dirty and naughty ones. lol. 
 So one night, Drew met this alluring brunette named Katherine 'Kate' Brooks in a club and yes, there was insta-lust in Drew's side (in a not-annoying way, mind you). Since then, he was not able to take Kate off his mind. And surprise! He learned one day that Kate's going to be his new co-worker in the company he's working which is owned by his dad. Now I won't get that far into describing the plot. Let Drew do the talking. Listen to him and prepare yourself for a bunch of laugh-out-loud moments because you'll surely get them here... all the freaking time! 
 Picture me while I was reading this 
 You might think that this book only features tons of craziness and sexual nothings. Not. I learned a lot of things from Drew. His relationship tips are so sensible, I tell you guys. You want relationship facts and tips from the playboy's perspective? Drop your Cosmopolitan and listen to Drew. 
 As a sample, 
 "Assume nothing. Even if you think you know everything. Even if you're sure that you're right. Get confirmation. That whole "ass" cliche about assuming? It's right on the money. And if you're not careful, it could end costing you the best thing that's ever happen to you." 
 "Women fall in love quicker than men. Easier and more often. But when guys fall? We go down harder. And when things go bad? When it's not us who ends it? We don't get to walk away. We crawl." 
 ... and so much more. 
 What also entertained me most was Drew's set of analogies and comparisons that he added in almost everything that he narrated in this book, like: 
 "She's like a Rubik's Cube. So frustrating at times that you want to toss it out the goddamn window. But you don't. You can't. You're compelled to keep playing with it until you figure it out." 
 There were no dull moments in this book. What it offered was pure entertainment. My favorite scene and the one that definitely had me cracking up was the dinner scene where Drew's little niece Mackenzie talked and spoke a vulgar word that had everyone immediately react in such a funny way. (Drew's dad choking, Matthew spitting up the juice right on Steven's face, etc.) LMAO. I laughed for about three minutes with that! Also, I didn't only admire Drew and Kate's characters but I also adored the secondary ones, especially Delores a.k.a. Deedee. She's one badass woman and I can't wait to read her story and Matthew's. 
 This book also built up a remarkable sexual tension which led to sexual frustration and then some. Basically, the relationship and character development was amazing here. 
 Tangled, as a whole, was a very entertaining rom-com book. It came packed with sizzling hot chemistry between the characters and it's simply designed to make you feel good and happy. I totally enjoyed Drew's POV here. The best! The ending was also wholly satisfying and it left me with a big smile on my face. This was my first Emma Chase book and it certainly won't be the last.

 However, I wasn't expecting her chemistry pen pal to be someone she knew. At all. I seriously doubted it was David or Lucas. I suspected that it was some random guy at school that had always gone unnoticed to her.

Like in the beginning of the book, when Lily woke up to find that she had to vote for one of the necklaces that were displayed on the counter. I didn't entirely know what was going on because the book didn't explain that her mom and dad force their kids to vote on whose necklace is better. It wasn't until later in the book that it was explained that her parents force her and her siblings to vote on everything. I didn't like that this wasn't given an explanation sooner, as I was confused in the first few chapters. I had to guess what was going on. 
 The more I read, however, the more I enjoyed the writing. I felt that it fit Lily's personality. 
 The characters were great. Not really unique, but good regardless. The main characters were really Lily and her letter writer. The rest of the characters were kind of pushed more to the back, including Lily's best friend, Isabelle. The character build was great. I felt like I really knew the main characters. We get bits and pieces of other characters too but not their full home life, personality, and all around aura. (Yes, I did just use the word "aura." Deal with it.) The relationships Lily had with everyone in the book was nice and well-rounded, but we don't see how things go down with David. I just assumed that Isabelle forced David to go out with Lily and once he saw how crazy her life is, decided that it wasn't for him. BUT THAT'S OKAY BECAUSE OF HER MYSTERIOUS LETTER WRITER! 
 Something that I found really cool is that Lily has siblings named Ashley and Jonah. Jonah is my brother's name, and I don't see it often. Also, I hardly find a character that's named Ashley that isn't a snob, so I found that nice too lol.

I get into some spoilsies later in the review so I guess "be warned". The short version of this review is that the book is overrated, boring and poorly written and I wouldn't recommend it. Ok, on with the review proper! 
 The Vision suddenly has a family! His wife is Virginia, his son is Vin and his daughter is Viv (oh the cute alliteration) and they reside at 616 Hickory Branch Lane (geddit, like Marvel-616, the main Marvel universe). Not a lot happens for most of the book until something does and then it's over. 
 So this was disappointing. I've heard nothing but praise for this series so I was really looking forward to it despite not being a Tom King fan. He's a writer who can take interesting setups like Dick Grayson in a James Bond-esque series or a cop investigating a murder in 2004 Iraq like in The Sheriff of Babylon and somehow manage to suck all the excitement out of them (to be fair he co-wrote Grayson with Tim Seeley). I'd say he does the same here with The Vision, which is a similarly boring read, except the premise isn't exciting to start with! 
 When did Vision make a family? I read quite a lot of Marvel and don't recall him doing or seeing any character mention this. More importantly, WHY did he make a family? Vision is one of those awkward characters who differs from writer to writer. Sometimes he desires to be more human, sometimes that's never mentioned at all. I tend to read modern Marvel books and I've never once read a story where he talks about wanting to be human, though I understand back in the '70s that was one of his things. 
 Moreover, it makes you wonder about the message this book sends out. Vision and his family are synthezoids but Vision, in this series, seems to desperately want acceptance among humans as one of them, despite the impossibility of ever being human. Especially in this day and age shouldn't the message be less of achieving an arbitrary standard of "normalcy" and trying to fit in by subverting your true nature, and instead accept who you are and asking others to do the same? Why try be something you're not? Vision is so unique and wonderful, why does he want to be as dull as his suburban human neighbours? 
 It's important to show the reader the creation of Vision's family and his reasoning behind it because that's the whole point of this book. It's simply not good enough to claim that the reader should know all about The Vision and to have read Uncanny Avengers or whichever series it was established (if at all) that Vision wanted to create his own family; this needs to be done in THIS series and can't be taken for granted. That's one of King's biggest failings with this book. 
 However I could have forgiven all of that if there was an engaging story or the book said something clever or original about the 21st century Western middle class, except it doesn't do any of those things. 
 Maybe this series is intended to be a satire on suburbia? It's not. It's definitely no Shirley Jackson or Ira Levin commentary on the nightmare of the 'burbs. What story there is, is underwhelming: Vin gets in trouble at school, Viv meets a boy she likes. Wow. Sure, it's "normal", which is what I guess Vision wants, but it's not riveting storytelling either. 
 Then a villain appears and Virginia ends up killing him because she was protecting her family. Fine - but why hide it from Vision? She was totally justified in killing him - he broke into her house with the intent of murdering her and her family; the dictionary definition of self-defence. But instead she hides his body and lies to Vision, and this provides the meatier side of the story despite being pure and utter stupid contrivance. 
 Pure and utter stupid contrivance summarises what happens next as someone films Virginia burying the body and blackmails her, leading to a commentary on America's useless and idiotic gun culture. Needless to say, the story is not impressive at all and the motivations behind the characters - particularly Vision's with that final page reveal - are inscrutable and silly. 
 King's not a very good writer. The narration throughout is flat and boring - maybe intentionally robotic-sounding but definitely not enlivening to read - while the dialogue between Vision and Virginia is dry and dull. They literally have mundane conversations about semantics! 
 King also inserts Shylock's famous speech from The Merchant of Venice ("If you prick us, do we not bleed") in a cliched and pseudo-intellectual commentary on the neighbourhood's perception of the Visions. It's an obvious and uninspired choice that feels like something a high-schooler would think was clever. Also, King's Vision claims to have saved the world 37 times, citing The Korvac Saga and The Phoenix Force as two such occasions - yeah, no-one else was involved in resolving those, just you, Vision, right? 
 Gabriel Hernandez Walta's art is fine but nothing special. Like in his Magneto series, he can sometimes bring out the horror in death which does give weight behind some of the scenes here, though otherwise his art style remains competent and somewhat drab. 
 I had high hopes for this one but The Vision, Volume 1: Little Worse Than a Man turned out to be yet another poorly written and conceived Tom King comic that was a struggle to get through. I think this one is meant to be a prestige series on the same level as Fraction/Aja's Hawkeye but it's actually little worse than the usual craptastic superhero-punching-supervillains fare that makes up most of Marvel's output.

An attempt to describe how people and families develop and adapt to their surroundings to survive in the modern era. 
 I really loved Franzen's previous novel, The Corrections, but Freedom just didn't hold a candle next to that one. It is probably unfair to compare the two, but I feel it is necessary at some level. Part of what I loved about The Corrections was the complicated and nuanced interactions between the characters. Thoughts or actions early in the book sometimes didn't make sense until you saw them mirrored later by another character. You could see how completely different circumstances brought out similar behavior from parent and child. There were fascinating parallels between parents, children, and siblings. Freedom tries to get that same feeling, but it came across as forced and artificial to me. 
 The story revolves around a husband and wife, their two kids, and their best friend from college. All of them have ups and downs, tragedies and triumphs, but little of it seems to mean anything. I didn't find any of the characters compelling enough to care what their outcomes were. 
 I've read that The Corrections was semi-autobiographical, and I can't help but think Freedom is as well. The obscure rock star character whose one heartfelt album suddenly propels him to fame on the indie circuit probably tracks pretty well with Franzen's own rise in the book world. The problem is, the rock star is always the smartest and most observant person in the room, which taints the book by making it feel like a vanity piece. He's not flawless, to be sure, but it was distracting. 
 Another bothersome aspect for me were several chapters that were supposedly an autobiography written by one of the characters. The language, style, and detail seemed no different from the rest of the novel. It strained my suspension of disbelief to think she could write that well or with such clarity. And if you're not going to adopt a different voice for those chapters, why bother with the trope of an autobiography at all? 
 I wasn't expecting to like Freedom as much as The Corrections, but I was expecting it to be different. Instead, it read like a failed attempt to recreate that book, rather than explore new territory. There were moments I enjoyed and some humorous passages, but overall I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.

Thursday Next is back for her second adventure in literature. Fforde does a good job of merging science fiction, fantasy, and literary references into a uniquely imagined 1985 London landscape. In addition to her pet dodo, Pickwick, Thursday also interacts with Neanderthals and goes on an outing to witness the mammoth migration. Then there's the newly discovered long-lost Shakespeare play, Goliath corporation's need to retrieve their senior executive from Poe's 
 The Raven 
 (see the first book in the series), and Thursday's father's warning that the world will end on Dec 12th unless he can figure out how to stop it turning into pink goo. Oh, and did I mention that Thursday's husband Landen has been eradicated and she has only her memories of him to warm her dreams? 
 I am completely entertained and intrigued by Fforde's highly imaginative books. My only complaint is that this one clearly ends with a cliff hanger, setting the reader up for a sequel. That's the kind of literary manipulation that drives me crazy. The author should have faith that he's developed characters and a story line that are so engaging that readers will want to come back, not try to force them to return by leaving Pauline tied to the tracks with a train approaching. (And for the younger set: that's a reference to the old serials that used to play before the main feature at the movies, enticing the audience to return next week to see how Pauline got saved - only to leave her in a barrel about to go over a waterfall next week. Google "Perils of Pauline.") 
 I listened to the audio book, performed by Elizabeth Sastre. She does a great job, in my opinion. Her pacing is good ... not too fast and not interminably slow. And she's able to use different voices to help differentiate the characters.

 Why I abandoned The Summer I Found You: 
 It could have gone so well. I can see what Jolene Perry set out to do with this book but I can't help but be disappointed by the end result. First of all, we have Aidan and my heart really went out to him. He had some tragic experiences in Afghanistan and the PTSD and daily struggle he faced is real. His story held a lot of promise but ultimately it's Kate that let him down. 
 I understand that she suffers from foot-in-mouth disease. Heck, I'm the ambassador of the charity! The first few times she slips up and points out that...you know...Aidan lost an arm, I cringed and accepted that maybe she's a bit ditsy. But it comes to a point where she's using every opportunity to slip up that it becomes offensive. I really liked her character in the morning but she became more unbearable with every page. 
 Which brings us nicely onto her own issue. Kate is a diabetic and I'd go as far to say that she's ashamed of it. Aidan can't hide his own disability, people pity him every day because of his missing limb so the fact that Kate feels her diabetes is something to be covered up, is disrespectful to him. Kate is irresponsible with her diabetes and it really made me angry. The amount of people who strictly follow a diet and work hard to get the disease under control just for their bodies to break down anyway while Kate faffs around with her insulin willy nilly drove me up the flipping wall. She doesn't seem to understand how dangerous it is to neglect her body's needs and I really saw no need to carry on and send my blood pressure through the roof.

 I was a tad precarious when picking up Gone, as I knew next to nothing about it, and the blurb sounded very similar to The Enemy by Charlie Higson. Not that I didn't enjoy The Enemy, but I wasn't sure if I wanted to read something so similar. 
 Boy, am I glad I decided to read this. 
 It was excellent! So full of suspense, and action, and there didn't feel like a moment where the story started to drag, something that can be a problem with longer books. 
 For those of you who may want an idea of the plot: 
 Sam is fourteen. So is everyone else in the FAYZ, because one day everyone fifteen and older disappeared into thin air. The kids left in the FAYZ are figuring out how to survive without any adults to help them, whilst trying to understand what the hell has happened. On top of that, some of the kids are getting freaky superhero-like powers, and then there's the crazy kids from Coates Academy...  (Yeah, I know it wasn't much of a description - but I don't want to spoil anything!) 
 I thoroughly enjoyed Michael Grant's writing style (this is the first novel I have read by him), and the way he described the area in which the kids live. After about halfway, though, I felt he got a tad lazy with the world building, as I found myself not really understanding the setting of a chapter, and the distances of things (there is one point where it seems to take characters a few minutes to get from point A to point B, when previously it had taken them hours, or even days - what was up with that?) 
 The characters were all very relatable, and didn't seem to lack depth at all, even if we didn't hear every single person's backstory (thank God - I don't think I would have been able to keep up!) I have heard that some people found it difficult to keep up with the number of characters, but I actually had no trouble at all! I only have two complaints: the first being that they all seemed too mature for their age (they're fourteen and seem incredibly comfortable - I'm eighteen in five days and I would have been shitting myself the whole time), the second is the stupid (nick)names some of them had (Cookie? Orc? BUG?) 
 Something else I didn't care for was the coyotes. The advanced evolution was a cool idea, but the talking coyotes were irritating and very weird - I didn't think they were relevant at all and could have been left out (though maybe they will have important roles in the later novels). I just really didn't like them and found their concept a bit silly and childish.  
 I was really pleased with how Michael Grant handled topics like autism and metal illness in the book; the characters weren't treated as victims, or seen as helpless; Little Pete is the strongest character in the book, and he was awesome.  
 There's so much more praise I could give for this novel, but its 11pm and my brain is dead. 
 I definitely recommend this book to everyone - if you like insane, evil kids with superpowers, then you'll really love Gone!

I really enjoyed Howl's Moving Castle, it's focus on Howl who was so annoying, his very cool castle, and Sophie's growth. This isn't at all like that. In many ways, I like it more. Our story opens in a warm climate, where Abdullah the modest rug merchant is beleaguered by his enormous step family. He has a decent little business in the bazaar, and plenty of time to construct elaborate daydreams about how he is a stolen prince and will get to marry a lovely princess. With the help of a magic carpet, his daydreams will start to come true. 
 But that's just the set-up. The princess is kidnapped and Abdullah sets off on an adventure to rescue her, relying only on his excellent manners and a very keen mind. Soon he is in Ingary, meeting magical cats and a strange, sly soldier, evading the law. 
 And then, Jones kicks it up another notch. All the characters are revealed to have hidden depths (for good or ill), much clever planning is executed, and the whole thing ends perfectly. The castle-as-character doesn't get much play, although it does amount to a running gag. What I loved so much is that Jones takes some stock characters and plot elements from traditional stories, and breathes life into them. And as much as I enjoy a good swashbuckling fight, the focus here is on very clever planning, and I love it even more when people think.

This review applies to all the Grisha novellas/Ravkan folktales by Leigh Bardugo. You can also read this review on my blog 
 When I reviewed The Assassin's Blade, a series of novellas from the Throne of Glass Series by Sarah J. Maas, I talked about how THIS was how a novella should be done. Because more often than not, novellas just strike me as being so superfluous and inessential to the series at large, and the reason that the Throne of Glass novellas resonated with me was because they are completely relevant and significant to the overall series story. 
 Well, I may need to eat my own words here because there are other instances in which I feel like novellas are worthwhile besides just being an essential part of the series story. Case in point: these Ravkan folktales that Leigh Bardugo published that have nothing to do with Alina Starkov's story in Shadow and Bone, but are all relevant to the Grishaverse and the Ravkan culture that we got to experience in Shadow and Bone. 
 The little hints of Ravkan and Grisha culture that we got to see in Shadow and Bone were my favourite parts of Leigh Bardugo's skilled world building. The best high fantasy stories to me are the ones that seem like they really could be legitimate worlds with an added magical flair, and having an author go that extra mile to think of unique folktales for that world is really special. 
 And as with folktales in our own world, they all come with their own morals, which is always interesting to decipher. So if you are a fan of The Grisha Trilogy by Leigh Bardugo and if you enjoyed similar pretend-folktales like The Tales of Beedle the Bard by J.K. Rowling, then be sure to check out these Grisha novellas by Leigh Bardugo.

 In this post-apocalyptic, dystopian world you either live in the colonies and go along with the communist program or be considered an outlaw destined to roam the decaying wasteland that civilization has become. Government has been replaced by a "Global Council" who have engineered society the way they see fit and let me tell you, it's not pretty. Enforcers, the enforcement arm of the GC, ruthlessly patrol the outlying territories searching for outlaws and bandits using lethal force to keep everyone in line. There's no more currency, only bartering and favors. 
 Connor is the reluctant leader of a band of outlaws. He is deliciously Alpha. One of those characters who is controlling because of circumstances not because he's neurotic or damaged. He plays hard to get with women because he can afford to be picky and I liked that about him. Connor is gruff, formidable, and a ruthless bastard by his own admission. Yet he's sexy, competent and effortlessly magnetic which is what catches the eye of our heroine, Hudson. 
 Hudson is on the run, being hunted by the Enforcers. She just needs a place to lay low when she runs into Connor and his crew. He is reluctant to take her in but being a beautiful woman worked in her favor. She's got plenty of secrets that she tries to keep hidden but Hudson also has a lot of skills to contribute to the group and she offers them in hopes that they will let her stay. Of course they do, right? Wouldn't be any fun otherwise. 
 With all the misery, uncertainty and danger in the outlaw territories the only real release, recreation and relief is thru sex and both men and women crave it in equal measure. It is a hedonistic culture steeped in "living like there's no tomorrow." Sex in this book came early and often. There's lots of dirty talk, threesome's, voyeurism, exhibitionism...it's pretty damn kinky all around. Umm, yes please! Thank you, Elle. 
 I was fully immersed in this world while reading and when I wasn't reading this story, I was thinking about it. Escapism at its best. The primary characters are well developed and the secondary characters are compelling, which is essential for the start of a new series. Claimed is a smoking hot thrill ride that keeps you on the edge of your seat. Ladies, keep your BOB or SO on standby for this one!

When I first saw this title, I have to say, I didn't expect much from it. I didn't even want to pick it up. But boy, am i so glad to have been proven wrong.
