There has been much chatter about this book from my friends on Twitter, especially Kati who encouraged me to request it from NetGalley - so thank you Kati. I love trying rock star books and with the premise that the hero and heroine get drunk and marry in Vegas the night they meet appealed to me. 
 The problem for Evelyn or Ev getting drunk and married in Vegas is that she wakes up the next morning with the mother of all hangovers and no idea who the man is sleeping next to her in bed. Or why she is wearing a 5 carat diamond ring. Or why she has the name "David" tattooed on her left butt cheek. When David wakes up and announces they are married, she is not sure it's the hangover or the shock of what he just said that makes her vomit. Not that David isn't sexy - he is all bad boy rock star: 
 David's dark hair had been tied back in a little ponytail with strands falling around his face. What should have reeked of scummy drug dealer worked on him. Of course it did. He could probably make a dirty back alleyway seem like the honeymoon suite. A gray T-shirt molded to his thick shoulders and faded blue jeans covered his long legs. His black army-style boots were crossed at the ankles, easy as you please, because he belonged here. 
 Girl. Get on it! *wink* 
 This doesn't go over so well for David. They were both drunk the previous night, but he didn't realize she was that drunk. Ev seriously has no recollection of the night before, she barely even recognizes the huge rock star and guitarist from the popular band Stage Dive as she is more of a country music girl. So when she flees Vegas to go back to her hometown of Portland and runs into the frenzy of the paparazzi who have learned she married David, she knows she is in big trouble. Ev has plans. She has plans to go to school to become an architect and other studious things. She didn't have in her plans to go to Vegas for a weekend and come home married. 
 David asks her to come out to LA until they can get the divorce papers finalized, and Ev decides that is probably the best place for her. As she spends time with David, and as he slowly tells her all the reasons he fell for her that night, she starts to realize, she likes him. She wants to get to know him and annulment plans get put on hold. 
 For a book that starts out kind of silly with a drunken, Vegas wedding, some real emotions come into play in this one. I actually liked the beginning with David feeling hurt that Ev has no memory of their special night together and how the media pressure and crazy LA lifestyle make Ev feel so uncomfortable. When David and Ev escape to his Monterey home, they very quickly decide to make a go of their marriage. This made me roll my eyes a little, I admit. I felt insta-love reared its head and I was afraid it was going to be all ooey-gooey the last half of the book. But thankfully that isn't the case. 
 David has issues from a previous girlfriend cheating on him (I believe he is in his late twenties in this book). Ev is twenty-one and in her first real relationship. There are bound to be trust issues and they definitely come into play in the second half of this book. They felt like real problems a couple like this would have. I think Ev handles herself quite well for being forced into a new atmosphere. Relationships are strained with her parents. Squeeing ensues with her BFF when she learns she is married to a rock star. And eventually, Ev has to find herself and her place in this new lifestyle. The emotions and drama that come into play took ahold of me in the second half of the book and I really like how it all plays out and ends. I still wish that these two hadn't decided quite so easily to stay married, especially toward the beginning, but I guess that is rock 'n roll man. 
 This book is definitely not all drama. Having a rock star hero means having rock star sex. One thing I'll take away from this book is the fact if you are going to have a serious discussion about issues, it's best to do it with no shirt on. David is a boob man. He loves her rack. No really. 
 "Mm. And I'm over there, trying to talk business with Adrian, but I can't. I'm totally fucking distracted because I love your rack." 
 Normal discussion in the kitchen about serious relationship stuff? Take the shirt off then discuss. It makes things much more fun. 
 David reached for the back of his T-shirt and dragged it off over his head. "Rule number two, if I take my shirt off you have to take off yours. The shirt-off rule now applies to these sorts of conversations. I know we need to talk about stuff. But there's no reason we can't make it easier." 
 Adding greatly to the story is the drummer and David's good friend Malcolm (Mal) who is a fabulous character. A total smart ass and I'm already in love with him. 
 I think this is a nice start to a rock n roll series. Very much looking forward to the next one.

Read 2 of my Cosmere chronological extravaganza 
 Instant five stars. 
 How can one priest convert the religion of two whole nations? 
 Hrathen, high priest of Fjordell and gyorn of Shu-Dereth, has three months to convert the religion of Teod and Arelon or else Fjorden will launch a vicious invasion. 
 How can one prince, taken by a tainted magic, turn a horrid and vile city into something that was once beautiful? 
 Prince Raoden of Arelon is suddenly taken by the Shaod, the magic-gone-wrong from Elantris, which was once called the city of the gods. His splotched skin does nothing to stop his ambition and goal of turning something ugly into something beautiful. 
 How can one princess, a widow who thinks her husband dead, stop the oncoming slaughter of a nation's warriors? 
 Princess Sarene of Teod has arranged a marriage to unite the nations of Teod and Arelon in a permanent alliance - with none other than Prince Raoden. But Raoden is dead - or so she thinks - and so she takes it upon herself to figure out a new way to ally the nations together... or suffer the deadly consequences. 
 Like I said, instant five stars. 
 I loved this book so much. There was magic, romance, politics, action, doom, destruction, war, intrigue and so many interesting characters. I loved the dynamics between all the characters, especially Sarene and Ashe, her Seon. Ashe just made me so happy. 
 The magic was very interesting, like every single one of Brandon's magic systems. None of the systems in the Cosmere are the same. In this one, there is AonDor. An Aon is a symbol that represents a particular theme or aspect of life. Ashe, for example, is light. When used and operated, the Aon will glow because of its illuminating characteristics. This was so interesting and I loved reading about it, also the history of it. 
 I adored the pace of this book. It is definitely Sanderson's slowest book - but that did not falter my enjoyment of the novel at all. Even what another person would call "dull" scenes, I absolutely adored. There was so much in this novel that wouldn't be understood much without a basic knowledge of the cosmere, too. And the ending of the novel left me in tears. The climax was just heartbreaking and a particular character's death just shook me from head to toe. I will never be over them. Hrathen loved Sarene!!!! :'(  
 I have many theories about what the sequel will entail, more than what Sanderson has given us anyway. I have a lot of theories and speculations about the Dakhor as well as AonDor and where that will lead the future of Elantris. There is undoubtedly going to be some conflict between Fjorden and the nations of Arelon and Teod, but I can't wait to see how it unfolds and is involved in the cosmere. 
 Also, loved that little scene with Hoid and his crew. So good! 
 Overall, an amazing book from Master Sanderson.

I read Stroud's Bartimaeus trilogy and liked it pretty well, the writing and the originality of the book (especially the ending) impressed me. THIS BOOK I think I can sum up (at least in my humble opinion) in 3 words... "OH GOOD GRIEF". 
 Now I am tempted to let my one star rating and those three words sum up my feelings here and move on. I see many enjoyed this book (actually, predictably I think). I didn't, so to be fair to those who would like more detail let me add another phrase, seven words this time, "been there, done that, got the T-shirt". 
 This book, like several other "youth books" I've come across (many of which have what Tom Sawyer and Huck Finn would call a "whole raft of awards") is far more "youth indoctrination" than "youth literature". This story exists solely to drill the desired "lesson" into minds of it's readers. Now while that in itself is a huge problem for me a worse one is...it doesn't even do it while telling a good story. The story begins somewhat slowly, becomes repetitive and beats the reader over the head with it's "persuasion" (brainwashing?), and it does it with all the finesse and delicacy of a howitzer shell. 
 So, should I tell the BIG lesson of the book? That would of course constitute a spoiler and therefore negate the necessity of you finishing the book. I could be doing you a favor...still there are some of you who I'm sure will want to read it for yourself, heck some will wholeheartedly embrace the indoctrination. So, I'll cover that below a spoiler warning. For now I give the book one (1) star. Why do I give the book one star? Because I can't give it less without it looking like I just read the book and didn't rate it. 
 I can't recommend this one. 
  So okay, now it's just us. What's the BIG lesson? What's the big reveal? Why it's that everything "you" ("you" being the "youth" who's reading the book and inculcating it's propaganda) have (you've) been taught is A LIE. The role models you were brought up to look up to even the ideals you were taught to embrace are all LIES. 
 There's even a place where we get the line "Halli realized all the ideals he'd been taught were lies". Thus my summing up, "oh come on". 
 The book starts out with Halli making a series of bad decisions meeting the results of said bad decisions (and the actions based on them) and rationalizing it all away because he was clinging to the stories of the "Heroes" this happens over and over in varying ways, these events running the gamut from (attempted) humor to (attempted) pathos. 
 Along the way the book sets up straw men that can be knocked down. For example, Halli is constantly almost coming to blows...or coming to blows to, "defend his honor" or his family's "honor". Leaning hard on the negative (and incorrect) definition of the word honor as basically overweening pride and ignoring the positive (and more correct) aspect of the word "honor". It (honor) is seen as "a bad thing". It's not understood as a basic honesty and respect for one's self and others, the thing that teaches us to do the right thing, even when no one is looking, the reason to play by the rules even when a "little cheating" will bring a win. This sort of thing goes on throughout the book. Halli doesn't learn that the "Heroes" were just human, with the "proverbial feet of clay". He (and of course the co-protagonist) discovers that the greatest evil of all is of course the hero he's been taught to revere. (By the way the hero's name is "Svein"...again the phrase comes to mind, "oh come on".) 
 If the lesson of this book had been that Halli (and by extension the reader) needed to learn to think for themselves, find balance, that he would come to realize that the "Heroes" were a mixture of good and bad, humans doing the best they could, making decisions both good and bad, people with "feet of clay", then I could have said okay. Poor story telling aside that's a good lesson. As it is the book (again in my opinion) fails on both levels. The main action in the book is set in motion by what amounts to a cruel practical joke Halli plays on members of the household of another of the "Great Heroes" (Hakon). It ignites (reignites) a feud and leads to all the "unpleasantness" that follows. All this never, even in the end teaches Halli to think. He moves from one set of indoctrinated ideas to another (what was all good is now all bad, of course) and after he and his "partner" and co-protagonist the girl Aud learn this they leave the Vally..as no one is supposed to be able to do. So the stories around them say they probably died killed by the Trows (the monsters the Great Heroes of legend are renowned for saving the valley from). So in the end the "lies continue" simply inculcating Halli and Aud into them. 
 So, my opinion, poor book on several levels. I've seen the reviews, many love it, I'm not among them, not being a big fan of brainwashing and BEING a big fan of good stories. My take, my opinion, for what it's worth, can't recommend it. If you like it, enjoy.

No one deserves that kind of treatment. 
 When I say I didn't like the actual story as much as the message, I meant that the plot itself was very common - I could guess every thing that was going to happen miles away- but it doesn't mean at all that it was boring nor uninteresting. I appreciated every information the author gave us about being intersex, it showed how much she invested herself and how well-researched her story was. 
 One thing that bothered me a little was that Kristin's decisions were mostly driven by her romantic feelings, maybe I would've liked something a little more developped, more focused on herself than the romance on the book (does that make sense?). 
 Anyway I recommend vividly this book, a great YA contemporary that reads super fast and with diverse characters.

 'Wishes have a way of twisting themselves, and there is nothing more dangerous than getting your heart's desire. The question is, are you willing to gamble? How much are you willing to lose? What are you willing to risk everything for?' 
 This book!!! I loved everything about it - the writing that was so vivid I could imagine everything as though as I was there, the fantastic world, which honestly didn't remind me of Aladdin in the slightest, but was instead fleshed out 10x more than the original movie was. 
 'The things that were once sweet to me are now bitter. The sun is not half so bright. The stars seem dimmer. All this wealth and luxury feels meaningless. All the world is in your shadow, Zahra. I cannot help but see you when I close my eyes.' 
 Aw, Aladdin. I have a really soft spot for you now, do you know that? Even though this Aladdin is not really like the guy in the movie... He had far more depth than the Disney Prince. He's a fool at times, and flirting at any girl with a pulse is practically ingrained into him, which would have made him seem like a first class DickChief, but I never hated him once! Watching his character change over the course of the book, as he realises his original dreams of becoming a Prince instead of the street boy he was, was shallower than he thought - and that he grew into a thoughtful young man was so nice. 
 And also, HOW does he manage to sound so sweet, without being cheesy? 
 Aladdin and the jinni Zahra (Zahra, oh magnificent Zahra, I'll get to her in minute) meet different kinds of people in the city of Parthenia from all walks of life: the poor who are sick of starving, those fighters in that seedy club, rich assholes who live in a palace and also rich but okay-on-the-inside people. 
 But let's go back to how the two meet: 
 'Have you never seen a jinni before?' 
 The boy clears his throat, his eyes fixed on mine. 'No, but I've heard stories of them.' 
 Turning my back to him, I look up at the stars. 'Of course you have. Tales of ghuls, I'm sure, who devour souls and war the skins of their prey. Of irfeet, all fire and flame and no brains at all. Or perhaps you mean the maarids, small and sweet, until they drown you in their pools.' 
 He nods slowly and climbs to his feet, brushing sand from his palms. 'And the Shaitan, most powerful of all.' 
 A chill runs down my spine. 'Ah, of course.' 
 Zahra was a powerful jinn. She was in fact, a Shaitan herself, one of the last few left. But even though she held mighty power, she was still vulnerable and worst of all, tied to the lamp, forced to grant wishes for 4000 years. 
 The story centers on her point of view as she tells her tale of how she and Aladdin fell in love, even though she made a vow to herself to never love a human, as jinns and humans could never love one another. 
 Okay, I won't spoil anymore! 
 But I had such fun reading this. I truly hope the author writes more stories centering this world! Maybe a story about the Queen Caspida? Btw, LOVED her handmaidens! The fact that there was NO girl on girl hate, and that the female characters showed love and loyalty towards one another made me thrilled.

Paris for One and Other Stories is a collection of nine short stories, the central theme around all of which is love in what is considered one of the most romantic cities of the world. All told from the female perspective the stories are about different manifestations of relationships and at various stages of life. Like any book of short stories some are better, some are less appealing. My favorites were the first one, Paris for One. Many have a relationship somewhere in their experience with a person who strung you along just enough to keep you around, but who was obviously not all that in to you. Nell is in just such a relationship with Peter. She's planned a romantic getaway to Paris for the two of them and he completely blows her off by staying in London. Her girlfriends back in London discover this and I tell you what....every woman needs a tribe like this bunch. It doesn't really matter though because Nell has made the most of her weekend without Peter. I also really enjoyed Last Year's Coat about a couple who are struggling financially but obviously adore one another. The rest of the stories were pretty average. 
 It is a quick, light read. I gave it 3.5 and rounded down to 3.

 Theo Decker is only thirteen years old when the museum that he and his mother are at is blown up by a bomb. Dazed and confused, Theo leaves the museum covered in dust and blood, taking his mothers favorite priceless painting home with him. Unfortunately, his mom died during the building and he spends the next few years of his life with his alcoholic gambling father, dabbling in drugs and bad habits, hiding away the painting all the while. Now as an adult, Theo has returned to New York, where he gets swept up in illegal art and antiques trading. 
 The synopsis here on Goodreads made this sound like it dealt with his adult life way more than it does, he is a teenager until about 60% of the way through the book. And while I did love the story, and there's no doubt that Donna Tartt can write a beautiful descriptive paragraph, I did feel like it was a little long winded for what it was. There could've been about 200 pages less and the story would have still been amazing. In all honesty, I skimmed the last 20 or so pages, because it was just rambling. I also thought the goldfinch painting would play a bigger part of the story than it actually did, it just sat hidden for the majority of the book, just to be brought back into the spotlight for the last 20% of the book. 
 This was one of my most anticipated books to read, and one that has been on my tbr the longest. I was a little let down. I still thought this was great, but it was just a little more slowly paced than I thought it would be, and at times a little bit boring. The size intimidated me and put me off of reading it for a long time, but I'm glad I finally got to it.

El Deafo is an amazing memoir, but written in such a simple and approachable way. But still, it tells a gripping story. 
 I will sum up my review this way: I wish I had read this beautiful book sooner. I had not initially read it in preparation for the Newbery awards because of the graphic novel format, not knowing if the committee would consider it. Well now I know! I'm so glad it won the Newbery. I definitely recommend it.

 This is probably going to be a weird review. I liked the book. As things progressed, I found it increasingly difficult to put the book down. I've gotten into lots of discussions about the book. I've rated it four stars. These are all really good signs that the book is, in fact, good. And yet, when I finished reading that last page, I couldn't help but feel slightly disappointed. I feel like some opportunities were lost. Or maybe ignored. So I'm probably going to write most about what left me disappointed, and that will make it sound like I didn't like anything. But remember all that stuff at the beginning, okay? I did like it. I just wish it had lived up to its potential to be awesome. (And full disclosure - The Book of Strange New Things has been getting a lot of comparisons, fair ones I think, to The Sparrow. I LOVED The Sparrow, so there was quite a lot to live up to. You may want to keep that in mind, as well.) I will be getting into some specific plot points, or lack thereof, so if you haven't read the book yet and want to avoid spoilers, you may want to move on. 
 Here's what I was expecting from The Book of Strange New Things, based on the publisher's summary and general buzz about the book: 
 *Science fiction, focused mainly on the discovery of and growing familiarity with a new planet, an alien race, and an alien culture. 
 *A story of developing disaster and tragedy on Earth, tied closely to the story of a marriage. 
 *A strong element of religion, faith, lack thereof, etc. 
 All tied up into one complex, thought-provoking story filled with zero easy answers. I wanted angst, and agony, and menace. I wanted to hear all about this mysterious organization that has taken the place of NASA. I wanted to know about what was happening on Earth, and why. I wanted to watch as Peter struggled with the inherently dramatic choice of staying on this planet, or leaving for the months-long journey that might send him to a home that has collapsed. This is compelling stuff! This is the foundation for something amazing. 
 But, for me, it never reached that mark. Faber does a remarkable job of building this world. Oasis feels like a real place, and even more remarkable, it feels like a completely alien planet. It's not the jungle with big-eyed aliens. It's not a big, empty desert with nomadic creatures on it. It's a kind of environment that I've never encountered before. And it's populated with interesting people, and run by a corporation that has an agenda. And this is where I start to bemoan all the lost opportunities. 
 I wanted more. I wanted to explore the nature of this big corporation. I wanted to know if the sense of evil intent I was feeling was just me, or if it was there on purpose. I wanted to know more about how the humans selected to work on Oasis were picked. In fact, the only question I had that was fully answered was why the Oasans felt such a strong pull toward Christianity. Everything else was developed clearly, completely, then abandoned. The voice of Peter's wife begins to fade. I understand that this is supposed to reflect their disconnect, but as a reader it also left me feeling disconnected from a huge part of the story. She felt absent, and since she's supposed to be a linchpin in the drama, that was a problem for me. Peter felt like he was floating along in a sea of obsession with the Oasans. Their unquestioning adoration of his religion and of him pulled all of his attention. That in and of itself doesn't bother me. It made him unlikable, but it made sense for the character. What I can't forgive, though, is that Faber made me go with him. I wanted to have the full story and be watching from the sidelines to see what move he would make. I wanted to really know what the stakes were. I wanted to have a dog in this race. And with such a meticulously built world, there was no reason why I couldn't have that. It felt like a waste. 
 That got a bit rambly. Hope it makes sense.

"If you want to know what a man's like, take a good look at how he treats his inferiors, not his equals." 
 Wise words, Sirius. Wise words. 
 The book where Harry and Ron hit puberty. At least that's how I like to see it, the way they behave. All the petty arguing, anger, and jealousy and the beginnings of crushes and heartache. It's funny how J.K. Rowling never really addresses puberty directly in a book of teens. Then again, considering it's meant for much younger readers, I guess I shouldn't be surprised. But the subtle hints are there. 
 Of course, the epic tournament and the (spoiler??) return of Lord Voldemort is a climactic episode which heralds the changing of the tides for the Wizarding World. And as such, it was written with many twists and turns, a multitude of humorous moments, full of heartening revelations and heart-breaking conclusions, and a build up of anticipation for what is to come in the future books. There was some major foreshadowing going on and some amazing character development, especially in Hermione's case. Man, she doesn't let anything get her down. 
 Let me get metaphorical now. I think this book was a symbolic expression of us as the reader hitting our own puberty in the change of tone signaled by  Cedric's death . It signified that our innocence will no longer be a shield as we open our eyes to the very real and very scary future of the wizarding world. From here on in, it's going to get ugly. Rowling masterfully made that a very evident but easy transition. Buckle up your seatbelts kids, it's going to be a bumpy ride.

 Every Heart A Doorway had beautiful narration, interesting fairy-tale worlds and it was slightly strange. I liked it much more than I thought I would. 
 Every Heart A Doorway is a diverse stand alone novel, surrounding the children that are taken to different lands through magical doors, wardrobes and rabbit holes. After they return to the world they were taken from, Eleanor West takes in these wayward children, and strives to helps them. 
 Nancy is one of these wayward children, and after a trip to her magical world she falls into Miss West's care as she seeks a way back home. However, while Nancy settles in to her new school tragedy strikes, leaving Nancy and her schoolmates in danger. 
 Since this is a review, below does contain spoilers, if you haven't read the book, don't read any further. You have been warned. 
 Short and sweet should be the way this book is described, running at a small 169 pages Every Heart A Doorway is packed full of strange children, magical doors and a little darkness. 
 The story's premise was fantastic, I love the idea of the children from Narnia and Wonderland ending up in a school to either help them assimilate back into society or find there way back to their respective worlds. This was a creative story, filled with wonderful diversity representation touching on asexuality, transgender and mental illness. 
 The writing within Every Heart A Doorway was beautiful and almost lyrical. I enjoyed this specifically during the first few pages, I think it set up the story nicely and made it stand apart from anything else I was reading previously. 
 I think the plot was well paced, the story flowed nicely and it was engaging for such a short book. I think considering the short nature, there was quite a lot done plot wise in the story. I especially liked the small amount of world building of Nancy's world and some of the other worlds that was created, although I would of enjoyed a bit more on her time within her realm. A disappointing factor I found, was in the ending. As soon our main character discovered she could learn to live in the real world again, and could see a life for herself there, her door opened again and off she went. It felt like all the building up and all the character development was torn down in this moment. 
 The characters were alright, unfortunately my favourite didn't stay in the story too long. I think some of the side characters were unbearable. The squad which included Nancy, Jack, Kade and Christopher, I enjoyed their dynamics together. Another enjoyable part was the fact that each of the children brought something back from their world that affected them, either personality or physicality. 
 You want to go back, and so you hold on to the habits you learned while you were travelling, because it's better than admitting the journey's over. 
 Overall, I enjoyed reading Every Heart A Doorway it was an interesting interpretation of what happens to children after they return from other world. 
 Favourite Quote: "You're nobody's rainbow. 
 You're nobody's princess. 
 You're nobody's doorway but your own, and the only one who gets to tell you how your story ends is you." 
 Rating: 3.75/5

 Arin's part of the story is what I found most interesting. There is definitely more to him than Kestrel realizes. That is not to say that Kestrel is a boring character.  The story is a fantasy adventure but not a traditional one. Don't expect great raging magic or the duck and parry and the swish of the blade of a master swordsman. The damsel is in distress but the distress builds rather than falling on her all at once. The struggle is epic and the end will leave you... not grinning madly, not sad but strangely content. The story is magical and real - nothing is perfect but things work out at the end.

 Oh, Harry Potter. So wonderful and yet so full of flaws. Continuing my re-read of this series, a book at a time when I need something a little different, I've finally gotten to the fourth volume, Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. 
 The third book was somewhat of a break from the direct Harry vs. Voldemort conflict, but Rowling doesn't waste any time getting back to things here, diving right in with a foreboding scene hinting at Voldemort's actual return and his direct targeting of Harry. But then things recede for a while as Harry returns to school and finds himself inadvertently entered into the Triwizard Tournament, possibly because they want him dead. The book is padded out with the Quidditch World Cup (to make up for a lack of quidditch as a whole) and a house elf rights campaign by Hermoine. Oh, and a vicious stream of gossip by Daily Prophet reporter Rita Skeeter. 
 Overall, this is a fun book. It's the first "long" Harry Potter book, but before the series takes a darker turn starting in Order of the Phoenix. The Triwizard Tournament is of course a highlight, particularly because it brings in other schools in the wizarding world, which we didn't know about before this point. The tasks are new and interesting, and there are a new cast of supporting characters to match them, like Mad-Eye Moody, Viktor Krum, and Fleur Delacoeur, in addition to some of the Weasleys we haven't seen before. But while Rowling has a fun book and one that works to get the plot back on track after the detour it took in the third book, there are still so many questions that, reading it years after the first (and second, and third) times through, I couldn't dislodge. 
 Like why is Harry allowed to just run around all year? If the antagonist lurking in this book wanted to save Harry for Voldy to kill himself, why not just nab him, curse him, whatever, and keep him stashed until the appropriate time? This is the main thing that dogs me throughout the entire book. There are so many opportunities for Harry to be "taken care of" that don't require him being in the Tournament at all, and so the Tournament clearly is meant to serve purely as fan service for readers. In addition, I am baffled by how easily Harry's concerns and stories about Voldemort are dismissed by everyone except his core handful of supporters, namely Ron, Hermoine, Sirius,and Dumbledore. Harry has repeatedly been proven to be a reliable source, and yet every gossip column that Rita Skeeter puts out seems to destroy his credibility, even among students at Hogwarts, who should know better. 
 And why are Slytherins (other than Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle) repeatedly characterized as evil? There doesn't seem to be a point...? Slytherins are supposed to be cunning, but making them into the "evil" house whereas the others are all "good" really seems to be a very shallow characterization and one that does not fit in with Rowling's other layered pieces of worldbuilding. 
 However, this is still a good book. The Harry Potter books are known for delving into issues that resonate strongly in our own world, and this is no exception. Voldemort is not Hitler, but his policies and actions sometimes bear a close resemblance; racism is a key part of politics in this world, and we can see that even Ron, who is one of the heroes and is a good person, dismisses Hermoine's claims that house elves should have rights just like humans should, and that he views Hagrid and Madame Maxine differently after finding out about their giant heritage. This is also where we really start to see the consequences of Voldemort's reign that we haven't seen before, like what happened to Neville's parents. It's a hint at what's to come, but still a rollicking story in and of itself. 
 I'm rather dreading moving on to Order of the Phoenix, which was always been my least-favorite of the books, but I have it lined up and ready to go.

Neil Gaiman is not only an excellent writer, he is also incredibly imaginative. He has the rare ability to conjure up the kinds of stories that are usually only available to young children who, by virtue of their youth and inexperience with The Real World, can still weave dramatic make-believe stories of fantastic creatures and events out of thin air. As an adult it is harder to make up tales of this kind because we've been around long enough to know they couldn't possibly be true. Which takes all the fun out of it. So we just go about our day and go to work and go to the gym and go to the grocery store and that's that. 
 But reading this book felt like being a kid again. I could once again feel the intense fear, the tender friendship, and the genuine fascination at the ways of a family that is not your own that I think only 7-year olds can feel. And although the adult Maria knew that it was just a story, and not at all true, and the narrator didn't actually have all of these fantastical things happen to him, it was probably just a memory of an elaborately imagined story he created to deal with the trauma of discovering the body of man who committed suicide in his family's vehicle, it still let me forget about going to work and going to the gym and going to the grocery store for a day. 
 My favorite quote: "I do not miss childhood, but I miss the way I took pleasure in small things, even as greater things crumbled. I could not control the world I was in, could not walk away from things or people or moments that hurt, but I found joy in the things that made me happy. The custard was sweet and creamy in my mouth, the dark swollen currants in the spotted dick were tangy in the cake-thick chewy blandness of the pudding, and perhaps I was going to die that night and perhaps I would never go home again, but it was a good dinner, and I had faith in Lettie Hempstock."

 AS the name suggests this is a book aimed towards females. Maggs talks about the discrimination of women in the nerdy world but empowers and encourages the reader to look forward to the female strong future of the industry.

 Tessa was terminally ill, she was diagnosed with a severe case of leukemia and no one could predict how long she would live. She barely lived her life so she decided to come up with a list, a list of things to do before she dies. 
 To-do list (not arranged accordingly), read at own risk :P It might ruin the fun though. 
 To-do list before I die. 
 1. Have Sex. 
 2. Prank calls. 
 3. Say yes to everything for a day 
 4. Break as many rules as you can. 
 5. Do drugs. 
 6. Fall in love 
 7. Travel around the world (but trade it for mum and dad getting back) 
 8. Gain fame. 
 9. Be there for Lauren Tessa Walker's birth.  
 To be honest, I hated the beginning of the book, and I was seriously considering whether I should continue reading or not. My first verse novel was I heart you, You haunt me by Lisa Schroeder so I am still a newbie at reading verse novels, and this book gave me quite an unlikely first impression. Tessa came across as someone pushy, bossy, self-centered (in my opinion), she treated her father poorly and pulled around her friend Zoey (whom I think is a bad influence) to do all the things on the list. Then she went back home, threw up and do that again. 
 I was very annoyed with Tessa, but after reaching the later chapters, I don't even remembered why I hated her. I normally dislike books that seemed rushed or lack in elaboration, but ironically, I wouldn't change anything about that in Before I Die (I noticed that verse novels are special in that way, and they made me very emotional). As I continued to delve inside the heart wrenching story of Tessa, I found myself discovering values that I never paid attention to, reading from a near-death teenage girl's perspective had made me realized how death is not to be taken lightly, and we should live our life to the fullest. 
 Tessa held on to the list, the list was her motivation to keep on living, but she never managed to accomplish it all, quote: ten is not enough. In the process of fulfilling her list, she met new people and make amends to her life. 
 Her friendship with Zoey deepened. Zoey came across as a spoiled brat and I disliked her character, however after a life-changing occurrence impregnated , they were brought together closer than ever. 
 She met Adam, a brave young man who was willing to put his heart at risk, knowing that falling in love with Tessa would only bring hurt to him in the end, still he loved her, cherished her. 
 She rekindled her relationship with her parents in the end. After her parents separated, Tessa was put under the care of her father, and her mother was rarely there anymore. Tessa's dad was the one who cared for her for 4 years, sacrificing everything just to give her the undivided attention she needed, and was the one who accompanied her through all her excruciating treatments. But as her condition worsened, she was the one who brought her parents together, and she finally accepted what her father does for her. 
 I was literally glued to the screen, flipping from page to page and my tears flowed to the extent I have to stifle my own sobs. And I couldn't have thought of a better way to end the story. It was heartbreaking, it was depressing, it was necessary. 
 It was a bittersweet ending. I love you Tessa! The memory of you will always be with me!

 The New Species are a genetically engineered mix of human and animal DNA that were created by and subsequently tortured by Mercile Industries. 
 The series starts around the time when the government raids the Mercile facilities. They capture the Mercile employees and begin rescuing the test subjects who are referred to as numbers. These "New Species" are genetically mixed with human and animal DNA (canine, feline or primate) and are strong, physically superior and much more immune than humans. Each book takes us through a progressive timeline going forward from this rescue while focusing on a different New Species character and their particular steamy story. 
 While there is a slight paranormal twist (genetically mutated/enhanced characters) that is the only part that makes this paranormal. Everything else is based on this planet, in this time, and amongst us and our modern day quirks.

Such a powerful novel. 
 This was my morning book; I read it for half an hour every morning after I took a shower and was waiting for my hair to dry enough to walk to school. After a couple days, I could feel "grit" gathering at the corners of my eyes. 
 I thought the "copulation" scene at the beginning of the 21st chapter captures the essence of the book: "Man's convulsions go on building endless layers of fossils. Dinosaur teeth and glaciers were powerless against this reproductive drive." We are prisoners of our own selfish genes; which is to say we are prisoners of our Self. The Sand Woman (Sha noNu ) is like the piece of rotting fish used to bait the crow trap, except that Jumpei takes the bait. We lead lives of relative misery or comfort, but when the species calls to us, we do what it wants. 
 I think it's significant that the woman submits to Jumpei (clearly, in a willing way, even if she feels degraded) but when he is going to rape her in front of the villagers (for their amusement, and to get access to the ladder rope) she beats him to a pulp. She is not defenseless. She is the dune--miniscule in the detail, unrelenting in the aggregate. 
 While reading the book, I couldn't help thinking of the Japanese "Internment" in America during the Second World War.(the 19th of this month marks the 70th anniversary of EO9066). With the exception of the camps in Arkansas, They were all places like this--battling isolation and the relentless desert grit. When you look at the pictures as they were being taken to the initial Assembly Centers, they (the "internees") also looked like they were off on a day trip (smiles and hiking boots). And when they got there, they too were surprised to realize that the guns and search lights were all pointing in the wrong direction. (Some of them too--like Jumpei--as bad as the camps were--ended up wanting to stay.) 
 This makes me really want to see the movie, and read some of his other books.

Review: 
 Protagonist: Hazel Grace has survived much longer than she thought she would. Armed with a quick wit, sarcasm, and her oxygen tank she embarks on the greatest and saddest adventure ever. I loved Hazel's character, and while I still believe that Kenzie from the Iron Fey: Call of the Forgotten series is my book soulmate, Hazel comes in at a very close second. She's brilliant, realistic, and will easily take advantage of "cancer perks" when she can. In the beginning of the book she's a bit reserved and really only interacts with the rest of the world when she attends her cancer survivor support group. Then she meets Augustus Waters and he opens her up to the world around her. She doesn't really become that much more social, but he gives her a reason to get out of bed in the morning. Her development through this book is amazing and I loved every minute of it. 
 Romance: So yes there is a fair amount of romance in this book, enough to make it more of a plot than a sub-plot, but it really worked here. Normally I'm not a big fan of too much romance, but in contemporaries it's different and this love story was epic! It felt real given the unlucky circumstances of their love. It progressed at a natural pace and it was the bright spot on this sometimes devastating book. The chemistry between these characters is electric, they aren't super alike, and at times they but heads, but at the end of the day they really love each other and they just fit. 
 Author's Writing Style: So this is the first John Green book I've read (I know, I know, what took me so long?) Since I'm so unfamiliar with his work I was absolutely blown away by how this book was written. It was profound, but not pretentious, and it was uncensored, meaning that these kids who any most other YA novels would have refrained from cursing or saying and doing things that in reality kids their age do, they act like real teenagers. Now I know the latter example was more character traits and development than "writing style," but it's a testament to how committed this author was to authenticity. 
 Sadness: So the one thing I kept hearing about this book was how sad it was, and that I might need a box of tissues, and yeah most of that was true. This book has a few really sad and emotional parts and yeah I did tear up when the most devastating part came, but in the end I think I built up too great of a sadness expectation that I wasn't as effected as I would have been had I just picked this up without knowing anything about it. 
 Predictability: So again, going back to how much I'd heard about it, I never heard any spoilers and I did everything I could to refrain from seeking them out, but I do think that the whole sadness factor plus the fact that I knew so much about the (non-spoiler) plot of the book, led it to be a bit too predictable. Now I'm not saying that I wasn't shocked or taken aback at any point while reading this book, on the contrary there were many times I didn't see something coming, but most times those were smaller things. It was the "BIG" thing that I saw coming the thing that left my best friend and my cousin in tears and probably a lot of people who read it. Since I saw it coming so soon I think that I wasn't as effected by it if I, again, knew nothing about the book and two wasn't reading it in public. 
 Ending: This book ended much later than I thought it would, but in actuality I was happy for that. It was sort of like having an extended epilogue. The ending while very somber in tone still added a lot of depth to the book. While I had hoped that some things would have happened differently I did feel that what happened was realistic. There was no sugar coating on the end and things didn't end particularly well, but it did end on a higher note. 
 Rating:

Partials focuses on Kiera, a 16yo medic who decides she has had enough of watching babies die and takes up the cause to find a cure for the RM virus. This sets off a string of events that bring her to learn everyone is keeping secrets. She was 5 when most of the world's population died. She has grown up in a seemingly hopeless world. Because of The Hope Act, any woman age 17 and up must be pregnant as often as possible. Kiera is quickly approaching this age and is desperate to change things. 
 Partials was a compelling book in many ways. I ultimately did enjoy it, but the book took me on an emotional ride. Throughout the book, I felt for the survivors and the hopelessness of their future. No baby can survive past 3 days of life due to the virus. The youngest child is 14. The Human Race will die out eventually. I also felt frustrated reading the book because the actions of some of the leaders seemed to make no sense. In eleven years, no one has come up with the same idea as Kiera? Their only idea is to keep having babies and study the newborns as they die. That was just disturbing and I was surprised there wouldn't be more depressed women walking around. When Kiera approaches her superiors with an idea, they immediately reject it because they still hate the Partials. Seriously, if the human race is in the balance, why wouldn't you give it a shot? 
 Kiera is a strong and tough female character but she does have the capacity to show emotion and compassion. I was happy to see that there was no love triangle. Even with Samm in the picture, I didn't feel there was a real potential for one. I hope it stays that way. I really did like Marcus. He was such a sweet guy who loves Kiera immensely and just wants to keep her safe. I really felt for him as he realizes he has to let her do her thing. There is a whole cast of characters who round out the story nicely. 
 There is so much packed into this book that I could go on forever. I know this book will keep me thinking for a long time. The next book, Fragments, comes out in February 2013. Since Partials ends on a cliffhanger, I am eager to read what happens next. If you are looking for a great YA novel with a mix of Sci-fi, dystopia, and lots of action, give this one a shot. There are no language or sexual situations, so I say it probably would be OK for the over 14 crowd.

 Mindy McGinnis once described Not a Drop To Drink as Little House on the Prairie meets The Hunger Games. I reacted to that description with doubt and confusion. The two books didn't mesh well in my head, and I couldn't figure out how such a book could be possible, and if it were possible, how it could be good. 
 Guys, I could sit here for days and still not find a better description of this book. And it. is. AMAZING. 
 After reading so much for so many years, it's difficult to find a book that is truly different, but I could tell from the start that Ms. McGinnis was giving me something fresh. Our MC, Lynn, lives in a dry, empty world, one that she and her mother make emptier by the day. It's just the two of them, Lynn and Mother, alone in their house by the pond. Their days are spent shooting coyotes, tending the garden, purifying water, and killing any stranger stupid enough or unlucky enough to step foot on their land. 
 We know the freshwater supply of the world is slowly disappearing. It's why Lynn and her mother guard their pond so fiercely, their last defense against a slow death by dehydration. Why the water had disappeared, we don't really know at first, nor does it matter, just like it doesn't matter to Lynn and Mother. All that matters is survival and the tools it takes to keep them alive - the pond, clean water, healthy food, and wood for the winter. The strangers down at the stream don't matter; they're city folk and are sure to be dead by the end of two winters. The tiny town to the south doesn't matter, so long as the menfolk don't attempt a raid on the house. Then they'll only matter until Lynn's bullets hits their skulls. Even their only neighbor, Stebbs, doesn't matter. He's stays on his land, and they stay on theirs. If he dies, it's nothing to them, and the same goes in reverse. 
 And then, one bright day, it all changes. 
 I've read books that could be called "gritty" or "real," and I guess those descriptions still hold true, but I've never read a book that felt quite as real as Not a Drop To Drink. I don't know that I can explain it. It's not like I was there, though I did feel immersed in Lynn's world. And it's not just that the scenario Ms. McGinnis presented was realistic and frighteningly plausible, though it was. But I don't think you all can understand it for yourself until you read this book. I could hear the crunch of the gravel. I could smell the soil in Lynn's garden. I could hear the howl of the coyotes and taste the wind-blown grit between my teeth. I could see Lynn go through her daily chores, though I've never witnessed someone purify water or skin a squirrel in my life. 
 Some, I suspect, might describe Not a Drop To Drink as pedantic. Certainly, Ms. McGinnis spends a great deal of time describing Lynn's daily routine. Lynn's actions, like her thoughts, are clean, precise, and controlled. Her story reads like a how-to survival guide, lacking only line-art diagrams. The details appealed to the part of me that loved Little House on the Prairie, and I believe the same will hold true to others. The details are prolific but concise. Ms. McGinnis does not waste her words, and every description, every task, shows us a little more of Lynn's life. 
 Often, the adjective "realistic" is overused in reviews. Sometimes "realistic" is used to mean "believable," and that's fine. Not a Drop To Drink is certainly believable (with one exception that I'll get to later). Lynn and her mother learn to survive through experience, practice, and issues of National Geographic. There are no superpowers or other special snowflake abilities. We don't ever learn the details of how the Earth's freshwater supply evaporated, but we do learn of the response to the shortage, and it is chillingly believable. Cover-ups, conspiracies, rebellions, and greedy capitalism - all the pieces are there, but Ms. McGinnis fits them together with such smooth simplicity, like the long, undented barrel of a gun. 
 So yes, "realistic" can and often does mean "believable," but in this book, it also can mean "unsensationalistic," a word that I gleefully just made up. In Lynn's world, it is what it is. It's a phrase she uses often, one her mother taught her. It is what it is. It - whatever "it" is - is a solid, immovable fact. No amount of sensationalism can change reality. Throw in all the adjectives you want, all the emotions, all the angst. Nothing will change the facts at hand. And so it is in Not a Drop To Drink. Lynn's world is a violent one, a harsh one. Awful, disgusting, unjust things happen. But nothing is ever graphic for the sake of graphicness. I never felt like I was being emotionally manipulated or goaded. It is what it is. People die. Water disappears. Supplies are stolen. Entire families are left to rot. It is what it is. 
 Because of this factualness, this realism, Ms. McGinnis is able to accomplish things in her world-building that might have drawn attention in other spheres. In other books, I might have laughed at the holes in Lynn's knowledge when it comes to the dangers men present. But in this book, it is what it is. Lynn only talks to her mother, and her mother never bothered to explain sex or rape to a young girl living in a manless world. It is what it is. And in other books, I might have noticed how few male characters there were, and I might have stopped to consider whether the story passed The Bechdel Test. Instead, this world where women are the strong ones, the survivors, the important ones, and I didn't bat an eye. Men exist as secondary characters, as the dead who motivate the living, and as villains, but the women outnumber them. I can't tell you the last book that I read that could pull that off without making it seem unique or noteworthy. 
 I do have a few nitpicks, nothing major. I thought the names of the female characters were confusing at times. Between Lynn, Laura, Lucy, Vera, and Neva, it took me a few tries to get everyone straight. I wish the editor had insisted on a more diverse nomenclature. One of these characters also possesses the only unbelievable plot point of the novel, the ability to sense water or "douse." 
 I also wish there had either been more of a romance or none at all. Lynn's romance with Eli did nothing for me. I didn't dislike it, but it didn't move me. I felt like the romance was an effort to "normalize" the book and make it more palatable for the stereotypical YA reader, though Lynn's story would have been fine without it. Or at least if you're going to go for it, then GO for it. No holding back, no half measures. 
 Oddest of all, Not a Drop To Drink lacked a strong narrative arc. I kept waiting for that One Big Thing, that One Big External Plot Motivator, but it never came. An external plot motivator came, to be sure, but it was handled quickly and cleanly. I never felt like Lynn was ever given more than she could handle. She was never truly bested, never completely overwhelmed. She lost in some things, yes, but I never felt like she had to fight her way back against insurmountable odds. It was... different. I'm not sure it was bad, just different, like the rest of the book. 
 So here's the bottom line. If you want something new and different; if you want a book that caters strongly to tough, fallible, diverse women; if you want a book that doesn't shy away from the squeamish, heartbreaking parts of life but never manipulates you; if you want a book that tells it like it is, then you should check this book out. If you don't like it, that's fine. If you do, that's great! In any case, it is what it is. 
 Favorite Non-Spoilery Quote(s): 
 A slow laugh rumbled through his chest and he opened his eyes to stare her down across the table. I don't know that your momma would approve of your soft ways." 
 "Maybe not," Lynn admitted, "but she'd like this next part just fine." 
 She shot him neatly in the forehead, leaving behind a black hole that was still smoking when she shut the door behind her. 
 Points Added For: Unexpected (dry) humor, a refreshing lack of sensationalism, wonderful characters, a kick-butt heroine, passing the Bechdel Test. 
 Points Subtracted For: Dousing, similar character names, the lack of a narrative arc. 
 Good For Fans Of: Little House on the Prairie, survivalist books, kick-butt heroines. 
 Notes For Parents: Language, murder, suggested rape, suggested prostitution, death, general life-on-the-prairie ickiness, animal death (though it actually made me laugh - don't judge!), and [spoiler]infant death[/spoiler].

 Taylor Jenkins Reid became an auto-buy author for me after I read After I Do and Forever, Interrupted, two of my all-time favorite books. 
 I was immediately intrigued by the synopsis of Maybe in Another Life and couldn't get my hands on a copy of this book fast enough. I loved the premise of this book. I was speechless when I finished reading this book. Maybe in Another Life blew my socks off. 
 Maybe in Another Life takes you on an emotional journey that shows how a simple choice can alter your life. Hannah has just returned to Los Angeles, her hometown after she has spent the last few years moving from city to city. 
 When Hannah returns home she goes to a bar with her best friend, Gabby. While there she talks to Ethan, her high school sweetheart. Hannah is given two options: leave the bar with Ethan or leave with Gabby. The story focuses on what would happen in Hannah's life with each choice. What if she leaves with Ethan? What if she leaves with Gabby? What happens in her life? We see each choice play out. We see both sides. We see what happens when she leaves with Ethan. And when she leaves with Gabby.  Maybe in Another Life takes an interesting look into the question, "What if?" It really makes you think about things in your life. It opens your eyes. Or at least it did mine. It shows you how simple choices impact your life. 
 Taylor Jenkins Reid's writing is incredible. Her writing is mesmerizing and beautiful. There were many scenes that I read over and over. Maybe in Another Life wasn't as emotional as her other books, but it was LOADED with feels. I felt a wide range of emotions while reading this book.

 Maybe in Another Life is such a refreshing, unique, thought-provoking book. I was immediately sucked in and was on the edge of my seat waiting to see what happened next. It was interesting to see how a simple choice could change someone's life. This book is one of the best that I have read this year. 
 Recommended To:

The Short & Tragic Life of Robert Peace, is a book I feel everyone should read. 
 This is a nonfiction piece written by Rob Peace's college roommate after Rob's death. 
 From the beginning, the reader grows with Rob. We see the different events and struggles in his life that shaped him into the man he became later on. 
 Growing up in Newark, New Jersey in his grandparents house with his mother, and many aunts and uncles, Rob showed signs of genius. He had loved to read, much to the chagrin of his father, and always wanted to know why. However, Rob did have a tough side. And whether due to his fathers reputation or his own stubbornness, this helped him in the streets ever since. 
 What I found really tough about Peace's story, is the fact that he was a genius. To go from Newark to Harvard and major in molecular biophysics... it's not an easy feat. If he had moved out of Newark, he could have worked for a large pharmaceutical company and make a decent amount of money in order to support himself and his mother. It was amazing that even though he held so much knowledge, he was adamant about staying in Newark and selling drugs. It seems absurd. 
 However, it could be the writing of Hobbs (who told us that he hardly talked to Peace after college, therefore doesn't really know the entire story of Peace's post college life) that made this seem ridiculous. But what isn't said addressed is the theory of being the product of your environment. This is not to say that everyone growing up in rough neighborhoods grow up to sell drugs. However, I personally know people, that are set in their ways. Selling a few ounce of weeds isn't a hard task, so its a relatively easy way to make money. For Rob, who was unsure of where to go after college, probably sold drugs in order to say afloat. 
 But despite his motives and actions, Peace's story really, really stuck with me. To know that Peace's murderers are walking free, that's scary. His mother never got justice for Rob's death. 
 And over weed! Weed is profitable but not as profitable as other drugs. 
 Despite the lack of perspective on Hobb's part, this piece of work will stick with me forever.

"You don't pass or fail at being a person, dear." 
 There is magic. There is magic everywhere. 
 I read a review of this book by Lev Grossman in Time magazine. I thought, "I like Lev Grossman. I like Time Magazine. This will be the perfect book for me." 
 And it was. 
 This is my first Neil Gaiman. I hope the rest are as simply complex as this one was. 
 There is The Boy. He is never named, and reading the book, you never want to know his name. Gaiman makes this simple, seemingly critical detail not necessary until you finish the book and think ... "What was his -name-?" 
 He just is. 
 And he is just only 7. 
 But that's not where is starts. 
 He's really 40, looking back at when he was 7, and an opal miner came to stay with his family. The miner steals the family car and commits suicide in it at the bottom of the lane. From this incident, darkness falls in the boys life in the form of Ursula Monkton, an aptly named villan. Light falls in the boys life in the form of Lettie Hempstock, an 11 year old girl who lives on a farm at the end of the lane. 
 It is her ocean The Boy is drawn to as a man, and it is her ocean that appears as a small duck pond, but holds magic and wonder and knowledge. 
 This book was amazing. 
 It was slow at first, but it grips you. The world is as the world is. Gaiman creates a magical universe that just is. There is no Harry Potter undercurrent explanation. There is just the Hempstocks and their farm. When The Boy meets Lettie, and his journey into understanding begins, there is no question or doubt, he just goes, as a 7 year old would and should. 
 The Hempstocks are not rationalized to fit the world we know and perceive. The Hempstocks exist, and after reading and living The Boy's life, it seems that the Hempstocks could very well live at the end of the lane, and any pond has the ability to be the ocean if you name is so. 
 That was where -I- faltered, because I kept turning the page expecting that closure. I began wanting there to be a clever code that made The Boy's adventure understandable, which is why the book took a few pages to latch on. However, it was the lack of something hokey and cute that made the story more believable that any magical tale I have read thus far.

 If you haven't read this book, you should. It's hands down the most quotable novel I have ever read. In my paperback version of it you can barely discern the print through all the cramped notes I've stuffed into the margins and the blobs of yellow, pink and green highlighter that take up a majority of each page. 
 What? I have a highlighting system, don't judge me. 
 For those of you who don't know the scandal-ridden history of this work of art, allow me to enlighten you. When it was first printed in 1890 by a British monthly magazine, the editors there, without the knowledge of the author, sheared off a little over 500 words from it because they thought it was "indecent". 
 It wasn't enough. 
 Victorian England was still outraged over it. Reviewers called Wilde immoral and hedonistic, and The Picture of Dorian Gray homoerotic, unclean, effeminate and contaminating. 
 Needless to say, the criticism got to the author. In response to it, the book was further edited, more passages were "toned down", deleted or re-written and six chapters were added to bring more depth to the characters and their actions in attempt to assuage the readers' 'delicate sensibilities'. 
 It wasn't enough. Again. 
 I won't go further into the life of the author as his story is even grimmer than that of his only published novel. Instead I'll say this; I hope to God that mankind has moved forward enough that his tale will never be repeated. We should encourage artists and their genius, not destroy them. For how can we make any progress if we repress our innovators? 
 So you see my five stars and here's where you're probably thinking "But what about the misogyny? Aren't you a feminist? How can you give this book five stars when it includes quotes like this: 
 "I am afraid that women appreciate cruelty, downright cruelty, more than anything else. They have wonderfully primitive instincts. We have emancipated them, but they remain slaves looking for their masters, all the same. They love being dominated." 
 I've read a lot of other reviews for this book and some people seem pretty irritated by passages like the above. I understand the irritation but let it be with the character and not the book or the author. I have Oscar Wilde's memoirs in my library. I also have two biographies about him and have done a lot of additional research (if you couldn't already tell). Wilde did not appear to be a misogynist. In fact, at one point he was an editor of a women's magazine and personally edited, published and lauded several articles on feminism and women's suffrage. The character of Lord Henry, however, is a misogynist, and I'm not arguing that. But there is brilliance in making him so disgusted by women and even though I don't particularly enjoy it, I applaud how it was done. 
 Here's a great article describing Wilde's motivations way better than I ever could. 
 Suffice to say, this book is one of my favorites. I can't properly review it. I just...can't. Everything has already been said, so why add my opinion to the masses when it would only be an outpouring of fangirling? And just in case you're curious, a few houses have recently published the unedited version of this book. I suggest you read both. 
 In closing, I leave you with some of my favorite quotes: 
 "...there is only one thing in the world worse than being talked about, and that is not being talked about." 
 "There is a fatality about all physical and intellectual distinction, the sort of fatality that seems to dog through history the faltering steps of kings." 
 "Experience is merely the name men gave to their mistakes." 
 "Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing." 
 "Live! Live the wonderful life that is in you! Let nothing be lost upon you. Be always searching for new sensations. Be afraid of nothing." 
 "What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world and lose his own soul?" 
 "All art is at once surface and symbol. Those who go beneath the surface do so at their peril." 
 "I can stand brute force, but brute reason is quite unbearable. There is something unfair about it's use. It is hitting below the intellect." 
 "Every effect that one produces gives one an enemy. To be popular one must be a mediocrity."

I have read this book three times already in just the past year because I thought it was perfect and I happened to love the characters. Madeline Hunter is one of my top 5 favorite historical romance authors. My favorite romance trope is the arranged marriage or "marriage to save heroine from social ruin". 
 In The Accidental Duchess, Penthurst marries Lydia to prevent her from being ruined by a villain. When Lydia and Penthurst were children, their mothers arranged for them to be married. But when Penthurst inherited the dukedom at age 15, he refused to marry her. He found the idea repulsive. For one thing, she was only five. 
 Lydia is described as soulful and reserved but somewhat odd. She considers herself a woman of the world, and in her own way rebels against society's constrictions. She is not particular about fashion and hides her grief behind an expressionless mask. Gambling is her favorite hobby, because it makes her feel free and alive. Penthurst is not particularly spontaneous and takes his responsibilities and position in society seriously. Like Lydia, he is something of an old soul. He is also somewhat old-fashioned and wears frock coats from an older era, instead of the current men's fashion in tailcoats. He is an upstanding gentleman, who believes strongly in honor and loyalty, and treats the women in his family and his personal life with respect. The only scar on his reputation is the duel in which he killed Lydia's brother's best friend, who was also Lydia's first love. 
 As Penthurst and Lydia discover the truth about the duel, they learn the truths in their hearts. They discover that that they are a perfect match and were meant for each other after all. I thought the ending was beautifully written. It is the final love scene in the book. Lydia asks her husband to make love to her. 
 "I want you to fill me. I want to feel you inside my body and my heart and know all the excitement of being in love with my husband." 
 He did as she asked, until they were joined so totally that she felt him in her soul. He moved, then closed his eyes and moved again. "It is perfect, Lydia." 
 It was perfect. She bent her legs to take him in deeper. She opened her heart, and allowed her love to be free and reckless.

 The Vagrant! The title itself is intriguing, begging the question how a fantasy story could revolve around such a person. But then you begin to read the book, and it all becomes so clear that Peter Newman is channeling equal parts Stephen King's The Gunslinger, Peter Ward's The Warded Man, and McCormac's The Road, as The Vagrant mixes the extraordinary elements of each of those books, creating something spectacularly addictive, which not only defies expectations but ignores all presumptions, as it knocks you right on your proverbial ass and drags you to a place you've never experienced quite this way before. 
 As the tale begins, the protagonist walks out of the shimmering heat of the desolate landscape. This mysterious mute a sword-wielding knight of some kind, who is on a quest with a baby and a goat in tow. The three of them traveling across a post-apocalyptic landscape toward the Shining City. Their every step forward dogged by demonic pursuers who have conquered and blighted this once peaceful and beautiful land. The world's dirty carcass infested with the warped remnants of humanity and the slowly deteriorating technology of the time before the demons. The different factions of a huge, demonic host introduced, shown in all their grotesque splendor, their infighting described, and their warping of mankind explored. The ongoing journey of the Vagrant tense and revealing of his true nature. Continual interludes dubbed "Eight Years Before" filling in the background on how the demon infestation began, who the Vagrant really is, why he is carrying a baby along, and where they are determined to go. 
 While this description of the novel might remind many people of other post-apocalyptic novels from the past, what sets The Vagrant apart is Mr. Newman's storytelling style. It is jarring at times, dark and depressing, sad yet joyful, simple but multifarious as well as demanding due to its protagonist, as a reader must search the non-verbal communication of this mute knight to determine his emotions, motives, and innate nature. The lack of dialogue turning from an annoyance at the beginning of the story to a masterful stroke by the end; Mr. Newman able to convey the deepest of sentiments and invoke the strongest of responses with a simplicity of words. The slightest expressions on our knight's face saying more than ten pages of internal monologue ever could. 
 As for the worldbuilding, it is an integral and irreplaceable part of the story. Mr. Newman dropping a reader into the midst of an eerie and unnatural world, then gradually revealing it not a new idea but very effectively done. Each tidbit of information growing upon the other until a complex world begins to take shape. The search for answers to the how and why of this place nearly as compelling as the Vagrant's journey. The demonic forces pursuing his small band even more ominous due to the lack of understanding of exactly why they are after our hero. And the author's slow revelations of all the answers (or, at least, most of them) mesmerizing in its gradual unveiling. 
 While I usually have to weed down my criticisms about a book to a manageable number (Yeah, I'm a hater like that, I suppose.), the only one I really had with The Vagrant was the repetitive nature of some parts of his journey. Naturally, he is moving through a desolate, formidable landscape, which doesn't transform too much from encounter to encounter, but several of his interactions with the demonic forces and with the dredges of humanity felt the same. Definitely, different events were transpiring, but they were so reminiscent in tone and scope to previous scenes that I felt like I was having deja vu. Thankfully, though, this problem did not persist the entire narrative, resolving itself as our hero's journey proceeded into new locales with unique challenges and fresh faces. 
 Reading The Vagrant was one of the more rewarding reading experiences I've had lately. It is a dark, unique, brooding (at times) tale, which still finds a way to incorporate immense beauty (both spiritually and physically) into its narrative. Sure, it was difficult to read, forcing me to keep my attention focused on the briefest of details in order to understand the goings-on of its silent hero, but that made the emotions it evoked deeper and more heartfelt. And, by the end, I found I was cheering for this quiet knight, a baby, a goat, and whatever castoff the Vagrant had picked up now to find some safety and sanity in a world gone mad. Highly recommended!

 I have truly enjoyed this trilogy! The first book was definitely my favorite. They just got more depressing as I read them and I've always been a fan of the "happily ever after." I still loved reading each book to the point that I was giving up sleep in favor of reading just a few more pages.

 Beginning the trilogy with Prim's life being in danger, and having the main character do everything that sparked the rebellion all to save her... only to have Prim die in the end, and spark the ending of the rebellion. Wow. It's really brilliant storytelling, I have to admit that. 
 It's also horribly depressing. It makes me want to read the first book again, just to find that innocence that still existed within both Katniss and Peeta. I feel sad for them, that neither can ever really be fully happy again. Even with each other. Katniss and Peeta still have their own personal issues to deal with. And after everything she did, I kind of hoped Katniss would get something out of it. Respect or fame or something. But instead she was shipped back to a burned out district to live life as an outcast. 
 So while I enjoyed reading all 3 books I'm left feeling, after reading this last book, just a little sad and wistful. I would have loved a happy ending with rainbows and unicorns - especially after all of the crap the characters all went through. 
 Something else that bothered me: I love to read books with strong female characters. In the first book, Katniss was just that. She was strong enough to sacrifice her own life for her sister, to risk death to keep her family from starving, and even strong enough and smart enough to do everything she needed to do to win the Hunger Games. She was awesome - no wonder they chose her as their mockingbird! 
 But by the third book she was a shadow of herself. She was being protected or saved by other people. She constantly being knocked unconscious. She wasn't "allowed" to fight. She was literally crying in closets. 
 She went from being the girl who was on fire to the girl who fizzled out. And that left me feeling sad. 
 I am still glad that I read the books, though, even if I did like the first book the best of all of them.

I loved the first book in this series, An Ember in the Ashes, and finished it in one sitting. That book was fast paced, well-plotted, and gave a good sense of Sabaa Tahir's Rome-inspired world. This book picks up pretty much right where the first one left off, but it didn't have quite the same magic as the first one for me. A Torch Against the Night follows Laia and Elias as they attempt to head to Kauf, a prison where Laia's brother Darin is being held be the Empire. The alternating POVs between Laia and Elias weren't as impactful this time, since they were traveling together for most of the book. Meanwhile, the addition of POVs from Helene, who was named Blood Shrike in the first book, and is reluctantly hunting Elias, lent a bit more interest to the story. 
 One thing that turned me off about this book is that it's incredibly violent, and there are no moments of reprieve for the reader. Something terrible happens every single chapter. It felt like reading A Feast for Crows, which was the book in the A Song of Ice and Fire where there seems like there is no hope for any of the characters, except I enjoy George R.R. Martin's writing a lot more and the world building/political intrigue is much better developed. This book just seemed to focus more on violence to prove that this world was brutal but lacked any political depth to balance out the endless descriptions of women and children being killed. I guess since it is a YA book we were at least spared reading about sexual assault like in a George R.R. Martin book, but the constant violence made it hard for me to get into this story. I don't really want to immerse myself in an ultra-violent fantasy world right now; the real world is scary enough. I found myself skimming towards the second half of the book, especially over the more violent scenes. 
 The reveal at the end of the book was not very well done, either, and I don't think that the magic in the book is ever really explained fully. This book just did not have enough world building or balance to make it live up to the first one for me, and I don't plan to read the third whenever that one comes out.
