 It's a rare, beautiful experience when a book totally catches you off guard and completely exceeded all expectations you had. Of Beauty And Beast was not a book I was particularly excited for, I was only slightly interested in reading it. Despite my skepticism, Of Beauty And Beast was exactly what I needed to read and I am so glad that I picked it up. This is definitely one of my top books of 2013 (so far) and I just can't describe how much of a perfect read it was for me. 
 I have read plenty of retellings in the past, but I've never really enjoyed A Beauty & The Beast retelling for whatever reason. Beastly by Alex Flinn was definitely not the book for me, even though so many readers seem to love it. OBaB succeeds where Beastly failed and brings to the table, a refreshing spin on a classic tale. This is definitely one of the best retellings I've ever read! 
 Isra is a blind princess and she lives in the domed city of Yuan. Every couple of years or so, the city requires a sacrifice to rejuvenate and continue to function normally. A monstrous named Gem is brought to the castle as a prisoner, and slowly Isra and Gem form a bond. Their relationship is completely unconventional and yet, it feels so right for Isra and Gem. Can Isra and Gem manage to save Yuan and their quickly deteriorating world? 
 I started OBaB with the intention of only reading a few pages, but I quickly was immersed in such a beautiful tale of hope and determination. Needless to say, I ended up reading more than a few pages and I was hooked instantly. I ended up reading the book in less than a day due to the addictive nature of the book and Jay's writing style. I didn't want to take a break or do something else, all I wanted to do was find out what happened next in the book. Seriously if you have chores or work to do, don't read this book! You will become so immersed in the story and invested in the characters that you will quickly forget whatever you had to do. Of Beauty And Beast is a perfect pageturner with it's fast-pacing and it's heartbreaking, yet beautiful story. 
 Stacey Jay perfectly explores what it means to be human and the thin line between humans and monsters. This book perfectly captures the essence of the beloved tale and adds in so many new elements to create a tale unlike any other. Gem and Isra's relationship is executed so well and this is YA romance at it's finest. I'll be honest, I usually hate romance in books but I couldn't help but fall in love with Gem and Isra. Romance can make or break a book; in OBaB the romance is one of my favorite aspects. 
 Overall, Of Beauty And Beast is an original retelling filled with a perfect blend of action, adventure, and romance. This is truly an extremely original book and I'd definitely highly, highly recommend reading it! I'm so excited that Jay has another retelling coming out soon and I'm absolutely dying to read it. I haven't read Juliet Immortal or Romeo Redeemed, but after reading OBaB, I'm dying to read both books. I can't praise OBaB enough, it is truly a must-read.

Mitchell is clearly a talented writer. Not only did he manage to create five equally gripping stories set in different locales and time periods and make them a cohesive, thematically-linked narrative, but he managed to write each part in a different tone and style. The choppy, action-based narrative of the Luisa section differs greatly from the letters of Frobisher and especially the first-person history of Zachry, for example. Some writers have a certain style and they write that way all the time - every book they write has the same narrative voice, it seems. And it's fine for some writers to do so (I would be annoyed if Stephen King, for example, dropped his in-your-face, crass, metaphor strewn third-person for an attempt at an 18th century, descriptive prose). Mitchell though, excelled at snatching you from the current story and dropping you into a completely different story, wherein you were instantly immersed in something completely different. 
 Likewise, breaking up the stories was a clever way of structuring the novel - Mitchell could have simply written five novellas and stuck them in a book, but making the reader stop reading one story in order to read another forces the reader to wonder why it was done, and to look for connections. And there's nothing I love more than a book that makes you think! 
 Hell, I can't even choose which story I like the best. It's probably a toss-up between Sonmi and Frobisher. I liked Luisa's story the least, mainly because mysteries like that bore me, and Cavendish's part made me laugh out loud quite a few times. 
 Anyways, I rarely write this much in my review unless I really enjoyed the book, so I totally recommend it to anyone who likes something a little different.

Ambitious and thought-provoking, but also long and at times tedious. I respect the writing craft here, but found it frustrating as a reader to have to constantly redefine Ursula's life and keep the characters' situations straight.

Well, this book has been a roller coaster of emotions. I loved the first book and I can say that I loved the second, can't wait to get my hands on the last one. 
 Regarding the story of this book I can say that I enjoyed it very much. We have two main areas where the narrative takes place, Eretz and Morocco. I found this book more raw and bloody, while the first was basically Karou and Akiva to get to know each other and an introduction to this whole new world. 
 In this second volume we see portrayed wars and battles between angels and chimeras, no mercy and a lot of deaths on both sides, both warriors as innocent people. Whenever I came to the end of a chapter I rested the book on my legs and looked in front of me, seeing nothing, simply stunned by what had just read. There were scenes so intense and so well detailed that stuck with me. There were situations that I was waiting and others that caught me by surprise and it's always so good, that's what makes the difference between a good book and a book that goes directly into the favorite's collection, as is the case of this. 
 Karou is devastated by what happened to her people, with all the memories and all that she sees when back to Eretz she blames herself for everything. I found this part understandable but a bit boring because she spends the whole book to blame her and to blame Akiva. She has to move on and do what has to be done. Thing she makes towards the end and it was another of the surprises that left me astonished. 
 Akiva, my dear Akiva, does he have to suffer even more? He did what he did to Karou's people because he saw them kill her. What he did was an act of revenge, to avenge Karou. If I agree with what he did? Maybe not, or maybe yes. If I understand why he have done? Of course I do. Throughout the book he tries to atone for all the evil that he made to the chimeras, trying to save as many of them as possible. He always tries to help Karou even if she continues to treat him so badly. Karou open your eyes please. 
 Zuzana and Mik are the perfect couple, love the interaction between them and how they get along. She really is Karou best friend. Her demand to find her in Morocco and stay to help in what she could against these new creatures. Zuzana doesn't care about the danger, she does everything to help her friend. It's nice to see a friendship like this one. Without Zuzana I don't know if Karou would remain completely sane. Mik always supports Zuzana's decisions, however crazy that her ideas are. 
 I reached the end so happy, I felt completely filled. I love it when a book makes me feel this way, such a roller coaster of emotions and always putting my heart racing. In the end I just wanted to read a little bit more, because even after reading more than 500 pages, it felt so little. One of my favorite books of all time and one of my favorite authors too.

I was inspired to read Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde on a walking tour of Edinburgh, where the guide pointed out Deacon Brodie's pub, named after a respected man who created a secret life of theft to support his debts which apparently inspired this very tale. It is the Scottish book in my mission to read a book from each country I visit this year. It is set in London, but Robert Louis Stevenson is Scottish so it counts. 
 It is much, much less scary/fun/interesting because we all know the twist already, which is a shame as I'd imagine it would immensely powerful if you didn't know. It is quite short, so it's not as in depth as you might expect, and told in a peculiar mix of reflections of an observer (the lawyer, Mr Utterson) and letters. So it's rather distant from the action. 
 It's interesting to read a novel this old and consider what has changed in fiction... and what hasn't.

Loved the characters, loved the tie-in with the podcast, and I loved the story. 
 Not so fond of the fact that the narration was very Cecil-like, despite not being from Cecil's point of view--which, y'know, seemed to be exacerbated by Cecil Baldwin's narration, which is overall not a bad thing, but I'd love to hear Night Vale from a different voice. 
 Something about the story seemed simplified and rushed near the end. It fit together nicely, but the pacing kind of made the denouement seem less earned than it should have.

 The whole twist of Emily having Isaac's baby was crazy! I sort of guessed it when she was sick in Jamaica but I didn't really put too much stock into it because it kind of got dropped, but holy moly! I wonder what ended up happening to her little girl! 
 Klaudia is an awful girl - I want her gone! Especially because she seems to be playing a trick on everyone with her ditzy nature & fake accent. 
 Spencer and Zach not really hooking up but it appearing that way was unfortunate for both of them - just when Spencer is starting to figure out her place in her family again she 'messes up' and gets blamed for something when nothing actually happened. And I feel really bad for Zach that he was outed and then sent away. 
 That skeezy photographer was really awful - I feel bad for Hanna because he preyed on her need to be accepted. 
 A is just pure evil - just as I think I maybe have an idea who it might be or what might happen next, I realize just how wrong I really am.

** spoiler alert ** 
 What?!? 
 Isla and the Happily Ever After 
 has me feeling a lot of feelings right now. It is, of course, still written in Perkins's cute, fluffy somewhat nonsensical style but... it's different. Not the way 
 Lola and the Boy Next Door 
 was different. In a harder to explain way that doesn't just involve a different set of characters and setting. 
 Isla 
 frustrated me in a lot of ways. It was cute, yes, but it had more substance than Perkins's books usually have. It dealt with insecurities about love and life. It had the same vein of self-discovery that Lola and Anna had but it came across as more annoying. 
 Josh and Isla basically fall in love with each other in a matter of days. It's pretty unbelievable and had me rolling my eyes when they were professing their love left and right when really, they only knew knew each other for a few days. It was a classic Romeo and Juliette type story. 
 I also really disliked the part where Josh gave her the manuscript and basically put his heart on the line so she could see the good and the ugly parts... And all she did was complain and cry about how Rashmi was a huge part of the book and she got eight pages. I understand Isla being upset over it, but really? The majority of Josh's book was written when he was dating Rashmi. He put everything out there--the good and the ugly--and the way she reacted was just horrible. 
 I did really, really enjoy their tender moments, Isla's relationship with Hattie and Kurt and, okay this isn't really part of Isla's story, but seeing Etienne propose to Anna... Swoon! 
 Still five stars. It really seems like I didn't like much about this one, but I did.

I received this book for free in exchange for an honest review. This does not affect my opinion of the book or the content of my review. 
 Armed with a new name former child star Olivia moved to Lucky Harbor with the dual purpose of losing and finding herself. Growing up in Hollywood with all the positives and negatives that comes with that, has lead her to become a very guarded and weary individual. Lying by omission has become her new mantra as friendships and relationships start developing, despite her best efforts. Cole is a native of Lucky Harbor who runs a charter business with two of his bestfriends. A few years ago with the death of a very close friend, secrets came out that his girlfriend and now deceased friend were perhaps not bickering because they didn't like each other. As a consequence, Cole has a very rigid line in the sand when it comes to any untruths. When Cole and Olivia meet chemistry instantly binds them together as past issues lurk to tear them apart. 
 While this is the 11th installment of the Lucky Harbor series I, finally, felt like it was fresh and had something new to offer, something that has been missing in the previous books for me. Even though families and all the issues that come with them was still a large part of this story, as it has been with all the other books in this series, there was energy to He's So Fine that pulled me into the story. The story dives right in (literally) as Olivia and Cole meet right away and produce sparks. They are always front and center and definitely have the chemistry to pull it off. Olivia has a big heart but never veers into sickening sweet and Cole is the everyday man that just so happens to be gorgeous and be able to give MacGyver a run for his money. Let's just say the man has the knowledge and a multitude of tools in his pants that are bound to impress. While Olivia and Cole have lead vastly different lives, they seem to have the same issues, trust, and ultimately are searching for the same thing in life, security with that special someone; this is what makes them work so well as a couple and enjoyable to read about. 
 Past main characters and townspeople (can't leave out Lucille!) are mentioned enough to bring a smile to dedicated fans of the series but not overwhelming enough to confuse any new comers. This is an easy and enjoyable enough read that if you have the time you'll want to read it all in one sitting. The ending wraps up a little too quickly as Cole's PTSD issues with the fire and explosion he was involved in with and Olivia's family drama are never truly resolved. I really liked this couple so maybe this is just me being greedy and wanting more of them. Anyway, I've previously complained that the latter Lucky Harbor books were all starting to run together but am happy to report Ms. Shalvis has stepped up her game again with this one. There is a huge infusion of sweet and sassy into the story and characters that have made He's So Fine one of my favorites of the series. I'm once again watching the calendar for the next installment which will feature Tanner the bad boy ex-Navy SEAL.

"I'll Give You The Sun" reads like an explosion of color and life. The story is about twins and how their past and present mingle to create the future. This story deals with love, family, betrayal, and loss. To use the book's terminology, I burst into flames as I listened to this novel and later transitioned to reading as I simply couldn't get enough of it. 
 Definitely read this. It doesn't matter who you are. Jandy Nelson reaches out and causes the reader's soul to ignite into color and life as you read!

"How do you... we... you know, faeries pollinate?" 
 "The male produces pollen on his hands and when two faeries decide to pollinate, the male reaches into the female's blossom and lets the pollen mix. It's a somewhat delicate process." 
 "Doesn't sound very romantic." 
 "There's nothing romantic about it at all." Tamani replied, a confident smile spreading across his face. "That's what sex is for." 
 "You still...?" She let the question hang. 
 "Sure." 
 "But faeries don't get pregnant?" 
 "Never." Tamani winked. "Pollination is for reproduction- sex is just for fun." 
 yesssss thats what I like to hear. 
 Aprilynne Pike has an interesting imagination.

 I remember reading Charade when it has less than a thousand ratings on Goodreads and look where this story has taken itself to! A huge deal with Hachette and mouth-to-mouth word about Nyrae and her talent. I'm so happy for her since she's an incredible author. I couldn't pass up the opportunity to read Facade since I've been waiting for this pretty forever. Adrian was one of my favorite characters in book 1 and his story touched me in ways I didn't expect. 
 "Your heart beats so strong, I feel it against my chest. You make mine want to catch up, to match the rhythm." 
 The story. Adrian is the kind of guy who, at first sight, seems careless, a typical party-boy who is always high. We saw that he has a sweet, caring side, but its hidden behind a facade. He carries a secret with him that explains all of his behaviour and this is where Delaney comes into play--she's connected to this crushing secret that's destroying Adrian every day more and more. The thing is thoug, Adrian doesn't know Delaney's involvement and it may very well be the thing that destroys any chance they have as a couple. 
 My thoughts. Adrian--my poor baby! I loved him so much in Charade and it pained me to see him waste away his life by being high all the darn time. Having these stupid parties and being with girls, but having incredible pain behind his eyes. I loved his bromance with Colt. I had no idea hidden behind his mask was unimaginable pain. I really thought I had it all figured out since Laney tells us her version of the story, but I couldn't have been a bigger fool! It turned out to be bigger than anything I imagined. It broke my heart and ugly-crying was involved in the healing process. 
 I liked their sweet, light romance which was actually a beginning of a really deep connection neither of them was expecting. I liked how Laney made Adrian work for her attention and time even though she wanted desperately to meet him, tell him how sorry she is for what kind of pain her family has caused him. It broke my heart to watch them open up and make their woonds worse, but I understand that it was necessary in order for them to heal which was beautiful to watch. The thing that maybe bothered me, was that the writing, while strong in general, for me Adrian's point of view was a little too similar to Colt's. It's probably just me though. 
 However much I loved Adrian's story, I liked Colt and Chey's more and I have to stay true to myself so the rating is as it is. 4 stars doesn't take away the meaning and amazingness that is this story which was absolutely stunning and painful. I know that Nyrae loves happy endings so I had no doubt that Adrian and Delaney would find their way to each other. I advise you to pick up Charade asap and if you've already read it, give Adrian's book a try. It was gorgeously haunting!

I just sat down for two hours and read this book. I've always loved the film, ever since I was a young teen and discovered it. It's only now that I've finally read the book, and it was beautiful. It's true, it's honest, it's insightful; I feel like I really understand Susanna, and I loved her voice. I may not have the same thing she was diagnosed with, but I have experienced mental illness and a lot of her psyche involves things that I can on some level relate to. It's beautifully written. I'm not huge on memoirs, but this was special, it reminded me of Plath, it read more like fiction yet it was still so very real. I loved it.

I am usually a big fan of Hornby's humor and writing, particularly his non-fiction and essays, but this novel did not do it for me. I found it less funny and more plodding than most of the other novels. Written almost entirely in dialogue, and covering too much time and ground, this was one of those wide-lens books that just did not ever quite connect to its subjects who themselves were too roughly sketched--each became a caricature much like the television show of the novel. The book felt like an entirely predictable mash-up of research poured into a slapdash manuscript. I think it should have either become a movie script (which he does so well, and which would have taken this rich period into a visual feast of style) or an editor (or agent) should have sent it back and said, "Great First Draft!" (I do wonder if this is a case of an author becoming so well known that editors shrink from the task of letting him know when something does not work.) Oh well, clearly others enjoyed it and I will look forward to the next Hornby to come out.

This novel written for MG, YA or adult audiences, ticks a lot of my favorite boxes. I knew it had a narrator who is autistic. I didn't know that it's set in Upstate New York. It's set before, during, and after a Hurricane like Irene, but it is without Salvage the Bones' bleakness. 
 It's about a girl who only has her dog. Because the story is told from Rose's point of view, it's spare, she's uniquely perceptive, but she's a 5th grader, allowing the adult reader to see more in her situation. It's about love and loss and grief, and about finding support when Rose needs it. I borrowed this amazing book from my public library. Recommended by Jackie Kellachan from The Golden Notebook on WAMC on 12/16/14.

The story was interesting, but the writing got in the way. I've enjoyed other Le Guin books I've read, but this one had far too much exposition and pedantic blather. Word choice was a distraction (e.g. enreddendhuged, ianroundian, hugendly, researchwise, vinyleathers). The characters weren't realistic at all, more like parodies. How this made it off the editor's desk in this state is beyond me. 
 Still... the story was interesting.

What to say? What to say? 
 I liked how Daisy and Matthew's story unfolded. It was written in a way that set this book apart from the past three books. The main difference is that the focus wasn't entirely on Daisy and Matthew. We get a chance to see how the other Wallflowers are doing. 
 The following may be considered spoiler-y. You have been warned! 
 Lillian and Westcliff's side story worked in nicely. I won't say what happened, but it called for everyone (all wallflowers and their significant others) to be present. And not only that, but actually band together as well. What a fun scene all around! 
 However, as far as the individual characters go, I felt like Lillian was a bit too much at times. Actually, in some scenes I felt like she overshadowed the others. Seemed like the character was just trying too hard. I like her intrepid character, but at times it seems it's to a fault and she comes off rather overbearing. Westcliff on the other hand, his contribution to the story only made me like his character even more. I was reminded of his powerful and authoritative nature. I just felt like rooting for him every time he said something. 
 There was something different about Annabel in this book. I'm not sure what it was, but I have come to like her more in this book than when she was the main character. Strange. As for Mr. Hunt, he was quite a treat. His humor--OMG! Only he can pull it off in the way that he does. I love him to bits. 
 Evie is still my favorite character of all time. She proved to be an excellent confidant for Daisy. And dare I say, she is rather sinful in an innocent kind of way. Oh, how I love her! The few scenes that had Evie and Sebastian together just turned me into a puddle of goo. Sebastian alone was made of awesome and win and everything good, soooo good that he's bad. Or in his case would it be the other way around? Is he so bad that he's good? lol 
 And now for the main characters, Daisy and Matthew. I don't see how anyone could fault Daisy in any way. She's just so darn lovable. And Matthew was awesome in every way. The perfect hero. I fell in love with him as soon as he appeared and he did not disappoint. Yayy for him for adoring Daisy right from the start, a nice change indeed. (I mean, heaven forbid that a man would love a woman at first glance /sarcasm) In regards to them being together, I just want to say that these two just BELONG together. The banter. The chemistry. The everything. Again, they just belong together. 
 In regards to the rating, I would actually give this book 4 and 1/2 stars because I felt it ended rather abruptly or like it was just thrown together. It left something to be desired. I don't know. Maybe it is because Devil in Winter just set the bar up too high for me. XD 
 With that said, Scandal in Spring is my second favorite in the Wallflower series. It was very nicely done. 4 and a 1/2 stars for being different, for containing these wonderfully memorable characters, for a mysterious plot that was handled beautifully and for just being a very very good read.

This is the story of the Creepy Clown Lady, later known as Pippa. I really can't tell you much about this novella without spoiling it, so I will just say, this helps brings several pieces together. You find out how Pippa is connected to both Dex and Perry. And how tragic her life was. 
 I did find myself feeling sorry for her and getting angry at her simultaneously. I suppose it is the whole "Hind sight is 20/20" but knowing some of the things I did, and some of the things she did, she continuously made terrible choices. But like I have said before, I don't always have to agree with characters decisions, as long as they are in character. So, she makes decisions that ultimately lead to her death. That is not a spoiler, you should know going into this she is dead. If you don't know that you should not read this yet. 
 While this story does answer several questions, it leaves me with new ones; Did Dex's mom see ghosts? What happened to his dad/mom/brother? Did Dex and Perry actually listen to this story on the tapes? Did they hear it together? What were their reactions? 
 I also want to know what happened to Dex between The Lying Season and On Demon Wings. Hopefully we get to find out in The Dex Files this summer. And maybe Miss Halle will be nice to us and release it early, like she did with Old Blood. :-) 
 OH! And it includes the first two chapters of Into The Hollows. GOOD LORD I cannot wait for that book. Get over yourselves and get together already!!! Ok, better now.

I am a total newbie when it comes to reading fantasy/paranormal. Several things drew me to this book, however: the lovely cover, the premise of a secret Library, Librarians who travel to alternate worlds to obtain unique books, plus personal recommendations from members of the FB group OSRBC. 
 I enjoyed it a lot. Irene is an interesting protagonist. As a junior librarian, she is given a mission and an assistant, and she accepts both. The alternate world she enters is a sort of steampunk version of Victorian London, but it is inhabited by Fae and other supernatural creatures. Furthermore, she runs up against Alderich, an infamous former Librarian who is determined to beat Irene to the book. 
 Irene's assistant, Kai, turns out to be a dragon. His abilities come in handy. Also, Irene and Kai join forces with alternate versions of Sherlock Holmes and Inspector Lestrade. 
 I still have a number of questions about the Library. Looking forward to the next books in the series '

I decided to read this book after everyone had told me it's awesome. I had very high hopes for it, and I was waiting for something life-changing. 
 The book was not life-changing for me, nor was it worth all the hype, at least in my opinion. It was entertaining - once I started it, it was hard to stop reading - but I was a bit let down. There were things that I liked a lot(for example Charlie's relationship with his sister), but then there were things that either annoyed me or just lacked the power to make me care about them. 
 First of all, I couldn't believe Charlie was 15. The narration was extremely naive and I got frustrated with it many times. Still, I managed to like Charlie - I didn't identify myself with him as much as I would have liked to, but he was a nice guy and I wished him well. However, somehow some of his friends came off as phony and annoying - I didn't hate Sam or Bill, for example, but something in them just really irked me. In addition, I disliked the fact that the group was nearly always stoned, smoking, or drinking alcohol, and that being a "wallflower" was seen as something negative. I like to observe, that's the way I live, and I'm extremely happy that way. 
 Still, I think it was interesting to read anecdotes about Charlie's family, for example, and there were a couple of scenes that I really loved and felt my chest ache for (Charlie driving his sister to get an abortion, Brad thanking Charlie for stopping the guys from hurting Patrick, Helen dying when he went to get another present for Charlie) . The end came as a surprise for me but it did made sense, story-wise. I was also really curious to know whether the receiver of the letter really read them and appreciated them, or whether he just threw them in the trash. 
 Most of all I liked the positive note the book had: even though you have bad times, they will pass, because that's the why the life is. There is always something good still to come, and we should all stick around and wait for it. 
 So not the best book I've read, but I still don't regret opening it at all.

I'm sorry but this was one of the worst book I've ever read! 
 The story turns high school drama in to some kind of mob... Maybe if I was some kind of angry teenager I'd like this book a little more... But as it is.. I find this story embarrassingly immature.

These were fun books. 
 Sabriel is pretty much a stand-alone book, but the second two are really one novel - Lirael ends right smack in the middle on a cliffhanger, and Abhorsen starts right where it left off... 
 The trilogy gives us a dual world - one which very strongly resembles Britain in the early twentieth century - and then, across the Wall, the Old Kingdom, a magical land which is currently in a dire state of anarchy and seriously plagued by the Dead - which rise as zombies and make themselves the sort of nuisance that zombies generally do. 
 Sabriel has been raised at a girls' school in Ancelstierre (Britain), but has always been aware that her father is the Abhorsen, a powerful individual with magical influence over the Dead. But when her father disappears, and Sabriel sets out to find him, she realizes that she has never been aware of even half of her father's abilities and duties... duties which are now on her shoulders, as she realizes that more is at stake than merely her father's life... 
 The second story (Lirael/Abhorsen) takes place around 20 years later, and deals mostly with the next generation... of course, things are even worse, plots are afoot to bring about the end of the world, necromancers are causing problems, and our young protagonists, Lirael and Sam, must both discover who they truly are, find their path/calling in life, and, oh, save the world. With the help of the snarky magical cat (?), Mogget, and the Disreputable Dog.

From what I understand, this book was originally published in 1999. How I wish someone had handed 13 year old me this book that year. 
 Well written, naturally flowing, and beautifully sparse, "Speak" should be required reading for all ninth graders. The author completely understands the psyche of that age bracket, and embraces all the craziness and random-ness of the freshman year. 
 Well done.

I am a glutton for punishment. Why do I keep reading these books? Because I just want to know how it ends, but in the meantime the reader is subjected to writing that lacks personality and depth. 
 Will I read the next one? Ask me later. 
 Would I recommend this book? Yes, but with an explicit disclaimer.

I've read every book in this series, and whilst I only really liked the first book and this one, I will continue to read other works by this author because she is such a talented storyteller. To understand this book and appreciate the history between this couple, you need to read all the other previous books in the series. This one takes us back to when Lucy and Cameron first got together at 15. Their story is by far the least angsty and Cameron is such a good, loyal character. I absolutely adore drunk Lucy, she is by far one of my favourite heroines and her drunken tirades are hilarious. Their relationship drama is the kind that you expect for their age group and I just love all of the secondary characters. Looking forward to reading more from this series.

So very Diana Wynne Jones - a world mostly like ours, with unexpected magic, where you're thrown in the deep end trying to sort it all out. I'm not sure I entirely get the logic of the conclusion, but the ride was so entertaining. Fantasy for people who like puzzling things out.

Loved it. Loved the awkward first meeting. Loved Phillip and how clumsy he was one moment and smooth and seductive the next. Loved how Quinn made me like Eloise despite her being a spoiled rich brat who prolly should have given more thought to people around here instead of making her mother worry herself sick 'cause girl just had to escape how boring she felt her life was becoming. I should really have hated Eloise or - at the very least - immensely disliked her, but she had her intelligent moments and seemed to be everything Phillip and his kids needed. 
 It was also nice to see a lot of chemistry between the two main characters - the first since The Duke And I. The others were pretty bland, which was such a surprise especially with Romancing Mister Bridgerton since I loved Penelope and Colin. I just didn't like them as a couple all that much. Have to see if the next Bridgerton book has at least a drop of the sizzle that was in abundance in the Daphne-Simon and Eloise-Phillip books.

Dr Temperance Brennan was suffering from a dreadful cold, so the unexpected call to a meeting first thing Monday was the last thing she felt like going to - but her arrival before 8am at the Law Enforcement Centre in Charlotte was to set a chain of events in progress that would horrify and disgust the most seasoned of them all. 
 On learning that an old adversary, Anique Pomerleau, had resurfaced, Tempe was filled with a feeling of guilt and spine-chilling fear. Pomerleau had been so close to capture years previously, but had slipped the net - Detective Andrew Ryan as well as Tempe had some scars to remember her by. Now she was thought to have made her way to the States where other young female victims were going missing - some whose bodies were found, others who were staying on the Missing Persons list - the Cold Case Unit had many unsolved files... 
 As the investigation picked up the pace, they were frustrated by lack of evidence - there was friction between certain detectives; Tempe found Ryan's attitude difficult to cope with at times; plus she felt she needed to spend more time with her mother. Then suddenly, finally there was a break in the case; but was it? What was happening? Were they headed for a bigger catastrophe than anyone had ever envisioned before? Would they ever catch this cold, calculating killer? 
 I absolutely loved this latest instalment by Kathy Reichs! A brilliant psychological thriller, the twists and turns were intense, each one better than the last. I found it hard to put down, and really enjoyed the unexpectedness of the ending. I have no hesitation in highly recommending Bones Never Lie to all Reichs' fans, and lovers of the genre. 
 With thanks to NetGalley and the publisher for my copy to read and review.

I fell so hard for Ian and Kate in Heart-Shaped Hack and was beyond excited to get an update. I imagined that married life would be a hilarious adventure for the two of them, and I wasn't really wrong. There were definitely scenes that made me laugh out loud (Ian is as cocky and adorable as ever), moments that had me on the edge of my seat, and I found myself thoroughly entertained. 
 What was missing for me in White-Hot Hack was more romance, I think. The love is there--and it is wonderful. The humor. The adventure. All there. But I never really felt the butterflies. The charm of Heart-Shaped Hack was in the pursuit and relationship building. There were times--before things really ramped up in this book--where things felt sort of mundane (in that way marriages get, I suppose). However, what it lacked in romance, it more than made up for in adventure, and the feels came in other ways. Please don't get me wrong--I wasn't disappointed in White-Hot Hack, it just didn't quite give me the same emotional experience that Heart-Shaped Hack did. 
 That said, Ian is still Ian and I freaking LOVE Ian. He's one of my favorite book boyfriends of all time. He's adorable, incorrigible, hilarious and possibly the best husband ever. I am as crazy about him as I ever was. I loved their life together, I loved the adventure pieces in this book, and I love how smartly written it was; it sucked me in and kept me entertained (and for a while, on the edge of my seat) from start to finish. 
 I'm curious and a bit intrigued to know if there will be more to this story. Kate and Ian's story wrapped up beautifully and in a most satisfying manner and yet...there are still some plot points dangling out there (Joshua Morrison? WTF?), which seem to be teasing me that there may be at least one more book in this series. I'd like that, as I've thoroughly enjoyed these two books.  I've always pictured Eibhear as a bigger version of Smallville's Clark Kent (big, gorgeous, bumbling, and sweet). Is that just me? 
 EDIT: Loved it! 3 parts action: 1 part romance - just as it should be with characters who are self-aware and intelligent and who know they just need to get their timing right. Yes, the planet continues to turn while you're waiting for Mr/Ms Right! This world just keeps growing and becoming more fleshed out and even when the characters & gods start to remind me a bit of The Belgariad Boxed Set or some similar series, the fists-to-the-face and the sexy times pull it back from the edge. Izzy is a worthy successor to Annwyl as an action hero and (in a genre where the sequel always features the heroine becoming destructively boy-crazy & getting into a love triangle of some kind) it was refreshing to see Izzy maturing into a woman who knows who & what she wants but isn't going to ruin her life & reputation to get him.

I liked building up the mythology around Molly Metropolis, and what you have to talk about if you're talking about someone that's as incredibly famous as she is, but somehow all the random references to music people were listening to on iPods (like, actual songs) smacked more of fan fiction. I really got into the background of the Situationists, the New Situationists, Mary-Helene, the transit maps--once that got rolling, I got really sucked in, and it was a real page turner. But the end felt flat. The tonal shift to really dark didn't seem to fit, and the epilogue ended my suspension of disbelief. But there was a good story in the middle of that!

She works for Grant, Dane and Cole, all survival specialists, all super built, hot etc. They all live in cabins on the property, so she comes to work in ratty t-shirts and boxers if she pleases. She has tattoos and bright purple bangs. All of this annoys the very serious and tense Grant. Grant lost his wife five years ago and has never re-entered the dating scene. This worries his mother who is always trying to get him set-up - so when she comes to town for a visit, Brenna pretends to be his girlfriend to give Grant a break from matchmaking. Brenna is very forward - so their fake kiss in front of his parents leads to them having sex, more sex...lots of sex. Brenna just wants it to be fun, no-strings attached sex, but Grant has a very difficult time with this. 
 Brenna really made me giggle the first half of this book. She is so blunt and silly. She is a horrible, unprofessional employee and paired with Grant who is so uptight - it made for some humorous situations. Grant has so much pent-up sexual tension that when Brenna pounces on him, he is shocked. Yet so, so dirty in bed. The sex scenes are done well in this book (and very plentiful). 
 I got a little tired of Brenna in the second half of the book. She pushes so hard against any type of long-term intimacy that it drove me a little batty. She lives with almost no possessions and anytime Grant tried to give her something or tried to have a commitment talk, she shut down. It also surprised me that Brenna would not know any details of how Grant's wife died. That seemed really odd to me. I also thought Brenna went way overboard when they hired a new employee, Rome. Basically sexually harassing him on his first day. I'm sure it was set-up to be funny but it seemed to be too much. (on a side note, Rome's book is next and I really want to know his secrets). 
 Overall I liked, but I will warn you that Brenna can be overbearing in this one. It's a sexy book though and I think you all will enjoy Grant.

 My favorite part of this book had to the the multiple discussions on topics like figuring out your sexuality, learning who you are, and a lot more. I know that my very short synopsis in the former paragraph made this book sound sort of shallow, but it really isn't. I just don't want to spoil anything for you guys.

 When I first picked up this graphic novel, the only thought running through my head was IT'S A GRAPHIC NOVEL FORM OF THE TV SERIES GRIMM OH MY GOD I'M SO PUMPED!!! 
 Turns out this was nothing like the tv series Grimm, but I still loved every bit of it anyway. 
 First of all, the backstory of the "Fables" is ingenious! Basically, all the fairy tales and magical creatures were living somewhat happily but divided in their "Homeland," but then this mysterious enemy called "The Adversary" came and picked them all off one by one. The few who survived created "Fabletown" and the "Farm" in the human world so that they could all live peacefully away from The Adversary, and that's where they've been for centuries. Now, we follow the Big Bad (reformed) Wolf and Snow White as they try to figure out all the crazy mystery, crime and drama that happens among the magical people in Fabletown and the Farm. 
 The artwork in this volume is simply stunning. Every character is expertly drawn and colored, and in a way that makes their features realistic and expressions relatable. In my opinion, the best parts about the art were the accents, borders and backgrounds because they really set the stage for a fairy tale-esque story. Well, a really twisted fairy tale-esque story. 
 Which brings me to the lovely characters. Right from the beginning, every character completely blew away any assumptions I had going into this book. Actually, I was really imagining something dark and Grimm-like and some standard princesses, princes, creatures, etc. before diving in, so I was pleasantly surprised by how bright and lively the characters and panels were. I loved how a lot of the most well-known fairy tale characters had very unexpected personalities like Prince Charming is a poor womanizer who sponged off of every girl he met then slept with while Snow White is the assistant deputy mayor. I also loved reading about how the magical-ness of pairings like the Beauty and the Beast translated to their actual physical appearances and feelings and such. 
 Definitely a must read! I recommend the first volume of Fables to lovers of suspense, scandals and badass fairy tales. 4.5

On June 14, 1941 Lina Viklas is taken by the Soviet secret police. Along with her mother and her younger brother, Jonas, Lina is forced to leave her home in the middle of the night to board a train to be deported from Lithuania with thousands like her. 
 As they are taken farther and farther from Lithuania, all hope seems lost. Lina's father has been separated from the family to be sent to a prison camp. Lina's dreams of one day attending art school or falling in love are dashed. With nothing but the clothes on their back and a few precious possessions, how can they survive? Will help ever come? 
 Refusing to lose her sense of self along with everything else, Lina clings to what she does have: her memories and her art. While dreaming of her past, Lina uses her talents to document the atrocities she and the other deportees are forced to endure. Lina may be far from everything she once knew, but she will survive. Any other options are too horrible in Between Shades of Gray by Ruta Sepetys. 
 Between Shades of Gray is Sepetys' first novel. It was also a finalist in the 2011 Cybils for Young Adult Fiction which is how I came to read it. Since its publication Between Shades of Gray has garnered a fair amount of accolades and even critical acclaim in the form of a finalist spot for the 2012 William C. Morris YA Debut Award. 
 Sepetys, herself a daughter of a Lithuanian refugee, brings light to one of history's darker (not to mention lesser known) moments when the nations of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia disappeared from maps in 1941 as thousands were deported and sent to labor camps and prisons. These countries did not reappear until 1990. 
 Because of its content and its deft negotiation of this bleak subject matter, there is no doubt that Between Shades of Gray is an important, valuable book. It will undoubtedly be added to many history class curiculums and will raise awareness about Stalin's cleansing of the Baltic region. 
 Unfortunately, being an important book does not make Between Shades of Gray a book without its flaws. 
 Both the story and its narrator, Lina, are difficult to connect with. The story has a linear narrative of Lina's journey with the other deportees interspersed with flashbacks and memories of Lina's old life in Lithuania. While the memories illustrate all that Lina has lost, they also appear abruptly and at little to the plot's forward momentum. The ending is similarly abrupt not only having a a fifty-four year gap between the last chapter and the epilogue but also a gaping hole in terms of what happened to many of the characters. 
 Although Lina becomes a strong character as the story progresses, she spends much of the novel as a petulant girl who enjoys rash behavior and jumping to conclusions with little to no evidence to support any of her seemingly random assumptions. 
 So much emphasis is placed on Lina's art but the book as a whole provides very little payoff in that department. Granted, Between Shades of Gray isn't that type of book but I can't help but wish that readers had been able to see Lina's actual drawings after hearing so much about them.* If any book could have benefited from illustrations to add another dimension to the story, it's this one.** 
 Between Shades of Gray is already a beloved book for a lot of readers. It will likely reach many more. The story and the characters are brimming with a potential that, in a lot of ways, was not fully realized. While Sepetys has created a story with many beautiful, compelling, important parts the sum of those parts never quite added up to a flawless read. 
 *Or at least to see a little more about what happened to some of the drawings Lina sent out into the world. 
 **Seriously, after you read the book, think about it for a second. How cool would that have been?!

As a novel of ideas, this is quite good. Genetic engineering allows the creation of children who do not sleep (or, it turns out, age, once they have attained adulthood). Somewhat implausibly, (almost) all the Sleepless are super-cool, rational, serious geniuses. (Implausibly, because there are already many people who need much less sleep than the rest of us slobs, just three or four hours a night, and they are not half-way between us eight-hourers and the Sleepless of this book. Still...) Their advantages open up a serious gap between them and Sleepers. The book uses this set-up to explore the limits of community, the individual and her relation to others, what the strong owe to the weak (the beggars in Spain, in one character's little speech), and so on. 
 This is well-done because Kress throws into the mix the presence of a philosophy, Yagaiism, that seems like a spiritualized version of Randian libertarianism. Many of the Sleepless are Yagaiists, especially at first, but not all, and there are Sleeper Yagaiists. In addition, the Sleepless end up creating a generation of supersmart, further genetically altered children, and find themselves in the role of 'beggars' to their own creations . All these cross-cutting currents make the novel quite 'crunchy' in texture; realistically rough and confusing and not neat. 
 However, as a novel about people, the work is rather plodding. The main characters are quite wooden and never really come alive. It's hard to feel much about them one way or another. However, much of the (sporadic) action is driven by the characters' psychological dramas. Consequently, the whole book was somewhat dull.

I really enjoyed this. It's highly readable with interesting characters, but what really grabbed me were all the interesting ideas. Nothing is clear cut in Uglies. While Tally and the Smokies are the protagonists, there are still a lot of ethical grey areas in their world. What kinds of sacrifices are acceptable for peace? And if the Smokies get what they want, what might be the ramifications? Nothing is absolutely good or bad, right or wrong, and that makes for a truly engaging read.

The first half of this book was exciting, suspenseful, and fun. The second half of the book slowed way down, and it pissed me off a little bit. 
 I understand that sometimes to keep the story fair, and to move it along, characters have to die. It's just not fair to force me to learn so much about the characters and then kill them off at the last minute  
 Like some movies, I think you could've cut about 200 pages from the book and been good. I rarely think this about books, but this one could've been shorter. The extra exposition really didn't add anything to it for me, and most of the time I was impatient to get back to the rising action. 
 Overall, it's not a bad book about vampires, especially if you're tired of the sparkly "Twilight" brand or emo "Interview" brands. If you want vampires that you can, if you'll pardon the pun, "Sink your teeth into", then it's not a bad read. It just needs to be a little shorter.

Well, I see that I'm in the minority here because most readers absolutely rave about this book. But I found it tiresome and tedious. While the dialogue and "flash-speak" may have been authentic to the setting, it seemed to me to be trying too hard. It made listening to the audiobook difficult because I don't speak that slang, so figuring out what a "kinchin" is, for example, was what I found tedious. I also didn't really warm to the characters or buy into the love interest angle. It's odd, because I do find this time period interesting. Maybe it just didn't suit my mood. I really wanted to like it, but meh.
Not sure what to say about this book that has not been said before, but it's a very decent old school fantasy every fantasy fan should read.

How to search for true love? 
 One could hope that a parcel, containing directions to find one's soulmate, fall off from heaven. But unfortunately, that is highly unlikely. There is no easy way to find the one. 
 And for Eloise Bridgerton, the search was definitely not easy. She endured a number of seasons only to accustom herself to a few years of spinsterhood. She refused six offers of marriage just to wait for her own epic romance of cosmic proportions. 
 And all it took was a simple correspondence to find him. This is an old school starting from penpals love story. With just a few letters spread throughout the years, Eloise has managed to find the one destined for her. They say that when you see the one, you just instantly know. But does it really happen that way? Since in Eloise's case, that certainly didn't happen. 
 Sir Phillip's last letter ended with a marriage proposal of sorts, where he was asking Eloise to spend a fortnight at his home, with a chaperon of course, to see if they would suit. But Eloise, hastily ran away to search for her destiny. She already imagined Sir Phillip to be immediately on his knees as soon as he sees her and propose his undying love for her. 
 Well, that was far from what actually happened. It was miles and eons apart from her imaginings. Sir Phillip just stood there, and it was awkward. 
 But somewhere along the way, love just happened. She didn't instantly know, but she knew that love must be it. Love must be what she had with Sir Phillip. 
 To Sir Phillip, With Love, is a fantastic and exquisite tale of finding true love and having it in the end. As usual, it's also absolutely hilarious and wonderfully touching. 
 And I have to say, what I feel for Julia Quinn's novels is love at it's very best.

When I started reading this, I wasn't sure I would like it as I tend to like a bit more story but I ending up loving it. I've been battling my way through "50 Shades of Grey" and I was worried this would be the same sort of thing but it differs in some important ways. Yes, the dominant/submissive thing is important in this story but there is love too, and feelings. It's not so clinical. I usually love Lora Leigh but the stories of her I have read have had more plot to them. This one was really just about the sex and the underlying love, but very enjoyable

This book was... slow. It didn't get interesting until over two hundred pages in. I thought it was kind of unnecessary, or could have been a little more... well thought out. I still like it, and am moving on to the third book in the series now.

*May contain spoilers* 
 I loved this short story. It gives us an insight into the struggles of Lena's mum, Annabell both during her time in the Crypts and during her adolescence. We are given insights into her rebellion from a young age and the inevitability of her marriage to Conrad Haloway. It was beautifully written allowing us to completely sympathise with her. She also grew up in a family that were entirely void of feeling and felt more embarrassment than concern at her leaving home. It's interesting to be able to draw parallels between the life of Annabel and Lena. 
 'But from the beginning, I knew that in a world where destiny was dead, I was destined, forever, to love him. Even though he didn't - though he couldn't - ever love me back.' 
 The only thing I wish that this short story had also shown was the several procedure attempts rather than just the one. It would have been interesting to read how Annabel handled this, and how she coped throughout her marriage. She was one of the lucky ones, finding and being matched to a man that she loves - even though he cannot 100% love her back.I would love to have read more about their relationship and to see how they react around each other. It suggests that Conrad was more than your usual Zombie - I wonder if his cure had messed up slightly too? 
 All in all, an insightful and enjoyable read and I'm looking forward to reading Hana and Raven!

2,5/5 
 I am not all that familiar with revenants, to be honest. In fact Amy Plum's debut novel Die For Me is the first book I read about them. Revenants, as described in DFM, are people who had died saving someone else, which means they had sacrificed themselves. Now they are dead and immortal, feeling the urge, the "compulsion" as they call it, to spend their immortal lives dying for other people, hence the title. 
 The revenant story and their arch enemies, the numa, along with the beautiful setting in Paris, were the best aspects of the book for me. I just wish they didn't keep calling the revenants "zombies". Why zombies? Because they are dead? Vampires are also dead but we don't call them zombies. Yes, vampires drink blood. But zombies eat human flesh, last time I checked, and thank God revenants did no such thing! So why call them zombies? I still don't get it... 
 Characters were OK enough I guess, but nothing extraordinary. I didn't detect strong personalities on either of them. Nor weak, for that matter. They were just meh, mediocre. Vincent, I never quite saw his God-like looks because I felt he was never described clearly and the same goes for Kate. 
 The best part of the book for me was when Vincent and Kate spent some time apart because Kate decided that she just can't handle the whole revenant thing. It was believable and honestly, an anticipated human reaction to hearing of people who cannot die! Unfortunately, as the story is told from Kate's POV, only her personality got to shine just a tiny bit when they were apart but alas, not Vincent's. As for the ending scene with the romantic date and the boat and all that, I don't know. Maybe I am getting old and grumpy because I thought it was way sappy for my taste. 
 All in all, if Die For Me took place in the US, it would have been like every other YA paranormal romance I've read. There is nothing in it that made it stand out from the other books of this genre. However, it isn't set in the US. It's set in Paris, which at least gave it an edge. Character-wise though, it just didn't do it for me. 
 Recommended to ages 13-15.

 "He makes me come three times, and I try to commit every second to memory because soon, memories may be all I have of him." 
 How far will you go to protect your sister? Will you be able to steal? Lie? Sell your body? In Brenda Rothert's latest new release, His, Brenda brings forth these question into light. When it comes to surviving and having food in the stomach, can a young woman sell her body for $500 for one night? But what happens when one night is not enough and he offers you safety, a home, money, and protection as long as you become his? 
 "I take his face in my hands and kiss him, trying to tell him without words how much he means to me." 
 Homeless. Cold. Hungry. And then toss in the fact, that Quinn and her sister are living on the streets and are on the run. They don't want to be found. And in desperate need for money in order to survive, Quinn agrees to one night with a stranger. 
 "Quinn broke down my walls, and I never want to put them back up" 
 When Quinn appears, Andrew is immediately drawn to Quinn's beauty, innocence, and personality. You could say a broken person could recognize another broken person. And for the first time, Andrew wants to be more than just a one night stand for Quinn as he gets to know her. He knows that she is hiding and running for something and so he makes her another offer. An offer to stay with him and be with him. When he Quinn accepts the money in order to help her sister, Quinn begins to see Andrew in a whole new light. This enigma of a man is more than his looks and wealth, and soon Quinn begins to slowly crack Andrew's armor. 
 As Quinn and Andrew begin to spend more time with each other, their past and secrets begins to be slowly unpeeled. Layers of truth and raw vulnerability begins to get exposed. And soon deep feelings for one another begins to surface. But what happens when this was suppose to be only temporary, can Quinn trust Andrew and give her heart to him? Will Quinn let Andrew protect her once he discovers why she is on the run? 
 "I've gone from my lowest point to my highest in a matter of months. From feeling forlorn about the future to feeling hopeful about it. My Prince Charming isn't always sweet, and he's still learning how to love. But he's mine, I'm his, and I wouldn't change a thing." 
 Brenda Rothert tackles a modern version of Pretty Woman with a deeper poignant, raw, and gritty emotional storyline. Ms. Rothert allows her readers to feel for her characters as she stripped them bare allowing readers to see that two broken individuals can find the love that they have been searching for. With Rothert's emotional and touching story line, she flawlessly brings these characters to life highlighting every mistake, imperfections, vulnerability, and most importantly how far will one go to sacrifice for love. So if you are looking for a story where two broken people in a city of millions get their fairy tale ending that they truly deserves, then be prepared to get swept away and become His. 
 Review can also be found on Four Chicks Flipping Pages: http://fourchicksflippingpages.weebly...Brenda Rothert

This was such a wonderful book! The author had a very distinct style which included beautiful details and rich descriptions that brought to life an exotic, magical, and dangerous world. This was definitely different from anything I have read lately, and I loved it! 
 The story certainly took a lot of twists and turns, and it wasn't something you could follow easily if you weren't paying attention. However, I think that made the story all the more enjoyable. The myriad of characters and their complicated relationships greatly enhanced the reading experience. Although, I have to admit, there was definitely a learning curve when it came to the names and terms used in this book. (Just check out that giant glossary!) However, I'm really glad that they were used because it gave the story a very authentic feel. 
 As far as the characters go, Shahrzad was definitely a feisty and independent heroine, my favorite kind! However, this book also shifts the point of view to other characters throughout the book so that the reader can get a more complete picture of the story. By the end, I really came to care about all of the characters, especially Jalal! Although Tariq did get on my nerves a bit... And of course I loved the mysterious and sexy Khalid. 
 Speaking of Khalid, there were definitely a fair share of steamy scenes in this book! The passion between Shahrzad and Khalid was off the charts! I loved their interactions, even the simple ones. I am very eager to read the next book because I need for them to have the happiest of endings. 
 Overall, this book was a real treat to read. It stands out in the YA genre for its culturally rich story and it was truly beautifully written. Shahrzad and Khalid were characters I loved getting to know and can't wait to read more about in the next book. In short, this book definitely deserves its hype and I recommend it everyone!

The writing here is beautiful, much like Maas' Throne of Glass series. I also enjoyed the twining of Beauty and the Beast into a faerie filled world; it works seamlessly. My only reservations are with the grown up language, sexy content, and rich violence. I'll probably handsell this mostly to our older teens, and let the younger ones find it on their own. It's a great fit for those looking for an EPIC romance though. Also: LUCIEN. He is my FAVORITE. I just re-read Lish McBride's Firebug, and he reminds me a fair amount of Ezra. Foxy, you guys.

If you read Brandon Sanderson's Mistborn Trilogy Boxed Set, then you may want to continue on with this one, too. The story is set many years later, to a time when the characters in the Mistborn Trilogy are legendary heroes. The same magical properties of certain metals apply. A different type of story begins--it seems like this is probably going to be the first book in a new series, as there are some loose threads left dangling. 
 The story is almost like a Western; a lawman hero in the rural areas comes back to the city to bring his house in order. But, he just cannot shake off his proclivities to act as a vigilante as a shocking crime wave overtakes the city. 
 My favorite character is not the main protagonist, but his sidekick, Wayne. Wayne has a wonderful personality that just makes me wish I were his friend. The back-and-forth banter between the two characters is engaging, and really makes the story readable. 
 This is a fun book, set in a somewhat strange society where horse-and-buggy days are just about over. I give it a thumbs up! 
 I didn't read this book; I listened to the audiobook. Michael Kramer is the narrator, and his reading is simply fantastic. If you can, listen to the audiobook--it is definitely a treat!

I gave up on this book after 60 pages. I got it for the Vaginal Fantasy Hangout's alt pick for November 2012. Luckily, my library had it. It just wasn't my thing. So I put it down and read the other two I'd gotten from the library. But before I took them back, I decided I'd give it another shot. I'm glad I did, even though I didn't love this one. I did end up liking it. I won't read any more in the series, but I did like it.

***** 4 'Living for Me' Stars ***** 
 Can be read as a standalone. 
 No Falling Allowed is a quick sweet read. Although you'll see some of the characters from Book 1, this can be read as a standalone. 
 Grace Soaring is a woman that just wants to be seen as a normal person. Some people feel nervous and intimidated around her because she is the daughter of one of the richest men alive. Think of her as Bill Gate's daughter. 
 When Noah visits NYC to take a break from life, he flirts and challenges Grace. He doesn't know who she is. He just see's a beautiful woman that knows what she wants. 
 They have one beautiful night together, but he needs to go back to his country town. Cricket Creek. 
 Grace's parents doesn't see the point of her being an event planner. They call it a hobby. This leads to her getting cutoff from her elite credit cards and full bank accounts, which also drives her to work harder. 
 When she gets a job to plan a wedding, she ends up in the same town as Noah. Sparks fly, but can they have to overcome their differences? 
 I really enjoyed this story, and I can't wait for the next book.

I really wanted to love this, given how much I enjoyed The Devil in the White City, but this one didn't just click for me. I did have to finish the last hundred pages or show in a rush, because I really wanted to know how it came out, but I was really only invested in one of the two main plotlines. I found Crippen's story much more compelling than Marconi's, and I found myself skimming Marconi's chapters to get back to Crippen. Also, Larson employed a lot of non-linear storytelling, which isn't exactly new for him, but it seemed way worse this time. I had trouble following the timeline at points. Perhaps because he knew he was jumping around and was trying to keep the suspense going, he kept using some very heavy-handed foreshadowing, and spent at least 2/3 of the book ending virtually every chapter, and sometimes every scene, with some variant of "And this would prove disastrous in the future," or "This did not seem important at the time, but later would be critical." Because he kept the majority of the action until the last third of the book, the first two thirds made me crazy. WHAT? What would prove critical? Why would it be disastrous? It wasn't suspenseful, it was frustrating. 
 None of that is to say that I didn't enjoy the book overall. I really enjoy Larson's writing style in general, the above flaws notwithstanding, and I as usual he made an event in history that I knew little about come alive. I don't know how I didn't know about this Crippen murder before; it's the kind of thing that I am very interested in. Also, I enjoy how the book kind of leaves the question open as to what happened to Cora--whether Crippen actually killed her, and how, and whether he was on his own when he did it. I think there are just too many unanswered questions to say for sure, and I find myself not entirely convinced that he did do it, although there really isn't another explanation. That was a truly compelling element to the story, and Larson told it well. Again, I overall enjoyed it, I just thought there were some structural weaknesses in how the plot was developed that caused it problems it didn't need to have.

Cat and Bones have had a very rough time of it lately and while they have come out on top in the last few battles, there still were loved ones lost and irreparable consequences. In this latest installment, Cat is still coming to terms with her new, mostly pulse-less status. She was unique as a half vampire, so it makes sense she wouldn't be a normal full one either. However, this spells trouble as a nasty Ghoul is using the threat of the "Red Reaper" to incite a war between the Vampires and Ghouls. They must scramble to round up their allies as well as try and find away to stop the war that could destroy them all. They seek out the help of Majestic, the Queen of New Orleans. The biggest question is not whether or not they will get her support, but if they will survive her "help" if she gives it, because one never knows just what the VooDoo Queen may have up her sleeve. 
 Cat has really had just about all she can take of dangers and threats to herself and her loved ones. So when her "borrowed" powers start causing her problems she scrambles to find a way to tone them down. She tells Bones that she isn't meant to handle them since she isn't a master vampire. This may be true, but when push comes to shove, she will do whatever it takes when her loved ones are at risk, even if it means using powers that wreak havoc and completely overwhelm her. However, I think most of her problems with the powers is that when she tries to use them, she over thinks it, as well as refuses to accept them as her own. Granted, they are only borrowed, but until they wear off, they belong to her, and I think if she could learn to accept them, she just might surprise herself. 
 I was so thrilled to see Cat and Bones fully together in this book. Their separation in the previous book was very hard to bear and they are by far my favorite fictional couple. In this book it seems they are closer than ever, and Cat is really trying to not repeat the mistakes of her past. Every time she has the inclination to run off on her own to try and save the day, she stops and takes a moment to talk herself out of it. She finally has come to terms with the fact that where she goes, Bones will, and no matter how much she may want to protect him, he will always be there at her side whenever danger strikes. Bones has even made some major strides in accepting that she will always have to be hip deep in the action and that he can't keep her on the sidelines either. I'm sure there will always be some tension between them as they are both extremely strong willed, but in the end they could not be more perfect for one another. 
 Since this is my favorite series, there always is the fear that the latest book will not live up to my admittedly high expectations. However, after reading this book I realized my fear was completely unnecessary, as this book was every bit as good as its predecessors. Be prepared for plenty of high stakes, heart pounding action, and plenty of steaminess. The book was jammed packed with emotions, and the ending will leave a smile on your face. Fans of the series will not be disappointed. If you haven't checked out this series yet, you don't know what you are missing.

 I have a confession, please don't scold me. 
 I saw the movie before I read the book... 
 Also, this review is 3.5 stars... 
 Reading this was sort of like reading Philosopher's Stone for the first time, it's exciting, intended for younger eyes and an easy read but it didn't hook me instantly (I am still in love with Harry Potter, easy 6 solid gold stars). It did however, give the impression that, it's going to be similar to Harry Potter in that, the next few books will feel older and the plot will develop into something amazing! 
 I loved Percy, Annabeth and Grover (Though I kept picturing him as a blue muppet, rather than a goat) and I really loved how everything fell in place! Although it's basically just 12 year olds on one massive road trip, it was exciting and the pace was brilliant. 
 The characterisation was just right for me too, I loved Percy because every 12 year old boy with behaviour issues that I know, acts like Percy! I felt so incredibly protective of him, he was so young, naive and stubborn, every time I knew he was going to get into trouble or run into something/someone dangerous, I wanted to guide him through it and help him! But Percy always managed to pull through, he was strong willed and determined to do the right thing and help. Rick Riordan was incredibly successful in creating a loveable 12 year old boy! (Harry Potter still holds the key to my literary heart though!) The fact that ADHD and Dyslexia was portrayed as a good thing in these books left me astonished, I still can't get over it! I think it's so great that somebody has finally turned around to the world and said "screw you" and made these so called 'bad things' into something unique and great! I love that demi-gods are dyslexic and I love that they have ADHD and I love that this is an advantage to them! Too often in books, we see things like these portrayed in the antagonist or as a major flaw in the protagonist and it was refreshing to see it portrayed in a different light for a change! I could go on about this for ages but simply put, I was impressed :) 
 The way the Greek Gods were portrayed was awesome. I've always loved Greek mythology but as it turns out, I have forgotten alot of information! So it was refreshing to read a book about a topic and have it turn out to be fairly accurate, seriously people, how often do you get accurate mythology is 90% of YA-novels? I felt Riordan gave each of the Gods great defining characteristics that weren't necessarily cliche except for Poseidon wearing a freaking Hawaiian shirt or something? - That is my work uniform :|  but they had definite personalities, although they were still Gods and therefore Godlike. 
 As for setting, it annoys me that the centre of the world is America. It annoyed me that the Greek Gods were in America (although this is roughly explained) and that pretty much everything is based in New York. One major thing that irked me was when Percy said that Persephone really did control the seasons by saying that when she was in the Underworld it was winter, and when she was above ground it was Summer. Sorry, but where does the other side of the world come into this? So, at the time of writing this, it'll be winter in America, so it's summer in Australia (YAY!!!), but according to this we are in winter still. Ahh! Rant over :) 
 The setting of the Underworld however, fascinated me! When I read about "Hades" in 'Hades', I wanted to punch the author in the face, when I read about the Underworld by the REAL HADES, I was so happy! I'm glad it wasn't just portrayed as Hell with the burning and destroying, blah blah blah, there were GOOD places in the Underworld too! Which makes sense! YAY FOR COMMON KNOWLEDGE :D 
 Overall, I thought this was great! I didn't love it, but I enjoyed it and will definitely read the others (plus I just got the boxset *dances*) and I have a feeling that because of the ending of this which was AWESOME, the other books will just get better and better :) Also, I have a thought I may turn into a fangirl of this series, but we'll see :)

I am really going to have a hard time rating this one. This is another young girl/older man romance which I knew going into. However, the dynamic between Danny and Ripper is a tough one to root for. I was okay with the men of the club being who and what they are all of the way until the end of the book when a few of them do something collectively with the full endorsement of Deuce (Club president) and a few other brothers, that as a woman, I just can't justify, rationalize, or accept in any way. Even though I own the next two books in the series, I am walking away from these. I just can't after what happened to an admittedly mean spirited and blood thirsty female character. I really just can't, which means I am most definitely not the target audience for these types of scenes. Full review later.

The Girl on the Train by Paula Hawkins tells the tale of a young woman's murder, in the voice of 3 of the characters, one of whom is the murdered girl. 
 I know this book was hyped up, and is soon to be a movie, but I struggled with the first half....probably didn't help that I kept putting it down to read something more interesting. Initially it was very confusing because the girl on the train is an alcoholic, who made up names for the people she saw, so we had additional characters that didn't really exist.
