Finally Percy stops being a Seaweed Brain and makes the right desicion. What would you have choosen? I would have tooken immortality in a heart beat. 4.5 STARS (closer to 5)

I didn't have many problems with the book as a whole besides choppy sentences and I wish some of the characters were fleshed out a little more. Other than that I had a blast with this adventure. I cannot wait to buy it for my collection and to read the next one when it comes out.

Don't let the cover art fool you! This is a smart, thoughtful, and highly enjoyable fairy tale. Although the main character is thirteen, she's a medieval thirteen--old enough to be apprenticed, to have survived wars and famines and make her own plans for the future. Reveka wants nothing more than to be an herbalist, and has the perception, curiosity, and logical frame of mind to become a good one. With her as the main character, and a well-researched, fully-grounded medieval Europe as the context, the legends of the Twelve Dancing Princesses, Beauty and the Beast, and Hades and Persephone all become a seemless, fascinating whole.

Shards of Hope by Nalini Singh. This paranormal has two assassin psys on the run who have no hope of life and so cling to each other all the more tighter. The heroine, Zaira, and my favorite hero in the series, Aden, are so perfect together. There's raw chemistry and emotions and a ton of action (triple threat!). Nalini is in my top five favorite authors, and I have already pre-ordered the audiobook.

 How did you choose your couple this time? 
 Nalini: I always knew these two would be the final couple in the first arc of the series. It couldn't be anyone else. But I didn't force it -- Aden and Zaira were ready. It's their time. 
 Tell us about Aden... I love Aden! 
 Nalini: Aden is a true leader. He'll go into hell itself for his people, and he will never, ever leave an Arrow behind. No matter what.

Enjoyable, but nothing amazing. Light read. 
 The issue I have is the last two books in the series is nothing like the first two. Book three (Luke's) is the conclusion of the big plot we saw in the first books. Very underwhelming. Ended really odd and quickly. It doesn't make sense to me. 
 Killian and Luke literally has the same plot. Girl owns successful business, has a little girl with a crimial ex (who isn't in the picture), guy helps girl with business. Girl is mad at guy from first meet even though they are both in instant lust. 
 I did enjoy the series for the most part.
Very very low-angst-high-cozyness factor in this one. It was a nice edition to the 'Scoring Chances' series, and I liked that nothing crazy or over-the-top-drama took place.

I grabbed this kind of at random. After reading the description... 
 When I started it was dull. Takes place in high school. Yuck! That can be a hard sell for me. Gave it a chance anyway, I'm cool like that. Then the character was all whining about his life and how he's such a freak. Yadda, yadda! Kept with it. Can't figure why. 
 During all the whining about his life we get gallons of angst. About a third of the way through I was eyeing the fridge door for a nice brain scratching. *que quite riot, bang your head* 
 Last quarter got a lot better. As in, something actually happened. Unfortunately, does not make up for the crimes that took place before the turning point.

Absolutely loved this book!!! I guessed the twist but that didn't detract from the story at all. The sexual banter and lead up to the sex was so freaking hot, that the actual sex scenes nearly paled in comparison... nearly LOL What a fantastic read!!!

Re-Read May 2017: This story will never be less than 5 stars for me. I love all my precious broken babies. 
 NOBODY TOUCH ME RIGHT NOW. 
 This book is perfection. Kaz, Inej, Jesper, Matthias, Wylan and Nina are perfection. Leigh Bardugo is perfection. Even the acknowledgements made me cry. That's just rude. 
 I'm going to go look at all the fangirl merch now. Maybe get a tattoo. You know, the normal reaction to finishing a series.

My recommendation would be to re-read the first two books and then dive into this book. (If you haven't read this series then go do it!) My reason being is Jodi, reacquaints us with all the characters that existed in book 1 and 2. Reacquaints isn't actually the right word. You get to know them on a more personal-ish level. Just to name a few, Sam, Kate, Dan, Coral, Mikael, Ruth Quinn, Sarah, John, etc. Every character is presented with a little bit of their own history and their relationship with either Ava or Jesse. With that being said... 
 I'm floating on Central Jesse Cloud Nine and I don't want to get off. After impatiently waiting several months to read it, this book does not disappoint. This final book has met all of my expectations and more. Who knew that The Lord of the Manor had so many secrets and such a tragic history? He knew it was time to confessed (ie, the pills, the drinking, the women, etc.) and be redeemed if he wanted a life with Ava. 
 In this book, you get to see a different side of Jesse that you don't see in the first two books. His reasons (confessions) behind why he's the way he is. You get to experience what normal is for Jesse and Ava. As always his love for her is intense, at times suffocating and quite honestly borderline unhealthy but at the end of the day, he just genuine love and care for her and just wants her safe. 
 I can honestly say Ava grew on me. I felt her frustrations with Jesse and can understand why she had some reckless moments. Given if it was me, I'd probably have more reckless moments than she did. 
 Before I end this review, let me just touch up on The Ava Wall. That part was one of my favorites to read. The notes that were written next to the pictures, you must read the book to read the notes. No spoiler will be revealed. 
 Jodi, did such an AMAZING job writing this 3rd installment to the "This Man" series. The plot, OMG! The plot! I wasn't expecting it at all!!! It is truly the cause to why Jesse confessed. This book is a MUST READ and deserves more than 5 stars. End of. 
 This Man Confessed 
 Jodi Ellen Malpas 
 P.S. This book has an Epilogue you don't want to miss :) Happy reading everyone!

A little background on how I read this. Yes, How I read this. My husband and I just started to travel with his dads bridge inspection company because he wants us to take over soon so he can retire. Our first jobs are flagging and for almost a month, we have been working in Alaska. Well on those cold as all holy hell days with no cars coming by for hours, we can either sing the entire soundtrack to "Frozen" to ourselves or do things on our phone....or both. After much work I finally found a copy of the book in which I promptly added to my phone. In between far and few cars...I read this with so much eagerness and it did not let down. 
 From the first two chapters I was hooked. I was drawn in honestly by the odd coincidences between Andrew/Andy and my husband. He too has a web/graphic design degree mostly doing freelance stuff in the past. AND at age 33 experiences]d retinal detachment after weird surgery. After those eerie similarities, I was hooked. I hated her. I really truly did. I can tel you some onlookers probably thought I was cursing at my phone, but really I hated Charlie with so much disdain. I didn't see the twist coming at all. That is what makes an amazing psychological thriller. This was my second book by Mark Edwards, my first being The Magpies and I can't want to get lost another one of his books soon!
Always a pleasure.

A heroine named Hero! I liked this except for the part where she is struck by her fiance. I thought he got off too easily for being a cad. 
 Borrowed from library.

I am not normally a fan of contemporary YA, so when I like a book in this genre, you know it must be good. Now, if I could just find a guy who would buy me donuts and a puppy for my birthday like Ezra, I would be set. I don't think that's asking for much.

Monsters inspired by other monsters. 
 I enjoy anthologies because: 
 1. Short stories take less time to finish 
 2. Short stories tend to get to the point quicker. (Which is both a strength and/or weakness sometimes). 
 3. The theme is usually intriguing enough for me to want to keep reading to see other people's takes on it. 
 4. Many different writing styles are compiled together. I enjoy different points of views when they're in different stories. 
 5. I can find new authors and/or enjoy ones I already like! 
 I've found an author in interested in reading more books by. The author is Megan Shepherd and her story was Hide-and-Seek. 
 I liked it because: 
 1. Even though it was a short story, I was eager for more. 
 2. It was a new story I've yet to read with a twist I guessed and a twist that made me smile with the cleverness. 
 3. I haven't heard of her before and I'm happy to have now. 
 My second favorite was A Girl Who Dreamed of Snow by McCormick Templeman, for it was strange, but intriguing nevertheless. 
 Though I kind of felt bad for a sub-character. 
 Overall, 3.5 entertaining stars. :)

This showed up at the library as an e-book so, being an ANTM fan, I snaffled it. It's over 400 pages. Wow. I couldn't get past around 150 though. It's all over the place. It's fantasy, SF, kind of weird; not what I was expecting at all. 
 It's strange is what it is.

*distant screams comes from the depths of my bed...* 
 This was an okay book, I didn't enjoy it as I did To All the Boys I've Loved Before but I did enjoy it a lot! It was another cute and fuzzy, sometimes frustrating read! I thought that ending was way too rushed, like she just threw it in there. *softly sniffles* 
 Lara Jean is in an official relationship with Peter Kavinsky, such a dreamy boy he is! In TATBILB their relationship was sort of fake, it had a contract and everything! We get to see Lara Jean and Peters relationship grow and still be all cutesy until things get real, and Genevive is sort of in the way of them. Her big secret that Kavinsky refuses to tell, Lara Jean finally finds out near the end of the book and... all is well with the love birds. 
 But! We are also introduced to John Ambrose McLaren, who is a boy Lara Jean lied back in middle school, I think after or before Peter. He finally received the letter that was sent in book one, TATBILB, and writes back, they become pen pals until the middle school gang meets up to open the time capsule they buried near Lara Jeans next door neighbors tree house. I enjoyed bits and pieces when the Assassins game was going on, it made me want to play it and I'm a nineteen year old college student! 
 I fell for John... I can't lie about that. I was head over heels for Kavinsky just like Lara Jean was, but I have to admit that John was a sweetheart and he was a keeper. It wasn't until Peter finally got some balls that I realized, yes, I choose you Kavinsky! Who do you think Lara Jean chose? Hmm? Hmmmmmm? 
 For those of you who haven't read To All The Boys I've Loved Before, go do that because it was so cute and adorable and then go pick this up because it's even more cute and adorable because Peter and Lara Jean are so cute and adorable that it might just make you sick but then you won't care because they're so cUTE AND ADORABLE!!! 
 The reason I rated this four stars and not five is because even though I did smile and laugh and love it so much it wasn't better than book one, so basically four and a half stars... GO READ THESE BOOKS BC CUTE AND ADORABLE!
Ugh! Stupid tears! Bax breaks my heart!

I feel about this book the way I feel about Anna and the French Kiss. Almost the same exact way. They're pretty similar actually. Stupid heroine, douchey male character, an interesting setting but a lackluster plot. 
 My first problem: Allyson. She is so dense. Getting on a train with a guy to go to Paris when you JUST MET HIM? Didn't even technically meet him..more like have lunch on a train and exchange minimal information about each other. She's giving girls a bad rep. We are smarter than that. And besides that she was just jealous of every little thing (I mean I'm jealous too, but honestly..) and she was annoyingly moody. 
 I felt like the descriptions in this book could get a little weird and confusing and I just didn't see the reason for half of the stuff that Forman put her heart and soul into writing pages about. 
 The book felt super long to me and I'm happy to be finished with it a little bit. The beginning was intriguing but then it got boring half way through then a little intriguing again, then once again, boring. So I would say it was 50% boring, 50% bearable. 
 I didn't feel warm inside reading about Allyson and Willem. Willem seemed a little....I don't know, I didn't feel much for him. I thought he seemed kind of funny and interesting I guess, but I didn't really get a solid feeling that I had for him. Over 369 pages. Oh well. 
 I know the ending is kind of cliff hanger, but I'm honestly not sure if I will continue to the second one. If I do, it will be after I finish the 100 some books on my to read shelf.

This is one of those books were nothing happens, but at the same time, absolutely everything does. The writing is beautiful. A little confusing at times, but beautiful nonetheless. It's full of different formats such as: interviews, letters and prose - which makes it all the more mesmerising. 
 I didn't really have any major issues with this book, aside from the 'post apocalyptic' scenes dragging on a little bit sometimes. That looks odd, but surprisingly, the life set in the era of now was extremely interesting. I think a little bit of that was encouraged by how gorgeous the post apocalyptic world makes ours sound. 
 All in all, this was a magical story, centred around characters and life.

Anne Bishop is one of my favorite authors and I love this series. This first book Written in Red takes the reader to a fascinating world where humans are subservient to the Others, paranormal creatures that rule the earth and look at humans as prey. 
 Meg Corbyn seems human but doesn't smell like prey. When she shows up at Lakeside Courtyard, Simon Wolfgard, the shapeshifter in charge, decides to give her a job. All of the Others are fascinated by Meg who is very childlike for a young woman. It turns out that she's a blood prophet who reads the future from cuts on her skin and a valuable resource to some humans. 
 Anne Bishop creates a world that I want to live in. The plot is very original and the ending very satisfying. While this is a series, Written in Red is a complete story with no cliffhangers. The surprises continue as new creatures appear and more of Meg's story is revealed. It' a great book and I recommend that everyone follow Ms Bishops Facebook feed as she has great (and funny) updates about the series.

Just as with Gilead, I was slow to warm to this, but its depth and humanity completely won me over. It's frustrating to spend so much time with characters who don't seem to help themselves, but Robinson really makes it worth your while.
CASSIE WHAT HAVE YOU DONE TO ME?! I'M A MESS

In my quest to read YA that isn't stupid garbage I came across this book and was pleased. The heroine is no shrinking violet crying over her lost loves; she is mourning her father and trying to find answers about his death. Pretty diverse cast for a book set in predominantly white Oregon. I feel like most issues about racism/eugenics/conversion therapy are handled sensitively and well-researched. 
 My favorite thing about this book is that Hanalee does NOT end up dating the boy that is mean to her. You think it might be going down this road, then the story takes a different turn. Take note, YA authors: if our heroine gets with a boy that is mean and rude to her I will stop reading your book. I'm not even going to mark this as a spoiler because if you're like me you WANT to be spoiled about this and don't want to continue reading if it's about shoehorned unhealthy hetero romance.
Own this on my Nook. One of the only books I've bought on there, and I'm excited! It was only $.99, so I figured I'd buy it. Can't wait to see if it's any good.

This audiobook was exactly what I needed in my life, I just had no idea I needed it. 
 Lauren is funny, honest, and on point. She tells the stories of her life, from her theatre days to her time on Gilmore Girls. 
 Long live Lorelai.

I was introduced to the Green Arrow by the CW show Arrow, a show I look forward to watching each week -- something I wish I could also say about Marvel superhero show S.H.I.E.L.D., but I digress. So when I saw this New 52 comic on sale for Cyber Monday, I jumped at the chance... to waste my money. What a let down. 
 The comic opens -- and mind you, this is the first issue of a rebooted DC line, so it is really the series opening -- with little to no introduction of Oliver or his supporting cast. In the first arc, he fights against a gang of D-list supervillains who party hard and upload their criminal exploits to social media. For some unexplained reason, they really want to record themselves murdering the Green Arrow. This is supposed to be a subtle dig at the current state of modern society and social media, but comes off more heavy-handed than a bad after-school special. More importantly, this stock batch of villains are all incredibly lame, so there is no tension in thinking they might actually come close to succeeding in their voyeuristic goal. 
 This subpar villain problem is somewhat resolved in the second half of this book, when Midas and Blood Rose are introduced. The Green Arrow is not any better developed here -- his signature snarky quips come off more juvenile and immature than funny -- but at least his antagonists are deserving of attention. Despite some improvement with these worthier adversaries -- which saved this from getting a one star rating from me -- there was not nearly enough between these pages to get me to continue reading this series. Not by a long shot.
Awesome. I didn't mind the slow beginning because once you're through that, it's just WOW!

It's pretty hard to get into a story that is poem based when all you've ever read are paragraph based. Ellen Hopkins does a great job telling a story about dealing with your inner demons while trying to find love in a cruel world. Even though it's pretty hard to get into, the plot is good and the characters stand out. The writing style is a bit weird at first but the main characters are so interesting that it doesn't bother me after a while. 
 The beginning is boring. I feel like Ellen Hopkins is trying to make the relationship between the sisters sound and seem very mysterious which it isn't. Also, the fact that they are complete opposites seems to happen a lot in books. I wish they had more in common for the characters to stand out more than they did. 
 The shocking secret that comes out of nowhere is my favourite part of this book. It will take you by surprise and leave you shell-shocked. I also like the tense parts between Kaeleigh and her dad because it's so controlled and perfect. It's easy to know what will happen while still leaving the reads to let their imagination run wild. The ending to this is really good too since things look brighter and clearer, I'm not left with any unanswered questions. Even though the ending is kind of typical, I'm not disappointed because there is just so much happening in the book that the ending couldn't ruin this for me. Recommended for everyone, especially if you enjoy realistic fiction with human-like demons.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This was a very good book. It was a great way to end an intense series. Where do I start. Cole...I loved Cole. I liked him just as much as Evan, and before Evan made his entrance in the book, I was really torn with whether I wanted Emma back with Evan or with Cole. In the end, I'm glad she ended up with Evan (which I knew she would), and Cole was a little bit of a disappointment because he didn't fight for her. But then again, she couldn't take any more drama in her life! Another element that I loved about this book was Emma's friends. Wow! How wonderful life would be to have friends like that! I'm not sure how believable it is that people would be that caring and look after someone as intensely as they did so quick, but maybe I'm just pessimistic. I'm so glad that Jared and Sarah ended up with each other too. One thing that I didn't like/didn't agree with was the way that Emma was forced to go to her mother's funeral. No one gave her a choice in the matter. She just went, and you knew that was going to be a train wreck! BUT, if she wouldn't have gone, she wouldn't have ended up with Evan. I hated that he had to see her at her very worst! I love what Emma said at her mom's funeral. It was perfect, because depending on how much you knew about Emma and her mom, you could have seen it as a sweet tribute or a searing jab at the hateful women she was. I loved the way Donovan took this book to not add another layer of abuse, but to have Emma finally deal with what happened to her emotionally and choose to live life despite of it.

I was surprisingly enthralled and moved by this book. Rowling proves herself as adept at creating characters you care about in the real world as in any fantasy realm. The sometimes darkly humorous, sometimes depressing dance of the dozens of personalities that inhabit Rowling's fictional hamlet of Pagford wends its inevitable way to tragedy. There are many people in the often petty, sometimes dangerous political dance to fill Barry Fairbrother's 'casually vacated' council seat, some of them noble and respectable, some of them small and hateful. They're all flawed, and they're all intriguing. 
 I think my favorite dichotomy of the book is what I see as that of the two characters at opposite poles of Pagford society: the jolly, corpulent Howard Mollison, first citizen and proprietor of the shop that hints at the finer things in life for the village's residents, and Terri Weedon, a junkie mother and denizen of the local projects that fuel the central political conflict of the story. They could not appear more dissimilar on the surface, but Rowling draws subtle and compelling parallels between them that serve to further problematize the question of right and wrong, good and wicked, just and unjust. It's a delightfully delicate touch she has here. 
 Well worth a read, and not just as a snarky literary curiosity but as a worthy piece of fiction in its own right.

 "What we've just done is no different from what Mary did to John." 
 "Do not compare my feelings for you to those of that strumpet. Mary never cared for John. He was a lover of convenience. I do not hold out much hope for Tom, either. Give her a week or two, and she'll have moved on to someone else."

I'm not talking about the thrusting, naked fumble in the dark sort, I'm talking about the melding of two hearts, two souls. Yes, reader, I am a romantic at heart. 
 This book didn't have any of the above. It was a boring, terrible love story with a weak-ass female and a regrettable waste of air, without much swashbuckling at all. Edward "Teach" (how the fuck is that a nickname?) the future Blackbeard, falls for his biracial servant girl. That's it. That's IT. 
 One of the worst things about the past is the class difference and how the upper classes tend to abuse those who are "beneath" them. This is particularly true (and particularly abominable) when it comes to master-servant relationships. Countless serving girls, maids, governesses, helpless females (and given the era, they truly are helpless), were subject to rape and sexual abuse by the men they serve. 
 "I could have you punished for what you did," he said, watching her closely. 
 She nodded. "Yes, you could." 
 "After that, I could have you fired." 
 "Yes, you could. But I'd rather you didn't," she said. 
 "And why not?" he growled. 
 The male protagonist in this story is one of those assholes, and yes, he said those things above.

 Because truly noble characters are chaste, right? 
 Anne is the one who constantly receives - and steadfastly resists - sexual advances. Teach is engaged to a highly sexualized (and villainous) woman named Patience.  Guys. I barely survived this whirlwind of a novel. It was so good. 
 In the three days it took me to read this book, it twisted me in and out. I have never been more splendidly exhausted from reading a book. And boy, what a good three days it has been. 
 When I first started it, I thought it was good, but not fantastic. I was ready to give it a solid four stars. And then something happened, about a hundred pages in. I stopped expecting Feyre, the main character of the book, to suddenly whip out Celaena Sardothien qualities and I started seeing her as her own, wonderful character. 
 Although this is intended to be (somewhat) of a fairy tale retelling of Beauty and the Beast, the similarities were very limited. Sarah J. Maas did an excellent job of bringing out the very best of her characters, but also their very worst. Feyre was never meant to be perfect, and I loved that. 
 There were so many things I expected this book to be, and despite some spoilers I received, I was still stunningly surprised. I thought it was going to be a feel-good book, that the stray mention of Amarantha and the court Under the Mountain would just fade away to the more prominent, more sophisticated love story between Feyre and Tamlin. About 250 pages in, however, I acquired a shocking amount of denial that Tamlin had sent Feyre back to the mortal lands . How could he! 
 There were so many blurred lines in this novel, so many purposeful confusions. I was supposed to hate Elain and Nesta, Feyre's sisters, was I not? (Especially Nesta) I was supposed to hate Rhysand... And yet, besides the otherwise obvious antagonists that included Amarantha and Attor, I started to actually like all those characters that had been portrayed as terrible human beings (and faeries ;)) in the beginning of the book. I started to understand all that they had to endure. 
 I loved the setting of the book and how wonderful it was to imagine the Spring Court every time that Maas described it, I loved the span of emotions I experienced during Feyre's trials that kept my eyes peeled to the page, I loved the riddle that practically broke the ending of the book, I loved the foreshadowing, I loved every time Lucien made me chuckle, I loved how insanely unbreakable Feyre was, and I loved loved loved Tamlin and his adorable shyness :). 
 In other words, this book was everything I wanted it to be, and more. I have the sequel sitting on my nightstand, and I am so excited to see what the next 600 pages of Maas's magical writing will bring. (And since it's been announced that there are going to be no less than eight books in this series, I am a super happy camper :))
I really like the story and all, but I think it's too fast-paced. I also found too many unanswered questions. So I guess this is a 3.5/5 for me.

Kazu Kibuishi is one of the people that fostered my love for graphic novels and not just traditional comics, and I was really excited to be able to read and review an ARC of the next book in this amazing series. 
 First things first--if you haven't read all of the books in this series before this book, you should. Not because the story doesn't make sense, but for two other major reasons. 1) The story doesn't make as much sense and 2) because the other books are worth reading. 
 In this book, I didn't think that Kibuishi went as far with his plot. However, he still packed a lot into this story and I really appreciated the way he went back into his story and answered a lot of the questions I'd had from previous books. My love for all the characters was made even stronger and I liked the way all the characters were put through different kinds of trials dealing with others--especially Emily's brother, Navin, due to their alliance with the other part of the war effort. 
 All the usual suspects for the characters I loved (or loved to hate) are there, and that's great, but I think with this book my love for Trellis as a character was fully solidified. Trellis has grown so much throughout the course of these books and I've come to really enjoy seeing how he progresses. I'm looking forward to what Kibuishi does with him in the next books. When it came to Max though, I was a little disappointed. I felt like Kibuishi could've done much more with Max. 
 As always, the artwork is amazing in this book. I didn't get to see a whole lot of the color in most of the regular comic part of the book since I got an ARC copy, but all the landscapes and what I did get to see of the colored work, everything is beautiful. I love Kibuishi's style and the colors and background team for this book did a fantastic job. 
 Then there's the action, adventure and supporting characters. I wish I had gotten to see more of Leon and the crew in this book, but I was glad to see what Kibuishi did with past characters from this series. The action is also great and I liked seeing Emily come to become even stronger in this book, not just as herself but in her relationships with the people supporting her. The pacing is great and there's a lot of explanation as to why things are the way they are. 
 I wanted to see more happen before the ending of this book, but it left me excited for the next book and overall, not disappointed. Fans of this series will love this book and I hope it will bring even more attention onto this series. After reading this book, fans of this series should also read his other works and the Flight comics, which are all awesome books. 4 stars.

After shelving Kenzie and Gennaro for eleven years, Lehane returned to his signature characters in 2010 with the series' sixth novel, Moonlight Mile. A lot has happened since we last left the detectives. Patrick and Angie have since tied the knot and brought life into the world in their four year old daughter, Gabby. Feeling the pinch of the recession, Patrick is stuck freelancing for a big investigation firm, hoping to woo them enough to be hired on fulltime while Angie is taking classes working toward a degree. 
 Patrick is approached by Beatrice McCready, the estranged aunt of the once missing Amanda McCready - the same Amanda that Patrick and Angie worked hard to track down twelve years ago (1998s Gone, Baby, Gone). Bea tells Patrick that Amanda, now 16, has gone missing a second time and once again requests Patrick's assistance in finding her. While initially reluctant, Patrick views this as his shot at redemption as he looks to ease the guilt over the results of the last time she went missing. 
 Revisiting Kenzie & Gennaro's most famous case was likely the right move on Lehane's part in resurrecting the series. I can't speak for everyone, but I know I was curious as to what happened to little Amanda McCready and in Moonlight Mile, Lehane is determined to put her through the ringer one last time. While the plot isn't quite as complex as Gone, Baby, Gone, Lehane keeps things interesting by introducing a plethora of bit characters that populate some memorable scenes. Russian gangsters Pavel and Yefim stole every scene they were in - so much so that I'd read the hell out of a book featuring just those two. Lehane somehow made Amanda's mother Helene even more despicable this time around and Patrick & Angie's encounter with a fitness guru yields some laughs, if only due to the man's missing moral compass. 
 If this is where Lehane chooses to end the series, it's difficult to come up with any complaints. While life doesn't often give us happy endings, it's nice to know that once in awhile, the truly good people out there do get what they deserve in the end.

I liked the characters and world-building, but the plot was a bit strange. 
 Going to continue with the series to see if it improves.

When college study, Avery spots the rough biker she knows one thing... she wants him. A girl that has always enjoyed the challenge might have met her match with Axton though. After the club shows up at the bar that Avery and her friend, Sloan work it, Axton feels drawn to Avery but he isn't the kind of man to allow a woman into his life or his world. 
 When Axton needs Avery's skills, she happily agrees to assisting him on his deal, after all it did earn her a ride on the back of his bike. But when shit hits the fan, Axton is surprised to find just how far Avery is willing to go. Even when his head is screaming to keep his distance, part of him can't seem to stay away from her. A woman who is slowly learning just what a man like Axton needs, and one that is willing to do whatever it takes to stick by his side. 
 This was my first read from SD Hildreth and I was instantly intrigued at the idea of reading a romance novel written by a male author. I love to see the spin on things, the way a man would write a particular scene or a character. There are far too few male authors in this genre and sadly of the ones that are, can often be surrounded by far too much fabricated drama to keep my attention. So when given the chance to read this book for exchange for an honest review, I was more than willing. 
 I enjoyed the story overall, although I found it difficult to feel too much for Avery as she confirmed to who she thought Axton wanted so much that I was left wondering if we really got to see the real Avery at all. She was also lacking a bit of confidence when it came to her body/looks - overshadowed by her friend Sloan who had the curves she lacked. I did like to see that she shifted her views on her looks as she gained more confidence. 
 I've read quite a few biker books and no two authors will write about the clubs and the lifestyle the same way. ** spoiler alert ** 
 Before I read this, I didn't read too much about what this novel was about--all I knew was that it was a story about mathematician/monks that ended up in space. Thus, I was a little broadsided when the whole thing turned to metaphysics and the nature of consciousness. Not disappointed mind you. Just quite surprised. 
 My first impression upon starting this book (one which lasted perhaps the first 100 or so pages) was that I'd never make it through the novel due to all his made up jargon. You'll spend a while as confused by the auts and cnoons of the avouts of The Concent of Saunt Edhar as the fraas and suurs therein are by the jeejahs, speelies, and other pieces of praxis of the extramuros, but you'll get over it. Probably more quickly than Neal Stephenson intended, since you'll spend another 100 pages or so just marinating in this world before Fraa Orolo's Anathem finally kicks the plot into gear. While not a major issue, I felt he could've gotten on with the storyline much more quickly than he did. 
 After things got going, I really enjoyed the plot. I'm a sucker for hard sci-fi first contact stories, and this was a pretty good one. Most aspects of this were excellently done--Erasthmus' journey to meet up with Orolo, the slow reveal of the alien (referred to, for a while at least, as the Cousins) ship and it's details, and the internal politics of the Cousins and the various misunderstandings between the Cousins and the people of Arbre make for a good read. I occasionally had a few issues with how they determined things (I was completely unconvinced by the way they decided the large orb on the ship needed to be a giant bomb) but overall good. 
 However, the ending went a little wrong for me. I've not mentioned until now one of the main components of the story, which was the long metaphysical discussion on the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics and human consciousness--that's because throughout almost the entire novels it doesn't really matter (nor, for that matter, is it particularly compelling). That is until the very end. To be honest, I'm still not entirely sure what happened. I think we traveled between a few parallel dimensions settling in one in which our main character survives and gets the girl. And thats pretty much it! For me it was almost as sudden as that, and as unsatisfying. 
 I really wanted to enjoy this book a lot, and I think it's fair to say that I did. It wasn't perfect (ocasional minor pacing problems during metaphysical discussions, weak beginning and end, and unconvincing metaphysical meditations on consciousness pop to mind as the worst offenders) but a fun read that I recommend.

Perhaps it's not surprising, since I haven't got along that well with anything else by Michel Faber either.

Ronan's dreams, Adam focusing the ley line, Blue amplifying, Gansey speaking the entire plan into motion. Adam had never felt so...intrinsic before. They had been a fine machine. 
 There's no way I can write this review without some "spoilers" that are bound to make someone mad. So I'm putting this all under a spoiler cut. Read at your own risk. 
 Story time: My sister and I went to Barnes & Noble on the 20th, and she asked me if The Raven King was out yet. I told her I doubt it will be yet, but if it was, I wouldn't freak out. I might not even buy it, I claimed. Then I went to the new releases table, and I saw it. I screamed. My sister took a video of me freaking out. Boy, was I fooling myself. This series is my third favorite series, I don't know why I told myself I would be okay. So, yeah, I bought it. Then I saw everyone reading it on Goodreads, while I just couldn't get around to it due to a busy schedule. I was terrified of spoilers. Luckily, I didn't see anything. 
 When I bought this, I told my sister as we were driving, "I have four requests from this book, and I hope that Stiefvater delivers at least ONE of these." They were the following: 
 1) PYNCH 
 2) A happy ending for Noah 
 3) Gansey doesn't die from Blue's kiss 
 4) No deaths of main characters (other than Gansey's, which I was expecting) 
 And guess what? She delivered about 1 1/2 of these. Yet I still loved this book. How, you ask? 
 Well, it's all about the development of the characters and relationships. I have a solid twenty-seven Post It Notes in my book, all Pynch moments. Yeah, Maggie delivered. The relationship was always more one-sided, with Ronan obsessing over Adam's hands, and Adam never being able to get over Blue fully (for the record, I used to like Adam and Blue until Ronan drove in). I'll just include some quotes under here. Just a couple. I'll try. 
 Ronan crossed his arms to wait, just looking. At Adam's fine cheekbones, his furrowed fair eyebrows, his beautiful hands, everything washed out by the furious light. He had memorized the shape of Adam's hands in particular: the way his thumb jutted awkwardly, boyishly; the roads of the prominent veins; the large knuckles that punctuated his long fingers. In dreams Ronan put them to his mouth. 
 His feelings for Adam were an oil spill; he'd let them overflow and now there wasn't a damn place in the ocean that wouldn't catch fire if he dropped a match. 
 A personal favorite of mine. Ronan's obsession with Adam's hands will be the death of me. 
 Inside, they pretended they would dream, but they did not. They sprawled on the living room sofa and Adam studied the tattoo that covered Ronan's back: all the sharp edges that hooked wondrously and fearfully into each other. 
 Ronan put Adam's fingers to his mouth. 
 He was never sleeping again. 
 Just...everything. Ronan's dream came true. Adam's feelings are mutual. I could die happy. 
 I have twenty-five other quotes than that. But we'll leave it at that. 
 I never was a huge fan of Blue and Gansey. I know they're soulmates and all that, but I just never fullheartedly loved him. I felt like they masked out the beautiful romance that was Pynch. Now that Pynch has become canon, I liked them a bit more. My heart broke when Blue cried over Gansey. 
 My only complaint with relationships/characters is that: 
 1) There wasn't enough Noah. Every time he did show up, it was just heartbreaking. There was no happy ending for this pure soul. 
 2) Some of the secondary characters were added for no reason it seemed. I mean, their stories were interesting, like all of the characters in this world, but I just didn't see the point for some. 
 Another thing about this book that made me love it maybe more than all of the others is that it wasn't as confusing. The first book was so confusing for me, making it my least favorite. The second one was just a lot to handle with the dreaming and all that. The third was a bit better. Fourth was just crystal clear. I think there was one thing that I was confused about. On page 328, I couldn't figure out the meanings of the words amae vias and oce iteres. If you know, please comment on this review (thank you!). 
 A lot of people said the ending ruined it for them because it was confusing, but I thought the ending was the best part of the book. The epilogue especially made me happy because we get to see that Adam and Ronan are "boyfriends," according to Adam's horrible father. It made me feel all warm inside, and I'm so thankful she included it. 
 I could rave about this series as a whole forever probably, but I think I'm going to end it here. The Raven Cycle. Read it, if you've been living under a rock for the last couple years.

Oh boy, this was a long read. I never felt highly compelled to power through the whole thing in one sitting but also liked it enough to make my way through all 850+ pages of this thing (though perhaps I really kept going due to a sunken cost feeling lurking in my head), hence the three stars. This is the first book by Auster I've read and I can't say I'm jumping to read anything more by him any time soon. 
 The good: He is a fine writer and he does a fantastic job of weaving together key moments in time, the value of friendship, and the revealing process of growing up. I enjoyed all four iterations of Archie Ferguson and became invested in the stories of each but can't say that I needed to know so much about all four. 
 The not-so-good: 
  
 Empty. That was the word for it, he said to himself, as he sat down on the sofa and took his first sip of wine, the same empty space Vivian had talked about when describing how she had felt after finishing her own book. Not empty in the sense of standing alone in a room without furniture - but empty in the sense of feeling hollowed out. Yes, that was it, 
 hollowed out in the way a woman was hollowed out after giving birth. But in this case to a stillborn child, an infant who would never change or grow or learn how to walk, for books lived inside you only as long as you were writing them, but once they came out of you, they were all used up and dead. 
 This quote, from Archie version 3.0, made we wonder whether this was how Auster felt about writing this book. Of course I can't know what was in his head, but the impression I got from reading the book is that Auster (or perhaps Archie version 4.0 who admits at the end that he is the "true" Archie) had so much dwelling inside him about his teenage years and early twenties that he had to write it all down. And once the book was finished, he'd have to step away from that time and move on. So, instead of a concise reflection, words upon words spilled out into the book - either as an attempt to capture everything or to prolong the writing process and delay completion (or both?). 
 Aside from the overall self-indulgence and extraneous details of the entire thing, my main issue stems from the fact that one of the main themes of the book is that it is a book about writing a book - the same book, in fact, that we are reading now. My dad and I used to remark at how often books and movies feature writers and actors because that is what the people behind those books and movies know. This is not inherently problematic but as a reader and viewer, it gets old after a while. The idea of the book within a book is not new so if the author chooses this approach, something else about the book must make my time worthwhile. Throughout the book I kept wondering, so what? What is the point of these 4 Archies? I hoped that the answer would be something other than a narrator telling us at the end that all these stories about writing were portions of a larger written book by one of the Archies. I definitely let out a giant "ughhhhhhhh" upon turning that final page. 
 I also did not understand whether the four stories were meant to represent four completely different people who were mostly the same but slightly different, or whether they were essentially the same person but led different lives based on the decisions of the relevant characters in each version. If the latter, then why aren't all four Archies interested in romantic or sexual relationships with both men and women? Archie 3.0 stands out in this respect but this can't be solely based on Archie 3.0's life decisions. 
 One last mini-rant: what was with all the lists?! I'm fairly certain about 300 pages of this book could have been cut out if the never-ending lists were cut out altogether or severely reduced. 
  
 This is the only book on the Man Booker shortlist I've read so far so I can't compare it to the others. However, I can't say I'd be overly impressed if it wins the final prize.

A captivating, almost otherworldly, book. The distinctions of character are revealed through seemingly typical conversations, and I have to admire how that applies as much to the adults as to the teens. The parent-child relationships were among my favorite qualities of this work: realistic, tinged with humor, at times strained, but grounded in respect and devotion. Cultural markers were integrated without seeming to make a lauded show of them, which is one of the best ways to make those exact points. 
 The theme most celebrated is what gives me most pause, but not for the reason you might assume. Personal convictions aside, it wasn't the struggle with sexual identity that made me uncomfortable. It was that it seemed almost pushed on Ari. It wasn't his idea. He loved Dante, of course, but it no longer seems allowed for deep same-sex friendships to not inevitably become romantic ones. Perhaps he would have reached the same realizations given time, and perhaps this is just my read on the story, but I was troubled by the fact that even as he was trying to sort out his feelings, nearly everyone in his life was hurrying him along to their own conclusion.  
 audiobook note: It is no surprise that the reason I moved this book up in my queue is to hear Lin-Manuel Miranda read it to me, and I wouldn't have had it any other way. He has a barely-restrained energy, an incisive empathy, and the old-soul wisdom with which to merge the facets of a unique spirit testing the ripples of adolescence. The pacing is quick or careful, reflecting the narrative beats, but you never once question the authenticity. It's perfect. I've read many of the reviews that take issue with the purported lyrical nature of the writing. Perhaps those readers needed Manuel to bring it to life.

David Eddings was my first foray into fantasy. Thank you, Mr. Eddings, may you rest in peace, for starting me out right in the genre and causing me to be a life-long fan. 
 Though this was the first book in the world of Belgarath, Polgara, and Garion, Guardians of the West was the first book in that world which I read, thanks to a random pull off my local public library's shelf. I loved it, gobbled up the rest of the Mallorean series and then went back to read the Belgariad. 
 That was back in the early nineties, when I was barely in double digits. Now, after my husband recently started reading the series for the first time from the actual beginning, I started with this first book for my re-read-through. And it's like meeting old friends. Polgara has been one of my absolute favorite fantasy characters for ages now. I couldn't wait to meet Silk again. I didn't realize how much I was looking forward to this. It's been long enough that I remember the general way things turn out, but not the details. I read on eagerly to see how things turn out specifically. It's great. I love how the different parts of the book focus on one country in the world as the assembled group journeys forth on their goal to retrieve the stolen Orb of Aldur. 
 I have a hard time reviewing just one book of this series, as all five books make a seamless, sweeping epic story together, especially reading them back to back as I am currently.

"My life has become a single on-going revelation that I haven't been cynical enough." 
 This is the kind of cheery thought one is apt to have when facing a narcissistic megalomaniac who has gained power by convincing some people that all their problems can be blamed on other groups while setting humanity on a self-destructive path it may not be able to recover from. 
 Geez, I thought I read science-fiction to escape reality. 
 The Expanse series took an epic dark turn in the last one, and this book is mainly about dealing with the fall-out from that as well as trying to resolve the new threat that arose. The short term stakes involve a fight to control the outposts outside of Earth and Mars, but the longer view will determine nothing less than the fate of humanity itself. 
 Like the other books this has a self-contained story that features all kinds of political intrigue and strategy as well as a healthy dose of interesting characters riding around in spaceships being all Pew-Pew!. Which is what The Expanse does really well as a general rule. The new wrinkle here is that because this is the aftermath of catastrophic events that there's a tone of shock and even a certain wistfulness in this one. Things will never be what they once where and everyone knows it. This makes the conflict here literally a fight for the future, and all the characters are under enormous amounts of pressure because of it. 
 There was one element I wasn't entirely happy about.  I absolutely loved the set up at the end that the Rocinante crew is essentially facing an Alamo situation where their best option is to die well while taking as many of their enemies with them as they can. However, it seemed like more than a little bit of cheat that they simply manage to make the Free Navy ships vanish via the ring gates, and it seems way too easy of an end for Marcos Inaros.  On the other hand there's still story to be told so I'm trying to set aside any feelings of mild disappointment I have about the ending here because it's likely that there is more pay-off coming.

Brilliant book! I love books where the author spends enough time in developing characters, with all their pock-marks and warts and what not. 
 I thought Eva's letters were heartbreaking at first, till I realized that she was a deeply flawed character. The whole plot device of writing to her dead  husband was nothing but genius. The shallow, selfish, narrow Eva and the story of her son Kevin, who goes on a rampage, killing several people a few days before his 16th birthday is a tale as dark as they come. 
 The story begins slow, slows down even further in the middle, and then accelerates to a nerve-wracking, gut-wrenching climax that leaves you sucker punched and feeling drained at the end. 
 Eva's epistolary style, and her almost detached sense of narration, makes her story much more powerful. Does she feel guilt? Shame? Responsibility? All of these? Intense emotions, and she's apparently condemned to feel them for as long as she is alive. 
 And her writing about Kevin makes him seem human and monstrous at one and the same time - clearly the mark of a good book by a good writer. Where's the depth in a one-dimensional black or white character? Kevin is oh, so complex. And evil. And disturbing. 
 Even though I lack the cultural context to a crime of this magnitude, I think it's an incredibly tough thing to write from the perspective of the mother of the perpetrator, and that too without assigning clear degrees of blame to any quarters. 
 Perhaps, one of the most disturbing books read by me this year!

 The Night Circus is, hands down, one of the most beautifully written books I have ever had the pleasure of reading. The language is superb. It is divine. It is one of only two books I can think of that I have actually savored. (The other is The Thirteenth Tale by Diane Setterfield) 
 Atmosphere is most definitely Erin Morgenstern's strong point. Every single page is brimming with rich prose that paints a vivid picture of the circus and its inhabitants. And the mystery. There is a mysterious dreamlike quality to the book that at time came across as just plain vagueness, but in the end played out well. 
 I didn't expect the magic aspect of it, and I didn't expect the romance twist to it either. Actually, I didn't really know what to expect when it came right down to it, but I was very pleasantly surprised. 
 The book features an ensemble cast, and we never really find ourselves drawn in to any one character. I didn't feel like any of them really stuck out as outstanding characters, but then this isn't really a character-driven novel. That isn't to say the characters are not likeable or they are poorly written, I just felt they were not the focus of The Night Circus, and that is completely OK. 
 Plot-wise, it is slow. The plot unfolds, as I stated above, at a very dreamlike pace. There are only a few moments where there is any real sense of urgency, and those are mostly near the end. Honestly, I was so entranced by the prose that I only noticed the slow plot once or twice in my reading. They were short-lived notices before I was distracted by the shiny prose again. Some of the plot devices seemed a little sloppy to me. There wasn't much explanation into the workings of the magic used, it was more just "Look, magic!". 
 Bottom Line: Absolutely gorgeous prose. Slower paced story, but still a lovely read. 
 I leave you with a quote. A book has to really resonate with me for me to quote it, so this should speak pretty highly of it. 
 "It is important," the man in the grey suit interrupts. "Someone needs to tell those tales. When the battles are fought and won and lost, when the pirates find their treasures and the dragons eat their foes for breakfast with a nice cup of Lapsang souchong, someone needs to tell their bits of overlapping narrative. There's magic in that. It's in the listener, and for each and every ear it will be different, and it will affect them in ways they can never predict. From the mundane to the profound. You may tell a tale that takes up residence in someone's soul, becomes their blood and self and purpose. That tale will move them and drive them and who knows what they might do because of it, because of your words. That is your role, your gift. Your sister may be able to see the future, but you yourself can shape it, boy. Do not forget that." He takes another sip of his wine. "There are many kinds of magic, after all."

 This book was soo good. The writing and the plot were very addictive and the romance was absolutely swoon worthy. Also, it was in many ways, very different from other YA fantasy books I have read, which I thought it was a really good thing, since sometimes it can feel like you are reading the same plot lines over and over. 
 The Winner's Curse is not like other books: 
 -The main character Kestrel is smart, but not physically strong or able, but that's okay, because she is still awesome. So often we seen books were the female main character has to be physically strong or have some kind of useful fighting skill in order to have value. Kestrel isn't like that. Instead, she is able to strategize and to win what she wants through cunning methods. She is smart and she doesn't make decisions without thinking things through first! 
 -The romance is such a slow burn! Honestly it was sooo slow, even though you could tell they were drawn to each other, they didn't actually move forward with anything for a really long time. There were some kind of sad things regarding their romance in the end, but I'm holding on to hope that the next books will have those two getting together. 
 -It is fantasy, but there is no magic. There are some "not-natural" things that would only happen in a fantasy world, though. While I would have like some actual magic, always, this book still presented an unique world with its own set of rules and costumes. I thought the world building was really interesting. The only problem I had was that I wish the world had been explored in a broader sense. I'm not really sure what sort of universe they live in, or the names of adjacent towns, what is part of the empire and what isn't. That kind of stuff wasn't very clear. But overall this didn't take too much away from the story for me. 
 -The plot was very romance-centric at the beginning, but towards the middle it got more involved in the matters of the revolution and wars. Personally, I prefer the romance part of the plot, but the other stuff was okay too. Honestly, I know this might be an unpopular opinion, but I actually prefer books that are more focused on the romance and on the action/war/fights sort of things. But there isn't a rule - it really depends on how the book works better. For me, this book worked better on the romance. 
 -The writing has beautiful moments that are well balanced between description, metaphor and action. I found it easy to read and quite addictive while at the same time it isn't too straight-forward or simplistic. Sometimes books can either have really descriptive beautiful writing that makes it slow paced and others it can be really fast paced but have no real substance. Neither is a bad thing necessarily, but I liked that this book was able to balance both well. 
 I strongly recommend this book and I want to read the rest of the series soon!!

 As for the story itself, I enjoyed it. There's a lot of mystery that doesn't get explained, and while that enraged me in The Colorado Kid, I think it works fine here mostly because this is a short story and not a pointless novel. A kid interviews his great grandfather, and gramps tells him about a dangerous something he got from his mother. Ghost is the story of Castle Crenshaw, aka Ghost, a young boy who learned he could run fast on the night his father shot at him and his mother. His father was arrested, and now he lives with his mother, who works at a hospital cafeteria and takes online nursing school classes in the hopes of moving out of the low-income housing block called Glass Manor where they live. 
 In a fit of jealousy while watching another boy run track -- who is this boy with those fancy clothes? that swagger? -- Ghost shows off how fast he can run. His fleet feet catch the eye of the track coach, who admits Ghost onto the team under one condition: that he doesn't screw up at school. 
 It's impossible to change overnight. Despite Ghost's best efforts, he soon gets into a fight at school. Later he steals some shoes. But the love and acceptance he receives from his teammates and his coach, a strong father figure he is lacking, motivate him to stay on a better path. 
 Ghost, both the book and the character, deal with the internal struggle to fit in more than the external struggle of, say, running a track meet. The book's dramatic arc comes from Ghost's spiritual tug-of-war, being pulled back and forth by conflicting forces. 
 Jason Reynolds, whose author blurb is written in a blatant attempt to seem cool to young boys, captures the voice of this character perfectly. The book moves at a brisk pace and doesn't overstay its welcome. 
 However, Reynolds does rely on a silly "world record" gimmick throughout, which doesn't always feel organically integrated, especially regarding the cumbersome chapter title like "World Record for Having the Best Secret." Also, I found Ghost's preoccupation with status and swagger, while realistic and understandable, to be annoying. But that's my personal taste, and why I don't usually read books with young male protagonists. 
 This book is labeled as the first in the "Track" series. I wonder if Reynolds plans to focus future installments on other members of his track team and their complicated racial dynamics, like Lu the albino boy or Patty, the girl adopted by white parents. If he does feature a different protagonist, I might read it. But as for me, I'm done with Ghost's story.

Sometimes the dragon guards the tower. And sometimes he stomps around inside despairing about his dirty housemate. 
 Uprooted takes the classic idea of the dragon-guarded damsel in the tower and gives it new life. Agnieszka comes from a small village where, every so many years, the Dragon appears and takes a girl of a certain age to stay with him in his tower for a decade. The girls are then free to leave and generally do quite well for themselves afterward. Meanwhile, a sickness plagues the people living closest to the Wood, that which the Dragon protects them from. The Wood is no ordinary forest, but alive and ready to spill as much blood as necessary to spread its roots across the valley. 
 This book reads like a fairy tale retelling, and I mean that in the best way. The world is defined enough to satisfy the reader for the time being while the plot continues to thicken. There's more to this story than a girl in the tower. Uprooted isn't a character-driven novel much like fairy tales tend to focus more on the story and less on the characters, even going as far as not giving them names. And when it comes to the plot, this book steals the show. Everything is crafted and drawn out in such a beautiful way that it's hard to stop reading. Is it original? Not when it comes to fantasies. Evil monsters, dark forests, magic controlled by unpronounceable words. It's been done time and time again. Are the characters a little bland? Yes. But this brings me back to my earlier point. 
 I consider Uprooted to be in the realm of fairy tales. Perhaps because of that expectation, I didn't care so much that the characters were a little flat. There isn't much development there and if this was the first book in a series, I would knock of a star for that alone. Later Novik attempts a romance subplot between the Dragon and Agnieszka which could have been done without but it happened and I realized I didn't mind so much. To be perfectly honest, I can't really remember the characters from this book. 
 The story on the other hand, I loved. The evil of the Wood always creeping closer became more than just the grand evil of the world but almost a character on its own. Initially, Uprooted focuses on Agnieszka's time in the tower but by halfway through, she was out...and I was really confused because what could possibly happen after that. The story was done, right? Instead, Novik took the plot on the twists and turns of a roller-coaster, knocking the characters down one by one until I couldn't imagine it getting worse. I read this book in one sitting, couldn't put it down. 
 Is this book the next fantasy bestseller of all time? Absolutely not. Did I really enjoy it! You bet. And if you go into it with the intentions of enjoying it instead of performing a critical analysis, I think you'll enjoy it too!

February 2012: When I first read it almost two years ago, I remember thinking that of the three Millennium books, Hornet's Nest was definitely the weakest, but either because I've really drunk the Kool-Aid by now, or because I've simply ceased to think of Larsson's creation as a fictional world, I liked it much better this time (and I did like it quite a bit before). 
 As I noted in my first review way back in June 2010, The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest is much less of a mystery-thriller than books one and two. Instead, TGWKTHN is more of an espionage-thriller. In the first book the big question was 'Who killed Harriet Vanger?" In the second, "Who is Zalachenko?" There isn't really a question in this book. We are treated to answers about The Section before the characters are, so the pleasure in this book, then, is in watching Blomkvist and Co. take down the men who ruined Lisbeth's life piece by piece, and giving her vindication. It's about airing dirty laundry and shaking things clean. And it is immensely satisfying (if a little unwieldy at times). 
 TGWKTHN is constructed around the trial of Lisbeth Salander. Blomkvist, Armansky, and several people within the police who believe her to be innocent, and even a faction within the Security Police, all work together to get Salander acquitted and take down the men of The Section, who have been committing crimes against the people of Sweden and infringing on their rights for decades. The build up to the trial is a little slow at times, but it's worth it in the end. 
 Stuff that I loved: 
 *All the random bits of Swedish culture and history. 
 *Everything to do with Salander. I loved her forced recovery period and her reluctant friendship with Dr. Jonasson. (Actually I love it period that so many unlikely people are able to see past her hostile exterior and plant themselves firmly in her corner.) 
 *Seeing all of the supporting characters we've met join together to kick some old balls. 
 *Seeing all those self-important wrinkly old white men get what was coming to them. 
 *Seeing everyone who ever mistreated Salander eat their words during her trial. 
 *I love that Salander dressed in her Sunday worst for the trial, just to scare the shit out of everyone who was there. 
 *The last line: "She opened the door wide and let him into her life again." 
 Stuff that should have been fixed but couldn't because Stieg Larsson is dead, you asshole: 
 *Blomkvist sleeps with yet ANOTHER woman (that guy is just a manwhore, but at least he's a likable one who is loyal to his friends and never pretends to be otherwise). I guess I like Monica Figuerola okay, but seriously, dude? At least he semi-commits to her at the end, but that might actually upset me more. Maybe I'm just a good old fashioned monogamist, but she isn't Lisbeth, and Blomkvist is hopelessly dense. Probably all of this would have been resolved in all of the books he planned to write afterwards, but he's dead, so that's not happening, and instead I will complain about it on the internet. 
 *I do not get the whole thing with Berger and the giant newspaper, or her thing with the stalker. it seemed out of place in a book that already needed to be cut for content. I suppose the impulse there was for Millennium to be in even more of a crisis than it already was, so thus we take away all-important Berger, but the book could have done without it. 
 *I hate that there isn't more. 
 All in all, this probably deserves four, or four and a half stars, but I don't care about being objective, as I've already stated, so five stars. 
 June 2010: Although The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest is not as tightly structured or frightening as The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo or The Girl Who Played With Fire, it is nevertheless un-put-down-able (not a word). 
 But I think it's slightly unfair to compare Hornet's Nest to the others for three reasons: 1) Where Dragon Tattoo and Fire were essentially thriller/mysteries, Hornet's Nest is more of an espionage legal thriller. There isn't really a mystery at all, unless you count the question of how Lisbeth Salander could possibly be able to get herself out of the mess she's in as a mystery, that is; 2) If we look at all three books, the first two are essentially set-up (#1 sets up the Blomkvist/Salander meet-cute or whatever so that we will care in #2 when everything goes to Hell for both of them, and the #3 is the conclusion to both of those stories). Conclusions are different by nature and should be judged accordingly; and finally, 3) Stieg Larsson is dead. There's no beating around the bush on that one, and I'm not using it as some sort of get out of jail free card, like oh, cut him some slack coz he dead, or whatever, but the fact remains that he dropped stone cold dead and never told anyone what he wanted done with his manuscripts. They were published post-humously, and who knows what went on with the editing (or didn't go on). From what I understand (and I'm certainly no expert), most writers and editors go through a lengthy process together weeding out the bad or unnecessary and beefing up the good. Larsson never had that chance, and Hornet's Nest being the third and last, logically he spent the least amount of time with it. 
 With that in mind, I've enjoyed getting lost in this trilogy. It's the kind of writing that makes you forget you're even reading and that forces you to stay up to ungodly hours. And, once again, Larsson managed to deliver an extremely powerful message on behalf of women everywhere, which is basically, don't fuck with us, you two-balled bastards. These books are the whole package. And who knows when I'll find *that* again?

 This was an odd book, and I'm not sure how much I entirely enjoyed it. I've been sitting on it for about three weeks, so I'm just going to lay it all out on the table and see where we land. 
 The main protag, Laureth, is blind, which I found unusual and interesting (especially given that the audio book I was listening to at the exact same time featured a deaf protagonist, but I digress). I liked that Marcus Sedgwick took the risk of having a character with a major disability because most a lot of authors in the YA genre give us characters who are Awesome, Unbelievably Awesome, and So Unbelievably Awesome It Should Be Criminal. And by "awesome" I mean, flawless. 
 So the change of pace was refreshing. 
 Laureth is on the hunt for her dad, who has mysteriously disappeared, and decides to fly from London to New York City with her little brother in tow, so he can be her guide of sorts. Someone found her author father's notebook and sent her pages from it, which in and of itself lends an eerie and sinister air to the story. What I had a hard time buying into was that she, as a sixteen-year-old girl, could easily fly internationally her brother and without parental supervision and only a simple note, without alarming any federal agents on either side of the pond. That just didn't add up to me and felt entirely too convenient as a way to get Laureth and her brother from London to New York with little hassle so Sedgwick could continue the story arc. 
 I also felt like the story lost a little bit of steam and meandered around while Laureth meandered trying to find her dad. I was fondly reminded of Home Alone 2: Lost In New York, just a little bit, when they checked into the hotel where her father was supposedly staying, because it reminded me of the adventures of Kevin MacCallister so many years ago, only much more serious and less fun. 
 I think overall I did enjoy this story, but so many things were just too convenient for me to really get into it. I did like the in-depth explanations on coincidence and how many times coincidence made an appearance in the story. I would have liked to have seen more from the stranger on the flight to NYC, because I felt that connection was interesting and instead it kind of petered out. I didn't like how Laureth was defensive of her disability. I guess I can understand it, but it bothered me because at the same time, she would say things like she didn't miss vision since she had never had it. Those two things didn't add up to me. 
 This was a good story though, and definitely unique to the YA genre, because there is nothing else like it that I know of. I enjoyed reading it, I loved the incorporation of philosophy and her father's letters and notes. I just think it could have been more.

5 Dregs STARS 
 "Six people, but a thousand ways this insane plan could go wrong." 
 How does she do it? Seriously, Leigh Bardugo has to be a blessing I was missing out because I just finished Six of Crows, after the Grisha trilogy, and I feel like she will ruin me for any other book in the future. 
 To say that I loved this story would be an understatement, especially because all the characters were so interesting and likeable. This is all told in a multiple third person POV, which I thought may be too much at the beginning, but I quickly realized it was just another perfect puzzle piece Bardugo creates for this book. I can't exhaust enough how amazing Bardugo's writing and world building are, but what may be the best, is how all the characters are made of deep multi-layers, that are rich in every sense. You get the good, the bad, the ugly; you get their thoughts, their feelings and what they long for. You get to see, feel and experience the stories of this rather dysfunctional group, and how they get to a point where they are just a another family, mighty criminal, looking out for each other. 
 "No mourners. No funerals. Among them, it passed for 'good luck." 
 So basically this is what you have: 
 6 characters, 5 POVs, 1 highly dangerous mission and way too many risky variables. 
 It makes for a great book, probably my favorite this year hands down. I think that the fact that I read the Grisha trilogy before this helped a lot to get into some world building context, but to say the truth, even if is in the same universe and just 2 years since the events of the GT ended, this book is based in a place that has nothing in common. You will get thrown to a different scenario, new characters with their own agendas and backstories that quickly catches your attention; so besides some Grisha culture, it wasn't much needed but I highly appreciated the fact that I read those books before for the whole experience of this story. 
 Even though we where missing Wylan's POV, the whole perspective of the book from Kaz, Inej, Jesper, Nina & Matthias was so well done, in a synchronized game of flashbacks and present actions that left me not being able to put this book down. 
 Kaz leaned back. 'What's the easiest way to steal a man's wallet?' 
 'Knife to the throat?' asked Inej. 
 'Gun to the back?' said Jesper. 
 'Poison in his cup?' suggested Nina. 
 'You're all horrible,' said Matthias. 
 The characters are just a group of teenagers, which at the beginning I thought it was gonna hard to relate, but that wasn't a problem at all. This world hasn't been fair to any of them, it has been rather cruel and some unlucky past events has led this 6 people to accept this risky mission: to steal the brain of jurda parem, something that would change the rules of all games, from the safest and most guarded place on Grisha world, the Ice Court. 
 "A gambler, a convict, a wayward son, a lost Grisha, a Suli girl who had become a killer, a boy from the Barrel who had become something worse." 
 They all had lived through a lot of things that has forced them to learn to adapt and grow up fast to find ways to survive- more than any other teens, especially given they live in Ketterdam's most dangerous side of town: the Barrel. Ketterdam, Kerch's capital, makes for a great escenario to this criminals, with its whole merchand vibe and turistic exotism. Also, as a side note, the component of the Komedie Brute that Bardugo creates for this culture (I``m ignorant about the topic and I`m not sure if she explained somewhere about what it is or where she took it, though I know is mostly similar to roman`s times and theatrical history) it is so aligned to this world and I counld't stop thinking how brilliant it was. 
 I have no words of how enthralling and captivating this book was. 
 All the characters are so well done that you dive from one head to another, getting to know them and seeing them interact, because the SASS, oh my, they had me laughing so much. 
 "We enter from the north as planned," Kaz said. 
 Jesper knocked his head against the hull and cast his eyes heavenward. "Fine. But if Pekka Rollins kill us all, I`m going to get Wylan`s ghost to teach my ghost how to play the flute just so I can annoy the hell out of your ghost." 
 Brekker`s lips quirked. "I`ll just hire Matthias`ghost to kick your ghot`s ass." 
 "My ghost won`t associate with your ghost," Matthias said primly, and then wondered if the sea air was rotting his brain. 
 Kaz Brekker is the big bad wolf, boss of the Dregs and probably someone with an intellect beyond measure because he makes sure that even the craziest plans work. There`s a lot of things behind the though mask he puts to everyone to look at, and most of it is related to why he seeks revenge from an old con artist. 
 "When everyone knows you're a monster, you needn't waste time doing every monstrous thing." 
 Inej Ghafa, the Wraith, is the queen of all Ketterdam`s secrets and dangerous with knives. She has a sad past, which has lead her to Kaz`s group as a powerful asset and to the closer to freedom she has been in while. I loved how she still was so close to her Suli culture and Ravkans Saints, but she was fierce to the core anyways. 
 Inej would find her own way in. The rules of fair play among the gangs were from Per Haskell`s time. Besides, she was the Wraith - the only law that applied to her was gravity, and some days she defied that, too. 
 Jesper Fahey, a zemeni boy who arrived to Ketterdam to study, but lost his way in the gambling dens. You would never see him without his guns, and he most certainly be ready to shoot his way out of trouble, but he definitely has a flirty side and one which he can`t make himself brave enough to face the truth about things. 
 Jesper just grinned and whispered, "Well, we've managed to get ourselves locked into the most secure prison in the world. We're either geniuses or the dumbest sons of bitches to ever breathe air." 
 Wyland Van Eck, son of one of Merchand Council's members. He is recruited because he is a safe way for this group to get paid, but there`s so much more to this guy than his knowledge of bombs and chemistry. Naive and good at heart, he is far from the criminal ways everyone else live by. 
 "Always hit where the mark isn't looking" 
 "Who's Mark?" asked Wylan." 
 Matthias Helvar, a Fjerdan druskelle or witchhunter, convicted for slavery in Kerch. Matthias was a great character because of his internal fight about if Grisha are good or bad, and the fact that him helping on this mission would make him a traitor again to his nation. Besides the fact that he struggles with his druskelle beliefs and all that he has know, he was still a person who believed in doing the right thing and all those moral thoughts will crash with what this mission has in store. 
 "Wanden olstrum end kendesorum. Isen ne bejstrum. The water hears and understands. The ice does not forgive." 
 Finally, Nina Zenik. She is a Grisha with a big secret and quite the mistakes, that lives in Ketterdam hoping to right a wrong that landed her in the island. She is such fierce, sassy and flirty character, I lived for her interactions because she always proved to be funny. Her being Grisha, Hearthrender, weights a lot on who she is and how she acts. 
 "You wouldn't know a good time if it sidled up to you and stuck a lollipop in your mouth." 
 Basically, I hope you get this books (the second book of this duology is out) and go read them ASAP!
