I picked up Legend with a lot of hope for a good, solid dystopian YA. However, what I found myself with was a fairly average story with a fairly average plot. 
 Let's break down the pros and cons of this book: 
  
 Pro - I liked the world building. I was fascinated by the idea that the United States had another civil war that tore out the very foundation of our world. I liked the trials being set up to separate the so called wheat from chaff. I also enjoyed the militaristic government that rules the Republic. For me, the world itself is set up very well. 
 Cons - The characters. They are boring and predictable. By the time the story wraps up, you can tell that 1. June and Day are going to fall for each other in a classic Aladdin fashion. Poor boy winning the heart of the rich girl. 2. Day's companion, Tess, will find herself losing the love of her life to said rich girl. This means she will employee every tactic she needs to ensure she digs her claws to prevent Day from leaving her for another. 3. Day will be the self acclaimed asshole. Because he will find himself in a tug-of-war between these two women, he will say things and do things that plays with the emotions of both. (just you wait, it's coming.) 
  
 I sat down and tried to figure out why these new beloved dystopian stories (Divergent, Maze Runner, and Matched being prime examples) leave me feeling empty and bored and I think I have figured it out. I grew up reading classic dystopains like The Giver, 1984, and Brave New World. So when I see these new main characters put into the situations they are in, all I can hear is them whining about how bad they have it and it just grates my nerves. So modern dystopians unfortunately are placed on a higher grading scale for me; greater expectations. Is it fair? No, but then it is a dystopian so fair is kind of the point. That being said, go pick it up and read it for yourself and make your own assessments about this trilogy, because when the rubber meets the road, there was enough intrigue at the conclusion of this book to encourage me to pick up the next.

A lot of people have problems with this book and why I can understand why, but in the hazy afterglow of finishing the story I just don't see them. Because what I see is that anyone could be Hannah. Anyone could have this experience, I am sure many people, both male and female, have. The best thing I can think to say to people who dislike/don't understand this book comes from another book about suicide, Jeffrey Eugenides' The Virgin Suicides, "Obviously, doctor, you've never been a thirteen year old girl." 
 While I think other books have done it better, I think this book does capture well what it is like to grow up and feel like you have no control over your life. To feel lost and alone and beaten down by everyone around you. To realize that the things you say or do may impact someone else without you ever thinking they will. Also, this is one of the fist novels I finished and didn't automatically IMDb the cast. Something tells me I am not going to be happy with the cast, don't ask me why.

 Look at the sun and see the clouds and the faces in the sky; what do you see? There are glowing animals and sharpened weapons, an eternity of possibilities buried within our own imagination. Pandemonium is the sky, and its cloud burn with a passion. 
 The beginning of Pandemonium is slow. Slow with a trail of beautiful words obscuring its monotonous events. It was dragging on and on, and though yes, I needed to understand and adjust to the Wilds, I had no wish for an abundance of gorgeous, plot-less language. 
 Enter page 165. This one quote (note, it's from the ARC, so it may be altered in the final copy) finally grounded me into the story... and from there on, Lauren Oliver captivated me once again. 
 "Her eyes have softened now, and I see how tired she is, and must always have been--to live for years and years and years this way, having to rip and shred just for a space to breathe." 
 After that halfway mark, you could hear a pin drop in the entire pandemonium of everything and everyone (pun intended). There were times when chills swallowed me whole, and I couldn't breathe. There were times when I wanted to smash the words apart, to rip the boundaries of fiction and reality and charge in for vengeance. Yet, as the action skyrocketed beyond expectation, and stakes reached above the edge of our sight, a subtle but constant annoyance slowly peaked within me. 
 Lena. 
 There was nothing specifically wrong with Lena. I could understand her motivation and intentions fairly well, and I can't exactly blame her for her choices--they had to be made. Except for one choice: and that is the one you see precariously inserted in the summary, that she may just fall in love again. 
 That, my dear friends, is my biggest problem. Oh, Lena, I know you thought your old love was dead. I know that things have been terribly hard and obscenely intense and staggeringly scarring, but were you really so desperate you could not help but fall in love with someone who couldn't possibly compete with what your old love did for you? I know love is a hopeless trap you can't claw your way out of once you fall in, but why oh why did you fall in in the first place? Did you forget? I know not everyone feels this way--quite the number of my friends certainly preferred Lena's new choice over her old one, but I'm sorry, I just can't see it. I'm torn between sympathy and understanding for Lena and fury at her for forgetting the most important thing of all. I suppose, then, that I will have to make my mind up in Requiem. Oh, please, will someone hand that aesthetic to me? Now? 
 Pandemonium is well worth its name. Its roads have diverged into the then and now, and without the fantastic imagination of the mind-blowing Lauren Oliver, it could have easily drowned in the deadly sea of second-books-that-suck-in-a-trilogy. 
 Even if it did--and it didn't--no matter. Lauren Oliver is known for her life rafts.

This book totally teetered on the edge of 5 stars for me. Adiga transports the reader to India with an outstanding first person narration. Balram is a servant with few prospects for happiness or self determination. The story highlights his attempt to change his life in the face of corruption and near enslavement. The portrayal of India and the wealthy class is not pretty. 
 For me, there were three components that really made this book great. First, Balram is not a uni-dimensional character. I found myself in his corner even while he does some pretty reprehensible things. It's hard to write characters like this, and Adiga does an outstanding job. 
 The author is also great with using words to create analogy and also a certain wittiness. He calls the uneducated "half baked" and identifies the situation that servants are in as being in as the "RoosterCoop", and his explanation of that concept is very good. He compares and contrasts the state of the India populace as either being in the Light or in the Darkness. These are just a few examples, but let's just say the prose is both thought provoking and illuminating. 
 Finally, in the context of today's world, the underlying themes are thought provoking. How bad does a situation need to be before it drives people to commit immoral acts to rectify it? In this book, on the face of it, Balram doesn't seem that desperate, but the author portrays his situation as ultimately untenable. To me, there are many parallels to this problem in other countries, and I read the book as more of a cautionary tale, but I think there are other interpretations that would be very interesting to discuss.

I am giving this book five stars too. I cannot believe I have read another marvelous book. I must be on a lucky streak! 
 I have read tons of holocaust literature, but this book deserves attention b/c there are fewer books about what happened to the people of the Baltic states during WW2 and their life under Stalin. This book is based on true life experiences, but put together in a novel format. It is totally convincing. It is also about a young girl growing into womanhood under exceptionally hard times. What can I say that isn't a spoiler?! We know of the horrors of WW2. These horrors were not restricted to those of Jewish background. You feel these horrors could happen to yourself. This book makes some of these horrors so real that they go beyond reading text in a book. You feel that what happens, happens to you. 
 Nevertheless, there is wonderful humor and kindness. I am not kidding; this book pulls it off. You laugh, you cry, you freeze, you are sick. You feel like giving up - but you don't because life is worth living. Some do not have the strength physically or mentally to survive, but some do. We must not forget why life is worth fighting for. 
 The writing is excellent. The author, step by step, makes you care for the characters, even the ones that at first seem insignificant or even disagreeable. I should give you several quotes, but here follows only one. The little girl in the following quote plays only a minor role, but when the reader reads this, you care about her too: 
 "Where's your doll?" I asked. 
 "Dead," said the girl with a hollow look in her eyes. 
 "Oh." 
 "The NKVD killed her. Remember how they shot the women with the baby? That's what they did to Liale, except they threw her in the air and shot her head off. Kind of like a pigeon." 
 "You must miss her a lot," I said. 
 "Well, I missed her at first. I kept crying and crying. A guard told me to stop crying. I tried, but I couldn't. He clobbered me in the head. See my scar?" she said, pointing to a thick red fold on her forehead. 
 Bastards, she was only a child. 
 "You couldn't stop crying either?" she asked. 
 "What?" 
 She pointed to the scar above my eyebrow. 
 "No, they hit me with a can of sardines," I said. 
 "Because you were crying?" she said. 
 "No just for fun," I answered. 
 She curled her fingers toward me, beckoning me closer "Want to know a big secret?" she asked. 
 "What's that?" 
 She leaned over and whispered in my ear. "Mama says the NKVD are going to hell." She leaned back. "But you can't tell anyone. It's a secret, okay? You see, Liale, my dolly, she's up in heaven. She talks to me. She tells me things. So that's a secret, but Liale said I could tell you." (72%) 
 I am not sure if it works to pop in and read just one section..... That a child thinks and says what this young girl says is so horrible. What has life done to a child to make them think this way. You are shocked about what she says because you have become attached to these people. Terribly attached. 
 Art is wonderfully worked into the book too. Do you know anything about the Norwegian artist Munch? Well, you will when you have read the book, and surely you will have sought more information on Wikipedia! 
 This is a perfect book both for young adults, and adults too!

A love song to Bayesian reasoning on par with http://xkcd.com/1132/. 
 Proposes an answer to a question that baffled me during the most recent economic collapse; why so many people driving the crisis maintained, with all apparent earnestness, that no one saw it coming while the record reveals that LOTS of people did. Lots of people spoke movingly about housing bubbles. Lots of people suspected that collateralized debt obligations were far riskier than rated and some were vastly overvalued. But the rating organizations Had Done The Math. They Knew The Risk. They Advised Their Clients. And They Caused A Whole Lot of Human Misery. Because, Silver said, they didn't get that risks could be cumulative; that it was quite possible a hiccup in the market could make people all around the country miss mortgage payments. And if the risks were cumulative, then the math is wrong. 
 Goes through a variety of forecasting and prediction fields and assays an analysis of what fields do it well, what do not. My attention wandered during the sports and gambling sections, but was riveted during the discussion of weather and earthquakes. He suggests that a little sharper analysis of the data would have shown that a 9.1 earthquake was quite foreseeable in Fukushima, and why the authorities thought it wasn't. The story of chess playing computers was great fun. 
 I think he gave a wee bit too much attention to climate skeptics. But I truly enjoyed his observation that "A conspiracy theory might be thought of as the laziest form of signal analysis. As the Harvard professor H. L. "Skip" Gates says, 'Conspiracy theories are an irresistible labor-saving device in the face of complexity.'" 417. 
 Great last line. "May we rise from the ashes of these beaten but not bowed, a little more modest about our forecasting abilities, and a little less likely to repeat our mistakes." (454).

Patrick Ness brings us Siobhan Dowd's last idea, a simple story about a boy called Conor, and takes us through the stages of grief as he slowly comes to terms with his mother's illness. I can strongly relate to Conor - I was 16 when my mother died of Multiple Sclerosis. It was a pretty horrible time and Conor's truth is something I can relate to - but I didn't feel guilty about it. I think Conor's age (14 I believe) may have something to do with why he feels so guilty, although 14 and 16 is a relatively small age gap, it's pretty huge in terms of mental development. 
 The curse of the hype - it gets to us all. There was so much hype surrounding this book, that I eagerly bought a copy, and read it with a lot of anticipation, waiting to be moved to tears when I got to the end. Only... that didn't happen. And now I'm left with a sort of 'is that it?' feeling. Don't get me wrong, the ending was beautifully sad, the drawings were as wild and destructive as Conor's monster, everything was perfect. But I was just waiting for more. The story itself is exactly what I expected. Simple, yet full of mystery until we get to that final chapter, the ending we've all been waiting for. I found the ending painfully obvious and spent a lot of the book waiting and hoping for a twist in the tale. 
 Altogether, the book really pulled me in and kept me reaidng from the beginning right to the very end which is pretty impressive, even for a short book. I do wish there would have been stronger character development, particularly Conor's father who was the most stereotypical character in the book. The illustrations are much stronger than the actual story which I'm not sure is a good thing but they were pretty amazing! If you buy this for any reason, buy it for the illustrator.

 This book was pretty darn awesome and it kept me hooked from beginning to end. It has a pretty original feel to it and that of course made me like it more. Also, it isn't a paranormal book that is romantically driven. Sure there is romance, but the main focus of the story is more to do with the demons and the trouble they cause. 
 Our heroine Riley is a very strong one. She is tough and determined and can hold her own. However, she is also very stubborn. She is possibly the most stubborn character I have ever encountered in all my reading adventures to date. She is the kind of character that just does not know when to ask for help and that is ALWAYS a trait that makes me crazy. She is also very argumentative. Because of this, there were a lot of moments where I wanted to punch her. However, in the end I do admire her as a character and I like that she isn't a damsel in distress. 
 The novel presents us with two guys. A love triangle, yes, but this is a good one and it didn't really aggravate me. First we have Simon. Simon is a good boy who plays by the rules. He is incredibly sweet and adorable and good hearted. So naturally, I don't trust him. Then we have Beck. Beck is cranky and overbearing and a general pain in the ass. Naturally, I adore him and want to huggle him. 
 Like I said though, The Demon Trapper's Daughter is not romantically driven. The story is about Riley learning to cope and survive in the face of a devastating tragedy. It is about her growing up and dealing with things you may not want to deal with. Of course this is all done with demons getting in the way. 
 I really loved the way this book was written. It is written in the third person and I love books like that. I love getting in different characters heads and seeing the story outside of one characters bubble. I especially loved seeing from Beck's perspective. It really enabled the reader to understand him. Had we only seen him from Riley's POV, the reader would think he is a jerk plain and simple and not someone who has Riley's best interests at heart. 
 All in all, The Demon Trapper's Daughter is a very engaging read. There is action from beginning to end and that keep you hooked to the pages. I cannot wait to start the next chapter of this story.

I think the title of this book should have been "How Adrian Got His Groove Back." I know so much more happened in this book, but, come on, Adrian becoming Adrian again tops all. 
 Ok, I will stop from my Adrian fangirling (for a moment). Indigo Spell finds Sydney still trying to figure out what to do about all of the changes in her life. She doesn't trust the Alchemists after learning more about their internal dealings, which leads her to track down Marcus, the only person she believes can help her discover the truth about her leaders. What she finds when she meets Marcus, isn't the save all/end all she was expecting. Instead Marcus wants things from her in return, things that Sydney isn't sure she can provide. 
 Along with the Marcus issue, Sydney's dealings into the art of magic have taken a more serious turn. Her teacher, Ms. Terwilliger, pushes Sydney to delve deeper into defensive magic when she drops the bomb that there's a witch out there draining the life and power of other witches. 
 And then of course, behind all of this, there's still the duty of protecting Jill and keeping their lives secret in Palm Springs. 
 What I loved about Indigo Spell was it finally showed Sydney beginning to break away from this mold that she had been formed into. Instead of just following orders without questions, she's pushing limits and not just her own. She's questioning everything around her and herself. Also, she's finally getting her own personality. 
 While this is a story told from Sydney's POV, I feel the side characters bring so much to the plot. I adore Eddie, I have since the Vampire Academy series. Jill is starting to grow on me. She stood up to Sydney in this one and was actually the voice of reason to a point. I'm still not a fan of Angeline, but I can tolerate her. 
 But of course, my main attraction to this series is Adrian. After two books of him moping and chasing after Sydney, I feel like we finally get him back in this book. Even though he still admits to loving Sydney and not stopping anytime soon... 
 "I'm going to just go on loving you, even if it's hopeless" 
 "You're my flame in the dark. We chase away the shadows around each other." 
 His charm and wit are back full-force, but so is his heart and his loyalty. 
 Indigo Spell found our characters is some stressful situations and also opened the door to future challenges. Along the way Richelle Mead never lost the humor. Both Adrian and Marcus, while involved in the heavy situations, provided much needed comic relief for us. I mean, who can resist Hopper? 
 I anxiously look forward to the next book based on what Mead left us with there at the end.

Emotionally-charged, epic story by Kristin Hannah

 is both heartwarming and heartbreaking. Have a box of tissues handy if you are planning to read! I picked this book up at a Used Book Sale this year -- after loving The Nightingale. Today, I just needed something different to read -- so I pulled it off the shelf. I almost couldn't put it down until it was complete! I was a bit late in picking my son up from swim practice (but traffic happens!!)... 
 This is a story about love, survival, and repairing relationships.... 
 I don't want to spoil the plot - so will keep additional comments brief. This book switches between two main settings - Washington, USA in early 2000's on the family orchard and Leningrad / St. Petersburg, Russia in late 1930's / early 1940's during Stalin's rise to power and then the German invasion. 
 The older plot line is developed in the form of a fairy tale. The two are effectively interwoven together and the change in setting is easy to follow. 
 The circumstances in Leningrad / St. Petersburg are beyond most reader's imagination, especially when the Germans have blockaded the city and food is scarce. More current plotline is of an upper middle class American family, with your standard dose of dysfunction thrown in. 
 Why not 5 stars? While I really enjoyed this read, there were events on top of events that were just implausible.... Obviously, did not have a major impact on my enjoyment of the book -- as I devoured it today.... 
 "We women make choices for others, not for ourselves, and when we are mothers, we...bear what we must for our children. You will protect them. It will hurt you; it will hurt them. Your job is to hide that your heart is breaking and do what they need you to do." 
 I would highly recommend this book to readers who enjoy historical fiction. If you liked The Nightingale, consider giving this book a try.

Henry DeTamble is a librarian in Chicago. What makes him remarkable is that he is a time traveler as well. Clare Abshire met Henry for the first time when she was a child and his appearances in her life have defined her existence. But can a time traveler have a successful marriage? And can a normal woman be truly satisfied with a husband who disappears with no control? 
 I really expected to love this book. I expected to feel anything but ambivalent about it. But that's exactly how I feel. For the majority of the time I was reading, I couldn't get the annoyance of this book being shelved in fiction instead of science fiction/fantasy out of my head. I'm sorry but time travel is SCIENCE FICTION. So, that definitely contributed to my ambivalence about the book. Additionally, Clare and Henry do not have particularly distinctive voices until the last third of the book. For the majority of the time, they are nearly impossible to tell apart. I didn't feel particularly drawn to either character and I didn't understand why I should care about them. Clare is particularly unsympathetic - poor Clare, money is so lonely and I'm sure it's incredibly difficult knowing your entire life who you're going to marry, especially if you already love him. Henry just seemed slightly unbelievable - I think his interest in punk was just a way for the author to demonstrate how hip and underground she was since it didn't suit his character at all. I was also slightly bothered that they never explained the specifics of Henry's time travel. I'll admit, that stuff usually goes over my head (like on the TV show 'Lost'), but I still would have appreciated the attempt. I know this sounds like I hated the book, but there were some parts I really enjoyed. The love and admiration between Henry and Clare was quite nice (though the sex seemed a bit unrealistic) and I especially enjoyed the scenes where Henry traveled to horrifying episodes of his life and his helplessness at those moments. I absolutely loved the ending, enough to cry. I just think this was a disappointment, not at all the masterpiece I expected.

Ok, so I've decided a few things: 
 1. The scribe virgin is a hateful bitch that I want to punch in her glowing face. I wasn't a fan in book one, but this one sealed the deal. 
 2. The brothers are all "tough guys" but are some of the whiniest characters I've ever seen. They throw the biggest tantrums, and pout. Sometimes I want to tell them to grow the fuck up. 
 3. I think Butch is the best. 
 4. Just as the story was rolling, the end. What? That wasn't an end of a book. It was the end of a chapter. 
 5. I have a problem - I will continue to read this series. Because I know it has an end (unlike Anita Blake where I finally had to throw in the towel). It is a sick addiction of mine to see a series through. 
 6. The unquestioned acceptance of the humans to the vampire's weird terminology, calling people male/female instead of man/woman, for example, baffles me. I would turn to someone and at least raise an eye brow. 
 7. Since when did the ability, or lack there of, to have kids make someone's life worth more or less in a book? Or in real life? And what does that say about those of us who are childless by choice? 
 All that aside, the overall story is good. I was able to get into the story more with this one, since there was less "getting to know you" even though the focus was on a different pair. 
 The Lessening Society make for creepy ass bad guys. And the fact they smell like baby-powder, well thanks for ruining THAT smell for me. 
 And I have to mention, that I listened to this on audio. The narrator is horrible. Very monotone. No inflection, and no different tones for each character. Which makes it hard to decide who is talking in long conversations. And the editing is bad too. There are some parts that have too long a pause, up to 15 seconds. Long enough I think it might be broke. Then there are the parts where a break is needed and there is none. 
 But like I said, the overall story is a good solid one, and I have a problem that compels me to continue with a series. But it won't top my TBR list, that's for sure. I know several people have loved this series, and especially certain characters, but I just ... can't.

Oh, and Arya's ringer. Poor girl. Arya should definitely just stay with Clegane and become an apprentice pillaging anarcho-knight.  Oh...and Theon Greyjoy isn't dead? He's like the only pseudo-baddie who isn't by the end of this book. Not sure why I care. Although it seems we're unlikely to hear from him anytime soon.

Man, she is going to be piiiiissed. 
 There are some serious critiques to be made of these books - they're not perfect and cheesy and draggy in places, to be sure - and some of the names are downright redonkulous - but I'm having too much fun blowing through them to worry about it. Satisfying, entertaining, chunky, like snorkeling through a gallon of rocky road ice cream without the stomach ache and regret that follows.

I don't know why I avoided reading Dashiell Hammett. I knew he was an influence on Raymond Chandler, whose work I love, but I only had the vaguest idea about what The Maltese Falcon was about. Turns out, it's not that different to Raymond Chandler's work, and Sam Spade is in the same mould as Philip Marlowe (well, the other way round, technically). It's the same sort of world, the same sort of morals, and though I think Raymond Chandler's writing was a lot more sharp and clear, a lot more new, Dashiell Hammett is nothing to sniff at. And, actually, I think his plots are that mite easier to follow. 
 Sam Spade's a good character -- it's hard to follow his motivations at times, hard to figure out what he'll do, but he also makes his own kind of sense. And he has some excellent lines.

As others have said, there is a somewhat lighter tone to the book overall, though it is still a dystopian world. The economy has collapsed, the prison system is being used as a socio-economic experiment of sorts, and there are, again, disturbing chicken practices. But that being said, I felt like Atwood honed in more than she has recently on characters -- more specifically, on just a couple of characters. Their disparate qualities, gender-conforming qualities (at first) play well off of one another, and we have gotten to know these two pretty well by the time additional strange characters are added to the mix. The Maddadam Trilogy didn't work so well later on for lacking this character-driven quality. I really enjoyed this book, and feel re-drawn to Atwood. Between the plot and the characters, Atwood still makes large statements about and battles against societal standards and inequities, but it somehow feels more manageable in this novel.

Lorraine Heath is such a solid writer and she's made a fairly terrible concept (to me, anyway) - young ruffian turned Lord hero, asks heroine to school his ruffian beloved for being a wife of a Lord and then, along the way, they fall in love instead - into something eminently readable. 
 Two strong characters at the centre of this. For me, the heroine, Catherine, outshone the hero. There's a lot of talk in romance novels of gutsy, interesting, intelligent women who don't even really fee like those things to the reader. Not so here. Catherine felt like all of those things and yet still felt period appropriate. Perhaps it stretches the boundaries of credibility that she was gallivanting off to a gaming hell in the middle of the night but, then, she is basically her own mistress because of her father's condition. I liked Catherine. A lot. 
 Luke, was less good. I'm going to have to blame Heath a bit here because for a clever man he is utterly unaware about the true nature of his 'love' for Frannie and that dragged on, for me, waaaaay too long. It also took the tarnish off the romance a bit because it meant he was cheating on Frannie with Catherine but not bothered by it. 
 Great romance though. Amazing sexual tension. Wish the sex had been a wee bit hotter for all that telegraphing. Early on Luke talks about pounding into a woman in a way that was hot and I wish we'd got some of that hotness in the follow through. That said, it was still good by any reasonable standard. 
 Some of Heath's language bothers me from time to time. She has a tendency to slip into fruity language, or drifts into the realm of the obvious with her explaining. It's so incongruous to me, I wonder if it isn't an editor at Avon saying 'this isn't clear enough' [when it is] or 'we need more feelings' [when they're already there, and all the better for the restraint with which they've been done]. 
 This is, however, a solid four stars every day of the week. I am looking forward to making my way slowly through Heath's back catalogue.

 Alice in Wonderland is a pretty trippy tale, and Splintered does a great job of taking the book's signature elements -- things like the looking glass, the Red Queen, the White Rabbit, the caterpillar -- and weaving them into a completely different story that's still true to the original. That old "girl who's afraid she looks/acts like her crazy/dead mother" isn't a brand-new trope in YA, but the "girl who hears bugs talking" certainly is. I loved the beginning of Splintered, which shows us Alyssa making bug collages, Alyssa plugging in earphones and heading to the skate park to drown out the bug voices, Alyssa visiting her mother in the mental institution. Alyssa's in love with her best friend, a fellow skateboarder and former juvenile delinquent named Jeb, who is in love with mean girl Taelor, who is just as annoying as the spelling of her name. 
 Most of the story takes place in Splintered's version of Wonderland. To me, this part of the book was strongly reminiscent of the fae fiction I've read -- rival queens and courts, tests to endure, characters under spells and curses. If you loved the Wicked Lovely series by Melissa Marr, Splintered will definitely be your kind of book.

I remember sitting in English Lit class in high school and discussing an overarching theme that appears in many great novels: Good vs Evil. As a reader, you desperately want Good to prevail. You want Evil to be vanquished. But what happens when, as it so happens in the real world, Good and Evil are not two distinct elements but present together in each individual person? How do we live in close relationship with people who are arguably as Evil as they are Good? And are we able to recognize that struggle within ourselves? 
 What would you do if you found a letter from your husband, written to you, to be opened at the time of his death? Would you open it? What if he was still alive? What if he explicitly told you not to open it? That's the choice laid before Cecilia Fitzpatrick. Her decision would change her family completely. 
 The Husband's Secret by Liane Moriarty is an incredibly compelling read that I could not put down. I sat in my living room and just read, gasping and telling my husband all about it. "You probably won't read this book, right?" I asked him, knowing full well that he wouldn't, no matter how good I told him it was. "Okay, good. Because I need to talk about it to someone!" I became fully engulfed in the sinews of the story; the way all the characters connected and the way that single decisions affected another character's whole world. 
 I think we all like to think of ourselves as good people. When we mess up, we want grace. We want forgiveness. We want people to remember the person we are when we are at our best and move on. But it isn't that easy. Our actions have lasting effects. And we feel the lasting effects of others' actions so acutely that we don't want to move on. We don't want to forgive. We don't want to forget. Should people pay for one evil action forever? Should we pay for our own actions forever? 
 These questions challenged me as I read through the The Husband's Secret. John-Paul did something completely awful and got away with it for a long time, except that he paid for it in his own way. He constantly made sacrifices to his guilt to atone for his sin. Every character in this book steps outside the parameters of what it means to be "Good". Cecilia finds out about her husband's misdeed through deception and it changes her life forever. As the story progresses, we're introduced to other primary characters who are living through the hurtful actions of others and trying to justify the hurtful things they do themselves. 
 Who are the good guys? Who are the bad guys? As readers, do we want John-Paul, a good husband and father who is broken by his guilt, to be found out? If he is, what will happen to his family? To his children? No, he's too "Good". Despite his actions, there needs to be some way out of this for him. Except, what about the family he hurt? What about the family that he forever changed? They've been feeling his actions for so long. Don't they deserve answers? They too are so "Good". And what about the man that is falsely accused? Doesn't he deserve to be cleared? There is no winning solution for the reader. The Good simply can't win in this book. 
 Liane Moriarty writes a novel that challenges a reader's morality while blurring the lines between right & wrong and good & evil. She accomplishes it all in a page-turner that simply cannot be put down. It was a favourite read of mine in 2013 and I will be suggesting it to other readers for a long time coming.

I think the ideas here are more successful than the execution, but I still really liked this. Set in Depression-era Seattle, the A-plot follows Flora and Henry - a black girl and a white boy - as they fall in love in Flora's underground jazz club. They're both passionate musicians, they're both orphans, and they're both pawns in a game played by Love and Death (yeah, I know how it sounds, but trust me - it works). If they choose their love, despite all of the obstacles, Love wins, and both players survive. If they don't, Death wins and claims Flora's life. 
 Flora and Henry are both nicely drawn characters, but their relationship never totally makes sense to me; it's very much the "instant connection from across the room" model of YA romance. Their relationship works much better in the context of the game - if you think of them as yet another star-crossed couple following in the footsteps of Romeo and Juliet, their relationship doesn't really need to be more than a stereotype, since they inherit all of the baggage of their forebears. 
 The Death vs. Love thing does lead to some overblown narrative towards the end, but I don't mind it, and I like the conclusion the book eventually reaches re: whether those forces are opposed at all, in the end. 
 Anyway: the writing here is solid, the setting is unusual, and the characters work really well even if they don't make sense together. And I'm a sucker for the ending. So I like this.

The 2017 Man Booker jury are to be congratulated for choosing such a strong longlist, in part for the quality of the books they chose, but mainly for resisting the calls to include this, the lovechild of 2016's winner The Sellout and 2014's nadir, To Rise Again at a Decent Hour. 
 At least those books had the merit of being relatively brief but this weighs it an 620 interminable pages of lame prose. "Later all of this blather will be edited out" we are told early on (in reference to the video of the Packer Attacker). Hopefully there will be a second edition of The Nix taking the same approach, and I may be tempted to revisit the resultant novella. 
 But as a reminder to myself why not to do so, a typical passage reads: 
 The kitchen urgently needed renovation: The countertop laminate was cracking and curling at the edges, and the dishwasher stopped working last spring, and the garbage disposal died maybe a year ago, and three of the four burners on the stove were useless, and the refrigerator had lately gone insane--the fridge side shutting down unpredictably and spoiling hot dogs and lunch meats and souring milk while the freezer side occasionally went hyperactive and locked all his TV dinners in permafrost.  The software's inner brain is made of literally millions of words written by the nation's high-school and college students, and Samuel sometimes jokes to his colleagues that of the software ever achieved sci-for artificial intelligence and consciousness, it would immediately go to Cancun for spring break. 
 I am genuinely glad for my GR friends who loved this - but if a scientist tried to concoct the perfect book tailor made for me to dislike, he would find Nathan Hill beat him to it. 
 By page 70 even the characters were getting fed up with each other.

This book gave me serious anxiety. The main character goes on a bit of a rabbit hole down a NYC society path and racks up unseemly amounts of debt while trying to amass social cache. I honestly had to flip ahead during some chapters because I was getting such bad secondary embarrassment.

Three Orsk furniture superstore employees, Basil, Amy, and Ruth-Anne, agree to work a dusk til dawn shift in order to catch the perpetrator of the strange occurrences that have been happening at their store and ruining stock and vandalizing property. During their all-nighter, they'll encounter horrors they never would have expected. 
 Horrorstor by Grady Hendrix is a fantastic horror comedy novel which is designed to resemble an IKEA catalog. It's a little slow to start, but I thoroughly enjoyed this story. Now, aside from being a librarian, I also work in a retail environment and you can see some really crazy things on a regular basis. Plus, you meet all sorts of people that otherwise you would probably never meet. That being said I could relate to this IKEA knock-off superstore's employees. Seriously, the cast of characters seem very real - I know people that are quite similar to those taking center stage here. Hendrix succeeds at creepy, and sometimes gory, horror as he is at creating characters and comedy. I don't want to spoil too much of it, but have you ever visited the "Squirrel Cage" Jail Museum in Council Bluffs, Iowa? In other words, it's really creepy, especially considering the huge empty store setting. 
 Overall, I highly recommend Horrorstor by Grady Hendrix, especially if you enjoy horror with a side of humor. If you're a fan of American Horror Story, I expect you'll love this novel. I'm really looking forward to his newest novel, My Best Friend's Exorcism, and I'm interested in seeing what becomes of the forth-coming Horrorstor tv adaptation.

Review of White Trash Beautiful by Teresa Mummert Book Blurb 
 A word-of-mouth bestseller that's captivating readers with its honesty, grit, and headstrong heroine, White Trash Beautiful is a story for anyone who has ever felt trapped in life, cheated by love--and longed for something more . . . Cass Daniels isn't waiting for her knight in shining armor. She knows that girls like her don't get a happily ever after. Not if you live in a trailer with your mom, work at a greasy spoon diner, and get leered at by old men. Maybe that's why she puts up with Jackson--her poor excuse for a boyfriend, who treats her like dirt. Cass has learned to accept her lot in life. That is, until he walks into her diner. . . . His name is Tucker White, and he's different from any man Cass has ever known. Tall, tattooed, and bad-ass gorgeous, he's the lead singer of the rock band Damaged. From the moment they meet, Tucker sees something in Cass he just can't shake. Something beautiful. Something haunted. Something special. And he's determined to find out what it is--if only he can get her to open up and let him in. . . . 
 My Review 
 I really wanted to like this book...I mean the name...the cover...I just knew I was going to be hooked. Eh, not so much. 
 The writing style seemed a bit rushed to me. In what world does a drop dead gorgeous rock star waltz into a run down diner to rescue a sullen waitress he just met. There was little interaction to warrent his night in shining armor routine. 
 The story was not well developed and left me full of questions...Why? Why? Why? 
 I tried to connect with Cass and wrap my head around why this young beautiful woman would allow herself to continue to live in the crappiest of situations. From her abusive good for nothing junkie boyfriend to her drugged out crackhead mother. Why Cass? Why??? 
 And the decisions she makes....damn Cass, you gotta brain honey, use it! 
 Then there is Tucker....what do we know about Tucker? 
 Not much at all. He's a rock star. He loves Cass. BUT WHY??? 
 The characters were not fully developed and lacked any real depth, especially Tucker. I came away from the book feeling like I hardly know anything about him and still having the question, WHY HER? 
 I just need a reason why Tucker falls instantly in love with Cass without having an actual conversation with her other than ordering a burger and a beer! Am I the only one frustrated by this?!?! Sorry, not sorry, this really bugs me!!! 
 I really wanted to love this book but it did not resonate with me. It's not relatable, it's not believable and most of it did not make much sense. 
 The ending was over the top and left me feeling a bit unsettled. 
 Overall I rate this book 1 out of 5 stars and would not recommend. 
 It was not my cup of tea to say the least!

I was screaming at her to knee him in his cheating man bits and run into the arms of the hot Nordic Sex God that comes complete with a life time supply of sex toys.  Lucien is not a man that loves, he can't and he sure as hell won't. He might lust and he might like and he sure as hell fucks - but love is not something he wants.  'Theirs was a closeness that went way beyond the physical proximity.

 Kitty French did an amazing job on the conclusion of the Knight & Play book. You got to see the strong and confident Sophie emerge. The Sophie that Lucien knew was lying just beneath the surface. And oh are there moments that will cause a lump in your throat. His struggle not to give in to the need he has for her, the fight to not love something when everything inside is pulling you towards it. It was crushing. I felt so much hurt for him in those moments. 
 He fought his love for her while she fought for him because she loved him enough. 
 "I don't want to wake up and find you're not really here," he whispered, not yet opening his eyes.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Generally speaking, when a book is the second in a trilogy or series, it tends to be weaker than the first. It's usually in the awkward part of the aftermath of whatever the first was setting up. It is also tasked with setting up for what comes next. So even though I was ecstatic to have a chance to read this, I was also leery of it being inferior to "Divergent". I am happy to report that I didn't feel this way at all. 
 Thankfully it picks up right where "Divergent" left off. There is no one month to year gap in which we have to play catch up on anything we missed during that time. I tend to get annoyed with plots/authors that carry on in that fashion. It wasted so much time recapping when the story could just have been told to begin with. We follow Tris, Four (as I refuse to call him Tobias), Caleb, and Marcus as they journey to the other factions (Amity and Candor) to make them aware of the teaming up of Dauntless and Erudite factions and make known the war started against Abnegation. Sadly, both refuse to get involved and only offer to take in those displaced from the war that's begun. All we really know at this point is that Jeanine Matthews (Erudite leader and resident genius) wants to collect all Divergent people for study purposes. We are unsure why they have become so important. All we know is that it is to *supposedly* protect the city from the outside. From here the plot can at times become confusing. Four's mother comes back into the picture as the leader of the factionless who are planning to stop the Erudite/Dauntless combination from warring on everyone else. There are some subplots going on as well that can make things confusing at times. 
 I'm not going to lie here. I loved Tris as a protagonist, but in this book, there were times she annoyed the crap out of me. She became reckless and was almost selfless to the point I wanted to slap her. Not to mention that her guilt over killing Will was drawn out up until the very end of "Insurgent". After awhile, it got really old. She was refusing to defend herself and was about to die because she thought it was for the best. UGH. Then there was Four... I cannot seem to make myself call him Tobias no matter how hard I try. I am not sure if that is because he was introduced to us as Four and that was the character I fell in love with or what. But he is always called Tobias here and it seems wrong. Perhaps he needs a new name altogether as he is a different person in this book. He is still the caring, lovable, sweet guy we know; but also has some harder edges. He becomes selfish in his love for Tris and tries to protect her, which she doesn't allow. The majority of the book, I felt his heartbreak over her carelessness and disregard for his feelings. Had there been another love interest for her in the series, I'm sure this would have been the point she'd have struggled with a love triangle. The two were either arguing or avoiding each other for most of the book. That in itself made me sad. The leaders of the other factions were all weak and pretty much unlikable here. Marcus had a large part and was obnoxious in his own right. His refusal to give up information drove me nuts. I wouldn't have been able to coddle him in order to get information. I'd most likely have used force to get what I wanted. I always had thought Tris's brother, Caleb, was odd. And he turned out to be a traitor as well. My heart did break for her here. The only family she had left betrayed her. All to protect something that was ready to be revealed to all. 
 Now, for the plot critique. "Divergent" hinted at being protected from the outside. There is more hinting of this until the end, when finally all is revealed. This was a lot of what kept me reading. I wanted to know WHAT it was. I wasn't entirely surprised, although we are still not aware of exactly how much is out there. Am I a tad disappointed? Yes. But now we at least know that much. It's almost like that movie "The Village". Separated by the rest of the world by a fence. Now though, the Divergent are supposed to be released in order to fix things. Hmm. And how? I'm curious to see where the story goes from here. All the simulations and murder were to keep everyone inside? That's it? It can't be... there MUST be more. The cliffhanger left us with a video of Tris's family member announcing all of this and reporting that she was to forget things and take on a new identity. So was it her mother? Grandmother? We're left hanging until the next book. 
 Overall, I really, really liked "Insurgent". It was a great follow-up to "Divergent" and really keeps the pace of the series going. It's not slow like many middle books tend to be. There is always action or some conflict going on; whether physical or emotional. Some characters take on different personas temporarily and it manages to work. The book definitely has its moments of suspense that keep you reading. You can't help but be curious to find out what is going on. I am so excited for the next book in the series!!

No lie, I am extremely conflicted about this book. 
 On the one hand, the writing is great. I've read Novik's other works, and this book shows how talented she truly is. It might be her best yet. It's unique and imaginative, while remaining loyal to the Old-Fashioned Fantasy genre. The world is bright and gorgeous, the action is fast-paced, and the friendship between Agnieszka and Kasia is sweet and believable. 
 Bonus points for a main character with a totally common, yet non-English, name. (Ag-nee-ESH-kuh and KAH-shuh, respectively, for those who are wondering.) The creepy forest is a recurring, and recurringly interesting, theme. 
 On the other hand: the Dragon. He's a total dirtbag, and Agnieszka just... takes it. Trying to prove she's worthy of his notice, over and over again, while the object of her affection (determination?) belittles and berates her like a child. Their relationship is so well-written from an insider's perspective of abuse that it inspired worry for the author. 
 While this book gets points for Agnieszka's process-- she eventually wakes up to the lolz-y realization the Dragon doesn't love anyone but himself and leaves him-- I could not, in good conscience, place this book in the hands of a naive and hormone-ridden young person, hoping they will take this story with a grain of salt. Especially because Agnieszka's reason for leaving the Dragon is not especially clear. From her perspective, it's more of a "you're a stick in the mud" than a "you make me feel like garbage" situation. 
 (If I sound like a stick in the mud myself, please remember all of the books undeservedly-banned for containing Real Talk about periods, death, or homosexuality in penguins. I never underestimate the power books have over their readers, or Helicopter Parents.) 
 On a third hand I don't yet have, far more believable is Agnieszka's devotion to her best friend Kasia, who stars as the hero in all her childhood games of make-believe. And who she trusts more than any person on earth. And who she would willingly endanger herself to save, no matter the personal cost. Whose thick, wheat-blonde braid is gloriously shiny. Whose eyelashes are long and beautiful resting against her cheeks, and whose eyes are liquid pools filled with emotio--nevermind all that, here is a grumpy male wizard. Agnieszka is totally straight, nothing but girl-girl friendship right here.

I've read the reviews for this book and I can tell it's really brought people together, because, as I said before, Cath loved reading, writing and all of the above just like us! It was a perfect combination. Rowell also does a great job of depicting how hard it can be for someone to move away from his or her loved ones, or the difficulties with the social aspects of college, or even the academic parts. It just seemed to truly combine what life can be or is for some people, while making a truly interesting story. 
 Story 
 The story was just great. Overall, there seemed to be a great balance with Cath's social aspect, at least in the middle of the novel, her struggles, her self-realizations, etc. Rowell did a fantastic job in portraying a realistic character-it didn't hurt that she was fun and exciting too. I liked the college atmosphere, even though we didn't get to see a lot of it, but I could tell when Cath spent time with other people apart from those she mingled with during classes. It was great to see Cath gradually progress into someone who we could all admire even more than we did in the beginning. I also admired how Cath never gave up, or sacrificed, what she believed was important. It's crucial to recognize authors who respect a person's true personality and make sure that there is an emphasis that it's okay to change a little but i's okay to remain the same too (some authors are too much on one side of the social spectrum, it can be hurtful (:). Regardless, Rowell did an amazing job with the story and I really respect the character developments she included with not only Cath, but also Wren, Reagan, and Levi (not so much, but there was some things) (because the other characters are just as important [sometimes I forget because I am too engrossed in one character]). 
 What made this book so special was the mini/stories of Simon Snow. It was like reading two stories simultaneously--I loved it! It was great to see how literature can affect people, and it was even better seeing how it affected all of Cath's daily activities and how everyone seem to know Simon Snow because it was that popular. I saw a few reviews where they described Simon Snow as our modern day Harry Potter series, and I couldn't agree more. There's something about paranormal, mythical creatures that brings everyone together! I also thoroughly enjoyed Cath (and I suppose Wren's) take on Simon Snow, Baz and Simon's wonderful relationship-loved it!! 
 Characters 
 Cath: Great! Just great! She was enthusiastic, she knew what she loved, while she didn't know how or what she wanted in life, or how she wanted to approach life (which was completely fine by me, cause I mean who really does?), she seemed to get through it. Her relationship with her roommate Reagan was realistic and just overall grand. I mean that's how people usually meet: super awkward at first and then the relationship turns into something more realistic, or it just becomes something irrelevant. I loved how mean they were to each other, and Rowell spared no expense when trying to show that it was okay to have fun even when sitting in a lunch room making fun of people-it's light, guys, she's not threatening anyone. I am just saying, while I am not advocating for bullying, it's realistic to say that doing something jokingly canbe okay. 
 Reagan: Loved how she interacted with people. I also found the way she reacted to (I cannot say specifics) certain events *cough* *cough* was super realistic, sweet and just laid-back, which seems to be the type of person Reagan is. Loved it! 
 Wren: While I didn't seem to enjoy her character as much as Cath, I did like the moments Cath and Wren shared together. Since I do not have sibling, I found myself getting extremely irritated when Wren would ignore or be rude to Cath, and while this "type of personality" (whatever that means) didn't stay for long, I couldn't find it within myself to be like "hey, Serena, it's okay. They're fine." In my mind, she was so rude and hurtful and I blame the fact that I am only child and wouldn't understand what a true sibling relationship would be. 
 Levi: I will not get too into his character, as I know I will spoil something, but I will say this: for some reason, from how Rowell described him, I couldn't seem to get a clear picture of what he looked like. Usually, I have a vivid imagination of what characters look like, but for some reason, Levi is just not being pictured together well. So if someone has any "celebrity look a likes" they want to provide me with, please go ahead! Anyway, Levi was fun and forward, which I liked, and he seemed to be an overall nice guy. That's all I shall say(: 
 I loved this book, I recommend it to the entire Goodreads community (it's just that good) and I hope everyone enjoys it as much as I did (like I know you will [I am reading this way too late, so I am sure everyone has already read it, but I'll recommend it anyway])! 
 -Serena

I didn't know you could write like this, Mr. Gaiman. 
 That's not to say I haven't enjoyed your other books. "Coraline" was a creepy joy, and "Sandman" felt like a very long, very sad and angry dream. Stardust never lived up to what I expected but that was alright. I haven't tried the Ocean at the End of the Lane yet. I will eventually, since it's on my shelf. 
 But "American Gods" was a Gaiman book I did not expect to love as much as I did. While I'm not exactly head-over-heels here, I enjoyed 99% of the book, and the parts that lagged in comparison to the others were at a disadvantage. Gaiman's writing soars so high here that when he takes a breather, you can tell, but you can forgive it. 
 I have a few nitpicks, of course. What was Laura doing in the story? I don't really want to know, because she was a fantastic part of the novel not to mention its heart, but I also wish I understood. I liked Shadow, though I wish we knew more about him. What about the Ifrit? Ah well. You can't have everything. 
 I read Diana Wynne Jones's "Eight Days of Luke" a few months ago. That book also had a strange ending, one where very little ends at all. You know it's just the beginning, but that's all the author wrote. I suppose the difference is that where Jones could have done with more meat during the story, Gaiman filled his book to the brim with details and every god he could think of. But Jones's ending wins hands down against Gaiman's. American Gods finishes with a sense of emptiness and freedom at once. The characters could go anywhere, but we are told Shadow has unfinished business in America. Jones's book ends with the knowledge that, while peace may have been finagled for now, there is a lot of war and loss waiting to spill into the world. There is a family, whose members love each other, who have done such terrible things and have lived such lives that, one day, they will face each other on opposite sides, and nothing will stop this. It's a strange ending. But I think I enjoyed Jones's ending as much as I enjoyed Gaiman's first three quarters. 
 Recommended for those who are interested in the TV adaptation and for anyone who enjoys mythology.

4.5 stars 
 ** Spoilers, people. ** 
 I thought this was a very good 2nd book in a beloved series. 2nd books tend to fall into this trap of "Let's just get through here so we can get to the end." 
 Not Insurgent. 
 The story picks up literally right after the events at the end of Divergent. If you have time, I'd re-read Divergent unless you've read it a few times over the past year. I hadn't. I only read it the one time last year after publication. A re-read was really helpful as numerous things are touched upon that happened then, especially when you're dealing with lots and lots of characters. 
 The Bad: 
 Sigh. This book is long, but only took me a day to read in between yard work and housework on my day off. I think a few of the scenes could have been condensed down and combined. On second thought though, sometimes after I re-read a book, I find crucial details I missed during the mad rush to get through it. Time will tell. 
 There's lots of running to and fro, from faction HQ's and all over the city. Almost too much. Its like they just get somewhere, and already they're rushing into another we-might-get-killed situation. 
 Tris,  cries, or is trying to hold back tears, all the time. She goes from selfless valor and kick-ass bravery to curling into the fetal position on the floor a few dozen times.  I totally get why. This is an emotional story with lots of death and loss.  She shot her friend (Will) in the head at the end of Divergent. This willful act of murder has consequences on her choices in Insurgent.  
 The World of Divergent: I'm not going to lie. ** Major Spoiler ** There is NO WORLD BUILDING in this book for the first 95%. Yes, you learn more about each faction, but only a little bit. But there is NO mention whatsoever about the entire earth outside of the fence. It's a nagging problem throughout, until you get to the end.  The last 5%, is just a taste of what surely must be coming in book #3. 
 Despite almost non-stop action, the plot itself seemed to stall half way through. Lots of dangerous 'mission' type things, either looking for information, or rescuing, or just clearing one's head. It starts a pattern for 250 about pages. But, there is important information imparted during those times that you might miss if you just skim those parts. Pay attention! 
 A major plot hole, as far as I'm concerned, is that they have a certain amount of technology, but not cell phones or radios. Radio is seriously simple technology and I'm thinking if they have 'simulation transmitters' and virtual reality type things going on, why isn't there at least walkies-talkies or something? It's a little thing, I know. It might not matter overall. 
 Also, there is a continuity error on page 207. I'm not the only reader that has caught it. But a few pages afterward, I was like, "Wait. What? He wasn't there." Not a big deal ... but I think she meant Uriah, not Zeke.  
 The Good: 
 Four is awesome, of course. I like him as a character although he does fall occasionally into the brooding, leave-me-alone-with-my-dark-thoughts kind of guy. Four, of all characters, had the most to lose during this book, as we all put him on a Pedestal of Awesomeness, right? I'm happy to say that he did have his bumbling moments, but for the most part was a strong character throughout. 
 Tris and Four's relationship was very sweet. I thought VR did a good job of keeping it interesting without making this aspect of the story the MOST IMPORTANT thing. It was a good balance between stolen moments of intimacy and knowing there's something big happening in their world. 
 The story was VERY engaging overall despite my complaints earlier about length and repetition. House/Yard work be damned, I just didn't want to put it down!! 
 The last 1/3 of the story is the big payoff. 
 I can't wait for book #3.

To me, the best thing about this book was the way it depicted what can go on in the mind of a person with cerebral palsy. Draper clearly has done her research, and anyone reading this book should view anyone with a disability with perhaps a slightly different viewpoint.

Many characters were too "good" or too "bad". Early in the book, what Claire could and could not communicate did not seem consistent. And even though she has extreme intelligence, her hippocampus would not have been developed enough for her to remember things at age one and younger. 
 I also had to keep reminding myself that these students were in fifth grade; at times the characterization seemed spot on, but at times they seemed older.

 This book was really bad. It wasn't the writing or the grammar mistakes. It was the plot - or better saying, lack of it - that made me stop reading it 20% through.

Let me point out here that when I say abuse, I'm talking almost rape, not counting the many years of molestation she endured up until her father tried to rape her. However, Amber is anything but traumatized. She says she is and that she can't stand people touching her but she sleeps with Liam, her neighbor and her brother's best friend every night, and is not in the least fazed that he is all over her and always wakes up with a boner. The only time she freaked out was when Liam touched her butt and when a random guy tried to kiss her at a party. 
 There are more things wrong with the story like Jake, her allegedly super protective brother that besides telling Liam to stay away from Amber, never seems to be there when Amber needs protection(like when random guy was kissing her). 
 The absentee mother was also too convenient. The woman had endured abuse by her husband, watched him do the same to her kids, and she wasn't the one who kicked the him to the curb (her son and Liam did) but suddenly she is a PA for an executive and spends most of her time away from her kids. Wait, what? It makes no sense, I know.

 I went into this book seeking a good summer romance book and came out with waaay more then that. I got a wonderful sweet read that was everything I look for in a book and more. 
 Next door to Samantha lives the Garret family. They're a big family (8 kids!) who are noisy, don't mow their lawn, have a million cars in the driveway, and they're messy. Samantha's mom dislikes the Garrets more then anything and she finds them disgraceful to the neighborhood. Samantha, however, is fascinated by them since they don't live the same privileged life she does. When Samantha meets Jase, she enters the Garrets world and ends up falling hard for Jase. Then when something tragic happens, Samantha quickly finds herself having to choose between the two families she loves. 
 YOU GUYS. My Life Next Door is without a doubt one of my favorite reads of 2013 and, well, ever. It has just the right amount of drama, romance, and summer settings that will make you want to keep on reading. 
 Samantha is a fantastic, realistic character. She was not at all stuck up at all, even though she had all the elements for it (like her mom being senator which also meant she had a lot of money). I found myself relating to her a lot and also feeling sorry for her because of her mother because was a completely and utterly self-obsorbed beyond an unhealthy amount. If I could've gone into the book to smack her, I would have. She made me want to scream. Sam's friend, Nan, also make me want to scream. She was one of those friends who seem real but I felt like she was actually fake. However, Nan's brother Tim, though he was a very hot mess, he still cared for Samantha which made me like his character. 
 Jase Garret a.k.a the boy next door, was SO swoon-wothy. I mean, seriously I wanted to go into the book and just hug him because I loved him that much. He was sweet and kind and didn't let anyone mess with the ones he loves. Jase was a great, real character and I loved him. (Wait, I said that already, didn't I?) The Garret's were a great family and honestly one of the best families I've ever come across in YA books. And my favorite sibling? George. He was so flipping cute with all the random stuff he would say. I wanted to adopt him as my brother! 
 I was completely invested in this story and found myself actually caring a lot about Samantha, Jase, and all the other Garrets. I'm not kidding when I say I stayed up until 3:30 in the morning to finish this book because I needed to know what happened after that tragic event took place (which by the way completely shocked me!). 
 The romance between Jase and Samantha was paced nicely and I didn't find it being rushed. It wasn't an insta-love, it moved slowly and was pieced together to a believable romance that didn't feel fake. I really liked this aspect because sometimes I feel that in romance books, the romance is insta-love and doesn't seem real. However the romance in this novel was very realistic. 
 The only tiny complaint that I have is the ending. There was a lot that I was hoping would be tied up at the end, but wasn't. However, I still felt satisfied and just made up my own happy ending scenarios in my head. So, it was okay but I would have liked to see more questions answered and things explained. 
 In the end, I highly suggest this book especially now that summer is coming. This would be a perfect book to read at the beach or by the pool.

 Dec. 6, 2013 Original Review 
 Oh. My. Gosh. This is an amazing book. Just amazing. I don't think I've had such an emotional reaction to a story since my first reading of Where the Red Fern Grows, and that was about 35 years ago. 
 Our narrator, Death, wastes no time slashing us with his beautifully sharp words. He meets Liesel while taking away the soul of her poor dead little brother as they travel with their mother on a train. Their mother was taking her children to live with foster parents after something happened to their (possibly) communist father in Nazi Germany. We get to watch Liesel as she comes of age during that horrible time. We see her laugh, steal, cry, and love. And we see her grieve. 
 The novel is about death and war, but it is the themes of family and friendship that will make it a story I won't forget. After Liesel loses her brother her mother abandons her in a house where Rosa, her foster mother, a gruff bear of a woman, terrifies the child. When Rosa demanded that Liesel call her "Mama" I was outraged. Then Hans, the foster father, stepped in, and there was hope. Later, Max, the apologetic Jew, comes to live in the basement for a time. And then there is Rudy. Always poor Rudy, who painted himself black in 1936 to be like American athlete Jessie Owens. I came to care for all of them as much as Liesel -- and Death -- did as her story unfolds. 
 Since I listened to this in audio format, I have to say something about the narrator. Allan Corduner does an excellent job giving voice to Death. His accent is very pleasant and he articulates nicely. Most importantly, the anguish he pours into Markus Zusak's words comes across as absolutely genuine. 
 This may be the best book I've read this year. I definitely recommend it.

300 years after the original trilogy, we return to the now-industrialized Mistborn world. New Mistborn powers are seen, but in both a Wild West setting and the city-scape. The main character is Wax, a nobleman who has been living as a lawman in the Roughs but must return to the city to solve his family's (boring) problems. However, it turns out that the city is not as safe as he thought, and once again he finds him fighting criminals. 
 I'm up in the air between which is my favorite--the original Mistborn book or this one. This book has well-written, complex characters (even the female characters that felt a little flat at the beginning become much more rich by the end). I really liked how the magic is simpler--no one is an all-powerful mistborn. Everyone has just one or two powers, and so has to use them really well. 
 I was quite surprised with the direction romance plot line, but I thought it was quite appropriate, especially as Wax is emotionally broken during the prologue. My favorite character is probably Wax's sidekick, Wayne, who likes to "trade" for things (steal, never!) and is always switching costumes and accents. 
 This book has been touted as Steampunk, which made me wary, because I honestly haven't read any Steampunk that I've truly enjoyed. However, this didn't feel like Steampunk to me. It felt Victorian-era (but in a Mistborn world) and it had magic, but to me that's not enough to qualify it as Steampunk, and it's a better book for that. 
 The book had really good closure, and like the original, did a good job wrapping up plot lines and character arcs while leaving room for a trilogy. If I had Marasi's powers, I would be very tempted to use a Cadmium Time Bubble so I don't have to wait for future books to come out. 
 I probably should've written my review right after reading it, rather than waiting a few days. My Facebook post had a lot more exclamation marks than this review (something along the lines of "It was amazing! I loved it! You must read it!") You get the idea. Basically, I strongly recommend it. If you haven't read the original trilogy, this book can probably stand on it's book. However, if you haven't read the original trilogy, you're behind the times and you're missing out. Go catch up, and then you can talk to me.

DEEPER is everything a New Adult read should be! Gritty, real and makes the reader so emotionally invested that it feel like you are reading a diary. 
 I am so glad that all my high school/college blundering happened before camera phones and social media! My screw ups are a distant memory but kids these days have a permanent record that even their grandkids will be able to peruse. That is what happen to our protagonist Caroline. 
 Caroline had plans. She had her life planned out that included a public persona but that was destroyed the moment she trusted her first love, her first everything, to take pictures of her during an intimate moment. Pictures that he used against her when they broke up. Pictures that would never go away, that made people judge her, that made her a target for the sexually depraved. 
 Reading it felt like internet rape. I felt how exposed she felt. Her humiliation and her fear. The internet is for forever and it was never going away. 
 I really related to Caroline and she felt so real to me, maybe because we have all trusted the wrong person but not many of us get burned this badly. 
 West is is our hero but he's not the typical bad boy with a chip on his shoulder. West does bad things but out of necessity and love for his sister. He sacrifices himself as the price he feels he has to pay so he can build a better life. 
 He has a powerful organic attraction to Caroline but she isn't part of his plan. He wants to take care of her, like he does with his mother and sister and he does to a point but with working three jobs, going to school full time and a few shady dealings just to maintain his ambition of making a better life he is stretched too thin. 
 This is beautifully written, so compelling and so gut-wrenchingly real. I'm not going to lie, I cried and then I was pissed because I have to wait till summer to read what happens next. 
 Bravo Ms. Robin York!

Have you seen Blade Runner, Ridley Scott's superb '82 Sci-Fi film? The paperback copy of Do Android's Dream of Electric Sheep includes the line, "The inspiration for Blade Runner". Even though it's been a long time since I watched the movie, I would agree with the term: inspiration. The bones of the book are in the movie, but it's only a part of what this book says. And at a page count of just under 250, it is deceivingly image packed tale. 
 Of Philip K. Dick's books, "Android's" is probably his most well known. That's probably due to Scott's film. It also seems like many consider it their favorite PKD work. This being my first PKD read, I cannot yet say. I can say that I thoroughly enjoyed it. 
 Here's why this book was so intriguing to me: Dick creates a world that surrounds an atypical, yet extremely engaging plot. It's like he has taken a thought, or premise and built a world around it. If the story itself wasn't intriguing enough, the setting certainly was. Our earth of the future is reflected as a broken, nearly desolate place, yet advanced enough to make Androids that pass as humans. When a group of the latest organic Nexus-6 model go rogue, it becomes Rick Deckard job to find them. The problem becomes finding what is nearly human among humans. This sounds like an out-in-out Sci-Fi work, but it is not. 
 In the film version, I have a vague recollection of a few animals crossing the screen. They are much more prominent in the book. The point of the animals in the story is one of empathy. People love animals in our own real world, but here they are prevalent (mostly) and often taken for granted. In this world, they are a rarity, precious to own. So much so, that replicate machine animals are manufactured and sold at a fraction of the cost. 
 My initial advice is: get past the first 10 pages. The beginning is not really understood until later. At first this book reads like a catch-the-criminal story. Half-way into his hunt, the tables are turned on Rick, and therefore on the reader. What is real and what is right? By the middle point, and certainly by the end, I found the book had become so much more than its beginning. It was deep-seated human story that questions humanity and compassion.

 Wow, this is one jam packed story. I was pulled in immediately, loved Jack right away, and was cringing and rooting for him (and Adder) through to the very last pages. 
 Jack was a con man. Unfortunately, on his one last big con, he was stabbed in the back and set up by his bf and their friend. He is sentenced to three years in prison where he is really unsure of how he will survive. Right off the bat, he finds out his cell mate is one scary mother*****r. But, Jack has a plan, and is forced to put it into action right away when he is forced to stand up to another inmate on his first day. Just as with every action in this place, there are two sides of results. Jack makes a positive statement about his position, but he also pisses a lot of people off in the process. But, better that than become the whipping boy to every inmate there, right? 
 There are so many thing to watch out for, so many different things going on with different groups, and Jack bides his time trying to soak up all the intricacies before deciding how best to act in any given situation. One thing he has going for him is that no one knows he is gay. This is all in addition to the whole cell mate problem Jack has. 
 Adder is a big dude who nobody messes with. He is serving a 15 year sentence in which he has not spoken a word. There doesn't appear to be anyone who has or even wanted to get close to the man, but Jack decides that is exactly what he needs to do to get through the next 3 years in one piece. 
 There is a lot of violence with inmates getting beat, raped, etc. but there is so much more to this story. I found the entire Adder/Jack relationship fascinating. Jack works very hard to get through to Adder in some way, often having to take steps back, or having to deal with negative attention as a result. But, eventually, he does what no one else has managed to do. He earns Adder's trust, and the two carry on a very symbiotic relationship for the duration of their stay. 
 There is actually very little on page sex in this story, but the emotions and sexual tension are very vivid. I was hung up on every word, and while I wanted the story to end so these guys made it out, I was sorry to see it end, as I was not quite ready to say goodbye to them. 
 I definitely recommend this well-written, fascinating and exciting story about enduring hardship, finding love and starting over. This was my first book by this author, and I can't wait to try something else.
