Melanie Winters and Daniel Montgomery shared a love most only dream of, one they believed bonded them together for life. When their world is shattered by a tragic accident, overwhelming grief and guilt distort the truth. Their relationship ends in uncertainty and unanswered questions. 
 For nine years, they drift through life, unable to forget the one who holds the strings to their hearts. 
 When their lives intersect, neither can deny the connection they felt so long ago. But will the power that drew them together be enough to heal the wounds from their past, and do they have the courage to overcome the insecurities and fears that threaten to keep them apart? 
 I was quickly pulled in to this storyline. I liked the characters of Melanie and Daniel and thought the flashbacks and alternating POV added to the mystery as this story unravels. I do believe in true love, but the whole idea of soulmates, I'm not so sure of. The pull that drew Melanie and Daniel together was almost unbelievable--sensing when the other was near and sending mental messages was just a bit corny to me. I had the ending figured out midway and I just have to say, no one's life turns out THAT perfect. Quick, easy read,but a bit unbelievable.

There was very little to endear me to this book aside from Manchee, the talking dog who I imagined as a bug-eyed small thing with his tongue lolling out half the time and a derpy running style. So, there's one thing that I liked. Let me list all the things that I didn't. 
 1. All the other characters in the book are insufferable. Some of them are incredibly 2D, like all of the "bad guys" who seem to exist simply to be bad. 
 2. Aaron. Dude, you keep losing parts of your face. Get yourself together bro. 
 3. I understand the writing style was because Todd is illiterate, but it irritated me nonetheless. If the story had more appeal to me, I am sure I would have forgiven it. 
 4. The setting sounded like Louisiana, except with a few Creatures from the Black Lagoon running rampant in algae thongs. 
 5. The ending is a ginormous cliffhanger. I know many other books which have ended on cliff hangers, but throughout the book there is at least a complete story. Books like those are a dinner where you don't get dessert at the restaurant, but you wait and go somewhere else for it, thus giving your meal a resolution. This book was like going out to dinner, and just when you think you're getting your entree, you are given a punch in the teeth and a wedgie. So then you're just confused and have lost your appetite entirely. 
 6. With the men having all their thoughts out there but not the women, I felt like the author had watched "What Women Want" and was like, "Hey, what if I reverse this into a dystopian future and add a lot of violence and less romance?" 
 7. The author kept having terrible things happen to these characters, and they keep managing to survive things that I am pretty sure they should have died from. What are these people? Bionic? Oh wait, someone is floating around with magical bandaids that regrow skin and make you a cup of tea while they're at it. My bad. 
 Ugh. I just hated it hated it hated it.

"Among other things, you'll find that you're not the first person who was ever confused and frightened and even sickened by human behavior. You're by no means alone on that score, you'll be excited and stimulated to know. Many, many men have been just as troubled morally and spiritually as you are right now. Happily, some of them kept records of their troubles. You'll learn from them--if you want to. Just as someday, if you have something to offer, someone will learn something from you. It's a beautiful reciprocal arrangement. And it isn't education. It's history. It's poetry." 
 Okay, this was just great ... Actually, I was very reluctant towards this book till once I read a few pages in library and I was totally taken by the passive language used in it. (That's what makes this book a figure of contraversy in literature) The protagonist actually felt so close - as an introvert bibliophile young adult one is passing thro' similar problems (but usually not at that extent as in the book) with changes in secretion of harmones at this age. 
 The book describes the journey of a 17 - years old boy (Holden Caulfield) towards alienation which is actually an act of self-protection with the cynical sense of superiority, this isolation is some stabilization in a messed up life according to Caulfield but is actually the source of all his problems. He actually fears the change and it's complexity which leads him to a fantasy of adult world as superficial and hypocritical. He even fantasizes himself as 'The Cather in the Rye' (the protector of children from falling into adulthood) which looks like a Heroic act. 
 The entire book and espicially the climax is structured magnificiently. The elements, symbols and motifs are skillfully used in texts and are so touching. A remarkable transition is described at the end not to be spoiled.

This book is the very definition of "it's not you, it's me." I can't think of anything "wrong" with it, there were just a few things that didn't work for me personally. It was a little too long and descriptive for me, and at times awkward and confusing with the amount of detail provided but there were still plenty of funny and sweet moments. I loved the knitting group and each of their unique craziness and am looking forward to continuing the series.

Okay, don't hate, but I loved this more than the Lux books. I loved the challenge that an Arum presented, that Hunter presented. The story kept such a tight focus on the two characters and their journey to tolerate each other, not kill each other, and ultimately discover there's a whole lot more to the Arum. And the book is hot. Armentrout knows her way around some steam. 
 Book can absolutely be read alone. Love that too. If they get another story, I'm there.

I love how each book focuses on a different set of characters. It keeps changing and broadening my perspective on the faerie world. I didn't expect to like this one as much as the others and yet I think I liked it more. I can't wait for Melissa Marr's conclusion to this series.

 Ishnara has a gift of seeing the future in her dreams. When she stops a bomb that was about to detonate in her own Hugh school, her world is turned upside down. Her powers stop, she meets the new student Ethan who is seems like a bad boy but underneath that exterior, is a good person. Their relationship starts to gradually increase in

Ethan is definitely mysterious, yet he volunteers at the animal shelter? I think I'm in love! He's an animal lover. I pretty much loved him after what he did. Such a sweetheart.

I'm looking forward to reading the next book, The Dark and Hollow Places!

Five stars for the first half  until shortly after he managed to get into the loop  
 One star for the second half  starting from the part where he just keeps visiting the loop without anything happening till the end with the "monsters".  
 The beginning was extremely promising. The prologue was perfect. I really really liked it. I loved the pictures. They were super creepy. I thought I was in for a creep-fest. I wasn't. And it wasn't long before there were too many little kids and "monsters" for my taste. 
 I think I'm having the same problem with it that I had with the Percy Jackson series. Too many kids around. And for this book, they were too many for a YA book. Too many for me to think of this book as anything but a children's book. But it's not a children's book. 
 The creepy parts:  were awesome. They gave me goosebumps! Abe's death. Jacob's visits to the old home. The fog and the island itself. It was going extremely well until he crossed the threshold into September 3rd, 1940 then things just started getting less and less interesting for some reason.  
 The "monsters": I honestly can't seem to be able to use the word "monsters" without air quotes. It's just not possible. They were super creepy at the beginning. The Abe death scene was epic. Then as the story developed, they grew less scary and more pathetic. They're basically what? Parasites? And the wights? Even less interesting. Though, I was genuinely surprised to find out that Dr Golan is a wight.  
 The Romance:  Why? Why does there have to be romance? It was unnecessary to the story. And Emma of all people? His grandfather's ex? It's not that bad but there wasn't even a real connection there. They were together because they were together. Like she was there, he was there, why the hell not? I didn't even like her very much. I think of all the people in the book I only liked Millard and Olive. And I felt genuinely sorry for his father. It looked like that marriage is going under.  
 The ending: Leaving his father behind like that was really selfish of Jacob. What would his father tell the world? I lost my son on a foreign island? Did Jacob think his parents would survive that? That their marriage would last a day after that? It didn't seem like he'd thought this through. Or at all. He didn't think much of them. He thought of his life and what would happen to him but that was it. He didn't even bother telling his father that he was not dreaming. That decision was just horrible of him.  
 Being peculiar:  I was under the impression that being peculiar is some sort of evolution. I mean, their abilities have to serve some evolutionary purpose, right? But I failed to see the evolutionary significance of something like the "back-mouth". Seriously what is that? The only explanation I can think of is that the author couldn't find a proper explanation for the picture of the girl with the golden locks but it was too creepy to leave out of the book and he just had to use it.  
 **With that being said kudos to Mr. Riggs for tying the pictures to the story the way he did. I can imagine how difficult that must have been. And while I think that some of the explanations felt forced, I have to say that I couldn't have come up with something better myself. But then again I'm not really a writer. 
 I expected something different from this book. It's not exactly a disappointment but to me it could have been much better if it had gone another way. I'm not sure exactly which way. Just a different one from that one. 
 The second book is out now but I'm not sure about reading it. We'll see.

The first two books of this brilliant trilogy were astonishing, addicting, and beautifully constructed. "Poison Study" and "Magic Study" had me at the edge of my seat, craving for more and more. Based off the fact that I enjoyed those first two books more than I did breathing, I obviously had high expectations for "Fire Study". Unfortunately, I can't say it satisfied me enough. There was a surplus of content that made the story overwhelming and overbearing at times. To be quite honest, there were moments when I read the book because it felt like a duty, not because I actually wished to continue. 
 As surprising as it is for me to admit, primarily because I loved the character of Yelena to a great extent, in this book, Yelena was simply annoying to me. She had been portrayed as such a powerful and determined character in the first two books, but she still had her flaws. She was stubborn, always rushed into things, never stopped to think, and put herself in danger the first chance she got. These qualities developed and became who she was as a person because of her experiences in Ixia. You'd think that by the third book, she'd learned to trust a few, to think, to not base everything off her own strength alone, etc.. However, that did not happen, since there was little development in her as a character. That alone disappointed me greatly. On the other hand, Valek was the character that kept me going. I yearned for him, and the events that took place in this book concerning him were surprising and emotional. He made everything better. 
 Even though this book did not do justice to the first two, I can't say I didn't enjoy it at least briefly. There were some great concepts in this book. I would recommend Maria V. Syner's trilogy to anyone who's in the mood for an adventure!

Not a bad read, but I had trouble connecting with the characters. Deeper was a nice New Adult read. It was okay and, while I didn't love it, I did enjoy reading it. 
 I had a big problem connecting with Rain. I understood her guilt, but I think she took it too far. Because she felt she was responsible for her almost-boyfriend's death, she decided she didn't deserve to truly live and she was going to continually put her life at risk and be totally reckless in the name of saving others. It just didn't sit well with me. And I couldn't understand why she kept calling Knight sexist. For example, when they were training the new lifeguards, he didn't want the girls to practice on the bigger guys since it would be more difficult for them. While that's not gender equality, it is kind of true. Girls are, on average, physically smaller than guys, so they would have more difficultly rescuing a guy. I consider myself I feminist and that didn't bother me. But Rain went on a rampage about it. Several times, I just wanted to tell her to chill out. In the end, I was okay with her character, but I can't say that I liked her. 
 Knight fared better for me. I understood how his past affected him more than I did with Rain. I connected with him more as a character. He was sweet and a genuinely good guy. He was the best part of the book. Though I didn't understand why he put up with Rain. But, I did like his character and I thought he was great. 
 The romance was sweet. There wasn't much spice in this, though there was obvious chemistry between Rain and Knight. They were a cute couple. 
 The plot was okay. I was kept interested the entire way through. And, though I wasn't riveted, I did enjoy the story. And the ending was great. 
 Deeper was a nice New Adult romance. Though it's not one of my favorites, I did enjoy reading it. If you're looking for a quick read that nice and enjoyable, then you should give this book a try.

There's something sort of nerve-wracking about falling in love with the first book in a new series, isn't there? I mean, I don't know about you but, when I really love the first installment in a series, I immediately start worrying about things like: 
 -- The other books in the series won't even come close to living up to the first one 
 -- The writer will introduce characters that are genuinely unlikable/that complicate the story unnecessarily 
 -- The character development for existing characters will hit a stand-still 
 -- The writer will try and stall the plot and everything will end up going haywire 
 -- The ending will end up being a huge disappointment (okay so I still have that fear since I haven't finished the third book yet but shh) 
 However, to my immense relief, I can gladly say that Leigh Bardugo's Siege and Storm did none of this. Yay! In fact, I actually though that, for the most part, Siege and Storm was even better then the first installment in this series. Let me tell you why... 
 "What is infinite? The universe and the greed of men." 
 Reason #1: The new characters were wonderful. 
 Like, really. I did worry about the introduction of new characters a little in this one, because I felt like the cast was already pretty big in Shadow and Bone. I wasn't sure how Leigh Bardugo would manage to craft more fully-fleshed characters, and have them integrate into the story easily... And then she did. So, uh, that was cool. 
 "I took a breath. "Your Highness-" 
 "Nikolai," he corrected. "But I've also been known to answer to 'sweetheart' or 'handsome'."" 
 Nikolai is written to perfection. I mean, I was a little like, "Seriously, is this going to turn into some sort of love square, because what even??" but then I realised that I loved him a little myself, and decided that I was perfectly okay with that. 
 Plus, if it gets Mal out of the picture then I'm cool with that. Still can't get to grips with the guy at all. 
 But yes, back to Nikolai. Not only was he crafty and intelligent -- he was kind and thoughtful and full to the brim with wit and sarcasm. Yes, good. I don't often laugh out loud at books, but I did whenever Nikolai hit out with one of his great one-liners. He was hilarious. However, there was more to him than just his sharp wit, and that made me like him even more. He's a smart and ambitious character, and I'm very excited to see where he ends up in Ruin and Rising. 
 Nikolai wasn't the only welcome addition to an already wonderful cast of characters, though. The twins, Tamar and Tolya were great, too -- and I really enjoyed learning a lot more about characters we'd met in the first novel, and even drastically changing my opinions on some of them from what I learned. 
 Reason #2: The characters from the previous novel continued to intrigue and amaze me. 
 I seriously love Alina now. I mentioned in my review of Shadow and Bone that it took a while for her to grow on me -- and grow on me she did. Especially in this second installment. In Siege and Storm, we finally get to glimpse the darker parts of Alina -- the parts of her that hunger for power, and for the Darkling, and for everything that she shouldn't really hunger for. Not when she's supposed to be the Sun Summoner. Not when she's supposed to be a Saint. But she experiences these things all the same, because she's human -- and, instead of making her unlikable, these dark thoughts only made her all the more relatable. She grew and learned so much in this novel, and I'm super proud of her, and I can't wait to see where she ends up in the end! 
 I still don't like Mal, though. At all. I don't know if my feelings will change towards him after reading the final book in this series... But all I know right now is that he doesn't love Alina like he should love her. Instead of accepting her for who she is, and loving her regardless of her "faults", he appears to only love the parts of her that aren't Grisha. I mean, he goes as far as saying that he wants her to go back to being the girl she was before she found out she had Grisha powers?? Um, no. You can't force someone to change themselves to suit you. That's not how love works. Thank goodness Alina has enough backbone to tell him that her powers are part of her now, and if he can't deal with it then, BYE. 
 ""I can't go back!" I screamed, not caring who heard me. "Even if you take away this collar and the sea whip's scales, you can't carve this power out of me." 
 "And what if I could? Would you let it go? Would you give it up?" 
 "Never." 
 I think, existing character-wise, my only problem with this novel was not enough Darkling. I'm still a little troubled by how much I like him, if I'm being perfectly honest... It is official--I've now read all the Austen novels! 
 Apparently I prefer the more mature, bittersweet Austen to the young romantically-minded Austen. While I enjoy a spirited heroine as much as the next girl, I appreciate that Austen's heroines all have markedly different personalities, and Fanny Price strikes me as one of the more difficult types from which to craft a heroine. Perhaps unfortunately, I see a lot of my teenaged self (and my current self--who am I kidding?) in Fanny--highly introverted, non-confrontational, perhaps a tad too moralistic, and what many people will dismiss as passive. After all, we like our modern heroines extroverted (but bookish, always bookish), confrontational, feisty, opinionated, and willing to rock the boat. Fanny is none of these things, but I can still identify her strengths--strengths that are not celebrated nearly enough, and which I wish I'd see more of. She is actually quite smart and opinionated, but she keeps these things to herself. Because she is an introvert and fairly easy-going, other people assume that she's a doormat and try to treat her like one. But she has a firm idea of where her values lie, and surprises people when she digs in her heels when they insult her intelligence. 
 Remember in Pride and Prejudice when Elizabeth initially fell for Wickham? Fanny Price sees through the Mansfield Park equivalent of the Wickham character in an instant. Everyone else thinks she's an idiot for not marrying the guy on the spot, coming from poverty (or "poverty" since they still have multiple servants) as she does. But guess what--shy little Fanny doesn't actually give a scallion's width for what other people think. She sticks to her guns...and guess what, she's right. That right there is inner strength. 
 Fanny also gets a bad rap for not actively pursuing what/who she wants, but I get where she's coming from. Fanny knows from the first chapter of the book who she wants to marry, but that person needs to come to realize it for himself. Filtered through her eyes, if she actively tries to get between the man she loves and the woman that man thinks he loves, she's doing him a disservice. Because if he finds happiness with someone else, then Fanny wasn't right for him. What can she do anyway, flirt? Flirting and pursuing a man is so inauthentic to who Fanny is, she would be betraying the very sense of herself if she did so, and drive the guy away. That probably doesn't make sense to anyone else but me. 
 Honestly, Mansfield Park probably has the most "downer" ending of all the Austens. Not being a hopeless romantic myself, I liked it for the honesty. Because coupling isn't a happily ever after. There's another 50+ years of ups and downs to get through as best we can, and I could tell from the vibe here that this is a mature Jane writing with a longer view of life and what marriage really is worth in the long scheme of things. Sigh. I'll miss you, Jane Austen. Thanks for the journey.

 If you've been following me for a while, you know that I'm a huge fan of Emery Lord and I look forward to every book she puts out. She is one of my favorite contemporary authors and favorite authors in general, and I've loved every book she's put out. Naturally, I was excited for The Names They Gave Us and read it as soon as I could. 
 While I loved this book, it fell short in a couple of spots and so I had to lower my rating because of those factors. It hurts me to give this book the rating that I did. But I couldn't ignore the problems I had with it. I'll wait until later to get to the cons, but I want to talk about what I loved because there's more good in this book than bad. 
 First off, the aspect I loved most about this book was the diversity and representation. Every page has a character that is different than what's in most young adult books. The main character, and many other characters we meet, but not to the same extent as the heroine, have heavy beliefs in the Christian faith. There's a character who's transgender at the camp; the people we meet deal with issues such as teen pregnancy, grief, family problems, health, just to name a few. I would have loved to see more of a dip into the characters and how it's affected their lives, but it was nice to get to see it in this book. 
 I also loved the friendship that Lucy has with everyone in this book. I loved how, as the book went along, we got to see how her relationship with the counselors and campers changed as she opened up. You could really see how she grew to care and love for everyone that she met at the camp, and how her reaction to situations (especially at the end) changed from how they were in the beginning of the book. 
 Like I mentioned in my previous reviews, two of my favorite aspects of her books are shown off once again: the realness of her characters and her gorgeous writing. The characters feel like real people, and you see how they grow and changed from when we first met them in the beginning. As for her writing, it was beautiful as always, with some lines wanting me to stop reading and taking them in full embrace. I will admit, I didn't experience that as much compared to When We Collided, her release that came before this book. But I still had those pauses and invested myself in her writing. 
 However, despite my immense enjoyment of this book, I had two specific problems with this book: 
 First off, the romance felt forced. It wasn't insta-love like in When We Collided, it took it's time before Lucy and Jones decided to get into a relationship. However, when they started dating, the next fifty or so pages become entirely centered on their romance, away from her relationship with the campers or her thoughts on her mother's cancer. There really wasn't a moment in this book between these two characters (save for one moment where they made up by the end of the chapter) where they had conflict or any struggles. I thought their relationship was cute, but it felt very forced together within the last hundred, hundred-fifty pages. 
 Secondly, I thought the ending was too short, too open-ended and abrupt. The ending of this book was intense, and I got worried as I got to the end that I would not be satisfied. Unfortunately, this story feels like we've been cut off from what happens and we did not get any answers of what happens. What happens to Lucy's mom with her cancer? What about some of the campers we follow at Daybreak, where do they end up? How does our ensemble end up after camp is over and where they go? I left this book with more questions than I wanted, and I needed to have another chapter or two to see what happens. It almost feels like Emery Lord couldn't fit in the ending that she wanted to, because it feels so abrupt and like we were not done with this story. 
 But, aside from the romance and ending, I loved this book and definitely recommend you pick it up. This is perhaps one of the more diverse books out there with religion taking a major role, the representation of transgender characters and kids that deal with tough issues, but I would have loved to expand more on the characters issues and how it's dealt. The characters and relationships (aside from the romance) feel as real as they've always been in Emery's books, and the writing was beautiful as her previous works. I am looking forward to whatever Emery's next book will be. 
 If you are looking for a summer read that won't take you long to get through, that has more depth than fluffy books, I highly recommend The Names They Gave Us.

In this story, Maisie's hired to find the missing daughter of an overbearing businessman, only to learn that her case has a link to Detective Inspector Stratton's latest murder investigation. When more bodies appear, Maisie suspects that the runaway she's tracking is the only one who can help lead her to the killer. 
 Maisie Dobbs continues to impress. The mystery is satisfying, and it's tied to the post-WWI setting really well. Their entire world is changing because of the staggering numbers of young men who either died or were wounded, and everyone is living with the consequences of the things that they did, and the things that happened to them, during the war. The characters are all trying to move on with their lives, with varying degrees of success. 
 One of the things that sets the first two books in this series apart from the pack is that they're really well grounded. Maisie is an impressive person. But as a woman of her background in that time period, she could never have gotten where she is without the help and support of those around her, especially her father, her wealthy patron, and her mentor. This sense of how Maisie's skills were developed and nurtured is often missing from my other favorite historical heroines, who sometimes seem to need elaborate plot justifications for their involvement in the mysteries they solve. Some of this difference can be put down to the time period and Maisie's working-class roots (most of the other historicals I read are about upper-crust Victorians), but it's also partly about Winspear's heavy focus on characterization. 
 I also enjoy that the book goes into Masie's crime-solving process. Her methods might strike some as kind of hokey, but they fit the character and the setting. It's certainly nice to see a different style of sleuth. 
 I'm looking forward to reading more about this character, especially now that she seems more ready to develop her personal life rather than just her professional one. I have to say, though, I don't really care for either of her suitors. That could be because of Maisie's own reluctance to get involved, but so far she doesn't read as if she has much chemistry with either.

I love this series! I have a huge girl crush on Mercy. I love Patricia Briggs' fascinating world where werewolves and fae walk amongst us. 
 In this installment of the Mercy Thompson series, Mercy is asked to investigate a few murders on the fae reservation. She accompanies Zee to sniff out several of the crime scenes. Mercy seems to have the power to act as a bridge between our world and the super secret world of the fae. The fae world reminds me of Dr. Who's tardis - what we see on the outside is not necessarily the reality. The fae reservation seems to be a portal to their Underhill, complete with a sandy ocean and a hungry selkie. 
 The characters are what make this series so special. We are treated to Samuel's musical side at the Tumbleweed festival, Warren and Kyle's homey and entertaining banter, and some very eye opening girl talk between Honey and Mercy. Ben, a character that I despised in the last book, redeemed himself with his revelations to Adam about Mercy. 
 I liked how we are given a glimpse of Zee without his fae glamor. Nemane, one of the Gray Lords, was a great addition to the fae cast of characters, as was the very hungry and scary Fideal. 
 It is in this book that Mercy's special role in her world is fully realized. Mercy understands that she walks a fine line between calming and inciting her wolves. She has a special place in Zee and Uncle Mike's hearts, too. Mercy is therefore under the protection of both the wolves and the fae. 
 The best part of the book was Mercy's self realization of her choice of mate. Throughout the first two books she vacillated between Samuel and Adam in a kind of love triangle (or square if you add Stefan). This competition between two dominant wolves was tenuous at the best of times. Mercy's thought process behind her choice was truly insightful. 
 I can't wait to read the next book in the series. I can't seem to get enough of this world.

 I'll be honest right from the start: I didn't like the first book in this series. Actually, I disliked it so strongly that I was convinced that I didn't like Richelle Mead (which, if you've seen much of what I've posted on this blog, you know that I apparently love Richelle Mead). But Vampire Academy was the first book of hers I'd ever read. I didn't like the characters, I didn't think it was well-written, and there were enough things that I didn't understand that it just couldn't keep my interest. 
 After a multitude of people telling me that the first book in the series was definitely the worst, and after reading and loving several of Mead's other books, I decided to give this series a second chance. 
 This book was definitely better than the first. I decided about halfway through that the primary reason I didn't like this one was just that I didn't care for the main character. I find Rose annoying and immature, and quite honestly pretty stupid. 
 But at least the writing was more up-to-snuff. As my mom commented, "It's like [Mead] figured out how to do this writing thing." 
 And by the end of the book, I realized that all of the things that bothered me about Rose were kind of the point of this book. Sure, it had a tangible plot that is clearly setting up for a significant macro plot, but the actual point of this book was Rose's maturation from an annoying teenager to a Guardian. And once that became clear, I was fairly impressed. It was a bit heavy-handed and clunky for my tastes, and it involved an awful lot of time in the mind of a teenager who I would absolutely never have gotten along with in school, but we finally got there. 
 I'm feeling better about where the rest of the series is going, and I'll definitely be approaching book 3 with much less skepticism than I did with this book. 
 Oh, and a quick note on titles: It took me a good 5 minutes after finishing this book to figure out why it had the title it did. When it finally registered (it really shouldn't have taken that long), I was a bit confused by the decision. Titles should have more meaning than just how they relate to a portion of the setting. Just my thoughts on that. It's why I hate coming up with titles.

I have had bad experiences with American authors writing books set in Scotland before, so I was a little sceptical going into this book. Thankfully I was wrong, this book was absolutely amazing.  The Falconer is set in Edinburgh in 1844, and it is clear that May really did her research. It was so brilliant to read a book set in places I've been and really be able to picture all of the locations, e.g. Princes Street and Arthur's Seat. May is really great at subtle but thorough world-building so I really felt like I could imagine everything. I also loved that it rained all the time, very realistic! 
 This was also the first steampunk book I have ever read, and I loved it! It's so interesting to see inventions and technology mixed in with a historical setting. The Faeries in this book were so amazing and I loved how there were so many different types. I have done a lot of research on Scottish folklore for my own writing so it was great to see everything that May included. Again, it's made me so happy reading a great YA set in Scotland. 
 The main character Aileana is great, I liked her instantly. The author did not give her a stereotypical accent, she instead added in some Scottish slang. I felt like she spoke a lot like me at times so that really helped me connect with her. The other characters were all very interesting as well, but I won't say much about them, it's better to go in not knowing them. 
 This probably isn't the best review because it's after midnight, but I really recommend this book to everyone. Especially Scottish fans of YA, it's so wonderful seeing ourselves portrayed well in books!

I expected to like Uprooted, I even expected to love it. What I did not expect was to love it quite as much as I do, which is almost beyond reason, tell-everyone-I-know, this-has-everything-I-wanted love. 
 There are a few reasons why this is one of the best books I've read this year, and so completely up my alley that I almost can't believe it exists: 
 - The Wood. It is nature being both terrifying and awe-inspiring. The Wood isn't exactly what it appears to be, but it uses a lot of trees and creepy creatures to get what it wants. If you ever wondered what it would feel like if nature decided to take everything back, or if you went on a hike and the forest wanted to eat you, or you just wondered if the trees are up to something shady - this is wonderful nightmare fuel. It's fantastic. 
 - Agnieszka and the Dragon. They are polar opposites, who somehow fit together by filling the blanks in the other, both in their magic and in their personalities. One is talent, the other skill. One nature, the other technology. One imagination, the other reason. It's a really compelling interplay. They aren't always happy with each other, or the way that they each fit into the other's life, but they are always interesting. 
 - Agnieszka, the protagonist, is the kind of person for whom "winging it" is a reasonable life strategy. This leads to all sorts of wonderful shenanigans. 
 - The friendship between Agnieszka and Kasia. Growing up, sometimes they were jealous and sometimes they resented each other and sometimes the pressure of assuming that Kasia would be "chosen" was too much to bear - but their friendship and genuine affection for each other overwhelmed all of the much more minor bumps in the road. This is an excellent, devoted female friendship, full of collaboration instead of competition. It's really enjoyable to read. 
 - Kasia. She's the character that would have been the "chosen one" in any other story, except here she isn't. And she has to grapple with that. And figure out what to do with her life in the face of being who she is, instead of who she thought she would be. Hers is a really intriguing story. 
 - the Dragon. He's been in his tower so long that he's kind of forgotten how to be a person. And is afraid to learn. He's great, basically. 
 - The logistics of magic, and how it doesn't work quite the same for Agnieszka as it does for everyone else she encounters. While she lives in a world that would, under different circumstances, supply her with a mentor to help her figure all this stuff out (and the Dragon certainly tries), she is mostly self-taught. She isn't some sort of chosen one (and this is emphasized by her being "chosen" but not actually chosen), and she doesn't immediately get good at anything. She has to fight for every inch. Which makes it really satisfying to see how far she gets along the way. 
 Basically, everything about this is amazing. While there are some things I wish got more of an explanation (are the valley people related somehow to the Wood people? shy do sorcerers live so long? does it have to do with trees? ), that explanation wouldn't be necessary to the story, so I can't really consider it a mark against the book. Instead, this is an amazing standalone that leaves a lot of threads hanging, so that it's clear that problems are never easily solved, and plenty of things take more time than a novel's worth of space. 
 Read it. It's great. There's magic and intrigue and sword fighting and evil trees. You'll like it.

To love someone was not what she had expected. It was like falling from somewhere high up and breaking in half, and only one person having the secret to the puzzle of putting her back together. 
 My heart is heavy, my emotions are everywhere, and this book is something to be treasured. 
 Boy, am I glad I bought this one. It is such an adventure. Guys, I haven't felt this strongly about a book since I read the Chaos Walking series two years ago. The characters in this. The plot. The setting. Everything was incredible and it transported me to Neverland. 
 Listen up, I don't even like Peter Pan that much. It's definitely at the bottom of my "favorite Disney movies" list. I was intrigued though to hear the story from Tiger Lily's point of view. Not only do we see the story from Tiger Lily, but Tinkerbell actually tells the story. Narrating a story from the point of a faerie. Just..brilliant. 
 I knew I was going to at least like this book when the book started because Tiger Lily is an amazing character. She's strong, but she doesn't pretend to be something she's not. She admits to her flaws and knows that she has weaknesses. 
 "I don't care what they say," she said, though she did care. 
 Finally, a girl that admits that she does have emotions and a conscious. There's so many "heroines" nowadays, especially in fantasy, that are just..too badass. Tiger Lily was just the right amount. 
 "You looked strange climbing in the tree like that." 
 Tiger Lily pulled her braids between her fingers her sudden self-consciousness feeling foreign and strange to her. "I didn't do it to look nice." 
 The dynamics in this book are some of the best I've experienced to date. We have Tiger Lily and her (not biological) father, Tik Tok. Tik Tok likes to wear dresses and wear his hair long in braids. And he's great. He's wise and mysterious, but the best thing is the relationship that him and Tiger Lily share. Tiger Lily makes a comment once that Tik Tok believed that people were all bits of each thing, boy and girl. Wow. 
 But the great character dynamics don't end there. We have Tiger Lily and her childhood best friend Pine Sap. These two were just perfect and Pine Sap ripped my heart out multiple times. You see, Pine Sap's mother verbally (and sometimes physically) abuses Pine Sap. He's quiet and doesn't quite fit in with the other boys who love to go hunting. However, him and Tiger are like two peas in a pod. I mean, Pine Sap is kind of my ideal romantic-boyfriend-goals. He build Tiger Lily a freakin' house. One word: d'aw. 
 But then, my feelings get all jumbled when Peter Pan comes along into the story and he's basically like Prince Charming. The chemistry between him and Tiger Lily doesn't help my feelings either. I mean, anytime they kissed or made any physical contact, my stomach did that thing it does when it's really happy and I could honestly feel my heart warm. This usually doesn't happen to me, okay? 
 She felt the warmth of Peter's arm under her neck, and it almost felt like he was an extension of her, and like if they had souls, they lay somewhere snug between their two bodies. Maybe all her strangeness, her curse, her always feeling like an outsider, had all existed so that she could belong here, with Peter. 
 Finally, possibly my favorite relationship between any two characters: Tink and Tiger Lily. Sound weird? Well, if you read this book, you'll understand what I mean. 
 You may think my jealously would have been enormous during those days after Peter gave Tiger Lily the smallest kiss on the neck. And you would be right. But these moments were swallowed by a bigger emotion, my tenderness for Tiger Lily, which had grown to take up most of the space in my body. 
 Then Wendy bird comes along. I had nothing against Wendy until I read this book. I wanted to punch her. Sorry. Whereas Tiger Lily grew to love Peter through friendship and doing things they both enjoyed together, Wendy shows up and insta-love occurs. This quote explains my feelings perfectly: 
 Wendy's heart beat for Peter immediately--there was no slow growing, no dark distrustfulness like Tiger Lily had had, no hesitation. Wendy didn't believe in situations she couldn't bed to fit her, so there was no need to be distrustful. She had the blissful confidence of someone who had never been put in a pot of turkey broth to die. 
 Although the ending of this book made me cry about five times, it was phenomenal and it actually provided me with better closure than I could have hoped for. There was one sentence (if you've read this, you probably know which one I'm talking about) that just about made me slam the book closed and give up even though it was so close to the end, but thankfully that passed quickly. I mean, even the last paragraph of this book is so lovely and makes you just breathe a sigh of relief for all of the characters in this book. 
 She said she thought there were different ways of loving someone, and there were some she used to think were the most important, and now she had changed her mind. 
 and also, 
 Sometimes love means not being able to bear seeing the one you love the way they are, when they're not what you hoped for them. 
 One hundred percent true quotes that, at least for me, gave me the closure I needed after that heartbreaking ending. I hope all of you who have read this book or plan to read this book can get the same closure I did because if not, I'm so sorry. 
 Sorry for all the quotes, but the writing in this is beautiful and I had so many Post It notes throughout this one and I just had to include some of these that either warmed my heart or I just found to beautiful. Please do yourself a big favor and read this book. I can without a doubt tell you all that this is my favorite retelling I am ever going to have the pleasure to read.

This is a first-on-a-series book. At first is a little bit of a slow reading, mostly because you have to get used to the idea of a different world. As a rare thing, in White Cat I found difficult to accept this alternative reality. But after several chapters, I found myself more comfortable with the story and suddenly what was so hard to understand at first, then it made perfect sense and became kind of predictable. 
 It is a good book and a good start for a series too. It explains how everything works in this world and still keeps you entertained. This was a new idea, with a fresh premise that I had never seen before in this genre. 
 About the plot: The world in the story is similar to the today's world. Aside from some very important details: Magic is actually a real thing, everyone knows about it, but just a few has been gifted with it and they use to be criminals associated with the mob (including the protagonist's brothers), because curse-work is forbidden and they're like the black market of magic. People pay them to do little curse works, such as erasing the memory of someone, beat the crap out of a guy who didn't pay his debts with a supernatural strength, make someone who hates you to fall in love with you in a second and all kind of things like that. Cassel, the protagonist, is a seventeen-year-old boy who seems to be the weird one of his family. Which is pretty odd itself, given the fact that he's actually the only one of this family who isn't a curse worker. But after a really vivid nightmare, Cassel begins to question everything he has ever believed in and he'll soon find out that his family has been lying to him for a long, long time. 
 About the characters: Cassel has always believed he killed his best friend, Lila, and that he's some kind of maniac who everyone should stay away from. So he tries to act normal, but always remains on the outside, beating himself up for not being good enough for his family or for the rest of the world. He is a very authentic character and I really liked him, because he is not some prince charming, he's damaged and he knows it. 
 Lila is a b*tch. I have to say it. I don't like her. She's selfish and childish and mean to Cassel. She should've stayed as a cat. 
 Cassel's brothers, Philip and Barron are nothing like him, they are selfish too, and they just want power and money and put that before his own brother, so I don't like them either. 
 I love Sam, Cassel's friend. He's a sweetheart and a really good friend. I consider myself as a good friend, but I wouldn't leave my house at six in the morning just because a friend -who doesn't even treat me that well- is calling me. I admire this kid. 
 About the writing: It was different, in a good way. I was written in first person, from Cassel point of view and I love it. His mind works in such an amazing way! I learn to love him on the way of the story. I love the style and everything, although it wasn't as fast-paced as I prefer, it definitely caught my attention. 
 About the ending (contains spoilers): I absolutely loved the ending. It wasn't what I was expecting, but the quotes of the last pages of the book, were cool and got me thinking. I have to say I hate Cassel's mom, she's such a nosey lady. Everything was finally falling into place and she has to stick her nose. 
 I would recommend it for: Lovers of paranormal books, and new worlds with magic and anyone who enjoys a male point of view.

 I just can't seem to warm up to Faith Hunter's writing style. I keep coming back to her books because they are great, concept-wise, but a good concept does not a good book make. 
 I had a bit of trouble following the story of this second installment in the Jane Yellowrock series because I read the first book a few years ago and although I remember strongly that I didn't like it very much, the story is all but forgotten. Still, after a few pages, I was pulled into Jane's world and the characters. I noted a marked improvement in Jane, she seemed less disdainful of females in general and less convinced she was super duper cool and good. I was also pleasantly surprised because, although there was description and the prose itself was still mostly too descriptive for my taste, it wasn't as bad as the first book (that I remember). 
 However, it didn't take long for me to realize that this book, like the first, lacked focus (narrative-wise). Jane runs around a lot, makes a lot of research but it's like the bits and pieces she uncovers make no sense whatsoever to the case she is investigating. It all seems so... random. Her investigative decisions make no sense. If she's investigating a rogue vampire, it does make sense to investigate crime scenes... but it doesn't make a lot of sense to delve into cold case files that seem to have nothing to do with the case at hand or going to vampire parties. 
 All of the things Jane discovered seemed like pieces of different puzzles that really didn't fit together very well in the end (because some of the information was superfluous). She loses too much time on other things, unrelated things. 
 It seemed to me the mystery was a bit too simplistic. When Jane uncovered a piece of it, it was quite easy for me, the reader, to understand what was happening... not Jane though; she may be "though as nails" but the sharpest tool in the shed she is not. This was... frustrating. Basically this mystery was not complex enough for a full length novel, in my opinion, and that is why Jane was so slow on the uptake and why she ends up doing so many unrelated things that add little to... anything, either character development or plot. 
 Overall, I still like the concept. The story telling? Not so much.

 I am a giant fan of Lauren Oliver. Whatever she writes, I read. This was actually the book I read before Delirium, and when I discovered Delirium I was ecstatic that she had written another book! Now I'm anxiously awaiting my chance to buy Pandemonium, but this is a review of Before I Fall, not Delirium. 
 For a book of Lauren Oliver's I think this book is sadly overlooked because of the excitement of Pandemonium and Delirium. Yes, those books are amazing and are going to be amazing, but Before I Fall is just as good. It doesn't have the romance that Delirium has, but it still has that style of writing that makes you feel as if something more is going on, something that will make you think over life again. In a way, Before I Fall is realistic fiction, everything happening is possible; except for the one thing that makes this book so unique. Samantha reliving her death. 
 In the beginning, I absolutely hated every single character in this book. Samantha, her friends, her boyfriend, the "loser", basically the entire bunch. Samantha seemed fake, petty, and selfish, her boyfriend was a total jerk (and not the good kind), her friends seemed cruel and empty (and like Samantha in that way), and Juliet seemed weak because she didn't fight back. It's only later on, I learned why. It's later on that I realized why Lindsay acted the way she did, and why she seemed so fake--because she was. 
 In the beginning, Samantha is all looks and little substance. She thinks she's crazy because she doesn't "love" Rob, her all-popular boyfriend. Pshh. I sort of pitied Samantha at that moment, she didn't know the value of her friends, her family, her life. It's only when she loses all those things that she slowly realizes. There's a lot of character development in Before I Fall, especially on Samantha's part. Of course, I didn't really realize it until near the end. Sam made a lot of mistakes, but slowly, slowly, she fixes them. Slowly, she's finally getting her last day on Earth right. "Learn from your mistakes" and that's exactly what she does. 
 Another plus is that Lauren Oliver played on the domino effect a bit. Samantha relives her last day again and again, so everything should be exactly the same, right? No. Each word she said, each look she gave, each action she did, changed something. Secrets were exposed, friendships were ruined, lives were saved, lives were killed. But those were all variations of the same day. It's amazing how Lauren Oliver did all that, but really, was there ever any doubt? 
 My absolute favorite parts were the italicized parts. They just sent a chill up my spine, which happens when I read a book that touches me. It was like Samantha had gone over her own story and added her comments, added her experiences to help us understand better. My favorite non-italicized parts, to be specific, were pages 419-420, 428, 438, and 468-470. These were the parts that made me cry my eyes out or just absolutely cheered for Samantha. It's amazing how the small things she does makes the people she cared about, or the people who hated her, happy. Samantha is a great character that shows what it means to have second chances to redo everything. In the end, she sacrificed one of the most important things and didn't hesitate. In short: Lauren Oliver's writing will capture your heart and touch you. She shows how everyone makes mistakes in their lives; that we can correct them, and the sacrifices people have to make in the end.

She hates the situation - and her husband - with every fiber in her and she doesn't hide it, except from the world. Troy doesn't feel different, he just hates the whole situation and hopes once he gave a credit card to his dear new wife, she'll leave him the hell alone. But neither expected the attraction they felt for each other despite the circumstances. 
 "Love and hate are similar in a lot of ways." 
 "Is there a way to love you away from me?" I snapped. 
 "No, but you could hate-fuck me all you want." 
 The heroine is a significant point for me in every book. If I can't identify or sympathize with her, the whole book becomes boring, annoying or just simple torture, depending on the heroine's character. I hate whiny women, I prefer girls who are strong and brave. Sparrow was what I love in myself and what I search for in every main girl. She had a smart mouth, threw witty comebacks in Troy's way every chance she got and it made the whole book not just sexy and misteroius but funny too. 
 "Opinions are like assholes. Everybody's got one, and they usually stink."

 "He gave me lies, and I ate them from the palm of his hand.

 I especially adored how they didn't say "I love you" until the very end. It made it more special and believable. I rarely go for this type of book. For years, I've rigidly stuck to fantasy, adventure novels that I can escape into. But this was free on the kindle and I'd heard good things, so I figured I'd give it a go, and I'm so glad I did. 
 17 year old Lennie is lost following the sudden and unexpected death of her older sister, Bailey. More like best friends than sisters, the two were inseparable until now. Life goes on for everyone else, but Lennie struggles to keep up and finds herself dealing with a whole lot more than just her grief. 
 I was daunted by the premise of the novel. Having a sister myself with whom I'm so close with, I thought I might find this difficult to get through. In places, it was emotional, but that's what made it so good. I loved this book because of the nature of the way grief was dealt with. This book is hilarious. 
 Unorthodoxly for my reviews, I'm actually going to start with character as opposed to plot. This is a largely character driven experience all provided through the eyes of grief-stricken Lennie. I really liked Lennie. She's got some really interesting quirks to her personality. For example, she's reread Wuthering Heights 23 times and will write poetry anywhere; on coffee cups, tree bark, empty sheet music and leave these scattered around for anyone to find. These help her with her come to terms with her grief, and enables her to open up to the people around her without actively seeking help. Lennie takes her loss personally and, in a way, selfishly. While that may sound harsh, she forgets that Bailey's death affects her grandmother and her uncle, without whom, Lennie would really struggle without. 
 Gram and Big are fantastic side characters. Nelson has fully developed these guys. They're not just set pieces to help the plot move along; I'm made to care about them and their grieving process as much and, if not more in some cases, than Lennie's. While not technically a spoiler, since it's revealed early in the novel, we know that Bailey and Lennie have been raised by their Gram and Uncle Big after their mother ran away. Therefore, with Gram, we have a woman who has already lost a daughter and now must come to terms with the death of her granddaughter.  The family are all creative and Gram is no exception. She paints, but only in shades of green, and her garden is famous amongst the townspeople. Big takes the form of the gentle giant, a man with a passion for insects and who falls in love often. They're both instrumental to a part of Lennie's healing process, and she's just as big a part of theirs. 
 I should probably talk about Joe. He is one of the most unrealistic characters going, but he's just so damn likeable. Nelson created that 'dreamboat' guy who just appears to be perfect. This is most likely because the story is written from Lennie's point of view, therefore giving us this impression via an unreliable narrator. Having said that, he is an honest, kind and incredible thoughtful young man who naturally stands out from the 'boys' of Lennie's class. I approve of Joe. 
 The plot gets somewhat lost behind all of the character development, which is why I've chosen to talk about it second. Reducing it right down to its core, we meet Lennie four weeks after Bailey's death and follow her as she copes with her grief. She has her Gram and Uncle Big looking out for her and Bailey's boyfriend, Toby, is a regular on the scene. He needs the families' support as much as they need his. While Bailey lived, Lennie had little to do with Toby - just saw him as Bailey's boyfriend. However, after her passing, they become each other's main source of comfort, believing themselves to be the two people who knew Bailey best. 
 I found this endearing at first, and it was comforting to me to see that the pair of them had someone to share their feelings with. After all, we were beginning to see in Lennie just how dangerous it is to bottle these kind of feelings up. However, this relationship becomes uncomfortable to the reader. I wouldn't call what occurs between them a romance, because there is no real 'love' shared. They find solace in each other - Lennie finding a bit of Bailey in Toby and Toby, essentially, finding a replacement to Bailey - but it certainly isn't love.  
 Upon returning to school, Lennie meets Joe, a new classmate who has recently moved to the area. What follows is technically a love story, a journey through grief and all the ways in which life goes on regardless. 
 The plot is simply a vehicle to explore Lennie's grieving process. It was effective and the pace wasn't compromised as a result. I could have done away with the love triangle theme, but my dislike for it didn't affect my enjoyment of the novel overall. It just made me feel kind of awkward for those short sections with Toby.  
 In a way, I'm kind of gutted to have read the Kindle version. Preceding each chapter is a poem or piece of writing that Lennie has written - on scraps of paper, sheet music, coffee cups - presented as images. On my tiny iPod screen, I couldn't enjoy and appreciate these. I found a physical copy in my school's library and just the presentation of these pages is beautiful, and that's before you read the words written upon them. It's these pieces which give a greater insight into Lennie's frame of mind.  There's quite a clever plan behind the inclusion of these writings. Right near the end of the novel, Joe reveals that he has been finding these words scattered across town. With works not written on tree bark or etched into park benches, he began collecting and collating Lennie's collection. Essentially, we 'stumble' across Lennie's scribblings along with Joe, and learn more about her with him.  
 Last Thoughts 
 I thoroughly enjoyed The Sky Is Everywhere and will be shoving a copy into my friends' hands for some time. This is brilliant. 
 Recommendation: Devour it! 
 TL;DR 
 A girl loses her sister and must come to terms with her grief. A beautiful, poignant novel.

 It was fast paced but everything were so trivial. It could have been more interesting if some of the selected guys would have told parts of the story. So at least we would know how and what they see in Eadlyn that made them liked her. Because that was a total sham. 
 Overall, this book was a disappointment. But since there will be one more to wrap up this story, yes, I will still read The Crown because I don't just abandon a series no matter how blunt it is. However, if there will be more than that, I don't think I will read it. 
 Final ratings: 1 star
This book was amazing!!! I'm so happy there's more Yelena and Valek to come!!
An amazing book. It's a little long but it's perfect. The heroine is flawed, which is good. I'm in love with it.

This was different than any Hercule Poirot novel I've read before. Poirot is tasked with investigating a murder that took place sixteen years earlier. While I enjoyed the premise, the story got a bit redundant. There were five suspects (hence, Five Little Pigs) and the novel showed both their verbal and written testimonials. I enjoyed trying to figure out whodunit from the facts, but ultimately my gray cells weren't up to the challenge, although I enjoyed the resolution very much.

Thank the sweet lord(s) above for this book. After finishing Allegiant, I was so not in the mood for a depressing, everyone-you-love-will-die book. I know a good amount of people who have read this book and thoroughly enjoyed it, and I had it on my to-read list for a while, so I figured, "Why not?" 
 I am so happy I decided to read this book. I knew there was somewhat of a romance within the story, but I didn't realize just how involved I would get with both characters! 
  
 The scene where Celia finally realizes who her opponent is had me giggling to myself. I immediately loved the cat-and-mouse game they played with each other, neither one admitting to being the mouse. I really didn't care for the story line with Bailey. There was nothing wrong with it, and I didn't hate it. I think I was just so involved with Marco and Ceila that I didn't care about anything else but their story. 
 I was so so so scared when it's revealed that only one of them can walk away from this fight. I had just finished a book where a main character dies; I couldn't handle it again!! I was so relieved when they found each other again, after Celia had bound them to the circus. When Marco tells Celia she's breaking his heart, they were breaking my heart! I don't think I could've handled it if they had never found each other again, or if one had died. 
  
 This was such a good read and I had to stay up until 2AM to finish it. I couldn't put it down! Definitely one I would recommend.

Loved it! I can't wait to start reading the other volumes! 
 Nicely paced and written. With believable characters and quite diverse too yet still oddly relatable!

I've been trying to read more diverse books -- diverse in terms of social issues, foreign authors and more -- and this book fit into a lot of those categories for me. 
 The book focuses on Max Walker, an intersex teen, and the trials that he faces. The story is mainly told through his eyes, with narrative chapters told from the viewpoints of the supporting characters, which I really liked. I thought it added a depth of character for those people and how they reacted and why they reacted how they reacted.

I suppose this book is supposed to be a "Silent Spring" wake up call for social media (and while the authors points are valid) I don't think he revealed anything that a tech-savvy user isn't already aware of. And unfortunately he wrote his screed around Meg a two-dimensional lead who is newly employed at a Google-esque workplace where Facebook-like privacy violations are overtaking the world. I thought most of book was predictable and wanted to rush to finish it and move on.

Devon Monk has built an interesting world, where magic is available to most everyone in some way or another, but using it comes at a price. 
 She does a good job of introducing the characters--Allie, who is doing pretty much everything she can to get away from the influence of her money-grabbing father; Zayvion, a mysterious man who was following Allie until the day she has to confront her father and then helps her out when she gets into tough trouble. There's also secondary characters that may or may not come and go through the rest of the series. 
 I actually accidentally started with Magic on the Storm on accident, not realizing that it wasn't the first in the series. Having gone back and started at the beginning, lots of things are starting to make sense and I can't wait to read the next book and figure out even more! 
 Magic in the Blood here I come!

I only read this book because I loved the first book in the series. Angel in this book is a little bipolar. The end just left me feeling confused, and mad. I didn't know whether or not Angel was still on Max's side or not. Max's clone is actually good. and Max is falling for Dylan, who I still considered a Dork. I really like the Max and Fang coupling. Technically it still exists with Max's clone, Maya, but still, it's not the same. Oh, I didn't like how Fang tried to recreate the flock with no-fliers. That was unreal

I normally don't read books set in this time period, but omg it is Lisa Kleypas so I had to. I think she did a great job with letting the reader get a feel for the time period, including the dorkiness of their clothes. 
 I love her descriptions of things it is one of my favorite things about her books. 
 Helen was seemingly fragile, but my wasn't that just a facade. I really loved her character, except that little bit at the end where I thought she went a bit off character in decideing too quickly. That, or maybe I just thought it was too quickly.\ 
 Rhhys, man I really wished sometimes that Kleypas heros were real, or at least if their are really men out there like them that I get a chance to meet one. He said at one point that he wasn't romantic, but that usually ends up meaning they are so romantic and that saying they weren't was just a way to psyke you out. hah 
 Some interesting characters were introduced in this book. I can't wait to get to read the good Doctor's book. Pretty sure the seemingly sociopathic friend will play her opposite. I'm also curious to read West's book, but I think he needs a bit more marinating before he gets his. 
 But, first Pandora ... Devil in Winter is one of my favorite Kleypas books. I'm *so* anticipating Devil in Spring.

Wow, this book was pretty incredible. I really didn't know what to expect, but it was very intriguing. The majority of the book is from the perspective of an 11 year old boy that was born in a basement. His family lives with him, Grandmother, Father, Mother, sister, and brother. The little boy doesn't really know why they are there or what's going on. As the book progresses the story is slowly unveiled, but keeping the reader mostly in the dark as well. At some point past the middle of the book, the perspective shifts and reveals everything, with the conclusion following. 
 The perspective being from the boy really makes this book work as you don't know who to really trust. Everyone seems awful in their own way and without knowing anyone's motivation it's hard to judge. Sometimes the family is nice and sometimes they are really really bad. My thoughts of what was going on ranged widely until the reveal chapters and I think I was wrong in every way. 
 The book is mostly about family struggle and what you would do for your family. Some people will go to some pretty lengthy measures.

I liked it better than the first book. I liked Maggie and Michael's characters, their story and romance better than Alexa and Nick's. I loved how they were so desperate for each other, before they even knew it. One of my favorite characters was Michael's mother, I loved that she took Maggie under her wing and taught her things her own mother should have done or at least someone else while she was growing up. Also I think his mother knew that they weren't really married yet too, she didn't let much get past her.  
 Also I loved the cat, Dante was really hilarious. I'm curious to see how Max and Carina's story will go. I hope it's just as funny, heartfelt and genuine at this one was.
I read this book on lunch at work and was like "uh huh, uh huh... WHA?!" So I took it home and read it again.

Orleans was definitely different from the normal things I read and definitely different from...everything. 
 In the best way of course! 
 I really did like Orleans, though I wasn't as into the story as I wanted to be. I think it was the odd-yet-common dual points of view in both first and third person and the...diction, I guess (YAY for Eileen...even if it wasn't the word I was looking for...) of our main main character (yes, that does make sense). I've always had a problem with that kind of thing, though I guess it does make sense for someone living in the conditions she was raised in, but I always hated the "He ain't" or "He got" instead of "He has". Yes, I am a Grammar Nazi. If you know me I DNF'd Blood Red Road because of that too. 
 But ignoring that (or getting used to it), Orleans was definitely a great read, though I can't exactly say I loved it. 
 I did like the characters though! Fen was independent and strong and ingenious in her own way! She knew how to survive in the ruins of Orleans and she took her promises seriously, I'll say that. She wasn't a character I could connect with, but I found myself cheering for her (silently, of course...maybe) throughout most of the book! She's an easy character to like and not frustrating at all, which is more than I can say for some! 
 Daniel...the way it was written and by what happened; I honestly feel as if Daniel wasn't really a main character or needed in the story. Sure, he made things a bit edgier, but the main plot really could've done a bit without him. 
 And no, you guys, they do not fall in love, I'll say that now! I dearly wish they would, but maybe in book two! (There is a sequel, right. There has to be! Goodreads HAS to be lying!) 
 This was definitely one of those adventure-type books I don't usually read, but absolutely love! The plot honestly was a bit all over the place, but it was still enjoyable and I loved it. 
 The best thing about Orleans was, without a doubt, the worldbuilding! It was thorough (well, except for the one question of HOW DID THE FEVER START?!) and I loved learning about what had changed, the events that led up to the Wall and to Orleans and all about the fever and how life in Orleans was. There were tribes and hunting and lepers and so much more! It was an absolutely fascinating fantastically created world that definitely shows you what the words national epidemic mean. ;)

It's too bad, because it started off very good. I've been having a hard time giving it up in hopes of finding that original magic, but I think this book cured me.

Once Drake sees her picture, he takes her case on personally, and becomes her personal live-in bodyguard. Though Zoey doesn't feel she needs a bodyguard or wants one. 
 ..."Listen here, Hulk. You can take your incredible body and vacate my home. I won't be needing your services."... 
 "Sorry, cupcake. Contract's signed. You're mine."... 
 I loved their chemistry and interaction. Zoey's way of saying things as they are and taking things literally was amusing. I also enjoyed the side pairing of Elle and Pink. 
 The romance between Zoey and Drake is definitely the prime focus of the story. The stalker aspect was minimal, but since I love Alexa Riley books for their romance, I didn't mind too much. 
 Overall, Guarding His Obsession was a fun and sweet story that I very much enjoyed and happily recommend.

You sneak back in bed, trembling, hoping it didn't see you, and then a huge hand snatches you right out of bed. No matter how much i like the BFG, I still don't want him to do that to me. I must admit that i'm not that adventurous.

It really hooked me for the first 100 pages, eventhough I found its style and language more suitable to teenagers than to me. Then, the plot slowed down and became almost predictable. Moreover, what I would expect to be a main character, Tamani, seemed too flat and superficial. I liked David more. As for Laurel, she's OK but far from being the outstanding and unforgettable character I'd imagined. To tell the truth, I was expecting something more magical from her wings! The final part has a bit of action, but it didn't actually make me hold my breath. I'll read its sequel because i want too see how the story develops but I must admit I'm somehow disappointed for now.

The plotting was uneven, and I never really felt that Vimes was in trouble. I could not help but compare this unfairly with The Fifth Element, an absolute masterpiece, and wonder how Pratchett's illness has affected his writing. Still not so great Discworld is much better than most of the fantasy novels out there.

When a movie based on his best settling book is turned into a movie, his only demand is that Ava Banks play the role she inspired. 
 Neither Ava nor Tucker really moved on in the five years they were apart. But for all the time they have been apart and the hurt that sent them in such opposite directions, once they are in close proximity again there is a very smooth transition into the present. 
 This was a sweet story with so much love. Ava and Tucker are one of those forever couples, even as time and their choices sent them in different directions. The connection between them is strong. I loved the flashbacks and memories of the time when they were a textbook example of young love: innocent, starry-eyed, and full of promise and dreams. It was nice to see some of that playfulness come out as they reconnected in the present. 
 This was a low drama book, but was filled with emotion. The easy way in which they come back to each other doesn't mean they don't have things to sort out, but they don't add extra tension to the already tense situation between them. 
 This books is filled with great cameos for fans of the Explosive series. Ava's brothers are a hilarious addition to the story. This was a fun second generation story and I look forward to more from the series, possibly Tucker's story, maybe even Ava's brothers as they get a little older, or the other children from the Explosive books.

The pacing is quick and events progress quite rapidly. I also liked the portrayal of Loki, the trickster god. The love interest is very swoonworthy and the way Paulson describes him, I wouldn't mind having a boy-next-door if that's how they come (they don't, I know for a fact, the boy next door to me is 12 and a brat). 
 There were a few aspects of the novel that gave me pause. Ellie's complete obliviousness that Tuck likes her. I understood that she is scared to trust her instincts but the boy is more than obvious - he's all but flashing a neon sign on top of his head. It's hard to imagine a better gothic romance than "Jane Eyre" -- gloomy vast houses, mysterious secrets, and a brooding haunted man with a dark past. 
 In fact, Charlotte Bronte's classic novel has pretty much everything going for it -- beautiful settings, a passionate romance tempered by iron-clad morals, and a heroine whose poverty and lack of beauty only let her brains and courage shine brighter. And it's all wrapped in the misty, haunting atmosphere of a true gothic story -- madwoman in the attic and all. 
 Jane Eyre was an orphan, abused and neglected first by relatives, then by a boarding school run by a tyrannical, hypocritical minister. But Jane refuses to let anyone shove her down -- even when her saintly best friend dies from the wretched conditions. 
 But many years later, Jane moves on by applying to Thornfield Hall for a governess position, and gets the job. She soon becomes the teacher and friend to the sprightly French girl Adele, but is struck by the dark, almost haunted feeling of her new home. 
 Then she runs into a rather surly horseman -- who turns out to be her employer, Mr. Rochester, a cynical, embittered man who spends little time at Thornfield. They are slowly drawn together into a powerful love, despite their different social stations -- and Rochester's apparent attentions to a shallow, snotty aristocrat who wants his wealth and status. 
 But strange things are happening at Thornfield -- stabbings, fires, and mysterious laughter. Jane and Rochester finally confess their feelings to each other, but their wedding is interrupted when Rochester's dark past comes to light. Jane flees into the arms of long-lost family members, and is offered a new life -- but her love for Rochester is not so easily forgotten... 
 "Jane Eyre" is one of those books that transcends the labels of genre. Charlotte Bronte spun a haunting gothic romance around her semi-autobiographical heroine and Byronic anti-hero, filling it with brilliant writing and solid plot. It has everything all the other gothic romances of the time had... but Bronte gave it depth and intensity without resorting to melodrama. 
 Bronte wrote in the usual stately prose of the time, but it has a sensual, lush quality, even in the dank early chapters at Lowood. At Thornfield, the book acquires an overhanging atmosphere of foreboding, until the clouds clear near the end. And she wove some tough questions into Jane's perspective -- that of a woman's independence and strength in a man's world, of extreme religion, and of the clash between morals and passion. 
 And Bronte also avoided any tinges of drippy sentimentality (Mrs. Reed dies still spewing venom) while injecting some hauntingly nightmarish moments ("She sucked the blood: she said she'd drain my heart"). She even manages to include some funny stuff, such as Rochester disguising himself as an old gypsy woman. 
 The story does slow down after the abortive wedding, when Jane flees Thornfield and briefly considers marrying a repressed clergyman who wants to go die preaching in India. It's rather boring to hear the self-consciously saintly St. John prattling about himself, instead of Rochester's barbed wit. But when Jane departs again, the plot speeds up into a nice, mellow little finale. 
 Bronte did a brilliant job of bringing her heroine to life -- as a defiant little girl who is condemned for being "passionate," as an independent young lady, and as a woman torn between love and principle. Jane's strong personality and wits overwhelm the basic fact that she's not unusually pretty. And Rochester is a brilliantly sexy Byronic anti-hero with a prickly, mercurial wit. 
 Of Charlotte Bronte's few novels, "Jane Eyre" is undoubtedly the most brilliant -- passionate, dark and hauntingly eerie. Definitely a must-read.
