 This book is not only the "can't-eat, can't-sleep, reach-for-the-stars, over- the-fence, World Series kind of stuff," (two points for whoever can name this movie!) but it also has a touch of magic. And we all know that magic can lead to some unexpected twists. I'm not going to ruin any surprises but I loved all of the plot lines so much that I really want you to experience it for yourself. 
 I loved the house. It reminded me of the house in Rose Red by Steven King. Where the lady of the house has to keep building on and "growing" the house. This book isn't a horror like that one, but the continuous construction on the house reminded me of that. 
 If you like sweet romances, modernization of fairy tales and just plain great stories- you NEED to check out Rapunzel Untangled. I loved this book. One of my favorites of the year so far! It is also my first book by Cindy Bennett. She has so many other books that I would like to try. Let me know which one I should check out next!
What a grat POV story I loved reading about Landon and what he went through in his life. I kind of wish that we got his POV first. He is a great character that had a rough life.

Paper Towns was my first John Green book. Therefore, in my mind, it holds a certain unique-ness that his other books don't quite have. 
 The balloon metaphor is still one of my favourite parts of a John Green novel ever and, although Q and Margo remind me of Pudge and Alaska A WHOLE LOT and I love them all equally, I think that Paper Towns will always be my favourite John Green book. (Unless he writes more ofc, please do, John.) 
 Damn I hope the movie doesn't cock my opinion of this book up. Please no please NO.

I don't normally write reviews of books I don't enjoy, but Nevermore was so anticlimactic, it hurt. It physically pained me to finish this book. 
 Where do I even begin? Max didn't 'save the world'; she complained and moaned about her love life and sat around MAKING PRO AND CON LISTS ABOUT THE BOYS while the world ended and she somehow survived. Are you fucking serious? You've been engineered to SAVE THE WORLD and blather on about it for 7 books; but instead of making preparations, you go to school like a normal kid and make pro and con lists about the 2 boys who trail after you like puppies. asdrtyuijkl NO. 
 The plot twists were dumb and stale. Every plot device (if you can call them that considering there was hardly any plot to begin with) has been used at least once in one of the previous 7 books. How many times can Ari come back from the dead? How many times can Jeb betray the flock? How many times is Angel going to act like a sociopath and have Max forgive her? How many times will Angel be kidnapped and experimented on, only to be rescued by the flock? Why did Iggy, Gazzy, and Nudge fade into the background only having dialogue every once in a while?Also where the hell were Iggy, Gazzy, Nudge, and the other mutant kids on the island after the world ended? Did the humans survive or did everyone die? They mentioned Dr. Martinez monitoring something or other, but then made it seem like the whole world died.  Why introduce Maya and Dylan as the perfect counterparts to Max and Fang only to make the irrelevant in the end? Why paint Dylan as the perfect guy and then have him go on a psychopathic rampage, terrorizing innocent people all because he saw Max and Fang having a 'moment'? 
 This book frustrated me till no end. The inconsistencies were horrific. I don't know how James Patterson can live with himself, knowing the ending to this series (which started out beautifully and had such fantastic potential) ended so shitty. He and his ghost writers don't deserve the money they raked in from the last 4 books of the series. 
 The moral of this story: Don't be greedy and use ghost writers just to put out more books so you can make more money. They WILL fuck up your story.

Book # 126 for 2013 
 The plot was very interesting - hence my adding it to my "to read" list, but alas, the actual story did not live up to it. :-( 
 The story starts off good, introducing us to the life of Grey and how she went on to becoming a stripper and how she struggled every day just to continue pursuing her dreams. Then one fateful night, she meets Dawson the movie star ---- this is when it gets absurd (for me at least). 
 Major Spoilers Ahead like I'm really gonna be giving out the story here 
 On the first night they meet, she gives him a lap dance --- he says she doesn't belong there. kisses her. walks out. 
 The next day they meet again, she becomes his PA --- he takes her to her dorm in his arms (some Christian Grey-ish thing goin' on with the feeding thing). Kisses again. walks out. 
 He saves her. I love you's get said. They make love. She freaks out. They reconcile. 
 And so it goes the fairy tale every exotic dancer is wishing for - a man who can see past the job and fall in love with her. Take her to the Oscars and propose to her in front of Channing Tatum and Emma Stone and a bunch of Hollywood celebrities. Oh Joy.
Wow, I loved it! I loved the romance, the magic, the action, the suspense and all of the characters.

4 Books in and these guys still deliver. Ty Grady and Zane Garrett are an amazing couple. They are not perfect and they still have a looong way to go, but I look forward to continuing their story. In each book, their relationship develops to the next level. These guys continue to be intense and interesting (and BADASS). 
 I liked seeing a little jealousy and it seems like they are both getting more comfortable with their situation. They are definitely more real with each other in this one, sharing feelings and intimacies beyond the physical. I think those moments when this happens are the reason I keep reading...such feels! Such emotion! Love it! I loved the way they took care of each other. 
 I loved the scene when they danced. 
 I loved that Zane was finally figuring things out.
A brilliant novel, full of twists and turns but also oddly predictable.

I liked this book, for what it's worth. I had problems with this book towards the end though. I feel like the authors experience with the family became too much of a focus. I don't want to say this was a bad thing, because its not. The family needed their moment in the spotlight. The book didn't need over a hundred pages of recounting the various medical problems and drama within the family though. The science parts were interesting but I wanted more on the societies treatment and medicines treatment of poor black sick women in the 1950's. That might be another book to look for.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The only reason I haven't given this book 5 stars is because I don't really buy the main character being 70 years old. It might not seem important, but she's so immature and emotionally stunted she comes off like someone in her twenties, maybe thirties, not someone who would have been in her late forties when Planetfall happened. Otherwise, this is brilliant.
"Who will survive?" Obviously, it won't be the readers. OR the characters!! There all going to die and I'm going to cry for ages because of the pain

This one actually started off a little bit on the slow side for me. I was worried I was going to end up disappointed, but then something amazing happened. Things started to pick up in a major way. And as I watched Aria and Perry's relationship evolve into something beautiful and deep, I couldn't turn the pages fast enough. Though their love story is the heart and soul of this book, Under the Never Sky gives you so much more than that. It gives you a complex and fascinating world that you can sink your teeth into. Everything feels real, and vivid and the atmosphere is incredible and something I could revel in forever. Overall, what really impressed me was the fact that the author took a really simple premise and did something completely unique and extraordinary with it. Through the Ever Night, COME OUT QUICKER, BECAUSE I NEED YOU NOW!

This book was packed with drama and suspense. Not all things are as they seem. The book just kept getting better and better the more I got into it, learned about so many secrets and so many hidden connections. Troy was a tough one to love, at first he was nasty, mean, uncaring but just like the story as it went he got better and better. Sparrow was feisty, Troy met his match with this girl. I was really surprised at the twist with Brock and I was on the edge of my seat not knowing what was going to happen page after page toward the end. Everything did not wrap itself up in a pretty bow right away but there is a HEA. I love the very end when Red says "I'm Sparrow Brennan now" she corrects. "I was only Sparrow Raynes when I used to be your nightmare." Troy says "You were never a nightmare. At first, you were business...and then at some point, you became my pleasure." Sparrow says "And what am I now?" Troy says "Now your my lovebird, you're my home." My heart is all a flutter, great ending.

What intrigued me: The second in a series. 
 What I liked: I impressed with the way the characters from the first book were still represented in the second. 
 What I didn't like: n/a 
 Favorite quote: "There was nothing like a Saturday - unless it was the Saturday leading up to the last week of school and into summer vacation. That of course was all the Saturdays of your life rolled into one big shiny ball."
I think this book was written especially for me. I want to hand this beautiful, important, brilliant, funny, sweet novel to every woman/girl I know.

There's just too many positive things to say about Easy. Tammara Webber has taken a sensitive topic, sexual assualt (most notably, rape) and created a story that is not only inspiring, but beautiful. I really do not know if I can do this book justice as it's just something you need to experience yourself. 
 Jacqueline is likable, easy to relate to and someone you'd love to have as a friend. Lucas is completely sexy, inspiring, and a guy you wished was real so you could have him for yourself. 
 Unlike some other books that have dealt with rape and just brushes it aside, Tammara Webber made sure it was always in the forefront of the novel. Jacqueline attends more self-defense classes, she talks to others who have been attacked, and does her best to make sure it doesn't happen again to her, or anyone else. There's even information in the back of the book for those who need help for themselves. It's easy to tell that this is a topic the author is invested in. I commend her enormously for it.

3 STARS 
 PLOT - 3 (Interesting and original, but I wasn't blown away or anything.) 
 CHARACTERS - 3 (The characters lacked depth and I just couldn't connect to any of them) 
 WRITING STYLE - 3 
 ROMANCE - 2 (I didn't like how the romance was written. It just annoyed me.) 
 UNPUTDOWNABLE LEVEL - 2

"We all came into the world as a single cell, smaller than a speck of dust." 
 Man, this book was a work of art. So poetic, so powerful. I was immersed in all the characters lives, and love how they were all intertwined in ways you wouldn't expect. War is so awful, obviously. Hitler was fucked. And I feel so lost after reading this book in relation to the recent turn of events in US politics. 
 'All The Light We Cannot See' is incredible. I don't think another book will live up to it.

Okay so I thought Mitch was pretty much awesome in Mystery Man. But Jesus, he made me lose my shit in Law Man. Absolutely swoon-worthy-toe-curling and just down right the perfect male specimen. Mara had to grow on me for a bit, her insecurities sort of annoyed me, even knowing she had her reasons for feeling that way. I wanted to hug and shake the hell out of her, badly. 
 But after years of watching and looking for his 'in' Mitch finds it - and that one moment puts him in position to come to rescue when she needs it the most, even if she doesn't see it...yet. He was all in from the start, seeing what he wanted and knowing that it was worth the fight. You got to love that. The man who has searched for the right girl long enough that he doesn't bat an eye to do what it takes when he finds her. Mitch won me over completely! 
 The fact that he steps up the way he does to protect and care for her, Billy and Billie was heartwarming. Even in the drama that happens (which was light), I could not wipe my smile from my face. Every time he did something or said some thing I smiled. For me this had element of a little heat, but it was more sweet than it was steamy. It was heartwarming and I even found myself getting a little lump in my throat in the epilogue. 
 So far this is shaping up to be a great series and I have no doubt that I am going to adore Tack in the last installment. And I get the bonus of an taste of Shy pre-OTW. 
 Between our fictional men of Seattle and Denver I would not be surprised if there was a population boom over the next 5 years.

I was pleasantly surprised how much I enjoyed this book. 
 When I first saw the cover of this book I thought it was going to be too much about the joys of visiting France, not that that is bad but I have read enough books like that in my life to not seek them out. 
 However, when I first started reading this book I knew I was going to like it right from the beginning. I enjoyed the characters and got lost in the story. 
 It is definitely a coming of age, Young Adult, Last year of high school kind of book but it was still good and different enough to stand on its own. 
 I look forward to reading the next novel in the series. 
 Great Read!

As mentioned in the review for the authors Dauntless novel, his mastery of conveying spacial warfare is unparalleled. I enjoyed this book a bit more because it, to me, flowed more. I finished it in two day. Again, hightly recommended.

This book was really good, completely suprised me... 
 I started reading this a couple days ago, because I had a friend staying with us I had to wait to finish it, and some of the smaller mysteries were really easy to figure out and I was thinking it was going to be another one of those corny little predictable books, but it took me completely by suprise, ending with a big BANG!
Re-read 9/17

2017 Reading Challenge: A book with a family-member term in the title. 
 An engaging story about three women whose lives twist together with murder, infidelity, a mysterious letter, first loves, revenge...and tupperware. I felt hooked the whole time, and although I saw some of the twists coming, somehow the foreknowledge made those parts all the more riveting. 
 I can't give this four stars, however, because one of the women is essentially pointless to the overarching plot. I realized near the end that she could have been omitted completely and the storyline would have gone more or less the same, yet a lot of time is devoted to her particular dramas. This made an otherwise tightly woven story feel like it had a random loose thread. 
 Last, the narrator was great. Her Australian accent was delightful, of course, and overall her tone was playful, wry, and memorable. I'll be looking for more books narrated by her.

Ms. Marvel returns! And now she has to face the Inventor! Working alongside one of her favourite superheroes and meeting Inhumanity for the first time, Kamala bands together with some of the most unlikely of people to stop Inventor before he does real damage. 
 I'm just going to apologise in advance. This isn't a review. This is me just flailing as I try to attempt to describe how GOOD this was! In volume one, there was something about it that stopped me from giving it 5 stars but Generation Why was even more enjoyable than No Normal. Kamala is even more adorable and hilarious. In Generation Why, Kamala learns more about the nature of her powers. After her encounter with Wolverine during a mission, both Wolverine and Kamala became more curious of her possible origins.4 
 Her self-appointed role as New Jersey City's superhero has caught the interest of Inhumanity. (Since I don't read comic books, I actually had no idea who they were but a quick google search cleared that up!) They send a superpowered watchdog called Lockjaw to aid her in missions. And this page is one of the funniest in the two volumes I've read. 
 In this issue, the villian sees the current generation of youth as shallow and I loved how Kamala faced the topic of how this generation is undermined by the previous one - calling us self-entitled, unambitious and lazy. I thought this was a great topic to tackle and it worked well using Kamala to tell it, a young teen who is suffering from a generational gap that everyone faces. She admits our flaws but doesn't excuse or condemn them either. I love how passionate Kamala is, and how she refuses to see her and others her age as a lost cause. She gives a speech, while cheesy as heck it was to read, it was well-timed moment of self-awareness which just stacks up the moments and things I love about her. 
 Simply put, this is so good! As always, the art is good and so hilarious! I recommend this to anyone. Go read it and see what you're missing out on!

3.5/5 
 Out of the 3 Liane Moriarty books I've read, this one is my least favourite (so far). The concept of this sounded great and I was really looking forward to reading this but for some reason the story fell flat for me. I found that I was never really fully engaged with the characters or the story. I also found the ending to be disappointing (why, I'm not really sure...It just wasn't what I was expecting, which I guess was kinda the point, however I felt a bit cheated by it...).

Okay, so I'd enjoy anything Mortal Instruments just because I love the world. But sadly, I've fallen out of love with this series. Don't get me wrong, I still enjoyed it while reading - but ever since City of Glass, the books have failed to leave a lasting impression on me. It's kind of like beating a dead horse at this point. I strongly believe that Cassie should have left this a trilogy, the way it was originally meant to be. 
 Like I said, I love the world. And I still enjoyed it while I was reading, but it was kind of just...fluff. It's not that it's a light and cheery book or anything, but it's the kind of book I like while the book is open and completely forget about when it's closed. 
 Remember when I said I'd fallen out of love with the series? I've also fallen out of love with the characters. I don't really care about Jace and Clary anymore, and I used to LOVE them. I feel meh about Sebastion, too, and I was drawn to him in the last couple of books. I'm not sure if the series has lost its magic, or if my opinion of it has changed. (It's also been a REALLY long time since I read the last book, I'm sure that doesn't help.) 
 The lack of emotion was the serious issue for me here. Shit, Simon flipping DIED and I didn't bat an eyelash. Partly because I didn't believe it for a minute. I just KNEW he wouldn't be dead. Cassie's characters rarely stay that way. *sigh* Emotion robbed. Honestly, I'd have liked it more if he had stayed dead, as sad as that sounds. Oh, and Raphael died too...I was so unaffected that I actually forgot until I saw someone else's spoiler. Whoops.  Like I said, I liked the story. But I didn't really care about the outcome or what happened to the characters. Plus, nothing felt dire. They were in a dire situation. But I didn't feel it at all. 
 My second complain was the length. This book was SO. LONG. I mean, it went fairly fast, but I still think that a lot of the filler could have been cut back to shorten it to a more manageable size. Oh and another thing, there are spoilers for TID in this book. I have not read TID and some major things were ruined for me. So beware! 
 Man, this review sounds pretty bad! I promise I didn't not like it, it just kinda sounds that way. Looking back I don't have anything exciting to say about it because I'm already starting to forget the story. I still like Cassie's writing, and I maintained decent interest throughout the story. Would I recommend it? Maybe not this book in particular, but I would still recommend trying the series if you like paranormal!

Beautifully subtle story about a young boy facing the realities of possible homelessness and s struggling family - there are no easy answers, and the ending is one of optimism without Disney-fication.

I SOOO wanted to give this 5 stars because I adore this series, especially Meda, but unfortunately an abundance of spelling and grammar mistakes rather marred my experience in this final installment. 
 The Crusaders are on their last legs, they're horrifically outnumbered and the demons are picking them off one community at a time. Meda wants to help, not in the way everyone wants her to, but Jo asked so she has to do it. Jo wants to help to, but what she does has dire consequences and could mean the end of Jo, the Crusaders, everything. 
 The final installment of the Soul Eaters trilogy is just as full of snark and sarcasm as the first two. And Meda is still on top form, but the best part of this book is Jo. She becomes a different person, almost literally, and it means that she's able to empathise with Meda's struggle and truly understand her best friend. 
 As I said, this book, like the rest of the series, is amazing, but there were a lot (and I mean a lot) of grammatical errors in this book. It was shocking, I don't remember the first two having any grammatical errors, so why did this one? Did I buy a bum copy from Amazon? Were the publishers in too much of a hurry to get it out that they didn't properly proof-read? Either way, it did mean I had to drop my review by one star. Other than that, top notch.
I would never have read this based on the cover or the description. SO glad I read a review of it online! SO funny, so heartfelt, with a fast-paced plot and plenty of good drama.

After reading the first book, I realized how much I want to read the rest of the series to learn more about the whole clan! I absolutely fell in love with Chase. I also loved Chloe, and completely understood her desire to try and stand on her own after her crazy ex husband. At times her thoughts got a bit old, though. I understand where her thoughts were coming from, but she was so blind to what was right in front of her! 
 I loved the setting of the vineyard, it was so beautiful. The vineyard is actually belongs to Marcus, the oldest Sullivan sibling. He was in a few scenes in the book, but the rest of the family didn't make an appearance until the last chapter. I would have liked to see them more in the story, but it did give the feeling that Chase and Chloe were alone in paradise, so to speak. I also liked the way they met, and how Chase saved Chloe from the speeding car. The romance and sexual tension was great, as were all the sex scenes (and there were quite a few). 
 I didn't think there was enough action. The dialogue was good, but most of the dialogue between Chase and Chloe was the same stuff over and over. There wasn't any other character development. The conflict was a little boring as well. The whole thing wasn't very believable, having spanned only a few days. 
 But I did enjoy the ending, although it felt a bit rushed. It really showed Chloe how strong she really is! And the family dinner was also fun, to get to finally meet the rest of the family! For anyone who likes a contemporary romance, I'm sure you will enjoy this book!

If you recall, book two of this series almost killed me (ok, not literally). As a matter of fact, the words I used were "I feel like my heart has been ripped out, stomped on and handed back to me after finishing this book." And they were true...I even did a re-read of the last few chapters to refresh how things went and it did it again. With that in mind, I jumped at the opportunity to read book three as I needed to know what happened to McKenzie, Aren, and Kyol. Trust me when I say, if you have started this series and enjoyed the first two books, you will definitely want to read this one when you can. 
 Warning: There may be spoilers here so I will tag it but be warned if you decide to continue. 
 It has been three weeks since Kyol created the life-bond with McKenzie and she left the Realm. She is slowly adjusting to sensing Kyol's feelings and trying to live a normal life. She has an apartment and a job...both of which aren't anything special but they are things she has done on her own without anything related to the Fae. 
 It has also been three weeks since she has seen Aren and despite him making the decision that he will stay away, she hasn't given up hope on their relationship yet. Even though McKenzie is determined to not give up on him, she does begin to doubt whether Aren loves her as much as she does him considering (as she sees it) he gives her up so easily. Just when McKenzie thinks she may be on her way to a normal life, something happens and she is pulled back to the Realm where she comes face to face not only with Kyol but also Aren. 
 As McKenzie goes back to the Realm, she is pulled into the fight for the throne again. Lena has not been confirmed as queen and there are a number of threats to her reign. The first being the high nobles as Lena doesn't have enough support from them to ensure she can keep the throne. Additionally, there is a group called the elari that are supporting a false blood who is making a play for the throne.  
 The majority of the story follows the group of normal characters through trying to secure Lena's place as Queen and includes a lot of action. McKenzie finally learns how to use a sword and fight and it comes at a good time as she really doesn't get an opportunity to rest. At the same time, McKenzie has to think long and hard about whether she really does want what she considers a normal life outside of the Realm. She also needs to figure out her love life. 
 I'm not going to give any of the story away as I think you will want to read it yourself. I will say there were some moments where I wasn't really sure what was going to happen and I will warn you, Williams is not afraid to kill people off (Sorry - I had to do it)....so make sure that if you have enjoyed this series so far, you pick this one up as soon as you possibly can. 
 Bottom line - I'm glad I stumbled upon this series and although I am sad that this story is wrapped up and I won't get to read about these characters anymore, it was well done. If you haven't started this series yet and enjoy Urban Fantasy with some pretty hot fae guys, I think you will enjoy this one. 
 Thank you to Netgalley and the publisher for the review copy.

Not my usual fare, and rather more sex in it than I like in my romance (But, I picked this up knowing that and tried to go in with an open mind). 
 Still, I'm not sorry I decided to buy this book on an impulse. Yes there were some problems with the writing (The author has a horrible tendency to over explain - a lot [really, a lot]); however, it is still readable - if you're able to ignore the overuse of a few words. It was simple, straightforward, and uncomplicated prose. 
 There really is no plot to speak of in this book. This would normally have me tearing out my hair. So much of the action in this revolves around the relationship between Danny, Paul, and Eve that if there had been a "main plot" it would have bloated the book into unreadablity. Maybe that means some of the relationship stuff could have been cut down to make room for a more traditional plot? I'm not sure. The pacing only dragged for me in a few areas, so maybe I just have to accept that some plots only revolve around the relationship in the book. It was a bit strange to me, and it made the book feel slightly one dimensional in some areas. 
 I think the reason I liked this so much really had to do with the fact that I identified with aspects of Paul's personality and his dilemma. Which kind of says something about me, to those of you that have read the book. Suffice to say the greatest point of emotional tension in the novel had me in tears - and I literally had to put the book down and blow my nose several times. 
 Danny was a total ass, but that fit in with his character's personality. He was also vulnerable despite his walls and I think the author showed that nicely. I liked Eve too, and her clear misery involving her failed marriage and career attempts in New York. 
 I think characterization is where the author really shined, and that alone made this book have an emotional impact on me. 
 I was shocked I liked this book so much. 
 **For those of you that cannot tolerate a ton of sex in a novel - I do NOT recommend you pick this up. For those of you that can - and/or like a lot of sex in your reading material, this one might well connect with you too.

** spoiler alert ** 
 OMG LEIGH BARDUGO WHY NOT JUST GO RIP OUT MY HEART 
 I loved this book. I love this duology really. It's just so wonderfully written and the world is so fantastically built. As someone in love with Amsterdam, Ketterdam was just such an amazing setting and Bardugo's description made me feel like I was back in a much-darker Amsterdam setting. It was wonderfully done. 
 But really, let's be honest, this book is really about the Six Crows - the characters - that through the two books we have come to adore. I have to be honest - I think I liked Six of Crows better plot wise (it was a little more action packed), but Crooked Kingdom really made me care more about all six characters - ALL OF THEM. I never loved Wylan until this book, and I definitely began to care more about Jesper and Kaz who I enjoyed reading about in the first novel but didn't feel connected too. Now I do. 
 But for me this book is the Nina and Inej show. Strong powerful women who kick ass just as much (if not more so) than the boys? Yes please. Let's start with Inej before I move onto my favourite girl Nina. 
 Inej is just a beautiful portrait of a survivor. She is strong and powerful and loyal, while also being deadly and vengeful to those who wrong her. She is clearly tormented by her past, the flashback in the silos were just such an accurate representation of a trigger to someone who has dealt with assault and abuse. Working with survivors, I can say that Inej is such an accurate portrait to me - she is haunted by her past, she can barely stand to be touched sometimes, but she doesn't let it stop her. She deals with reminders daily but she know she has to keep going. Some of her chapters made me want to cry because it was just such an amazing portrait and so accurate, and I am so happy Leigh Bardugo wrote Inej because I've read far too many cliched "sex-worker" types. Inej is amazing, and I love that she always has hope. Her ending just made me so happy. I don't love her with Kaz (because I don't like Kaz - sorry don't hate me) - but I think she is what he needs and vice versa. 
 Now lets get to my precious Nina. Nina is my favourite character in the whole series. She is just so FUN. She's sassy and witty and she just reminds me of Buffy the Vampire Slayer - strong heroine who is both girly and kick ass and always has a comeback to everything. Nina is just the greatest to me. She brought all the humour to the books. And her and Matthias? I adore. I love them. Again its a Buffy the Vampire slayer territory where your greatest enemy is also your greatest love (cue Angel/Spike angst). I just adored them together. On his own Matthias is a wet blanket but his description of Nina and the way he constantly looks for her is just so .... cute. I loved it. It was the little moments with them that just made me reread pages because their intereactions are so genuine even in the face of a tragedy or in the middle of a heist. 
 If I had one complaint about this book it is that Nina did not get a proper ending. Look I was HEARTBROKEN about Matthias. Literally going "NOOOOOOOOOOOOO" very loudly when I read about his death. My little ship sank right then and it killed me. But I do understand his death. I don't think Matthias would ever 100% get over his revulsion to the Grisha and would not have adapted to Ravka well. At his core he's a Fjerdian (did I spell that right?) and even though he loves Nina throughout the book he mentions his immediate hatred of Grisha and Ravka numerous times. I don't think in the long run it would have been enough, he would've been miserable even though he had Nina. So I get the tragedy. Much as it breaks my heart - I think death is the only future for Matthias unless he would become a bitter old man. Nina though - girl just goes off to bury him and travel to Ravka and then what? Literally all the other characters are in Ketterdam getting their happy endings but what about my beloved Nina!? Inej says she hasn't heard anything and I NEED TO KNOW. I can't have her ending be her going off to bury her beloved. NO, just NO. THAT IS NOT ENOUGH. 
 Ms. Bardugo please give me a whole series about Nina and her future. Because I am not satisfied with her ending. It can't just end like that. Even if the series is about her dealing with Matthias' death I NEED IT. 
 Anyways, fabulous duology - well-written, fast-paced and with characters you get hooked on and way too attached too (hello see my rant about Nina above). I need more books like this.

Have you ever wondered what a soap opera would look like in written form? Picture the melodrama, romance, tragedy and action all described in detail, without the dramatic background music. 
 Even though, to be fair, I don't feel that this book was trying to be a soap opera as much as a dedication to all the old, forgotten books of the past. After all, aren't soaps just a transition from pages to the tv screen? 
 It is a very full book, saturated with characters and emotions and winding plots that diverge and converge in an intricate tangle. It was for the most part predictable, with a few plot twists and macabre incidents. 
 But what made the book tolerable, and at times really enjoyable, were the characters. Despite their sheer number, the author did not skimp on endowing each with a rich personality, enhanced through the relationships between each, and viewing them through the different narratives. A cruel, abusive husband and father is really just a victim of life's hardships, who seeks retribution. A young boy's love interest appears innocent until the emotional manipulation is made apparent. 
 And then there's Fermin Romero de Torres. Ah, Fermin. A walking witticism, a man of innumerable talents and personalities, life's wisdom incarnate. He really carried this book through, giving it the spice and appeal that would otherwise make it a dull read. That, along with the enchanting atmosphere of Barcelona. 
 I respect that it doesn't try to be anything other that what it is, a tribute to the lost art of story-telling.

 To give a quick summary Don't Get Caught is about pranks. The schools notorious Chaos Club sends a group of students to get caught after one of their pranks, including Max. Max is just a no one, invisible nothing spectacular in his life kind of guy who loves heist movies. Feeling betrayed and humiliated by the set up Max goes by a simple heist movie rule, get payback. He decides to take down the Chaos Club. 
 I love heist stories. Don't Get Caught has so many amazing and on point cinematic references that left me shaking my head in agreement and also wanting to re-watch them, though I couldn't put the book down to do that. It's epic in a high school way. Things many of us wish we could have pulled off in school. The pranks themselves both from planning to the follow through to the aftermath was pure hysteria for me. Each of the water tower five had their own motives and unique personality, like any good crew does. All from the perspective of Max as he gets to know each of his crew better and sees there is more than your first opinion of anyone, even the evil administration. 
 While I loved seeing all the pranks ensure the story also has more depth to it that you don't even realize until you're in the middle of some deep and life altering questions. Max is a fun and entertaining person to see things from, maybe because he reminds me of myself loving movies and not being the social butterfly and all but he learns more about himself as the book and pranks progress. We get to grow with him through the book as he comes to some harsh truths about life and what he wants to stand for. I really enjoyed the story and so have the urge to prank someone now, though maybe I shouldn't have told that to the whole internet and ruin the element of surprise, drats. 
 Overall I think anyone who enjoys any good heist plots, contemporary, comedy, or anything could enjoy this without complaint. There is so much happening but you never lose pace and it never felt the least bit slow to me. I need a physical copy of this book for my shelf it was so good, and that cover is just perfect. I hope the author does a book event near me I'd love to hear how he came up with some of the pranks and such he came up with. Genius level stuff. Now I'm off to go browse my heist movies and find the best one to fill the void of reaching the end of the pranks in this book.

Although this installment was easier for me to read than Furies of Calderon (my groans were cut down by about a third, I'd say), I liked this second novel no more than the first one. It has been two years since the events of Furies, and we're plopped right back into the action without so much as an update, which at first had me a little miffed. The problem with plowing through novels so quickly is that proper nouns quickly find their way into the oubliette, so even though it's only been about two months, I was still playing catch up trying to remember who the characters were. 
 On second thought, let's not blame me. The names just aren't very memorable. I was 3/4s of the way through this book and explaining it to a friend and I had to grope for the main character's name. T...t...it's T-something I swear! Tavi? No wonder he's powerless, he sounds like it. Yes yes, I can finally easily remember his name now that I know his full name, Octavian. I cared so little about this series that the not so subtle hints went right over my head.  
 From the first page, Butcher sets up the story, and from there on out it is non-stop action. I like a good action scene as much as the next bloke, but in this case it really started to grate on me. The characters are never given a chance for introspection, besides sparing a thought or two for "I wonder where this other character is right now? No matter, off to another near death situation!" So once again, one of my main problems is the lack of character development. I know what the author wants the characters to be, but they never seem to get there on their own. We're just told they do, and I am baffled at people who say these characters feel "alive." Only alive in the sense that fire is alive; expanding the story and going new places but leaving nothing behind to appreciate. Honestly the only character I felt became a little more interesting in this novel was Fidelias, who I hated in the first book, so that's saying a lot. Making bad guys likable is always a plus in my book. 
 What really interests me about this series is the weak (well, relatively) main character. Tavi uses his brains and quick wit to talk himself out of - or into - situations. Usually in fantasy novels, any sort of magic is regarded with suspicion, a la X-Men. Someone with crazy powers and inhuman strength is usually incredibly frightening to the layman. In these novels, however, Tavi is the only weak character without magic, and he's the weirdo and regarded with suspicion. This flips my thoughts on magic and powers on its head, and I like that. I can't help but be gut wrenchingly involved whenever Tavi is in the middle of the action. I always want THIS to be the moment when his powers manifest. 
 I could have done without the weird women's rights story line. I know I know, I'm always touting about how sexist fantasy is and give me my strong female characters dammit. But in this case, it just came across as schmaltzy and a thoroughly fake story line to throw some pretend politics into the mix. Without it, there would have been next to no politics in the novel, and Butcher obviously wants us to be aware of the political situation in the realm. 
 The love story between Amara and Bernard was uncomfortable at best and gag worthy at worst. Here's my favorite quote from page 453: 
 Amara let out a nervous little laugh, and her cheeks flushed hot. She took two steps to Bernard and leaned up to kiss him again. He returned it, one hand touching her waist, a possessive gesture. 
 Please! Hopefully it picks up a little in subsequent books. 
 Pick this up if you want a fun romp with non stop action, with little consequence but also small reward. It definitely improves on the first novel, but not enough for me to legitimately like it on its own.

 I started Young Elites expecting a usual no-nonsense Young Adult novel--apparently I had no idea what I was getting myself into. I ended up finishing the entire trilogy in a span of two and a half days. 
 Finally, something different. 
 This review covers the entire trilogy so heads-up: Heavy spoilers ahead. 
 For the first time, the star is not a hero--but an antihero. Adelina stands out among today's crop YA heroines because she is exactly what they are not. We've seen it a hundred times: A seemingly ordinary girl who eventually becomes the key to the world's survival or something like that. It's a tale as told as time, and frankly I've grown tired of it. Young Elites is none of that. This is a story of the rise and fall of a villain--and her eventual redemption. In this series, I saw a mirror of our reality: how nations are born, how they are conquered... how one dictator falls only to be replaced another. It showed problems our society faces constantly each day: How hate begets hate, how it becomes a cycle that gets nurtured until it peaks. It's dark, it's mature, and amidst all the powers and fantastical world: there is truth. 
 Young Elites started with Adelina as a weak little girl, not knowing her place in the world and how to use her power. I journeyed with her through her torments until she found the first group of people that accepted her. I saw how she fell in love and how she got betrayed over and over. I watched how the bitterness of life slowly took its toll on her. I knew what was happening: How the darkness in her slowly brewed, cultivated by her sufferings and the people who hurt her. I stood witness as her power heightened and slowly corrupted her--how her ambitions and cruelty grew stronger each page. I knew she was no hero--yet I couldn't bring myself to hate her. Because I knew her story. Nobody here was pure. Each character had darkness in them--even sweet Violetta. In a way, I rooted for the villain. I think that's what the author wanted. Because in reality, we all have darkness in us. We all want to succeed, to become powerful, to be on top. Adelina was our personal darkness personified. 
 Honestly, I think the series could've stopped at book two and succeeded. I thought that final sentence at the end of Rose Society was perfect on its own. The beginning of Midnight Star felt a little out of place. I found myself doubting the author, "Where is she going with this?" The first two books were so strong and I didn't want to be disappointed with a weak conclusion. The third book started off weak, yes, but the final chapters were what saved it. That part where Adelina was bargaining for her sister's life and was contemplating what she has, would, and could become was beautifully written. My heart broke as she pictured her future with Magiano--a future that she'll never have. It felt like it was also being wrenched away from me. I wanted them to have more time--I wanted them to have a life. The voice in me wanted her to stay. Who cares about Violetta? She's had an easy life! It was as if I've become the dark whispers in Adelina's delusions. I wanted her to be selfish. I wanted her, not Violetta. But then as she wrestled with her thoughts, so did I. She was right. And it was devastating because I knew it was the right choice--the only choice. Still, my heart broke for Magiano. I finished the book with a little hatred for Violetta. Why did she get everything Adelina worked so hard for? Her life has always been easy--and in the end Adelina's life work was just handed to her on a silver platter. It's not fair! But then again, life is never fair. I guess, like Magiano, I'll just have to live with what we are dealt with.

 In this final installment of the marriage between Dean and Olivia West, things have definitely evolved. Olivia has a new business with her friend and Dean is dealing with a spiteful student, Maggie, who has accused him of improprieties in oder to get her own way. 
 Dean leaves town on an excavation in Italy, not only to give Olivia some time, but to also stay out of the line of fire from Maggie. This is the first time that he doesn't have a plan or control of the outcome in his life. But, he and Olivia seem to get closer and closer, through their "dates" over the phone and during his return trips home. 
 But when Olivia's very manipulative mother comes to visit, Dean is afraid she may take Olivia away. But Olivia isn't the woman who needs to be taken care of and protected anymore. She's growing into the woman she's always wanted to be, which is nothing like her mother. Her absence from Dean is allowing her to learn to stand up for herself and find out who she would have been without him and who she wants to be in their marriage. 
 The time in the hotel "dating" was so sweet and HOT at the same time. 
 Dean's desire to protect Olivia at all cost, even to his marriage made me a little nuts, but I liked how he had to learn to evolve with the relationship and even take a step back from being so over protective. 
 This series was hard for me because the first book was a little hard to get into . I just felt like it was all internal dialogue between the two with the back and forth between their past and present. I was most angry with Dean as I felt like half of their problems could have been resolved if he'd just spoken up and said what he felt. But I guess he behaved the way a lot of men do, which is probably why I'm still single. I need communication... LOL 
 But each in each book the relationship grew and matured and became what they both needed from each other, which makes this a great series and went from such a dramatic low rating to this high rating. 
 I would definitely recommend this series and preface to anyone to just get through the first one as it is a set up to much more emotion and drama to come, with some great and hot chemistry between this lovely couple.

I don't exactly know where this book and I went wrong. I really wanted to like it, and in a sense there were parts in the book that I did enjoy, but overall this was a big disappointment with me. Which sadness me because so many of my friends loved it, and I was so eager to read it myself, that it just turned into an absolute failure. 
 First, when I read the opening chapter I was excited. Grave digging, my imagination ran wild, I had all kinds of hopes for this book that ended up not only disappointing me but it fell completely flat. 
 Where do I start? 
 Jo. I honestly kind of hate her. She is a 17-year old that acts like she is younger, much, much, younger. Not only does she appear obtuse sometimes, but she is also naive, childish, melodramatic, too trusting, and overall not the smartest crayon in the box. Like in one scene while she is in Brooklyn, after facing so much danger already and learning the dark side of New York City, she goes ahead and thrusts some out of the mill older woman who offers her a ride back home, not even contemplating what kind of danger might be facing her trusting this woman and her husband. Now let me tell you something. I was raised in NYC and if some random older woman and her husband offered me a ride home while I was alone in a neighborhood I am not familiar with, I would run the other direction screaming fire. I guess it might just be me, but as an ex-New Yorker, I actually learned how to not trust people - an issue my husband and I choose to agree and disagree on. 
 Conveniently for Jo though there is always someone there to rescue her from her bad decisions, most notably Fay. 
 The romance was lame and honestly felt a little forced and fake. There were a few scenes that left me questioning if Eddie was actually using her for a story like her uncle has mentioned. Which in itself was never explained. When Eddie was confronted about it, he denied ever saying it, but the author never explained how Jo's uncle pulled that one out of thin air. There wasn't any tension and felt kind of instant. 
 I don't understand why the book was over 400 pages long. It dragged a bit at times. I found myself wanting to finish it in hopes of a better ending, but everything I predicted at the beginning of the story came true, which actually only disappointed me more because it was that damn predictable. There had been parts that also felt a bit rushed and not only that but oddly written. In example, this scene, just found weird the way it was written: 
 "Oh, look!" Jo said. "The man sitting next to her just stood up. He knocked her gloves off the counter. Go return them to her, Oscar!" 
 "He's crazy about her," Eddie said as he watched his friend go. 
 Jo smiled. "I never would have guessed. Is she really a medical student?" 
 Maybe I would have to backtrack a little more for it to make sense on here, but stuff happened conveniently and the actions kind of felt odd? 
 There was mostly just the bad side of NYC at that time and good part. Not much in between. 
 I wanted to know more about the Tailor, he seemed kind of creepy. 
 I only really liked Fay in this book. 
 And the prologue or whatever it was that gave us a glimpse into what is happening later in the book, did not really reflect what happened later. It didn't match. I can't go too much into it, but the feelings and actions of the moment just did not match. 
 I also thought this would be more creepy due to the cover, but it really wasn't. I was surprised Jo could not see the answers in front of her as the evidence continued to pile on, since I myself already figured who done it right after it happened. 
 Also, in one chapter her mother sucks.This review was originally posted on Night Owl Book Cafe

 Every time I pick up a new thriller, I'm hoping to be surprised. I want to be sucked in, lied to, encouraged, tricked, deceived - and Mejia does all that. But at the end of the day, I want the ending to be the type of surprise that hits me out of nowhere, yet makes perfect sense in retrospect. I love authors who make me suspect everyone. If I figured out the killer within the first few chapters, I'll never read the author again. So... that's the point of view I'm coming from when reading this type of book. 
 The prose is excellent. Mejia is a talented writer. She weaves a fascinating web in dual timelines with multiple points of view. The story pulled me in from the second chapter, and I read 2/3 of it in one sitting.

Well, Elantris is a book by Brandon Sanderson, and that alone for me anymore ensures a certain level of quality. It's a bit more of a mixed bag than the Mistborn trilogy, but still has many fantastic elements in the story. 
 The strong points of Elantris were very clearly in the setting and in the characters. The idea of Elantris: a place where pain never fades away and the inhabitants live in the ruins of the city of the gods, is simply a fantastic setting and I thoroughly enjoyed every scene which was set in Elantris. Really awesome worldbuilding there. In addition to this, the character of Sarene was very interesting and her personal backstory made her that much more of an unusual and fascinating character. Add to all this many unexpected plot twists, some very intriguing religions present in the book, and some surprising character arcs, and this lends to a very satisfying read. 
 There were some weak points to the story, though. It took me a long time to get into some plot-lines in the book, and since it utilized a one chapter following this plot line, one chapter following the other plot line mechanic, this meant that for a while I was pretty bored with one plot line, since--as interesting it was--it just wasn't matching up to the Elantris plot line. In addition to this, some aspects of the story's ending, while partially explained, were still kind of confusing and not as clearly wrapped up as I'm accustomed to with a Sanderson novel. 
 Nevertheless, on a whole, this was a very engaging read that very much gripped me until the end and which combined so me great characters with a surprising plot and some solid world-building. Great standalone novel by a fantastic author. 
 Rating: 4 Stars (Very Good).

 "That's all I do all day. I'd just be the catcher in the rye and all. I know it's crazy, but that's the only thing I'd really like to be." 
 I'm not really sure how I feel about this book. Damn, it would be easier if I were neutral but here I am... 
 This book was meant for those, who dig deeper. Not only reads it, puts it aside and grabs another book. At first, I was just reading it for school. I didn't try to understand, I just read. And later I began to read about it on the internet, try to understand what the author meant, when he wrote chapter after chapter. What I found - changed my perspective entirely. 
 I began to see this book for what it truly was. Not just a book about a teenager hating the world but also an individual going against the society and the rules that control all of us. Holden said screw it instead of playing a happy teenage boy. He questioned things not being afraid of sounding stupid. He lied, manipulated, criticized, cursed. But the truth is, he was right to do so. If we follow the rules the society tells us to, what is the meaning of life? There is none. Just doing what everybody else expects you to do, going through the motions - that's not really living. 
 "It's funny. All you have to do is say something nobody understands and they'll do practically anything you want them to." 
 All in all, this book was well written, thought-provoking and unforgettable. I have to say - I didn't expect it to be this daring and I'm glad I read it. I would definitely recommend it but The Catcher in the Rye is not for everyone and I know more than a few people who didn't like it.

 - I quite like Kaz's characterisation. I do. At first, with Six of Crows, I didn't quite get the fuss. Eventually, With his backstory and his "affliction" and no, I'm not talking about his limp, i started to find him a lot more interesting, because he was who he was, no excuses, no attempts at "heroics". Basically, I really appreciated that Leigh Bardugo didn't try to pull an uncharacteristic act to make him seem more like the romantic hero in any way. He stay perfectly flawed until the very end. There were no magical cures, nothing convenient about him in any way. So I found myself really rooting for him. If anything, the fact that he didn't have a magical character change and only subtle little changes is what ultimately made me really love the character. 
 - Friendships developed. It wasn't just about a group of people who embarked on an impossible heist together, it was about a group of very different people who embarked on a heist together and somehow, against all odds, ended up caring for one another and being friends. The chemistry between the characters was really great and each of them started to get close on a deeper level and find common ground that was beyond the fact that they all-pulled-the-impossible-and-survived. It also offered some great humor among the characters and I found myself laughing a lot. Mostly at Nina's shenanigans and the fact that Matthias cannot comprehend sarcasm. 
 - I liked that this book focus on the action, the world-building, the setting, the heist, the characters and not so much on the romance. It wasn't romance-heavy. There was some romance, obviously, but unlike other YA fantasy book, the focus didn't veer off from the main events only to giving readers their sailing "ships". It would give the romance it's due, and then move on. 
 - The action itself and the plotting was really great in this book. I honestly just read through it without thinking and trying to guess what would happen next. I just allowed myself to be taken on the ride somehow trusting that Kaz Brekker knew what he was doing even when all else seemed impossible. 
 - Van Eck was a great villain. Absolutely marvelous. Despicable through and through, but I would have liked to have seen a bit more two-dimensionality to his character, because every time you think you see the bit of good in him, it's staunched by finding out that it was merely an act on his part and I would have liked, at the very least, that some of his concern for his young wife and his unborn child was real beyond his build for a legacy. On the other hand though, Pekka Rollins was magnificent because he gave me what Van Eck didn't. His concern and love for his son went beyond anything in the world: his riches, his legacy, his life. And gosh-dern-it! I actually really liked him in his two final scenes (the first with his showdown against Kaz and the second during his last chapter). So I thought it was really interesting seeing those two put side by side and seeing how each one of them reacted differently to their family vs. their legacy in jeopardy and the choices they made. Pekka man. He was the biggest surprise. 
 - I loved the ending as it was. I love that it left the reader wanting more, that it allowed the reader the space to imagine a bit what-could-have-been and what-could-be. There was some happy and there was some sad. 
 - This may sound awful but I appreciated Matthias's death. Maybe not the way he died (although I can also appreciate the cause he died for) but the fact that he did. The fact that not everyone gets their happy ending. The fact that not everyone came out of the battle unscathed and alive and well. 
 No mourners, no funerals.

To start off, let's just admire the cover for a bit. Isn't it exquisite? Okay, about ten minutes of googling failed to bring up the name of the cover designer and this is perturbing because I want to know! How come they are not credited on the credits/copyright page?  Anyway, moving on to the book. I liked it. I thought it brought a sort of originality to the young adult fantasy genre. Evie is an engaging character and it is very easy to root for her as she navigates her paranormal life. The world Ms. White creates is fascinating and convincing. And well, I thought the book was pretty awesome when I read it. 
 But now that some time has passed and the afterglow of the initial read has faded and I am able to think (again) in an objective manner, I feel compelled to make some observations. 
 I felt that Reth was a bit too one dimensional in his pursuit of Evie. I felt that Reth lost out a lot because he wasn't given a backstory, emotions, reasons, something more than what he has. I hope the sequels bring more to his character than the premise of the series did. Give him some layers, I mean. 
 I know that the author really really wanted me to feel that the love story between Lend and Evie was nothing short of epic but I was not convinced. I felt that their chemistry was being forced on me - too much, too fast. When they fall in love, I was simply objectively observing, instead of the usual - falling in love along with the main character. I wish their love story hadn't been so rushed so they could have taken time to become friends and then progress to something more. 
 Actually, I wish the book was more about how Evie found out about herself and the enemy. What the subsequent revelation of her humanity (or the lack of it) affected her on a much deeper, psychological level than was portrayed. I am probably asking for too much considering this is meant to be an entertaining, fun read but I just wish...well, I just do. Especially because there is so much potential in the plot.

Her best friend is Bailey, her cousin and they lean on each other to get through the tragedies of childhood and high school. Fern has been in love with Ambrose since she was 10 years old and has tried to get him to notice her but why would a guy as handsome as Ambrose want a homely girl like Fern? Everything comes out in the wash when Fern writes love letters to Ambrose for her friend Rita and Ambrose finds out. It is then, Fern confesses her true feelings for him and he walks away. 
 "You read smutty romance novels and quote scripture." 
 As the ugly duckling grows into a beautiful swan, so does Fern while Ambrose is away fighting in war. When Ambrose returns home, Fern is faced with a challenge of getting him to open up and live again. Will Fern be able to get Ambrose to love her? Will she finally know what it feels like to live out the fantasies she reads in her romance novels? 
 "I think about your long red hair and your sweet mouth, and the way your little body feels when it's pressed up against me, and I just want to put my hands on you. Everywhere. And I forget that I am ugly and alone and confused as hell." 
 Ambrose 
 The picture perfect handsome man who excels at everything he does in life. He is drop dead gorgeous along with being champion at wrestling. He is everyone's hero or as Bailey calls him "Hercules". But does Ambrose want to continue to try to live up to the town's expectations of him? No, instead he decides to run away to the Army and talks his 4 best friends into coming with him. 
 Ambrose comes home from war alone suffering from a battle wound which disfigures his face and makes him look like a monster. He is blind and deaf on his right side and thinks he will never be able to make a life for himself and lives with the guilt of his friends' death. 
 "I used to be afraid of going to hell. But now that I'm here, hell doesn't seem so bad." 
 It isn't until Fern starts leaving him little messages at his father's bakery and slowly pulls him out of his shell, that Ambrose begins to heal. It is through Fern and Bailey, that Ambrose learns he still has strength not only physically but emotionally as well. He sees the life which Fern and Bailey have been dealt and realizes that not everyone is better off than him. 
 "Because terrible things happen to everyone, Brosey. We're all just so caught up in our own crap that we don't see the shit everyone else is wading through." 
 Bailey 
 Ahhh sweet Bailey - how my heart broke for you in this story. Bailey was an old soul in a broken body. He was the true hero in this story who was the foundation between the town. Even though he couldn't wrestle, he was at every practice, camp and game helping out any way that he could. He never let Fern down and was always there trying to make her life a bit more happier. 
 "Problem is, how am I going to get a handful of tit if I can't lift my arms?" 
 He was also the emotional strength behind Ambrose. Bailey was the one who told it straight and didn't pull any punches when it came to helping a friend out. Bailey made the best out of the life he was given and lived each day to the fullest. 
 "I think that's the worst part. The thought that no one will remember me when I'm gone. Sure, my parents will. Fern will. But how does someone like me live on? When it's all said and done, did I matter?" 
 Minor Characters 
 Rita 
 She is friends with Fern and Bailey and is the most beautiful girl in town. Fern wrote the love letters to Ambrose for her and Bailey was madly in love with her. 
 Becker 
 Asshole villian of the story and is a typical bully. He picks on Bailey through school and Ambrose confronts him. He also plays a pretty major part in the last part of the book. 
 Grant, Jesse, Bean and Paulie 
 Ambrose's best friends who signed up with him to go to war. 
 This is a book which will make you cry but leave a smile on your face. If you don't come away with a lesson from this book, you didn't read it good enough. 
 If you don't do anything else this year.....at least read this book and give your heart a bit of a jump start!!

Loved it. A very engrossing story. The second half or maybe the final third flew by. So, maybe I'd have to say it had a slow start because all of the action happened at the end. But still, great story - can't wait for later installments.

A delightfully twisted Japanese crime novel in the long tradition of delightfully twisted Japanese crime novels. For those familiar with the genre there aren't a lot of surprises. The structure is that pseudo-Rashomon format where one character narrates a chapter, then the next chapter throws new light on the previous one, possibly even revealing that the last narrator lied or met a hideous end. Still, it's well executed and the twisting is fun to figure out.

Of the three books in this trilogy, I enjoyed this one the most. I feel that the majority of the build up and movement towards the conclusion of the series was wrapped up well in the middle volume. This book was more active and engaging for me. The first book was a long, winded buildup of the characters, backgrounds, a part of the mystery and environments. The last book is mostly a recap of events that leads towards the conclusion. In terms of overall enjoyment, I really enjoyed this book because there is a nice balance of character development and plot movement. 
 It's astonishing to me how popular this series is all over the world. The basic premise behind Salander is a horrifying past that has scarred her forever and marks all her actions in the future. There's a no holds bar vision of what happened to her and her apt yet barbaric revenge. The other half of the series deals with corrupt, international business shenanigans that caused the leads which Blomkvist follow despite the dangers he face. I wouldn't have thought such a premise would come about with such a large following but it has. If a friend had asked me if I would be interested in reading a story about a rape victim and corporate espionage, I don't think I would have said yes. 
 I read the series because of the impact it made on a good friend of mine. While the book is not something I would have picked up on my own, I did enjoy exploring the world and characters that held a steady fan base all over the world. Kudos to Reg Keeland for writing a great translation of an interesting novel. 
 Are you looking for startling characters that grab your attention? Need a little mystery to sink your teeth into? You've come to the right place. Settle in and take a look into the Millennium Series.

When I first found out that there would be Aiden's point of view novella, I thought it would be some kind of "thank you" or gift from author to her readers who love Aiden and Covenant series. But Elixir was so much more. Aiden's point of view was definitely needed for the sake of storyline development and to be in his head was incredible. He is exactly a person Alex always thought he was, if not better. I have always been Team Aiden girl all the way but now my love for him is even stronger. 
 My Aiden: 
 Even though this was only short read, so much has happened. Readers will find out new info about whole Apollyon thing, new Gods were introduced, couple of emotional scenes took place and much much more. If this is only a glimpse of what is coming in Apollyon, I seriously cannot wait!

Now that's more like it. A return to the world of Earthsea at large - with even more magical shenanigans and DRAGONS! It's cool to see how much Ged has matured since the first book, and he feels much more like a Merlin figure here given that the main point of view character functions pretty much as his apprentice (despite not actually being a mage). 
 The story here functions as a conclusion to Ged's story featuring a counterpoint to the quest we saw in the first book - what if Ged had gone down the dark path he originally sought after all? - framed within the story of the disappearance of magic from the world. What emerges is an exciting (though ironically not that fast-paced) journey filled with lot of philosophical musings and wise words about the nature of magic/power and death spoken by Ged in the process. There's a lot to take in considering how short the book actually is and its young target audience, and it merits some re-readings to digest and really understand what Le Guin is going for. 
 Arren is less annoying as a POV character than Tenar was in the last book, but he still has his naive moments that require him to be [gently] schooled by Ged at several points. Sometimes I wondered why he even needed to be there at all, but he makes up for it by journey's end just the same (almost akin to how Dumbledore needed Harry in the Half-Blood Prince). 
 Not exactly what I would call a happy end to a series- which seems a bit unusual for a teen/young-adult targeted fantasy series, but a very much altogether satisfying one (although I have yet to read books 4-6 that came out a couple of decades later).

THIS BOOK WAS PURE PERFECTION. 
 I know I'm writing the review a bit late (a year since I actually read it haha), but it had to be done, because this is definitely one of my all time favorite books, ever. It is THAT good. 
 I loved everything about it, it was one of those books that I literally just couldn't put down. Seriously, one time, my friend had to drag it off me because I was reading it in class. 
 The characters were all so well-written, and they had realistic personalities as well. In some books, certain characters are always completely perfect and nice and happy and selfless all the time. But in Divergent, the characters all have flaws and they all have their imperfections that show up some times, and I love that. It makes the characters more human, more realistic, and much more relatable. 
 The plot line had lots of twists and turns, too. I'm not going to lie, some of the twists, I had expected and I predicted them to happen, but there were a lot of plot twists that literally had me gasping out loud in shock! 
 DEFINITELY ONE OF MY FAVORITE BOOKS OF ALL TIME.

I have mixed feelings about this book. 
 What I liked: 
 - an interesting world-building 
 Amy Bartol has elaborated a particular world with Ethar, with 5 nations, distinctive flora and fauna, biology and astronomy. It could be more defined and explained, but I suppose the author keeps some info fro the sequels. 
 - Kricket's human past 
 Kricket's character has flaws, due to a difficult childhood, of which we catch some glimpses through what she accepts to tell others. It makes her more "human" and credible in her reactions. 
 - a fast pace in the second part of the book 
 After a few slow chapters, it was nice to read some action and twists! 
 - promising material for the sequels 
 The author has everything to make an interesting sequel, with a perilous situation coming, changes in the status of the characters etc. 
 What I didn't really enjoy: 
 - the supermodel heroine (necessarily tall, platinum blonde, slim but with curves) who is smart and so irrestibly sexy 
 Kricket is such a cliche! I would have preferred a character who's appealing to some people "only", not to every single male... Kricket looks more like the living dream of a teenager rather like a beautiful, credible protagonist. I would have preferred a character who's appealing to some people "only", not to every single male around ... 
 - the multiple descriptions of Trey's abs and bust 
 After too many occurrences, and as an adult, I was so bored/irritated by Trey's physical descriptions (he's hot, we got it, thanks!), and more generally by all those sexy-but-chaste moments. Let's face it, they were cheesy. One is ok, two, why not, more is too much. 
 As a conclusion, I give 3 stars to the first installment of this series. I may read the sequel to learn more about Ethar, but I am not sure yet. This is definitely not a bad book, it's enjoyable in many ways, but some features prevent me from fully loving it.

I felt the construction of it had been rushed, there were plot holes, lots of repetitions (the book could've easily been cut by half), and a lot of "easy" plot solutions - for instance, introducing random characters to suddenly and conveniently explain why something occurred, or give background to an event, etc. 
 But still, I loved Evie, Jericho, and Sam, and the book did leave me wanting more. It also got me out of a reading slump, so was definitely entertaining!! It's lagging behind the amazingness of the first, though - and unfortunately so.

What an interesting modern take on being inslaved and not knowing it, whether by your family culture, your friend, your job, etc. Also kind of entertaining to read, which didn't hurt.

This is another of those books that baffles me by the number of 5star ratings it's received. Honestly, I just really did not find anything interesting or intriguing in it.

 The characters were all very 2d, and very contrived.

Ok, so it could be argued that they have this long history together or whatever (I haven't read the other books) but Maggie doesn't remember that so, for her, it's very much the cliched 'I barely know you but you are so the one' type affairs.
