Warning: Absolute Spoiler Alert (and very emotional and heavily wordy review) 
 You should've read the book already before you read this. 
 1.5 STARS 
 Initial Rating: I refused to rate 
 UPDATE: After days of reflection, thinking and meditation (lol) I still carry a heavy heart and frustrations about those what could've been in this story. I can't get over my hate to Cooper's Dad, Jace's stupid actions, and the unnecessary angst and issues. That doesn't mean that this is a BAD book. I will still recommend this to someone. A LOT actually. But I guess I have to go on my personal, subjective view of it since after a day, 1.5 star is the rating that settled on me considering all the negative feelings that I harbored after reading this 
 Uhm. I am not sure. I don't know. This is very emotionally-complicating to read. Let alone to review. I wanted to give this a 5-star rating but what's my justification for that? 
 Did I enjoy reading the book? No. 
 Did it make me feel happy, warm feelings? No. 
 Did it depressed me? HELL YES. Made me shake in anger, even 
 Did it make me angry? AGAIN YES. 
 But then, the book is so well-written, delivers the goods as the author intended, and if the intention of this book is to make the reader experience the different facets of pain, then it succeeded beyond Anyta can imagine. She completed all the facets of emotional pain in this one hell of a book. A good feat for a writer but a problem for me since I just don't see the point of it at all to be compiled in this book. 
 The emotions portrayed in this book are so effin real that I hard a hard time letting go of my emotions as I read through it. The story progressed in a 12-year time frame. Since the emotions portrayed in this book are so real, a reader can sometimes be stuck to the emotions of one time period and finds it hard to connect to the situation when reading a scene that jumps years later. I am still seething in anger to Cooper's dad while reading the rest of the book, making it hard for me to enjoy the great moments. 
 I struggled with some of the characters' decisions and emotional reactions. For example, I am not sure if Cooper's mom is emotionally dysfunctional since I really can say that her reaction to all of this is somewhat bland. I was looking for that RAGE. Acceptance of the situation, fine, but still there should be RAGE. Cooper is right, she is a FOOL for accepting that situation and stupid for not considering the feelings of her kids with that kind of setup. It's like the parents just thought about their own emotional issues and expected the kids to come to terms with whatever their decisions and situations without any emotional impact to them. 
 I am very much affected by the negativity (and the stupidity) that is all over this book that I honestly think how on earth did the family story settled happily that easily? This story presented a very grave offense a father and a husband can do but the emotional reactions are quite unrealistic. You can't shit people like that and expect them to accept and be happy for your decisions. The angst is there, and it's so real but the rage, and the emotional reactions are so unrealistic. Impossible, even. 
 I see Cooper as a martyr. I see Jace as a weakling. And because of this, I did not enjoy the "HEA" ending. I hated Jace throughout the book. It's not satisfying to me at all. Jace does not deserve Cooper. And there are way too many unresolved issues/questions for me (which I hate) 
 So, my question: How will I rate this book? Based on how it was written or how it made me feel? 
 What's important is that the book was very interesting and emotionally engaging enough that even if it feels like I walked through many thorns just to finish this book, I conquered. And that is a very hard feat for an author to do. I HATE all the angst that was presented in this book because I find a lot of it as silly and stupid, but she was able to pull me to the finish line. And if only based on that, I'll give her all the stars in the universe. She's a great writer. Brilliant actually. I just hate this particular story. So much. 
 I RECOMMEND THIS READ if you don't have any issues about family or daddy issues. This is a GREAT, WELL-WRITTEN BOOK all things considered. But the issues presented just hit home for me that's why I am spluttering all these hate and negativeness. 
 With that, please excuse me while I nurse my heart back to health. I just read Lightning by J. Bell and this book back-to-back and I DESERVE a rest on angsty books. Or I'll die like Lila. 
 PERSONAL NOTES: 
 * Jace says that he is a fool for doing what he did i.e.  Exploring his sexual urges, while still in love with Cooper. That damn tryst with BLOND MOP nearly killed me!  I say he is stupid. Ugh. The reason why they did not open that stupid brown envelope is because they did not want to know what it says. YET, he selfishly presumes the worst and ended up hurting Cooper in the process. I just don't get that he made the possibility of their relation an issue and underwent in an unnecessary relationship spree that brought heartbreaks to Cooper many times then afterwards, he'll decide that it didn't matter anyway. I thought the reason why they didn't open the envelope is so that they can continue what they have. But no. Both of them agreed not to open the envelope but Jace presumed they are brothers anyway and then, let Cooper suffer with his barrage of boyfriends and girlfriends. If they opened that damn envelope in the first place and confirmed they were brothers, at least Jace's actions will be justified. Cooper won't be hurt because he'll understand Jace's actions. And for this reason alone, I can't help but declare that this whole situation is a waste of emotions and just an unnecessary angst. It could have been easily avoided if they just have enough brains. What made me angry at the end is that IT DIDN'T MATTER ANYWAY IF THEY WERE BROTHERS... So with that said, I really don't get why Jace have to set Cooper in that kind of situation. It's like he purposely made Cooper suffer for his own emotional enjoyment. Gosh, he really find it necessary to bring a boyfriend home after Cooper tried and tried to reach to him despite the distance? Really Jace? Ugh. 
 * In addition to my point above, I am pretty sure Jace knew how Cooper dreaded his inevitable Journey to college. It was established very well in the book. Cooper tried to reach Jace, excited with his calls and even planned to go to Otago to surprise him. Trying very hard to cling to him. As a reader, I have this foresight that Jace will do EXACTLY what he did in this book, but brushed it off since it IS impossible since Jace loved Cooper that much and I am pretty sure that he won't subject Cooper to experience the latter's worst fear: For Jace to find someone and choose someone's company over him. And that's EXACTLY what he did. And I hated him for that. He even brought that BLOND MOP home. And I HATE him for that. Hate him for that. Did I just mention how I hate him for that? Sadistic scumbag. UGH! 
 * Cooper is the loyal one in this relationship. Jace? He is the coward one. And, honestly? I hated him since that scene with the Blonde Mop. I never felt sorry for him afterwards either. He doesn't deserve Cooper one bit. 
 * What happened to Zach? He was sacked unceremoniously in the story, and I thought there was more to that "Hamish-Zach" part which ended as an unnecessary filler. 
 * I don't think I can forgive my father at all if I was Cooper or Annie. Being left 2 weeks at a time for a "business trip" only to learn that he is playing House with someone just a few neighborhoods away, the thought alone makes my blood boil. I wasn't able to forgive Cooper's dad for this and I don't think I will be able to at all. He's selfish for expecting the kids to blend well in his newly-established family. I can't imagine myself experiencing that trauma is I was Annie or Cooper. It was mentioned in the book how every year they planned a great Halloween birthday for their dad that took almost the whole year to plan and after that horrible revelation about his "dating his love of his life" everything stopped. Imagine how lonely and betrayed Annie and Cooper at this point. But HE EVEN INVITED THEM to his relatively-better home with better Halloween Party that obviously Annie and Cooper wasn't part in the planning. If I am a kid in Annie or Cooper's age, I would definitely feel so bad that my father was able to replace us that easily and he was able to create a great Halloween Party (Yes, he WAS IN THE MOOD for a party after shattering his first family's heart) And to think about the planning involved in creating such a party, I can imagine him planning his party to be held in that new home before he broke the news about him leaving Cooper and Annie's mom. That echo in Cooper's mind "We're better than you" is very very accurate and understandable. And the only reason for all this shit is because he wants to be with the love of his life?! It's like their father said "F*ck you all, I'll live my life?" To say he is a scumbag is definitely an understatement, don't you agree? Ugh. 
 * This book is very well-written. The words are carefully woven to ensure the readers can feel the trauma that the kids who had just experienced a broken family. I just can't say I enjoyed the journey at all. NOT AT ALL. 
 * I can't relate much on Cooper being chummy with Lila too much. I am more of an Annie on this situation, actually much worse since I won't be seeing my father or the witch in any way after that.

Reading this book gave me a serious urge to watch The Big Lebowski again. 
 Larry 'Doc' Sportello is a private investigator in LA in 1969, and he's also a damn dirty hippie who smokes dope constantly. Doc gets a visit from his old girlfriend Shasta who has been seeing married and wealthy Mickey Wolfman. Wolfman's wife and her boyfriend want Shasta to help them with a scam to get Mickey committed to an asylum, but Shasta feels guilty and wants Doc to help Mickey out. 
 Doc no sooner gets started than he gets blamed for a murder by his arch enemy LAPD Detective Bigfoot Bjornsen who has nothing but contempt for hippies. Mickey and Shasta have vanished, and while Doc tries to wrap his foggy brains around these developments, he's also approached by another woman who claims that her boyfriend, a saxophone player in a surf band that supposedly died of an overdose, is still alive. 
 The Crying of Lot 49 is the only other Pynchon I've read, and this one has the same kind of hazy vast conspiracy lurking in the background . And like that one, I was left kind of liking the book in a general sort of way while thinking that Pynchon is just fucking with me on some level. There's a lot going on in here in terms of information and secrets with a friend of Doc's feeding him info he's getting from the first primitive form of the Internet. 
 The spacey and affable Doc makes for a unique main character to guide us through a noirish but laid back landscape, but it was Bigfoot Bjornsen with his constant stream of anti-hippie comments that I found the most enjoyable. 'Cause much like Bigfoot and Eric Cartman, I am also a hippie hater. 
 I get why Pynchon is worshipped as such a post-modern master, but there's just something about his style that isn't engaging me at the gut level.

I've never felt so lukewarm about a book before. 
 I don't think this book elicited a single feeling from me. I'm trying to recall any part of it that was at least somewhat memorable or impressionable to me but I'm coming up short. Simply put, this book had no plot. I am completely baffled by just how little happened in the FOUR HUNDRED AND THIRTY-THREE pages of this book. There were so many scenes that added absolutely nothing to any aspect of the story. They didn't forward the plot, didn't add to the character development, nothing. There were actual scenes where a character would literally show up, say hi to another character, and then leave. That's it. Even the ending of the book, which was supposed to be an exciting payoff to the (meager) suspense that had been building up throughout the story, was anticlimactic. Yes, there was some conflict and lingering tension, but it was resolved and everything ended up fine for the most part. There was one loose thread left in the end, but it certainly wasn't enticing enough to make me even consider reading the sequel. It didn't make up for the complete and utter lack of narrative that this book had. I cannot emphasize this enough: NOTHING HAPPENED IN THIS BOOK. 
 Onto character development, or lack thereof. The characters in this book were essentially blobs with names; they barely had any personality. The main characters were bland, the side characters pretty much interchangeable. The story mainly follows four people's perspectives: Simon Wolfgard, a Wolf; Meg Corbyn, a blood prophet; Monty, a policeman; and Asia Crane, a woman hired to dig up dirt about the Others. Here's the thing: I didn't care about any of them. My feelings towards these characters ranged from indifferent to irritated. Yes, Meg was sweet and all, but she was also painfully boring. She wasn't boring because she was sweet or innocent. It's just that the way she was written made her feel quite flat. 4.5 stars. I loved Showtime's "The Borgias" even though I know it's not all that accurate. How could you *not* love the juicy story of a family unafraid to bribe, murder, or conquer anyone who stood in their way? Showtime billed them as "the original crime family" with plenty of reason. So when I learned that Sarah Dunant had tackled this infamous family, I had to pick up the book and dive in. 
 In "Blood & Beauty," Dunant sets out to give us a far more accurate accounting of the Borgias' bloody misdeeds, and the result is no less engrossing. No matter how despicable the Borgias are (especially Rodrigo and Cesare), you almost want to root for their tremendous ambition and utter disregard for the rules. You even feel a bit sorry for Cesare at times; he was incredibly intelligent and capable, yet his father took far more pride in his loutish second son, Juan. 
 Lucrezia, who's often been portrayed as every bit as ruthless as her father and brother, is given a much more sympathetic treatment in this book, and she's the story's beating heart--an innocent young girl who gradually learns how to navigate the treacherous political web she's been thrust into. 
 Despite my interest in the subject, I did find the start of the book a bit slow, and I had trouble connecting with the characters at first. However, a few chapters in, and I was hooked. So hang in there--it's worth it. 
 "Blood & Beauty" ends just as Lucrezia marries her third husband in an attempt to solidify the Borgias' hold over much of Italy. Dunant plans to write a second book about the family, and I'll be picking it up when it comes out. Highly recommended for those who love historical fiction.

I had always heard that this series gets better with each book, but I had NO idea that each book would be so much more intense than the last. I can't even imagine what the last book must be like!  Although Rose nearly drove me insane in Vampire Academy, I did nothing but admire her fire and strength in Frostbite. Sure, she still makes tons of mistakes, but don't we all? If anything, her ability to handle even the toughest of problems makes me appreciate her even more. Plus, I LOVE how she can kick butt and stand up for herself. If there is one thing Rose isn't, it's a damsel in distress. Really, her character development is the novel's biggest strength. 
 Not only does Mead pump up the drama and romance, but she also turns up the intensity. The plot is more fast-paced than the first book's. In Vampire Academy, I felt like we had to wait until the very end of the book before we got to the real action. In this book, the action starts in the first few chapters and doesn't let up until the very end. The climax had me squealing and flipping pages faster than lightning. 
 Mead sets things up perfectly for the next book, Shadow Kiss (which I immediately grabbed and began to read after finishing Frostbite). I cannot wait to find out what happens with all of the characters, especially Dimitri and Rose. Their love is so addictive, and I can't get enough of it. I can only hope that the third book is as captivating!

 Don't get me wrong - I like the author's writing style and I feel like she stays true to the characters and the world she has created. And perhaps part of the problem is that I read this on the heels of a YA book with lots and lots of action but very little world-building. But still - this book seemed to move at a frustratingly slow pace. With the first two books, I enjoyed that they took their time building the world and describing people and places with detail but without long-windedness. This time, however, I found myself impatiently skimming nonessential paragraphs repeatedly, craving the pages when something would actually happen. 
 Again, it could just be that the jacket sets you up expecting this huge event up front that doesn't happen until you are almost a quarter of the way through. That's enough to make anyone impatient. But it also could be that the author is starting to fall into the trap that many series-writing authors succumb to - stretching out a series for all of its money-making worth. I sincerely hope that I'm wrong.

I'm not afraid of zombies because they are dead bodies who want to eat people. What I'm afraid of, is actually that idea of a contagious virus sweeping the globe and putting an end to society/order/safety/life. The idea that there's no one to turn to for help, no safe space to run to. Your life is now basically just you, permanently on the run from whatever threat is looming over you, forever and ever until you finally die, probably alone. I can't lol. 
 So basically, I went into this book expecting a survival story, but maybe like a fun camping survival story, about a fun traveling theater, you know? But actually most of it read like a straight up horror story to me lol, especially since large portions of it take place during the initial outbreak, which, ok, terrifying. I really liked the premise, and it could have been a very amusing read, had the execution been as good as the idea behind it. One of the first things readers will notice is probably the lack of new material. I realized rather quickly that crediting the author as "Jane Austen 
 and 
 Seth Grahame-Smith" was no mistake, as most of the prose and dialogue in 
 Pride and Prejudice and Zombies 
 was lifted directly out of the original and only tweaked to suit the zombies theme. This was initially funny; the modified version of the famous opening line to Pride and Prejudice is probably the best example of this: 
 It is a truth universally acknowledged that a zombie in possession of brains must be in want of more brains. Never was this truth more plain than during the recent attacks at Netherfield Park, in which a household of eighteen was slaughtered and consumed by a horde of the living dead. 
 Unfortunately, when this is done repeatedly at the expense of new material and dialogue that could have added some spice into the novel, it becomes tiring. For readers who are extremely familiar with Pride and Prejudice, in particular, it reads like someone regurgitated Austen's writing and randomly inserted the words "zombies", "blade" and so on. This improves slightly later on when there are more events to zombify, but not by much. 
 Secondly, the fact that this should be a rewriting of the original around a new theme seems to be an afterthought for the author most of the time, which results in a certain awkwardness and lack of flow when Elizabeth or any other character speaks of killing zombies or their fighting training with "Orientals." For example, Darcy suddenly introduces the topic while dancing with Elizabeth, to which Elizabeth replies that she finds the thought distracting while in a ballroom, before the dialogue abruptly returns to a slightly modified version of their original banter about prejudice and character. It's like the author suddenly realized that it was beginning to resemble the original too much, and hurriedly inserted a few lines on zombies. 
 The brief mentions of "Oriental" masters are also grating after a while. Had the background been expanded upon rather than seemingly thrown in there as a stereotypical idea of Chinese and Japanese martial arts masters (Elizabeth is a student of shaolin and has mastered the seven-starred fist, har har), it might have made a little more sense. As such, it just makes me wonder whether Grahame-Smith had watched too many Jackie Chan films! The humour is actually far more natural when Grahame-Smith forgets trying to force laughs with cheesy plot points like these. That scene where Bingley "politely vomited into his hands" from watching Darcy behead his zombified servants was hilarious. 
 Pride and Prejudice with zombies really is a very clever idea, and I honestly believe that had it been done better, it would have been quite a fun read for both Austen fans and non-fans alike. Sadly, the execution was lacking, so while one can appreciate the premise and have a giggle over a chapter or two, it's a waste of time to read the entire novel. Grahame-Smith made the mistake of lifting too many passages verbatim, without the ability to insert new dialogue himself that maintained the Austen flavour without being a carbon copy.

I often don't mind when nothing happens in a book or movie. I actually really like reading stories about people simply going through their lives, thinking about their situations or reacting to whatever mundane things are happening. These stories are relatable and often make me more emotional than stories which have more going on. The problem with this book is not that nothing happens, as I kind of expected going in, but rather that things actually do happen. 
 In fact, a lot of things happen. A lot of insane, crazy things. Things that would never happen in the real world. Things that are just plain magical. Murakami contrasts these fantastical happenings with his characters, who are dull, bored, and disaffected. These are not negative qualities, in my opinion. I really liked most of the characters in this book; their thoughts felt real and their dialogue, while a bit too erudite for the casual feel that their interactions had, mostly rang true. The problem comes when Murakami inserts these characters into the dream worlds he has created for them. 
 Every time a character entered or found him or herself in a bizarre situation, I could not help but lose interest. I did not want to read about someone coming to terms with someone who was telepathic, or having visions, or something like that. These were not situations that I could relate to, and they said and meant very little to me. Furthermore, they were not entertaining or exciting, because of the muted nature of the characters who were experiencing them. Hence, I did not get a series of revealing episodes which made me empathize with the characters or imagine myself in their situations, nor did I get something that was so insane and crazy that I wanted to keep reading to see what would happen. 
 Of course, this complaint is somewhat about myself. I was not willing to put myself in those situations and involve myself in their proceedings. Part of the reason why I did not do this is that I do not have a very good imagination. However, another part is that the end result of these situations is almost always the status quo, at least in terms of the characters' emotions (particularly those of Toru Okada, the main character). One could also say that this is very realistic, which I can agree with, but in that case, then I don't really know how the magical realism adds anything. All it did was take me out of the moment and make me feel like the novel had very little to do with me, and even if I imagined that it did, didn't have many opinions on how a person like me might deal with being in such a story. 
 But maybe this isn't a book that is supposed to be relatable. Maybe it's a "mood book" that puts you into a state where you can kind of lose yourself in the constant happenings and pleasant prose. I think there's something to that, but that feeling was undercut by the book's inordinate length. It just kept going and going, and the more I read, the more I felt like it wasn't worth the time it was asking for. Eventually, the almost singular tranquility that I did feel at the start was replaced with a vague boredom, and nothing was really able to pull me out of that. 
 It might also be the case that I didn't relate to this book because I am not Japanese. There might be references that I'm not getting, like in A Wild Sheep Chase, or the war stories might have meant more, or something. As is, I found the war stories in particular to be digressions that didn't do anything for me, and did not enjoy them at all. 
 Of course, I did like some parts. I really liked May Kasahara's dialogue and narration, especially by the end, and thought them to be relatable, thought-provoking, and uncontaminated with the magic that infused the rest of the book. I also liked the ending, which wrapped up a lot of the loose ends nicely. 
 I thought I would really like this book. It felt right up my alley, with its modern, vaguely disaffected characters and Murakami's propensity for describing the mundane as though it is extremely important. In the end, I feel like it didn't really do anything to me. It's not going to stick in my head, and it didn't teach me anything. It wasn't incredibly entertaining, and I felt glad to be done with it. I don't necessarily think it was a waste of time, because there were some worthwhile moments, as one would expect in a 600 page novel by an accomplished writer, but it was too close to that for me to like it much.

Andi has meaningless relationships. Her longest running was three weeks. Then in comes Clark, cute, geeky and a little awkward, he's the author of a best-selling fantasy series. When a fluffy white dog named Bertie brings them together for the first time, Clark starts to realize that planning everything and controlling everything may be the best thing that has happened to her. 
 I fell in love with Morgan Matson's writing with this one. She knows exactly what it's like to combine wonderfully flawed characters and eventually have them realize the error of their ways by the end. I gobbled this 528 page monster. Don't be intimidated by the high page count because you will fly through this one. She combines not only romance, but includes the importance of family and friends. I loved every moment of it. 
 Andi is always going to be the one who plans everything. Having her have all these plans be cancelled last minute makes her anxious. I could easily relate to her in this way because this is how I am too. I loved her character growth, her relationship with her father. And all of her best friends who are all so likeable as well. Clark is the sweetest guy with his cute dimples. He is a book nerd's dream come true. If you read the book, you will know what I'm talking about. All the other secondary characters like Toby, Bri and Palmer are there for support, and as a group unit, I loved reading their emoji messages. The cutie pie Great Pyrenees dog named Bertie stole the show for me. He is the cutest and so full of life. 
 You'll need to pick this one up if you're looking for a great summer read that will have you laughing, and also sighing with relief. Morgan Matson is definitely a favourite contemporary author of mine and her latest book will have readers clamoring for more.

I used to have a penpal from Kaunas, a lifetime ago when my only dream had been to see the world. Now I know that I didn't really have to travel far - I just need to open a book! What I learned about Lithuania's past from this book was beyond what my penpal offered me. He did send me the usual banknotes and stamps as common courtesy, and a 4x6 self-picture of himself (rather older than I was back then), but up 'til I picked up this book I didn't know that Hitler did invade Lithuania. 
 15-year-old Lina and her family were forced out of their home and transported to Siberia. She's just been accepted to the art school in Vilnius, because of her sheer talent, but due to his father's important position in the university, her family's on Stalin's list to be out of their country. 
 The book describes the hardship that Lina and her family had to face. She and her 11-year-old brother Jonas and their mother Elena, were seperated from their father. They were sent to a beet farm in the middle of Siberia and survived the winter until they were picked for another transport to a remote outpost near the North Pole. I mean, who would survive the North Pole during the winter months, not me!! What a harrowing account. 
 Since I've also been a devoted reader of anything on Holocaust, it's hard to not linking the war in this book with that of the other war. However, readers would appreciate how the author pulls them to the experience of being in a labor camp. This book might as well be a good introduction for me before tackling the Gulag Archipelago! 
 The only thing I regret is reading this book right after reading The Daughter of Smoke and Bone. This book is not a roller-coaster ride, but the book delivers much more than history - it says more on how to survive adversity without losing your soul.

Sigh, the premise is cute, and I can tell that the author has many stories within the world she has created but this story would have been much better served with some editing and the cutting down of characters. As many have mentioned repetitiveness is what brings this book down along with lack of feeling for any of the characters.

The novellas in the Kate Daniels series are usually pretty good so it is hardly a surprise that Magic Stars, with Derek as lead POV character, was an super enjoyable read. 
 After a family are murdered Derek is tasked by Curran with finding, and dealing, with the culprits. A task he completes quickly and brutally! Afterwards he investigates why the family are killed and discovers they were after a magical stone. One of three that a Warlock is seeking to reunite. The job of tracking down the Warlock and the Stones is made both easier and more difficult by the arrival of Julie on the crime scene. Derek is forced to accept her help in tracking down the stones because she has the talents to locate them and because she would just hunt them on her own no matter what he decided! 
 It was a fun story. Like all the Kate Daniels books the story had a nice mix of humor, action, and drama. My only criticism is that the story was a bit short. Lets be honest: we need a whole spin-off series focused on Derek and Julie! Despite the short size the story gave us a good glimpse into Derek's mind and an alternate look at characters like Curran and Julie from Derek's perspective rather than Kate's which was interesting. We also learned a few interesting things about Julie. Mainly that she is a lot more capable and kick-ass than Kate seems to realize. Also possibly, given her colourful vocabulary, that she has been spending too much time with Ascanio! The most shocking thing about this novella was possibly Derek's frail mental state. I never realized things were so dark for him. He hides it well most of the time. 
 All in all a very entertaining read. 
 Rating: 4 stars. 
 Audio Note: I do like Jeffrey Kafer as a narrator, but for some weird reason I did not feel like he was a good fit for Derek or this story.

This whole book is stripped of extraneous world-building in lieu of cutting to the important parts and showing character through the narrative. It never felt hollow or forced. Her story is interesting and it's fun looking for real world clues but it's not one where you're hunting for obscure bits mentioned fifty pages ago. No one seemed particularly flat or needlessly offensive. There's an anarchist and a biracial lead and circumstantial criminals and the story is driven by not one but two brave and fallible and likeable young women. I like that it's a standalone novel in a field of overstretched series. If she does serialize it, I'd love to see the full Princess X story as a graphic novel rather than a traditional sequel. I was totally into this book to the extent that... well, I'm not saying it's the only reason I called in to work to finish the book in one day, but it was one of the four or five reasons I didn't want to go back to my soul-sucking job. I've come to expect tight, fast, exciting, interesting, full stories from Cherie Priest's adult works (the last two Clockwork Century books just became my next two reads) and her foray into writing for young adults is just smashing. A++ I'll give this to my kids if I ever have them. 
 EDIT: Oh! I didn't even notice until I read other reviews. There was no romance. None. Nada. Zip. Tada! Teen girls don't have to fulfill their dreams with men. There were tiny mentions of queerness and one allusion to predatory men though, which was refreshing given how coercive relationships are mythologized.

"A fantastic ending to an awesome series" 
 Listening to Clockwork Princess was gripping, emotionally touching, and amazing! The third and last book in the Infernal Devices Trilogy was not a let down. Sure, it had the signs of closing and resolving all issues of the series but it didn't disappoint. If you followed my review from the Clockwork Angel to the Clockwork Prince, you would know how psyched I am about this book and this series. 
 Clockwork Princess starts off a couple of months after the end of Clockwork Prince where we were introduced to Cecily Herondale, Will's youngest sister who came into the institute to be trained as a Shadowhunter. We also see the continuation for Tessa and Sophie's training by Gabriel and Gideon Lightwood. I cannot continue giving a short summary without giving out spoilers but I will really try my best. Please be aware that I may reveal spoilers so if that is not to your liking, just skip on and read my thoughts on the audiobook and the narration. In this book, we finally find out the real reason why Benjamin (?) Lightwood, Gideon and Gabriel's father is in league with Mortmain and why he wants Charlotte Bramwell out of the Institute. Without spoiling much, I will only say that the Lightwood brothers are torn between family and Clave with Gideon choosing to join the Institute and Gabriel staying with his father. With Benjamin (?) Lightwood was defeated, Gabriel joins forces with the team at the Institute while Charlotte still tries her best to keep her position, Tessa and Jem plan their wedding. It is at this point where Will confesses his love to Tessa and Will and Jem's relationship as parabatai are put to the ultimate test. 
 This book is just explosive! I love the way the pace of the book felt. I was almost waiting for a fight to pop in at any second - yes, it was that thrilling. I love how the team joined forces - with Magnus helping Henry with his inventions (we see the origin of the portal that was used in The Mortal Instruments: City of Bones). The twists in the book where really unexpected. From Jem to Will and Tessa to the attack on the Clave - I just cannot begin to describe how very well thought out it was. 
 When the final battle came, Ms. Clare did not disappoint! It was very well written and full of thrills and surprises. I wasn't actually expecting the way Mortmain was defeated and how Tessa used her Clockwork Angel and her abilities to help in his defeat. 
 Overall, the book and the whole series was very well written. The story was plotted out impeccably from the first book to the last. 
 THE AUDIOBOOK 
 The audiobook is narrated by Daniel Sharman - a male. I had doubts about why they picked him as the narrator. I was wrong. Daniel Sharman was the perfect pick to narrate the story. Before I move forward, I would like to add that this book had a lot of declarations (emotional) by the male characters: Will and Jem. By picking a male narrator, these declarations were multiplied tenfold in their emotion to move the listener. To be honest, this was the only book that I cried. Sharman's reading was perfect and I would not change anything. His calm voice, pacing and the different voices (even the female ones) he used where spot on. It didn't even bother me that his "female voices" did not sound feminine or female at all and I did not have any questions as the the gender of the character he was reading. Narration is a definite 5! If you want to read this book, I recommend picking up the audiobook instead. You will not regret it!

The memories of his tramper friends. The letters he wrote. Anything that he did himself. Examples to enlighten you: 
 It is the experiences, the memories, the great triumphant joy of living to the fullest extent in which real meaning in found. God it's great to be alive! Thank you. Thank you. 
 Begin to boldly do things which you may previously never have thought of doing, or been too hesitant to attempt. The very basic core of a man's living spirit is his passion for adventure.... [Joy] is in everything and anything we might experience.

 I was sobbing at times while reading. This book was a home hitter. The pathos evident was so honest, that you can't help but be affected by it. You feel for Chris. You feel for his family. You feel. The prose was well done, clearly telling Chris's story when he wasn't able to. The organization and time line of the book was a little wonky, and at one point I gave up and made a timeline. (I recommend that you do the same.) You can definitely tell that Krakauer is a journalist because he uses that kind of precise-yet-imagine-y writing style. He puts you in Chris's shoes, but he is also throwing information at you at all times. His characterization of Chris was spot on, and more than once I yearned to meet Chris (then the harsh reality set it once more and I was a mess). He showed just how intelligent a man Chris had been. How innocent. How quirky. How everything. He didn't leave any rock unturned when it came to Chris McCandless. 
 And that may be in part to his mild obsession in the boy. I mean, he basically stalked Chris's journey for a long time after he wrote the small article on him, searching for answers. He followed Chris's footsteps. Spoke to the same people. Visited the same sights. He did everything, and it gave off some stalker vibes. He was so divested in this story that it was heartwarming. I will make a side note, though, that I could have gone without the Krakauer backstory parts. It threw the rhythm off and kind of set me on edge. It just didn't flow properly. 
 "[Chris] seemed like a kid who was looking for something, looking for something, just didn't know what it was." 
 This is all of us. We are all looking for something in the world, and more often than not, we don't know what that something is. We're all "misfits and dreamers." We all go on grand expeditions to find whatever it is we are looking for. I hope that for some of you, this novel helps you find that something. I hope you find your own way, as I did, while reading Into the Wild. Adventure is out there! 
 The best to luck to you all. I hope you find yourselves prosperous on your journey. 
 Thanks for acting like you're paying attention.

He was the Duke of Montgomery. He'd successfully blackmailed the King. He was about to blackmail himself a wife. No one loved him. 
 And that was the way he liked it. 
 The hero in this book, Valentine Napier, the Duke of Montgomery, is a villain. He blackmails everyone. (no, really). He murders people. He is cunning, arrogant, but he also has this child-like playfulness to him - I'm not talking giggles but more - his childhood was so messed up that he has this immature side. He wants to play, but doesn't know how to play nice - and never mistake his playfulness for weakness. 
 The Duke of Montgomery was as deadly as a coiled adder discovered suddenly at one's feet. 
 The only person that can wrangle him, is his housekeeper, Bridget Crumb. 
 Bridget loves her job - she runs Val's house to perfection, keeping all the servants in line, no matter how poorly Val treats them or his eccentricities he puts on display. Bridget was born to an aristocratic woman, but her father was a footman. Her mother hid her pregnancy and then placed the baby with foster parents. Bridget knows who her mother is (readers of this series will too) and the only reason she took this housekeeper position is because Val is blackmailing her mother. Bridget's goal is to find the letters Val is using to blackmail her mother, retrieve them and give her mother some peace. But Val is sly. Very, very sly and finding the letters proves to be quite difficult. 
 Val's childhood was horrific. His father belonged to a secret society that had annual initiation rituals including kidnapping, rape and murder. Val was a witness to all of this, and an attempt to initiate him also occurred. His father would give Val kittens at a young age, and when Val grew to love them and care for them, his father would kill the kittens in front of him. Val was taught that everything he grew to love, would die a horrible death. His mother hated him too - so let's just say, as an adult, Val isn't 100% stable and his idea of loving someone isn't healthy. 
 Bridget is definitely wary of Val and his moods, but she is also intrigued by him, and downright attracted to him. Val walks around in the nude around her, as he pretty much has zero shame. Val is very sensuous in this book, but he is such a different type of hero. He isn't growly or big or grumpy. He isn't serious and arrogant (well, he is arrogant) and broody. He is flamboyant. He wears pink and bright blue, and walks around in a dragon robe. His hair is long and wild. He is more on the shorter, slender side. Did I mention he has a full nude portrait of himself in his bedroom? 
 "You really are the vainest man in the world," she said wonderingly. 
 He stopped chewing. "This is the first you've noticed?" 
 He looooooves to shock people. He loves attention and games. When he kidnaps someone in this book, it's so thrilling for him. He has grown into an adult and missed the conscious and ethics line that adults shouldn't cross. For him, power is everything. Absolute. So, anything to gain that power over someone - be it blackmail or kidnapping, is something Val yearns for. 
 Bridget recognizes this to some degree. She is very smart and mature, and is able to look past Val's theatrics and understand what his main goals are. She is very practical and I adored her (he calls her Seraphine because she refuses to tell him what her first name is): 
 "Oh, Seraphine," he rasped. "Are you making advances?" 
 "I'm wiping vomit and sweat from your body," she said with rather too much tartness. "Nothing more." 
 "Are you...sure?" And she thought she saw his lips twitch as if they tried for his usual smile. 
 She blinked hard. "Yes. This isn't a moment for flirtation, Your Grace." 
 "...always a moment for flirtation," he whispered, the beginning of his sentence to low to understand. "Especially...when you're handling my cock." 
 "That's Mehmed." 
 "Pity. Though he has very soft hands." 
 Bridget and Val start this unlikely friendship. He loves having her around. She stimulates him with conversation and can keep up with his chaotic lifestyle. She also challenges him: 
 He leaned over it, reaching for the headboard, and opened the concealed compartment. 
 Empty. 
 Oh. 
 Oh, Seraphine. 
 He felt the grin spread over his face, felt his cock throb and stiffen. Suddenly the day was bright, singing with vibrant colors and stratagems. 
 She'd outmaneuvered him. 
 And that? That hadn't happened in a very, very long time. 
 She isn't afraid to tell him when he is being crazy and then she starts to fall in love with him. I loved it. She isn't a virgin, which shocks him. She has raven black hair with a white stripe in the middle and this drives Val crazy with lust. 
 This book is sexy, with such a unique hero and a heroine I totally fell in love with. Plus there were so many scenes that made me laugh. 
 You don't need to read the previous book to enjoy this one.

'Persephone' is a fun, imaginative, smart retelling of my favorite myth, fusing modern culture with a rich world of magic. I had such a great time reading this. I ate it up in just a few days. With its irreverent sense of humor and its intelligent references, it reminds me most of Joss Whedon, in particular the livelier, funnier seasons of "Buffy" or "Angel." 
 Persephone, a modern high school girl, is more than a bit surprised to learn that the Underworld is a real place, her mom is a real goddess, and she (Persephone) is on the verge of coming into her own powers. Soon Persephone gets temporarily stuck for her own protection in the realm of Hades, who's a hot and introverted immortal (his introversion really endeared him to me), and through her we get a visit to a richly and cleverly drawn paranormal world. 
 Kaitlin Bevis has done her homework. The side characters are nearly all inspired by mythology (some famous, like Orpheus; some more obscure, like Pirithous), but they are all fleshed out as individuals. The Underworld's features include lots of the geography we know from myths: various rivers with different magical properties, a hell-like area (Tartarus), and an awesome palace for the royalty. But it also has fun modern features like the ability to transform your rooms into a spa, and redo your wardrobe telepathically. But among the diverting innovations and renovations, darker and sadder scenes crop up, as is fitting for the afterlife: Orpheus will move you (naturally), and you'll cheer for Persephone when she demands to know why the hell the gods allow all the horrible things in the world to happen. (Though it's not like anyone can be expected to have a good answer to that.) 
 As a sucker for the Persephone/Hades relationship, I thought the romance was quite well handled. They keep up amusing banter, which lapses into sweet tenderness when Hades leaps in to protect Persephone from dangerous forces, and they share a couple of good "KISS HIM!" moments. It's clear they love each other, enough that I felt satisfied with where things end in this installment, but I very much look forward to watching their marriage of convenience mature into a full-blown steamy one in the next two books!

 I was practically a whole cheerleading squad to see Jules and her younger siblings who escaped a deplorable home life get their chance along with grieving and self-blaming Officer Theo Bosco who lost a canine partner to cancer and then his human partner to depression. Secrets abound and it was a nice level of tension to see how things worked out with Jules hiding big stuff and Theo being a cop. In this instance, the secrets are justified because its one of those sad situations where the law can't help the victims here at least for now when they are most vulnerable to a crime that can't be proven. 
 The secrets of Jules and her relations were only part of the suspense element. I enjoyed the action suspense element of a shooter and a night prowler. 
 But most of all, I enjoyed this sweet and spicy slow burn romance. It was fun how it awkwardly started. He might have called her 'squirrelly' and she might have found his sour face and disposition a bit off-putting, but they got beyond that and it was all for the good. 
 I also was excited to meet all the players in small town Monroe who I can look forward to seeing more of as the series progresses. It was a great start and I'm rarin' to go for Rocky Mountain K-9 book two. You don't need to have read the earlier series to jump into this one so you're getting in at a good time if you're interested in a solid new romantic suspense series.

 First of all, I did not realize this was geared for a young adult audience. I really do not read too much YA so I tried to take that into consideration when rating the book. I also found out that this series is a spin off of an adult series by Shana Abe... interesting. I'll have to check that out because maybe that would be more appropriate for me and my middle aged mentality. :) I ended up tasking my 16 yr old to read this too so I could try to rate it fairly. 
 So, this book has a beautiful cover... very well edited... and it's a full length novel... not too long and not to short. My daughter and I both read it easily in one day. The story is set during the World War in England. You have a girl who grows up in an orphanage and she doesn't know who or what she is and she is a very misunderstood child. She eventually is forced to move away from the orphanage and London to a boarding school because of the war. At this boarding school she is immediately drawn to two young men... one who mentors her and helps her find "her inner dragon" and the other is sort of a mystery until the end of the book. (Trying not to spoil things too much.) A sweet romance develops which is where I began to understand the title and it's strong connection to the story. You'll have to read to find out with whom! The romance is very age appropriate to a younger audience. We're talking hand holding, first kiss type of romance. Nothing too dramatic or shocking. The ending was a bit of a surprise and brought on a brief teary eyed moment.

The heroine ends up in a snobby boarding school so there is a lot of snarky girl drama. :) She also said that she felt it was a very well balanced novel in regards to the history, action, romance and drama. So Twisted by Melissa Marino is the first book in her Bad Behavior series. A debut novel with the story told in dual POV, the main charcaters are Aaron and Callie.

Josie became fairly whiny though out the story. I don't want to compare her to Alex, since Alex and Aiden come back in this story...  but if there were a competition to see who the better heroine would be, it's Alex hands down.  OK... let's get into the main event of the book. The big climatic fight scene. All the rest of this will be in spoilers so no one has to curse my name... Everyone thought it was Alex because hello, she killed Ares. I always thought that she became the God Killer because Seth gave it to her. I always felt like he was the real power source in that. I don't know if that theory will really factor in to how he is now the God Killer or not. I just want to feel justified in my crazy fangirl-dom!  
 We just scratched the surface of all these new character developments. Seth kept mentioning that he had this essence inside him that's constantly seeking aether. Perhaps the God Killer is a separate entity that's linked to him? Josie keeps getting headaches and weird dreams and foreboding feelings... maybe she's having some oracle tendencies?  I want answers now and I have to wait an entire year to get them. UGH!!!! I will always love this series but in the scheme of things, this installment was a tiny bit lacking. I just wish it really drove the plot forward more. 
 P.S. Hercules is a douche-bag but I think he will be a big ally to Seth in the rest of the series. MARK MY WORDS! Also, I'm glad they found a new demigod, Gable. Hopefully, we will get to know him better in The Struggle and find some more of them.

To begin with, this story is told in two different time periods by three different women. 
 In the late Victorian era (no year is ever mentioned) Kitty and Esme, two sisters who were born in India, are taken to Scotland to be raised as proper European ladies. Kitty takes to this grooming immediately, but Esme is resistant and finds herself the center of her mother's, grandmother's, and classmate's scorn. This is not helped by the fact that Esme was alone to witness a tragic, family-shattering event back in India and her parents assume her a bit 'touched' by the incident. 
 Iris is a young woman who lives alone in the more modern age. She owns a shop that she inherited from her parents after they passed away and she is simply trying to find herself. 
 The story begins when Iris gets a call from the local psychiatric hospital about Euphemia Esme Lennox, a woman who has been there for the past sixty-one years, and whose contact card has Iris's name. Euphemia, they explain, is the sister of Kathleen Lockhart, Iris's grandmother- but they're wrong, Kitty never had a sister. 
 I can't help but be a little disappointed in this book. I try not to go into a new novel with any preconceived notions, especially one which people tell me has a 'tragic' ending. As a connoisseur of all endings sad and unfortunate, this was recommended to me by several people, including one person who compared it's sadness and ability to haunt the reader to that of Diane Setterfield's "The Thirteenth Tale." I am here to tell you that no, it is not in any way like "The Thirteenth Tale," but it's not a bad book overall. 
 * SPOILERS AHEAD! BE FOREWARNED!* 
 Iris was one of the few female characters who didn't really frustrate me. She really was just a young woman lost in her own world, unsure of people, uncomfortable in her life, and willing to let things happen as they would. She's having an affair with a married man, a man who claims he wants to leave his wife to be with her, but unlike most women in novels who are sleeping with a married man, Iris is under no delusion that he will ever actually leave his wife, and she doesn't stake her entire being or happiness on his decision either way. Meanwhile, she maintains a close relationship with Alex, A man with whom she was raised and considers a brother, but the relationship goes deeper than that when it is revealed that as a teenager she had lost her virginity to him. 
 I liked Esme as an old woman and as a small child. For a little while she touched upon the feministic characteristics that I find distasteful in novels, specifically the stereotypical "I'd rather READ because reading is FORBIDDEN and DEEP." and the "I'm going to BUCK TRADITION because I am a WOMAN who wants an EDUCATION!" I realize that these were real issues in the time period in which she lives, but those two themes have been repeated so many times and with so little originality that they grate on my nerves. However, as she gets older she finds herself less resistant and more anesthetized to her role in society, coping by removing herself mentally. In fact, she removes herself so much from her present situation that when she is raped, it takes her almost a full day before she realized what has happened. By that time, her screams mean nothing to her family and they make the decision to erase her from their lives. Thus begins her long incarceration at Cauldstone Psychiatric Hospital. 
 Kitty can never quite understand her sister. Even though they are very close in age and were raised the same way, Kitty always embraced her mother and grandmother's rules of societal conduct. She dresses up, she goes to parties, she observes the proper decorum, and she goes along with her mother's desire to find a suitable match. She falls in love with Jamie, the man who eventually rapes her sister, but finds herself married to a man who doesn't want to have sex with her. She is so in want for a child, that when they find out that Esme is pregnant, she adopts the child and takes him home to raise as her own. As she gets older, Kitty falls victim to Alzheimer's. We get small glimpses of her past through this confused haze. It takes a little bit to get used to the narrative style, but it is actually very effective. 
 !MAJOR SPOILER! MAJOR SPOILER! 
 I didn't find the ending that sad, actually. In fact, I didn't find it sad at all. Esme never struck me as a vengeful or vindictive person, so when she kills Kitty by smothering her with a pillow, it seems more like a mercy killing than anything else. Esme is bitter toward Kitty for most of her life, frustrated that her sister would take so well to their mother's lessons and she so poorly, as well as feeling betrayed that Kitty never came to visit her, only coming to Cauldstone once to take away Esme's son. However, I don't think it was out of this bitterness or resentment that she suffocated Kitty. Although I can't put an emotion to Esme in that time, I sincerely don't think she was trying to get revenge for anything. It felt like an act of love.

3.5 Stars | Warning: There may be minor spoilers (a.k.a. Quotes). 
 I loved the prequel to A Court of Mist and Fury, so naturally, I had high hopes for this book. Before ACOMAF's publication, I thought of all the amazing possibilities there were for this series, and find myself a little disappointed by the direction this book is headed in. However, I did enjoy reading this book. 
 The plot of this novel was not remarkable. The first quarter of the book is essentially stagnant and Feyre is melancholic most of the time. Feyre's broken state came across really clear, perhaps too clear (it was emphasised so much), to the point where I almost lost interest in continuing the story. Thankfully, the pace picked up soon after that. Like Maas' other books, there is wonderful action contained within these pages... but all of the action is near the end, making the last third of the book extremely action heavy, and the ending chaotic. There are also some twists, but none of them were really shocking. 
 Even though I talk about being really bored when Feyre got so detached, I still think that part is important, because it paves the steps for Feyre's eventual rediscovery of her true self. This meaningful, well written character development is definitely what won me over. 
 As usual, the main cast of characters in this book is utterly amazing. By the end of the book, I pretty much became emotionally attached to Rhys, his gang, and Feyre. Their friendship chemistry is simply awesome and the occasional witty banter made me enjoy their exchanges. 
 Her eyes fell on the open threshold to the bedroom hallway, and she grimaced. "Why," she said, "are Amren's eyes there?" 
 Indeed, right above the door, in the center of the archway, I'd painted a pair of glowing silver eyes. "Because she's always watching." 
 Mor snorted. "That simply won't do. Paint my eyes next to hers. So the males of this family will know we're both watching them the next time they come up here to get drunk for a week straight." 
 Each and everyone of Rhys' gang has a hidden part of their personality that makes them interesting, three dimensional. More about Rhys himself is also revealed and it allowed me to empathize with him at a level I could not before. Another character I liked was Tarquin, and... I hope he survives the next book. 
 On the other hand, there were other characters who were poorly neglected. For example, Lucien's fiery personality which I had loved so much in the first book is now nothing more than a few embers, a remnant of what he was before. It was super disappointing. Tamlin, who was also one of my favourite characters from Book 1 just became nothing more than a flat character who had an overwhelming obsession with protection (his "wry humour" has all but disappeared). A lot of characters were sort of... trampled upon just to make way for the main gang. 
 Velaris was a lovely setting. I'd love to visit Velaris if it existed. *Sigh*, the troubles of a reader. 
 The Rainbow of Velaris glowed like a fistful of jewels, as if the paint they used on their houses came alive in the moonlight. 
 In general, the night court proved to be more complex than the spring court and thus, it captivated me a lot more easily. Outside of Velaris, there are also tribes of Illyrians. The traditions of the Illyrians were really interesting. Although the traditions are brutal and unjust (clipping their wings is just cruel beyond measure), it did show me another side to this world. 
 Before the events in A Court of Thorns and Roses, there was a war between the King of Hybern and the courts of Prythian. The characters who had a part in this war were often mentioned, and I really wanted to know more about them but it was not talked about much in ACOMAF. Hopefully, more parts of that particular story will be revealed in the next instalment since the war sounded pretty epic. In all seriousness though, a brief but informative history would make ACOTAR's world much more believable. 
 Finally, the romance. The romantic arc in this book was a little frustrating. So much attention was placed upon the romance, that some attention was taken away from the plot, which is equally important. Also, why does Maas mess with my shipper heart all the time. In this book, my favoured ship sunk, but it's ok, because I also love the ship that did survive. The romance between Feyre and her love interest is developed in a way that is simply beautiful. But let's be honest here, all of the possible love interests for Feyre are 100% hot and also awesome. 
 And he'd be here during the summer, flying over the meadow, chasing me across the little streams and up the sloped, grassy mountainside. He would sit with me under the stars, feeding me fat summer berries. And he would be at that table in the town house, roaring with laughter-- never again cold and cruel and solemn. 
 The romantic arc is a little similar to the overarching romantic arc in Heir of Fire and Queen of Shadows, so if you didn't like the romance in those books, you might not like it in this book. Nonetheless, I do urge you to try out this book though, because there are definitely some great parts. :)

 Pleasepleasepleasepleasepleaseplease no love triangle between Rhysand, Tamlin, and Feyre. But considering the reason why Feyre went through all those trials, I think it'll be unlikely that she'll love someone else... 
 ...unless Tamlin isn't her other half.

Before I start you need to know that after this review nothing meaningful can be written about the Clockwork Prince. 
 My second disclaimer concerns Ms Clare's writing in general. I had the misfortune to read the Mortal Instruments series before the Infernal Devices trilogy. This experience, amounting to trauma, influenced my reading of the Clockwork Prince. However, if you approach the Shadowhunters' world for the first time, the objections below may seem unsubstantiated. 
 In a sense these objections will be repeated exactly because the Infernal Devices regurgitate several themes/motifs/scenes/characters featuring in Mortal Instruments. Accordingly, a more seasoned reader might feel cheated or bored or, possibly, both. Nevertheless, it is better. It has better writing, more plausible plot, characters displaying more than two dimensions, banter, ambiance; shortly - everything. Including romance. 
 Let's be clear, it is a romance novel. Not a fantasy tale about a sinister threat of a clockwork army or a girl on a journey towards existential self-discovery; it is essentially a love triangle story, and a quite skilfully written one. Once you accept this premise, and reconcile yourself with with the fact that everything else in this book serves as a means towards this ultimate end and needs to make sense merely as an enabler or a set prop Example: Why was Will's father forced to abandon the Shadowhunter community for marrying a mundane, if they have the Ascendant procedure? Couldn't they just turn Will's mother into a Shadowhunter? No, otherwise Will's drama couldn't have unfolded and he would have been a perfectly ordinary boy, unfit for the love-triangle purposes , the to-read-or-not-to-read dilemma becomes a non-issue. 
 Then, the only problem is whether you are cheering for Will or betting your family heirlooms on Jem. Because if you think yourself partial to this emotional conundrum and could not be more bothered whether it is the neither or both of them, I would advise you not to pick up this book.

I gave up. After reading more than 100 pages (which is more than a quarter of the book!) I decided to let the book rest in peace. I still wasn't drawn into the story, still wasn't gripped. Rather than keep hoping the story will improve, I'll read something else. 
 What stands out about this book when you flip through it, is that it's written in Present Tense. I myself have only ever gotten as far as writing fan-fiction, but one of the first lessons was NOT to write in Present Tense. It has an odd feel to it. It made me like the book less, instantly. 
 It reads slow, like a 'quality' movie. Very long introductions. Gemma's boredom is very feel-able. Okay, her mother is almost killed by a shadow-demon-thingy and then stabs herself with a knife instead, but was it the vision, or real? The action isn't that well written, blurry descriptions. I didn't understand what the shadow-monster looked like or where it came from. 
 Also, you're not really in the middle of things, they're not embracing you and pulling you in. It's like you're watching from a distance and are unable to loose yourself in the reality of the book, as you are supposed to. 
 It's not until page 50 or so Gemma finally reaches Spencer's and (tiny) things happen. I like that she hates being a lady but all her thoughts and mental comments are a bit overwhelming. Not always as funny or witty as they were probably meant to be. Kind of obnoxious. 
 Spencer's setting is eerie enough, it has potential despite not being that original. 
 I did like that Gemma stands up for 'poor' Ann and that way draws the attention of the popular girls. I like all the details about what ladies are supposed to act like (especially to her brother Tom) and the way society works and looks. Like they're not supposed to look out the carriage window when they ride through the slums. Literally closing yourself off for misfortune. 
 The church scene after dark where Gemma has to obtain the wine is creepy. But the 'mystery' surrounding the young Indian man is too... hazy. Too childishly simple, so far. Too easy. 
 From reading the bit I've read so far, clearly this book is meant for a much younger audience, not for teens. 13 Year olds would probably really like the mystery and girls' relationships. 
 I'm not saying this is a bad book, it's just not for me. It didn't grab me. Young girls might like it though. Perhaps, had I been that age, I would have loved it too. Part of me thinks that would have been the case. Alas, I am not that young anymore. 
 I'm just glad I didn't buy the whole trilogy in advance and get to spend my money on more interesting books. Or, so I hope.

I am very happy with the way her story resulted though, she had been through hell and back again and I have no words with which I could comfort such pain. This is the only reason why I'm rounding up my 4.5 to 4 instead of 5. Rating: 3.25 (I'd like to give this a bonus start for originality, but I decided to stop doing bonus stars.) 
 This book has two narrators. One is Bo, who is in a mental institution. The other is his sister, Phoebe. Bo thinks his school just pretends to be for the mentally ill when it's really a school for people with super powers. The school is currently under investigation because of a studen'ts suicide, which Bo says is a cover up because he lost the girl in the past. You see, Bo has the ability to move through time, but he doesn't have the best control of his abilities. When he took Sophie with him, he got sucked back to the present, and she got stuck in the past. 
 Throughout the whole book, Bo tries to save her and keep his abilities hidden from the investigators. 
 The whole time you feel like Bo is an unreliable narrator, but you desperately wish he isn't. You want Sophie to be alive because he's in love with her. 
 I won't confirm whether he's delusional because that's half the fun. What I will say is that Beth Revis knows how to create something fresh and original with subtle references to Doctor Who. As much as I love Doctor Who, her take on time travel is more creative. Bo navigates his way through strings of time like one of the Fates, traveling back in time but unable to warn anyone of what's to come. There are restrictions to time travel. Even so, Bo stays faithful til the end. 
 Speaking of the ended, it goes out with a flame, an eruption of heart-pounding suspense leaving you worried about the fate of our dear Bo. 
 When you're done reading, there's a lot of reflection to do. What makes a person crazy? Can a person be defined by mental illness? How do their lives affect their family's? 
 Regardless of whether Bo is mentally ill or not, you're forced to see him as a person and not a loon. I think everyone will be able to see themselves in him. And that's great because it takes away some of the negative stigma against people who have mental illnesses. I highly recommend you read this. If you're a teacher, get a classroom set and add it to your curriculum. It fits multiple genres, and there is so much to be taken away from this book. I also deem it appropriate for all ages since the worst thing in it was the D-word as far as I recall. 
 Anyway... 
 If you like this book, I recommend Shutter Island 
 . I've only seen the movie, but they have some definite connections.

I enjoyed this short novella, though I didn't feel like I was able to taste enough of the world to really make an opinion of it. But I did read enough to be interested in a longer novel. The story also teased out several questions for a book: What is this virus that kills people young? What is outside of the closed gates? Why hasn't the king been seen in ages? . The dystopian society, built on a past time (not sure if it was one time period or a jumble - regency England? King Arthur's court?), was intriguing, and I'd like to learn more about that as well. I think part of my problem with this short story was that I was genuinely suspicious of Xander for much of the tale. He just seemed too nice, and Fallon was clearly someone who was playing a double game, so I assumed that he was as well. It wasn't until the very end when it became clear that he didn't have a hidden agenda. Fallon came across as a strong capable character, and I'm hoping that he'll also pop up in the future novel, giving a better sense of himself. Also, I thought that everything moved too quickly. While I don't think that just these elements could have made a full length novel, there could have been a lot more added to Xander and Fallon's story. And with the teased question, a longer tale could have been written. I guess I'm not sure why the author didn't just go for a full length book, unless she'll be working with completely different characters and wanted to get this story out of the way.

"Pride and Prejudice" is undoubtedly one of the most beloved classic novels in history -- it's had countless adaptations, sequels and homages lavished on it over the years. 
 And Jane Austen's grand opus is still beloved for a good reason. While it's rather stuffily written much of the time, it has a vibrant core of witty dialogue and strong characters that shine like lanterns in the night -- and the best part of it is the interplay between the two strong-willed main characters, whose initial dislike of one another blossoms into love once they learn how to overcome his pride and her prejudice. 
 The Bennett family is in an uproar when wealthy Mr. Bingley moves into the neighborhood, and Mrs. Bennett is especially happy when he takes a liking to the eldest Bennett daughter Jane -- since their estate is entailed and there is no Mr. Bennett Jr., a good marriage is considered essential for at least one of the girls. But her forthright, independent sister Lizzie immediately butts heads with wealthy, aloof Mr. Darcy, who scorns the rural village and seems haughty about everything. 
 A flurry of proposals, road trips and friendships happen over the course of the following months, with Lizzie fending off her slimy cousin Mr. Collins, and befriending the flirty, hunky Wickham, who claims to have been wronged by Darcy. Lizzie believes Wickham's account -- and she's in for a shock when Darcy unexpectedly proposes, and reveals what Wickham won't tell her about both of their past lives, and what Wickham did to offend Darcy. 
 And finally things take a scandalous turn when Lizzie's idiotic younger sister Lydia elopes with Wickham, while staying with a friend in Brighton. The family is plunged into disgrace, which also wrecks any chances of a halfway decent marriage for the other daughters. The only one who can set things right is Darcy, who will do whatever he must to make amends to Lizzie -- and unwittingly establish himself as the man she loves as well... 
 Reading "Pride and Prejudice" is a bit like watching someone embroider a piece of cloth with subtle, intricate designs. Lots of balls, dances, visits and drawing room banter between Lizzie and virtually everyone else, and interwoven with some rather opinions from Jane Austen about haughty aristocrats, marriages of security, entailment, and the whole idea of what an ideal woman has (intellect and strength). 
 The only real problem: Jane Austen writes very much in the style of her literary era -- it's rather formal and stuffy much of the time, and the narrative is kept distant from the characters. So, not for casual readers. 
 But despite that formality, Austen's brilliance as a writer is evident -- she slowly unfolds the plot one act at a time, with several intricate subplots that tie together and play off each other. She also wrote some unbelievably sharp-edged dialogue with plenty of witty banter between Lizzie and Darcy ("I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine"). But Austen also weaves in startlingly romantic moments between them ("No one admitted to the privilege of hearing you, can think anything wanting"). 
 It's hard to imagine a better fictional couple than Lizzie and Darcy, despite their rocky start (a major-league snub at a dance). Both are witty, smart, and a bit snotty in their own ways, with quick minds and even quicker tongues. Darcy is a selfish, rather haughty man man who gradually becomes warm and kind, while Lizzie is strong, independent, and Darcy's equal in every way. And neither will marry for anything but true love. 
 It also has a solid supporting cast: the painfully practical Charlotte Lucas, slimy clerics, virtuous-looking rakes, sisters ranging from saintly to snobby, and the lovable Mr. Bingley and perpetually optimistic Jane. Lizzie's family also adds plenty of color to the story, including the screechy and hilariously mercurial Mrs. Bennett and the barb-tongued Mr. Bennett ("Your mother will never see you again if you do not marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again if you do"). 
 Despite its mildly stuffy style, "Pride and Prejudice" is the ultimate Jane Austen novel -- a powerful and romantic story about two people who grow and change because of love. An absolute must-read.

This is a great graphic novel version of a classic piece of literature. It does a wonderful job of transforming the text into pictures, and keeping the spirit of the original intact. It stands up well on its own, and it peaks the readers interest in the source material of the original novel. 
 The illustrations are spot on. The scenes of the fires are thrilling, the four wall televisors frighteningly predictive, and the atmosphere of this particular dystopia is rendered flawlessly. But my strongest praise is reserved for the way in which artist Tim Hamilton draws Guy Montag. In a story where so much of the action centers on Montag's internal struggles with his own actions in the context of his society, the artist's renderings of naked Montag in the shower, the image of Montag tilting his head back to taste the rain, the silhouette of Montag tucking a book inside his fireman's jacket, and the mask like blankness that descends on his face during the card game with Beatty all serve to amplify the critical moments in his journey. The drawings of Clarisse are also well executed, and capture the sense that she is the only character who really seems alive in the early portions of the novel. 
 Of course, in a Fahrenheit 451 world, this adaptation gives us far fewer words of the story to memorize and preserve. This renders the mechanical hound a little less scary, Montag's hidden vent book collection a little more startling, and the vagabonds ability to recall for memorization books that have only been read one time a bit too convenient. But you gain almost as much story as you lose with the visual element that this adaptation brings to the table.
