"Tell me something about yourself that no one else knows. Something I can keep for myself." 
 I have been itching to read Confess since that gorgeous cover reveal and I'm happy to say that the inside matched the outside. What a beautiful and emotional story! I was a little nervous to dive into this one after Ugly Love failed to live up to my expectations but Confess got to me within the prologue. I'm talking about big, fat, ugly crying. It's been some time since a book hit me this hard and it was just a sign of good things to come. 
 "Some secrets should never turn into confessions. I know that better than anyone." 
 What I love about most CoHo novels is how unique her story and the characters are. For example, Owen, he is the artist that catches Auburn's eye. If it wasn't his boyish looks, it was his sheer talent in creating works of art from people's confessions. If you follow CoHo online, she has stated that these confessions are ones readers sent to her. My favorite one was "When I'm With You, I Think of All the Great Things I Could Be If I Were Without You". I mean how deep is that? I like to think that I'm not easily swayed by pretty writing but Colleen has a wonderful way of giving feeling to her words. I felt Owen's passion when it came to his art. I also felt the anguish that both Auburn and Owen felt in their daily lives. I am so against spoiling anything so I apologize when I don't give you a recap of what this story is about but it's because once it starts unfolding it makes you question things like happiness, and fate, and sacrifice, and consequences. 
 "I'm scared I'll never feel this again with anyone else," I whisper. He squeezes my hands. "I'm scared you will." 
 I only had a slight issue with the progression of Auburn and Owen's relationship. I wouldn't say this is love at first sight or insta-love, but there was an intensity right from the get-go that felt, at times, a little forced. By the end of this book I felt like I was in a place to understand the bond between them. The end also had me in tears, which again, has been rare for me as of late. Confess is a work of art with a ton of heart and swoony moments. If you are a fan of Maybe Someday I can easily see how you would love this as well. 
 4 stars*

A must read! Four 1/2 Amazing stars! I'm near speechless. It feels like I've been away on a journey so incredible I'm still trying to decide what aspects were best. 
 Watching Jamie and Claire grow as a couple was probably the most amazing romance I've ever read. It gave new meaning to soul-mate. In the early stages, I got angry with Jamie for his macho behavior, but he was also written with such strength, tenderness and vulnerability, that I couldn't help but fall in love with him. Claire was a strong, likable heroine with a level head on her shoulders. Their "pillow talk" and intimate conversations were a guilty pleasure. All of the characters were very "real" with human flaws and emotions. Jenny, Jamie's sister, made an incredible impression and I hope we hear more from her in future books. 
 There are layers upon layers to ponder in this book. It's not "just" a romance between Claire and Jamie. It's a piece of historical fiction that gives us a glimpse of life in 1743 Scotland and the political struggles of that time. The time travel adds the element of mystery. I do have several unanswered questions, but being the first in a series, that's to be expected. There are elements of violence that aren't for the faint of heart. 
 I was a bit intimidated by 800 some odd pages and put it down months ago after the first 67 pages. Now I'm glad I went back and stuck it out. This isn't a book one can really rush through. It should be pondered, absorbed, savored. I'm a bit of an action junkie. Maybe that's why I found the first 100 pages or so a bit slow, but they are necessary to the story. Once Jamie and Claire met, I became more engaged and found a comfortable pace, alternating between falling through the pages and reading with near frenzy. This is definitely a book I'll re-read. 
 I plan to continue this series.

I read the Mortal Instruments series fairly quickly after it was released -- I basically fell in love with the entire set of characters, and Cassandra Clare gave me several books to lovingly inhale. :) I don't know what took me so long to read the Infernal Devices series, but per usual, I bought all three last weekend and have already completed them. 
 Cassie Clare has an undeniable talent for making you root for several opposing people at one time -- it's both incredible and infuriating! I have never struggled internally more than when I read her books. Who do I ship? Who do I support? Who is the enemy? But is he/she really that bad? 
 IMHO, that just means Clare is damn good at her job. Snape Syndrome 101. 
 I thought the entire series was incredible. I loved seeing references to details or things prominently featured in TMI, and the foundation of so many others. This entire series was not just the icing, but an entirely separate, but equally wonderful, shadowhunter cake, lovingly baked created by Clare. 
 The one specific part I will reference is the epilogue. SWEET GOD THE EPILOGUE. Mind you, I read this on my lunch break and failed miserably at keeping my shit together at work. I was crying, with that horrible pain in your chest when you know your heart is basically breaking. I know it was meant to be beautiful -- and it was -- but goddamn, if it didn't shatter me into pieces. The final component, or reunion I guess I should say, left me feeling so whole, so fulfilled, so satisfied. Well done, Clare. 
 Recommended for: Those who want their Shadowhunter tales served with a historical fiction twist.

 This was on no account The Hunger Games. Rather than the contestants fighting each other to the death - they were gossiping each other to death. The closest we get to action in The Selection is a bitch slap. And it wasn't even a good bitch slap. 
 The specific motive that caused me to pick this up is because it sounded like an enjoyable read. The blurb stated thirty-five teenage girls competing for the marriage of a handsome prince. Yes, it didn't sound particularly clever. But I still decided that I would pick this book up just for entertainment. Nevertheless, the book was agonizing due to the fact we've countlessly read so many books about characters like America Singer (What is up with her name, anyway?) Unless, you're J.R.R. Tolkien or J.K. Rowling, please don't make up names out of your head. Just simply search normal girl or boy names on the web. It's very straightforward. Anyhow, America Singer's character was hmm...the exact word to describe her is monotonous, nothing remarkable about her. 
 Facts about America Singer: 
 -	Very pretty 
 -	Poor 
 -	Very nice 
 If there were other facts about America Singer, I'm not going to attempt to remember them. Wait. I think she could play an instrument. Oh, who cares? She was boring! 
 I like the attempt on how the author tries to make this as dystopian as possible, but achieving very little. One of the funniest was how the girls were supposed to wait till marriage to have sex. Is that the most original idea you've ever heard of or what? 
 I remember one quote from the selection though, strangely. (It was that bad). 
 "Aspen was dressed in white. He looked angelic." Um, you'll need slightly more description there. There were some tremendously cheesy quotes in The Selection that made me want to gag. 
 The male interests were just as flat as America. If I were asked to pick out one of the two male interests, I would choose none and I'll keep a safe distance from them, just in case I don't die out of boredom. Interesting fact: Did you know the Prince hasn't even had his first kiss. I'm sorry, but that's just not believable.

I thought this book was brilliantly written. The book is about the event that took place during the Nigeria-Biafra War in 1967 to 1970. The story starts before the war, in the early sixties, and continues on until Biafra lost the war. It talks about how ugly war is... especially in a place like Nigeria where little existed in the first place. It was so heartfelt and brought me to a verge of tearing a few times. Many people in Biafra died of starvation during the war, including many children. 
 Even though it's not a "feel-good" kind of book, I take from it that human are resilient. Sometimes fighting to survive leads to more violence, but sometimes it gives you strength and courage that you thought you never have. Both Olanna and Kainene went through horrific ordeals, but they pulled through and became stronger because of them. 
 I thought that Ugwu represented innocence, who grew overtime through unpleasant experiences. He was a very likable character until he participated in the gang-raping. He hated himself for it, and I could only imagine how he felt when he found out his own sister was gang-raped and beaten to near death. It was touching that the war brought Olanna and Kainene closer to each other, even though it also pulled them apart when Kainene went missing. I was getting so sad in the second half of the book, after they all evacuated their homes and the tragedies started. But in the end, I liked the fact that the author had Olanna remaining positive about her twin sister's disappearance. It's hope that sometimes keeps you alive.

 Some of the short stories were definitely better than others. 
 The Keeper: It was interesting to see the Michelle story line. How she ended up with Scarlet, how she ended up with Cinder. 
 Glitches: This was the story of how Cinder ended up with her step-family. We got to see that Adri was always horrible and that Peony was always sweet. It showed us how Iko came to be, and how Cinder was so good at fixing things. It was devastating to see how much the death of Garan really did impact things. 
 The Queen's Army: This was the story about how Wolf came to be. It was not surprising that he was always a little defiant of his "calling" that he did not want to be part of his. But, once he was part of it he refused to go through the surgeries again; he refused to be made more beast than man. It was heartbreaking to see how Wolf came to be, how he became Alpha. At the same time that led him to Scarlet, which I can't be mad about. 
 Carswell's Guide to Being Lucky: This was one of the weaker stories. Carswell has always been an incorrigible flirt and this just proved it. It was nice to see him question his methods, and develop real feelings for Kate. And it was sad how little his family cared about him. But, overall this story was just meh. 
 After Sunshine Passes By: This was the story about how Cress ended up in the satellite. It was sad. A little girl works so hard to get even a little praise, a little warmth, but it never comes. No matter what she did, nobody cared because she was just a shell. This was devastating. 
 The Princess and the Guard: This was the early years of Winter and Jacin. It showed us how Winter became crazy and why. It was sad watching Winter realize that what she considered helping might not have really been helping. This is a prime example of the cliche "the road to hell is paved with good intentions". I was glad to see her take responsibility for her actions and to decide to change. It was nice to see that she fell in love with Jacin before she became crazy, and it seemed like that was mutual. Watching him make the choice to give up his dream to stay with her, to protect her was heart wrenching. This was one of the better stories. 
 The Little Android: This served to show that Iko was not the only android with a malfunctioning personality chip. This story was not about any characters we already knew and I was not invested in any of the characters. This story was irrelevant. 
 The Mechanic: This was Cinder and Kai's first meeting from Kai's perspective. It was wonderful to go back to that moment; to relive it. It was nice to see that Cinder was not the only one awestruck and unsure. Smooth, confident Kai was dumbstruck by a mechanic. It was wonderful to relive the beginning of their relationship. 
 Something Old, Something New: This was the story of Scarlet and Wolf's wedding. It was charming and actually brought a happy tear to my eye. How much they love each other was beautiful. And how everyone came together to give Scarlet a small, press free wedding, was adorable. I loved everything about this. It didn't hurt that it started with Cinder leaving Luna after abdicating her throne, or that it ended with Kai proposing. All the feels for this story!

Jonathan Strange & Mr. Norrell is a decidedly unique book. Whether that is good or bad is a matter of perspective, but it is most certainly distinctive and different from almost anything else you'll read. 
 Parts of this distinction are Victorian-esque spelling and grammar; detailed footnotes relating to imaginary books and stories to further worldbuilding; meandering plotlines; and incredible length, measured not just in pages or word count but in drawn-out pacing. 
 To cut to the point, would I recommend this book? Not to most people. But that doesn't mean it isn't good! It has charm, and kept my attention. But it is long and slow and indistinct--it really isn't a book for everyone. 
 And if you do read it, save yourself the arm ache and read it as an ebook. I didn't, and my book seems to have a cracked spine in a few places, despite my caution. 
 Anyway, what is the book about, you ask? Well, funny question: I went most of the book without being able to give a clear answer. It's ostensibly about two Victorian-esque magicians who quite literally bring magic back to England. But it's really not. It's also not about a rivalry between these two; though it flirts with the idea, that's a red herring. So basically it's a book you should read if you've got time to kill and an interest in Victorian magic and glacially slow plots. 
 I do appreciate the writing. It must have been incredibly complex! There are layers upon layers here--but I just didn't care that much. My biggest question, having finished it, is how in the hell in today's publishing market it was allowed to be published in this format?! There was a lot here that I didn't really need to read and which would have been easier to digest as two or three books in a series. The resolution would have been about as satisfying (ahem: not), and it would have given me a bit of a brain break from the wandering story. I mean, some people are really going to enjoy it--and it is masterful!--but that doesn't inherently make it a good read. 
 Generally, you should probably just watch the TV show for this one.

 There are quite a few things I expect - and get - when diving into a Megan Erickson novel: 
 Unique characters 
 Witty dialog 
 Realistic plot 
 Sexy times 
 Heartache for daaaaaaaaays 
 I have said it time and time again, she has this way for writing such realistic and relatable characters. Each character is unique and genuine, and she is a master at bringing those characters to life. How she does it time and time again is just mind-boggling. 
 What I didn't expect was the dark undertone of Focus on Me. Riley has a lot of deep-rooted issues that are brought to the surface and his struggle was just heartbreaking. I can't imagine how tricky and painful it is to write a character with not only one, but two mental health disorders. 
 Not only was Riley suffering from said issues, Colin has his own struggles to which Riley's tie into. Colin's self loathing as a failure mixed with the realization that he couldn't FIX Riley brought on the flood gates. As hard as it was, I appreciate how we got to see the struggle of how these mental illnesses can affect everyone, not just the person suffering. Colin wanted to be enough for Riley and wanted to fix everything but the reality is, you can't. 
 Riley's mental state was never glossed over by any means. Yet, TO ME, the book's focus was on both characters, not just Riley. 
 The romance build up was slow, to which I loved. Both Colin and Riley slowly let each other in and their even though they had plenty of challenges to overcome, they worked through it. Their story isn't over yet - both have many things to overcome but I am happy where things ended. 
 The secondary characters were minimal but played such an integral part. The families are SO supportive of each other, and helping Riley get the help that he needs, all the while, supporting Colin as well. And just in case you were wondering -- Justin and Landry make appearances and even play a major part in Riley's life and recovery. 
 All in all - I loved everything about Focus on Me. The characters, the romance, the road trip! Best of all, I love the message behind it. Focus on Me is a gem and one to be cherished. Highly recommend.

This book was an utter fucking mess. I have never read a book cover to cover and been shocked into disbelief and felt such disgust as I have with this. It actually frightens me that teenagers could read this and see it as nothing but a semi-tragic romance where everything is happily ever after in the end. 
 1. I could go on until the cows come home about how idiotic Nyx is during this entire story. She doesn't know whether to be filled with hate and loathing or remorseful and filled with good intentions. It's constant shifting back and forth. Nyx is chaotic, and not in a constructive way. One moment she's hating her twin sister and her family, and the next moment she's all "I shouldn't be so hateful, I'll fulfil my mission for her and love her." It's a constant back and forth and the more this book goes on the more bewildering it gets. 
 2. Hermetics. What the fuck. Is it. Never explained. It's just a thing. Nyx is supposed to have trained in it for nearly 10 years so she can defeat the demon, but she does absolutely nothing. 
 3. This is perhaps one of the unhealthiest "relationships" and forced romances I have ever read. Nyx is forced to be the demon's wife, and comes to his castle married, and is rightfully frightened and angry at him. Ignifex, the demon, reveals himself to be a Class A bastard. I laughed at his first appearance because I couldn't believe this absolute laughing stock was our "evil but not evil" prince needing saving. 
 Let me make it clear, Ignifex is a godamn bastard. He torments Nyx in the beginning, belittles her, mocks her, and is condescending toward her. She knows this, BUT !!!! he has a pretty face so it makes her put aside these irredeemable flaws and lust over him. Because he's dark haired and pale and beautiful. Gag me. 
 For a good 200 pages or so, it's like this. There is no believable development between Nyx and Ignifex, but more so with her fellow "captive", his shadow, who takes corporeal form at night. She thinks she's fallen in love with HIM (Shade) yet still feels this lusty pull toward Ignifex. In the same way she went back and forth between hating and loving her sister, Nyx goes back and forth constantly between doubting her mission to kill him and being confident in killing him. 
 Oh, but he's working his magic on her. All it takes is that moment when he saves her from the "darkness" and suddenly he's no longer a cocky bastard. He shows his "vulnerable" side and she's smitten. I'm just in utter disbelief that this is what I read. 
 When it comes to the point where they've admitted to mutual "love", he still talks to her condescendingly, like she's a pet, and doesn't respect her enough to tell her anything. She's deluded herself, is what she's done. She loves him and she can fix him. The entire "relationship" in this story is unhealthy and dangerous. I don't care if it's intended to be seen as akin to a Greek tragedy, it's billed as a romance and this kind of dynamic is toxic, no matter that this is a fantasy world. 
 If you couldn't tell already, reading this book angered me like no other. Little to no worldbuilding, a toxic romance, and pathetic, uncreative characters and plot had me shouting out my disbelief and anger to my friend as I read this book in her presence. 
 The tagline reads "Her mission was to kill him. Her destiny was to love him." This right here tells me that if women only try to fix men, they can find love regardless of the consequences. This was a sorry excuse for a Beauty and the Beast retelling.

** spoiler alert ** 
 King at his horrific best. 
 Stephen King flexes his horror-writing muscles in this tale of seven misfit kids who must confront the profound primitive intelligence of the most vicious creature to ever inhabit planet earth. In the process of telling his story, King draws what is perhaps his best portrait of the personification of evil... not Randall Flagg, not the Crimson King, but IT! 
 The monster arrives from beyond space and time into the swamps that will eventually become Derry, Maine. Eventually IT takes over the labyrinth of sewers and tunnels under the city. IT usually shows itself to Its victims as their worst nightmare (right out of literature, comic books, or movies): the giant eye, Rodan - the monster bird, the werewolf, Frankenstein's creature, the mummy, Hansel and Gretel's witch. But Its most common and perhaps most terrifying incarnation is Pennywise, the child-eating, monster-screaming, mass-murdering, shape-shifting, sardonic Clown. (And, as King reminds us, who doesn't love a clown?) 
 Of course, in reality IT is far more horrific than any of these, more horrific than the giant spider whose shape it assumes when humans come close enough to see IT in Its lair. The real demon, the monster within a monster, is so incredible that to get a clear look at IT is to die of terror. 
 But that's not all! IT can also take over the minds of townspeople, visitors, entire segments of the population, anyone IT needs. IT can color their thinking and drive them to insane and terrible acts that only serve Its purposes. And Its main purpose (besides eating bunches of children, sleeping it off, and staging insane bloodbaths when it wakes to begin killing again) is to get rid of the seven kids who once almost figured out how to destroy IT. 
 The misfits (six uncommonly geeky preteen boys and the pretty preteen girl that all the boys all are in love with, have amazing imaginative powers, and a real leader in stuttering Bill Denbrough. They also have a historian, a kid with engineering savvy, a guy who never loses his direction, a neat freak, and their own personal class clown (no relation to Pennywise.) 
 The misfits are hounded by the neighborhood bullies, by irrational parents, by their own fears and shortcomings, and by a promise they made when they first confronted and bested IT. They swore that, if they hadn't really killed IT, they would return to Derry as adults, go back into the sewers, confront the monster in Its lair, and finish the job. Of course IT knows this and is ready for them. 
 The book features King's usual insightful philosophical observations, his great character development, his strong powers of description; there's the typical sweet love story, and some very unexpected sex. There's also the sense of living through it all, and confronting King's ultimate monster.

The Winter King encompassed much of the elements from all five books of Tairen Soul into this slightly longer but compact storytelling. The romance elements is just as exciting as the mythology in the book around the weathermages, the Ice King, Roland, the politics of the Wintercraig and Summerlea, the war and action packed, complex side characters that made the book something more than just Romance but a genuine solid Fantasy. If you're the kind who judge the book by its cover, the cover seems lacking. There should be more lightning and cyclones and ice zombies and a flaming sword and loads of fire and ice apocalypse. Hell, there are more songs of fire and ice in this book than all GRR Martin's books combined. 
 To be honest, the story began much like "The Mark of the Tala" except I totally abhor the characters and the storytelling and it began fairly predictable. The story was set around the surrender of a Summer kingdom which was besieged by this Winter King because three years ago, the Summer King's prince started a war with the Winter kingdom who killed the Winter King's brother and kidnapped his fiancee. On top of that, The Winter King possessed this awesome ice power after he took this god-like substance, The Ice Heart, and he was able to defeat the Summer Kingdom but at the cost of his humanity. But the Summer King also have this elemental ability and so does his children. There was this youngest hidden princess with an ability to control the storm but was hated by her crazy father because she accidentally killed her mother when she was three and found herself being manipulated to wed the Winter King instead. The Winter King on the other hand never really care about who he might married to but wanted to humiliate the Summer King but found himself dangerously attracted to this servant girl who sneak into his room which was formerly the dead queen's room and later grew ballistic when he found out that he married the wrong girl but reconciled about it quickly when he found out exactly how she was being treated by her father for her consent. But everything doesn't always go right between the Storm and the Winter king. Yes, its Khamsin and Wynter. I know. 
 But the story was very layered and very very intricately well-crafted and thought over that somehow it was harder to think about any plot holes in it. In fact, it was harder to find a good Fantasy with this kind of tight plot. The story was still about the romance between the two very unlikely characters but it is about acceptance, betrayal, family, trust, relationship, war, violence, magic, loads of blood.. yeah, you get my drift.
I thougth I had a thing for Will and Jace herondale but gosh I tottally had a thing for Herondales in general.

This book was dense but was very easy to read. I love the way Elizabeth Chadwick writes. Her narrative pulls you in and captivates you. 
 This is the story of Eleanor of Aquitaine's life up til her marriage to King Henry. The strongest part of this story are the characters. I loved how you really got inside their heads and understood motivations, fears and hopes for the future. Eleanor is strong and intelligent. Her mind was constantly working on how to please and influence her husband into action and on how to protect her lands. I didn't always agree with her but through the writing I did understand her. 
 The book was tense, unexpectedly so, as you read of Eleanor's claustrophobic marriage to Prince Louis. Though heavy with history - this book never dragged. I found every word interesting. I never skimmed. Again, loved the writing. 
 Looking forward to The Winter Crown, the next book in the series.

Oh, so many reasons to love this book. 
 The prologue. *Squee!* 
 I was hooked right from the start, and it comes back in later, and it sets up the whole conflict really well. 
 And better yet, the action sequences generally felt like I was watching a super hero movie. Wonderful descriptions that really captured the scene (I was re-imagining the climatic moment into the day after I finished this book... *squee!*). Downside: Right in the middle it felt like we were getting a little too much action and not enough story plot... but that was quickly made up for by suspenseful situations which ended up fueling questions about the other epics. 
 Steelheart follows one (non-powered) guy's desire for vengeance on Steelheart-- an epic (super villain, in this case) who can turn things into steel. 
 The book follows pretty close to this plot, and doesn't really tangent off in other directions, but you still get plenty of interesting tidbits from the power system, and the classification systems for the powers was fascinating (and you're left wanting to know why epics tend to go evil when they use their powers... and what Calamity really is... and I'm looking forward to the next book) . Side note-- I happen to really like Brandon Sanderson's magic systems: here, in Mistborn, and in Warbreaker-- so I'm not too surprised at enjoying this one. 
 Another bonus: the romance wasn't heavy-handed. Actually, I'm not sure you'd call it romance. More like David (the main guy), trying really hard to impress the girl and generally failing miserably. The bad metaphors were a great touch. 
 And the characterization was easy to place. I didn't get lost in the who-is-who of the story, and it was easy to tell who was who. Though a couple times I was reminded of characters from other stories (namely Abraham reminding me of the scholarly guy from Mistborn), but I really didn't mind that. 
 One thing I've consistantly enjoyed in Sanderson's novels have been the ultimate guessing game of figuring out who's really behind everything, and what's going to turn out unexpected. Without giving away details, I did manage to guess a couple people would turn out to be epics (though I hadn't realized they would both be, nor their relation to other characters), but I was surprised by how the ending was resolved... and the epic (no pun intended) climax. 
 Now, for my favorite part of the book. First time we see Prof with tensors. Pure... awesomeness. Didn't see that coming. 
 Easily one of my favorite books I've read lately, it was just what I'd been wanting to read. If you like Mistborn, and if you like superheroes... give Steelheart a read. Forget my review because my review doesn't do it justice. 
 Just start with the prologue. It'll do the rest.

Austen, boy of her dreams is great but I just didn't feel the same pull to him as I did Cooper, alive and in the flesh. 
 J Sterling did an awesome job of fleshing out all of the characters and the friendship between two college roommates. I also really enjoyed the hockey element, the setting and the concept behind the story. 
 I like that the main girl is from California and is living in the East. There is a big difference between the two coasts (which I know since I've lived on both) and I liked the way Sterling added that into her book. 
 What I struggled with: The storyline is constantly shifting between the thoughts of all the characters which got a little confusing for me. 
 I received what I am guessing was an advanced reading copy from the author- there were several typoes, weird spacing and even font changes which are a bit distracting. For some reason I just didn't feel a connection to Austen so I think the pull in the story between two men didn't carry the full emotional reaction it otherwise would have. 
 Content: Moderate swearing, college drinking and co-ed sleepovers. No sex, very mild violence. 
 Bottom Line: Yes, I would recommend reading In Dreams and I would read it again.

But when things like that happen, I tend to blame the author over the character because it's so unbelievable it takes you right out of the story. 
 Candace is a college student who's been sheltered (repressed) all her life. She's a virgin and completely under her parents' thumb. Brian is Evan's younger brother (Evan is the hero from Unleashed, we meet Brian for the first time in that book) and Candace's cousin's ex-boyfriend. He's a rebel in his family with tattoos and piercings and an attitude. It doesn't matter that he owns his own body art business and has developed a great reputation at his craft, they still seem to look at him like he's got horns and a tail. 
 Can these two mismatched souls find accord? Of course they can! Especially because Candace is more than ready to jump off the V-train and wants Brian to do the deed. She's been drooling over him since he dated her favorite cousin. Oops. Complications! It all works out well, though.

 Wizard for hire Harry Dresden has more enemies than he can count on one hand, and they all want him dead. When there are serial killings that seem like the work of a bloodthirsty werewolf, he makes a few more. Will Harry be able to keep his head above water, and maybe restore his police friend Murphy's trust in him? 
 I like Harry's voice, and Mr Butcher is a good writer, yet still there is something about his book that is... itchy. I don't know how to describe it. I want to love them, but I just never get there. There is something about Harry, about the story that stands in the way. I can't put a finger on it. 
 What I can tell you about Fool Moon is that it is quite werewolf-heavy, in a good way. There are different kind of wolves, all with different strengths and weaknesses, which I found very interesting. Usually urban-fantasies only sport one kind of werewolf. Mr Butcher managed to create quite a few, and made them all distinct species. 
 For me Fool Moon felt a lot darker than the first book in the Dresden Files series, Storm Front. There is tons of violence, and because the main villains are wolf-like, there is a lot of gruesome detailing of people shredded to bits. Not only was there more violence and fighting, I also felt like Harry was not quite his cheerful self. He felt quite depressed, like he had lost all hope. And not just during one situation, but throughout the whole last half of the book. I'm wondering if this is how the whole series is going to be like. Maybe the darkness and bleakness of the book is why I'm not that eager to continue reading. 
 These are good books, and I will keep reading the series, but I'm not really rushing to get to them.

This was the most affecting book I have read in many years. I very nearly burst out crying at the beautiful last few pages when I finished it a few minutes ago. Since I'm sitting in a cafe in Nairobi, surrounded by latte-drinkers, that would have been rather awkward, so I held it all in in much the same way as Franzen's characters did throughout most of their lives before finally unfurling. 
 I know the detractors say the focus is too narrow, on people of a certain colour and background, to be the great American novel others say it is. It's an irrelevant argument. I don't care if it is the great American novel, because it is just a beautiful book. The focus is narrow, yes, but it is all the deeper because of it. It's a thin drill boring down into human existence rather than JCB digging massive, shallow chunks from the earth. 
 I didn't expect to love it so much, as Franzen comes across as a grumpy old luddite in his interviews and I've read far too many family sagas. This, however, is just about the best such work I've read, and, judging by how well he seems to understand the human condition, Franzen is an insightful and tender human being.

All He Ever Dreamed is another solid series entry. I loved Katie, who'd been in love with her best friend Josh forever--her love/hate relationship with cutting his hair was particularly cute. Josh was a typical clueless guy--the scene where he finally notices that his bff is an actual woman with girly parts was just too funny! Sure, there were times that I wanted to smack him upside the head for his dogged insistence that he HAD to leave town in order to be happy and fulfilled, but Katie was absolutely right when she said that if he never went anywhere he'd eventually come to resent anyone and anything he perceived as having kept him from it. My only complaint is that I wish this one were longer, because the ending felt a tad bit rushed.For example, it would have been nice to have seen some more of Josh and Katie's correspondence while he was gone--especially an example or two of his "here's where I am right now" picture/texts to set us up for the final one. A closer look at his experiences while traveling, too, wouldn't have gone amiss. He'd been looking forward to doing this forever--surely he had some memorable experiences while he was gone?  Still, though, I definitely can't complain about the ending. It was very nicely done. 
 Sigh...now the downside. All the Kowalski boys are finally taken. Surely this means it's Liz's turn next, right? And then maybe the "Friends and Acquaintances of the Kowalskis" series, so we can see Max and Hailey get together, perhaps? (Heck, I'm even willing for Mallory, Drew's ex, to get her own HEA, once Drew is all taken care of. That's how much I enjoy Shannon Stacey's writing style. I'm just sayin'....) Please, Ms. Stacey, can we have some more?

Well, I found the travelling and the people, and the thoughts and feelings one goes through while in a strange land and not really having a clue as to what is going on very authentic - Garland captured, for me, what it was like in India, very well. And then we hit the ethic of the group, and realise these things can work, if everyone is willing to do their part and get along. 
 The problem is, usually the people most vocal in their creation of such a utopia are the fucked up ones, who will turn out to be arch-hypocrites, and screw the whole thing up for everyone else. This, again, totally rang true. Anyone who has spent any time on the hippy trail, or hanging out with reactionaries, revolutionaries, hippies , free-thinkers, etc., will have found a few people who could really carry this off. The problem is, they are not interested in the petty power of control, and such groups are soon dominated by the liars, who believe their own bullshit, but actually, are so self-centred they have absolutely no idea how self-centred they actually are. 
 As a morality tale, The Beach shows just how many people actually are in this group, only really on the fringes, because no one else will have them. As such, it is a great reflection of the kind of people you meet. It goes a bit bonkers for the ending, but in a very Lord of the Flies way, takes such conclusions about people to an extreme. 
 I gave this 3 stars before i wrote the review, but going back over what i learnt from it (i read it about 13 years ago), I realise its power and accuracy. I have not seen the film, and from the reaction of 'real' travellers i know, am glad. I will keep the book with all its flaws, because it says a lot about human beings. If you have ever travelled, read it. If you haven't, yes, travel in the far East is really that mental ;-) 
 As an aside, i once hitched a lift with one of Garland's mates, soon after The Beach went global. He said that most of the characters were based on real people they had both met out in Thailand and the Far East. I can well believe it.

Perhaps because the premise and eventual reveal of 
 The Stepford Wives 
 has long been a part of the American zeitgeist, the story does not land with much of an impact. Part of it may be tied to the timeliness of it; I have no memories of the early 1970s (as I was not alive until the mid-1970s), but Levin does little to frame the era and the tensions of the maturing Women's Liberation movement on couples just trying to have it all -- careers, family, independence, and self-satisfaction. These crucial elements are left unwritten because of how real they were (and would have felt false in the moment). Unfortunately, it leaves the modern reader with a mostly blank canvas that will be informed by personal experience, and that may not fit the mood and aesthetics for which Levin was aiming. 
 My real disappointment came with how washed-out of any real terror/dread/horror the climax is. It feels as if it were entirely conceived for how it would play visually rather than on the printed page. Indeed, in its economy of characters and development it evolves like an episode of 
 The Outer Limits 
 (complete with budgetary considerations). 
 Worth reading, sure. But like any story that relies on the reveal as the make-or-break, it isn't helped by the foreknowledge of almost every reader as to just what, exactly, the reveal is going to be. (And it is also spelled out in the forward in case a reader managed to maintain ignorance up to this point.)

Usually I'm prepared to be a little more lenient on a debut, since it is the first book from an author and usually has some flaws. Sanctum is incredibly well written and has a strong plot and wonderful characters, making me super excited to read more from this author. 
 Sanctum is the first book in an urban fantasy series. It's a rather dark fantasy on the more mature side of YA (trigger warning for suicide and rape, neither graphic but come up throughout the novel). The story follows Lela, and girl who has grown up in foster care and has a rather dark past. She has become best friends with Nadia, a girl who looks like a typical queen bee from the outside until Nadia befriends Lela. When Nadia abruptly commits suicide and it's up to Lela to walk into Hell (literally) to save her best friend.  This is a story that doesn't stick to the typical YA fantasy tropes. Our main character, Lela, is a person of color. She has a strong female friendship with Nadia, without any of that girl on girl hate. The love interest is edgy, but never in the creepy way that so many love interests are.

Prince of Fools runs parallel, at least chronologically, to Mark Lawrence's Broken Empire trilogy. Lawrence is close to the top of my list of new(er) fantasy writers and the Broken Empire trilogy is one my favorite reads probably in the last decade so seeing a new title is exciting news. Prince Jalan is a bet far down the line from the throne currently occupied by his grandmother The Red Queen. Jalan spends his time shirking responsibility, running from conflict, and basically spending all of his considerable effort in looking out for the most important person in the world: himself. The Red Queen summons her lineage to hear the testimony of several prisoners who claim that war is coming and hear the Jalan first sees the Northman named Snorri ver Snagason. Jalan thinks little of Snorri's tale of the dead returning to plague the living and see him for what he: potential profit in the fighting pits. Jalan's selfish decision to suborn Snorri's freedom sets forth a chain reaction of sort that snags the young prince and the stoic Northman in events both dangerous and dire. 
 It is interesting to note that there a some skeletal similarities to Prince of Fools and the Broken Empire trilogy. Both series lean on a character whose moral constitution is, to put it mildly, limited at best. Both Jorg and Jalan are primarily selfish characters. The main plot of Prince of Fools as in Prince of Thorns is predicated to a large degree on the selfish nature of the main character. It struck me early in the novel that as selfish as Jalan is he is in many respects a "anti-Jorg." Where Jorg's selfishness has fired in a forge of violence and rage, Jalan's has instead been honed by indulgence and idleness. Jalan is a spoiled nobleman, unused to hardship and fully cognizant that the primacy of his own safety and survival makes him a coward in the eyes of those around him. He just doesn't care. 
 Snorri is the complete opposite of Jalan in every way. A commoner on a quest for revenge Snorri is a man used to hardship and hard work and the two characters work quite well as foils for one another. Their contrary natures is further compounded by the magical spell that binds them together. It is a clever device and Lawrence implements it so that the spell interacts with the basic natures of both men in an interesting and unexpected way. The novel leans heavily on the notion of opposites and the idea that they both attract and repel; it is in many ways the primary thesis of the novel. The opposite energies of the spell that infects both Snorri and Jalan contain the power for great destruction yet it is that same destructive energy that fuels the quest both men inevitably set forth on. The tension created by the opposing binary natures of the two men is frequently the catalyst for events in the novel with Jal's shortcomings often playing into Snorri's strengths and vice versa. 
 Prince of Fools feels like its more layered with nuance than the Broken Empire novels. While Lawrence sacrifices none of the action from his previous series he still manages to engender a sense of wheels within wheels over ther course of Prince of Fools. While Jalan and Snorri remain the focus of the novel they are in many ways pawns, albeit pawns with some personal agency, of other powers. Both men are manipulated throughout the story, and for Jalan perhaps even longer, into the positions they find themselves forced to act (in wildly different manners) in accordance to their natures and strange magic that binds them together. The world of Prince of Fools is one that I am endlessly fascinated with and more adventures in this strange, yet familiar, land are always welcome; doubly so when they manage to build upon the depth and mystery of previous novels. Prince of Fools marks the beginning of something new and subtly different from Lawrence's previous work and I definitely look forward to seeing where this new series takes readers.

 Boys, Bears, and a Serious Pair of Hiking Boots by Abby McDonald is a fun book that takes place mainly in the wilderness of a small Canadian town. The pages flew by as I immersed myself in this natural world of adventure, misadventure, romance, coming of age experiences, and friendship. 
 Being a Canadian, I'm sometimes offended by the stereotypical representation of people from Canada, but I wasn't offended at all by this one. The characters were treated like normal people (which they were) and just because the author picked a remote part of Canada as the setting of her novel, does not mean that she was saying we are a mainly remote country. She just simply wanted the story based there, end of story. 
 Phew, sorry, had to get that out. 
 I loved the fun vibe that McDonald creates in this one as her protagonist, Jenna, strives to fit in with the teen locals. Her ideas of what is right and wrong when it comes to the environment, and our treatment of it, is seriously challenged as she enters a world full of what she one day swore to protect. She learns that we can't control everything and that there are usually more sides to a particular situation. 
 This novel also encourages other characters to grow as they encounter situations that challenge who they are and how they see their world. This one's definitely a coming-of-age novel that teaches the reader the importance of finding who you really are and not being afraid to be honest with those who love you. 
 One of the small cliches in this one is the ruggedly handsome adventure addict love interest. I'm not saying who he is (and you shouldn't read the synopsis if you don't want it ruined for you), but it's fun watching how he goes from being one of Jenna's antagonists to a guy she can't stop thinking about. 
 I'm a sucker for coming-of-age adventure and romance novels, so I loved this one!

 I am a huge fan of Caisey Quinn's but I have to admit that I put off reading this book for quite awhile. I wanted to read Leaving Amarillo as soon as I saw the gorgeous cover, and honestly I had no idea what the story was even about. But then I heard that there was a cliffhanger and I decided to wait. Usually cliffhangers aren't my favorite, but I can deal with them easy enough. I was really glad that I waited here though, because as soon as I got to the end I was ready for the next one! Luckily now that they have all been released, there is no waiting if you haven't already started the series. Just make sure you are ready to spend some time reading though as once you start you are not going to want to stop! I couldn't put this book down, and I barely came up for air. 
 Dixie and Dallas Lark lost their parents when they were kids and were raised by their grandparents. But with the inspiration from her grandfather, she learned to play the fiddle and grew up with an appreciation for music. Now ten years later, Dixie and Dallas are in a band with their best friend Gavin, who Dixie has been in love with since they were kids. Though Gavin has never made a move on her and they have never crossed that line, Dixie is determined to finally get him to see her as more than just his friend's little sister. So when Dixie decides to put a plan in motion to spend one night with him and get him out of her system, she has no idea just how much everything will change. 
 I was frustrated with both of these characters throughout this story and they did several things that had me wanting to slap them around a bit. That isn't to say that I didn't like them, because I really did. I just had some problems with some of their choices and actions. Dixie is talented and sweet, and I loved how much she cared about those in her life. She would do anything for anyone she really cared about, and yet that was also what drove me the most nuts about her. She would fight for Gavin and refused to hide her feelings from him, yet she also gave up everything for both him and Dallas. She always put others first, and sometimes I wanted her to focus on what she needed and wanted. Gavin had a rough childhood and the bright spots for him were Dixie and Dallas. He had made a promise to Dallas to stay away from Dixie, and I liked that he was trying to be a good friend. At the same time that bothered me as Dixie made him happy and was always there for him and yet he refused to let himself go there for so long because of a promise he had made to Dallas. These two had such intense chemistry, and it was clear that it had always been there between them. I don't know how Dallas didn't see what was happening right in front of him with the sparks that were flying. Dixie and Dallas had a great connection, and I really liked that they had a lot of history. They had grown up together and knew each other really well, yet they were still getting to know one another and their bond just continued to get stronger. 
 If you have read anything by Caisey Quinn, you will know that her stories definitely have angst and Leaving Amarillo was no different. There was a lot going on here for the characters to face, and I will admit at times it was a lot. Their band was beginning to take off and they had issues there, then there was the stuff going on between Gavin and Dixie and them worrying about Dallas finding out. All the while there was something going on with Gavin that Dixie was in the dark about and yet Dallas knew about it. I really thought that we would get some sort of explanation about that here, and while we did get clues and I could make some guesses, there wasn't anything actually revealed besides some bits and pieces. If I didn't have the next book ready to read when I finished this one, I think I would have been extremely frustrated. I also have to say that I really wanted to throat punch the band's new manager and Gavin's mom. Each of them definitely deserved it at times, and I hated that neither of them were dealt with here. I can only hope that they each get what is coming to them as the series continues. I love Caisey's writing style and I am a huge fan of her books even if they are filled with angst and frustrate me at times. The stories are good though and Caisey Quinn has a way of drawing you in right from the start and not letting you go until you have read the entire book in one sitting. I would recommend this book and I think a lot of readers will really enjoy this one. Just keep in mind that this book is not a standalone and be prepared to dive into Loving Dallas as soon as you finish Leaving Amarillo.

 To be perfectly honest, I was more that prepared to dislike The Plague -- I was actually relishing the idea of hating it. Let's just say that my first encounter with Camus, The Stranger, did not go well. That book was one of the most annoying and frustrating reading experiences of my young life, second only to Ethan Frome, the book I love most to hate. But based on the amount of respect given to Camus by friends whose opinions in books I usually trust, I knew I had to give him a second chance. It was indeed possible that The Stranger was an incredibly interesting book, and that there was only something about my state of mind at the time that kept me from appreciating its subtle nuances. As much as I wanted to believe that, the thought of picking up and reading it again filled me with a sick sense of dread. So I chose an alternate route: I read The Plague, instead. 
 From the beginning, I sat in a state of anticipatory judgement of the book. I didn't want to like Camus. And the beginning of the book just did not win me over. Having both seen and read Stephen King's The Stand, and read entirely too many brutal and thorough books on the AIDS epidemic, it was highly unlikely that any description Camus might give of the plague would shock or move me much in comparison. As his book is set in relatively modern times, there was also not the shock of general filth and sewage running in the streets that might have been present in other accounts of plague. 
 If shock or horror would not draw me into the book, I didn't anticipate compassion to do so either. As in The Stranger, the characters of The Plague are not an emotive bunch. The doctor, Rieux, watches hundreds die every day and is separated from his wife for the duration of the plague -- he grinds on. His closest friend, Tarrou, keeps a detailed journal comprised entirely of observations of other people, the only personal details he records come very near the end of the plague, when he is presumably too exhausted to censor himself. "Well," one might say, "those are men, those were different times, you can't expect men to express their emotions, what about the women?" What about the women? What an excellent question! The only women in the book are the exiled wives from whom, conveniently, nothing can be heard, and Rieux's mother, who is even less emotive than Rieux himself. 
 I might have set the book aside entirely had it not been assigned for me to read for the 100 books list, and for that I am grateful. Because after plowing doggedly through the first three parts of the novel, it was in the fourth that the book finally set its hooks into my chest. In a brief moment of respite, Tarrou and Rieux sit on a terrace overlooking the town, and Tarrou tells Rieux how he came to be the man that he is. I don't want to spoil anything for anyone, so I will just say that Tarrou finally gave me something to identify with and a reason to be involved in the book. His struggle as an athiest pacifist riveted me, and from that point on I could hardly bear to put the book down. Unfortunately, there was little left to the book after that point, but it was enough. I was converted. I could finally agree with all of those who consider Camus to be a great author. 
 But will I ever give The Stranger another try? Perhaps in a few more years....

Once there she must learn to uncover the politics and truth of the city while determining what she really wants out of life. 
 I liked the story and found the concept of the trolls interesting. I definitely want to learn more about them and where they came from and hope the second book fleshes this out more. The setting is interesting and well described, I had an easy time picturing the city of Trollus. 
 Cecile is quite spunky and often does what she wants. I really liked this about her and though she is often impulsive, it is a nice balance to Tristan's planning and thinking. I also like how she thinks quick on her feet and though impulsive tries to make good decisions. Tristan is more thoughtful and though he tries to keep his distance from Cecile you can see how he starts to care for her. I thought their relationship was well-developed over time and liked how they got to know each other.

You know when you have been reading a lot of the same stuff for a while and you are just so burnt out on it that you are making snarky comments in your mind? Rolling your eyes, saying "oh brother!", getting frustrated enough to murder your family? Oh, or is that just me? 
 Anyway, I've been reading too many books with the alpha male thing going on lately, so I'm just done. I think the only thing that would make me happy at this point is to read about a female serial killer that targets asshole men. Yeah, one of those books. You know, cuz the market is saturated with them. 
 I'd settle for some alpha females. If anyone has recommendations for strong female lead characters, please let me know. You might just be saving a life. 
 Okay, so this book had Marcus, an alpha male werewolf, chasing after Roni, a female werewolf. He decides that he wants her because he is so deep. 
 There was just something about her... Maybe it was that she was so very different from the females he usually dated. Maybe it was that she didn't stroke his ego, didn't fawn all over him in that way he'd come to find distasteful. Or maybe it was just that she had the most luscious ass he'd ever seen. 
 Stop, please, you romantic poet. Who could possibly resist your charm? 
 Yeah, so Marcus decides he wants to nail Roni and Roni tells him "no". Five seconds later, he nails her. 
 "I never stood a chance, did I?" 
 "Of what?" 
 "Holding out against you." 
 "Nope. I was too determined to have you." 
 First of all, she never held out. Maybe she doesn't understand what "Holding out against you" means. Maybe she thought she was supposed to hold his wiener. 
 Secondly, this is a good life lesson for us women. 
 Young girls, gather round, I have a story for you: If a man decides that he wants to nail you, and he's good and determined, you will be nailed. Don't bother resisting, girls. That would be a foolish waste of your energy. Energy that could be used to please your man. 
 So, before my head explodes, I am off to read something different. If there is an asshole man in it, and he doesn't die, you will see me next on the evening news.

I enjoyed Stolen Songbird very much. Cecile (without the accent mark) is the stolen songbird of the title. Obviously. Because she sings and she is kidnapped in the book... And no, that isn't a spoiler. That is obvious. Too. 
 Tristan, the future king, has a very big ego. Well, it is a bit complicated. But he is a great guy. Or troll. And yes, he is literally and figuratively a troll. Just like the trolls you see in the Youtube comments or anywhere else. Internet is full of them. However, he is such a great guy, but his comments are so witty and hilarious. I mean, he is a Sassy Prince. I'm not kidding. His sass just kills me. I love it! 
 Cecile (without the accent mark) is a very special girl. She has red hair (which is totally rare) and she knows how to read. In the Middle Ages, few people knew how to read. Most of the readers (who knew how to read) are men. It is rare for a girl to be able to read. Kind of interesting, right? Yeah, I think so too. The girl is smart and intelligent. I don't know if she developed Stockholm's Syndrome, but if she did, then I have it too. Because Tristan (who is indirectly involved in her kidnapping) is really hilarious and lovable. 
 So the book has strong characters. What about the plot? It is really good. I never wanted it to end (but of course, everything that is good must end). The plot goes by fast, and it never lost me once. The political world of Stolen Songbird intrigued me, and I enjoy reading and reading. It is really good, but I don't recommend it. Or at least until the next book comes out. Because this one is just too darn good to read so early! 
 The ending ends in a cliffhanger. It is the major reason I don't recommend reading this book right away. At least wait until the sequel comes out. 
 Because you are going to get so angry and vicious. 
 Overall, Stolen Songbird is a great book. I would recommend it once the sequel comes out, but until then, don't read it. Strange advice, isn't it? Methinks not. It is a great piece of advice. Reading books, saving people, the family business. 
 But the book is really fun to read. There is humor, there is good characterization, and there is a hottie/love interest. 
 Rating: Five out of Five

I was really surprised when I finished this in a day! Okay. Honestly, thanks to blackout in our area that I was able to finish this within 24 hours. It was so hot and humid in our house that I found it hard to sleep so instead, I read this book. Anyhow; 
 I like Kiera Cass' books because it was quick and easy to read. But I am not sure what to feel about The Elite. It was one heck of a roller coaster of emotions. Throughout the book, I was so confused and frustrated. I really don't know what to say about it. But there were a lot of times that I was pissed off like I wanna rip out my hair and scream 
 "WHAT THE HELL?!" 
 I really felt that this book was like a girl who cannot decide what the wear for summer. That might sound stupid but I haven't read anything like this that confused me so so so so much! 
 I had tons of problems with this book too. First, it was America. Boy, this girl had some attitude, I tell you! Every time her temper flares, she impulsively does something stupid that she regrets in the end! 
 WARNING: SPOILER AHEAD 
 Like there was a part in the book where I got really pissed with America. It was when Marlee, one of the Elites and her best friend, was caught having an affair with the palace guard, Carter Woodwork. First, let me explain that once you enter Selection, you become part of the palace's, especially the Prince's, property. Therefore, you ought to be devoted to the Prince only. So whatever and whoever will do something against him will be punished. (that is according to the book. So, if you're confused, don't blame me. I was confused myself.) 
 Of course, Marlee and Carter were punished and sentenced to be caned 15 times and stripped of their castes to the lowest of the low, Eight. However, America was unable to watch her suffer and attempted to free her friend. She thrashed and shrieked while two of the guards stopped her. She put up a fight. A really good fight. End of story, she failed and was pissed off with everyone who kept this a secret. 
 So, the next day, the queen talked to her and told her about her actions. There, she said; 
 "For the first time, I truly felt bad about how I reacted." 
 Hello? America, baby, you just don't regret something you did right for a friend! Especially if it's your best friend! You fought for her, dear! And it was a good one. 
 I was really pissed off and annoyed!! 
 She was the most complicated character I've ever encountered! So far. Ugh. 
 Then, there was the weirdest and tangled relationship I've read in my life. Either you're Team Maxon or Team Aspen, I don't really care. We all know who she'd end up anyway. What I was concerned with was on the first few chapters of the book, she was most sure that she'd choose Prince Maxon, that she liked him. Or maybe loved him. God,she was so sure! But Marlee happened, and some dumb things. And so, 30% of the time she was like "I'll choose Aspen. He knows me well. He comforts me well. I am best with him. Blah blah blah." 
 Clearly, she was using Aspen as her safety net. So whenever Prince Maxon decides she goes home, she has someone who she can be with for the rest of her life! 
 Somehow, I didn't blame her. Okay, she had a two-year solid relationship with Aspen. And you just don't let go of a two-year relationship just like that, chiefly when you planned your future together! But damn, she screwed up so many times. If he really loved him, why can't she just let go so they can be both free? Why couldn't she commit to one person once and for all? Really, there were a lot of parts that I didn't want to read (but I did in the end) because I knew she'd changed her mind again. And again. And again. Oh, by the way, neither Prince Maxon nor Aspen really deserves her yet. They were annoying as hell, tbh. 
 I also have some problems with the dystopian part. It was like more in the past and not in the future. No internet, no cell phones, and all the techie stuff. Uh, what happened? How's that possible? Also, the history books were kept hidden. Why? It was never explained. Or I was asleep when that one passed? And the caste system, the rebels had me gone ??????? I really did not get it. At all. Though, admittedly, there were some parts that really felt like a real dystopian. And this is a book, anything can happen. But still. 
 The romance part was not so romantic at all. Yes, I was expecting heavy and extreme cheesy lines. I was prepared for it, and it did not fail me. There were tons of it! But when it came, it wasn't swoon-worthy at all. I didn't feel anything. It was toneless and monotonous. I was on blank state whenever I passed on those corny-cheesy-unbelievable lines or convo. Was it me or what? 'Cause really. 
 I really liked it when Cass' finally put some action-packed scenes, though mostly it only involves crying and running. Regardless, Cass' successfully set some tension in the story, aside from the never-ending bullying of the rebels. 
 I loved Celeste. I really loved her! She was a real biatch. Her character was perfect in the story line. And K. Clarkson was absolutely the worst King I've known yet. King Clarkson and Levana of Fairest can be a good tandem. No matter what, I loved them. Both of them put up some spice in the story. And honestly, I was thankful that Cass at least considered them. 
 I can't say I hate this book. I like it despite it's flaws. It was a bit predictable, yes. But it doesn't really matter. I'm giving 3 stars because. And I honestly dived into the third book after reading this because I had a hunch that it'll be better than the first two series.

 Romancing the Duke: He's Given Up Being the White Knight and She's Given Up Expecting One 
 Book provided by publisher for review. No remuneration was exchanged and all opinions presented herein are my own except as noted. 
 I have loved everything I've read by Tessa Dare but I had a hard time getting into this at the very beginning of the story; the "damaged duke" trope is so often used (Injured Earl, Marred Marquis, Broken Baron), I find myself sighing when it comes up. However, Tessa quickly individualizes her characters and makes the trope more appealing. Then the story heats up until we know that there is a very naughty girl hiding under that skirts of England's favorite fictional character based upon, well, another fictional character (although within the world of the book she is real). Those thoughts aren't the only thing she's hiding either. 
 A theme here, and a recurring theme in Tessa's books, is the inequity women experienced (and continue to experience to some degree depending on location). And, she has a way of combining humor, love, lust and the foibles of the upper crust of 19th century British society (AKA the Ton) into a charming, hot, poignant and humorous story. Her prose is often lovely and it is always accessible. 
 And when I say heats up I mean it is rather hot under those skirts. I thought it was a little more erotic and regarded sex with more modern sensibilities than Tessa's Spindle Cove series. 
 The Duke is hiding something as well, although not under a skirt; something that has caused his damage. Here, the story is complex because while the duke, Ransom, is damaged physically, the more important damage is emotional damage from his childhood, as well as the imperious attitude granted by his ducal title, and a host of other titles. 
 Another theme is the "white knight charging to the rescue;" only in ROMANCING THE DUKE the female love interest. Izzy, has finally rejected all the themes young women were, and often still are, brought up believing. In the end, I wasn't sure if she really had a large nose and ugly hair or if she just thought she did because other girls were cruel. Even in that time there was an ideal English beauty and with dark hair, light blue eyes and Izzy with her abundant and dark, frizzy hair would not have met the standards. As the owner of a rather largish nose myself, I can say we don't grow into them physically - but we have to own them! 
 Tessa's characters are always a bit to type, but with enough characteristics to make them individual. They are often somehow atypically employed for that character's position. But, the hero is the hero and occasionally an ass. The heroine is usually physically innocent, often the one left on the shelf. But there is enough difference in them to make them worth reading and they always win my affection. 
 There is a certain fairy tale feeling to this story as well: Weird pets, unsympathetic solicitors, and fans engaging in the world's first readers' con. It's a spiders web of fictional fantasy such as a young woman whose life was very difficult could imagine. I seem to be having a hard time distinguishing between Izzy's fantasy and Tessa's. 
 I think what ended up making this story interesting was the way the two love interests not only get together physically but how they help each other emotionally, how strong and resolute Izzy actually is, and how the stalwart duke learns he is open to emotional growth. So, yeah, I liked all those things and that it is hot -- very, very hot. I highly recommend this or any of the books in the Spindle Cove series. This one is the first in a new series though and a great chance to be in at the beginning!

I'm torn on the rating of this book because at first I was enthralled by the idea of this plot. I was ensnared within the first few pages, but then it grew stagnant and while things constantly happened it was really nothing at all. Even though those small things, later on, amounted to everything. Every little moment that happened in this book contributes to the overall story. 
 "We are that tree, she thought, 
 holding the richly scented sprig to her nose. 
 We defy death, to grow." 
 And so much little happens in the book that adds up to the bigger picture. At times I felt utterly bored with the story and how it went nowhere - except it did and does. Every moment Lada spends forming her calculations mounts up to her epic moments. From the time she is a cruel, vicious girl to her young womanhood in these times where women are perceived as property, as something to bear children and bear no thoughts. Lada doesn't stand for this and defies society's views left and right. Her views of those who disrespect her simply because she was born a female are a testament to her strength and wisdom beyond years. 
 "They are beneath our notice! 
 They are less than the mud. 
 You do not get angry at the mud 
 For clinging to your shoe. 
 You wipe it off and never look at it again." 
 While her vicious quality can be tiresome, it is who she is and she remains true to herself, even when faced with passion, she does not betray her beliefs. 
 The overall story was rather complex and constructed in such a manner. You feel as if you have plunged into the world of the Ottoman empire along with Lada and her brother Radu. I enjoyed reading the story in both of their tones, the way Radu grew and still remained true to himself, too. The world building was appropriate for a tale that was based around character development. 
 I really did enjoy this book, because the tone was so dark, Lada was so twisted. She is an obsessive creature, cold and withdrawn from tender sensibilities because she never wants to be seen as weak or having a weakness. 
 Which is why this is a difficult book to rate because it was good it was soo good but it was also drawn out. I don't think I began to really devour the book until a little over 200 pages. After that, I just began to gulp it down. 
 Not at all a fantasy read, but it's an alternate historical fiction with an unending game of thrones. If you're into political intrigue, warfare, historical fiction and strong female characters, this is definitely for you.

I managed to read the last 60 % of the book in 2 sittings, which says a lot about how captivated I was by the first 40 % of this book and this is one of the reasons it gets a star removed. 
 May contain spoilers! Read at your own risk! 
 Ok, so maybe I didn't really show much enthusiasm when I went into this book seeing that at the end of Ruby Red, Gideon and Gwen do nothing else except kiss, after their lives had been threatened but that's beside the point. So maybe my lack of enthusiasm to getting into this book was justified. 
 There is no significant shift in tone or whatnot. The plot just continues on from where it left off in the last book. However there are a few changes. A few characters are introduced, some of which are completely functionless, are there just to help the characters out of dilemma or otherwise improve the book by a whole lot :P. 
 Xemerius was the improvement character of the novel. I did not understand his purpose at first, thinking he was a typical comic relief and the eyes for Gwen when she was off doing something else, and the reader needed to know what happened with Gideon. (Man this girl is seriously obsessed if she's sending an invisible dead gargoyle to spy on her crush/boyfriend.) Then another idea struck me: this little guy is often the reader surrogate that is hyper-observant and points out short comings of some situations and character actions (like him saying how she's overreacting to Gideon's bad temper and acts like it is the end of the world - that made me burst out in laughter). And I seriously mean it, half of the humor from this book is delivered by Xemerius and his snarky remarks and they are so enjoyable to read. He is such a great character and a great addition to the story. 
 The same cannot be said for Mr. Marley (or whatever the fuck his name is, I'll just call him Ginger, like Xemerius does), Raphael (Gideon's younger brother, who for some reason I thought he was younger and less good looking, I may be confusing him with Dorian Havilliard's much younger brother - god I hate that kid) and that Lord Alastair. 
 Gwen, more than in the first book, acvted like a love struck teenager, and it was really getting on my nerves, I mean seriously do we REALLY need to have a description of how she feels EVERY time she kisses Gideon like it's some special event. It may be for her, but I was interested in the plot more or less. This book has so much teen angst in it, I was constantly eye rolling. *facepalm* Gwen is overreacting to everything Gideon is and does, sobbing every time Gideon does not reciprocate her love and the book ends with an ANTI-climax in which her heart is broken... I mean what the effing eff? 
 The reveal that the "magic of the raven" is actually her ability to see dead people is not actually a reveal at all, from where I stand. See here, I fancy myself a smart reader - and I checked and rechecked the prophecies here a few times to be sure - and I figured out that THAT was her "magic of the raven" since book one. Sheesh, all subtlety went down the drain. 
 Gideon gets more descriptions in this book, and is forgiven fairly quickly, even if he was (justifiably) cold towards her. He is a nice guy, but man he can't keep up the jerkass facade if he wanted to, he isn't like that, that's why I dd not buy this whole "Gideon resents me" fiasco. I was mad at Gwen for falling for it instead of - I dunno - fucking TALK TO HIM, and at Gideon for not saying what's on his mind. 
 Another thing that I don't like is the fact that he can't make Gwen listen to him, when he wants to talk to her, instead of saying "Gwen, Gwen Gwen" over and over again I would have said "Can you shut the fuck up for a minute girl, I'm trying to say something to you. Look at these damn papers Paul gave me!" 
 Speaking of which, the actual climax came in the epilogue. . . WHAT?! O.o The climax is in the epilogue? See, this is why I hate 1st person narrative, it limits the narration to what only the main character, the one who is narrating knows. And then you get stupid situations like these that end the book in a... GODDAMN CLIFFHANGER! You fucking book! Sorry I'm pissed off, because now I am forced to read further, because all the loose ends don't tie up and there are still unanswered questions. 
 One thing I did like though was the way he handled his "anguished declaration of love", which was not anguished, far from it. It was more... clunky, that's the word, clunky as in mixing words that are both slight insults and a bit praising to justify why he fell in love with her. My sparknote for the moment says it all: Gideon: Just keep quiet will you; XD smooth. 
 The highlight of this book was the party they had to attend with the count and to tell the truth all I did when reading that 2 or 3 chapter long part was laugh, continuous state of laughter, from Gwen's observations of how spiteful she's gonna make her dancing master Giordano, her getting herself completely wasted to her wanting to sing any song from a musical to Gideon's reactions at the very idea of her singing and his statement "I hate musicals." (*thumbs up* My man!) It was an enjoyable read and it really shifted my opinion of the book, since up until then I was thinking of giving it a 3 star rating. The entire ball soiree part saved the rating in my eyes though :P 
 Ok now about the other things that happen in the novel, admittedly not much happens, the first 43 % of the novel is spent preparing for the soiree and Gwen and Gideon smooching, so that's why I found it uninteresting. Though in between that we have two endearing meetings between Gwen and her grandfather's younger self. It was heartwarming to see her love her grandfather so much and mourn the idea of not being with him. Those were my favorite parts from the boring first 43 % of the book actually and it gave me an idea for a novel plot that quickly left me to tell the truth tho :( 
 At one point there was a talk about discontinuity of time travel where in Lucas berates himself for he is not going to warn Paul and Lucy about traveling further back in time and stop supporting young Lucas' risky idea. I was left, kind of dumbfounded that he did not remember to tell them in his old age. But, oh well... Timey-whimey. Oh and as an added note, despite Gideon telling her that she is clever, the first 50 % of this book show Gwen as being SO thick.
