Oliver Twist could stand on the strength of its colorful characters alone. Dickens used his insightful eye to take in and store away all the images he was seeing in London's poorer neighborhoods back in the days when his own family found themselves in and out of the debtor's prison, always on the verge of utter ruin. 
 However, the book is more than just interesting characters. It's a wonderfully enthralling tale to boot, seldom slowing down for long stretches. Certainly there is melodrama, but even the most harden heart has to melt just a little for poor little Oliver, his slender shoulders so often put-upon. 
 The author is sometimes criticized for these characters' outlandishness or dramatic flights of fancy. Cantankerous comedy and theatrical bombast aside, surely colorful personages parade about from page to page, but if that's what Dickens saw on the streets he so often tread in his youth, how can he be blamed for describing them so realistically? More valid in my mind are the criticisms again Dickens' female characters. His heart-of-gold prostitute Nancy feels a bit flat, her lines too scripted. But perhaps this is an unfair, modern sensibility seeing something old and haggard within something that was not so hackneyed in its day? And since Oliver Twist was one of the author's very first works the condemnation should be tempered in consideration.

This isn't the setup for a joke: what do you call someone who just gives handjobs - not a prostitute, who does everything else, right? Sex worker? So anyway our nameless narrator is a handywoman who, after giving thousands of handies, now has carpal tunnel syndrome and is thinking of a career move to something that requires less repetitive motion... Luckily (handily?) her place of work also doubles as a psychic reading shop and she decides to begin her career as a fraud, I mean charlatan, I mean psychic! 
 There she meets Susan, a distraught mother of two at her wits' end who believes her Victorian house is haunted - the walls are bleeding! - and that her 15 year old stepson Miles is possessed of a malevolent spirit: Handywoman to the rescue! She doesn't believe in ghosts, exorcisms, etc. but knows that she'll make decent scratch pretending to "cleanse" the house. And then she meets mega-creepy Miles and everything changes - maybe true evil does exist? 
 Gillian Flynn's The Grownup is a short story that originally appeared in George R. R. Martin's Rogues anthology last year and consequently won an Edgar Award for its refreshing and inspired take on the classic haunted house tale. It's being published by itself in just a few days (not in time for Halloween for some strange reason) and it's also really good and genuinely scary! 
 The first part with the narrator talking about handjobs felt very weird and unusual until you get to the final few pages and realise it's key to how everything plays out. The misdirection is indicative of the story as a whole - that summary I gave above is not at all how things turn out to be and it's a good too as what it actually is is even creepier than something generic. 
 The one thing that bothered me was that our narrator works in a shop that gives handies to male clients AND psychic readings to female clients - do such places really exist? Because it feels like a creation made purely for this short story to work. It definitely feels contrived because without it the whole tale collapses. Maybe places like this do exist and I'm just not very worldly? 
 Otherwise: bravo, Gillian Flynn! The Grownup takes numerous horror genre tropes and spins them into something absolutely brilliant and new. I read it straight through (at night by lamplight, of course!) becoming increasingly beguiled with and drawn into the narrative and loved how Flynn played with our expectations of the characters. You can't predict where it's all headed as Flynn deploys her famous story twists that made Gone Girl such a success. If you're one of those readers who doesn't like open-endings, you might be peeved at The Grownup's resolution, but I loved how Flynn left the interpretation up to the reader - what is Miles really and was he telling the truth or not? Has the narrator sealed her fate? What's real and what's not? So clever. 
 If you can get your hands on a copy of George R. R. Martin's Rogues, it's definitely worth seeking out just to read this short story on Halloween - it is perfect for the season! Otherwise, check it out next week when it's published. It's easily one of the best, most original horror stories I've read in years!

Secrets of Seduction was a very sweet romance with a delightful twist on the tale of Beauty and the Beast and I really enjoyed it! 
 Lady Skye Wilde has secretly loved the Earl of Hawkhurst since she was a girl. After learning he's returned to England to make a marriage of convenience, Skye arrives on his doorstep determined to persuade him to choose her instead. Hawk vowed never to love again after the tragedy that left him physically scarred and took the lives of his wife and young son. However, Hawk didn't count on Skye and the passion she would bring into his life. Soon, Skye helps Hawk see the joy in life again and he's left with a choice of love or duty to the organization that saved him in his darkest hours. 
 Skye was definitely my favorite Wilde cousin in the previous books in the series. She's incredibly passionate and is determined to get everything she wants out of life. I admired her confidence that she'd be able to convince Hawk that she's the best person for him. I don't read many historical romances where the heroine is the instigator in the relationship, so that was a nice change of pace. Also, as with all of the other Wilde cousins, family means a great deal to Skye and you can really tell how much this family loves each other. 
 Hawk suffered through a terrible loss when his wife and young son died and he was too late to save them. After their deaths, he left England and joined a secret division of the government which led to him risking his life over and over as he no longer cared if he lived or died. Upon returning to England, he's a very reserved individual and isolates himself from nearly everyone. He's definitely a grump and has a tendency to growl at anything that displeases him. He doesn't believe his marriage will be a happy one and is convinced he can never love again. 
 Skye and Hawk definitely had a very passionate relationship. These two had great chemistry and their first scene in bed was fantastic (and came way sooner than I expected). There is a lot of push/pull in their relationship as at the start Hawk is determined to wed the grand-niece of the head of the organization he works for. Watching Hawk slowly fall for Skye despite not wanting to was a lot of fun to watch. Plus, when these two finally get together, it's incredibly sweet and I was very satisfied with how everything turned out. 
 The original way Skye convinced Hawk to let her stay was that she hired him to help find her uncle's long lost love believed to be dead. Skye and Hawk's quest to find the missing woman and reunite her with Skye's uncle was enjoyable. It provided some great scenes where the two got to be alone without anyone interfering. I also was very happy to see Skye's uncle get a chance at happiness after everything he'd done for the Wilde cousins. 
 Overall, Secrets of Seduction has been my favorite of the Legendary Lovers series thus far and I look forward to reading more books from this author.

Lalala love this book. 
 It has a Austen vibe which I loved, but also reminded me of my favourite PNR/fantasy books like Throne of Glass or Soulless. 
 High society girl living in Victorian Edinburgh witnesses her mothers brutal murder at the hands of a powerful fae. Not the sort with glitter and wings but the soul-eating, monster sort with sharp teeth and claws. 
 She vows revenge, and with the help of a darkly handsome fae called Kieran she is trained to kill her enemy at night, while attending high tea and balls during the day. Obviously things get a bit scandalous and rumours abound due to her disappearing acts/shreaded clotihng etc... 
 Warning: there is a love triangle, which I have no idea how the author will work out as I loved them both... and also a cliff-hanger which left me in despair when I realised that the next book is not out till 2015!

Okay, let me just say one thing: this book screams TRUST. 
 TRUST TRUST TRUST. Like, the READER can't even think straight because she/he doesn't know who to trust. 
 And neither can the characters! 
 This book is all about trust basically. The word "trust" is pretty much on every page. Heck, the book might as well be called trust. 
 So yeah: 
 The 1st Wave was totally boring, but really sad because there's no iPhone or YouTube. 
 The 2nd Wave was more interesting. Bye-bye, coastal areas. 
 The 3rd Wave was deadly. A disease that killed billions of people? Whoa! You can't TRUST birds. 
 The 4th Wave actually starts getting interesting. 
 The 5th Wave? CHAOS. :D 
 I don't know what to say, actually, except this book was TOTALLY AWESOME. LIKE WICKED AWESOME. 
 Cassie is TOTALLY bad-butt. Okay, she might be stubborn, and maybe even a tad bit annoying, but she's hilarious, and makes sort-of okay choices. 
 And she's actually really smart. Doesn't second-guess trust as much as normal people could. 
 I feel like this book was more about Ben, though. Don't get me wrong, I love Ben. He's a great character. 
 What sucks is that I started shipping him and Ringer, but now . . . Cassie . . . =/ 
 As for that man, the Silencer. I totallyyy love him. Totally. DID HE ACTUALLY DIE? HE DIDN'T DIE, RIGHT?! PLEASE TELL ME EVAN DIDN'T DIE. :C  
 Just remember, TRUST is something you can't forget. Jeez, it was so hard to NOT trust Evan, and I sort of half gave up at one point XD 
 I'VE HAD ENOUGH HEARTBREAK AFTER Shadow and Bone, even though it was so freaking obvious. 
 I'm an idiot sometimes. 
 Lemmie talk about the plot now: 
 Okay, the plot is wicked awesome. I'm not going to lie, this is my first YA book about aliens (Pathetic, I know. But I've only read what, 88 YA books so far?) 
 But the plot was A.M.A.Z.I.N.G. I loved it! There's something about guns, bombs, death at almost every corner, not sure who to trust, surprises and a few plot twists all in one book that REALLY makes me happy. :3 
 Of course, I did have some stuff to fault with. 
 Like I said, I feel like this book is more about Ben than Cassie. And Cassie's on the freaking summary! And who's NOT on the freaking summary? 
 Oh, well lookie there, it's Ben Parish! Ben Parish is NOT on the freaking summary! 
 I don't know why, but the summary to me is a very important part of how I judge a book. Because of the summary, I'm sort of EXPECTING things. 
 And you know what I expected? This whole book was about Cassie's adventure. 
 But no, more than half probably is about Ben and how he's fairing. 
 Another thing: WHY DOESN'T IT SAY WHO'S POINT OF VIEW IT IS?! I mean, sureee I sort of realize who it is at one point after I get into the book some more, but seriously, giving the name of who's POV it is would seriously be helpful. 
 Last thing!: The middle was kind of . . . Boring. 
 I'm sorry, okay? 
 I mean, yeah, we need character development. We need to get a feel for the characters. 
 But it sort of felt draggy, and I'm like, "Umm, where is the action?? I feel like the training stuff with Ben was almost unnecessary, and Cassie freaking out about Evan and all that stuff was hilarious but . . . It was long, okay? 
 But the beginning and ending! God, reading through the middle is HECK worth it. 
 ADRENALINE RUSH. 
 The beginning got me totally hooked, and that ending was a page-turner indeed! So much was happening, it was REALLY exciting and intense. 
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
 I DEFINITELY recommend this thing. DEFINITELY. 
 The plot is so intriguing, so cool, you HAVE to read it. 
 You fall in love with the characters pretty easily, and you just don't want to let any of them go.... 
 I really want the next book now! >_<

Resending the Hero by Moira J Moore is a fun, exciting read. The story is set in the a world with a unique "magic system" to it. There are the Sources with power to avert a supernatural disaster from occurring and there are the Shields who make sure the Source doesn't die. . . plus all of the boring tasks such as paperwork. The main character is a Shield bound to a Source she can't stand. The story is a welcomed rarity in that the main character is a female and it is her job to save the hero. 
 Only two things detracted from my enjoyment of the book. The feminist allegory, while warmly welcomed, was at times heavy-handed. Additionally, Moira J Moore has a habit of starting a new chapter off with a jump, that isn't fair, a hop in plot. On more than one occasion, I found myself flipping back to see if I had missed something. 
 The characters in the story were excellent and the plot was very entertaining. Moira J Moore did a phenomenal job of tying in most, if not all, of the loose ends. I was extremely surprised to see this too. I thought for sure one major plot item was going to become the seed for the sequel. 
 If you like light fantasy and/or a strong female characters, I recommend you pick this one up.

Perhaps I shouldn't have been surprised at how thematically similar these stories were. An anthology about power armor will necessarily have recurring elements, but so many of the authors (with wildly different plots and settings) addressed the same issues in the same ways. 
 Some of the shorts were very enjoyable, and a few were even thought-provoking. Several cross into other genres, but in general, this is just good, escapist, military sci-fi.

I loved this book so much. It's very intense and relatively fast passed. I've been looking for a novel like this for some time, and I'm glad I came across this one! 
 I did find the first half slightly hard to get into, but I think that was more character building. The second half was amazing, and I found I couldn't put the book down (even after one in the morning). Once the characters got more into the adventure, it got better and better. 
 Nicely written, and definitely something I want to read more of.

4-4.5 stars 
 This book hurt my heart. :(. It was written to raise awareness on the issue of underage prostitution but I appreciated that it didn't feel like I was reading an after school special, if you know what I mean. I thought the main character was well developed and the end was realistic but with a bit of hope thrown in. 
 For a much better review check out LadyVigilante's excellent review

I thought that this book really just expanded our knowledge of the world and people we were introduced to in Unholy Ghosts. This book picks up about four months after the events in the first book. 
 Whereas Unholy Ghosts really introduces the readers to the characters and gives us a look into their past, and introduces us to the world of Downside, Unholy Magic digs even deeper on the character side of things. There's not too much additional knowledge of the world that we learn, instead we learn a lot about our characters. Namely, Chess and Terrible. 
 There are reviewers who have called this book heartbreaking and I would have to agree. There are moments that I feel so sad for these two characters and what they have been through and what they will inevitably go through. I know Chess has a lot of problems in her past and she uses drugs in her present to keep those thoughts from coming back and haunting her. I think if Chess could find that one thing that is worth more (cough* Terrible cough*) she would see herself better. I was saddened by the comments she would make about herself not being worth it. While I'm not much for a pity party, I think Stacia Kane did the right amount to remind readers how Chess feels about herself, but not throwing it directly in our faces at every turn. 
 Terrible really grows in this book. We get to see beyond the enforcer that he is, and we really get to see his heart. We saw the beginnings of it in Unholy Ghosts, but in this book he really opens up which makes it that much harder to see what he believes in come crashing down. Stacia Kane really did a wonderful job with making you want to see the characters find happiness, only to watch it get ripped away. 
 But I haven't given up hope. We do see at the end Chess fully realizing what it would mean to lose Terrible and it really is a beautiful moment. I am interested to see how things will be for them in City of Ghosts. 
 I really am enjoying this series and I can't wait to read the third book. I little sad that I will have to wait until March for the 4th book, but from there I don't thik there will be as big of a gap between the books in this series. Until Then!

"This book is nothing short of a brilliant, hilarious thrill-ride that is instantly infectious." - John Corey Whaley, Printz Honor-winning author of Where Things Come Back 
 This quote sums up Grasshopper Jungle perfectly. The writing style, although rather repetitive at times, was really enjoyable and the adventures of Austin, Robby and Shann were so intriguing that it was hard to put the book down. To anyone looking for a taste of something new, I advise you to give this book a go. At the very least, Grasshopper Jungle is without a doubt thought provoking. Andrew Smith certainly made me think differently about some topics, most prominently the world being taken over by giant, praying-mantis looking bugs which only have two things on their minds. A weird-as-hell and fascinating book; Andrew Smith's Grasshopper Jungle will definitely always have a place on my bookshelf.

I really like the mystery that Sara Shepard has created. This book really keeps me guessing, I have no idea who killed Sutton as all the characters seem suspicious. I really like how Shepard intertwines Sutton's thoughts with what is happening to Emma. I like how we are slowly getting bits of Sutton's memories. 
 This series has so many twists that it keeps you guessing the whole time. A character will be cleared but then they will do or say something that makes them a suspect again. Laurel seemed very cold in this book and I am not sure about her. 
 I really like this series and I can't wait to read the next book. I hope that we will get some answers in the next book as I really want to know what happened to Sutton.

3.5... I love how this book breaks quite a few of the young Adult cliches, while still being a typical YA novel. I also love the main character, Sophie is great. 
 Also, I have a super-power, yes I am bragging, I can usually figure out the ending after the first round of hints--either I'm off my game or this book duped me (me = :) to be duped). 
 What the book lacked-- I just wanted more! More characterization more of the day to day school stuff- the teachers the classes- it just felt skated over- great world idea- little building on it. And the (very) ending pissed me off.
Solid storytelling...Fun...Magical...Exciting. I can't imagine the last book will be anything less than epic and probably really long too.

Rereading this in 2015 with the IA Addicts

 Second Read: Rereading a great series may be the best way to get out of a book funk ever. I've been inundated with the new and shiny and they've been killing me. So I'm raising this from four stars to five, because it's just awesome. I love the games and I love how the heroine grows. On to the next one!

Hate the title...and the begininning felt very juvenile (especially since the authors are setting up all 3 books, all boy/girl/boy/girl/boy/girl)but it picked up after a few chapters. I liked it though, it was a quick girly read, nothing too surprising but still fun.

(4.5 stars) What a yarn. 
 The world that Victor lives in is an alternate reality, if the Civil War had not happened. Slavery is legal in four southern states and the rest of life is eerily similar to ours -- same politicians, same big historical moments (minus Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation; the history in this book is that he was assassinated right before he was going to give it), same celebrities and music. Victor, a free black man, is a bounty hunter for the US Marshals, bringing back runaway slaves. We follow him at the start of a new case, but something about the case is a little off. 
 The writing was rich and detailed, and the story was full of surprises, keeping me guessing the entire time, with lots of reveals. Super interesting and one I'd recommend to others, for sure.
Just what I needed to put some steam in my unruly life [?] ;-)

The first three chapters didn't engage me. They felt like they were establishing the background, and I worried that the switching between the third-person sections and Agnes's first-person narration was a failure on the part of the author to develop Agnes's voice. 
 Chapters four through nine were great. There is a tension between the different voices here, and Agnes's situations (in the valley today, in the valley when she was younger, and in Illugastadir) are fascinating, suggestive, and well presented. The triangle of piety (and Pietism), superstition, and atheism turns in each of the main characters. The difficulty of life in bleak conditions is brought across but not overstated. There are sweet subtleties of exposition (such as why Blondal is called that). 
 But then the last three chapters flounder. Agnes loses her confidant and we are increasingly given what are apparently internal monologues; it suddenly seems like the author made a mistake in not directly presenting Agnes's past. Secondary characters stand around doing nothing, looking awkward with too much earlier investment. The revelation of Agnes's past turns out to be banal and pathetic. We are denied details of her trials and incarceration (in particular, what prompted her move from Stora-Borg), and I thought her character now seemed alarmingly undeveloped and unlikely. I also had assumed Agnes had murdered Natan. I worry that, without this incorrect assumption, the middle chapters would not read so well.  
 A mixed bag.
Unreliable narrator. Was interesting for the first half, but I found myself just trying to read to finish the book and move on rather than to enjoy the story.

Oh my gosh guys, this book was adorable! I really needed something happy and this hit the spot. 
 Over the summer, Vivian (Viv) spent most of her time smooching the hottest boy in school, Jake. But once summer is over, Jake ignores Viv leaving her feeling very confused and very much used. After an embarrassing confrontation with Jake, she decides she's never going to let her heart get broken again. Love is for fools. What she needs to do is find a boyfriend logically - as Spock would do. Yes, Spock from Star Trek. 
 Viv thinks up the RC list - yup, you guessed it. The replacement crush list. Boys who don't rate high on her zing meter, but there may be a connection. And there's no way she'll fall in love. What Viv didn't count on was new to town Dallas. 
 This book made my nerd heart happy. Every chapter began with a Star Trek quote - mostly from or about Spock. And Dallas -aka McNerd - was nerdy in the most absolutely adorable way. He knows about Viv's list and is determined to make her see that love isn't logical and you can't force yourself to like someone. 
 Hearts get broken. Dreams get shattered then renewed. There's a hot celebrity and a talent show. There's book clubs, book blogs, and a book store - three things I absolutely love. There's the adorable charm of a small town. There's a cat named Hiddles - Tom Hiddleston happy alert! 
 So why not 5 stars? There were just a few little things that didn't sit well with me. The main thing being the book blogging part. Maybe if I didn't write reviews myself, or even read ones here on Goodreads I would think differently. But having been in this world for some years now, I felt that the blogging aspect took me out of the story. There were a few of Viv's online book reviews inserted throughout the book and they were just very mediocre at best. I thought the author, being as talented as she was writing this book, would offer more. I don't know, maybe that's me being nitpicky, but like I said, when these happened it just seemed to pause the plot at times when you really just wanted to continue reading. 
 But overall, I adored it. If you need a light pick me up, this is definitely the book for you. I mean, just listen to Spock! 
 I received a copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review.

First a quick note for when this appears outside of Goodreads (on my blog, for example): This review will have SPOILERS and outside of Goodreads I don't think the spoiler tag is going to work to shield you from the spoilers. You have been warned! 
 In my last review I (rhetorically) asked Ms Rowling to surprise me - to make Harry lose sometimes and perhaps have the kids not always succeed at saving the day. Ms Rowling gave me that and so much more. As I noted before, she delights in Red Herrings (these books being something like Teen Wizard Noir), so my attention was on high alert this time around. Looking back at my status updates I was right or almost right about the following (will be in a spoiler tag): 
  
 -At 33% I predicted that Hermione's cat was Black or worked for Black. The latter proved to be true and the former showed I was on the right track for the climax - the Animagi reveal. (I restated this around 68%) 
 -At 36% I thought Lupin might be a Vampire or Dr Jekyll/Mr Hyde type. This was due to the potion he had to drink. I was on the right path with the fact that he's a werewolf, but completely missed the name clue - Lupin. I think I might have been more keen to that clue (lupus=dog in latin) had I not known of Lupin III and thought maybe Ms Rowling was an anime fan. 
  
 Yet, even though I'd somewhat guessed a lot of the reveals, I was wholly unprepared for the twist. The reveal that the rat was Peter and that HE was the real traitor! . 
 It's also funny that the saying be careful what you wish for came to pass with Harry. I wanted a more realistic ending and,  He loses his chance to have his godfather as his guardian and also has no proof of his godfather's innocence. . 
 This is one of the darkest books yet - the Dementors are pure nightmare fuel and the ending is pretty dark to match. 
 Of course, Rowling is quite aware of Chekov's Gun (look it up on TV Tropes if you don't know what that means) so Hermione's method of attending class became a key part of the resolution of the climax. I was a lot quicker on the uptake than Harry and Ron that Hermione was clearly attending more than one class at the same time. I'm surprised that, as characters in a magical world they couldn't figure that out, even if they didn't know the mechanism by which it worked. That also caught me by surprise, but I was happy, having recently discussed the Time Traveler Paradoxes  with my wife that Ms Rowling is quite consistent and nothing about the narrative  we see the first time around before they time travel  needs to be retconned. 
 This appears to be the book in which Rowling begins the transition from middle grade book to young adult book. With the exception of a very subtle attraction between Harry and another girl betraying the fact that these kids are pretty unhorny for 13 year olds, the book definitely marks an uptick in the maturity of both the characters and the situations she puts them into. Again, once the full extent of the Dementor's powers and methods are revealed, it's pretty clear the Wizarding world is much more dangerous than we were led to believe in the first couple books where the evil was of a more cartoonish nature. In fact, if you consider what was supposed to happen to the Hippogriff  and how this book reveals that justice does not always prevail over at least two different occasions with life and death on the line, this book presents a very realistic view of how the world can be disappointing and not even the Great Dumbledore can magic people out of every situation. Except he kind of does with the Hermione reveal. Still, it was only by trickery and neither his powers nor his reputation that he is able to help them save the day

The book opens with an unusual scene where parents at Pirriwee Public are dressed in costume (either Elvis or Audrey) and attending trivia night. The night ends in an puzzling death. I thought this was a brilliant way to start the mystery. Since the parents were all in costumes, it is not clear who is who even as the book starts introducing the characters. We don't even know what caused the ordeal until the end of the book because the second chapter rewinds back to 6 months before trivia night and restarts the story from there. 
 The mainly follows three mothers whose kids start kindergarten and have different circumstances and struggles to deal with; being a single parent, living with domestic violence, handling a rebellious teenager. The middle of the book was slow and bordering boring but maybe it was to drive the point home about how life-altering decisions aren't made that quickly. Come trivia night, a surprise was delivered and it was jaw-dropping. Overall Big Little Lies was a well-crafted suspenseful mystery.

Such a cute, fluffy book. Here is me melting.... Sigh. 
 Despite so many logical flaws(which I would normally focus on, but in this book's case, I can totally make an exception!), I loved this book a LOT!

lovely and emotional 
 Milan has certainly given her hero and heroine difficult emotions to wrestle beyond those for each other in this book. Though very different, their past traumas- one at the hands of an emotionally abusive father, the other at the hands of a selfish father and cruel society- allow for them to both sympathize and to dig each other out of despair. Certainly a good match. 
 The political background was also important and a driving setting. Milan goes farther than many at suggesting the reforms that would eventually change England. Instead of resting heavily on the nostalgia of aristocracy as many in the genre do, Milan instead leans on what will and what could be, containing more a note of feeling a need for justice in unjust times without dragging the reader into a Dickinsonian despair. 
 Any further details would simply spoil you, and I encourage you to read it yourself. I am certainly looking forward to obtaining other books in the series.
This piece of shit awesomeness had me bawling like the little bitch I am.

I've read many reviews that said they were expecting more. I feel the same about it. Not enough world-building and especially I'm troubled by the character development that is reduced to Bran only, and that too is not really well done. The ideas behind this story, though, are interesting enough to give it such a rating. I'm thinking here on the slaves trainers in a institutionalized background that unfortunately is not explored seriously in order to obtain a better understanding. Training or re-training implies an important dose of psychological input, but here we see nothing of it. I guess this wasn't one of the author's intentions, but it would've been nice to have an image of the training techniques from different perspectives. 
 I haven't read many slavefics, but I came across two titles that are very good in portraying the life of a slave and the challenges this status offers for him: Hidden Boundaries by C.S. McClellan and The Violet and the Tom by Ocotillo.

Delightful! I wish Patricia Wrede would write a million books. :) Reminiscent of Seventh Son, by Orson Scott Card, in its alternate frontier and unusual magic, but with a lighter and more personal tone. Loved it.

Reread, original review below. I still loved this as much as I did the first time. It was interesting to reread this knowing Blue's Identity, but it was even more interesting to read it knowing Leah is bisexual, it puts a different lense on some of her interactions with Abby, and it's really something to think about when she talks to Simon about him not coming out to her, considering she hasn't come out to him. I'm happy to read my review of this from a couple of years ago with the knowledge that queer YA has improved, and there is now a much larger variety, I hope it continues getting better. 
 Original review: Too many Young Adult books have characters who are either far too adult or way too childlike, but this book hit the perfect sweet spot in the middle. The book was just a lot of fun in general, something that can't be said all that often about "coming out" books, but then again that's not really what this books is, it's like the anti coming out book in the best possible way. I hope this book inspires more like it so we begin to see more fun queer YA instead of the more serious books we often get. I didn't think much about the red scribble until I actually started reading the book. The first page after the dedication - but before the "Prefatory Material" says "The following work of fiction is partially based on fact." This immediately put me off and I spent the rest of the book wondering, well, which parts of the book are actually fiction? This annoys me far more than I think it really should, and there might be something to that. Or maybe I'm overthinking it. 
 I also wondered why Ball chose to synthesize some aspects of the story into narration, yet leave others as transcripts. I guess for the effect of presenting evidence to a jury? 
 The book doesn't use the usual tricks of the trade to draw the audience in and make them sympathize with the characters, which made the whole thing seem a bit flat to me. I also found pretty much all of the characters to be some variety of insane. Some are just pitiful, some are actually psycopaths. I seem to require sympathetic characters in order to enjoy a book, so I did find this a bit discouraging. 
 Altogether this is a bleak and unsettling book that I'm finding it difficult to assess.

I am not particularly shy when it comes to my general dislike of dystopian fiction. I tend to get angry when I read it, and since I read primarily for enjoyment and entertainment it makes little sense for me to seek out stories that do not provide those things. (There is also the fact that so much of the dystopian fiction I have read has strained my suspension of disbelief to the breaking point...that does not exactly recommend the genre to me.) 
 So with that in mind, based on the way people have shelved and tagged Partials on Goodreads and other book sites, I shouldn't like it. The thing is, while there are definite dystopian elements to this book, I would not classify it as dystopian fiction. It is much more a post-apocalyptic survival story, and that is how it is presented from the start. The dystopian elements are not the front and center focus of the story, and with that I find I can care about the characters. I think it not being in first person also helps with this.

 May 2012: You guys, I'm so conflicted about this book. I wanted to love it, I really did. But it was kind of a mess? I guess I'll have to settle for merely "like" and hope book three is back up to the standard that Roth set in Divergent. 
 Insurgent picks up right where Divergent left off, with the factions of Chicago at war with each other. The Dauntless are scattered and mostly dead; Abnegation has all but been wiped out; Amity is sitting pretty, far from the conflict; Candor is neutral at the moment (I think?); and Erudite continues to belligerently attack everyone. Tris, Four, and the other Dauntless/Abnegation refugees wander all over God's creation trying to find shelter against Erudite, who is hunting them for some reason I can't really remember (not a good sign . . . I only finished the book three weeks ago). 
 Meanwhile, Four's abusive dick of a father, Marcus, knows a secret that the Abnegation died trying to protect, and which Erudite is willing to kill to cover up forever. This is a pretty important plot point, but it's mostly glossed over in favor of hanging out with a traumatized, PTSD Tris who feels such extreme guilt over her part in killing Will in Divergent that she can barely function. She puts all of her relationships in jeopardy and basically has a death wish for the entire novel. It is exhausting. There's a couple of big battles, Tris goes batshit and gets herself captured on purpose, and then some other stuff happens that I can't really remember. Also also, we meet the Factionless, who are headed up by a not-so-secret person from Four's past, and who play in a big role in the final battle of the war, which surprisingly concludes in this book. Most authors would have dragged it out, but Roth makes the excellent decision to end it with book two and up the conflict in a different direction for book three. 
 If I had to sum it up (which I don't, because this is my review and who the heck cares anyway so why am I even typing this, I don't know), then I would say that Insurgent suffers from classic middle book syndrome. Since the war is over by the end, it's clear that it wasn't the focal point of the trilogy, and the big important stuff is still coming. That means that this book and this war served more of a transition function than anything else. Admittedly, it must be really hard to write a middle story (whether it's a film or a book), but it can be done, as evidenced by The Empire Strikes Back. And I have to say, Roth was almost there in terms of the actual events of the story, but the book is so muddled it's hard to tell. 
 The unpleasantness of hanging out with PTSD Tris (however accurate and true to character) is a close second, but my biggest complaint about this book is its complete lack of structure. One of the reasons Divergent was such a fun reading experience was that it was incredibly well-structured. That's a weird thing to say about a book, and maybe it's only something other writers really care about, but the net effect is the same: better structure, better book, even if you can't necessarily put a finger on it as a non-writing layperson. I just felt so lost the entire book, like I never knew what to expect page to page, but in a bad way. Only the most experimental avant-garde authors fuck around with structure, and there's a reason most people don't read those assholes anyway. We like structures. We like expectations, even if the only point of expectations in a book is to frustrate them. I felt like Insurgent just flowed along with things happening here and there along the way, and even though it was a fast read, the good stuff wasn't necessarily emphasized at the right times or in the right ways, and the frustrating stuff was more often than not front and center. Again, it's hard to put into words and I'd probably have to read it again and take copious notes to figure it out, but it's not like I'm writing a frickin' dissertation here so shut it I'm done with my arguments. 
 Anyways, still excited for book three, and I'm hoping that Roth turns out to be just as good at endings as she was at beginnings.

 WUTHERING HEIGHTS by EMILY BRONTE 
 Emily Jane Bronte (1818-48) wrote this novel in 1847, a time of post European renaissance reflection when the British elite were trying to come to grips with issues such as existence, religion, philosophy, and the progression of modern science. A year later Emily died of tuberculosis, a disease like many others incurable by the Victorian era advances in medical science. In order to better understand Emily's narrative style and portrayal of her characters and scenes we need to understand the influences of her time. 
 First we will observe what authorities of philosophy and religion believed prior to Emily's time. Old Medievalism was a period when monarchs ruled the world in tandem with religious piety. Scholars and adherents of the Renaissance likened Medievalism to conservatism and corruption, a period of Popes rising to become rulers, pagan superstitions, witch hunting, and barbaric priest-ridden centuries of darkness where free thinking was suppressed and blind faith was the law. 
 In revolt to medievalism, John Locke (1632-1704), an empiricist, wrote in 1689 that the only knowledge humans could have was a posteriori i.e., based upon experience. To him, the mind was a tabula rasa--blank tablet--on which life's experiences leave an impression, and that knowledge is gained through the contemplation of events transpired. This view was held first by Aristotle and was adopted by stoics during ancient Roman times and proliferated through the ages by Islamic philosophers of the 9th and 10th centuries. 
 The Irish Anglican bishop, George Berkeley (1685-1753), in response to Locke, in 1710 put forth a treatise challenging empiricism; his belief was that God fills in the voids of human perception by doing the perceiving when humans are not around to do it for themselves. 
 Scepticism, atheism, rationalism were spin-offs to these struggles between the philosophical and religious doctrines and led to an Age of Enlightenment in Europe (1715-1789) where everything that had gone before was subjected to scrutiny and reasoning in a Sapere aude "Dare to know" attitude. Rationalism, which has its roots in the Socratic life of inquiry, argued that truth has an intrinsically logical structure that can be applied to logic, mathematics, ethics and metaphysics. So, in essence, having a clear, unbiased frame of mind, using rational thought, man can reach out and, like Michelangelo's fresco painting 'The Creation of Adam', touch God, the epitome of Truth. Rationalism was prevalent during the Georgian period (1714-1830), a time in which Britain was in continuous conflict with other European (France, the Dutch, and Spain) and trans-Atlantic powers (Americas) in her bid to become a dominant world power and was the herald to the empirical Victorian epoch and the Pax Britannica. 
 In the aftermath of the Napoleonic Wars (1815) and the Battle of Waterloo where France was utterly defeated, Great Britain entered a period of economic and political instability. The Radical party emerged in a bid to champion the rights of the working and middle classes and was the forerunner to several upheavals and events. One such was the Peterloo Massacre (1819), in which protestors in Northern England demonstrated against famine, chronic unemployment, and the lack of suffrage. The king's cavalry charged into this crowd of 60,000 protestors with sabres drawn leading to 15 deaths and 400-700 injuries. The massacre was named in an ironic comparison to the Battle of Waterloo. 
 The early ninth century in Britain saw a time when Evangelism was on the rise, challenging traditional religious structure that emphasised a code of honour for the gentry, 'suitable' behaviour for plebeians, and faithful observances of rituals. One such patron of Evangelism was the philanthropist Hannah More (1745-1833) a religious writer who became involved with the literary elite of London becoming a leading member of the Bluestocking group comprised of learned, intellectual women. Elizabeth Montagu (1718-1800), a British social reformer, patron of the arts, salonist, literary critic, and writer, helped organise and lead the Blue Stockings Society. 
 Hannah More joined the group campaigning against the slave trade which peaked in the two last decades of the 18th century, and coincided with the events of Emily's narrative, which is no coincidence since the author of Wuthering Heights delves deeply into the issue of humans being viewed as property both as a consequence of the patriarchal system, but also as residue from the slave trade; Emily makes disturbing references to gipsies, black devils, poor, dirty children speaking gibberish no one understands. Unlike Moore, Emily's writing challenges the hierarchical structure of English society and goes a step further than Evangelism by challenging religious views on Good and Evil. 
 We witness, through Emily's dichotomous representation of Heathcliff, her protagonist, how she challenges the commonly held views of her epoch that Good and Evil exist in their purest forms, and argues rather that someone who is perceived as evil can also have some good in them, and someone seen as wholesome and good can in fact have mortal failings which lead to consequences of greatest evil. 
 Emily belonged to that caste of writers of the early Victorian era that gave rise to Romanticism and the Gothic novel. Romanticism, not to be confused with romance and romantic novels, was a revolt against the aristocratic norms of the Age of Enlightenment which sought to quarter and rationalise/categorise nature. Romanticism was the attempt to revive the life and thought of the Middle Ages, by tearing out any influences of religion (as represented by Berkeley and other religious/papal authorities of the 18th century), empiricism that had gone before, and the rationalism of the Georgian period. 
 In Romanticism and revived medievalism the narrative attempts to escape social structure, industrialism, and what society blithely accepts as agreeable behaviour, and expresses nature in its purest form, embracing the exotic, unfamiliar, unchangeable and untameable. Romantics were distrustful of the human world and self-imposed limitations/ restrictions, and believed that a closer connection with nature was healthy both morally and mentally. Romanticism embodied a restless non-conforming spirit which violently sought to break through cramping boundaries, longing for the unbound and indefinable. 
 We mentioned before that Romanticism in literature awoke together with the Gothic tale. Examples of this which Emily, as a learned scholar, was surely aware of are Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) and John William Polidori's The Vampyre (1819). In her pursuit of Gothicism, Emily uses as a backdrop the medieval mansion of Wuthering Heights, a dark brooding place, and spins her web of supernatural themes where she challenges everything that has gone before: religion, social order, division of the classes, rich and poor, master and servant, relationships between men and women, romance, horror, good and evil. Every aspect of her late Georgian and early Victorian period is placed under scrutiny and examined from all angles, allowing the reader to draw their own conclusions. 
 But, however many times we may read her novel, each time we find a new unexplored avenue, a new angle with which to view her work, and the themes she hits upon are as applicable in our time as they were ahead of hers. In fact, Emily was so ahead of her time that, after her subsequent death, her sister, Charlotte tried desperately to downplay Emily's work and tried to defend her sister under the scrutiny of the literate urban public view which took offence to this Yorkshire lady's apparent discrediting of society and the law of the land which was in place at the time. Even though the monarch, at the time of writing, was a woman, the woman's role was subject to patriarchal control where a man had rights of ownership over his house, his wife, his sister and daughters. Women in the UK were not granted suffrage until 1915. 
 In keeping with her love and study of nature and everything wild, in Emily's Wuthering Heights we see a distinctly canine imagery and symbolism in her scene settings: dogs and their behaviour feature prominently from the first chapter and abound throughout the narrative, indeed permeating her protagonists' characters and their thoughts and behavioural patterns and social groupings, her characters acting at times like a wolf pack with dominant alpha males and females and words such as howled, growled replacing more genteel expressions. This has been attributed to the author's childhood where she grew up in a home with dogs. Emily, with an intense nostalgia, brings out the supernatural aspect of her protagonists, Heathcliff and Catherine senior, who are as much a part of the wilderness of the moors as the stunted trees and the rocks that litter the landscape. Emily also brings in sharp contrast the Gothic aspect of ghosts and grave digging as opposed to civilised propriety and the benign honouring of the dead who, once buried, should be left in peace to reside in heaven. The pacified pastoral, Christian, English late eighteenth century placid belief of what heaven should be like comes into direct conflict with Emily's protagonists' passion for the natural, the supernatural; like spirits of the moor they see heaven as a perpetual existence, like the wind amongst the creatures and flora of the untamed Cambrian moors. True to her Romanticist views, Emily creates protagonists who remain indefinable to this day, even though our greatest scholars have made brave attempts to dissect and pin them down, with none having managed to do this entirely. For all boils down to personal perspective, and this is Emily's clearest message and greatest triumph; man, like all creation, is continuously evolving, changing, and what is thought correct today, might mortify future generations, and in this her work remains eternal, supernatural, a perpetual struggle with no conclusion.

 First, let's just get this out of the way. Make no mistake this is any good feminist's worst nightmare. Rape, Stockholm syndrome, I mean all kinds of abuse is kind of thrown in a pot and stirred up in a way that could only possibly be titillating in a work of fantasy. What makes it worse is how well it is written, and that all of these awful traumatic interactions between the two mains are consistent and truthful to the characters & their histories. In other words, Prisoner cannot be dismissed as yet another campy, granddaughter of the bodice ripper. In fact, I would not be surprised if the authors wrote this as a deconstruction of the genre. 
 It is a well written story; it is also an incredibly fucked up story. 
 Prisoner starts off with typical 'forbidden love' flirtations between a creative writing instructor and her prison inmate pupil. Then it takes a dramatic turn reminiscent of the Ben Affleck movie, The Town (2010) which is in turn inspired by the film Prince of Thieves (1948). Finally - and, the authors admit the comparison up front by referencing the infamous duo in the book - the narrative turns into a full on action/pursuit, psycho, crazy-in-love homage to Bonnie and Clyde. Ending TBD. 
 I can't rate this book. Kind of how the characters struggle with wanting what is wrong, do it anyway, and have to cope with the emotional fallout of forcing/being forced in a relationship so very unhealthy... That's how I feel about this book. It's intriguing but I need to hate it. 
 Maybe I'll update this review after finishing it but this is basically a warning to all those of you who may be jumping into this based on all the glowing, euphemistic reviews.

This was my first real reading of a Shakespeare play, aside from some childhood dabblings in Macbeth and Hamlet. Some intriguing references to The Tempest in three different novels I read this year (for the record, Christopher Morley's Thorofare, Mary Stewart's This Rough Magic and Jennifer Freitag's Plenilune) made me decide this was a good place to start. What particularly struck me was the swift-moving interest of the multi-threaded plot, with subplots taking place among different characters on different parts of the island at once, and the aliveness of the bluntly human characters--and the humor! Good heavens, Shakespeare invented witty banter. Sebastian and Antonio's impertinent running commentary on Gonzalo's speeches, Stephano and Trinculo's bickering, and Prospero's rather dry asides about Ferdinand and Miranda's romance had me very much amused, and pleasantly surprised to find Shakespeare so much fun. A very nice way to begin our acquaintance.

The cover and the title drew me in, and no doubt that they will seal the deal for you as well. So I plucked the book off the shelf and read the summary. Guess what? The summary DOES NOT TELL YOU ANYTHING. You can read what was on the front flap verbatim on Goodreads. But other than that, the authors are sort of expecting you to read to find out. I was sort of offended, but I read anyway. 
 And yeah, I didn't really find out anything until like page 130 of the book. And even then, it was less than a page of conversation. This is literally what happened: 
 Lena: I'm a caster. 
 Ethan: [Oh my god. Come on Ethan, breath in breath out.] Oh, so you're... a witch? 
 Lena: Don't be silly. That's a stupid stereotype. 
 Ethan: That's okay my household is weird too. 
 Lena: [Sort of sad] 
 Ethan: [Oh god oh god please kiss me] 
 HOWEVER, I do have to give props to her for the writing. It's simplistic. Yeah. But most YA fantasy is, and the authors give us enough room to think and guess what's happening, and don't overload us with thoughts. 
 That's another thing. A lot of people agree that for a boy narrator, Ethan is rather effeminate in his retelling. Okay, yeah, sure, he reads a lot of books and talks about Gone With the Wind a lot. I didn't think this was a problem because one, mostly girls read this anyway, so they won't notice, and two, the detailing is, again, simplistic enough that it's believable. But yeah, sometimes he is a little girly. I guess that's what makes Ethan more than a one dimensional character. I think that's sort of nice. 
 And to be fair, the authors do make some attempts at total guy-ness. Ethan asks his friends if the "new girl" (Lena) is hot. But that is not what propels Ethan to fall in love with Lena and her with him. It's the fact that Ethan is the only person who's nice to Lena. 
 Oh yeah, and we never really learn what Ethan looks like. I'm imagining that he's also hot because apparently one of the two hottest girls in the school used to date him. I just imagined him as African American because everyone else in the story was white. WHITE. 
 And despite all of that... I found myself rooting for them. I kept asking myself WHY. WHY ON EARTH WOULD I LIKE A ROMANCE LIKE THIS? And I did not have an answer. I mean, it has all the elements of a bad romance. You know they're gonna end up together and it should be tedious. But I read ravenously until they had their first kiss. And then I sort of stopped reading after that, because it got too much about saving Lena. 
 And the other thing that I wanted to address: the southern setting. I live in South Carolina, where the story takes place. People seemed to be taking the southern setting very offensively, and I more or less don't really agree. So I live in Greenville, South Carolina, a more populated area. But parts of the southern life sound correct. 
 For instance, Savannah [a ridiculously popular southern name] and Emily are two dyed blonde girls with over-bearing mammas who have a lot of influnce on the community. Sounds about right. Down here in SC, you have a lot of white girls tanning themselves and sticking their pelvises out in pictures so their fat PTA moms can be proud. 
 And Lena is sort of goth and is bullied. Sounds about right. I had a goth girl in my school who wore tutus and drew butterflies on her face as part of her makeup. Now maybe Lena doesn't do that, but this girl in my school was bullied to no end for being goth. And mostly by the tan, duckface whores like Savannah and Emily. 
 But another part is the cooking. We don't have biscuits and gravy for breakfast. At least, I don't think so. But there was a time that Ethan had egg rolls for dinner, and that's more correct than I've ever noticed. 
 And the end. The end was... weird. I had to read it over and over again. And I guess I was sort of tired because this book was about 560 pages and by then I just wanted to pick up another book. 
 I guess what I'm saying is that if you have the patience and you like a book where you can think for yourself, read this. The plot was entertaining at least, so if you're one of those people who read and see the book in their heads like a movie, then go ahead. It killed time.

Really great book with a new twist to it. The planet of Lorien was over taken by an evil alien species known as the Mogadorian. Several of the Lorien children were sent to Earth with hopes of their planet one day returning back to normal. The Mogadorian followed those children to Earth though searching, killing, and now wanting to take over our very own planet. This is the story of one of those children, number four, who has made Earth a home for himself and will do anything to protect it and the ones he loves. 
 John (number four) and Henri have spent their entire lives running and hiding from the Mogadorian. That is until they reach a town called Paradise where John realizes he's tired of running and finally wants to find a place to call home. With numbers 1 - 3 already being killed the Mogadorian are on the hunt now for number 4, so staying quiet and hidden is kind of sort of really important. It would've been an easier job if John hadn't started crushing on the head jock of the school's ex girl-friend. Sarah, the girl, is such an honest and genuine character that she's hard not to fall in love with though. Despite everything that she goes through with John she never let's their love waiver. Talk about Lorien love, right? 
 I really enjoyed John's sarcasm. He would be so blunt to his friends about being an alien, but they would just brush it off like he was joking. Specially all the conversations with Sarah such as "They're just lucky I didn't use my superpowers and throw them into the next county." 
 Now on to read The Power of Six! To find out Who sent that fax?! Who took the picture for the newspaper of four jumping out the window? How did that article find out about the Mogadorian in the first place? Will Four ever see Sarah again? Why were they meant to end up in Paradise, Ohio? & so many more questions left unanswered!

 I didn't even remember that Allie had a twin. Oops. Shows you how much I disliked the last book's fairy plotline. Oh well. I liked this one much more right off the bat. For one, Junior is back. We also don't seem to be too immersed in Fairyland this time around. Weird things are happening again-a creepy fairy is acting as Allie's guardian angel and the government has managed to find out information about the moonstone. Allie has to be on the lookout for Trimarks and the government in this one. She's searching for her twin sister, plus she has all the other Purdy-related family drama to deal with. Since I assume this is the last book, things should start coming to a head soon. 
 Despite not being immersed in fairies, we do meet a new one, namely Jessie, a dark fae dating Kizzy's horrible daughter, Carmel. So it looks like Allie's on the run from the dark fae as well. The Trimarks are planning another uprising, so Allie has to move fast. I was slightly horrified by the addition of stereotypical Irish mannerisms being added to the stereotypicality of Brothers' Hispanic characters, so excuse me if I indulge in a little written eye-rolling. Ireland is a really tired location for urban fantasy. We get it, Ireland is magical and fairies and druids and omg Celtic Wicca, but seriously, as someone whose grandfather emigrated from Ireland, I just want it to stop. Let's go to, like, Croatia or something. Anywhere but Ireland. 
 Luckily, we don't dwell on Ireland for too long. Allie spends most of this book learning about and trying to locate her twin, Anne Marie Scott. She recruits Junior and a runaway named Sammie tags along as well. I had my suspicions about Sammie right off, but she was a welcome addition to the Allie-Faye-Junior parade. When things finally start getting real, I found I really enjoyed this one. It brought Allie back to who she was in the first book, and the story was smoother as well. 
 So, in all, I enjoyed this series. It's just as good as most other paranormal YA series out there, and I've certainly seen worse. I'd check this one out if you liked and read the first three. Marilee Brothers commented at the blog to let us know she's writing the fifth, and last, book now, so we're almost done with Allie's story!

 To say the author has written an all-out no holds barred story, would be an understatement. This is a challenging read and I didn't get to the end unscathed. From the first page, I had a strong suspicion that the ride was going to be a hard one and I wasn't mistaken. Every imaginable feeling hit me like a ton of bricks so if violence in the first degree isn't your cuppa, my advice to you is read the blurb before one-clicking. The baddie is such an evil character that regardless of my need to jump into my Kindle and strangle him, I most certainly wouldn't have been able to knock off a psychopath hell-bent on one thing only. Death! 
 Quote: "...this was no threat; it was what Alik did. He killed." 
 Kisa is the one and only person that has the ability to calm him down. And only slightly at that. Alik's way of letting off steam is simply abusive and makes the word brutal look pathetic. He is not though. Ooh no, he is the best killing machine The Dungeon has ever had in the New York Russian Mafia. Driven by the fact that one day he will inherit it all, makes him unstoppable. No opponent is a match... He has no remorse, no ethics, no fear and the author has described his persona down to such perfection that he scared me sh*tless! 
 Quote: Where the fuck have you been?" he snarled, the hand on my left bicep inevitably moving upward to clutch the back of my neck." 
 Kisa is his world. She is so meek and mild that at times I got really mad with her. I couldn't understand why her father never stood up for her. Alik cannot survive without this young woman. Like him, she was born into the 'family'. She does what is expected of her and never questions. Alik dominates her to the point of dismay. However, she has a secret that has never been told. Ah, this my dear readers, this is the backbone of a story which will have you reading quicker than quick. 
 Quote: "So you know, 818, I can still taste her dripping pussy in my mouth. I just fucked her hard, real hard." 
 Now let's get down to the nitty-gritty of this story. The protagonist. My heart bled for '818'. You won't forget this number easily. Branded with it since a teenager, he is treated like a ferocious beast in a place comparable with hell. The Gulag. However, he is not sure why he is there, or why his very soul pleads for vengeance. Deception rules, abuse stronger. Will he have his comeuppance? Does this man have an angel, a saviour who is capable of helping him recuperate everything he has lost? You can't help but love this man who doesn't understand the word love. He had a long time ago. All he needs is the right person to show him that it does exist and what it means. 
 Quote: "Those eyes...those eyes were imprinted into my brain, they were soldered onto my soul. My voice was stolen by shock of what I'd just seen." 
 This isn't a lovey dovy read. It is beyond harsh and nothing that I expected from this author. She has managed to make my stomach turn inside out, my nerves jump out of my skin and my hair stand on end. You Ms. Cole, are a phenomenal writer. I haven't awarded your book five stars, which I might add was impeccably written and highly recommendable to those who enjoy dark reads, solely because I am not a lover this kind of genre. I cannot dispute that your penmanship is above excellence. Bravo to you!

I have a problem with this book. I am going to attempt to explain my problem clearly and calmly. My previous attempts at writing a review have all lapsed into inarticulate rage. I will admit that, as I did not finish reading the book, it is possible that Peter V. Brett redeems himself later on. I do not consider this likely. 
 Here is the problem: 
 The sun goes down, and demons overrun the earth. Protection is provided by defensive wards which get drawn on houses, barns, fence posts, etc. If a living creature is outside of these protections when night falls, that creature will be ripped apart and eaten. There is no way to fight the demons. 
 Eleven-year-old Arlen lives in a village with his parents. A messenger from the city shows up, carrying mail and salt. Arlen gets the job of showing this man around, and during the tour the man tells Arlen about a country far away in which young men train to fight and then go out at night in the hope of finding a way to defeat the demons. They all die, but the point is that it is not in man's nature to cower in safety while demons walk the earth. Men want to fight, and when deprived of that opportunity they become weak, depressed, and suicidal. The messenger's argument is supported when, during the tour, they come across a man from a nearby town who has hanged himself to death from a tree limb. 
 So Arlen takes this putrid idea to heart, and starts haranguing his father about how cowardly it is to stay safely inside the wards when there are demons to fight. I think this is very stupid, because if every man took Arlen's advice humans would have died out long ago. At this point, though, I am willing to give the author the benefit of the doubt. Arlen is only eleven, so it would be a bit much for me to expect him to act sensibly for the entire book. Perhaps he will learn the error of his ways. 
 Arlen is living with his mother, father, and a woman who recently lost her family in a demon attack. One afternoon, the sun sets more quickly than they were expecting because some clouds moved in. The adults and Arlen scramble to move the animals to safety. They run back to the porch, and then realize that the dog is still chained to a post in the back yard. Demons are about to start sprouting from the earth, and the dog will suffer a horrible, agonizing death. The guest runs out and unchains the dog, which bolts to the porch. The woman moves more slowly, and as a result gets a chunk ripped out of her leg by one of the first demons to spawn. Seeing this, Arlen's mother runs out into the yard to help the woman back to the house. Demons start attacking the mother, and drag the guest away to be eaten. 
 Arlen looks at his father. He realizes with disgust that his father is too afraid to move, so he jumps off the porch, beans a couple demons over the head with a nearby bucket, and drags his mother to the safety of the pigpen. They hang there till morning, when Arlen's father comes out to help them. Arlen gives his father a cold shoulder, and goes on and on about how cowardly he was, etc, etc. 
 I was filled with disgust, and stopped reading soon after. Why? 
 Because it became obvious that the author agreed with everything Arlen was saying. Not only that, but in his pursuit of setting Arlen up as The One (or whatever), he had to stack the deck in the kid's favor and kill/injure a few women to make the point. 
 Problem one: 
 A preteen farm kid should not have had any more success at fighting/surviving/staging a rescue from demons than two grown women. 
 Problem two: 
 Who demonstrated the most courage during the demon attack: the woman who risked death to save a dog, the mother who risked her life to save a woman who wasn't even part of her family, or the kid who risked his life only when his own mother was in danger? I think the answer is obvious. 
 Who demonstrated the most common sense during the demon attack: the kid who ran out into a yard full of hungry sprites to attempt a rescue that two adults had just failed at, or the father who stayed on the porch instead of running out there and leaving his kid an orphan? Also obvious. 
 Arlen is the loser by both metrics. If the author treated him the same as everyone else, he should have been eaten. And yet he lives so that he might make his father's life miserable. He lives, but not once does he say, Father, why couldn't you have been brave like Mom? 
 After that, I was afraid of what bits of blindness and idiocy the rest of the book might contain.

I think this is a 2.5 star book for me, but I feel like it's a little too harsh to just go for two... So I'll flip flop back and forth until I decide. 
 I know this definitely definitely had the odds stacked against it, seeing as it was read right after I finished a series I absolutely adored. I knew that coming down off that everything else might pale in comparison but... This book has had such raving reviews from reviewers that I admire and have similar tastes too, and it had the making to be a book that I could enjoy. Aussie YA, diverse characters, a bittersweet love story.... 
 I think I just could not connect to the character. It wasn't that she bugged me, in fact, she's a lot more sensible than a whole lot of YA narrators. I guess it was the obsession with the eighties, at first. I mean later it makes a WHOLE lot more sense on account of the whole being another Amy Lee in a past life?  but whenever I read 'modern' characters that are stuck in some decade that doesn't fit, I wonder if perhaps it's just excuse to write the decade in which they grew up/they are interested in. And I mean that's okay! But a modern teenager isn't going to connect with all of these references, and the level of this book meant it certainly wasn't directed at an adult audience. I do know the odd eighties reference. It's very very hard to live in this world and not understand some of them -- like the Princess Bride or the Labyrinth, or the odd music reference -- but many went over my head and, at nineteen, I'm at the older end of the spectrum of intended readers. 
 So perhaps that missing nostalgia left me out of the loop. After having to google the first few, I resorted to the random picture in my head to substitute game, so the references certainly did not have the intended effect. Amy's voice didn't get me in, and so though I could understand the ups and downs of the books emotionally it kinda passed me by. The love was sweet, but I didn't feel it, if that makes sense. 
 I'm not a fan of insta love at all. This one was a little more picky with me because she said she didn't want to fall in love with anyone because of her parents but it felt less like a motivation and more like a point to make the story angst-ier. It's not a bad motivation, I suppose, but it didn't feel like the character really believed that.  
 Also, I could not stand Rebecca. I'm not sure if she was intentionally horrible. It's hard to believe that she was anything but. I know that people like that... kinda exist. In that those are things that people think and ways that people might act, but I think just leaving the character as that and nothing more was not good at all. I'm not sure if we were supposed to like her? Nancy was much more bearable -- in fact I liked her quite a bit once you saw there was more to the character than the stereotype that Amy saw her as. I have no idea why Amy was so rude to her 99% of the time???  
 Also why was the Michael side story a thing? He was really cute, don't get me wrong, but it took away the sting of losing Logan and also the legitimacy of Amy feeling unnoticed by the guys.  
 My one last complaint with the book is of something I also liked the idea of. Just not the execution. I liked that past lives and Chinese mythology was brought into this. I liked that that made it a more complex tale. I really liked the use of the birthmark story, a way to mark children that died young so you could recognise them in the next world. My one complaint lies in the way this reincarnation happened. I mean perhaps it is an issue of belief systems, but I understand it to be that reincarnation means you are a new person but with connections to your past lives and connections. So it makes no sense to me that one of these girls is IDENTICAL to her past self and the other has the exact same name?? At least with Logan we know he was a ghost so he was frozen in his past form, for lack of a better way to explain it. How does this work? If they are identical to their past selves, and they only died twenty four years ago and apparently in the same town, how did no one else notice until now?

2.5*-3* The best I can say about this book is it would've made a great short story. But unfortunately, as a longer work it was unfocused and repetitive. Many romance novels have no real plot other than getting the two leads together for an HEA, and that sometimes works. But this book tried to have several plots, and none of them seemed to have much purpose other than to lengthen the book. The plot lines did little to increase the reader's understanding of the main characters' motives and actions, or to move the main story (ie, the romance) along. There was some good material in the book, especially the unfolding of David's background, but it was lost in the pages of unnecessary drama. 
 Another problem for me was Sophie's yo-yo personality. I've never read another character that could change emotions and personalities so many times in one scene. She was a vamp, a shy innocent, mad as a wet hen, and afraid, all in the space of about two pages, or less. I found the conversations between David and Sophie to be repetitive and often confusing. 
 This book needed some focus and a good editor. The good stuff is there, it just needs to be cleaned up.

I have to admit that I'm really not sure how I feel about this book. 
 I generally found the concept of gods being brought to America by the belief of immigrants and fading away because there isn't much belief in them anymore to be interesting. The new gods were conceptually interesting, but I feel like Gaiman didn't really show enough of them. I honestly don't have much of an idea of what they're like, and that disappoints me. I did find the old gods to be handled well, and I'm quite happy that the Norse pantheon was quite prominent. 
 Shadow was...well, he was a more or less well written character. But I didn't find him particularly compelling or interesting. I often felt like he just did whatever he was told because he was told to do it. I know that is meant to be the case, but whereas some characters that are like that work for me, I didn't see enough evidence of why Shadow was like this for me to really find him relatable. 
 The other characters were good, and I'm very disappointed that Sam only appeared briefly. I'd really like to read more about her. 
 The plot was the real reason I'm not sure how I feel about this book. The first part is fun, though towards the end of it I started to feel like I wasn't getting enough of the roadtrip with Odin that the back cover seemed to promise. The second part was competently written, and I enjoyed the portrait of a small town. All the characters seem like real people and Lakeside very much felt like a real place. However, it felt like I'd veered off into a completely different book. Not a bad book exactly, but not the one I thought I was reading. The third part got back on track and was generally pretty good. If the whole book was like it, I'd have enjoyed this a whole lot more. The fourth part wraps up some plot points and did help to make the second part feel like it mattered, though it still feels like it was a second novel awkwardly stuck in as a subplot to the main god war arc. 
 Overall, I enjoyed this enough to read the whole thing, and it definitely was fairly well written. The last third or so of the novel does a fair bit to make up for my mixed feelings about the middle, but it isn't enough for me to love this book as much as the other stuff by Gaiman that I've read. Hopefully Anansi Boys will be more unambigiously enjoyable. 
 (Though I've given this a three star rating, it's really more like three and a half stars - more than totally average, but not enough for me to be really fond of it.)

 I had a little peruse of some of the reviews of this book on Goodreads and I was surprised to find that opinions of this book was quite polarised. I went into it not expecting to like it much, as I don't tend to rate young adult contemporaries higher than three stars, but I was pleasantly surprised. 
 Flora is our main character who suffers from amnesia and cannot form new memories. Flora is seventeen but all of her memories are from when she was ten and younger. I really warmed to Flora, I thought she was adorable. Due to her memory problems she has to write herself loads of notes using paper or her arms just to remind herself of what has happened and what she needs to remember, she reminded me a lot of Dory from Finding Nemo and I just loved her. 
 A lot of the criticisms of this book centre around the repetitiveness of Flora's narrative, lots of things are repeated many times but this didn't annoy me at all. In fact, I found it fascinating to be in the head of the amnesiac, and I know that repetition is a tool everybody uses to help them remember something. In Flora's case she forms a memory of kissing her best friend's boyfriend and she repeats this many, many times. The excitement of actually having a new memory leads Flora on a crazy adventure, which was so funny and entertaining. 
 There were a lot of layers to this story as well, it's not just boy meets girl, girl needs to find boy, the end. There were twists and turns a plenty. I really loved the ending as well, I hoped Flora did go on to recover fully from her amnesia but it was open to interpretation which I felt worked really well. 
 In summary, I would advise to just try this book for yourself if it sounds interesting to you and form your own opinion. I'm glad I picked it up and I thoroughly enjoyed it.

A cute read!

It's clear to everyone--from Viv's hormones to her BFFs to the little old lady who uses Viv's mom's bookstore as a weekly escape from the retirement home--that she's making some TSTL moves (and LOL, she even uses the phrase "TSTL" to describe herself at one point! At least she's self aware to an extent), but at the same time it's easy to see where she's coming from. Who wasn't been tempted to go a little overboard to protect yourself after being hurt? 
 Once she does manage to get her head out of her...posterior region she does a stellar job of making up for her earlier behavior. Her "grand gesture" is viral-video worthy, and inspired by The Wedding Singer. 
 So you know it's quality. ;) 
 I loved that she is a romance book blogger--reading her reviews at the beginning of a few of the chapters was so much fun! The Star Trek quotes were a nice touch, too--the one from The Wrath of Kahn actually made me a little weepy. Dallas is a worthy hero--for all of his stellar book boyfriend qualities, he too made a few bonehead moves (Kylie) but also made up for them, as a good romance hero does. 
 Overall, a fun read. Go, Vulcans!
