The rating on this is one I debated on a lot. I really genuinely enjoyed this from start to finish and it was exactly what I needed at the moment. It also had a number of flaws that I took note of and I wasn't so enthralled that I didn't notice them. 
 The good: It was fun. It was funny. It was charming. I loved the connections to Alice in Wonderland. I like Gena Showalter as a writer overall. Even though the characters weren't all as well written as they could have been, it never detracted from my enjoyment of any of them. It was an interesting twist on zombie stories. It had sad moments that did have me genuinely sad. Overall it was just a really fun and enjoyable read that I got sucked into and just what I needed. 
 The bad: I wished there was MORE connection to Alice in Wonderland. I expected some sort of other world and while I did like the more subtle connections, it was just a bit underwhelming. Knowing that Showalter has become more religious made me feel like the characters were occasional a mouthpiece for her in that regard. Lots and lots of cliches on all fronts. Teen fiction cliches, zombie cliches, romance cliches. They didn't pull me out of my enjoyment but I definitely wished they hadn't been so obvious. 
 I enjoyed this more than a typical three star read for me. But I didn't feel like I could give it a full four when the problems were ones that I felt were so noticeable. I would rate it higher for pure enjoyment and about the same -ish, maybe slightly lower if just going for the flaws. Ultimately I'd recommend it to my friends who are fans of the particular brand of YA that Gena Showalter has to offer. Others might find the flaws too much but I know that fans of this kind of novel will enjoy it for what it is.

I really liked this one. It captured my attention from the beginning. I only had a couple of problems and it's that I wish we would've learned more about Jason and Derick, that the story was a little longer. I think the story behind Derick's injury could've been just a little deeper. Those are the only problems I had. 
  
 Derick and Jason are both characters that I loved. I liked that they both had their struggles and that Jason wasn't the stereotypical bad boy star athlete that we always see. I loved how much of a smartass Derick was, and how real Jason was. I really do wish we could've learned more about him and his dad though, especially about how his mother died. I also liked that Jason didn't go through a drawn out thing of being in denial. He just took it in stride. I nearly lost my mind laughing at his jealousy and how he ruined Derick's hookup. 
 I loved that everything didn't go perfect, like Derick starting, the two of them arguing over making their relationship public, and Jason's ACL tearing. I am going to admit that as an athlete, the first thing I did was cringe when Jason said he felt something tear. I automatically thought about his ACL, because that's a serious nightmare for an athlete. I also liked that he didn't have a miracle recovery that put him back in the season, because though it's not impossible it's unlikely. So all in all, I liked this story very much and can't wait to read more from Hendricks.

Not too long ago, it appeared that Stephen King was finished with writing. Following a harrowing traffic accident, he seemed ready to hang up his hat. Then, rather suddenly, he began to write new books, and thank goodness for that, because two of the best novels he's ever written, Duma Key and this one, have come out since that time. 
 I won't go into the plot and what I specifically liked about the storyline; plenty of other reviewers have done that. Instead, I'll leave you with this: you simply must read this book. Yes, it's more than 800 pages long. Yes, it's about a traumatic event that changed the nation forever. But it's worth it, oh so worth it, and if you don't pick it up and delve into its engrossing pages, you'll be missing out on one hell of a ride.

I want to start by saying SEP is one of my favorite authors. Specifically, one of my favorite romance authors. 
 That said, once upon a time I would have given this book five stars. It's just that I've read almost all of her books and they're starting to all feel the same. The reason I love SEP is because I laugh continually at the witty banter between the characters. I like that her heroines have a wide variety of interests, but it would be nice if the tables were turned and the guy wasn't mega successful all the time. Where are the average joe guys to go along with the average joe women? 
 The way they get married at the end reminds me way too much of the ending of Ain't She Sweet?--and while Ain't She Sweet? is my favorite SEP book, I don't want to see all its elements repeated. I want it to be different. The first time they sleep together (sorta) reminds me of a similar plot element in Natural Born Charmer. 
 Also, Cooper pissed me off royally. The whole "macho" man thing is overplayed and overdone. If he did half those things in real life a woman would be kicking and screaming with rage, and is, in my opinion, way worse than her screwup. 
 Also, why do so many of her heroines exercise extremely poor judgment, while the men typically don't do that? And the girls are always a bit wacky and do cringe-worthy things. Again, the men don't do that. Why? 
 Aside from these things, though, I loved the part where they go on their little road trip with their friend and thought that mini subplot was refreshing and different. I loved Jada and Cara's stories. The NERF fight was inventive and fun. SEP books hold the promise of laughter, and of course this one delivered as well as all the rest. SEP is the master of banter and of subplots, always enjoyable. 
 And for these promises being upheld, I offer it a solid three stars. I just hope she changes things up a bit for future storytelling.

An exceptional book by an exceptional doctor and human being. It is hard to explain how deeply this affected me, but after losing too many friends to cancer over the years, I continue to search for answers and understanding of their experiences, knowing they are terminal, and deciding how to spend the time they have left. Paul Kalanithi spent his remaining days continuing to be a neurosurgeon until his body was no longer able, writing this remarkable memoir, being a loving husband to his wife Lucy, and a devoted father to their daughter Cady. And up until the end, he continued to think and examine the meaning of life in a way most of us never do. Remarkable and moving; this one will stay with me for a long time.

I picked up this audiobook after reading Gayle Forman's Leave Me which was aimed at adults, not teens, but this is her most popular book, so I thought it was worth a shot. That, and it was short and I am near the top of the waitlist for several other books. Why not, I thought. And now I think "Why"? I know that this is not the general consensus on this book. People love it. People whose opinions I respect. But uuuugh, the whole thing, just blarg. 
 Where to start with what I don't like about it: 
 1. I don't like books about teen suicide. It's not that I don't think it is a valid topic for books, but I'm a mom, I don't want to read about kids making that choice. I read for enjoyment, and to think about new things, but that is not enjoyable for me. And while Mia's choice isn't exactly suicide (if she stays or if she goes), but it isn't exactly not either when you give her agency in this choice. I disliked this book, but not with the venom of hatred I have for Thirteen Reasons Why which is one of my least favorite books of all time. 
 2. I didn't really understand the paranormal elements in the book as there is no setting of the rules of the universe. Mia is wandering the hospital as a spirit, apart from her body, but she can't walk through walls. But she can open doors, at least the first 6 hours or so. What, a door suddenly opens with no-one opening it and that's not noticed by the dozens of nurses? And no-one else is in the state that she can see? Why not? She's in the freaking ICU? And then her energy level drops remarkably, but no explanation as to why. Listen, I'm a sci-fi fiend. I've read all sorts of altered realities. But the universe needs to have some rules and some explanation, or you're just making sparkling vampires. Please, no more sparkling vampires. 
 3. Oprah book club levels of unnecessary awfulness for our protagonist. What is the hallmark of an Oprah book? When given the chance to throw your poor lady protagonist a bone, the author stabs her a couple more times first. Spoilers  Case in point - The Light Between the Oceans, the timing of Lucy's reunion with her dad. Case in point for this book - Teddy's storyline. Seriously overkill. What the hell?!?!? Isn't it bad enough that both her parents die horrific deaths, but her little brother too? I just kept waiting for the hospital elevator to crash and kill her boyfriend, best friend, and grandparents all for good measure.  
 4. Mia. I'm not a teen girl. I'm not the target audience. But I've read more than my fair share of YA fiction, and Mia is annoying. She's too perfect, has a too perfect boyfriend, is a cello prodigy, and has really no reason other than sadness to even contemplate "leaving" but she does. For the entire book. Barf. 
 ok, I've said enough. Other people obviously found something that they liked about this book. I tried hard. Here's the best part - it is quite short. I don't think I could have powered through if this narcissistic navel-gazing had gone on for much longer. I think the author is talented. I just really didn't like the premise, the central dilemma, the characters, and pretty much everything.

It's a really unique story complete with a kingdom at war with another country, strange people that live in nature, and a religious prophecy centuries old. The female protagonist is not the stereotypical princess but has her own strength. She appears weak in the beginning but as the story progresses she becomes braver and stronger. Her character is well developed and likable in terms of the strong, intelligent female roles people like to see and encourage nowadays. She's unconventional, and that is what I like about her. 
 There are many surprises in the story, the biggest shock caught me completely off guard. It's not something most people would expect because it isn't something that usually happens in this genre. I give Carson props for writing it, cause I certainly wasn't happy about it. I cried a lot actually. 
 Anywho, it is a great debut novel for Carson and a wonderful beginning to what I know is going to be a successful career and a wonderful series.

The Torrance family moves to the Overlook Hotel in order for the recovering alcoholic patriarch, Jack, to start his new job as caretaker. But bringing his family with him proves to be a huge mistake for Jack, since his psychic son seems to bring out the worst in the old hotel. 
 Nicely plotted and well developed with realistic and believable, somewhat heart breakable (Jack in this instance) characters and plausible actions and reactions, this books flows more along the lines of psychological thriller than straightforward horror. 
 The suspense builds up so slowly that the true horror and evil creeps up suddenly and (almost) unexpectedly, although it also has its silly moments that break the flow of the story and the slow, inexorable progress of the creeping evil. 
 What also breaks the stride of the story is the length. It felt overblown, overdrawn, and was slowly getting very boring indeed. Fact is, it took me ages to finish. But maybe it was just me having an adverse reaction to King's narrative style.

 "Who said I had a girlfriend?" he said, raising his scarred eyebrow. His dark eyes crinkled. 
 "No one," she said. 
 "Well, I don't anymore, if anyone's interested." 
 "Who's interested?" 
 "Are you?" He looked her straight in the eye. 
 "I could ask the same for you," she scoffed. 
 "So what if I was? Interested, I mean." He shrugged. 
 "It wouldn't be a surprise," she said. "I'm sure half the crew has a crush on me." She rolled her eyes. She wasn't sure what she was doing, but it was fun to rile him up a little. So he was interested, was he? About time he admitted it. 
 "Only half?"

This is volume 7 of an ongoing series. It's not the place to start. There is no question that any person of good taste should be reading Saga, but you should start at the beginning with volume 1. 
 I suppose that because the last volume made me very happy, this one was going to make me sad. Damn you, Vaughn and Staples and the emotional roller coaster you send me on. Temporarily stranded on Phang, a tiny comet that Wreath and Landfall have been battling it out over (like they battle for everything else), Elena, Marko and their little family are trying to find enough fuel to get away from their pursuers, they just need to to find some fuel. 
 Their brief stay extends to more than six months, and Hazel and her parents and their strange extended family make new friends and form new bonds. We meet The Will, Gwendolyn and Sophie again, and I'm happy to report that Lying Cat has a much more prominent presence in this volume than in the last. Gwendolyn is getting more actively involved in politics, and Sophie is faced with a difficult choice. As the tension on Phang escalates, our little band of refugees have to fight for their existence once more, and sadly, their interlude on Phang does not come without casualties. 
 I'm always excited when there's a new volume of Saga, the wait in between is always so very long. Due to a massive work load, I didn't actually get the chance to read this immediately after its release, having it lying on a shelf taunting me for a few weeks. Had I known about some of the developments, I may not have read it during my most recent Readathon, as it was really quite an emotional read, which I've already mentioned affected me. Still, it's not the first time this comic has made me cry, and I'm sure it won't be the last. I just hope the next volume is a little bit more upbeat again.

Then she is sent to court to do Mortrain's will. Basically to save and serve the Duchess Anne, the true heir of Brittany from being taken by France.

However, with just ONE WORD from Ismae, they both do what she says and they are completely obedient. The Fool intrigues me especially; it as if the more I know about him, the more I need to know. His answers only raise more questions. I think Hobb came up with a wonderful way for us to keep track of other beloved characters throughout the book, and I never felt I was missing out on anything. 
 This is a great book and I enjoyed the whole trilogy a great deal. It took me a long time to read The Farseer Trilogy, but I'm glad that I did, and I'm excited that there are more books set in this world for me to discover.

 Let's say it straight: This book has been a huge disappointment to me. Not that it's bad, but I think it hasn't been well advertized: it's more erotica than fantasy, and I am a fantasy reader, not an erotica reader. 
 Upon the king of Akielos' death, his son Damen was supposed to replace him as the king, but his half-brother Kastor gets on the throne instead of him and then send him to the enemy kingdom, Vere, to serve as a slave for prince Laurent. I didn't know that by "slave", the author actually meant "pleasure slave". Had I known that, I would have started the book with different expectations, and maybe I wouldn't have appreciated it any more, but at least I wouldn't have come back to earth with a bump. 
 I was expecting a fantasy novel about two enemy princes having to side together, with political plots and rivalries in the background. Well, there's a bit of this, I can't deny. But it definitely wasn't deep enough for my taste. This fantasy background, the plots and rivalries between the kingdoms, that's what interested me the most, and they are the only reason why I kept on reading the book. Yet the author doesn't go much in-depth about this part of her story. For instance, we know that Akielos and Vere are enemies, but we don't know why exactly. And the cultural differences between both kingdoms, that we can guess are many, are only evoked through Damen's memories, but never developed. 
 All in all, it seemed that all the fantasy background was there only to justify the erotica part, and that's what annoyed me the most. It really annoys me when authors don't want to openly say that they write erotica and try to hide this by selling their book as fantasy/thriller/anything. There is nothing wrong with writing/reading erotica, so please don't hide and label erotica books as such, so that you will only target a better audience. Because clearly, I wasn't the right reader for this book. Detailed sex scenes make me uncomfortable, and the Vere's culture, with all its debauchery and orgies... it really made me ill-at-ease. Well, before you start making wrong assumptions: I didn't feel this way because all sexual intercourses depicted were homosexual. I would have felt the same if they were heterosexual. It was just the general atmosphere, with the constant sexual tension... And also the fact that rape and pedophilia seemed so common and normal in this society. 
 I didn't care much about the characters either. Laurent probably was the most interesting one as you can feel he has more than one layer, but I wish the author had dug a bit deeper into his background and his personality. To me he mostly appeared as cold, selfish and manipulative, and the moments when you sense there is another person beyond the mask were too few to make me change my mind about him. As for Damen, well, we see the whole story through his eyes but I don't feel like I know him in the end... Oh, and don't expect any romance between these two. There isn't. 
 In short, Captive Prince was a book with an interesting premise but it turned out that I wasn't the targeted audience at all. Perhaps erotica fans would enjoy it, but to me the atmosphere was too crude and quite sickening, and the fantasy plot too minor for me to find it interesting enough. 
 I recommend this book to you if: Fantasy fans, go your way, and let this books to erotica readers.

A lot of these early reviews coming in for this book have reported that this book has no love triangle. I decided to include this in mine anyway, because it feels so important to note. This is a fabulous book about a seriously realistic college experience. All too often, I feel like these NA books portray college life that would never really happen. I highly recommend checking this book out! 
 Before I get into more about how great the characters and the plot are, I want to reveal more about the romance. I know that some people want to be aware exactly what the romance is, and this synopsis hints at having some sort of secret that the MC keeps from the love interest. So I'm going to spoil that specific part so you guys who might be suspicious of love triangles can know exactly about this and then decide whether or not this is something you want to read. 
 Nora has sex with Kellan in a closet at a party. She's shocked when she finds out that the boy she's been emailing who is looking for a responsible roommate is really Kellan, a total partier and womanizer. Kellan doesn't remember having sex with her, but she remembers right away. This is the big secret she keeps from Crosbie as they become friends and then begin a relationship. So we know that he is eventually going to find out, but it's before they even met, so it's really not that big of a deal. Naturally, there's some drama because of this, but it's mainly just the instant hurt that he feels.  
 Nora is a fabulous and relatable protagonist. In high school, Nora was under the radar and was what some may consider to be boring. Once she gets to college, she starts to get caught up in going to frat parties with her friend Marcela. After getting arrested, she decides that she needs to get her grades and act together so she can still attend school. She enjoys her identity around Kellan and Crosbie, they view her as being a nerd, and don't know about her partying past. She's just an honest and real character to me. One of my favorite things about her is that she doesn't know what she wants to do with the rest of her life. Her major is still undecided, hence the title. I like how the author shows that it's totally acceptable to not know what you want to do after college. I know there are other NA stories out there with this similar storyline, but I always find it refreshing to see. 
 You guys, Crosbie is the book boyfriend I've been waiting for. Yes, he's in a fraternity and he has a reputation of hooking up and partying, but there's so much more to him than just that. This book has no insta-love. I will say there is some instant attraction going on, but there's still a strong buildup to the relationship. Crosbie is a track star so he clearly has a nice body, which Nora tries and fails not to notice. One thing that is different about this incredible boy is that he likes performing magic tricks. Excuse me, he actually calls them illusions. This is a small detail, but I think it shows that he's more than just an athlete or a frat boy. He's never been in a real relationship before, but let me tell you, some of the things he says to Nora and the gifts he gives her will pretty much make you melt. 
 Honestly, there's so much to like about this book. I've never read anything else by Julianna Keyes, but I did read that this is her first NA book. If I didn't know that, I would have thought that she's been writing these stories for quite a long time. She just knows so much about college life. I feel like each character was well developed, even the supporting ones. It's hard not to love Kellan, even though he's a complete manwhore. I can't wait for Keyes to give him a little happily ever after of his own. I also want Marchela and Nate to get a book of their own. Anyway, you guys need to look out for this one when it releases April 4th!

 However, good story-telling is what it is and Maggie shines as one to hold up as an example and say, "Now this is how you show a story." 
 Never have cared much for the term "story-telling", when the really good ones aren't told at all. 
 Maggie drags the reader into her world, into her characters, makes you wish you knew them. Or maybe makes you recognize yourself in them. Or crave to be them. Or feel jealous of what you lack. She makes you believe in love again. 
 We all need to remember that sometimes. Even, or most especially, as adults. 
 This isn't a "young adult" book. It's a beautiful story that just happens to have teenagers as its leads. 
 A bit like Romeo and Juliette.

I gave it a 5, but I really wish we could give half stars. This book came out of nowhere for me, but I really liked it. It wasn't perfect by any means, but I'd definitely give it a 4.5. There are several typos, but if you can get through them, you're good to go. In fact, it's one of those books that I couldn't put down until I knew I had to go to bed or I wouldn't be able to function the next day. 
 Plot: 
 Ember thinks she's having hallucinations. To make matters worse, every time she loses her temper, something explodes ... in this case the gym during the school dance. Because of this incident, the local sheriff and the principal decide it would be best to send her to a school for troubled teens. There, she meets Eli, who - for no reason - appears to hate her. The director of the facility forces them to work very closely on a special project, and even though they have a love-hate relationship, they can't deny their strong attraction and their connection to each other. She wants to trust Eli, but his hot-cold attitude makes it hard. She becomes even more confused after Torin, who professes to love her, starts appearing to her in visions and dreams and warning her that something is coming to get her. 
 Characters: 
 Ember is your typical loner/outcast heroine with an undiscovered special ability and a hidden past. Eli is the tattooed bad boy who is so secretive, you don't know whether to trust him or not. When the two do speak, there is a LOT of sexual innuendo, and some of the comments are downright hilarious. Normally, I don't like it when a heroine uses her snarky remarks to mask her vulnerability, but these two cracked me up. It did irritate me a little that she kept referring to herself as being stupid for liking or trusting Eli, and yet she would continually seek him out. As readers, we already know it's stupid to go for the bad boy, but hey ... that's part of the fun! 
 Ember's mother was murdered (and Ember discovered the body), so she has lived with her stepfather Mark since she was young. It's an interesting relationship because he cares a lot about her, but he begins to worry about her sanity, too. She tends to try and hide her visions from Mark and her two friends, Ryan and Kennedy, who were the only people to approach her when she started attending the same school as them. As friends, they were likable enough. Ryan is a boy crazy gay high schooler, and Kennedy is not only sheltered, but sometimes voices some really odd thoughts. Eli's main companion for the majority of the book is Sam, another of the directors at the school. Although Sam is beautiful and appears friendly to most of the people around her, she immediately begins to hate Ember, which makes us immediately hate her. 
 There are several more characters, but the only two who really appear frequently enough to make an impact are Torin and Lorcan. Torin frequently tells Ember that she is his heart and that she and he were meant to be together. She finds him amazingly attractive (in a different way than Eli), and because he tries to protect her from the evil coming her way, she feels like he may be the only person she can trust. She feels the complete opposite about Lorcan, who is Eli's creepy and sinister brother. Of course, he makes it pretty clear that she shouldn't trust him or Eli and tells her that he will be watching her. 
 Writing: 
 There were a several grammatical errors, but the story was compelling enough to help me push through. Brown makes us feel everything that Ember feels, and that is a lot considering how much Eli draws Ember to him and then pushes her away. 
 The Bottom Line: 
 Darkness of Light reminded me a lot of Obsidian, which I loved. The sexual tension was unbearable ... in a good way. Be prepared, there is a HUGE cliffhanger, so you might want to have Book 2 (Fire in the Darkness) on standby, so you can jump right to it.

This has got to be one of the most powerful books I have ever read. 
 The main story is about Kevin - a disgruntled teenager who carries out a massacre at his high school and is subsequently jailed. However, the themes of the book run a lot deeper than a simple "shoot 'em up" story. The book is written from the point of view of Kevin's mother, Eva, in a series of letters to her husband Franklin, which examine their life together, their parenting skills, and the ups and downs of family life. The storyline actually starts before Kevin is born and follows through to the current day, with interlinked references to current events from the early years of the 21st century. 
 The book is slow to pick up, and the language is a little difficult to get into, but the final third of the book is totally unputdownable and the reader gets caught up in the letters, the unfolding story and the climax of the shooting itself. Some of the "surprises" were a little transparent, but despite this the ending is very powerful, and is one of the few books I had a physcical reaction to as well as an emotional reaction to. 
 When finished, it is also worth reviewing the book from the point of view of Kevin. The book is solely written from Eva's point of view, and it is easy to see how there may be an alternate, equally valid, point of view for the unfolding events. 
 I can't recommend this book highly enough. If Lionel Shriver continues to write novels like this, she will have a very successful career in front of her.

I read this about a year ago, but yesterday I had the chance to see it being performed live at the Fringe festival in Edinburgh by the very young company Cambridge Shortlegs, so I decided I should write a few words about it. 
 For me to rate an Atwood's book with only three stars is an extremely rare occasion. It's not that it's not good, or that it doesn't fulfil its retelling purposes. It clearly grants a voice to those who weren't given one in the original myth. But the way it does so is so in your face that it lacks Atwood's natural charm for subtle criticism. Although, her dark humour is there alright. It's the text's saving grace and what makes it undoubtedly Atwoodian. 
 The performance was incredibly good, I'd say. The scene when the maids are raped  was very impressive and visual. Cambridge Shortlegs clearly does not shy away from the hard scenes. It was refreshing. I think I'd rather recommend seeing The Penelopiad being performed rather than reading it. It just gains a new dimension that certainly favours the directness and sarcasm present in the text.

 Alright first I have to say that I absolutely loved this book! I have been in such a slump lately, and this book pulled me right out! Wicked Heart by Leisa Rayven has left me with a huge book hangover, and the second I finished reading it I wanted to start all over and do it again! Wicked Heart is the third book in Leisa's Starcrossed series, but this book can be read as a standalone. The first two books are about Ethan and Cassie and while I loved them and they are on the top of my favorites list, Liam and Elissa actually topped them for me! I never thought that would be possible, but Leisa proved me wrong and her writing just gets better and better! 
 Elissa Holt has only ever loved one man, and he broke her heart. Six years later, Liam Quinn is Hollywood's hottest star and has just been cast in the show she is managing. Not only is Elissa forced to see Liam again, but his gorgeous fiance is set to star in the show as well. Though both of them try to keep their distance, late night rehearsals have Elissa and Liam remembering everything they once shared and making it more apparent than ever that their feelings have never gone away. But with Liam engaged to someone else and Elissa scared of getting hurt again, they find themselves torn between what they have and what they have always wanted. Can they find a way back to one another, or is will their story end in tragedy? 
 I loved these two so much. I have to admit there were times that I was extremely frustrated with Liam here. I really thought that if he would have just talked to Elissa, so much heartbreak could have been avoided. I hated that these two had to go through so much hurt and it made me sad to think about all the time that they lost because of everything that happened. Yet as frustrated as I was, I really understood why Liam did the things he did. He really thought that he needed to do them and I admired his reasons even while I didn't like them. Elissa was amazing! She is the type of heroine that you read romance novels for. Strong and sassy, and so easy to like. She was funny and witty, and I loved that what you saw with her was what you got. Honestly she was so genuine and sweet that she is the type of girl you would love to have as your best friend. Not only that, but she was gorgeous and real, and I loved that she was described as curvy. She struggled with believing that she was beautiful at times, especially when faced with Angel, but I was so glad that she had those in her life that reminded her that she was. Liam and Elissa had a ton of chemistry and I honestly couldn't get enough of them. The attraction and connection was there from their very first meeting and these two understood each other in a way that no one else did. 
 Overall, I loved everything about this book. It was stunning and I was captivated from the very first page. Leisa Rayven is a truly talented writer and she has a way with words that is impossible to describe, but just needs to be experienced. I really didn't think it would be possible to love anyone more than Ethan and Cassie, but Liam and Elissa are absolutely my favorites! I have to say that I really loved the secondary characters here as well. Elissa's friend Josh and Liam's fiance Angel were just as amazing as Liam and Elissa. While it would have been so easy to hate Angel (and I will admit I kind of wanted to!), it was impossible! She was fantastic and I loved her. I really can't say enough positive things about this book, but this is a must read to me and I highly recommend it! If you are read the previous two books in this series, I think that you will love this one even though you don't get a ton of Ethan and Cassie here. But if you haven't read those yet, this is the perfect place to start and I think readers are going to love this book as much as I did! I can't wait to see what Leisa Rayven writes next!

I'm glad I did because I really enjoyed this story so much it kept me thinking beyond the end. I find it has the same flaws as TCV in that it's overwritten and locaquious to a fault.  The story revolves around private detective Cormoran Strike. Strike was in the military until he lost part of his leg in an explosion and returned to England to be a private detective. He's just broken up with his rich but volatile girlfriend so he's living in his small, cramped office. A temporary secretary, Robin, shows up for work and he reluctantly keeps her on even though he can't afford her. Strike surprisingly gets a wealthy client, John Bristow, who wants Strike to prove that his model sister's death was murder and not suicide. The high profile case involves a number of potential suspects and participants and Strike's methodical investigation actually manages to find the truth. 
 I liked the book but it took a bit to hook me. There plot is a serviceable mystery with a beautiful, rich model (also with a volatile boyfriend) who dies on a snowy night. Three months later her adopted brother wants to know the truth. There are numerous suspects and Strike slowly and methodically interviews each one, reconstructing the events of that night and the days preceding. The book is extremely, extremely detail orientated. It slowly and thoroughly introduces each character with considerable background. The events seem to happen in slow motion and in that way there is not much action. It's what I would think of as a realistic mystery for the most part as there are no real heroics until the end. 
 While the plot eventually hooked me so much that I didn't want to put it down, I can see where others may have more trouble than I did. The writing is bloated and often awkward. The descriptions lack the clarity and clean prose of her children's books but instead are convoluted. They try too hard and leave weird images instead of easy to understand visual descriptions. I think the writing is better than the first book and I hope it continues to get better and more streamlined as the books go on. What hooked me the most was the depth of characterization. There are numerous characters, probably too many, but I liked them and the level of depth was impressive. Strike is a bit of a know-it-all in figuring things out but that's to be expected from a detective novel. 
 The mystery itself was pretty good. It had enough potential suspects that I honestly didn't see the end coming, which is unusual for me. I didn't really like the ending as it felt too easy and neat with Strike figuring everything out too easily. However it works and fits with the story itself. I'm interested to see what new cases Strike and Robin take on.

It was like a normal book- nothing amazing about it. Then, I was whisked off to a mysterious and frightening place called 'The Glade.There came so many mysteries and questions that you just wanted to know all the answers.The Glade was confusing, but Dashner didn't leave you hanging on too many questions just so that you would keep reading.I loved learning about the new world and everyday Thomas would get further in finding out more about the mysterious place. I was hooked by the book because I think there were so many concepts and ideas that you became fascinated. After a while, it kind of got repetitive- he would wake up and do the usual stuff until Teresa came along.I loved the idea of telepathically communicating. This was when the book was actually starting to get its plot. 
 I felt as If I were Thomas.I had so many theories about the maze and being a runner. At one point, when Thomas was trapped in the maze, I thought it was the end for Thomas but it wasn't. I was quite annoyed by The Changing. Nobody told Thomas about it and no-one ever talked about it either. It kept bugging me because I really didn't understand it. Then he solved it all. Finally, I know a lot about The Maze.I loved the idea of the Grievers and The maze, but the Changing still haunts me! :) I loved the mystery. Teresa, The maze, the code, the escape, their purpose all seemed so real. I think It was an amazing book and the characters were all so different and unique. 
 My favourite character was Chuck. Alby was just a bit annoying to be honest, I mean really? He didn't believe Thomas. Milo was a great character along with Newt who I thought was just a really good-natured person.The thing is I hate Gally. I know it wasn't entirely his fault, but that doesn't change the fact that he was so rude and I just didn't like his character. I loved the ending, but Chuck dies.It felt so sad when Chuck dived in to save Thomas and I just wished it never happened. 
 Altogether the book was just so good! The new world had so many features I really recommend this book and it received 5 stars on my Goodreads. An adventure-packed book full of many twists and turns along the way. I can't wait to read the next book! The Maze Runner was fantastic and I hope Scorch Trials will be even better!

This was so, so not a Julie book. I knew going in that zombies weren't my favorite subject matter, but I am a unicorn fan, and most of the stories were written by authors I'd read before and in some cases, have a great respect for. 
 So imagine my surprise when the anthology featured: one zombie story that was so gross that I couldn't even read the rest of it; a rambling unicorn story involving bestiality; a story about a thinly-veiled actress and her tribe of (drooling, undead) adopted children; and a story about a suicidal serial-killing unicorn. Seriously. Unicorn. Serial. Killer. 
 There were a couple of stories I didn't mind, like Carrie Ryan's "Bougainvillea" (ironic since I really, really did not like her zombie book, The Forest of Hands and Teeth). I also didn't mind Cassandra Clare's "Cold Hands." 
 Diana Peterfreund's story made a lot more sense being that I'd read Rampant, and I probably enjoyed it more than someone who hadn't read the other book first. (That reminds me: I have to read Ascendant!) 
 I was sad to find that Scott Westerfeld's "Inoculata" was no more than a giant "MEH" for me... he is one of my favorite authors! 
 The one story I really, truly enjoyed was "Princess Prettypants" by Meg Cabot, which made me laugh out loud repeatedly. I guess that one was just more my speed, instead of the dark, dark, darrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrk stories in the rest of the book. 
 I'm sure there are plenty of people out there who will love it (or already do), but it wasn't my cup of tea.

My heart broke for him. He is only 8. He shouldn't have had to live in such fear. 
 I loved seeing his character grow. He becomes more and more brave. With the help of some friends of course. He meets little Elysabeth Victoria Mortimer, who is a granddaughter of a duke that is serving the king. I can't get over the spelling of her name. It's gorgeous! I wasn't really sure about her at first. She seemed to just be one of those annoying little characters that wasn't going to have a lot to do with the story. Boy, did my mind change quickly! She helped Owen discover his voice and helped him to be brave. I adored this little girl. Her nickname that Owen gives her is adorable. Evie. Isn't that just the cutest?? I hope I get to learn more about her in the next book. 
 My favorite character had to be Ankarette Twynneowe. Don't even ask me how to pronounce that. She is the queen's poisoner. She helps Owen and attempts to save his life along with his family's life. I can't even begin to describe what an incredible character she was. She was motherly and intelligent. She helped Owen but also didn't coddle him. He had been coddled most of his life so it was refreshing to see him grow under her care. She knew that her job was dangerous and it required killing people but she had no qualms about it. She knew what she had to do. It was refreshing to see her be honest with Owen as well. She did not hide things from him because he was a child. 
 My favorite concept of this book was the Fountain. In this world, those that had special gifts such as seeing into the future or persuasion, they were considered Fountain blessed. Often times, people found out that they were blessed if they were thrown off the cliff and survived. The Fountain is like their God. They praise the Fountain. Those that are blessed are looked upon with the greatest amount of respect. I thought this was such a cool thing. I don't know how original it is, but it's original to me. This and Ankarette is what really pushed the book to 5 stars for me. 
 I was just super nervous about this book. Besides Harry Potter and Septimus Heap , fantasty is not my genre. I essentially downloaded this book because of the absolutely beautiful cover. I don't really know how to explain it. Fantasy was just never my thing. But this year, I made myself a promise to read more classics (which I have been) and read more fantasy. I feel like I have done that. This book has shown me that fantasy is a really fun. I'm going to continue with this series and continue reading this fun genre.

I liked this one! It's no award winner, but it's a nice, cozy romance to curl up with. I'm a huge fan of the time-travel historical fiction genre, but I try to be picky about which ones I choose because some can be unbearably cheesy... But I didn't feel that way with this one. The romance wasn't instant, the time period (while not exactly historically correct) felt authentic, and the focus was more on the history and the plot than the "intimate escapades" of the two protagonists. Also, I found it unique enough - as a time-travel romance set in the Scottish highlands - that Outlander wasn't constantly coming to mind. (Actually, in some ways, I liked this one better than Outlander...ahh!) One complaint: I wish Bre had more in her arsenal than the "damsel in distress" card... I like female protagonists that stand up for themselves instead of waiting to be saved. (Though she did put herself in danger to save others, which is commendable...) 4 stars

Rating: 4/5 
 ***Minor spoilers, big spoilers for book one!*** 
 Onyx begins shortly after Obsidian ended. Daemon and Katy are just beginning to learn what their new connection due to Daemon's healing of her does. They're becoming closer and are undeniably interested in each other, but Katy is unsure if this is due to the new connection. Not long into the book, we learn that the Department of Defence is in town and they're suspicious, like always. This isn't really good for Katy, who's starting to have some weird alien abilities of her own due to her bond with Daemon. If she isn't careful, she may expose herself to the DOD and put all of the Luxen in danger. 
 I thought this book was much, much better than the first. The only reason I didn't rate this higher is because Katy really annoyed me in this book. There was a bit of a love triangle that I can't even call a love triangle because Katy doesn't even actually care for the other guy. She continues to lead him on because she doesn't want to confront her feelings for Daemon. She's was hurting both of them in a way and she seemed so oblivious to it, or maybe she just didn't care. I just wish she spoke to Daemon sooner. 
 I thought the prospect that Katy was getting Luxen abilities because of their bond was pretty interesting. It was also believed that since Daemon is super strong, she would be super strong as well. My issue was that Katy didn't seem to want to train with Daemon, but instead wanted to train with another new kid in town named Blake, who was a "hybrid" like her. I have no idea why she didn't want to learn with Daemon, who she knew she could trust with her life. It also seemed like everything Blake was telling her, Daemon could've done as well and been a lot nicer about it. Some of Katy's decisions in this book just didn't make sense to me. 
 My favourite thing about this book was probably the connection between Daemon and Katy. Things were getting more romantic between them and they were able to be in the same room for a long time without fighting. They seemed to have a new respect for each other and a new trust that I really enjoyed. I only with that we got to see more of their romance. If only Katy didn't have to run to Blake all the time. 
 Overall, I loved this book a lot, more than Obsidian. The plot was more interesting but I actually disliked Katy more in this book. I'm hoping that in the next book Katy isn't as idiotic and will actually listen to the opinions of other people. Regardless, I'm excited to continue on with this series when I can.

This was definitely a quick read, mainly because it was a graphic novel. But don't mistake the quickness of the read as a sign of the depth of the story. There's a lot to absorb and a lot to think about in regards to the picture that Yang paints with his imagery -- through pictures and through text. The lives of the three characters that star in this graphic novel are very intentional. And each one has a story that can hit you right in the feels. 
 Even though this story encompasses the experience of the Chinese American, indirectly and directly, I felt a lot of similarities between my experience as a Black woman living in America. And there was a lot of unexpected introspection that was prompted by the happenings throughout this book. 
 I really enjoyed it. Yang tells a great story and his voice is definitely heard throughout it.

I really enjoyed Team Human. It was a terrific satire based on the supernatural creature craze - and the title couldn't be more fitting! Mel was a real delight for the main character. Did I agree with everything she said and did? No, but at least we have a young woman who is actively trying to engage in the world and not mindlessly drooling over some guy, constantly needing to be protected. She has room for growth, and her journey of trying to get to the root of her prejudice against vampires seemed genuine. Part of the ridiculousness about any kind of prejudice is that it really doesn't have to be caused "by" anything happening... sometimes it's just fear or unwillingness to understand. This was well portrayed in Mel's situation. 
 I would love to have had a little more history of the world here, because the parts mentioned were very fascinating, particularly with the overlap between real world events and what they could have been like with the addition of vampires and zombies. The action and pacing were great - I found the book very engaging. Great for those who are willing to take the supernatural scene a little less seriously.

I don't really know what to say about this conclusion to this amazing series. 
 First of all I'd like to say that I absolutely loved the first two books, especially Insurgent. I could really relate to the characters in Insurgent, especially the development Tris and Four went through. That was also the case in this book. 
 I do have to say that I found this last book kind of boring, nothing much really happened except for some characters who died, I didn't really care too much for. Maybe if I marothonned the trilogy it would have made more of an impact on me, but now it didn't. When I was half through it started to get a little better, but I did found myselff pushing myself to keep reading. Then the important stuff happened, for those of you who have read the book, you know exactly what I'm talking about. That was just beautiful, I loved it, I'm glad I finished it just because of the ending and the stuff that happened nearing the ending. Even though everything before that didn't necessarily have to be there.. 
 Let's talk about Tris's death... I will tell you my horrible and kind of mean opinion, but if Tris didn't die I would've been happy with the outcome of this story. Just because the story was such a slow burn, something terrible had to happen for people to like the whole story afterwards. I think it was really smart what Veronica Roth did with this, because I literally gave this book 3 stars instead of 2,5 because I loved everything near the ending so much. It was a big finish and it was amazing, even though everyone hated it that she died and I'm probably in the minority with this opinion. I especially loved her death, because all of the inspirational psychological scenes and thoughts, it was just really thought provoking and it made me realize I should tell people I care about them more.  
 I did love all the scenes between Tris and Four their relationship was so real, they argued and had discussions and everything, they questioned eachtother's beliefs and I think that's an important thing to write about, to write a good, real relationship. Also the struggle Tris faces being vulnerable and open with Four, it's a really good thing to teach people about that fear. I think you should find someone that makes you strong and better in that way. 
 So even though I was a little dissappointed with this book, it still had it's great moments.

 The vintage photos, above all, added excitement and colorful realism to the book. Perhaps, the sole reason for younger thrill-seeking readers to enjoy the read! 
 Jacob's grandfather, Abraham Portman, escaped the Nazis during WWII, though his family were not as fortunate, but there are other 'monsters' that continue to haunt him. In contrast, Jacob has spent most of his 'ordinary' life listening to his grandfather's 'fairy tales' of mysterious children who can levitate, become invisible, and play host to a swarm of bees. Jacob was left with no choice but unravel the mysteries of what his Granpa Abe left him. 
 It is slow, but doesn't at all drag, perhaps making you anticipate the story more. Although you might first assume that Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children is a horror novel, it is neither horror nor a thriller, but instead a spectacular, bizarre mystery. Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children is a wonderfully unique and inventive book with colourful characters, a mysterious story, and a splash of historical relevance, incorporating vintage photographs that bring the story to life.

Bear in mind: Franzen will tell me that because I'm not American I don't get it. Both those things are absolutely fine with me.

 For example, I read something about the pharmaceutical industry etc, so I assume Franzen is making a statement about the evils of such companies in America, but that's not really the message I take directly from his writing, rather my assumption of what it is about, cause I find it all a bit flat and aimless. There's an old man with Parkinson's, so I assume it is in part about the bittersweetness of a family banding together to care for a loved one, but again... that's a theme I apply to his writing based on the situations and characters in the book, but what message came through his words about that topic? And may I ask, what does he know about caring for someone with Parkinson's? Did he just imagine a man with Parkinson's and what it might be like? I did a bit of reading and it's to do with his dad's struggle with Alzheimer's I guess... Well, I can understand that, then. But not enjoy it. 
 What can I say? I thought the metaphorical talking turd was the most fitting thing in there hahaha! 
 Franzen admits to being a bit shameless when he takes ideas from the experimental writers, Gaddis, Pynchon and the like... Dude, you're not shameless enough! I would totally read the next Franzen novel if it was called Jonathan Franzen's "Gravity's Rainbow" by Thomas Pynchon :-) 
 If you would like something about Americans that is entertaining, please listen to David Bowie's "Young Americans" continuously for the length of time it would take you to read a Franzen novel. I think you will find it a richer experience. 
 Take it away, David!

Not a bad story at all, but it suffered from the same problem I've had with nearly all of these stories - a lengthy, relatively detailed introduction followed by the middle part (where the actual plot happens) that is hurried and not nearly meaty enough, and a short, rushed ending. 
 I wasn't initially happy to find out Nine wouldn't have Rose as his companion in this one, both because I liked Rose a lot better with the Ninth Doctor than with Ten and because I expect this means she'll be in Ten's story instead of Martha or Donna (both of whom I liked much better in Ten's era), and, well, Nine & Rose just seem like an inseparable package deal. 
 That said, and slight disappointment aside, I actually ended up liking the way this was handled. It was nice to get an alien as a companion even though she thought and acted a bit too human-like for me to suspend disbelief entirely - I assume it was part of the whole reveal, to make Ali sound like a regular human girl to start with and then only gradually reveal that she's not from Earth and then, in a way clearly designed to surprise the reader, describe her very much alien looks and beliefs.  And also, it fit into the canon TV timeline better than I'd expected, and Rose was certainly present enough in spirit, if not in body. 
 The plot itself... not the worst I've read and not the best I've read. Ancient Babylon was a cool destination, but I felt the Starman part of the plot was rather weak. 
 On the plus side, I could actually hear Christopher Eccleston's voice for Nine's dialogue, so at least to me, Higson got Nine's voice down just right.

THE DEMON LOVER follows Callie McFay as she accepts a faculty position at an obscure liberal arts college that turns out to be far more than she bargained for. I give this book 4 stars, because while it's certainly a romance, and there are plenty of sex/erotic scenes, there's actually a story in between. It's sort of a fantasy-mystery hybrid that involves folklore and many beings from different mythologies. 
 The identity of the "bad guy" kept me guessing, and the ending was tied up well, not ending abruptly like quite a few books I've read lately. The characters could have been fleshed out a little more, especially the mythological ones, but the plot kept me intrigued. The book goes from New York City to Fairwick (the college town) and back, which makes for interesting scenery. 
 I have a feeling that there is more to this tale, so we might see a sequel sometime soon, and I'd be glad to read that too.

"What a treacherous thing to believe that a person is more than a person." 
 The book took a while to get into, and it didn't give me the feels that John Green books usually do. HOWEVER, I still really enjoyed its message. I loved the concept of people being mirrors vs windows. Basically, it makes you wonder if we ever really know someone. Do we see someone's true, unique self (a window that we can see through), or do we just see what the person wants us to see (a mirror casting a reflection)? 
 For most of his life, Q, the main character, has put Margo, his neighbor and crush, on a pedestal. He thinks she's this amazing, popular, attractive person who can do anything and doesn't care what people think. But when she runs away from home, Q begins a quest to find her and ends up learning things about her that he never imagined, stuff that contradicts the Margo he thought he knew. All in all, the book isn't really about Q finding Margo. It's about Q learning that people are complex and that it's unfair to idolize people or think they are something they're not. 
 Like I said, I absolutely loved this message. It's something that (I think) we've all experienced. We've all labeled people too quickly and later found out that our judgments were way off the mark. What I think Paper Towns does well is show us how easy it is to forget that our minds make these erroneous judgments. Q went years thinking he knew who Margo was, and he never made an attempt to find out if he was right or wrong. This book made me wonder how many people I know who I only see as mirrors instead of windows.

I just hope when I get to read the rest of this series Tris stays true to herself.

I always promised myself I'd be honest in my reviews, so I have to be honest: I almost completely hated the first half of Partials. It's full of so many terms that I don't think are explained well enough - the Hope Act, the Voice, Defense Grid, the Partials, and even more. Eventually I was able to guess what they were from the things people say, it was extremely frustrating for me. 
 And then there's Kira's boyfriend, Marcus. It wasn't only the first half I didn't like him, it was the entire book. Maybe because I just find him boring, I'm not sure. 
 The thing is that I feel like nothing gets done in the first half. It's mainly just a bunch of confusion for people like me and all of the characters trying to control one another. I almost stopped reading. The beginning alone is probably a one or two star for me. 
 But I kept going, and I'm so glad I did. It got interesting as soon as Samm, a Partial - an engineered being that can easily be mistaken for a human - came into the picture. There aren't really any hints of it, but I have high hopes that Samm and Kira will end up together by the end of this series. Just because I love him so much. 
 Partials is written in third person, and while I don't have problems with it, it's not very often that it happens. Dan Wells did a great job with it, and I completely loved Kira. She's not afraid to stand up for what she believes in, and she's definitely a kickass heroine. 
 That fact that Partials is so original is almost surprising. There are so many dystopians right now that they're all starting to blend together for me with all their similar plots. But Partials is so different that it's amazing. There are so many new concepts explored that you can't help but be interested. 
 Overall: Once I got past the first half, Partials was a very original, action-packed book full of hope and desperation. I have so many questions, but not in a bad way. I can't wait to see how everything is explored in the next book. 4 stars.

Defy the Stars by Claudia Gray is an amazing story where Ms. Gray creates an expansive sci-fi universe with interesting worlds, technologies and futures to explore. 
 Noemi Vidal is a young fighter pilot in the last weeks of prep for a suicide mission that will buy her world, Genesis, time to better prepare to fight the incursion of merciless Mech (terminator-esque battle drones) armies, sent by an Earth low on resources to exploit her home world. 
 When a minor battle causes her to make an emergency landing on an Earth ship, abandoned 30 years ago during the on going war, she comes face to face with her worst nightmare, the most advanced experimental Mech ever created. However, instead of killing her, it informs her that as the only human on board, she is now its commander. To top off the strange turn of events, Noemi finds it knows a way to destroy Earth's ability to attack them... 
 What is a girl to do? Obviously... go on a voyage around the circle of worlds in the known habitable universe, avoid getting blown up, get chased across said universe by battle Mechs, make new friends, have some narrow escapes, and of course...the most important bit and my favorite part... get an awfully lot closer to a surprisingly human android than she ever thought she would. Like I said from the start...amazing story! And that's barely touching the surface. 
 More than anything, what I liked about Defy the Stars was the growth of the characters. While Abel, a recently sentient AI has some obvious growth to do, both Abel and Noemi learn more about themselves and each other than they ever imagined. I wish there had been another chapter or two at the beginning to get a better feel for Noemi in her native environment, but we learn a lot about her as we go. I enjoy Abel's transition from a rather know-it-all android to a more human character and that Noemi is the one who causes this final development, from a machine which just barely did more than fake humanness, to one with his own feelings. I also liked how in many ways it brings out Noemi's own version of development as she learns more about herself, Abel, and the scope of the universe she is adventuring in. 
 In the end Defy the Stars gives you both a sense of satisfaction in the characters who you've spent chapters bonding with, but a serious case of wanting more. I'm ready for the next Noemi and Abel adventure and the ink isn't even wet on this one. I wholeheartedly recommend!

The Harlem Hellfighters was the nickname for the the 369th infantry regiment in World War I, which was all African-American. They were reviled by many whites in their own military, under-supplied, often humiliated by their own superiors, and spent more time in combat then any other U.S. unit. However they fought tremendously well and were highly decorated. 
 This book discusses not just the specific experience and history of the men in this unit, but the war itself. It's not like bombs, gas, or even the lice that tormented them discriminate between soldiers based on their skin color. Canaan White's drawing here don't flinch from some of the horrors. But what they go through also brings us closer to these heroic warriors as Brooks tells us their individual stories. 
 Really glad this exists!

The only reason why this book took so long for me to read was because of my hectic schedule and the fact that I took out too many books from the library all at the same time and had to prioritize with them first. When I did finally pick this book up again and start from the beginning it took me only a couple of days to get through it - it was engrossing. 
 I liked Juliet's character. I like how she ended up admitting her faults and coming to a much greater understanding of everything and herself at the end of the novel. She was made vulnerable in a way that was believable and wasn't done in an exaggerated manner. Her growth and transition and inner struggles with love and understanding is one that made sense and I was able to feel empathy and sympathy, different one for different situations, throughout the book. Her journey was a really long one and this book contained an amazing amount of character growth. 
 I enjoyed the spin off on the Romeo and Juliet story. As well, I was really satisfied with how Jay decided to end Juliet's part of the story - it was well-deserved and didn't feel like the cliche-d kind of ending most books would receive. Romeo's journey obviously still continues and I'm interested where this journey will continue off to, whether he'll be able to reach his goal or not. Even as the villain in this version of the story it was pretty hard to feel hatred for Romeo when he was just so blatantly lied to and spent the whole book overcoming his own challenges. 
 This was very impressive. I picked the book up for $5 at my local bookstore on a bargain book sale. I wasn't disappointed by what I read, as my general rule is that I take books out from the library first before deciding whether or not I'll buy a personal copy for my collection. This one deserves the place on my shelf.

Hmmm. I quite liked this series as a whole. For once, a fantasy that isn't Euro-centric, some very interesting gender play, and a smart, willful central character who is independent and capable (but still somewhat annoying in her youth). 
 While I did enjoy all of these books, I sort of liked this one the least, and it's a little hard for me to peg why. I *think* that it's because something was a little different with Flora. Or maybe, it's that something was exactly the same. She was whiny (which she's always been) and impetuous (which she's always been) but somehow, I don't want to accept that in book three. Where is her growth? She's had some crazy adventures in previous years, seen some crazy things, dealt with a number of harsh realities, and learned some truly sad tales about the people in her life. And yet, she's still so dang pouty! And refuses to believe that anyone else might have things going on. Throughout this whole book, she keeps being upset that the adults in her life don't trust her with information - but judging from the way she makes decisions, I can totally understand why they wouldn't. 
 All that being said, I still like her chutzpah. And I LOVE hearing all the continued snippets from Nini Mo's writing throughout (some of the phrases have actually helped me in my real life!). And I really have to say that the author has a definite sense of humor. Plus, for a book that's marketed to middle-grade readers - there's plenty for adults in here! Wilce is quite masterful at innuendo, cursing, and subtle adult humor that manages to stay in line with those of "delicate sensibilities." (She's also got a thing for making her heroine vomit, apparently, but it's never grotesque). 
 I'm not exactly satisfied with how things ended with the Wer-bear vs. Udo in Flora's affections. It all just felt sort of dropped. This whole book she builds this entire relationship with Wraathmyr only to have it completely wither/fall apart when she needs to go home? Unfinished. And having her love for Udo removed? While it's kind of clever to have that mean that she can start fresh with him, it seems to have hardly any consequence at all - which makes it seems like she didn't sacrifice anything at all. I want to believe this means that the author has more in store for us, but reading her various answers regarding that question leaves me feeling like that's not a definite. Confusing!  
 Overall, I enjoyed the process of reading these books, but I feel like there's more here that hasn't been covered. Here's hoping!

 This book captivated me from the very first word. It's a book of rustic magic and mysticism and the story is fantastical and yet still realistic. It's a masterpiece and I thoroughly enjoyed reading it. 
 Set in Medieval Russia this book explores the old mythology of a newly Christian nation. Religion and mythology are at the centre of this novel as everything supernatural is considered a demon and people who can see them are often driven mad by their visions. Vasilisa is a strange child, one who has the sight and can see and speak to the creatures that inhabit her home and her father's land, and she is the only one that can save her home from the evil lurking in the woods, something much more terrible than the Winter King that haunts local folklore. 
 Each character is fantastically well written and they all influence the story in their own way, despite the fact that Vasilisa is the main character. I really enjoyed the characterisation of Vasya's father, a strong man who cares deeply for his children, despite the fact that he blames Vasya for the death of his wife. Vasya's brothers and sisters are all equally well characterised and it's wonderful to see such a great family dynamic in a story such as this one. 
 The final parts of the novel weren't as good as the beginning or middle because it was used to set up the sequels but that doesn't mean that it was bad. The ending was actually very good and I was fully satisfied by the ending. I wish that this book was a standalone because I enjoyed the ending so much, it just felt right for the book. 
 I would recommend this book to all of my friends because it's such a richly detailed novel with a captivating plot. It feels as though you have stepped into a fairy tale and I love that. I will definitely buy this book for myself and I will re-read it several times in the future. 
 I look forward to reading the sequel when it comes out in January 2018.

Meh. That's really all I can say. The beginning had me pretty pissed off, and, if you followed me on twitter when I read this (in December...according to Goodreads, Dec 17), you would see my tweets about my irritation at how cliche this was, how racist and sexist it seemed (I know, I know, that's the point, but still. Irritation? Plus, I have friends in the US who have friends on the "rez". Doesn't sound very accurate...maybe?) and how perfect Ryan seemed. It was just...meh. Not to say it wasn't good! I'd read an insanely good book right before starting this, so I think it just raised my standards! 
 Bad things first, like usual: 
 Ryan seemed like a perfect guy, and, as someone pointed out on Twitter, looks like a human Ken doll according to the cover. So he was just a bit messed up in the beginning, but there were only really 2 or 3 incidents where he didn't seem perfect, or, as perfect as a literary character gets. I mean, he was rich, his family was a bit broken, he was dating possibly the most popular girl in school, he was the best on the team (until Fred came), etc. and as much as I hate to admit it, he was pretty much the epitome of perfection. And...it really bothered me. I love real characters and if you haven't caught that by now...well, then. 
 Also, how does golf make you popular? At least, in my area, only football and basketball raise your social status here. Is it different somewhere else? Anyone? Curiosity calls! 
 I wanted to smack a lot of these characters' heads, no joke. Fred was so optimistic and judging sometimes, that I wanted to shake her. Seth (Ryan's best friend) was so racist and sexist, I wanted to run him over with a car, and Ryan was so hurtful sometimes, he's the only one I actually wanted to smack. Not to sound rude. I mean, besides these it was a pretty decent book, of course! 
 So what was good? 
 The romance. It was cliche (the outcast with the popular?) but I do enjoy fluffs! Also? those hate/love relationships make me giddy and squee, and even though it's cheesy, I always love when a guy rescues a girl. Even though sometimes, if it's done wrong, I hate the girl looking like a DID (Damsel in Distress). But in this case, Fred was good enough! In the end, I did love her. 
 It was unique in the way of backgrounds and I didn't have a problem with it--what I did have a problem with was how prejudiced the characters were! But I loved how they were so different, but so alike, and it made sense to me that'd they'd fall in love. Even if I was a bit indifferent at first. 
 And I did like how Fred felt--lost and alone, but determined to do what she loved. THAT'S the kind of character I'm talking 'bout! 
 Hooked was a book I was excited about, but definitely fell flat of m y expectations. It was okay--just not one I really liked or loved. It went uphill in the second half, but by then, my interest was barely there and the only thing keeping me reading was the review I'd be writing. Thankfully, I did finish, and I did enjoy the ending which wrapped up the book perfectly!

Their constant bickering through the years has always been his way of disguising his true feelings for her.When she decides that it's time to add some authenticity to her sex columns, she decides that Sam is the perfect candidate to educate her. Will he be able to resist her? 
 "We're going to regret this," he said when he opened his eyes and gazed at her. Her eyes lit up at the implicit acquiescence in his words. "Maybe," she said softly. "But we're going to have a lot of fun doing it."

 Sophie Heyer has spent her life trying to live down her mother's reputation, the whore. Sophie has always felt like she needed to be the good and quiet girl in town, memories and scandal have long lives. Even twenty five years later she's reminded how much she looks like her mother so people assume she must also act like her. 
 Alex Bishop grew up in chaos. His father disappeared when he was barley a teenager and his mother believed he would just leave them. He must be kidnapped or hurt someplace. The family spent much of his teenage years roaming the country looking for him. At eighteen, Alex left home and never looked back. Recently after running into a family acquaintance that relayed some news about his father, Alex felt compelled to check in. His brother Shane convinces him to come visit for a few days. Alex knows this isn't a good idea. It's never good to go back. 
 Everyone has issues and all children are affected by things their parents do and say. This story is a perfect example of that. Both characters suffered major trauma as youngsters and now that they are adults the trauma is still affecting them. I understood Alex's actions and reactions throughout the story. I could see the line connecting the dots between what happened as a child and his actions as an adult. I thought I understood Sophie's actions and reactions too. However, by the end I realized I had only seen a small piece of who she was and why she was that way. When I got to the deep rooted issues in her life I had an "oh my goodness" moment, mouth hanging wide open, tears forming in my eyes, the whole shocked shebang. I really enjoyed this book. It seems a bit slow at times while I was reading it, but by the end it all came together. There is A LOT of hot sex in the book and that is always a plus. I give this book 4 stars and 4 hands down the pants.
