Epic, fast-paced, romantic love story that had my stomach in happy knots in the beginning, then twisted knots somewhere near the end. 
 I loved being in Mia's head. She's such a nut, I felt like I understood her. Her insecurities, humor and candidness really lit this book up for me and made me that much more invested in the story. 
 AND OMG LUCAS. Where do I even begin. I WISH I HAD A LUCAS IS ALL I'M SAYING. So sweet, funny and swoon-worthy. I loved how spontaneous he was, and that he was always consistent in his belief about the future and what it meant, because that's realistic! 
 And I think that's really the best part about this book, is that it shows how 2 people who obviously wanted different things from the relationship actually sticking by that but realising that sometimes life throws you a curveball and you can choose to ignore it, or run with it. That brief separation was so bittersweet because I actually understood and felt for both Mia and Lucas, but still I held out hope that LOVE WOULD INDEED CONQUER ALL, which of course it did. :D
Amazing! Loved the ending, it was so unpredictable.

I am so glad that I decided to keep going with this series. I actually enjoyed this book more than You. This may sound a little odd (considering that Joe kept killing people in this book), but the author took away a little bit of Joe's "crazy". He was still OCD, but it was scaled down enough that I began to sympathize with Joe even more than in the first book. Or, perhaps, I just got used to how his mind worked and became immune to the crazy. That is part of what makes this book so scary. How am I being brainwashed to become sympathetic to a serial killer??!? And, yes, the people he kills are mostly annoying, but that doesn't mean that it is ok to MURDER them. I had to take my nose out of the book for a moment at certain points to remind myself of that. That definitely takes some skill from the author. 
 I also preferred the California Joe to the New York Joe. California Joe was actually finding some happiness in his life. Plus, it was fun to read about the characters the author developed in California; some of them were actually pretty amusing. (For example I loved Harvey, the manager at Hollywood Lawns apartment complex. He kept saying, "Am I right or am I right?". I kept imagining him as Matthew McConaughey, the strip club owner, in Magic Mike.) And, that darn jaywalking - gets people in trouble all the time! My interest is still piqued enough that I would pick up #3 if the series keeps going.

And I know not everyone will get to love this book, but people please, don't kill me if I love this book so much even with the flaws.  Inescapable is simply amazing. It got me thinking and asking myself a lot of questions. I've come to so many conclusions but not even half was correct. I really love how this has made me grinning idiotically at cheesy moments and when I can't help it, giggles escape me because of the funny scenes. And I love the mysterious atmosphere of this. I also love all the characters omg. 
 Buns and Brownie. I didn't expect that they were angels. It never actually crossed my mind. But still, I love these two cheerful reapers. 
 Freddie. Well, he was one of my favorite characters. I even love that Evie thinks he is like her evil twin brother. Well, she got the evil part right. Still, I have a soft spot for evil characters. It always make me think that it isn't there fault they've turned evil; that maybe something happened to him or broke him that led him to a shameful fate. Part of me still believes he can be saved; part of me hopes that he's just acting out of madness and given a chance, he might change. 
 Zephyr. I may have shipped Zee and Evie for a while hahaha. I love how he finds Evie so funny and how he himself is funny. I love Zee, I just do. No explanation needed. 
 Russell. Same thing for him. I just immediately fell in love with this character. But I didn't like when he thinks he owns Evie. I mean, that's good but I'm Team Reed. I may have pitied him a bit.  Reed. Well, who doesn't love Reed. 
 Evie. I love her sense of humor and that she isn't afraid to die just to save Reed from a fight. I love her courage and the way she thinks. There are so many things I love about her and I just can't say them all. I just think that being selfless isn't all good. Maybe she should've thought that facing the demons together with Reed would be better for both of them. 
 Then Intuition. I got surprised there were others than angels. I didn't expect Gancanagh . I didn't even know them that time. I really hate that Freddie got this far in making Evie suffer. I almost want him to change and help Evie instead. It was really a shame their friendship wasn't entirely true. But now, with new enemies the series just got better and better. 
 The Dominion. It was a really heart-pounding part because I don't know what will happen to Evie and Reed. Good thing, there was Preben to help Evie a bit. I may have shipped him with Evie too xD 
 I also now love the quote of Shakespeare: 
 Doubt thou the stars are fire; 
 Doubt that the sun doth move; 
 Doubt truth to be a liar; 
 But never doubt I love... 
 I love thee best, 
 O most best, believe it. 
 I cannot believe Evie and Reed went through these hardships. I'm glad they were able to still be together. 
 Indebted. omg. I have come to love Brennus now and Phaedrus too. I didn't think Brennus can be so kind. I didn't like when Finn got Molly though. I may have shipped him with Evie too hahaha, I ship a lot of people with Evie. Anyway I love everything. I love how Evie is able to wield magic. It makes everything better. Then with the fallen and ifrit involved, the book becomes more thrilling. I think I cried most in this book. I was crying because of Molly being turned. Evie regrets it so much and I just couldn't stop crying. Also, when Lachlan died, I cried a lot. I have learned to love some Gancanagh the way Evie did. I just feel bad they didn't learn to be good. 
 And now Incendiary. This killed me the most. More questions arose and more characters too. I have no words for this. I love that Russell finally found his aspire. But this makes things even more confusing. And to add Xavier to that. I may have shifted to Team Xavier for a while. When Evie started to remember, I was hoping she ends up with him. It's like I feel bad for him because he loved her since forever but she can't remember and she doesn't want to. I feel so bad for Xavier. What if they never got called back to Paradise? Even Tau wouldn't lose her daughter like this (because now she hates him). But I just couldn't take Xavier's agony. This book gave me feels. Especially the last part omg. The Shakespeare quote again. It makes me cry. I was so relieved Evie got to save Reed. But, Brennus still lives. I'm afraid her feelings for him might grow and I don't want that to ruin Reed and Evie. So I was Team Reed after all. 
 The worst part is: I didn't know Incendiary isn't the last. While I was finishing Incendiary I was silently hoping it would be the last because if it isn't then I would have to wait for the last and I don't want that. But I still have a thousand questions in mind and I still want to know what happens to Xavier and Brennus. 
 So now, I wait. 
 I love this book series so much. I know I said a lot but I want to say more. This is really my favorite angel story I want to cry. 
 Amy, you're a rockstar :D

 The thing that kept me hooked though, was not knowing who to trust, and pretty quickly realising that not only can you not trust anyone, but nothing is what it seems. 
 Would definitely recommend if this sounds up your alley!

Ah! Good to know that I'm not unduly prejudiced against fantasy. I had, at one point, thought that I'd finally grown up, and had stopped liking all of this silliness. Like an adolescent version of damn-I'm-getting-old, I suppose. I see that I can still come to Faerie for vacations while spending the greater part of my time in Wall. Go childhood! Yay! 
 So why'd I like Stardust? Because it's whimsical and silly, and yet, by then time I read the last line, deep and moving. Look, just because it's a fairy-tale, it doesn't mean that it can't be for adults. It's very ingenious, what Mr Gaiman's done with the novel, often using fairy-tale tropes, primarily the style of prose, to create a fantastical feel (totally works), with interjections of sex (okay, there's just two sex scenes. And the second one I'm not willing to call that) and violence, more akin to something like a Grimm's collection than a Disney movie. That's not to say that it's an adult book. It's perfectly appropriate for children in their mid-teens, especially for the fact that the plot's got a touch of bildungsroman to it. 
 Speaking of the plot, when I had first read the premise, I'd found it quite silly. Like "Eh? A chap wants to retrieve a fallen star for the girl he loves? Isn't that a little too..." and I had refrained from even using the word in my mind, for that would mean tat I had finally crossed over, permanently, into Wall. However, childish this book is not. 
 It comes with several elements of usual fairy-tales: a quest for a love, princes vying for a throne, search of true love, magic (oh, I'm coming to that), witches and an ending where the protagonist... you little minx! You almost had me spoiling there, hadn't you? Well, I'll have none of that! 
 The magic in Stardust is something I've long missed. Although Harry Potter and Bartimaeus, are fantasies, they treat magic almost like technology. That's not to say that I don't like them, especially the first which remains one of my favourite fantasy series, and seven of my favourite books ever, but that it was refreshing. Magic here is... well, magical, there's an irreverence to it, a certain charming lack of logic that had me enchanted. Several things such as the teleporting candle, the glass flowers, the murderous woods, the little hairy man, and of course, the flying ship, are left almost without explanation. And we don't need one either. Gaiman wants us to lose ourselves in a world where everything is possible, limited only by his (and our) imagination. His prose as Wikipedia puts it, is pre-Tolkien in style, meant to heighten the fairy-tale feel. Of especial note, I would say, are the dream sequences. It's marvellous how Gaiman simulates the experience of dreaming with words! 
 That is not to say that this book is all fluff. Gaiman, while conforming to fairy-tale tropes for most of the time, occasionally subverts them to bring maturity to the novel and the world that it is set in. Stars swear, for one. And some wounds never heal, like Tristran's burnt hand or Yvaine's limp. In the end, Tristran and his love don't live happily ever after, though. It's remarkable how Gaiman managed to choose which parts to make fairy-tale-ish (for the lack of a better word) and which parts to keep real without contradicting himself. For example, he chose to make his characters rather simple, as is usually found in a fairy-tale. 
 To start off a man has sex with a completely unknown girl from a foreign land who is chained to a caravan with a chain that's made of cat's breath and moonbeam frozen by a witch, and who somehow, manages to send the child born of this one-night stand back to Dunstan Thorn across the Wall. The boy, after growing up to be seventeen, is a thoroughly naive idiot, being infatuated with the local hottie, Victoria Forrester, a girl who plays with his emotions cruelly, and then makes him go to Faerie to retrieve a fallen star because she doesn't know how much of a self-sacrificing dunderhead Tristran is. Simultaneously, the 81st Lord of Stormhold on the mountain Huon kicks the bucket, but not before sending the Topaz of Power into space and knocking a star down (the fallen star in question) in the process, leaving three sons, all of whom are murderous (especially Septimus. I like Septimus) in mutual competition for his throne. Simultaneously the eldest of the three old witches wins an animal organ lottery and gets the opportunity to drink the last of the youth potion (which is obtained from the heart of a star) and hunt down the star knocked down by the 81st Lord of Stormhold, to carve it's heart out. Have I mentioned how bad-arse I think the name "Stormhold" is? Also, stars are sentient, singing, humanoids who drink light and eat darkness, and sort of appear like a blonde albino girl (this, by the way, is how you write about sparkly love interests. Suck it Meyer), and have an impressive vocabulary with the cherry topping of a choice of colourful insults and an F-bomb. As the book slowly progresses towards the end, it gets more mature, maybe reflecting Tristran's own growing maturity. Many of my favourite scenes are from the last chapter where everything is resolved. 
 Gaiman balances and unites the three plot threads and the characters driven by straightforward motivations and devices adroitly with a twist that will blow your pants away, leaving you in your underwear, reeling back, trying your utmost not to say "Holy shit!" because you're an atheist and it's kinda hypocritical to use the word "holy". 
 So, does Stardust, with all it's ingenuity and innovation herald a rebirth of the fairy-tale for adults? I doubt it. The book isn't entirely faultless. While it's efficient at holding your attention, the lack of elucidation often borders on the annoying. How did Tristran meet up with the little hairy man? Who is the little hairy man? Is he a man? Why is he so hairy? Is he from a failed Willy Wonka experiment or just a dwarf with hypertrichosis? And most important of all: Does he have genitalia? Such questions shall plague you before you submit to the fact that you shall never get answers and also that it doesn't matter all that much that you won't get answers. Yvaine being called a "star" objectifies her, and though I know that's what Gaiman intended, well, I find it very horrible. I dunno why. I mean, just ask her name and call her by it, dude! Plus, Tristran and all the other characters often act unnaturally (it's a fantasy, after all) which sticks out more than the "adult content". Why is everyone, even the witches, so careful about not breaking their promises? Why are they so trusting of everyone else? And why is the only person who isn't gullible freaking paranoid? Oh, right, because of Septimus. It's world more innocent than ours, I get it. But, frankly, it's irritating. 
 Stardust is a thoroughly enjoyable read with a clever bit of literary ingenuity thrown into the mix. It might not be the future of fantasy, but on the crooked road of this genre of literature, it does serve as a refreshing detour.

I went into this book cold, that is to say I knew no more about it than its famous title. I was intrigued but at the same time worried about the quality of the language or like ability of the story. I needn't have wasted my energy - "The age of innocence" is a masterpiece that has that essential flow that enables one to read it hours on end without ever getting tired but ever more urged to read on (which is how I came to finish it in about a days time). 
 The world Wharton describes is to me as foreign as anything out of the Arabian nights and I feel glad to never have been any sort of member of this kind of 'society' which is described with a painstaking detail that resonates of authenticity. The rather off-hand but sometimes scathing comments on this society are lively and can inflame a heart even decades later while serving to remember that the setting of this book is not that far off really. 
 I thoroughly enjoy Wharton's writing, her easy shifts from feelings and actions, though (and I don't mean this in an negative manner should it come across as such) but Archer has the definite touch having been written by a woman. The whole text is feminine to me, which should be read more as a statement than a judgement, from someone who will now on count Newland Archer as one of her favorite literary characters. 
 Quotes: 
 On society - "Archer had gone to the house an hour earlier in full agreement with Mr Letterblair's view; but put into words by this selfish, well-fed and supremely indifferent old man it suddenly became the Pharisaic voice of a society wholly absorbed in barricading itself against the unpleasant." 
 An example of where I find a (well spoken) feminine agenda: "It would presently be his task to take the bandage from this young woman's eyes, and bid her look forth on the world. But how many generations of the women who had gone to her making had descended bandaged into the family vault? He shivered a little, remembering some of the new ideas in his scientific books, and the much cited instance of the Kentucky cave-fish, which had ceased to develop eyes because they had no use for them." 
 It is lines like that that make me feel that ''The age of innocene" should be more mandatory to read in schools than is "Madam Bovary" or Jane Austen. Edith Wharton, the first female winner of the Pulitzer price deserves a wider recognition than she has gotten.

Mr Eugenides is a man with a beautiful and compassionate soul: not a single one of his characters escapes its touch. He is a treat and a treasure and we're lucky to have him. 
 Apparently he can also weave a compact fact-pacted swashbuckling multi-generational epic. Its just that-- I say this about a lot of books-- the compression required to get readers to the end of such a story is counterintuitive to the space required to allow characters to meander their way poetically across the stage. 
 Also, as the story moves through its symphonic movements as each generation of the family becomes the focus, the novel itself loses its centre. 
 Cecily told me this is more enjoyable when re-read, and I can believe it. I've entered many a book so shocked by how its appearance differs from what I had in mind that I haven't even recovered by the end! DFW's "Oblivion", Munro's "Hateship, Loveship..." (you cannot let a single character's name slide!), Saunders' "Tenth of December"- I've just discovered the trend in typing this: I handle compression poorly. 
 I commend the work. 
 I lament the loss.

A truly grown-up fairy tale. 4/5 stars. 
 This review was originally posted on my book blog. 
 Of all the fantasy stories I've read this year, Uprooted stands out thanks to its depth, which is fitting for a story obsessed with figurative and literal roots. 
 For all of you who shy away from fantasy thinking it all too far-fetched or frivolous, I suggest you give Uprooted a try. This is a grown-up fairy tale which is mercifully free from characters who spend their time navel-gazing, complaining to their friends about their problems and going through developmental angst. The characters in Uprooted all have bigger things to worry about besides themselves and deal with their issues by taking action. 
 As you read, you get the impression that Novak had been thinking about this book for years before sitting down to write it. There wasn't a glimmer of superficiality anywhere: not in plot (which was always planned about 5 moves ahead of where we were, providing some excellent surprises), character or setting. The narrative is underpinned by the author's knowledge of Polish and Russian folklore which gives it a timeless quality. Also, Novak deserves praise for keeping things clear: although there's a lot happening simultaneously on several levels, I never felt lost or left behind. 
 Even more praise should be heaped on Novak for her female characters, particularly Agnieszka and Kasia. We get to watch our heroines develop from young girls who seem to have no choice in determining how their lives are going to pan out, to powerful women who get to decide their own fates. 
 Overall: if you're looking for a truly grown-up, complex fairy tale, I recommend you check out Uprooted.

 Overly complicated plotting, with secret plan on top of secret plan and so much double dealing and straight up lying that it was impossible to keep track of? Check! 
 A protagonist who followed plans that were clearly doomed to failure alternately because she was too stupid to think them through and because handwavey Wonderland logic? Check!

 I will say that the cover was the reason I wanted to read The Jewel SO badly. I mean, that dress? The sparkles? A cover that's slightly reminiscent of The Selection with the mirrors? I was so in to read this one and absolutely desperate to get my hands on it. However, right before starting this book, I had a sudden suspicion that I might not like this book. It sounded like a mix of Megan McCafferty's Bumped and Kiera Cass's The Selection, along with an unsettling cliched dystopian-feel to it. I also read some reviews and some of them... well. Let's just say they didn't paint the brightest picture of this book so my expectations sunk despite the gorgeous cover. I was, however, pleasantly surprised when it came to reading this book. The writing flowed so well, and the author really had built up this world beautifully. While there were some problems with the book, I found myself lapping it up huge chunks at a time and immersed myself into the world of The Jewel. 
 I think the problem with many dystopian novels today is originality. There are so many novels set in the future and sometimes it can be really hard to come up with ideas that standout. I've read a ton of dystopian novels that all sounded very similar, and while I overlooked it due to other factors, it can get annoying if it's too repetitive. The Jewel seemed to be made up of some of these already existing books. For instance, the scene when Violet's being prepped before she's going to be presented in the auction, there's her stylist, Lucien who really supports her and thinks she's different from the other girls he has prepped in the past. Sound familiar? If you thought of The Hunger Games, you are correct! Round two: the idea of caste systems or rather ranking by the area you live in in the city. Girls competing in an auction (which doesn't last too long but still). Any guesses? Yeah, I was right when I thought of The Selection. It's not just the dresses people! 
 While I did root and empathise (slightly) with our protagonist, Violet sometimes annoyed me. She's feisty, I'll tell you that, but sometimes, she does the stupidest things that make you want to hit your head against the wall. The love interest Ash elicited a similar reaction. I don't think it was something wrong with the characters but rather the idea of insta-love that kind of through me in a loop. Thankfully, it's only the second half of the book that it starts, so there's plenty of other things going on that distractedly me from the ridiculousness of how fast they both fall for each other. The Duchess, on the other hand, was an interesting character. I loved the two sides of her: some of the stuff she does in this book is really evil, but suddenly, she'll reveal a much softer side to her - you never know what she'll do next. 
 If you've read some of the other reviews of this book, you'll notice how much everyone freaks out about the end. Um, THEY HAVE GOOD REASON TO. I was completely blown away by the end! Some characters are not who they seem (and I had a sneaking suspicion), and now I'm dying to get my hands on the next book. So much happens and I had to re-read the last lines over and over again because I couldn't believe what was going on. Excited and a little bit freaked out to see where it picks up again in the sequel. 
 When I got to the end of Amy Ewing's debut, I instantly wished I had more to read. The Jewel is a stunning start to the trilogy that had my eyes wide open, scouring the pages as I devoured more and more of this delicious book. Incredible world building and a plot that thickens with every word, I have no doubts that the next instalment will be as spectacular as this one. Can't wait!

 Anyway, regardless of the cover art, I actually really enjoyed this novel. 
 The narration is in third person, mostly from Kami's point of view, though you often got Jared's feelings, too. The style was witty, interesting and engaging, and certainly a large part of what I enjoyed about the book. Kami (an amateur journalist/sleuth - think Veronica Mars) says on like the third page that when she sits down to write articles, jokes just pour out. Obviously, Brennan feels the same, as the novel is just littered with them. The dialogue, because of this, is often fabulous and funny, and made me laugh out loud quite a few times, not to mentioned increased my love for a lot of the characters. The problem I did have with this though, is that people don't actually speak like that in real life. No one has that many one-liners at the ready, and definitely not a whole group of very, very witty people. However, I'm willing to forgive this, because what does it matter, really? I immensely enjoyed reading the novel, so it obviously paid off, stylistically. 
 I liked Kami. As well as funny, she was curious and stubborn and determined. She played an active role in the story - things didn't just happen to her, she caused a lot of things, and reacted, too. It was great to read a character like her - someone who was unapologetically herself, even though she had flaws (curiousity killed the cat, anyone?) 
 I liked Kami and Jared together, and I though Jared was an interesting character, who I wished we could find out more about. I felt for him a lot of the time, and he obviously often felt very alone. His connection to Kami was strong, and I do really believe that they loved each other. I kind of hated them both for the ending, though. I wonder if that happened is reversible? (I'm being purposely vague because I don't want to spoil it for anyone.) 
 The supporting characters are interesting, too, and well-built. I cared about them, and their relationships, just as much I did for Kami's. 
 Brennan has written a very engaging novel, one which only just began to reveal what was actually going on in the small town of Sorry-in-the-Vale. I certainly want to continue with the series to see where it leads.

I was initially very invested in this memoir. The first half of the book does a wonderful job of melding memoir and sociological exploration. However, at about the halfway mark, it shifts to entirely memoir and Mr. Vance makes a noticeable shift as well. At this point, the book lost a bit of its esteem for me. I think Mr. Vance is obviously introspective about his connection to the societal problems of Rust Belt and other places dominated by the working poor, but he is also has acquired a certain level of privilege that only social ascension can offer, and while that's not necessarily a negative thing, it does seem to alter his paradigm on the societal issues he explores and ultimately makes him seem a little naive and/or myopic. 
 I would highly recommend this book to many people, and even gifted it this Christmas season, but it did not meet my expectations of social exploration based on the initial content of the book.

18-year-old Miss Percy (a nickname, her real name is a lot more feminine) Parker arrives at Athens Academy in London, having left the convent where she was left when her mother died in childbirth. She has nothing to remember her parents by, except a phoenix pendant she wears every day. Percy is an albino, with milky-white skin and hair, and pale, nearly luminescent eyes very sensitive to sunlight. All her life she has lived shrouded in veils and gloves, with tinted glasses to shade her eyes, and to keep people around her from being upset by her eerie appearance. She has a remarkable affinity for languages, being able to learn them almost as soon as she's heard them. She has been haunted by strange visions all her life, and can see, and speak to, the ghosts she so resembles. 
 At Athens Academy, not all the faculty are what they appear. Miss Rebecca Thompson, the headmistress, and Professor Alexi Rychman, a brooding and mysterious scientist, are both part of a small group known as the Guard, whose task it is to protect London against supernatural threat and something known as the Darkness. All six of the Guard were called to duty when they were only teens, and for nearly 20 years they have waited for their prophesied seventh member, whose coming will increase their powers and abilities, but also set in motion a possible war against the Darkness. 
 When Miss Parker arrives at the school, and shortly after, the stunningly beautiful and mysterious Miss Lucille Linden approaches their group seeking refuge from her cruel master, it seems as if the Prophecy will be fulfilled at last. But which of the remarkable women is the true seventh member, and which is the evil minion sent to lure them into further danger? Professor Rychman clearly wishes it to be Miss Parker, as the two are inexorably drawn to each other, despite the impropriety of a teacher-pupil relationship. But could the long years of waiting have dulled his instincts? 
 The Strangely Beautiful Tale of Miss Percy Parker is the first part in a series, a fact I only discovered after I started reading it. I would classify it as a historical fantasy with romantic elements, but while some might disagree, I did not think that the couple getting together was the main narrative driving the plot - the finding of the prophesied seventh member to help the fight against evil was more important. I saw one review that mentioned steampunk, I don't know why, as as far as I could tell, there are no unusual technical innovations, the setting appeared to be Victorian London, albeit a London haunted by ghosts and the occasional hellhound. 
 The supernatural threat that the Guard are battling, does not seem to involve vampires and werewolves and other such paranormal fantasy fare. Simply ghosts and the occasional demonic possession. As the arrival of the seventh member grows near, a demonic multi-headed beast haunts the street of London and brutally murders prostitutes (yes, in this book, Jack the Ripper is a hellhound). All the members of the Guard can see ghosts, but only the timid Miss Parker appears to be able to talk to them. 
 Miss Percy Parker is an unusual heroine. Named after a goddess of Greek myth, she is used to people being frightened and unnerved by her otherworldly looks. She is very self-conscious of her ghostlike appearance, and having grown up in a convent, is afraid that if people find out about her abilities to communicate with ghosts, her visions and portentous dreams, they will think her insane and have her committed. She is rather shy, studious and timid, and makes her first true friend at the Academy. She also falls head over heels for the tall, dark and brooding Prof. Rychman, and despairs that mathematics, his chosen subject, is the one that appears a complete impossibility for her to learn. 
 Alexi Rychman is a classic Gothic, romantic hero. He is gloomy and tortured, and his friends constantly make Hamlet jokes around him. Having convinced himself that he is fated to love the seventh member of their group, he has held himself distant from anything even vaguely resembling a romantic relationship for years, and he takes his duties as the leader of the Guard very seriously - thus leading to much anguish when he becomes unsure whether his feelings for Percy are caused by too many years of loneliness, or if she is really the answer to the prophecy. 
 The story is filled with allusions to Greek myth, which I liked. The book has some flaws as well, though. It is revealed to the reader quite early on who the evil minion is, and instead of this causing added tension, it just makes the members of the Guard seem rather gullible and stupid, despite all of them having good educations and preparing for this event for decades. Speaking of the other members of the Guard, with the exception of Miss Thompson (who frankly isn't given that much of a fully-formed character), most of the members are poorly sketched out, and the reader is given very little insight into who they are and what drives them beyond some rough character traits. However, since this is the first book in what appears to be a series, I'm hoping they will be more developed as the series goes on.

A 3/5 doesn't mean I didn't enjoy this book; there were numerous things I liked about this book. I loved the magic and the fresh take on it- it wasn't just black and white, but purple and green and red and blue. I really enjoyed reading the different stories- the story of Tristan and the star, the story of three brothers, the story of Dunstan and Lady Una, the story of the witches who desire to remain forever young through devouring the heart of star- and how they intertwined. I loved the world of faerie- it was so whimsical and magical yet full of dangers at the same time. The cross-over between the mortal and faerie world were also great and I wouldn't have minded reading a bit more about the divide. The book was full of quirkiness, and these small quirks- such as Tristan's mum having cat ears and being bound to a witch until the oath was fulfilled- made this book great. The writing was beautiful- it was poetic and the descriptions were wonderful. I really enjoyed the film adaptation of this, and although the book was different, the differences weren't bad. 
 But there were a few things that notched this book down and my expectations were not fully satisfied. The book started off with a great pacing from which you could gather a sense of the story, but near the end I felt as if it was rather anti-climactic. Certain events which had been building up momentum and it seemed as if would cause a lot of trouble, were easily resolved. There were also certain places that could do with a bit more elaboration and the characters fell slightly flat without the certain insight required. Tristan didn't have much of the depth that normal protagonists have and I didn't really connect with him as a result and the star, Yvaine, remained that, a star. I didn't get much of a sense of her humanity, although it was apparent in the movie. 
 Overall, I enjoyed this book (regardless of its faults) purely because of Gaiman's writing, the world and the eccentric and original story. If you're a fan of fantasy, magic and fairy tales, this book should move up the ladder on your to-read list. I'm definitely looking forward to reading more of Neil Gaiman's books.

Ah, there it is. That's the book I was looking for. 
 I went into reading this rather tentatively. After the disaster that was the second book of this series, I wasn't sure Cass could bring her reading back around to what had interested me about the series in the first place. Luckily for me I was oh so very wrong. 
 This book does away with the bloody love triangle within the first 50 pages. Decisions are made and kept and the book really gets into what intrigued me the most; how two young people could work to save this messed up country. I loved that it also highlighted each side of this issue. Was it something that should be done with grand, open gestures like America? Should it be brought about with violence like the Southern rebels? Or should it be done slowly like Maxon, all the while conceding certain wrongs as you go? It was a fascinating issue and Cass wrote it very well as America truly starts to mold into the task. 
 Then there was the actual idea of what the characters here were doing. This was very young adults being thrust into making very major mature decisions. In that light, they are allowed to make some mistakes. And there was one hair-pullingly juvenile moment of it  but lets face it, Maxon has as bad of a temper as America does. So, when confronted with the Aspen relationship of course he flipped out at first. Utterly juvenile but it made sense. And the way it was resolved was fascinating.  But all in all it surprisingly progressed the story along. 
 Really I just loved the true maturing of the characters and their relationships in this book. Everyone had to come into their own and it was done so beautifully. I was in love with each character for their own ways by the end and I simply couldn't think of a better epilogue than the one that was written. 
 This book seems to have saved it; I would totally recommend this series again!

Alright. Buckle up, kids. This review is going to be a wild ride. 
 Let's start off by saying that I genuinely and truly do not understand the hype that this book gets. This is one of the most well-loved books in the community, and while it's good, it's nothing to write home to your parents about. If somebody could please explain to me what the obsession is, I'd be happy to listen and try to understand. 
 That being said, this book is by no means bad. It's entertaining, and sometimes that's just the kind of reading experience you need. Is it life changing, though? Worth being an all time favorite? Er... not to me? 
 The Good: 
 - The beginning was definitely great and completely drew me in. Before the inciting incident, you totally get a feel for the characters and the world, which was awesome since it's something that a lot of young adult books lack. 
 - I mean, it's definitely not boring? Mostly. 
 - The characters are cool, I guess. 
 The Bad: 
 - This in no way needed to be a Beauty and the Beast retelling. Like I cannot express to you how unnecessary that was. SJM forced this storyline that absolutely did not to be there and it was dumb. Like the masks? No freaking point to that. 
 - The first 2/3 of the story are completely different than the last 1/3, almost to the point where it's not even the same story. It took this weirdly dark turn, and I don't think it fit with the story at all. 
 The Downright Ugly: 
 - Problematic much??? 
 - We have non-consenting biting going on, which honestly was just fucking weird. 
 - We have the MC being drugged and used like a fucking puppet in front of a huge crowd of people several times, and yet we are supposed to LIKE the character that does that to her? Okay, hey, just a thought, how about no? In my personal and humble opinion, if you do this to someone, AND also use violence against them as a form of threat to get them to do what you want, that's kind of unredeemable. Sorry. Oh wait, no I'm not. 
 Yeah, I don't know. I have no clue if I'm going to continue with this series, but I am definitely sure that I'm gonna get real tired real quick of all the hype about the new book coming out. I mean, happy reading y'all, but I just can't join your excitement on this one.

I finished this a while ago, before I moved actually, but was pretty busy and didn't get around to writing the review until today. 
 If you just gave me a plot synopsis of this book, it would not sound like my thing at all. Basically a curmudgeonly widower finds an abandoned child and ends up taking in the child and growing as a person. That sounds like a book I would not want to pick up. 
 However, the organization/structure of the book is what makes it interesting. Our protagonist is a bookstore owner, and the child he takes in is found in his bookstore. Each chapter opens with the name and synopsis of a famous short story and his thoughts about how it relates to some event from his adopted daughter's life. I thought this was a clever and fun way to set up the narrative. It still has some elements I didn't like (basically I tend to shy away from like, emotional type stories) but I thought all the literary references redeemed it.
Beautiful. Just beautiful. I have no words. I can't speak. Wow.

This is actually a review upon my re-reading it - some of my opinions have changed slightly since the first time I read it, which was August 2013 
 There are so many beautiful things about Daughter of Smoke and Bone. No one could deny the beauty of the writing. Laini Taylor has a way with words that makes me so insanely jealous. There's something so fragile and beautiful and descriptive about her writing. Her talent also lies in the fact that no matter how descriptive she is, it's never pretentious. It's not unnecessary. 
 There's also something so ultimately beautiful about two people from warring species that fall in love. Star-crossed lovers isn't anything new, but it doesn't stop being moving or ferociously beautiful - I am always touched by the idea that people can love amidst so much hate. The love in this novel is all-consuming and fierce, and it makes these characters better. Of course, they are still themselves, but they are their best selves, when they are in love. Their wish for a different life, a better life, is really quite human and really amazing. There's something about it that gets to me - the idea that both sides are trapped in the same war, in the same horrible life of fighting, for a reason long forgotten and long insignificant, but that these two people dream of the end of it, of something different and better. 
 I found Akiva's character especially interesting; 'Everything he had done since, it had been because he had loved Madrigal, and lost her, and lost himself.' He loved with such intensity, and the glimpse of him before her loss was like seeing another person. I thought his character arc was believable and well-written, and heartbreaking, too. 
 Karou was interesting and witty and I was enchanted by her feeling of 'lostness'. That missing part of her that she felt so strongly, was described so well. I actually that she was made 'whole' too easily by the revelation of who she was, and I hope that theme of lostness is present in the next novel. I don't want it to be that easy. 
 Though I could rave about this novel quite a bit, there were also some parts I wasn't necessarily enthralled with. Though I thought Madrigal's and Akiva's romance was touching, I felt that Karou and Akiva's progressed too quickly; it was too intense after such a short time. I know what Taylor was going for, but I would've liked a slower progression of their relationship. I wanted to see them really get to know each other; I think it would've made the ending so much more poignant. 
 I also felt Madrigal's story, which took up about the last 100 pages of the novel or so, really disrupted the pacing. I won't go so far as to say I didn't find it interesting, because that's not true, but I certainly found it harder to read - at least the first couple of chapters of it. Though her story is integral to the plot, and to Karou, I felt that it really slowed the pace right down and the novel started to drag. I didn't feel like it sustained itself very well. Maybe it's just me? I think it's because it takes you so abruptly out of the present moment; a lot of the novel had been concerned with Karou reuniting with Brimstone, and to be dragged so suddenly out of that, and into a more contained story with a different motive, was too disconcerting. As it was the 'past' I felt it was less urgent than what was happening to Karou, if that makes any sense. I also wonder whether it was a slightly too easy device to answer a lot of the questions from the rest of the novel. It felt a little exposition-y, if I'm honest. 
 The romance, and the execution at the end of this segment were incredibly moving though. 
 However, these problems don't stop me from saying that I found Daughter of Smoke and Bone a really very interesting read, and I shall definitely be continuing the series (in fact, the next one is sitting right next to me). I think the world Laini Taylor creates is gorgeous, and so much work has gone into the world-building that it shows. Ultimately, I didn't have issues believing the world or the events, and so often novels set in AUs tend to have significant plot holes, but I didn't find this. Taylor has an amazing talent - her writing is simply beautiful, and I encourage you to read this novel, I really do.

This novel is a Young Adult historical fantasy. It's set in Brittany in 1485 (I think), and is set mostly at the court of Anne, the Duchess of Brittany, and involves much of the politics surrounding the court at the time. Ismae is the protagonist, a handmaiden of death (and daughter of the god of death, Mortain) , and has been sent to the court by her convent on an assignment. She ends up doubting her assignments and what she has been told about her destiny. 
 I really enjoyed this novel. I thought the world was well created and a really strong background to the novel. There's a lot of political manoeuvring in this novel, and it's based on a few true events (I don't know that much about the history of Brittany - I only know it from the point of view of Tudor history). It was a really intriguing part of the novel. 
 The fantasy part of this novel comes with the mythology - the old gods that the Bretons used to worship. Ismae is actually the daughter of St. Mortain, and after a terrible childhood with an abusive father, is taken to the Convent of St Mortain, where she is taught to be an assassin, to serve Mortain's wishes. As the novel progresses, the morality of this profession is called into question and Ismae comes to doubt a lot of what she is taught. I found the whole mythology interesting and liked how Ismae gradually started to really think for herself rather than just rely on what she had been taught. 
 I liked all of the characters, too, especially Ismae. She was brave and interesting and dedicated and loyal. I liked her narration, and I really grew to like her. She stands up for others (especially Anne) and she tries to do what she think is right, even if it clashes with her instructions. 
 The relationship between Ismea and Duval. I thought it developed well and they had some really sweet moments together. 
 However, I did find some parts slightly predictable, like who the traitor was. And I wasn't overly impressed with the way the Reverend Mother told Ismea she'd have to be Duval's mistress. Then there was the lessons they got at the convent on the 'womanly arts'. I just wasn't impressed by the idea that women were strongest when they were having sex, and that was when they were at their most powerful. I know we have to sort of take the context into account, but at the same time, there is so much more to women then their sexuality and it got on my nerves a little. 
 Overall, though, I did really enjoy reading this novel, and I am looking forward to the sequel.

It is always sad to come to the end of a trilogy. To say goodbye to favourite characters. Robin HObb did a good job of wrapping up the story of FitzChivalry. There has been room left open for other story lines that I hope she takes up in further books.

 Davy Hamilton is a musical prodigy. At the age of three she sat down at a piano and started playing perfectly, with no prior practice or training. Her life has always been set, she'll graduate from high school and attend Julliard, where she has already been accepted and do something musical with her life. Or so she thought. When her test results comeback saying she is a carrier for the HTS gene (the one that causes homicidal tendencies), everything changes. Suddenly everyone in her life is shunning her and she is forced to change schools and be around other maniacs with the kill gene. There had to be so kind of error, but she knows that that can never be fixed now and she must try to make the best out of this terrible situation. 
 Davy is that perfect girl with all the right friends and the hot popular boyfriend that most people fantasized about in high school. It was more than a little fun to watch the rich popular girl get knocked off her pedestal, though the more you come to care about her, the less fun it becomes. She's such a strong character, but she losses all her confidence when the gets labeled a carrier and she almost losses herself in the struggle to keep her shit together. I imagine everyone would go through a similar transformation if life as they knew it was ripped from their grasp. 
 Sean O'Rourke is that bad guy you momma always warned you about, or is he? He's the classic bad guy with a heart of gold, who has had the carrier label since a young age. He even has the carrier brand around his neck because society deemed one of his actions so dangerous that the world need to always be aware that he was a carrier. As much as I wanted to be irritated at him for being a bit cliche with the bad boy imagine, he's ability to always save Davy's ass melted my heart. Against his better judgement, he always comes to her rescue, while spouting those annoying "it's better if you stay away" sentiments. He gets over that eventually, but I wanted to punch him every time he even implied it. 
 This novel has all the things I look for when I'm reading, like good characters, interesting story, great writing, all that jazz, but what really gets me here is the philosophical question it presents about the characters. Are these people really violent deviants who are genetically coded to murder and pillage or do the majority act out based on the fact that society pushes them into that role? Yes, it's obvious that there are a number of carriers who truly deserve the label and are violent beyond reasonable understanding, but aren't we more than our genetic code? Don't we have the choice, in most cases, to act as violently as our hormones command us to or to stop and think about our actions? If society is going to treat us like shit regardless of if we fight our urges or not, why bother? These poor people are shunned and abused by society as a whole and even each other. You'd think they'd band together to create a support group, but there are too many who'd rather just accept the role society has placed them in and act out than fight the injustice. And things that are normally acceptable, like slapping your ex-boyfriend for being a jackass, are now a sign that you really are a carrier for the kill gene. 
 This is my first Sophie Jordan novel. I know, this chick manages to write books in all three of my favorite genres (young adult, new adult, and historical romance), so I don't know why it has taken me so long to get around to reading her novels, but if they are all this good, sign me up! This novel had very few issues for me, no love triangle, no instalove, and no cliffhanger. The ending doesn't wrap everything up in a nice little bow, but things end on a hopeful note which is all I ask for. My only minor issues are the cover and the length. Despite the fact that this is almost 400 pages, it felt short. When I flipped to the last page on Luna, I couldn't believe it was over. There was still so much more territory that needed to be covered! It's not that it felt underdeveloped, but I was just craving more. The cover also doesn't really match the story at all. I don't see at all how the levitating girl gives any indication of what this story is about. Maybe I'm wrong, but it just doesn't fit to me. 
 This is one of the more unique YA novels I've read it a while. Jordan manages to wholly captivate her with her story and leave them desperate for me. I will definitely be on the lookout for the next novel in this series, as well as anything else attached to this talented woman's name. If her new adult novels or her historical romance novels are half as good, I'm in for a real treat!

I'm rereading this book; I think I've read it about twenty times over the years. It never gets old, it never gets dated, and I love it just as much as the first time I picked it up years ago. 
 I started the Anita Blake series in an odd place; with Blue Moon, the 8th book. A friend received it as a birthday present from an unsuspecting Aunt who thought it was tame, for vampires. Who knew this book series was going to turn into the sex filled romp it did at that time? 
 I'm one of the few Anita Blake fans that never minded where this series went. Zombies, Vampires and murder were the beginning, and the whole succubus/incubus thing later was not a disappointment but a change I enjoyed. 
 But here is the earliest one, when Anita clung ferociously to what she believed in and didn't compromise it for anyone or anything. She's strong, confident and independent. As the books go on she loses a bit of the independence, but never really who she is. 
 This book contains one of the scarier villains of the series; Nikolaos. We see Anita solved the vampire murders, and a little of what she does as an animator. It is a great beginning to the series, and introduces some of the characters that become important later on. Edward of course, being one of them. Somehow, he's always among my favorites, perhaps because their is no tension between him and Anita. 
 If you like your vampires beautiful but dangerous, sad and enigmatic, then this series is for you. It's not all guns blazing, and it turns into a major love fest, be warned, but the first ten are fine if you aren't into that. Still, sometimes I wonder where Anita would have been if Philip had lived, but that's another story.

When I was a toddler/preschooler, I wanted to be the poky little puppy. I had poky little puppy pajamas, and got all the kids at daycare to play poky little puppy with me. This mostly involved getting down on our hands and knees and eating snow (it was winter in Minnesota, what can I say?).

This was a positive story. About a young girl who has a horrible past, but there are some happy incidents. In the start of the story she was an outcast with a goofy brother and a small family. By the end she is young woman with a full family backing her and an identity both culturally and personally.

A very cleverly written but frustrating book. I can imagine some people quitting on this book before they've even reached the middle, because both narrators are extremely narcissistic and a lot of the detail at the start seems unnecessary. However, persistent readers are rewarded, because the twist is interesting, and the second half of the book is more suspenseful. Who do you choose to root for as a reader? There are plenty of characters all working against each other (though none of them are easy to sympathise with). The strength of this novel is how complicated the crime at the heart of it is and how cleverly the author manipulates you. Near the end, all the little clues fit together to form to total picture and you just have to admire the scope of it, even if you sometimes want to pull your hair out with frustration because THINGS JUST NEVER SEEM TO GO WELL and you can't trust any of these characters.

** spoiler alert ** 
 After sleeping on it, I did downgrade my rating to 4 instead of 5 stars. The last 25-40% of this book really swept me up in the urgency, but the first 60%-ish, while still enjoyable, did not have the same level of intrigue and magic for me that the first book did. Maybe it's unfair to compare the two, and this book is still really enjoyable overall. I just found some bits of the plot and whatnot didn't fit together as smoothly as the first book did. 
 First, the blossoming romance between Blue and Gansey I'm finding a little hard to believe. Not just because I still like Adam best of the Raven Boys; I know Blue and Gansey appear to be fated to be together, but because of that it almost seems Stiefvater slacked a little on the making it feel real/like a choice Blue is making. Maybe that's intentional. I buy Gansey's attraction to Blue. But at the end of the first book, she seemed to still be enjoying/crushing on Adam. And although Adam's bargain with Cabeswater did change him, there just seemed to be little buildup between the end of the first book, where their relationship seems fine, to the beginning of the second book where suddenly Blue doesn't know what to do when Adam shows her affection. If this was supposed to be because of the Cabeswater thing, I don't think that was clear enough. (I think some amount of time passes between the end of the first book and the beginning of the second, but that's a pretty important bit of development to just skip over.) Then Adam kicks one box in anger and Blue's affection completely dissolves. 
 In my head I go back and forth on this: I would not expect Blue to stick around if Adam is showing signs of violence. I don't think people should stay in relationships hoping to "fix" the other person. And I like that Blue is sensible and headstrong. But it also kind of feels like because the relationship starts to get hard, Blue bails. And I hate that trope in all stories (movies, other books, TV shows, etc.) because it's unrealistic, yet it's EVERYWHERE. Later, she has a moment with Gansey where she describes that relationships should be like that--she knows exactly what to say, how to touch him and respond to his touch (get your heads out of the gutter). But I dunno...relationships, even platonic ones, are hard and full of misunderstandings and awkward moments, and that doesn't always mean they aren't right or worthwhile. Obviously Blue stops being attracted to Adam at some point, and that is a totally legitimate reason to no longer be with someone. But the underlying implication that her attraction stopped (or was facilitated by) the relationship getting hard kind of didn't sit right with me. (And by "hard", I don't mean the anger/outburst; again, violence is a legit reason to leave someone. I mean that she felt like she didn't understand him or what to do, and that seemed to be the larger determining factor. The thing about that is, everyone knows Adam is being affected by his sacrifice, but no one wants to talk to him about it or figure out if the negative effects are reversible, not in a "fixing" way, but in a "getting their friend back" way (or "seeing if it's possible to get their friend back").) 
 Moving on, all the stuff with Kavinsky felt a little...weird in the beginning. Like, the interactions with him and Ronan just didn't make sense. He's in the first book for about two seconds, and it's clear they race each other sometimes, but then he suddenly becomes such a major part in this second book. It was such an odd jump in significance that I figured out almost right away he had to know what Ronan was and either had similar abilities or knew someone who did. So when that part was finally revealed, it felt too late. Because without that additional connection between Ronan and Kavinsky, there was pretty much no convincing reason for Kavinsky to be constantly showing up and harassing Ronan (at least no convincing reason that had been previously made clear). 
 But I really loved the development we see in Ronan's character in this book, and in his abilities. Same goes for Adam, although some of that felt oddly paced as well. After he calls Gansey when he sees the woman in his apartment, I was like "Hi everyone, you know an entire house full of awesome and badass psychics; why don't you suggest Adam go visit them for help/advice?" Instead, no one talks to Adam about the apparition again, and no one wants to admit that Adam is falling apart--which on the one hand I don't mind, because teenagers and adults do that ALL THE TIME, but on the other hand it was pretty obvious and I can't imagine ALL of them not being concerned enough to do something. Later, when Adam DOES go to 300 Fox Way, there is a hint of conversation that it had to be by his own choice for it to work. Okay, fine, but someone still could have suggested it to him earlier, because nobody but the psychics knew that it had to be by his own choice. Then he could have refused, or gone there and had the psychics tell him it wasn't time yet, or whatever. 
 I was worried about halfway through that Adam was being set up to become the villain, and I'm so glad that doesn't seem to be the case after all. I love that he becomes the Magician instead. Ugh I just love Adam as a character so much. And goodness, if he ends up being bisexual I think my love will just shoot off the charts. I'm hoping he and Ronan will end up together, since Ronan seems interested in Adam. I'm hoping it won't end up being the "Oh, sorry, I'm straight, but we can still be friends" thing on Adam's part in the end. We need more representation of the B in LGBTQ (and also the T and Q, but I don't see any hints of that in this series yet), so I am really, really hoping that is where Stiefvater is planning on going. I also loved how she treated Ronan's sexuality--it was such a non-issue, it doesn't change his character at all and it wasn't causing him angst or anything. It's just one of many facts about Ronan Lynch. 
 Also, I forgot to mention in my review of the first book, but I LOOOOVE everyone at 300 Fox Way. An entire house! Of women psychics! Each of them very distinct but working together! And how Blue says that men just can't cut it in the Sargent household (or something to that effect)! Adore everything about it. 
 So my issue with this book was mostly the pacing; lots of action in the last part, but the first part was a little bumpy. But the characters and character development for the most part are still strong and compelling. I once again bought the next e-book, Blue Lily, Lily Blue, immediately. 
 ETA: I'm rereading this book right now (3/17/15), and I think I just read it too fast the first time. Some of my criticisms don't hold up on the re-read--I think Blue losing interest in her relationship with Adam makes more sense this time around, for example, AND her starting to become more attracted to Gansey also makes more sense. Just updating that here for my own future reference.

My Love Lies Bleeding (Hearts At Stake in the U.S) was a quick, fun read. Quirky characters, a close friendship, action aplenty, a smattering of romance, original vampire lore, hilarious banter and sarcastic comebacks made for a clean, entertaining YA read. 
 Solange is prophesied to take the throne of the vampire queen (much to her disgust) but first she must go through the bloodchange, the life threatening transition from human to vampire. With seven over-protective brothers, a kick-ass mother and a fierce best friend watching her back, how hard can it be? 
 Solange and Lucy share equal billing in My Love Lies Bleeding but for me, fiesty, funny Lucy steals the spotlight. Chapters alternate in first person between the two best friends and in my opinion this really worked. I've always liked the alternating viewpoints style of writing; when done well it gives added perspective and a real feel for the characters' personalities, so kudos to Alyxandra Harvey for pulling this off. The romance between Lucy & Nicholas and Solange & Kieran is sweet and funny, the tension simmers but it stays quite innocent making this a great read for the younger teen. 
 The original take on vampire lore was something else I really enjoyed; The Host, Hounds and the evil Hel Blar, and what's a vampire tale without vampire hunters? Bring on the Helios Ra. It did take me a while to get all the names and affiliations straight in my head but it definitely made things interesting. 
 At only 256 pages a little more detail would have made this one a lot more satisfying, a bit like potato chips really; 'moreish' but not very filling. As I happen to love potato chips I'm keen to read the next installment in the Drake Chronicles due for release 1st July 2010. Blood Feud is Logan's story (one of Solange's brothers) but I'm keeping my fingers crossed that we'll also see more of Solange and Lucy and their love interests.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I liked how this started out. The narrator was fresh and the narration was succinct, the world equally fresh and interesting. Pierce doesn't dally with his writing, isn't wordy, though still succeeds in creating a rich world. The beginning was, honestly, my favourite. I appreciated that Darrow started as a compliant slave and was thrust into the world of politics and resistance by dramatic forces. Although I think I might have appreciated a bit more world set up before the plot catalyst. 
 But as the book developed, I found myself getting increasingly lost. I feel like most of this is because of the narrator, unfortunately. I don't think he does a great job differentiating between characters, and so it was difficult to tell who was speaking. This is no fault of Pierce's, obviously, but it did make it difficult to engage in this book. 
 I got a little confused with the rules of the game - Titus is executed for cruelty, but didn't all of these golds kill another person to get to this point in the game? And other subsequent executions aren't treated with the same horror and taboo, at least not consistently. Also, as Darrow was preparing for life as a Gold, he is educated on their lifestyle, which is painted as ruthless, cold, cunning, and very elitist. But the second the real game starts, this entire history fades away, as the Gold players are shown to be pretty normal. It's not clear (at least to me) if this history only applied to Gold adults, or if this was a major inconsistency. 
 I was also a little bothered that Darrow's espionage was reduced to a few Red curse words. I feel like after his surgeries, it stopped being a novel of espionage and became just one long battle. I would imagine his position in Gold society would be a little more precarious than that. 
 I'm not sure if my disassociation with the book was a major factor, but the subsequent "reveals" were not very climactic for me. I think it may have had something also to do with the pacing, which upon looking over some other reviews of the book, was a common complaint. It started out well paced, then slowed way, way down at the "35% mark," then sped up WAY too much by the end (I find it very interesting that Darrow's confrontation with the proctors is practically nil, a sum up of one sentence). 
 Overall, I enjoyed it, though I think I might have had a richer experience if I'd read the physical book.

She has this habit of hating herself, hating for being born a girl, hating for being born at all sometimes. She had this constant need to always apply lipstick and nail polish, only for her to peel her nail polish off every time she's nervous. Even though Kellan doesn't really have a presence, just his name sets something off. You hate that it happened to her but there's nothing to be done. The sad reality is it's too late for her to report it unless other people step up which they probably won't considering the circumstances in the book.

In each chapter opening there were small cracks. They just looking interesting there isn't much else to that. Writing? It was three-dimensional. We get to know Romy in different ways: victim and fake. She continues to carry this sort of facade around everyone that she is fine and still standing but her character literally breaks down as the story progresses that forces her to confront the truth again.

 There isn't a whole lot of pulse pounding action, but there isn't ever a dull moment either. The storyline was engaging and I kept reading because I wanted to find out what would happen, but also just because I liked spending time in these worlds (the jinni caves! the library!) and with these people. The romances and side characters are predictable, but I found that to be a comforting plus. Zayele and Najwa are very different, but both equally likable. 
 Goodreads shows this is book one of a series, and while I would definitely read a sequel, I also think the story wraps up well as a standalone. 
 Bottom line 
 I love these kinds of solid stories. They're my go-to type of book when I'm looking for something that will make me happy and isn't too taxing. I can see this appealing to a wide audience as it's perfect for Goddess Girls readers looking for something a little older but still engaging enough for adult readers who enjoy middle grade books.

 This is an older book of Ms. Eden's, but recently someone pointed out that I hadn't read it yet. I've seen many reviews rave about how this is the best Romantic Suspense ever, and since it's only $.99, I had to give it a shot. Well, I've read it now, and I agree. 
 Ms. Eden has a knack for getting into the killer's head, and it never feels forced. She can make the killer someone you have multiple page time with, and you never even realize it's him until the end. I thought I had this one figured out. I've read a lot of her books, I like to think I know how she'll pull it off. And I was wrong. 
 FBI Special Agent Monica Davenport has survived hell. And she's stronger for it. So what if her nickname is Ice. She might not like it, but she cultivated that icy exterior on purpose. 
 Luke Dante can see through her. He knows she isn't only Ice. He sees too much though, and it frightens her. That's why she left him after they hooked up several years back. He made her feel too much. 
 They're on the same team now though, a special team for hunting down serial killers. Just being in the same room becomes hard for her. She can't stop thinking about how it was with them. Luke wants her to let him in. He's known since the day they met that she was his woman. Now he just needs to convince her to give them a shot. That's hard to do when bodies keep turning up. 
 The main focus of the investigation is on the killer, but what they aren't seeing is that the killer is closer than they think. And his end game is Monica. 
 I loved Luke. But I really thought I was going to hate Monica. I ended up really liking her though. She was strong, tough, never TSTL, and for once, didn't use herself as bait. I was sure she would, but I was surprised. 
 I can't wait to dive into the next book in the series. I think since it's only 3 books, it would be a good one to binge read. I know what my weekend will have in store. 
 This book has it all. A capable and likeable heroine, a sexy hero who wants to protect the heroine, and an intense roller coaster ride of a plot. It's an older series, so you can glom it all at once, I know I will be.

For a pretty straight forward story, I had a lot of thoughts tumbling around in my head while listening to it. First, for some reason, all I could think of was a mash-up of the movies Heathers and Mean Girls (even though none of the characters were necessarily of the Plastic variety). Second, I vacillated from hating the book and characters to loving them to hating them. Third, the audio was also a love/hate. The narrator sounded like a spoiled brat who "really didn't have time to be reading this but whatever I'll do it anyway" kind of voice and attitude. While her Kardashian vocalizations made me want to punch her at times, it grew on me. And, it fit well with the story and the minor characters. Lastly, I am forever thankful that I did not grow up in the age of social media. I cannot fathom what kind of teenager/person I would be and how I would have managed my NKOTB crushes at the time. Quite frankly, it would have been embarrassing. 
 The boy band in question is The Ruperts. Five British boys, all named Rupert, tried out for a talent show individually. The music execs saw dollar signs and put them all together. It was easy to see what, ahem, 'direction' the author was headed with this band. Flash forward a few years and The Ruperts are making money hand over fist with their mediocre music and have amassed a large following of boy banders. The story centers on five girls who met through fan sites, Twitter, and Tumblr who meet at the New York hotel where the Ruperts are staying for a Thanksgiving show. Since they don't have tickets, this was the next best thing. The plan was to just hang out, maybe stalk a few hotel rooms and see if they can find them. What that evolves into is one of the Ruperts (don't worry, he's the least popular, cute and talented one) becomes a kidnapping victim of the girls. And that is the good part of his day. 
 It took me a long time to get there, but I really ended up enjoying this book for its social commentary, a blend of dark comedy/caper hijinks, and utter disregard for morals and ethics. I truly hope this doesn't ever happen, but the way it plays out is something I can see happening. One last thing I should mention is the use of the F-bomb. It's pretty prevalent throughout the story (as are other words) and I am sure some will think them excessive, and I can see that, but it worked for the story and the girls in it.
A more enjoyable story than a dysfunctional family should be. I liked how despite the neglect and addiction issues, you could tell she still loved her family.

Fabulous debut in historical romance. The premise is one I've never seen before. The heroine, Martha, is recently widowed. Her estate will pass to her brother-in-law unless she is pregnant with her deceased husband's heir. She is not pregnant, but realizes that if she can quickly become pregnant, and the child is born male, she can avoid being disinherited. And she knows her husband wanted very badly to prevent his brother from inheriting. (Over the course of the novel, we learn why.) So she determines to get pregnant by someone suitable, fast. 
 She picks someone and hires him for the task and what follows are some of the most hilariously unsexy sex scenes ever written. I usually skim the sex scenes in romance novels because they're just the same thing over and over again--when it comes to romance novels, I'm all about the character development, romantic tension, and witty banter. But these sex scenes were so different from anything I've ever seen before that I was fascinated and read every word. These scenes take every standard romance trope and turn them upside down. Take this dryly written passage, which had me in stitches: 
 "'Is that Irish linen?' she said of his shirt, just to be saying something, and 'Yes, in fact, it is,' he answered before lifting it, a bit slowly, over his head. 
 "Clearly he was expecting to be admired. He would be used to it, well-proportioned man that he was. His musculature altogether outpaced what she had seen in Mr. Russell [her former husband], though Mr. Russell had set no very difficult standard to surpass. That mattered to some women. Muscles and so forth. Those taut flat ones across his stomach, for instance. Or the ones that stood out on his arms. Women who didn't place the proper priority on a man's character had doubtless taught him to be vain of his physique, and even a woman of principle could enjoy, on some aesthetic level, the picture he made with his shirt removed. 
 "Then he let his pantaloons fall, and that was the end of the enjoyment." 
 You may notice that the writing is exquisite. It's that way throughout the entire book, and I've never read any historical novel that felt truer to period, especially in its dialogue. I felt like I was reading Jane Austen again, albeit a much racier Jane Austen. 
 Does this book have any faults? In my mind, no, it doesn't. I absolutely loved it. But I can see why it's getting some negative reviews along with the folks who are raving about it. Some readers are bothered by the fact that the heroine is doing something sinful. I understand that objection. But for me, that makes the book way more interesting. There are moral gray areas here. She's committing a sin to prevent a much greater sin from taking place, and the moral gray areas are deeply explored throughout the course of the book. Trust the author. She's going somewhere with this. 
 A few readers find it boring. I get that too--although I disagree with them. It's a slow paced, somewhat cerebral book. The early sex scenes are deliberately unsexy. I find them hilarious and fascinating, but if a reader wants titillation, she's not going to get it in those early scenes. 
 This is a story about a sort of heroine who isn't written about very often--the type of woman who has to fall in love with a man before she feels physically attracted to him. If you love books with moral complexity, emotional honesty and exquisite language, this is a book to be savored. I normally prefer fast-paced books, but for a novel this enjoyable, I have infinite patience. Highly recommended, for the reader who can appreciate it.

"Ready Player One" is an awesome book to pick up is you want to let your geek out. 
 The plot feels exactly like a video game, and Wade is the ultimate quester. The story is an epic adventure packed with classic video game bosses and challenges and a touch of dystopian/post-apocalyptic themes. The part of me that fangirls over everything Nintendo (Pokemon is my life) went wild over all the geekery that went on in this book. 
 Cline brought up the best parts of gaming as well as the worst. The main characters, most notably Wade and Artemis, use OASIS to create versions of themselves that are more physically appealing, confident, brave, badass, etc. They create versions of themselves that aren't ... losers. This is something I'm sure all gamers -- and bloggers -- can relate to: the amazing freedom of being anonymous. On the other hand, Cline brings up the all-consuming nature of video game addiction and the horrible lack of ... realnesss. The characters find themselves wondering Do I really know him/her? What's missing? 
 I was pleasantly surprised by the romance in "Ready Player One." I didn't expect romance at all, but I'd never say no to a few kissy scenes. I found it really interesting how Wade falls fast for Art3mis, but she's convinced he loves her avatar not the real her. 
 Art3mis is my favorite character. She's a major badass, and she knows how to rock a pair of Converse. I've always hated the stereotype that only men enjoy gaming. I hate that so many women in games are sexualized and clad in chainmail bikinis or something equally disgusting. 
 As much as I enjoyed the video game geekery, "Ready Player One" had a few things that just didn't work for me. 
 The 80's references totally flew over my head. I'm a late 90's baby. I don't think it's possible to get the full effect of the plot unless you have a relatively good understanding of the 80's. 
 The pacing drove me crazy. The first part of the book is a huge info dump before the actual plot kicks in. From there, I'd read a small section of plot that spans a short amount of time, then there's be a huge time-lapse and the gaps would be filled in with another info dump. At times, I felt totally disoriented, and I didn't enjoy that feeling.
