...and it reminds me that my mistake was not in speaking out. 
 No, my mistake was staying silent for too long. 
 Wow. Wow. Wow. So, it's been a while since I've written a review, but I managed to find time to write one for this book because it was awesome. I have to say, this book did surprise me, since the first few pages started out with me hating the main character, Chelsea Knot. The book starts out with Chelsea at her best friend, Kristen's, party. There, she accidentally stumbles into two guys making out, and goes on to out one of those boys. She was immature and seemed to disregard the feelings of other people completely. At least, that was the impression I got from her. She did, however, redeem herself very quickly in the beginning of the book, by righting a wrong. 
 Thus, begins her "spiritual" journey of staying quiet so as not to ruin other people's life. She's taken a vow of silence. Until when? She doesn't know exactly. And why? She's not really sure, either. She just knows that for some reason, when she speaks, she somehow manages to create trouble. Needless to say, I got frustrated at her silence, because she gets bullied and harassed by her peers, people who were her friends before she told on the boys who beat up Noah, and all I wanted was for her to yell and bite back with the thoughts in her head. But, I admit, it took a whole lot of patience to read through, so I must imagine how much patience Chelsea must have had, how much restraint it took to stay silent. It was a refreshing take to read about, and it had never occurred to me how powerful communication can be through silence. 
 I wonder if she's thinking what I am. How it seems so impossible that someone could look at them, see how plainly they care for each other, and find anything ugly or shameful or worthy of hatred for it, when all I see is something beautiful. 
 I loved the characters. They were unique, fun, sarcastic, and the type of people you want to hang out with all the time. Well, the new friends Chelsea makes, not her old ones. Andy, Dex, and Lou balanced out Chelsea's silence perfectly by offering humor and playfulness to the conversations. Asha, the girl Chelsea meets while in detention was the perfect friend. She let Chelsea into her world and allowed Chelsea to somehow forgive herself in the process. She also helped out Chelsea with her geometry, and I found all the geometric puns throughout the book hilarious. And there's Sam. He was so wonderful and sweet and complemented Chelsea's newfound journey in a way Chelsea probably didn't even know was possible. I was rooting for him the moment he ran his hand through his dark hair. He's just so sweet and attentive, I really loved him. There are also Chelsea's old friends, who weren't the people I want to hang out with, but just as memorable. Specifically, Kristen. She and Chelsea had been best friends since eighth grade. It's always sad to see a friendship end, so I felt Chelsea's emptiness there. But Kristen proved to be the nastiest, by throwing away years of friendship for something so immature. 
 Aside from the characters and the plot, what I really loved about the book was Chelsea's character development. Granted, a lot of other novels have great character development, but this one stood out to me in particular, because Chelsea started out as such a shallow and mean girl, that I just couldn't see myself ever coming to like her character. But, I was wrong. She had always been second in place to Kristen, but there was something empowering about Chelsea's newfound independence from Kristen. Chelsea becomes her own person, not even realizing Kristen had always underhandedly been controlling her life. She finds herself through her vow of silence, and what it really means to speak up. She grows into a great and lovable character and her pain and regret is deep enough for me to forgive her and want her to become a stronger, better person. I also loved how in the beginning, at the party scene, Chelsea's mind had been written to be rash and impulsive. When she had walked in on Noah and his boyfriend, she hadn't stopped to think about the consequences or what might happen. She just spoke. But, as the book progresses, she really begins to think before she speaks, and there was something so beautiful about the way it developed as I read. It was great to see. 
 A lot of issues are brought up in the book, namely gay people, discrimination, and school harassment. They were dealt with in a manner that showed how these issues really happened in real life, or in this case, high school. It's sad to think these things actually happen, but they do. All in all, I loved this book, and when that last page came, I was screaming for more.

I am not a fan of military Science Fiction. If I was I think I would have loved this book.

 This series starts after things have settled down after the return of magic. Magic powers randomly manifest in a small section of the population, much like mutant powers. There seems to only be about ten different powers that can manifest. You don't see how the world reacts, only see it after the fact. 
 The main character is already in the military, and he manifests a rare power. He finds out that the military has a great deal more knowledge than it has made public. There is a lot of intentional grey vs grey morality, so if you get annoyed that the "good guys" seem to be violent hypocrites don't think the author is a fascist, they are supposed to seem like violent hypocrites. 
 Several things presented as fact seemed unlikely to me. I couldn't see Americans being okay with the forced conscription of all American citizens who manifest powers or them being okay with the disappearance and rumored execution of everyone conscripted who has the most potentially harmful powers. An Islamic superstate is somehow created in the Middle East and Europe. It executes everyone who manifests powers. I could not believe that any EU countries could be conquered especially when the EU would have magical powers supplementing their regular military. 
 If those things won't bother you and you are a fan of military Sci-Fi, you will love this book.

Celeste Price is a sexual predator - only attracted to 14-year old boys. She's constructed her entire life to help her fulfil her fantasies, from the strict skin care regime that keeps her looking younger than her 26 years, to her shame marriage that looks Hallmark perfect to outsiders, to her profession. Celeste is an eighth grade teachers and she views the boys in her classroom as targets, not students. 
 To say this is a disturbing book is an understatement. The book is narrated from Celeste's point of view, so readers spend 300 pages inside her psychotic head. She is unrepentant, unreflective and thinks about little else then the erotic potential of 14-year olds. Usually, I'm a big chatterbox when it comes to what I'm reading... but how do you casually bring up this book in polite conversation? 
 Many other readers have made the obvious comparison to LolitaLolita. And it's true that both Celeste Price and Humbert Humbert are manipulators and predators, but Humbert suffers from a level of self-loathing that Celeste could never understand. She is a textbook psychopath, totally lacking in empathy and totally in love with herself. In the end, Humbert suffers. Celeste is made briefly inconvenienced. 
 In my mind, the book that Tampa is most like is J.G. Ballard's CrashCrash. Both deal with sexual fixations that society deems inappropriate and ooky. And both books dwell on that fixation to the point of pure, mind-numbing boredom. Celeste was impossible to care about and since the rest of the characters were viewed through her monstrous perspective, they were impossible to care about too. The two boys Celeste sleeps with are mere objects, her husband is a mindless oaf and the other teachers in the school are naive complainers. 
 But the intention of this book is not for the reader to like it. I imagine. I hope. DNF thus no rating - just an explanation as to why I dnf'd 
 Originally posted at For What It's Worth on 2/20/15 - http://www.fwiwreviews.net/2015/02/re... 
 :It takes almost a herculean effort for me to DNF a book. No matter what's going on, I feel compelled to see how it ends. Even if I just skim. But this book made me so mad that I just couldn't continue. 
 Let me backtrack a little. 
 I grabbed this book off Amazon Vine for review because it seemed like the fun, chick-lit type of book that I enjoy most. Within the first few chapters I already knew the writing style wasn't for me with the abrupt POV changes, and almost all the interactions are telling not showing, but I did enjoy the characters so I let it go to see where it might lead. 
 Then the hero starts making little comments about "bratty women" and how Amanda's ass is big enough for his hand - alluding to spanking. Hey, I'm fine with that kink. I've read a lot worse and enjoyed it. It was the "brat" comments that irked me. But again, whatever...the romance as Chase tries to woo a reluctant Amanda into giving him a chance was cute and sometimes it takes a while to develop a character. 
 Then I get to the sex part and NO. NO. NO. I have a thing about safe sex and discussing protection beforehand - not in the throes of passion where you are distracted by six pack abs. I've read many books where there's no mention of condom use or they equate birth control with safe sex. Which is not the same thing. Not getting pregnant doesn't mean being protected from STD's. Blah...blah...getting ranty now... 
 So anyway - this book crosses a line that just had me fuming. I've since read multiple 1 and 2 star reviews on Goodreads that mostly concern the hero and the spanking element of this book (I never made it that far so I won't comment), so I'll discuss what was my deal breaker scene that no one else (that I saw) mentioned. 
 They are having sex for the first time. This is where Chase tries to talk Amanda out of using a condom. 
 I'm going to quote the passage that pushed me over the edge, it's a spoiler, so I'll give you the option to click the button if you wish to see it - or ignore if you still want to pick the book up to read. 
 "Amanda," he said in a rush, "I use one of these every time. I don't want to use one now. I promise I'm disease-free. Are you protected and safe, and do you trust me?" Chase didn't actually care if she was protected or not. He couldn't think of anything he'd like better than holding the shotgun at the wedding. He didn't really care if she was safe either: the seed had already been planted in his mind that he'd be willing to die for her. But her trusting him meant everything.  
 AREYOUF*CKINGKIDDINGMERIGHTNOW? No Amanda - you should not trust this man. 
 So, epic irresponsible handling of sexual safety by the hero - and a heroine who is too distracted by a hot body to think clearly. That's a total turn off for me so I didn't continue. 
 There are several 4-5 star reviews for the book and those reviewers seemed to like the witty banter between the characters, the alpha hero that brings out Amanda's naughty side, a full figured heroine and humor - so ya know - I just can't recommend this book myself but to each his own and maybe it will work better for you. 
 Some people can overlook things like that but it just takes away all my respect for the hero and ruins the romance for me.

I'm a big fan of anything Alice in Wonderland related, I have read book and manga adaptations, played games, watched movies/anime... I even have a Cheshire Cat phone case. 
 You can probably imagine how excited I was when I found this book. 
 I'm no mathematician, but: 
 one of my favourite stories + my favourite genre (horror) + great reviews = GREATNESS 
 Except, it was a major letdown. 
 *YOU ARE NOW ENTERING SPOILER-LAND* 
 It started out so well with Alice in a mental institution after her trip to Wonderland turned out to be more sinister than one could imagine. We also meet mentally unstable Hatcher, her axe wielding, serial killer "roomie" who she communicates with through a mouse hole. 
 After a fire breaks out and they manage to escape, they find out the Jabberwocky (Hatcher's psychically linked monster BFF) is also free. Bad news because, you know, the Jabberwocky likes to drink blood and make grown men cry for their mothers. 
 Bummer. 
 They both know they can't let the monster go all "All you can eat buffet" on the people of the Old City so they have to kill it. 
 So far so good, but things quickly deteriorated. 
 First of all, Hatcher couldn't remember his own wife or daughter, but he could navigate through a massive city with ease. And I'm just sitting here like, I need one of those horse blinder things just to make sure I don't get lost on my way home. 
 Like so: 
 Secondly, we find out that the city is controlled by bosses who trade in girls, namely The Caterpillar, The Rabbit and The Walrus and Cheshire. I kept imagining these as mascots for some sport, completed with the outfit and it got really confusing. We're told that these furry mascots men are ruthless, powerful psychopaths who controll thugs and soldiers and whatnot. 
 So imagine my confusion when these baddies were easier to kill than a baby. Seriously. 
 The first boss to meet its maker was the Caterpillar. He owned a strip club/brothel (with security guards), yet after about two pages of dialogue, Alice pretty much reaches out and slashes his throat. 
 Alice and Hatcher walk some more, they come across the Walrus (the famous evil dude who eats girls alive whilst raping them), Hatcher goes to fight him and you just know shit's about to go down with his axe BUT OH LOOK HERE'S A GIANT FUCKING RABBIT WHO'LL EAT THE WALRUS INSTEAD SO NO EPIC FIGHT SCENE FOR YOU SUCKERS. 
 Then they walk some more to find the Rabbit. Now the Rabbit was the main goddamn reason Alice was in a mental hospital because he drugged and raped her when she was 16. He was supposed to be the worst of the worst, a person who haunted Alice's nightmares for 10 years. We get to his place which is LINED WITH GUARDS because the Rabbit knows Alice is coming to kill him. They also meet Alice's traitor ex-best friend, Dor, who handed her over to the Rabbit for money, yet Dor was the one who got stuck with him. She's now channeling her inner grandma even though she's only 26 (i.e. she's weak, old, and barely standing on her own feet). 
 So here we are. The long awaited showdown of Alice vs the Rabbit. Anything can happen. get ready for the battle of the centu... OH NEVERMIND, GRANNY DOR WITH HER ARTHRITIS JUST STRANGLED THE RABBIT AND ALICE LITERALLY NEVER HAD TO LIFT A FINGER. 
 This made me so angry that even though I was around 90% into the book, I didn't give a damn anymore and refused to finish it. 
 Such a letdown....

Cassandra Clare has written a beautiful, perfect love story, it's just such a pity that not much else in this trilogy is worthy of the same commendation. 
 Series rating: 3.5 stars 
 Clockwork Princess rating: 3 stars 
 This was a hard review to write, and for fans of this trilogy it might be hard to read. But I'll say up front that for all my criticism I did find reading this series entertaining, and some of the characters are truly wonderful and memorable. It's just that those things are not enough for me to overlook the rest of the issues that I had. 
 Having read the trilogy over the course of a few months I strongly feel that there was a story worth telling in there somewhere, but not enough to justify a whole set of three books. There are some beautiful passages and incredible quotes, Clare has a real flair for 'quotable' phrases. But there is so much about the series that is unnecessary. It had me wondering about the context in which it was written. I don't know enough about Clare and the Shadowhunters fandom to say for sure, but at times this series felt like the kind of fan-service found in anime series that have their own in-jokes, and information is included for a purpose outside of the actual plot of this series. 
 When reading a novel readers are happy to accept one or maybe two 'miraculous' events, but when the impossible becomes possible over and over again those miracles lose their narrative power. That's how I felt reading the Infernal Devices, by the end I could no longer care about the dangers or risks the characters were exposed to because I just assumed that Clare would invent some 'miracle' to save them or defeat an enemy, or turn the tide in every single battle. 
 For that reason, amongst many, I won't be reading any more of Clare's works. I think it is unfair to those who love her work for me to read something that I know I am not going to enjoy. That's not why I read, and I don't want to set out to diminish other's enjoyment. 
 From here on out there are spoilers for the plot of Clockwork Princess, please only read this section if you have already read Clockwork Princess, and be mindful of others who may not have finished the trilogy when commenting. 
  
 The epilogue is the main reason my rating for this book is only 3 stars. It was completely unnecessary in anything except a fanfic written to assuage the fans who had held out hope for the Jessa ship. The reminiscing about Will's life was painful, as though nothing in his life would change and grow: he would forever be the literature loving, duck hating, Tessa obsessed teenager, who writes terrible joke poetry, even as his grandchildren surrounded him. That whole section made me feel as though the dimensions I had seen in Will's character were paper thin and designed to create the perfect 'book boyfriend' with just enough flaws to make him a project for redemption. 
 Jem's section of the epilogue had me groaning in frustration. First he becomes a Silent Brother by way of a 'miracle' and then he leaves the brotherhood by way of another one. All throughout this series Clare declares that a very specific scenario is impossible, she puts clear rules in place, and then almost immediately breaks them. Now this is forgivable in the case of kind-hearted Charlotte keeping an eye on Will's parents for the little boy in her care, even though it's technically against the law. Perhaps I could also forgive one 'this shouldn't be possible' moment, but Tessa's angel transformation, her existence, the angel in the pendant, the demons in the automatons, the portal, Jem as a Silent Brother, Jem as not a Silent Brother, Jessamine as a ghost, everyone in the institute pairing off as a happy convenient couple despite family grudges or difference in station, etc means that all the 'miracles' big and small become hard to stomach and cheapens the effect of these impossible things becoming possible. As a reader being told 'a gentleman could never love a parlour maid' and then finding out he actually does is not unusual, and disbelief can be suspended. 
 But when you are told that all the things above are impossible and yet they happen with an alarming frequency, by the time I got to the epilogue I'd given up on the 'rules' of the universe Clare has created. She seems to create rules for the express purpose of moving her characters into particular scenarios. The result is beautiful interaction and tension and love stories, and a plot that is a battlefield of cliches. 
 It's particularly telling that the book continues for so long after the 'bad guy' is defeated. My biggest frustration with this series was that the plot seemed like an afterthought. The Infernal Devices that give the trilogy its name never felt like a credible threat, and the characters were far more interested in each other than in solving the 'mystery' in any meaningful manner. The only reason Mortmain was defeated was one of those 'miracles' I mentioned earlier, if you take that possibility out then Charlotte would have been responsible for the death of the handful of woefully unprepared people that were fighting. 
 The reason they didn't have backup was a plot line I absolutely hated; the Consul's abrupt transition to a misogynistic coward. I couldn't suspend my disbelief for that, the idea that someone who had apparently been a reasonable leader would suddenly become so short sighted as to endanger their world to such an extent, and that no one else would dare disobey him was absurd. Especially as 'everyone breaks the law' is repeated over and over throughout the series. Would there be no one sympathetic to Charlotte who was willing to risk missing a meeting to save the world? Or perhaps not because that would introduce new characters to the final battle who weren't part of the love stories that needed to be progressed.  
 Finally, I'll mention here for posterity the final writing quirk that bothered me, it's totally petty, but I can't get it off my mind: 
 Hair curling at people's temples or the nape of their neck due to sweat or humidity. This happens dozens of times throughout all 3 books, I understand the impulse to create some kind of visual atmosphere, but it is repeated so often that it becomes redundant. Are Shadowhunters really so sweaty?!

I think this may be the most boring one out of all of the arrangement series. Don't get me wrong, it was still a really great read but it didn't live up to the others, in my opinion. 
 Since the very beginning we have been waiting to hear Sean's secrets and what really happened regarding his wife and child. I had my assumptions, and after #6 we had a bit more of a clue but I actually felt disappointed in what was the truth. It felt like such a huge build up to something not quite as shocking as I expected. 
 "I'm not your savior, Avery. There's no knight, no horse, no happy ending - not with me. That shit isn't real." 
 As you can see, Sean is still struggling with his feelings in the beginning. No matter what Avery says and how much she tries to force Sean in to seeing they could have something beautiful together, he is just too closed off. I'm still liking Avery, although her job situation is starting to irritate me. She so desperately wants her and Sean to have a life together but she isn't willing to bend to accommodate his wants and needs too. In the sense of giving up her job with Black.. 
 "No one saved me. I've fallen so far that I can't see the way out anymore. I'm at the bottom of Hell and I found you." 
 The author mentioned in the blurb that there was a more shocking scene than we are used to in this instalment but I didn't think it was so bad. Perhaps I just used to darker reads these days but I felt it was a really important scene to include. We know Sean has his issues and we know that he has certain needs and wants when it comes to his sex life. He needs control. There is a scene here where it demonstrates that in a really strong way but after that, we get the total opposite and it was just so interesting to see both sides to Sean. 
 "I want you so broken that you can't trust yourself. I want you to give all of yourself to me." 
 I do love this series.. I really do but I am having a hard time wanting to continue it. I love Sean and Avery's story but I'm beginning to feel as if we are going through unnecessary stuff with these two. I don't want to end up being invested in a series that is being dragged out for no reason. All good things must come to an end and I think this one is getting there.

This is one of my most anticipated books this year. I've always loved Trip. Layla, though, not so much, but she's still likeable. 
 I remember I wasn't that carried away with book 1. The reason, I assumed, is because everyone spoke hormones, you know, being teenagers and all. But that's fine. I might not like it, but it's real. Contemporary is about realness. 
 Book 2 is my favorite. It's easy to see why. Trip was on his way to be a mega movie star. Their reunion was sweet. The fact that they were not together added extra pluses into the ratings. You can feel the tension and for once, their banters were not childish. Guarded, but still sweet. 
 I've expected the finale book to be much more different than this. I expected the book to open up with how Layla had been coping up. I expected her to be a little bit tougher, more mature, bitter even. She's allowed to be bitter. It's life. Instead, she remains the same. (in my opinion) 
 The first three chapters were still okay. But then, right after they were back together, everything (as Layla herself pointed out) went back to being seventeen. Even Layla's narrative turned seventeen. I skipped most of the interaction between Layla and Trip, Layla and her friends, Layla and Trip, Layla and Trip. Trip, in my opinion, took the hardest fall here. I didn't get his Hollywood persona. 
 Anyway, though it was rather disappointing for me, I still love the idea of the story. High school sweetheart's theme is my favorite. It reminds me of my youth (it also reminds me of how old I am now). For this reason alone, this book earns two stars. The half star is for Torrest's copyright page. If you have her copy, go back and read it. It rocks. Really rocks. I love her for that.

I couldn't put this book down. Sports! Friends forming a family! Dramatic misfits! Such cute (with that I mean hardcore) characters! 
 First, let us get this out of the way: this book sucks the first pages. Probably the first two chapters, or even longer. But do not give up on it, because the rest of the book is completely worth it. So is the rest of the series, which I read in less than twenty-four hours. 
 This is a book about family, but not only the biological one. It is about the importance of support and friends, how they can change your life and you change theirs. "The foxhole court" family is not perfect; they are a bunch of misfits thrown together with only one common goal: to be champions & make people stop laughing at their Exy team. That is: except for Andrew, because he is an uncaring, high (and protective) jerk. 
 "The Palmetto State University Foxes were a team of talented rejects and junkies because Wymack only recruited athletes from broken homes. His decision to turn the Foxhole Court into a halfway house of sorts was nice in theory, but it meant his players were fractured isolationists who couldn't get along long enough to get through a game." 
 And yes... this is a sports book about a sport that does not exists outside of "The foxhole court"s cover. Exy is completely fictional, but seems like a mix between lacrosse and... Rugby, perhaps? A more violent twist to the sport anyway. It seems like making up a sport was preferable in how certain rules and the whole sports culture had to be different from what we know, for this book to be what it is. We already have Quidditch, so why not Exy. Easier name to spell too. Fictional sport or not, this book has an authentic i-will-do-anything-to-be-the-best feel and passion, which I like. Nothing better than jealousy and threats to motivate you. 
 There is no romance in this book, for reasons you will realize if reading the rest of the series. I found this really refreshing? There is a lot going on with backstories, trying to get these fucked up teens on a straight path and be sort of friends/teammates. There is definitely enough drama to go around anyway. A lot like the raven cycle, this book has the notion of a coming romance, but is too busy that it is of importance. 
 "Hope was a dangerous, disquieting thing, but he [Neil] thought perhaps he liked it." 
 I will be the first to admit that this book got some problems, much like the characters in it. I love "The Foxhole Court" and its characters anyway, with flaws and all. Uncommonly, the series only gets better from here, and at the end of the first book, it was pretty exciting already. It was an easy read, but with dept as well. And with a squad you will love.

 This is definitely one of the better comics I've read lately and probably my favorite Superman comic. Mark Millar works the original Superman lore and characters into the Russian setting and it works so well. I really enjoyed the moral issues Superman faces and it was definitely interesting to see how he works to justify and spread the communist ideal across the world but also has to confront what to do with people who disagree. The art in this was fantastic, it had a kind of retro vibe to it that I loved a lot. This was very well done and executed wonderfully and I appreciated that this Elseworld didn't feel unbelievable or corny. All around just a great comic.

 When I first set my eyes on the blurb, I was taken in by the amazing possibilities and sure promises that this will be a great read. I was looking forward to be reading this and was sure that this will be one of the dystopian books that I love. However, I'm disappointed (as I've been a lot lately, not sure why) when I finished this book. I had a disastrous experience from reading Aimee Carter's previous work, The Goddess Test. I thought I could get The Goddess Test out of my mind so that I can give Pawn the chance it deserves. I thought surely the author has become better in her works and will not make the same error in judgement like she did in The Goddess Test. I was wrong. 
 The Goddess Test haunts my mind as I'm reading Pawn. I couldn't help but dissect and analyse every bit of the story. I started to see similarities in the flaw of the characters and in the story itself. I really tired to give this book a chance but in the end it fails to entice me and thus gave me another bad experience from this author. 
 First and foremost, what kind of name is KITTY? Had anyone seen that coming? How absurd it is that a heroine and savior of this glorious universe is named KITTY freakin DOE?? You've heard of Batman, Superman, Wonder Woman and yeah, Catwoman but Kitty? Look it's a bird, it's a plane, it's.....KITTY! *sigh 
 It's kind of hard to take someone so seriously when her name is "Kitty". Also, that name sound so kinky!. I thought it suit her well when she wanted to work at the club and become a prostitute. 
 So this book has the same character flaw as from The Goddess Test. It is one flaw that I absolutely loathe and get sick of! Kitty was constantly feeling bad for herself. She started whining from the very start of the book. I might be able to handle it if she had not continued on for chapters onwards. Better part of the book was spent with reading about how Kitty is feeling sorry for herself and how the people around her keep saying things to make her feel better. I mean, cut it out! Stop whining! I cannot stand it! 
 Did I mentioned she was a selfish b*tch? 
 I had tried to steal that orange. Benjy had offered to run with me. We all dodged bullets from the moment we turned seventeen. Sometimes they caught up with us and there is nothing I could do about it. Feeling sorry for myself and Tab wouldn't bring her back and had she known what was happening that i was getting a VII, she would have smacked me upside down the head for risking it all because of her especially when nothing I did would change what happened. People died and were send Elsewhere all the time. It hurt like hell when it happen close to home but what made Tabs any different from the others who were punished for breaking the law? I never cried for them. I never thought twice about the articles Benjy read to me about executions. People were they one day and gone the next and they were the ones who had risked it. It was different when it was my friend but at the same time it wasn't. Life still went on. Daxton still ruled the country and I'm still a nobody. At least I'm a nobody with a VII. 
 Omg, she is so self-absorbed! I feel like strangling her!! Also, her "suppose" cleverness: 
 Benjy sighed and reached for me but I sidestepped him. I couldn't take his disappointment too. He slouched. "I don't understand, sixty-eight people who were tested were IV". 
 "Yeah, well I guess I'm dumber than sixty-eight percent of the population". 
 I kicked a puddle of the rancid rainwater splashing a few rats that squeaked in protest. 
 "Eighty-four percent actually including the V and above", said Benjy and he quickly added, "But you're not. I mean you're smart. You know you are. You outsmarted the Shield out there". 
 Excuse me, but outsmart what?? All she did was lied, and a bad one at that! The Shield wouldn't even trusted her if it weren't for Benjy! 
 I know what the author was trying to do. She's trying to make our heroine seems smarter. I appreciate that but in that scene, Kitty didn't really do anything significant to warrant being called a "smart". Kitty was portrayed as being very smart though and her only problem that made her failed the test was her inability to read because she have some form of dyslexia or something. Still, I find it very hard to like Kitty. 
 It seems like the other characters were formed just so you will have the bad guys. Every story needs a bad guy right? In this case we have the Hart family who were evil for fun. I don't think there were reasons for them being evil. They just conveniently are. If there were reasons, I didn't notice any. It was so predictable and it was so clear to see who's side everyone is on. On this line you've got the good guys and on the other line is the bad ones. I feel like the characters were bland and it's hard for me to connect with any of them. 
 Also, I find it hard to like the story. It seems like there's a lot of sub plots and it's hard to keep track the things going on. Even the "plot twist" was so glaringly obvious and I could see it coming from miles away. 
 In all, this book is an utter disappointment. What could have been another great dystopian turns out to be another failure due to the characters and plots that were utter crap at its best.

 Before I get to picking on Vampire Academy, I will say I did like it this book and will continue on with the series... 
 But there were flaws. Flaws that personally irritated me and probably wouldn't bother the majority of the readers. The author brought the Russian Orthodox Church into the book, yet all her references were wrong. It isn't "mass", it's "Divine Liturgy". We cover our heads in church, we cross ourselves upon entering, we light candles and there are no long sermons and no sitting down. The "long boring sermons" part really irritated me. There aren't really any long sermons in the Orthodox church, just brief messages towards the end, but that's the quickest part of the service. It would have been better if the church would have been neutral and she hadn't picked a denomination. It would have been even better if she put effort forth to research it since I see how she wanted to tie it in with the Russian and Romanian background. The majority of Russians and Romanians being Orthodox Christians and all. 
 The other thing that bothered me and I might just be going overboard with this, but Lissa is not the nickname for Vasilisa, nor could it be. Vasilisa is pronounced "Vah-see-leesa". Leesa sounding like Lisa. So, Lisa would be a more valid nickname, though the nickname for Vasilisa is actually Vasya or Vasyona. Rose mentioned that she liked her "American" version better, which would had to of made it Lisa. Also, the female guardian with Dimitri who's first name slipped my head had the last name "Petrov". She's a girl, so it would be Petrova. Like in my instance my husband is Kurlykov and I'm Kurlykova. 
 Now, putting that aside it was an interesting read and drug me in. At first I didn't like Rose much at all. But she did show some growth throughout the book and by the end I warmed up to her a little more. I'm hoping for more growth and maturity in the coming books. I was kept in suspense throughout the book and I honestly didn't know who done it for a long time. I only figured it out right before Rose did. Rose could be a little too self-confident for my taste at times and I was ready to reach in the book and slap her for being such a jackass sometimes and then other times I wanted to reach in and shake her for being so passive. Sometimes the way she referred to Dimitri was silly and immature. The whole 'badass god' thing got old. It's cool that he's strong, but it would have been nice if the vocabulary expanded. The writing wasn't amazing and a lot of phrases were reused, but I think the story was interesting enough for me to put that aside and enjoy it. I really like the fact that we get to see Lissa's views through Rose. That really enhanced the story and I loved her character. 
 What I really liked about this book was the lore though. Vampires are an interesting subject, but everyone represents them differently and I really liked Richelle's version of vampires and the whole world she's created.

Ok so I loved this book. But it annoyed me too! This was a mix of two of things. My favorite kind of love story and my most hated conflict. 
 I loved Angel. One of my favorite situations for a story is when a player/bad boy is emotionally brought to his knees by a girl. When he just can't help falling in love with her and doesn't care how whipped he is. I love that. That was this book. 
 But I hate it when a character is hiding something and keeps putting off telling the other person the truth. Then the longer they hold off the worse it looks for them when they actually come clean and tell their secret. Ugh it is a pet peeve of mine. That was also this book. 
 So basically I love, love, loved Sarah and Angel's relationship. He couldn't stop touching her and thinking about her and wanting to be with her. And on the flip side Sarah was not your typical annoying girl. She is not too clingy or possessive or jealous. She has a moment where she gets upset about girl from his past and she confronts him and he takes care of it. I liked all that. I liked their dynamic. 
 I DIDN'T like that she wouldn't just TELL him about Sydney. She should have told him the first time he referred to him as a her. I HATE that that ended up being the major conflict, because it was so frustrating. 
 I also had to agree with Angel that Sarah and Sydney's relationship was a little weird. I kept wondering if Sydney was gay at the beginning of the book. Which is terrible. I've had guy friends in school. But most of them ended up wanting to date me, so I can see Angel's point. But, just because that is most people's experience doesn't mean that a guy can't be good friends with a girl and not want a romantic relationship with her. But I think wrestling around on the floor and holding hands, would blur the lines. I don't see how a teenage boy would be able to continue to think of a beautiful girl as his good friend when she is holding his hand and physically wrestling with him. Just my opinion. She said she thought of him as a brother and a best friend... but I don't hold my brother's hand or my best friend's hand after not seeing them for a long time. Just saying. 
 I hated them being apart. I hated Angel's stubbornness, and unwillingness to listen to her reasons, even after he cooled off. It was sort of gut wrenching. I hated that they were both hurting. But that makes the reunion so much sweeter, and yet, I wish the reunion would have been dragged out a bit. One second they were yelling at each other and then they were kissing and smiling and acted like the last few weeks hadn't even happened. I wanted some more... something, emotion maybe? I expected more relief from Angel when he understood everything, but he just jumped her. Oh well, I need to stop being so picky about these things. It was still a great book that I really enjoyed. But despite the lack of emotion or whatever it was I was wanting more of , I was SO glad that it didn't just end right there.  After their reunion I was SO scared that that would be the end of the book, but I turned the page to a new chapter and had to breath a sigh of relief. I'm SO glad she wrote more. That made me so happy. :) 
 I also loved how she set up for her other books. There were two other relationships that were started and primed for more books. Now I can't wait to read them. On to the next!

 "[...] I just don't want to smother you Angel. I want you to still have your space." 
 "You have it all wrong, Sarah," he said "If anyone is gonna have to watch the smothering, it's gonna be me. In case you haven't noticed, I just can't get enough of you."

This one is a bit more intense, probably because the hero is the broodiest of the Moretti brothers. Vincent and Jill has been "together" as work partners for 6 years - both are brilliant NY homicide detectives, the yin and yang to each other's good cop/ bad cop routine and the Morettis have been waiting for the day when Jill finally becomes more than a work partner to Vin. But one day after a long absence from work Jill returns and announces her engagement to another man and Vincent realizes what's been in front of him all these time. But he's got issues of his own - he doesn't believe that he's capable of loving or receiving love from someone. Add to that, this one particular murder case that might just be the one that they couldn't solve. 
 There's a lot of tension and dancing around each other, not a lot of romance in this story. Of all the Moretti brothers, Vincent's the hardest to like as he seems cold and unfeeling, often apart from the rest whereas Jill is the total contrast. Again, with the help of the nosy yet loving Morettis, the story is saved from being tedious and frustrating and the love story plods along towards a decent ending. 
 I didn't enjoy the story as much as the second one but the appeal of the family makes up for the anti-love story here. What i really want to read now is Marco's story - i hope he doesn't end up with his girlfriend, the vapid Hollywood actress wannabe Mandy, goes back to NY and has a nice little love story with a decent girl, just like all his brothers. Also, I want to read about Elena and perhaps a story of her own. Can't help but want more of the Morettis.

I can usually finish a 400 page mass market paperback novel in a few hours. It took me approximately 4 weeks to get 40% of the way through this particular book. 
 Granted, this might have been because I kept putting it down to go read and finish other books, but I was determined to finish this one as it had been on my to-read list for while. Thunder & Roses contained one of my favorite tropes: a good girl reforming a rake. What I didn't count on was how boring Clare was and how traditionally a bodice-ripper this book was. 
 Act 1. Scene 1. 
 Clare, the schoolmistress, marches up to Nicholas, demanding that he come help save the people of her impoverished Welsh village. 
 Conclusion: So far, s'okay. She's a plucky determined heroine. 
 Act 1. Scene 2. 
 Nicholas agrees if she gives up her reputation to go live with him for an agreed amount of time. 
 Status: This is a regency romance written in the 1990s; silly plot twists are allowed. 
 Act 1. Scene 3. 
 Nicholas must be allowed one kiss with Clare each day. 
 =___= : Er...okay. 
 The setup is already stupid and ridiculous, even more so than usual regency romance fare. But the problem lies mainly with the execution. Clare is just so good. She's so good that there is nothing else to her but her goodness. She's not particularly witty; she embodies the good and naive stereotype; she makes her one bold move in the beginning and then ponders incessantly about how she feels in his embrace. She sometimes turns into a nag and kind of ends up bursting into tears way too often for my liking and I really don't get why Nicolas likes her - when he's thinking about her, it's kind of like reading something to the effect of "milky white skin", "large innocent [color] eyes", "heaving [small/large] chest", "fiery determined spirit", "so good", etc. Basically generic bodice-ripper heroine adjectives. All of which, are probably kind of unlikely, due to the fact that she's also been described as rather plain, which I guess in romance-speak means all of the above adjectives. This is boring. 
 Nicholas also fades into the background, being a dark (but not too dark!) brooding rake with a tragic childhood and past. I sincerely feel like nowadays, if an author is going to do a rake, don't make him just a rake with generic background pain + womanizing behavior. Give him hobbies, motivation, passion: make him a real character. What's also especially egregious was that Nicholas here wasn't really much of a rake to begin with. All he's basically done is steal a few kisses from Clare here and there -- b-o-r-i-n-g and not really rakish at all. His half-gypsy background seemed interesting to include, but didn't really factor in that much into the book (well, for the part that I've read). Lisa Kleypas' Hathaway series does a much better job with Romany heroes, and Anne Stuart's House of Rohan series does rakes so much better than this book. 
 In conclusion, I give up. I give up on this book.

 The idea of using matchmaking to control the world around you is an intriguing one. Of course, the practice of entering into a marriage for political alliance and gain is something that's been around since practically the dawn of time, but this book takes it one step further. 
 Imagine an entire empire that is required by law to submit to matchmaking, and any "self-matched" couples are shunned and treated like lepers. 
 Our heroine, Sage, is the offspring of self-matched parents, which resulted in her mother's parents disowning their daughter. Sage and her parents live a pleasant life, even though everyone around them looks upon them with disdain. 
 When her parents die, Sage is forced to go live with her uncle, who tries--and fails--to make her conform to the society's notion of a marriageable miss. I mean, could you imagine the horror of a female who is interested in the sciences instead of how best to tilt her head in order to catch a husband. *rolls eyes* 
 When Sage is recruited to be the high matchmaker's apprentice she dives into her job with gusto. She never imagined that her powers of observation would capture the royal army's notice, leading them to enlist her help as their spy. 
 Here the story takes so many twists and turns that I don't want to spoil. Suffice to say, it was a white-knuckling experience. 
 I loved all the secret identities and code names, although I did suspect that "Mouse" wasn't exactly who he claimed to be. The only thing that bummed me out and made me yell at the book (true story!) was Charlie (If you've read the book you know what I'm talking about). 
 Recommend to all fantasy lovers.

David Mitchell is my favorite author, I think, so this one probably suffers from high expectations. Perhaps it deserves a 4, but I'll need some convincing. 
 The thing Mitchell always has going for him is his investment in and sympathy for characters. Arlo Guthrie frequently complained of being stuck downstream from Bob Dylan on the river of songs and the Bone Clocks is Mitchell hopping upstream of Neil Gaiman. Instead of some saccharine darkness where you know things are going to get weird, but eventually end up just fine, here you get to inhabit real solid beings with natural and varied reactions to unnatural events. Every character is an individual and full. You could read pages of any of their internal monologue and not be able to guess who wrote them; man or woman, urban or rural, foreign or domestic. It's impressive. 
 All this brilliant characterization and layered lives builds up an impressive foundation, however, for what is a sadly scant and implausible climax. It's like the massive silver pedestal of the Stanley Cup, engraved with the names of everyone that contributed to momentous seasons, topped with a bruised chunk of coffee-stained styrofoam. The Bone Clocks only loses one star for this, because the rest of the writing is fantastic. 
 The second star (or maybe just a half) comes off the top for a denouement that is less falling-action/summing-up than an added novella with shared characters.

Aw man. Aw man. AW MAN. 
 That was... I can't... Hm. 
 The last book of a trilogy I've grown to adore so much and now... I have no more. And it feels as dejectedly crippling as it sounds. 
 But on to the review. 
 The beginning of End of Days starts a bit on the slower side, with lots of repetitive descriptions to remind the reader of what happened in previous books - something a little hindering for someone who had just finished World After. 
 But regardless, the remnant of this book was really, really good. It was not perfect, admittedly, but it was the closest thing to it, save for a few aspects. 
 First of all, there is some major character development for almost everyone. Beliel is especially well represented since we get to know his backstory, as well as the other Watchers' and everything Raffe went through previously (as shown briefly by his sword's flashbacks in book two, but in much greater detail now). It was such a nice thing to add to the plot because it all made sense: it showed why Beliel ended up the way he did and, in a way, it was actually due to Raffe and Penryn's decisions  - which is mindblowing! 
 It also connected wonderfully with plot points developed earlier. In fact, all the wrapping up done in this book was wonderful. It made sense. It was well thought of and well planned and just masterfully executed. Flawless. The things mentioned along the way in the previous installments (the tons of deja-vu moments for Penryn, for instance) and that I sometimes got confused or curious about, were laid out and explained whenever necessary. Other times, they just winked cleverly at the reader, as if to say "gotcha". Plain awesome. 
 Beliel was, hands down, one of my favorite villains in the book. Because he was not just a villain for the sole sake of being one. He was not even one at the start; he was Raffe's loyal companion and it was his "betrayal" and "abandonment" who made him like that.  You finally understand him, and his motives, and you sympathize with him, despite all the evil he's done. Uriel, on the other hand, is hard to connect to, because you see no reason for his evilness other than his thirst for power. He is flat in comparison, because we don't get to glimpse into his past at all. Sure, he does much more horrible things than Beliel, but they don't seem to impact you as much on an emotional level. 
 Almost every character was flawed in some way. You couldn't really call anyone "hero" or "villain". They had to do what they had to do to survive or, at least, to make sure their species did. In this whole angels versus humans war, no one was really wrong or right. At the end, they were all just confused and scared and driven by ulterior motives and their own nature, basically. 
 There was a bit less humor in End of Days, as already exposed in World After, but I think that was purposeful because things were getting more serious by the minute. We're edging the literal apocalypse, after all. Still, there was time for little humorous moments here and there, some of them more memorable than others. And that's what was great about this trilogy: it didn't take itself so overly serious as to leave you rolling your eyes at the occasional cheesiness. 
 Penryn and Raffe are love and always will be. OTP material. There's no discussion about it. However, due to circumstances in the second book, there was barely any Raffe and that ended up affecting my reading experience. In this book, Raffe is also not always present, but there is a lot more interaction and we get to see so much of his inner turmoils and of his life before the Great Attack that we feel a lot more connected to him. We understand him better. Penryn, too. 
 Also, I was not prepared for the steaminess that occurs. Short and sweet, as always with this couple, but damn if it didn't make me gape at the pages. The romantic scenes are still pretty realistic, even if they are a bit unexpected after so long of not having them in this trilogy. I can't tell if it was refreshing or just plain weird but I can't deny that I throughout enjoyed them. They also don't play that big of a part on the story and both get their head back in the game after pulling themselves together. 
 Which brings me to the coolest aspect in this book: the way the relationship is portrayed. In most YA novels, it's always a hit or miss for me. There's either too much mushiness and unrealistic standards or complete awkwardness with no chemistry to speak of. With Penryn and Raffe, things are not as simplistic. They are enemies, their "races" are at war with each other. Now, that's not original at all and we've seen it played out so many times before it's actually a pretty popular trope. But that doesn't make it a bad trope. It's the way people write it that gives it a bad rep. And I think Ee totally pulled it off in her book. 
 Yes, Penryn and Raffe come from different worlds and falling in love with one another causes problems. But not for one moment do you get drowned in the angst of it all, nor do they make it seem like the end of the world in comparison to, well, the actual end of the world. They are so level-headed. Yes, they love each other and yes, they will do anything to protect each other. But they don't forget the world's at war. They don't forget their loved ones or what's at stake: everyone's survival. 
 Huge spoiler for crucial parts of the book, which you can skip: When Raffe first needs to leave to get his real wings back (again), their goodbye is so sad and heartbreaking, you can taste it. But the story doesn't stop there. Does Penryn go wallow in some dark corner because her lover went away? No! She doesn't have time for that. She has stuff to do. She gets kidnapped, instead.  
 On their second goodbye, things are probably even more heart-wrenching, because it's the unpenth time we realize they might not get to see each other again. And it's so anguishing. But still, neither of them try to stop it because it's what needs to be done. When Josiah comes to warn her to take herself and her family into cover during the blood hunt, Penryn could have taken the easy way out and protect herself and her family while everyone else gets murdered in such the angels' ruthless, animalistic game. She gets conflicted and realizes that, maybe, it finally comes the time where Raffe will turn on her species in order to win the trial. Because that's the sensible thing - he's an angel who will do anything to protect his own, and she's a human who will do the same. And both are on the same page on this; just because Raffe wants to spare her, doesn't make it ok for him to go and murder the rest of humanity. 
 And knowing this, knowing she probably, maybe, likely will have to fight against Raffe and his Watchers to save the rest of mankind, she makes the choice of not sparing herself or her family and instead goes into war to try and save everyone.  She realizes her biased opinion of the guy she loves can't affect her judgment. And because she chooses to do this, she ends up leading the Resistance and inspiring tons of people to follow her into a bloodbath, the chances of survival being close to null.  Whereas she could have sit down and cried and done nothing, while waiting for things to happen on their own. While waiting for Raffe to save her. 
 She doesn't even hold it against anyone who doesn't want to participate in the battle. Her ultimate priority is to just make sure they all live. And she's prepared to die for it. Sure, she gets scared, petrified even, but she doesn't back down at the last minute and becomes a beacon of hope for everyone who once sought for that same quality in Obi. Without her, everyone would be dead.  
 And of course she thinks about Raffe throughout the whole ordeal, it's only natural. But she doesn't allow that to command her movements. She shoves those thoughts to the back of her mind and moves on. 
 If that doesn't show you an amazing, strong, reliable and badass heroine, I don't know what does. 
 There were some minor things that I disliked about the book, such as the twins as they (sometimes) do feel kind of forced and awkward comic reliefs. I also found the "elections" thing pretty weird and random at first, but it seemed to make more or less sense at the end. 
 The world building was fine and consistent, and much development occurred since the first book, shedding a lot of light into several subjects. The writing was action-packed, with some gore and cringe-worthy moments to boot. The plotting was clever and exciting, always with bits of humor here and there to lighten up the mood. 
 The ending was satisfactory. I wouldn't say I was completely happy about it, just because it was so short and I needed a lot more to fill my insides with joy. But I didn't feel like it was rushed, either. I think the pace for that particular moment was appropriate, because it was somewhat shocking and unexpected and since we follow Penryn's POV, we get to feel how she feels. And in that moment she felt all sorts of emotions, from shock to anguish to confusion. The author was able to convey that really well and I liked it. 
 Just, you know, needed more. I'm still giving this whole trilogy 5 stars because of reasons. 
 I adore and hate you, Miss Ee. You're amazing.

"I missed you every hour. And you know what the worst part was? It caught me completely by surprise. I'd catch myself just walking around to find you, not for any reason, just out of habit, because I'd seen something that I wanted to tell you about or because I wanted to hear your voice. And then I'd realize that you weren't there anymore, and every time, every single time, it was like having the wind knocked out of me." 
 This book had been sitting on my shelf for so long. Despite hearing so much good about it from several people, I just didn't know what to expect, so I stayed away from it. Now I'm glad I finally picked it up and could kick myself for letting it sit there for so long. 
 First of all, the characters are amazing. I think I'm in love with all of them, even the antagonist. He really confused me and I'm still not 100% sure whether to hate him, or love him, or just be a fangirl of his powers. 
 Speaking of which, the powers. The whole magic system was entirely new to me, and as I don't read fantasy regularly, complex magic systems usually confuse me and put me off books. But this one was well thought out, and properly explained through show instead of too much tell. I really liked the idea of the elements playing a big part, but also that everyone can still have their own "thing" apart from that.

The setting is merely background noise (except that it's cold, but it could be cold anywhere in the world), and the Russian words might as well be just made-up words from a fantasy realm. 
 I think "Shadow and Bone" was a great start back into fantasy, and it's definitely on the PRO side of the list of whether I will read more fantasy this year or not.

I want to start this review with two positives: 
 1. I loved the book Seraphina so this is not written to be mean. 
 2. The sheer depth and interesting history of the world of Seraphina is wonderful and I loved those aspects in Shadow Scale. 
 Now on to the disappointment, reading this book made me have a lot of theories as to what went wrong in the publication of it: 
 The publisher was pushy with Hartman getting something out. My evidence: 
 1. At some point I realized that Hartman actually didn't really like Seraphina any more, where as the previous book had been about a character with passion, substance, intelligence, art, and learning to accept herself and recognize that imperfection and difference were part of the human experience this book was none of those things. At 75% finished I gave up when I realized all the beauty of the previous book was gone except for the world building. This was story that consistently had Seraphina in the role of idiot traveler, making blunders that seemed so out of left field, but also as though the author had just gotten sick of writing her. 
 Part of me believes the publisher told Hartman she needed to continue Seraphina's story when in fact what she really wanted to do was explore the world she had created through different characters. Shadow Scale easily has too many characters all with far more interesting back stories than the story explored with Seraphina. 
 2. The lack of editing and direction. A good editor should have helped Hartman develop this better. 
 3. The quest story that had no real point until the issue of Seraphina's uncle came up. I feel like this maybe was supposed to be quest story but Hartman could not pick out the reason for the quest and then just started throwing ideas at the wall to see what stuck. First idea: it's a quest to get the rest of the half-dragons to join in the fight for Goredd and about halfway though Hartman gets bored with this idea because Seraphina is in fact no diplomat so the lesson Seraphina must learn repeatedly is no one wants to come with her. Second idea: A quest to get rid of Junnoula? Except Seraphina seems too goddamn dumb to recognize this other half dragon as a threat until it is too late too many damn times (this was one of the most frustrating and eye-rolling aspects of this novel). Third idea: We are going to find out who the saints really were (perhaps my favorite idea and the most tantalizing), but suddenly Seraphina is the least curious and blundering idiot there ever was. Fourth idea: Let's explore Pphorory (Please excuse the spelling mistake I was listening to the audiobook)! Awesome, this place is really interesting and seems to have a lot of really interesting characters except we are stuck with Seraphina bumbling around like a ninny. Fifth idea: We need to save Olmer (once again please excuse spelling mistake)! Ehh, at this point everyone in Seraphina's world is in some sort of treacherous circumstance and this just seems like overkill, out of the blue, and really out of character for Olmer. 
 And then I just gave up.

Follow Me Back is so far outside my usual wheelhouse that it's barely on the same field (truth be told, it might not even be the same sport). But I had so much fun with it that I devoured it all in a single sitting one sunny afternoon. 
 Our protagonists are Tessa Hart and Eric Thorn - the former an agoraphobic pop fan, the latter a tweenage heart-throb tired of his own fame. Sick of his fans, Eric creates a fake Twitter account to lash out, but ends up striking up an unlikely friendship with Tessa. 
 As someone who spent a good chunk of her teenage years dopily following around boybands, the insight into fandom A.V. Geiger provides is utterly accurate - especially the awe and irritation surrounding those "Big Name Fans" who are first with all the hot new gossip. Honestly, this book made me hugely grateful that my own boyband days transpired before the Twitter age. A digital trail of teenage obsession would be too cringe-worthy to bear. 
 As well as a budding romance, Follow Me Back is also a thriller. A major plot thread follows Eric's paranoia after a boyband member is murdered by an obsessive fan. The book ends on a major cliffhanger, calling into question all that came before. I'm not absolutely certain I'll be back for the sequel, but in its own rights Follow Me Back was a hugely enjoyable read. 
 Sincere thanks to Sourcebooks Fire for providing a free copy in exchange for an honest review via NetGalley.

 The characters themselves were pretty great. Emmy was actually funny sometimes (I find that a lot of supposedly-funny YA characters end up not being that way). Oliver was fairly cute, too. Caro was cool, and Drew, despite being a bit stereotypical, didn't drive me crazy or anything. 
 That's one of my only complaints about this book, actually. Everything can feel a bit exaggerated. Both Emmy and Oliver's parents are that cliche of being too strict so that they can have a big fight at the climax when their offspring scream at them, I'm not your little girl/boy/walking-talking-stereotype anymore! But it was a little too much. It made sense in Oliver's case, because he's just returned after being kidnapped by his dad. But in Emmy's it was insane. She's almost 18 and has a 9 p.m. curfew and 10 p.m. bedtime? She's not allowed to go to college? I would have just spontaneously combusted if that was my senior year. 
 My other complaint is the insta-love. It's somewhat excusable because Emmy and Oliver were childhood friends, but they spend very little time catching up after a (very crucial) decade apart before they start mackin' on each other. It's not the worst I've ever read, just a bit grating. 
 Bottom line: It's not perfect, but this contemporary is refreshing, cute and fun. Also I think I like surfing books now. Regardless, I recommend!

Malcolm Gladwell's books are all in the same style. Gladwell writes interesting anecdotes and then generalizes them, showing common themes, behaviors, or morals. Whether or not these generalizations are valid, his books are vastly entertaining, and this book is no exception. David and Goliath is perhaps the most entertaining book I read this year! 
 In the introduction, Gladwell reviews the biblical story of David and Goliath. The popular conception is that Goliath was a mighty warrior, and David a meek shepherd who was clearly the underdog. Gladwell turns the story around, and by analyzing the biblical verses, he shows that David was not an underdog at all. He had a number of advantages that should have raised his odds of winning. 
 This is the major theme of the book; many apparent disadvantages can turn out to be advantages, while many apparent advantages can turn out to be disadvantageous. Each chapter is a compendium of anecdotes from all spheres of life, that give evidence for this turnabout. 
 Gladwell describes a father who volunteered to be a basketball coach for his daughter's team. Neither the father nor the girls had any experience with basketball. But because he was desperate, the father came up with an atypical strategy that turned the team into a powerhouse. 
 Gladwell shows that although dyslexia is a learning disability, it can help mold a person. A person with dyslexia, given the right aptitudes, can overcome the handicap and excel where other people have lesser abilities. At a meeting of prominent university donors--mostly successful businesspeople, a neuroscientist asked how many had been diagnosed with a learning disorder. Half the hands went up. 
 A medical doctor who had a terrible, traumatic childhood developed a cure for childhood leukemia. Other doctors with normal childhoods were too squeamish to experiment and find such a cure. 
 Gladwell shows that ultra-small class sizes are not always advantageous. Selective, elite schools are not necessarily good for all the students--they might only be good for those students at the very top of the class. He wrote that "...if you want to see the positive effects of elite schools on self-concept, you are measuring the wrong person. You should be measuring the parents." 
 The chapter about elite schools follows up with a very interesting observation, that it is better to be a big fish in a "small pond" than a little fish in a "big pond". As evidence for this, Gladwell cites statistics about college students completing a STEM degree (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics). He writes that "the likelihood of a student completing a STEM degree rises by 2 percentage points for every 10-point decrease in the university's average SAT score." If you are in a university where many people seem to be smarter than you, it is more likely that you will drop out of a challenging curriculum. 
 Gladwell writes about the apprehension in London before the expected bombing blitz by the Nazis. Courage is not something that you already have that makes you brave when the tough times start. Courage is what you earn when you've been through the tough times and you discover they aren't so tough after all. He shows how the Germans thought that the bombing would traumatize the city. Instead, it made the British more courageous than ever before. 
 I heartily recommend this book to anyone interested in psychology, as a fast, entertaining look at human behavior.

I'm torn between giving this book four stars, for its phenomenal premise & potential, or three stars for the actual execution thus far. So, I suppose we'll go with three and a half. I was extremely excited to read this because the premise had the sci-fi fangirl in me drooling with anticipation...a world where people are born with *two* souls instead of one?! Sign me up! 
 I did enjoy the story, but it wasn't quite as epic as I had hoped. The basic framework is as promised: Addie and Eva are two souls sharing the same body. Eva, being the recessive soul, should have faded away by age ten which is when most people in this society "settle". Naturally, that didn't happen or we wouldn't have much of a story. Addie and Eva are "hybrid", the worst possible taboo in this society, and live in fear of discovery because hybrids have a tendency to be abducted by shady government agencies and never heard from again. Fascinating questions are skirted around, such as what it means to truly be human and free...and the depths of terrible secrets a person can hide within their mind. 
 Unfortunately, the beginning is surprisingly mundane and slow, especially after a rather compelling prologue that lays out Addie and Eva's situation immediately. We know the stakes already...and are then forced to plod along as the girls go through their everyday lives at school. There are flashes of intrigue, such as a trip to the museum that gives us tantalizing glimpses of the wars that created this society, but then it's quickly back to the routine. It takes about halfway through for the story to really pick up speed, once Addie and Eva are outed as being hyrbid. Come on, now, that wasn't a spoiler, anyone could have guessed it! ;) 
 After that halfway point, I was finally so pulled into the story that I couldn't put it down. There was still that frustrating sensation of just barely scratching the surface of something incredible - tiny little flashes of the history and forces behind this world - but always falling short of ever truly *answering* anything. This book is the first in a series, of course, so I didn't expect a lot of grand resolution...but it still would have been nice to have *something* of the grand design revealed. 
 In terms of style, this is a very easy read. Zhang has a nice, clean prose that flows very well and does not use awkward structure or description. The story is told from Eva's point of view, and is thankfully *not* in the present tense that has been infecting all of teen fiction lately. The action is fast and furious once it gets going, and what little romance is present (extremely scant and fleeting) takes a backseat to the life-or-death events. This entire world is a very different, fresh take on the dystopian genre and I am definitely going to read the next book. Zhang makes a decent start here, but she could still create something epic if she stops merely scratching the surface...we will just have to read and find out!

Tale as Old as Time by Liz Braswell, is not the Disney Beauty and the Beast you know and love. 
 It's not better than the movie, but it's also not worse. It's different, for sure, and exciting, and interesting, and truly enchanting. What is it? It's all of those head cannons, tumbler threads, and out there theories combined into one book, and used as serious plot points. 
 Was the Beast eleven when he was cursed? You bet. What ever happened to Mr. Potts? You will learn. 
 If Gaston is the villain, why does the Asylum director look like the Crypt Keeper? It's a very good reason. What is the Beast's name? No clue. Your book is not cannon Braswell, suck it up and name your protagonist! (I'm still rooting for Adam myself.)  
 The book is divided into three parts, with each part departing more and more drastically from Disney's 1991 animated movie of Beauty and the Beast. This is something I embraced rather than raged against. The story is much better for having been allowed to grow organically from each plot alteration, instead of tying to cram it all into the confines of a ninety minute movie. 
 So if you are a fan of Beauty and the Beast, I really recommend this book, in a "if you liked __ you will also like __" capacity. Just don't pick it up expecting to read a novelization of the movie. That's an entirely different book.

Off-Campus has finally come to a close and I have a lot of mixed feelings. Not just about The Goal but the series as a whole. I may actually have to do a whole post on the series by itself. It started out so strong but I feel like it just devolved into something cliche and just not good. There were a lot of things that bugged me, especially in the last two books that I don't think it would be fair to put in a review for just The Goal. 
 When we left off, it was the end of The Score and Tucker drops a truth bomb of epic proportions- he's going to be a dad. I personally thought it was amazing because I love babies in romance. Couple that with the mother being Sabrina, Dean's nemesis and I thought it was doubly amazing. It was probably one of the highlights of The Score for me because, well, I have way too many thoughts about that book. 
 The Goal opens well before the end of The Score which didn't surprise me. Most of the stories in the series run rather concurrent, it just took time for us to get everyone's story. Unlike the other books in the series though, I feel like The Goal was much more Sabrina's story than Tucker's. All the other books focused a lot more on the guys, which made sense to me considering they revolve around a group of male friends who live together in an off-campus house. We see her trying to work her way through school, trying to become better than she was raised, and eventually become a mother. We don't get nearly the same characterization from Tucker. 
 From the previous books I never could get a read on Sabrina. I never thought she was a huge bitch that she was made out to be, but I didn't think she was a super amazing character either. She was known for sleeping around with the athletic population at Briar and that's about it. Besides because the bane of Dean's existence, of course. But in The Goal we're introduced to a young woman fighting to better herself. Someone who knows where she comes from and what she needs to do to make sure she doesn't stay there. She's something I rather admired except for a lot of the hate she had towards herself. But that also made a lot of sense considering her surroundings. 
 In the end, I did enjoy The Goal, but it's not without it's faults. Yes, Tucker and Sabrina were extremely hot together, however, their relationship was very much flawed. I feel like Tucker got a taste of Sabrina and became obsessed. There was on point where I feel like he was stalking her- he asked his advisor, who had no relation to Sabrina, her class schedule so he could find her. Um, hello? Red flag anyone? Mind you, Tucker is supposed to be the "good" one of the four roommates. There's quite a bit of misogyny going on as well as abuse. I rather wish the first quarter of the book didn't exist. It's just so problematic to me. 
 The Goal is a good end to an overall good New Adult series. Yes, it's full of cliche and eyerolling moments but it's enjoyable. I came to adore Sabrina and Tucker really is a stand up guy. I fell so hard for him when he was around the baby and how he treated a pregnant Sabrina. It was great to finally get into his head considering there wasn't much to go on in previous books.

 For one,  they never solve the case from twenty years ago! The case that's the big, intriguing hook from the description. What happened to those kids? Well, we still don't know.  Second, I found the first half or so to move really slow. Not much develops in the current case they're working on, and I guess that's the point--they themselves are frustrated that they're stuck, but because it was that old case that intrigued me, I kept waiting to see how it connected to the current case. Third, once it finally did pick up and we progressed on the case, Rob's character also progressed...in a not so positive way.  I know he's messed up by his past, but there still comes a point where that can't be his excuse in life. He makes more and more mistakes--messing up when he's at the trial, blowing up at Devlin, and what finally pushed him over for me was how he treated Cassie. The one person who knew his past that he could have perhaps opened up to, he instead pushes away. Although for as much as we hear of Cassie's great profiling skills and how she keeps spotting psychopaths, you would think she would have maybe suggested he do something about his own demons. Counseling? By the end Rob's negative spiral has really fucked up his life. I mean, I certainly wasn't expecting sunshine and rainbows for an ending but I hadn't imagined such a sad ending involving one of the detectives. Although my feeling of sadness was more a general, outsider look because by the end I went from feeling angry at Rob to just not really caring what happened to him. Like, sucks for you, buddy.

I related to her so strongly, and that's some writing skill, considering she's an assassin and I am not. (Or am I?) 
 Chaol is my dreamboat, and I love him, and Dorian is so painfully dull, but the romance is on the back seat just enough that it doesn't have to matter if you don't want it to. And it's okay because in the end, Celaena decides that her dream of freedom is more important than a dalliance with a prince, and that was the moment in which my eternal fealty was pledged to her. This is a heroine who is practical and who won't trade her goals to stare starry-eyed at a dude. That's important, guise, in a genre where the heroine is always the one to offer the sacrifice in order for her and her "true love" to be together - whether it's losing her humanity or killing herself or leaving her family and friends or giving up her education or giving in to having children when she doesn't want to. In this genre, women are the sacrificers, and their men look on, forlorn, "applauding" their "bravery" while remaining unchanged and ultimately only receiving without having to give at all. So that's why Celaena's dresses and her books and her little dog don't, in my eyes, make her 'annoying'. Because she takes control of her life and her sexuality and that's the sort of heroine we should be falling in love with.  
 The plot fell apart a little bit towards the end, enough to knock off a star from my rating - I was rereading passages, confused about what was going on. And honestly? I don't know that I would have picked this book up if I'd known we were dealing with faeries. I don't like faeries. They irritate me. I find them dull and confusing and ultimately, their stories are too small for me. There is only so much scope when you're dealing with forest deities that lead backpackers into bogs. That said, the good parts are mega, and the dialogue and writing hold it all together, even when it starts to hobble on shaky ground. Good save, Sarah. Good save. And to be honest, now that I'm into the story? I don't mind the faerie thing. Like, whatever. I'll get used to it for Celaena's sake. Who knows? Maybe I'll change my mind about...oh, who am I kidding. I'll try and push past it.  
 So, yeah, I'll be following this series. Hell, yeah. I've already started reading Crown of Midnight, and I'll be picking up Heir of Fire when it comes out in paperback (man, hardbacks are expensive these days! Whew!). 
 So, how's that for a review? See, sometimes I'm nice. Sometimes I'm a fucking delight.
