 Reader thoughts: Actually, my emotional reaction to the book is what makes it a 4 instead of 3 stars. In truth, I wasn't totally impressed (somewhat, though), but I was caught up enough to feel for the characters. 
 I don't quite understand why this deadly game (Fives) is so interesting. Maybe it has to do with the same reason so many people like football? Except this is closer to a coliseum-level of danger. Jess insists on participating and risking life and limb. It makes her interesting. She has passion and dreams, and they have nothing to do with boys. 
 Well, a little to do with a boy, an emperor's nephew.  Whom she betrayed in the end! Even if it was to save her own hide, I wanted her to find a way to let them both win. I guess that would have been too unrealistic. At least he's not dead, just sent to war. She'll still be watched at every step, though. So, neither of them won, really.  In some ways, it's shocking how close they become so quickly. She uses his connections, and he keeps letting her! Is he that besotted, or just that trusting? I can't figure him out. I like Kal, but he really could have been smarter. Maybe book 2? 
 This social structure is odd. It's racist against the natives (who are darker-skinned) and only lets the patrons (lighter brown-skinned) be in charge. There are strange rules about who can marry whom and how far certain people can rise in power. In one chapter, it says Jessamy's father could never rise beyond a sergeant. Then he's a captain, and it says that's the farthest he could ever rise because of his low birth. Then he becomes a sort of general person, and now that's the farthest he could ever rise. Which is it? The news lost its impact after the contradictions. 
 The weird dead rituals creep me out. They bury 4 or 5 women with each high lord corpse? There's some historical reason for this that doesn't make sense to me. These women are apparently fed for a while or the rest of their lives or something through a tube in the gravestone. 
 And there are forces that can reanimate a corpse. And Jessamy can see those "sparks," and this was where the story went from odd to paranormally unnatural. What do oracles and walking dead have to do with the spider machines? Is the young brother actually alive or just reanimated? I guess we'll find out. 
 Writer thoughts: I kept trying to figure out which culture Kate Elliot was basing her world on. Even if she did pull from some real-life cultures, none of them would have the Fives game nor the walking dead problem, and so it doesn't really matter. There might have been hints of Egypt (Kohl), but some parts sounded Oriental (I think there were katanas?), and the army ranks sounded European. 
 This blend is useful because it lets people from multiple backgrounds find resonance with the book and characters. It is also useful because KE can borrow ideas without having to invent new ones. Because she blended them, she can make this society her own without offending people that she may have gotten something wrong.

 Its funny to think about how this book started and progressed into a much darker tale of a line lying between hope and despair. 
 For one thing I LOVED AELIN. I know she's technically Celaena, whom I had a hard time accepting over the course of the past 3 books (yes, I read the prequel before book 3) only when she accepted her true self and accepted that name she began to grow on me. I could be biased with all the Rowan and Aelin is end game hints but I really loved them together, from the moments where they hard on each other (lets be real it'd be mostly Rowan) to the moments where they're vulnerable. She found in him what she lost in Adarlan, and I think that love is heartwarming (please get married already). I love when Rowan said "I claim you, Aelin, to whatever end" those words were so powerful and that specific moment where he renewed the blood oath with Aelin was so impactful, same goes for the "Carranam" moment  
 This book made me understand the main characters (as well as the newly introduced key characters). I have mentioned this countless of times, however I do appreciate when authors give us a chance to understand the characters we're going through this adventure with. SJM does it so well (only to rip our hearts out and tear them apart then restitch them without anesthesia) 
 The fire represented depression, loss, anger, grief, and everything despised and feared. So when Aelin couldn't control that it was symbol of those elements overpowering her and overwhelming her. Becoming the driving force in her life. Celaena was always strong, but this time she was broken. And I loved seeing that side of her, I thank you SJM for showing us that side of Aelin.as the book progressed and she got a hold of this power. It symbolised her being able to get a grip and acknowledge that these were parts of her, but not her. With her torture at the hands of the Valg princes and being thrown to a bottomless pit of despair, it symbolised how even she was getting the hang of things, she still was tested with that whole encounter with the Valg. After all, the point of having any faith is when its tested again and again. In this case, her faith in herself. Her rise from that gloom as a fearless warrior, conquering her fear and making the Valg burn with the fire she once feared. Making that fire a mark of her courage and those emotions a reason of strength  
 Even Brannon his nameless mark was once a sign of his pitiful state, until he rose from those ashes with his fire. Now generations view this mark as the opposite, something to be proud of rather than ashamed  
 Off to Adarlan now? 
 Now I've seen a side of my baby Chaol that I foolishly only noticed just now, his fear despite his position as a warrior. He isn't a coward by any means, yet especially at the beginning of the book when his father asks him about Anielle he seems to be confused as to what side he's on (which is completely understandable given the events of the previous book. Having fought for one side only to be shockingly shown the reality of the battle he was fighting) He fears the steps he's about to take and pushes away what he couldn't understand  Only when Aedion and the rebels came into play did he start to accept the truth of the war. At first he was a bit hesitant, yes he was doing the right thing yet how can he leave a world he was a part in so easily? He did amaze me in the end when he threw away his title and his honor for the fate of the world that lay, at the moment, between his palms. He is definitely a nobleman, and I don't think anyone could say otherwise.  
 Ok Dorian is a whole other story  after that conclusion I can't think of how he was before that. Having the blood of the woman he loved spilt on him and her head tumbling before him. His world fell apart in front of him from his friends and title to the Wyrdstone collar. Being kept in the dark for so long only to be plunged into a larger unknown. 
 He has broken my heart for multiple reasons in the previous books yet this one still has me thinking. Fearing.  
 As for Manon, she is an interesting character and I definitely hope to see more of her. She seems different from the other witches in terms of the feelings she has shown Sympathy, for a Blackbeak especially, is a big no-no. For her to refer to her heart more times than once (which, for someone who lacks it, is pretty odd), see the value of a bait Wyvern rather than jump for Titus, whom she wanted. And that moment with the Crochan was the icing on the cake. What changed for her to exchange her cold-blooded demeanor for a heart? Her brutality for sympathy? Wasn't she once so infuriated with the Crochans? What made her listen that witch she got the coat from? 
 And I do think the words are tumbling through her head I want to know how her story will connect to the others. Because it seems so distant here. 
 The story was slow at first, yet it does get very fast paced as it nears the end. It gets darker as you go in for everyone. And I do hope there is light at the end of the tunnel.

Lily Parker is so not thrilled at being sent to St. Sophia's, a snooty boarding school in Chicago so that her parents can go on a sabbatical in Germany. She's not resentful of her parent's acceptance into their program, but she feels trading her upstate New York home for a used-to-be convent in the windy city totally unnecessary. Regardless of Lily's feelings, though, she's now a St. Sophia's girl, for better or worse. It seems like it's for the worse based on Lily's first experiences at the school. A trio of uber-rich brats is intent on ruling the school and terrorizing anyone who gets in their way, Lily's new friend Scout keeps disappearing late at night, and there are strange people showing up around the school. When Lily finally learns the truth of what's going on, it threatens all she knows about the world. It turns out, there's a whole other side--a magical one--to the people around Lily, hew new friends, possibly her parents, and just maybe even herself. 
 I have to admit that Neill knows how to tell a story, and Firespell is certainly a good one. I must first remark that the pacing of this story is near perfect; the main action doesn't come too soon or too late. That in mind, I was quite satisfied with the story itself as well. Neill combines traditional interpretations of witchcraft with a version of vampirism in her dangerous world of magic underneath Chicago. In it, there are the Reapers, who refuse to let go of their power but must take energy from others to maintain it, and the Adepts, who vow to give up the power when it's time. The good versus evil is pretty obvious in black and white, but that's okay because it's not the entire concentration of the book. Where the story really starts getting interesting and complicated are the connections between the Adepts and Lily's only life. On the level of originality, Firespell ranks only moderately, but with its supernatural danger, intrigue, and romance, this novel sure is an enjoyable one.

There are some things about Looking for Trouble that make it one of Dahl's best yet. And there are others that make me waffle a little in that assertion.

 Alex...Alex Alex Alex. He is definitely one of my favorite Dahl heroes (Jamie Donovan holds first place. I do love me a man in a kilt.) He's got a surprisingly sweet side, and his obvious interest in Sophie was kind of awesome to watch. When he found out just how their pasts intersected, he just sorta shrugged and said, "So?" and I wanted to smother him with kisses. 
 Sophie's got good reasons for her prim, buttoned up exterior (though the stockings are a fabulously naughty touch). But so much of her is just reminiscent of Tessa (Good Girls Don't) that I had a hard time just losing myself in the story. Like Tessa, she's determined to keep her family together, by any means necessary. And like Tessa, she bugged the crap out of me. I don't have a good explanation why. There's just something about her that irks me. 
 The sex is absolutely some of the hottest Dahl's ever written, though there's one scene that made me scratch my head. But for the most part, they're creative, intense, and surprisingly emotional. You felt Sophie and Alex's connection from that first encounter. 
 While the focus is their growing relationship, the conflict that threatens to keep them apart is never far from the page, and it's woven in with an expert hand. Here's where Sophie's fears are easy to swallow - when you look at it in the context she sees it in, especially when Alex's mom is on the warpath (hateful woman. Ugh.) 
 Absolutely worth a read, and I'm looking forward to the next book.

This is first and foremost a mystery. Lots of time is spent covering the details of who "did it" and why and how. The chance that the events in this book would happen is minimal. Not only is the ending incredible but also the motive for the crime is feeble. I have learned that I value credibility. 
 Another aspect of this book that annoyed ME, was all the discussion of food. Lots of people love books where every other paragraph reverts to what is being eaten. I have learned to value other aspects of life than food. Why? Because I am a T1 diabetic and food just leads ME to trouble, I am the exception. Many adore books about eating and talking about delicious food. So again, a book for YOU, but NOT me. Go ahead, enjoy it. 
 A fun cozy murder mystery filled with yummy food. Not everything has to be credible for most people......except me. 
 Adam Sims narrated my audiobook. HE did nothing wrong whatsoever so go ahead and choose his narration if you think the book will be good for you! 
 ETA: I am getting braver. Here are more complaints: 
 There is simplistic philosophizing. You know that the criminal accused in the middle of the book will NOT be the right one. Nothing is done with the theme of the French versus English communities in Quebec. Popular themes of bullying and discrimination against gay people and women and Black rights - all covered but only superficially. It is set in a cozy fictive town in Quebec, but nothing is delved into with depth. Does cozy have to mean superficial?

Review for Zack (Cold Fury #3) by Sawyer Bennett 
 Zack is the third book in the Cold Fury series by Sawyer Bennett, this is a sports romance with erotic elements. Bennett has a great writing style and creates characters that are relatable. She's also got a way of writing sexual tension in a way that isn't overly angsty, but still frustrating in a good way. 
 Zack is a heartbreaker. His story is so devastating from the death of his long time girlfriend to the guilt he feels over things that are out of his hands just tears you apart. I hated every minute of his self-imposed torture. There are moments I wanted to shake him until his brain rattled around because he was so stuck on things that he couldn't change. Especially when Kate came into the picture and it became obvious she was so good for him and his son, Ben. 
 I adore Kate. She's sassy and sweet. I laughed at her little jokes and the way she teased Zack and Ben, pulling them out of the sadness of loss. Ben's instant love for Kate was beautifully done. Bennett showcased how resilient kids really are. 
 Zack and Kate had some pretty intense chemistry and because of the need to keep things professional it caused a good deal of sexual tension. Once they gave into their baser needs it was pretty darn hot. And the almost innocent way Kate was determined to be all that he needed without suffocating him or making him give her more than he was prepared to give her was so endearing. While on Zack's side of things it was frustrating and at times made me hate him a bit. 
 This book is a very emotional story that will probably have a few tears shed, but it's completely worth a read. Four stars for the storyline and five wet panties for smut that doesn't stop!

A tale of treachery, madness, royalty and badassery. All brought to you by no other than William Shakespeare. Anyone in? I am. 
 On this occasion, we have King Lear, an old king who wants to retire. Thus, he decides to divide his realm between his three daughters, but the share they receive goes proportional to the love they feel for their father. The elder ones tell him they extremely love him, while the youngest refuses to exaggerate her love for him, deceiving him into believing she doesn't love him. And so, he gives equal shares of the realm to the elder ones and he disinherits the youngest one without knowing that his decision will bring him to his downfall. 
 I think King Lear is the most tragic play I've read by Shakespeare so far. After finishing it, I was left with a feeling of sadness. Everything could have ended better. You think you have read tragic things? Then, read King Lear. In this one, also, the tragical end didn't seem neither forced nor exaggerated. It felt perfectly normal, given the circumstances surrounding the action. 
 Shakespeare is quickly escalating his way in the list of my favorite authors. And the fact that I like his name (William) is just adding more points in his favor. Perhaps what I love the most in his works is his writing -his beautiful prose--, but either way, he's one of the best writers in history, and I'm glad I'm reading (and liking) his works.

Ok, so I read this series a few years ago, WAY before I started with goodreads and blogging, but with the final book (City of Heavenly Fire) coming out I decided to re-read all five previous books to reacquaint myself, and thought I would write my reviews whilst I'm at it. 
 Firstly, wow these books are even better then I remembered, and I thought they were pretty awesome to begin with. The amount of imagination that has gone into creating this Shadowhunter world for not just this series but also The Bane Chronicles, The Infernal Devices and soon to come The Dark Artifices, well it's just amazing. If I had one wish it would be to get to live inside Cassandra Clare's mind just for one day and see how she came up with this phenomenal world. 
 Review: 
 So, just when we think that everyone has finally settled everything finds a way to mess itself up again! Here starts the second trilogy in the the Mortal Instruments series! 
 As Clary finally finds her place in this new world Jace seems to loose himself even more. Thankfully they finally know that they are not actually related and can be together but stuff keeps getting in the way. Clary's mum (wish she could have stayed in her coma) decides to become totally over protective and thinks that Jace isn't right for her (even though he has saved her life like a bajillion times and obviously loves her and makes her happy!) and at the same time Jace starts to pull back as well. For a character who was so confident in the first book it's so sad to see him so lost all the time. 
 Things just seem to keep getting worse and worse for Jace. After everything he goes through you think he has finally found peace. But instead things just get worse for him and again he really starts to loose himself all over again. Thankfully he does eventually let Clary in to help him, but unfortunately it's just that little bit too late. The whole thing with the dreams and possession is very cleverly done and I really didn't see it coming until it was too late.  
 But Jace isn;t the only one struggling. Alec & Magnus although totally in love and great together are having issues with the whole mortal/immortal thing and Alec becomes kind of self conscious over Magnus' past. They are both obviously keeping secrets from each other and you can feel the cracks starting to appear. 
 Simon really struggles in this book with "coming out" to his mum and trying to get her to accept him even though he doesn't accept himself. He still rejects becoming a part of the vampire 'clan' and is desperate to keep in with his Shadowhunter fiends who is he is also worried will one day reject him for being a downworlder. He is also petrified of his future and the fact that one day everyone he loves is going to die and he is going to be left all alone. Plus, with the Mark of Cain on his head things start to get difficult for Simon. 
 After the action packed City of Glass this book can seem a little slow, but with new characters and a new villain and new problems for our characters the book keeps our attention just as much as the previous three did. And with a really really great ending it's going to be really exciting to see where the next book takes us and how things develop even more.

Perhaps the cutest YA I have read in a long time. Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda centers on Simon Spiers, a sixteen-year-old gay guy who only reveals his homosexuality to Blue, the quirky online boy he emails and has a huge crush on. One day, a classmate of Simon's stumbles upon his correspondence with Blue and threatens to shove Simon out of the closet unless Simon hooks him up with Abby, one of his friends. As more complex dynamics and dramatic developments emerge from Simon's family and friends, he has to balance his more-public-than-ever sexuality and his growing feelings for Blue, a guy he has yet to meet in-person. 
 Becky Albtertalli's debut novel acts as a wonderful piece of brain candy. She crafts a compelling and not-too-dire plot to amp up the story's entertainment level, and she includes several little nuances in Simon's voice to make him more relatable: a penchant for Harry Potter, an obsession with oreos, lots of social media usage, and more. She balances the issue of adolescent sexuality well, making it an important part of the story but not its pith. 
 I do not give Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda a five-star rating only because the story felt a little too perfect. Yes, the Martin conflict never quite resolves , but Simon gets away with a lot at the end of the book just by having a couple of conversations and a a cute boyfriend, aka Bram . This novel did not inspire me with its depth or nuance, however, it did make me smile and go along with Simon's struggles and joys. 
 Overall, recommended to those who enjoy a good, lighthearted contemporary young-adult novel. For more serious and/or nuanced titles, I would recommend Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe, What They Always Tell Us, and Gives Light, amidst others.

1Q84 was a very unique book. Overall I enjoyed the plot and the characters, but I did have some signifigant complaints. 
 This is the first Murakami book I have read, so all my observations of his style are derived strictly from this book. I really like the premise for this plot, and much of how it develops. The lectures on fiction vs. reality and the interactions between them were intrigueing, and the convergence of the A and B plotlines is always welcome. My first complaint is the overabundance of sex scenes in this novel. While many of them we're used as symbolism or to make a relevant point, this could have been accomplished in other, less intrusive ways. Aside from that, Murakami seems to be particularly bad at writing sex scenes. Granted I am not a connoisseur of such literature, but Murakami's are by far the worst I have read. My second complaint is the length of the book. 1Q84 is written at a very leisurely pace, and things take a long time to develop. Having read series such as Robert Jordan's "Wheel of Time", I'm used to such writing. However Murakami's pace is borderline lethargic. It becomes tediously slow at some points, and he repeats things frequently for emphasis. This book would have been much more interesting had Murakami eliminated one or two of the side plots, developed his characters a little less, and reduced the size by 200-300 pages. That would have helped the novel signifigantly. While I enjoyed the concept, unfortunately the problems with this book lead me to not recommend it to those who have not read it.
Still not as good as the first, but better than the second. Even though I already know a lot of this.

Okay, so this is a review by someone who was (and still is, to a lesser extent) abused by her father. 
 And yeah, that's important, if you've read this book. 
 Book content warnings: 
 abuse 
 child abuse 
 homophobic slurs 
 alcoholism 
 So if you look at the book's page, The Bone People has a rating of over four stars, which is pretty darn good on goodreads. Reviews sing its praises, etc. etc., and I just . . . can't relate. 
 My problem with this beautifully-written book? You guessed it! The abuse!! 
 I just can't get past it. 
 I don't know a thing about Keri Hulme's background, but unless she's faced a similar issue, her coverage of child abuse is so damn distasteful. It's like a slap in the face to all abused people who read this. Let me tell you why: 
 The book centers around three well-written, completely-rounded out and fully-fleshed beautiful characters: Kerewin, a rich ex-artist who's holed herself up in a self-built tower and prefers to be alone and lonely; Joe, a Maori man with a drinking problem and an equal spread of temper and charm; and his foster child Haimona (Simon), who's mute and probably one of the best characters I've read in a long time (also the reason this is 2 stars instead of 1). 
 So, mostly when he drinks, Joe beats Haimona, or finds a reason to beat him. And Haimona is repeatedly labeled as a "difficult" and "troubled" child. He runs away from school, steals things, sometimes breaks property, etc. And even when it's brought to Joe's attention that he does these things because he wants attention (even if it's the wrong kind of attention!), Joe continues to tell Haimona that he's a bad, BAD kid. 
 It's like a self-fulfilling prophecy: the kid is told so often he's BAD, that he'd begin to believe it and continue to act out. Is it not obvious to any of the characters?? (or to the writer?) 
 But anyway, Haimona continues to do things in his own way to communicate with the adults, and they continue to lash out at him in the worst way, and the worst thing is the book continues to say it's O K ?? Because they still somehow love him? 
 In one part, Joe tells Kerewin that it's okay, because "it's not like I'm beating Haimona, I'm beating the 'badness' out of him!" like W T F!? It's the most abusive thing I've ever heard in my life. And stuff I've heard personally. You are still literally beating your child. The things you tell yourself while you're doing it to reassure yourself literally doesn't matter at all, okay? It's not about how you feel while you're doing it. Literally. It's about your child. 
 And then in the middle-ish part of the book, Joe  beats Haimona viciously enough that Haimona is hospitalized and almost dies. His head is bashed in on a door frame, and he risks permanent head trauma. Like what the fuck, I'm sorry, but really.  
 You know what the book does afterward? The book goes on to talk about how baaaaad the poor abuser feels, oh waah. I couldn't care less about how Joe feels after hurting his foster son, I honestly couldn't. At this point, it honestly feels like this book was written to make people feel sorry for child abusers. Like the author said "how NOVEL would it be if I wrote a book from a child abuses point of view and made people sympathetic to their pain?" HA HA. Listen, if you beat your child up, it's never, ever, EVER the child's fault. 
 It took me 26 years to learn this. And I'm finally standing up for myself. I'm finally distancing myself from my abuser and learning to say no and cutting him out of my life. And for this book to be sympathetic for the abuser and say the child is better off with the abuser after all is just disgusting. I'm sorry. 
 I love Kerewin and Haimona as characters, but the book is nasty. 
 Nasty.

I didn't want to read this book. A story about Ernest Hemingway and his first wife? All I knew about Hemingway was from high school English classes in which I read The Old Man and the Sea and The Snows of Kilimanjaro and tried to tease any sort of symbolism or nuance out of the stories to appease my teachers. But, the book is for book group, and after returning it once unread to the library, I resigned myself to read it the second time I inadvertently checked it out. 
 Within the first few pages, I was instantly immersed in the story. I liked Hadley, Hemingway's first wife, and while I knew the inevitable fate of their marriage, I couldn't help but enjoy reading this account of their love story, how they met, fell in love. After a time, though, the story became so sodden with drinking and partying that I felt like I was slogging through the story. Once the cracks in the marriage started to appear (besides those early red flags from the very start), it was like a train wreck and while I didn't want to read anymore, I simply couldn't put the book down. It was depressing, sad, and while I respected Hadley throughout, I'm afraid Hemingway comes off poorly (though who would who wants to keep his wife with a mistress on the side? All I can say to Pauline is that what goes around comes around; it's called karma, and can I say I feel somewhat vindicated for Hadley that Pauline was unable to keep Hemingway, either? ha!). Maybe Hemingway is just the tragic artist who couldn't seem to bear his own genius and live a respectable life, but I found him a poor excuse for a man. Ew. 
 In the end, I can't really recommend this novel because it's so dreadfully depressing. Also, a warning to friends that it can be explicit at times. Mostly, though, they just drank like fish. Lovely.

The very ending of the ending is something different, it kinda gives me consolation but also I feel so powerless. 
 I JUST WANTED THEM TO BE HAPPY AND LIVE PEACEFULLY BY A RIVER OKAY. ;__;

Ugh. Hated this! A ton! I heard so much buzz about this when the movie came out, so I decided to give it a chance, but I absolutely hated the main character and just didn't care what happened to her. On top of that, I didn't care for the heavy-handed anti-religion theme and motif throughout the story. I don't mind that it's anti-religion (I may be religious, but I can appreciate a book that shows a different perspective), but I'm not a fan of authors shoving their agenda down your throat. I don't care for most Christian fiction because of that, either. The author takes a one-sided approach to the topic and does so in a very clear manner that makes it obvious where the author stands and how he's trying to get the reader to stand on the issue. 
 The only thing I did like is that the magic of the land. That alone kept me reading through it, but it wasn't enough to make the story any good for me.

reader interested with cliff hangers and action. Tally, the main character, is an "Ugly" who is almost 16. When people turn 16, they undergo a surgery to become a "Pretty". When the time comes for her transformation, Tally ends up going on a mission for Special Circumstances instead. She must find her friend, Shay, and reveal the location of "The Smoke" in order to become beautiful. The story takes the reader through Tally's outrageous adventure to the wild, while giving insight on all of her thoughts and feelings. Will Tally decide to betray her friend to become pretty or to live as an "Ugly" forever?

The only reason it took me a few weeks to read this book was because it was so accurate I had to keep putting it down to recover. 
 American Fascism as described by Lewis is Corpoism, a belief that the state should be run like a corporation, and the fascist leader (and his shady behind-the-scenes right hand man) are fairly elected. 
 I do kind of wish Sissy had been the main character, but all of the women characters are excellently drawn and get their fair due. 
 The book can be funny, although some of the satire stings a bit more right now than it might otherwise have done. I felt real affection for many of the characters, and it was easy to get drawn into this world. Overall I feel It Can't Happen Here is a better match for the current political situation than 1984, if that's why you're reading it. 
 As far as trigger warnings go:  Obviously racism and anti-Semitism are discussed in 1930s terms, but they're soundly condemned by the book. Homophobia is more problematic. There's frank discussion of rape, but none actually happens, and in the last 20% of the book there's a lot of violence, but it's not torture porn. (There's straight-up torture, but it's there to shock and appall you, not titilate.)

Say what you will about the Dresden Files, but for me it's just endless fun. Brooding wizard battling the forces of evil, screwing up a lot and spouting sarcasm along the way? Hell, yeah! 
 Here in Summer Knight, Harry Dresden finds himself in the midst of a faerie war, and, like always, he faces it the way I face adulthood; you know, just winging it.

This is the fifth book of the series and it is written very much like a penultimate book, unhappy ending included. That's exactly what's wrong with the book, that it goes according to the unofficial script of YA fantasy penultimate books. I mean Maas really outdid herself here: 
 -The compulsive pairing of the main cast (with writing sometimes straight out of historical romances, which considering the fact that I actually like historical romance wouldn't be a bad thing except that it all felt very contrived. No, seriously, what are the chances? Or is it the 'we might die tomorrow' vibe that's making everyone pair up?). 
 -The Mary-Sue that is Celaena--I mean, Aelin. Seriously you will never find a stronger, more cunning, more awesome person. I, for one, am amazed at her foresight. I mean who needs Baba Yellowlegs when you have Aelin? 
 -Squad goals. Y'all this is the time the whole squad finally came together. Right before that disastrous (disastrously predictable) ending. 
 -The jump-cut writing style when you want to bring a big story together but do not wanna get caught up in the details. 
 -Bonus: characters I have never heard of since I refuse to read the prequels are suddenly all over the place. 
 I very nearly gave this two stars. 
 Let me just say, @Maas, book 5 is where you separate this series from all the others of its genre, not when you actively work to make it cookie-cutter New Adult fantasy. 
 Side note: Maas has made me eat very humble pie once before when I accused her of being too cliche, I'm really hoping the sixth book will not be more of the same tired script. The thing with Maas's writing is that it is like reading a very enjoyable trope-that-isn't-a-trope fic and so there is always the danger of slipping too far into been-there-done-that territory.

I had forgotten how much I adore this book. 
 One of my favorites, by far. 
 I desperately need to read the sequels.
WOW THAT WAS SERIOUSLY AWESOME. Both the story and the art are amazing. Love it. A very solid first volume which does a great job in introducing the concept of Lazarus and Families.

I have been reading too many books with the same theme. Intense but forbidden love and a story interspersed with letters. Maybe because I read The Forgotten Garden before and fell in love with it this one did not fall upto the mark. But still it had a poignant love story or it had two but I liked that of Jennifer and Antony. That of Ellie lacked in depth. The love letters were simply beautiful.

Another lovely read in the Hathaway series. Poppy and Harry's story. Poppy is the third Hathaway sister, and she just wants a conventional life - to marry a nice man and settle into a quiet life of children and family. Unfortunately due to the unconventional make-up of her family, the ton is largely closed to her, and after several seasons she's still unmarried. But all that is about to end, because she and Michael have fallen in love and plan to marry. Michael, who is a member of the upper classes and will eventually inherit a title. But he hasn't been brave enough to tell his father yet or to openly be with Poppy.... 
 Then Harry Rutledge comes into the picture. Harry, a driven, lonely, brilliant workaholic who owns and runs the hotel where the Hathaways stay in London. He and Poppy meet by chance at the hotel one day, largely due to the pesky behaviour of Beatrix Hathaway's cute ferret Dodger. Gotta love Dodger! Poppy and Harry like each other right from the start, and it isn't long before Harry decides he needs to 'acquire' the fascinating Poppy, as if she is a piece of property he can simply own. But life isn't that simple....... and Poppy has a mind of her own! 
 It's an interesting plot. Some of Harry's behaviour is quite reprehensible in his quest to secure Poppy away from Michael and into his own arms. And Poppy lets Harry know what she thinks! It's not an easy path for either of them. But Ms Kleypas is a skilful writer and the reader does not hate Harry - in fact as we learn more about him, like Poppy, we sympathise with the difficult hand life has dealt him. 
 Once again, I was carried along enjoyably by the eventful plot of this book, and by the end I was left still feeling as if the Hathaways are such an interesting family of loveable, slightly eccentric and very warm people. Next book is about Leo and the fascinating governess, Miss Marks, whose secrets have started to be revealed in this book, but obviously she has more to reveal.... :)

Captured takes us to a dystopian future in which the world is ruled by vampires and the remaining human population is reduced to being used as servants and slaves. A small band of rebels still holds out in the woods, and the vampire rulers would like nothing more than to destroy them all. When Aria, only daughter of the rebel leader, is captured and claimed as a blood slave by none other than a vampire prince, she fears her worst nightmare is about to begin. Determined to keep her identity hidden at all costs to protect her family, at first she seeks only to escape. Little by little, however, that begins to change as she gets to know her captor and is astonished to find that he may not be quite the monster she expected. 
 A short but great YA paranormal romance read with a strong protagonist - looking forward to seeing where the story goes in book 2!

Pretty exciting read! A real page-turner, for sure. I didn't guess some of the twists so I was in auspense. My only quibble was Max was a weak MC - everyone made decisions for him, the story was going to move on even if he stood still. But fun read other than that.
What an awesome simple read. Such a refreshing storyline I can't wait to read the others.

Fanfriggentastic!!! I mean I am blown away. I love Kiera and Kellan and this book totally rocked. The ending was PERFECT!!!! I don't really have anything major and deep to say about it except I want a drama filled love story like Kellan Kyles and Kieras, it's filled with so much passion that it's palpable. There love for each other is beautiful and real...I love that they had thing's in this book that they needed to develop and grow from. Real relationship problems that seemed so hard to overcome in my mind! They really discovered true love in this book. The sex and chemistry in this book was even better than in the first book! I loved it...overall if you haven't read this series stop what you are doing and read it! It's amazing :)
Killing Floor isn't bad, I liked the author's prose, but it's very predictable and the characters didn't seem realistic to me.

The second book in this amazing series, and I enjoyed it as much as the first one. I'll try to keep this as spoiler-free as possible, but most of this will make no sense if you haven't read this book. Just some of the thoughts I have swirling around in my head. 
 Kaylee's abilities are developing, she's finally learning to control herself and her powers, and Nash is with her every step of the way. Did I mention I adore him already? I love their dynamic and their chemistry, especially when the room temperature rises above critical levels. 
 Rawr, baby. 
 I wasn't blown away by Tod in the first book, but I really like him now. He's cute, funny and I just love it when he gets on his brother's nerves. He seems to be getting closer to Kaylee as well, and I like that. It's not like he has a lot of people in his life and I think it's good for him to have her around. As long as he keeps a safe distance... *scowls* 
 I really didn't like Addie in this book, my god what a pain in the ass. Nash setting her straight towards the end even got a "BLEEP YEAH!!" out of me while I was reading that part. But she redeemed herself eventually, which left me feeling quite satisfied with the outcome. 
 I have one silly remark, but it's something that seems odd after a while: Nash and Kaylee hold hands constantly. All the friggin' time! A little less hand-holding, a little more action please. Cause I love how graphic the action is in this series. *winks* 
 Next!

This is the first (possible future) current NY Times Bestseller that I've read in a long while. I forgot how much fun they could be. 
 Take a few distraught children, throw extra brutality at them when young, then fast forward 30-some years and see how they have survived. Though this formula has been done by many different people with varying successes (recently I read It which follows a similar premise), I appreciated John Hart's take and like what he did with the main characters of Julian (our broken adult still coming to grips with the world as he sees it), Michael (protector, vigilante, mafia enforcer) and also Abigail (savior figure for Julian) and Jessup (Abigail's bodyguard). 
 When finally all of these characters have been introduced and the real story gets moving along, the pages turn fast. Though it is possible Hart tried to weave too much together (which means that after the story that starts this whole book ends, he still has over 100 pages left to tie loose ends together) I did enjoy the additional layers involved. Once the initial sections of elaborate descriptions are finished, Hart is usually good at economically using words, though too often I found myself skimming paragraphs and sentences to just get to what had to be coming up next. Not that they were bad, just that they were delaying what was inevitable and - like his wordy descriptions during the first chapter especially - unnecessary. 
 The major drawback to this book, though, was in the character of Elena. Though she is supposed to be the kinda sorta savior figure (in a sense) for Michael (as Abigail is to Julian, though in a VERY different way), her character never gets the treatment it deserves. She is by far the weakest and I still feel that she was there more for plot device than as an actual human being. 
 That aside, the story was fun, the mysteries were neat and it was great to see some action sequences that went far enough to let the mind wander but reined it in just enough so that it didn't traumatize the reader (opposed to, say, certain scenes in The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo). 
 Full disclosure sake, I got this ARC via a Goodreads first reads competition.

Nice read, but there's not much to say. I ended comparing this to the movie nonstop, since I've watched the movie like million and one times! And I must admit, both have pros and cons. Book had less embarrassing moments, when the movie was filled with embarrassment. But the movie had more scenes with Darcy and Daniel, which I missed in the book. 
 I think I like the movie better, since I'm going to watch it yet again this Christmas (because you just have to watch it when it's Christmas!), but I don't see myself reading this again. 
 Oh, and I was all confused when there was all this talk about answering machines etc.! Then I had to check out when this came out, and realized I was only about 10 years old back then, and cellphones came few years later, so no wonder they didn't have cellphones.. 
 But huge plus for the fact that this was written ages ago, yet still didn't feel outdated. Except for the part about answering machines.

I don't know what I expected from A Fractured Light, but it was a lot more boring than I expected. Looking back I realize that I gave A Beautiful Dark a higher rating than it deserved, and I also realize that I really didn't like it much at all and only gave it the high rating because I couldn't think of a reason not to.

http://snoopydoosbookreviews.com/bone... 
 When I saw this on Netgalley I thought it sounded really good and interesting. 
 It is interesting and a really cool idea and I sort of liked the first half of the book. Thinking that a lot of the questions will answered. 
 But they really didn't. It just got worse and really it started to get really confusing and it got to the point where it was hard to follow the story. It also most seemed like the author lost focus on something, went to something else and back to the first part. There were some pretty good plot holes staring half way through the book. 
 Characters also seemed pretty flat and didn't seems to grow much. 
 Overall. I liked the idea and the first part of the book in hopes it will answer a lot of things but it just got worse and worse. 
 Story and characters were just all over the place and it was neither enjoyable anymore nor made it a lot of sense. 
 I rate it at 2

I really enjoyed this! I wouldn't necessary label it "YA" even though it does read like one. 
 Very unique and mysterious. Great world/s building! I feel like I know some plots points for the remaining trilogy, but also know Schwab will throw a few twists and turns in there for us! 
 I thought the idea of Vampirates was hilarious, but MAGIC pirates just sounds like something I need to literally be part of.
3 stars for myself, but 4 or five if I'm thinking about younger readers, especially those who enjoy fantasy and can hang in there for some world building.
This is on my recommend list for sure. Love finding unique stories.

I didn't know about this book until a patron requested it. Once I had it in my hands, the cover was so beautiful, I had to find out what it was about. Beyond that, the description compared it to Gabriel Garcia Marquez! OK. Must read it. 
 I listened to The Snow Child as an audio book and loved it. It is the story of Jack and Mabel, an older couple who moves to Alaska as homesteaders in the 1920s, unable to shake the memory of their stillborn child. The homesteading is difficult and their relationship is suffering. Upon the first snowfall, they build a child out of the snow, only to find her gone the next morning. They also start seeing a young blond girl racing through the woods and hunting with a fox. 
 The beauty of this book is in its quiet. I could feel the cold. Without any major, fast action, I got a sense that everything was going to fall apart at any moment. The isolation was palpable. Ivey's prose is, at times, breathtaking. This story is slow to unfold, but it is just so good.
Oh that cliffhanger!!!! can't wait to read the next installment on the series!!!

It was good as always. I am a huge fan of Rachel Caine and I read all of her series and liked them all. Her books are always interesting, with great characters and a lot of action. And "Unseen" is not exception to this. 
 I find Cassiel an excellent character. She is unusual and memorable in this huge amount of urban fantasy lead heroines. And what I think is making her distinctive is the way she thinks. Other characters often use "cold" to describe Cassiel. But she is not. She is just very logical, pragmatic and calm (she is totally opposite to Joanne in Weather Warden series, who is impulsive and all her action came from her fillings). 
 In "Unseen" we finally get to see a development in Cassiel and Luis relationship. I like Luis, but sometimes I get this feeling, that Cass is stronger than he is. And not in physical sense but in mental one. She is always the one who made tough decisions and have to deal with the consequences of it. 
 The problem that I had with this book is the mortality level in it. It is the third book in series and in every one of them people keep dropping off like flies. Only we get introduced a new character, BAM, he is dead. In Weather Warden series a lot of people died to, but it can't compare with mortality in Outcast Season. Ms. Caine, please, stop killing so much of your characters (especially children)! 
 I really hoped that we get to see main characters from Weather Warden. I miss Joanne, David and Lewis. But the events in "Unseen" occurred in time of Warden sea travel, so we don't get to see any of them. I just hope that there will be crossovers in the next books. 
 Conclusion: the quality of Outcast Season is the same. And in Russian we had this saying that "Constancy is the sign of great talent".

This falls between 'didn't like' and 'it was OK' for me. 
 I liked that Sam began really seeing herself and made changes. However, I cannot forgive her for not calling Lindsey out on her crap. (Yes, she did the one day, but she should have on the day that counted.) 
 But in the end, she didn't do enough to save the book for me.
I really enjoyed this, but I felt like a lot of important details slipped through the cracks.

I'm not exactly sure what to say about this book. I've not read a lot of books by the author so I can't say I'm a huge fan or not of her writing and can only talk about the ones I have read. 
 Poppy is just ... too perfect. She can do everything and has no trouble with any task. Despite how she says that something is hard she has no trouble with doing it. When it came to descriptions I got rather tired of hearing how she had red hair and especially how she had red eyebrows, maybe it is just a thing since I'm not used to an author mentioning what color a character's brows are, but it just bothered me a bit. 
 Godric, well I can see how he has this uber position, but I couldn't really see him working as he is supposed to. I mean it was easy for him to put stuff off, go stalk Poppy, eat lunch with her, and well whatever else. The revelations as to what/who he is near the end of the book was sort of surprising since I would think that someone who has that position and clout would ... I don't know work harder? I just saw all of the results and none of the work that had to be done to get there, if that makes sense. 
 I think the world has a good foundation to build from, but I think that there wasn't enough conflict throughout the story and what little there was was easily remedied. When it was taken care of it seemed to all be taken care of "off screen" or too easily. Whatever happened to Brandon and Jonathon? With Brandon the one or two lines that talked about what happened with him wasn't really very satisfying. Just when it seems to be getting interesting the story ends so I guess this was more of a short prequel or extended epilogue? I'm not familiar with Ms. Dawn's other works so maybe it is the norm. 
 The groundwork created for the world was pretty intriguing. I enjoyed what little information she gave for shifters and how it all works. Introductions went pretty quickly so I'm guessing they will be expanded on in further books. The world itself was pretty cool, but I'd like to hear more about how everything is compared to before. I think the whole bit with the gun was sort of ... well silly. If you are a general's daughter and have some good martial training, wouldn't you recognize a weapon even if it were banned and there aren't any more now? Also I get why there is the big alpha guy and the tiny delicate looking woman ... but do authors ever think as to how the logistics actually work when they come together? 
 Just a pet peeve about the snoring ... I just didn't find it amusing. There are medical reasoning's as to why people snore and if you snore really loud you should really get yourself checked out. Snoring when tired or stressed makes sense ... snoring loudly just because makes me think of serious medical type issues.

Beg acts as an excellent introduction to the rest of this series, but it is both pacey and HOT! 
 The author develops the characters, their relationships and their hang-ups. 
 Monica is a great singer, and her best friend, Gabby, accompanies her on the piano. The play gigs at night clubs and bars, but are still awaiting their big break. They feel that it is bound to come. Gabby knows the names of all the people in the music industry who can help them towards their goal. However, she is unstable and depressed. So depressed is she, that she bounces in and out of being suicidal. 
 Between Monica and her ex, Darren, who is also Gabby's brother, they keep a safe watch on her to make sure that she doesn't terminate her life. This adds stress for both of them, and impacts their social lives. 
 Of course, like most aspiring musicians who are working hard for their big breaks, Monica has to work at a day, or night, job. She waitresses. 
 But she is easily distracted. The result is that she tips a tray of drinks into the lap of the billionaire owner, Jonathan, and gets fired. 
 You can read more of the story in the book description and all of the reviews. The short version is that Monica and Jonathan fall for each other. Jonathan is a divorcee who doesn't want a serious relationship, and would like a string of women who will submit to his dominant tendencies. He does NOT want a long term relationship with Monica! Will he? Won't he? On the other hand, Monica wants Jonathan so much that she will do ANYTHING he asks. 
 The outcome is SMOLDERING! 
 Other characters are developed and come into play, but you need to read the book to find out more. 
 The end of the book is such a cliffhanger that you are compelled to pick up the next one. I found this a little irritating as there is no need for it. Songs of Submission (Beg, Tease, Submit) is not what I would call a proper trilogy. It is a novel which has been unnaturally sawed into three pieces. 
 If you can take this, then you are about to pick up some top class erotica.

Mini-review originally posted at http://shelversanon.blogspot.com 
 I'm afraid I was less than pleased. I wanted to like it. No, I wanted to love it, but so many of the stories fell flat. None of them made me shiver. None of them made me gasp. Very few had any strong connections to the rhyme chosen (okay, the one based on Hickory Dickory Dock did a pretty good job both at being interesting and connecting to its rhyme). Only a handful made me wish for a full-length tale based on the characters presented. In most cases, the authors seemed to think that having someone die qualified the tale as "dark." As someone who has read and reread Alfred Hitchcock Presents: Stories That Scared Even Me, I beg to differ. Now THAT is a dark anthology. 
 Note: I was given an ARC of Two and Twenty Dark Tales by the publisher for review via NetGalley.

After a fairly interesting premise, John Scalzi writes a war book with a tiny thread of romance. Which is fine, but I'm not really into war. I kept wanting him to do more with the premise, like give characters peculiarities and quirks and surprisingly useful talents from their previous lives, but he never did. It is well written and well paced, and not remotely misogynistic, which does set it apart from much sci-fi.
Easy to digest as far as sci-fi goes, but a little lacking of substance. I've read much better distopian fiction with similar themes -- for example, "The Handmaid's Tale."

Do you know when you realize that you are reading a good book? When you can't put it down, when you even dream about it! Well, this is one of those books. 
 DiSemblance is an original techno-thriller novel. It grabs you from the start and you can't stay away from it for too long. 
 In DiSemblance we meet Jason a 17-year-old boy who has lived his all life almost confined to his house. After saying goodbye to his father, who goes away for the weekend, his life changes from one second to the next. He sees him involve in a strange case of a serial killer and in a fight to save his life, his brother's and the girl next door. 
 The story moves extremely fast. With chapters very short (mostly 3 pages long more or less) you can feel the action through the pages. And things change with a speed that gives you the sensation that you are living them. 
 The book has some moments that blow your mind. You end up feeling like you were hit by a wall. Most of the times the news was so surprising that my mouth hang open for a while. I was like... "Wasn't he or she supposed to be dead?" Or saying "is this real?" 
 The most amazing thing was that you really don't know where the book is going. I love that it isn't predictable. Maybe at the end you have a feeling of where it was going but it still has a great ending. 
 Jason is an amazing character, a mature, brave, intelligent boy who is willing to do anything in order to clean his father's name. His brother Isaac his so funny, I adore him. Being totally opposite to Jason he is a bit annoying but anyway he is sweet guy. The detective Durante is the perfect adult character that this book needs. And you couldn't have a great book without a girl! Boston is the lady in question; she is the perfect match for Jason. 
 The whole holographic reality is outstanding; it's excellently explained and is the perfect background. Besides being original DiSemblace makes you question a lot of things. In a world dominated by technology this kind of book makes you wonder some things. 
 This truly is an excellent book, which is perfect for YA and adults as well. 
 (I received a copy of the book from the author in exchange of an honest review)

DNF. 
 Have you ever found yourself browsing books, stumbling upon an interesting series, with good ratings, good reviews- the whole package and then thinking something like: oh, an average of 4.20 stars. How can this book go wrong? 
 Yeah. 
 So, the question: why did this book not adhere to my liking? 
 Within minutes of seeing each other-meaning they were merely strangers- the guy strikes the girl. A slap on the face that sends her sprawled over the floor. 
 I'm sorry but- what the fuck? 
 I cannot tolerate a guy hitting a girl. I cannot. I don't care what the circumstances are. You do not get to raise your filthy fucking hand. This book is nothing but a sad attempt. That's what it is. The author accomplished no feat. Everything sucked- the writing, the characters, the romance (or the lack of it, really because hitting a girl- a fucking stranger, too- is the lowest fucking thing a guy can do). Moreover, the fantasy? LOLOLOLOLOL. I'm not even going to comment on that. I don't know how the story progresses so I have no clue if it gets better (or if it even gains the capacity to get better lmao) but upon reading that little hitting bit, I don't even care if this series turns out to be one of the best. It's gonna remain the lowest for me. Don't read it.

OMG I just love the Fuentes brothers! Carlos, oh Carlos. You are so annoying sometimes, but I gotta love you. Carlos, you just don't realize how lucky you are! And Kiara! Way to hold your own girl! 
 I just loved the Kiara/Carlos romance! So sweet, and yet Kiara knew how to stand up to Carlos, which I loved. The cookie thing was genius! The feud and the love/hate relationship between those two was very entertaining. And Kiara was just so...dedicated. She refused to give up on Carlos no matter what. And Carlos's decision in the end...perfect for him. And Alex! so great to see him again in this, it's cool to see him as more of an adult, see the way he really looks after his brother...thought Carlos was a total ass to him most of the time. And to see Alex and Brittney still together was great! (and sorry, I know I say 'and' a LOT in this but I can't seem to help it). Kiara's family was sooo amazing to Carlos, taking him in, and I think it added a whole knew sweet level to their relationship. It was so nice to see her parents really believe in Carlos and accept Kiara's relationship with him, unlike Brittney's parents. Love, Love, love the Fuentes brothers!!!!! 
 Also, I'm writing this review after I finished Luis's story, so I had to delete a bunch of stuff cuz I was getting them mixed up, but I think I got rid of it all. For those of you that are reading this, make sure you read Luis's story too! I did a review of it as well, but it's slightly shorter, though I'm sure I'll add more to it, as I'm sure I will to this one, too.

Nice. Good summer read, flows well but I just didn't feel great engagement with either main character. 
 Victoria is a divorce lawyer who moves into the apartment next to Ford. They have a series of almost meets which gives her the wrong impression about him but end up working together to help Ford's sister. 
 I think there was maybe just too much that was contrived, they both had father issues they needed to deal with, their failed meet cutes etc.

Overall, an enjoyable read although it didn't start that way. For the first 175 pages I was not really loving this book. This book was divided into 7 parts and each part was better than the one previous. There are a TON of characters in this book and part 1 is a lot of set up, so it is a bit of a struggle to get into because you are just waiting for the story to progress. However, once you get past those first 200 pages the book really comes alive and then you cannot put it down! 
 The characters are all very flawed but the reader still manages to find a likable or relatable quality in each of them. Even though this is an "adult" book I still think Rowling was at her best when she was writing from one of the teenage perspectives. 
 The tone of the narration is very intimate and omniscient which I enjoy. Saying this book has multiple perspectives is an understatement, there are at least 17 perspectives and sometimes it is difficult to keep up. At times the reader spends 5 or 10 pages with a character and other times it's merely 5 or 10 sentences. 
 Overall this book has a leisurely pace is humorous, dramatic, sad, hopeful, reflective, gritty, harsh, and moving. 
 Side note: I did need some time to adjust to this book, being a Harry Potter fan it was weird to read Rowling using swear words and while this book has violence, child abuse, drug abuse, teenage sex, child molestation and rape, it is not gratuitous and adds to the tone and message of the novel.

Fitz has always been dumb, but he was just a little too dumb in this one for me to really like it. The reader sees all the surprises coming many chapters before Fitz himself does, because they're foreshadowed so strongly. It really hurts the suspension of disbelief when someone supposedly trained in spycraft can't figure out really basic stuff like the fact that the first messenger was a white sent from the fool  or likewise that Bee is a white herself . The catalogue of his mistakes and failings as a person would be almost as long as the book. 
 Which by the way is way longer than it needs to be. Where was the editor? I don't need to hear for the fiftieth time about how Bee wants more attention or about how reluctant Fitz is to be drawn back into the Farseer family's business.

What an incredible book. 
 Eliza and Her Monsters is an fascinating look at internet culture, mental health, and the value of doing what you truly love. The characters are complex and (for an internet-obsessed, introvert like me) relatable, the dialogue is funny and clever, and Monstrous Sea is an amazing side story. I loved getting to see Eliza's web comic and especially loved seeing the artwork, which made this book more of an experience than your usual book. 
 Although there's a lot to love about Eliza, my favorite thing has to be the way it portrays relationships. There are a lot of different relationships in this book--familial, acquaintance, friends--but what it does best is show that you can be friends with anyone anywhere thanks to the internet. Internet friends are really unique to those of born in the computer age, and so we know that we can be friends with people we've never actually met or even seen a picture of; just because we communicate with someone solely online doesn't mean they're any less of a friend. Unfortunately, because this type of friendship is so new, a lot of older folks don't truly understand the value of internet friends and sort of poo-poo upon these relationships. Case in point: Eliza's parents. They're not trying to be mean or to punish Eliza by wanting her to live in the real world more, they just fail to understand that Eliza is connecting with the real world, she's just doing so with people in other places. 
 That's not to say that Eliza doesn't suffer from some issues that contribute to her preference for the indoors. This book provides a very realistic portrayal of social anxiety as well as panic attacks and depression, and yes, that may seem like a lot of mental health issues to tackle in one story, but it's handled so well. It never feels like these issues are shoe-horned into the plot just to make it more complicated; no, Eliza and Wallace's issues stem from events in their lives that have left them scarred, and their reactions are all too natural responses. It's really heartbreaking to see both characters dealing with their separate issues, especially after certain events leave both of them suffering on their own. At the same time, though, it's inspiring to see Eliza and Wallace begin to overcome their anxieties and ask for help and support as they work through things, and I was so glad that Eliza especially reached a place with her family where they could being to understand who she was and what she was feeling so that they could be there for her. 
 This book also does a wonderful job at exploring Internet fandoms through Eliza's web comic. Like I said, I loved reading the bits and pieces of Monstrous Sea and meeting Wallace and other fans of the series. I would absolutely love to see a full version of this story at some point, although for now I can live with the teaser over on Francesca's Wattpad (which can be found at https://www.wattpad.com/user/ChessieZ..., along with The Children of Hypnos, which Eliza and Wallace read in Eliza). 
 Overall, Eliza and Her Monsters is a solid 5-star read. It has plenty of fandom, drama, and snappy comebacks, and its focus on mental health really sets it apart from most other contemporary YA books. The featured artwork also takes the story up another notch and helps mesh together the story of Eliza's life with the story she's writing. I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a contemporary read that strays a little from the familiar and tackles some hard subjects with honesty.

 Firstly I had no idea that this whole book is from a child's perspective. The book's basic premise does deal with a very serious topic . But the way it has been written somehow makes it easier to read (I did not have the heavy feeling that is associated with most of the classics). 
 The start of the book reminded me of all the children's book I have ever read- the world is innocent all around and life is all about fun and games. But as the story moves forward and the main protagonist (Scout) becomes aware of all the evil's that surround her, we too experience this awakening with her. I really think this was a very unique way of making the reader realize how the innocence of this child is shattered and there is a stage of awareness of the rights and wrong (We all have been through that). 
 The author has also beautifully iterated to the reader that it is easier for the children to differentiate between right and wrong than adults who are prejudiced by their own narrow view of how the world should be.

If I wanted re-imaginings I'd stick to Gregory MaguireGregory Maguire , although I got sick of him pretty quickly, too.

I admittedly LOVED Lamb: The Gospel According to Biff, Christ's Childhood Pal and will always consider it one of my favorites and that's a riff on the Bible I'm a bit of a hypocrite, sue me.

But the book is breezy and fun even though the concepts are actually pretty heavy. Lily working on a crisis line was close to home for me (as I'm a social worker who does this as a job), and while I certainly don't think she was portrayed as being a good clinician I can appreciate the absurdity of distracting someone threatening suicide with literally anything that will stop them from acting. Disruption has been on my radar ever since I finished reading another book by this author. Disruption is a book that drew me in with it's synopsis. The whole idea behind the M-Bands both fascinated and scared me. Imagine not having to go on pointless dates, wasting time and money on people you'd rather not be with, and using the band to find your match, to jump the queue and go straight to them. But having something so small have such a big role in your life is also scary, it's a small step to taking away your free will, your feelings and opinions. 
 Maggie doesn't believe in the M-Bands, grudgingly getting a band and only turning it on at registration, before disabling it. She dislikes the way it takes your feelings away from it all, not having a choice in who you want to date and spend your life with, even more so with the disappearance of her Father. Determined to fight the system and somehow find her Father, with the help of an unwilling accomplice, Gus, Maggie finds a way to win the hear of Quentin Mercer, heir to the M-Band throne. 
 Disruption was a book I enjoyed reading, there were a few moments where I thought it dragged on a bit too much for my liking, but overall I liked the progression of the story line, and Maggie's plan. Maggie is someone who I admired for not being afraid to be different, to stand out from the crowd and not be a follower. She is also resourceful and determined, and we see these qualities come out more the closer Maggie gets to finding the answers. I wasn't particularly keen on how she obtains help from others, but looking at if after the book is over, there isn't really any other way that this could have been done without it. 
 The characters within the pages did grow on me, despite some of thier attitudes, and towards the end of the book I did worry about thier outcomes. I liked that we get to see people from all walks of life, and that it's not necessary the popular, rich people that get to call the shots. 
 Final Verdict 
 Did I love Disruption, no. But I did enjoy reading it. I liked that we get brief explanations about the important details to the plot, and we don't get too much information thrown at us. The ending of the book wasn't something I expected, and I am excited to see where it picks up in the next installment.

I must say I'm not a big fan of anthologies/novellas. There usually doesn't seem to be enough time to flesh out the characters adequately. That said: 
 Julia Quinn - Something Old. LOVE her. Good introduction to the characters. Glaring error between this and the Something Old story - did Anne need to be married by the time she was 21 or 25? Four Stars 
 Stefanie Sloane - Something New. About Anne and Rhys. How have I never read this author before? I loved this story. All the characters were likeable, and I liked them spending time together without quite knowing why it was so important. Four Stars 
 Elizabeth Boyle - Something Borrowed. Kipp and Cordelia. They are childhood friends. He's almost engaged, and she doesn't want to marry, just travel the world. There were a lot of people in this story, so the story of the couple wasn't as engaging. Also, back in those days, having sex in a garden with the fear of being discovered? I don't think so. Three stars, I guess. 
 Laura Lee Guhrke - Something Blue. Lawrence and Cordelia. This story would have been better if it had been longer. Lawrence is trying to find evidence against Cordelia's father for selling shoddy guns. So she "hates" him because of this. We're three-quarters of the way through the story before she discovers that her father was guilty (discussion with her father was a short blurb in the story), the father leaves the country, Lawrence decides he's going to do whatever it takes to bring him to justice, and all of a sudden Cordelia is fine with it. I'd give it 2.5 stars. 
 Julia Quinn - and a Sixpence in Her Shoe. Frederick and Beatrice. IMHO, it was brilliant to end with Julia Quinn, because it makes it will to forgive the shortcomings of the other stories. I loved this story. Frederick and Beatrice were both wonderful characters, and I loved their interactions with one another. Her honest, inquisitive reactions to his eye injury were touching, and his interest in her mind was very endearing. Her issues with the sixpence were funny. 4.5 stars.

Yearning to Read 
 Ella of Frell has never really known her father. She and her mother are best friends living a happy life with their Cook, Mandy, for company. But Ella is not your typical girl. She was given the gift of obedience as a baby from a fairy who never gives good gifts, even when she has the best of intentions. This gift means Ella must obey any and all orders - whether it be to sweep the floor, hop like a rabbit, or cut off her own head! 
 After Ella's mother dies, Ella must deal with her grief alone - for not only is her mother gone, but her father is sending her to finishing school with the two most horrid girls in the world - Hattie and Olive. She wishes she could stay in Frell, enjoying the menagerie and her new friend Prince Charmont, but her father, who knows nothing of her curse, has ordered her to go. 
 But Ella is not one to shy from adventure, or to bend the rules of her obedience charm. Ogres, elves, stepsisters, and possible true love wait in her future. If only she could find the fairy who gave her the curse in the first place... 
 ___________________________________ 
 My thoughts - 
 At first, it was hard not to compare this book to the movie, which I've seen about ten times. I still watch it every so often with my sisters to laugh and relive childhood memories, as silly as the movie is. I wanted the book to be different but...the same. Same characters, same order of events, same climax and turnout. 
 I got something completely different, and was at first surprised by this. I wasn't sure how much I liked it - it lacked the action and intensity I was expecting. 
 But I soon got over this and found myself in a fluffy, light, floating fairy-tale that involves more silly magic and character development than action. And then I was hit with the climax - and I went to my sister, who had already read the book, laughing and giggling and bursting about the story with her, while she tried to get me to stop hugging her with joy... ;) 
 In any case, I was so happy, by the end, to find how different and how much better this was from the movie, which I don't know if I'll ever watch again. How could they have ruined such a beautiful story?! 
 Character notes - 
 I really loved all these characters. They were three-dimensional and full of life and so different from each other. I admired Ella (even though I thought she cried a lot), despised Hattie, and said, "Poar Olive" every once in a while to get a good laugh. (Yes, I meant "poar".) 
 Prince Char, where to begin? He started as a boy, and grew into a man, lovable, tender, and loving. He lived up to my standards and definitely deserved this story's heroine! 
 Story notes - 
 Like I said before, I wasn't too happy with the lack of action and suspense...but it was hard to stay disappointed. I found myself enjoying the story just as much as I'd been hoping, just in a different way. It focused on Ella and how she came to be a woman, so whether this involved taming ogres or sewing for finishing school, it became an adventure. A few of the scenes weren't as well written or executed as the others, but the turnout of those scenes always made up for it. 
 My favorite scenes involved the love letters. Love letters always add the most touching and tender side to a story. I'm so glad this story had many!! 
 Summing it up - 
 Lively - like skipping by a lake in the cool spring breeze. I'm so glad to have gotten to know Ella, her friends, and even her enemies. I want to read more of Levine's novels now!

 "Now can we please go inside? I'm freezing my butt off and I need my fluffer to warm me up." I narrow my eyes. "Excuse me?" She blinks innocently. "Oh, I'm sorry. Did I say fluffer?" Her smile lights up her whole face. "I meant boyfriend ." Sweetest words I've ever heard in my life.

This was a pretty great series. I enjoyed it and it was short and sweet so to speak. It speaks volumes about what it is like to grow up in a small town where there are cliques, bullies, rumors, the rich, the poor, and a place where everyone has some sort of history. It shows growth and change in a girl just trying to get through high school and then her life changes drastically over night. It was a good story and a quick read.

Overall this 3rd book of the series was outstanding. The action was great and the story unfolded quickly. I liked seeing Tally in her new, highly functioning "skin". She seemed much more in control of herself and her emotions and was able to see the world for what it was. 
 However, the last part of the book had me more than frustrated. I stood by her when she switched so carelessly from being in love with Peris, then David, and then even Zane (admittedly my favorite of the bunch). But this most recent change in her ever-so-fleating love interests has me fuming! How can she possibly think of starting over again?! Ugh! 
 But again, other than Tally's misguided feelings for the men in her life, I really enjoyed the new world that is being created in this book. The Random Town that Tally found is just the right mix of futuristic bubbliness and Rusty thinking. I had some trouble really picturing everything that is being described in the town (something that has been lacking in all three of the books so far is good, descriptive world-building). But honestly, I have been free to let my imagination wander and make their world whatever I want it to be. 
 The ending of the third book is not at all a cliff-hanger in my mind. In fact, I have serious doubts that the fourth book should have been written. Kind of like a TV series that goes one season too long, I wonder if the fourth book will do more harm than good in tying up any loose ends. Maybe this one would have been better off left to each person to imagine the rest of the story and what happens to Ms. Tally Youngblood.

This is NOT a romance. Not erotica. Not a love story of any type or description. WHAT. SO. EVER. Anyone who picks this up expecting yet another version of 50 Shades, only darker and more BDSM-ey, is in for the shock of their life. 
 Break Her is a psychological thriller unlike any I've read in recent memory. The protagonist is pitted against a villain that defies description (by me, anyway). He is completely without conscience, a pure psychopath. Fuck the nicey-nicey personality disorder titles they give that stuff nowadays; this guy is a complete fucking psycho. 
 I'm not going to say much about the story - that would give it away. It is tautly written, fast-paced and mesmerizing. I couldn't put it down. Nor could I look away, even when the author was describing assaults so brutal that I literally couldn't imagine getting through it. 
 (WARNING: Anyone with any kind of sexual assault triggers or history shouldn't touch this book with a barge pole. Any merit to the discussion of rape and its use and effect contained in the book is miniscule compared to the graphic descriptions that accompany it.) 
 I was riveted while reading this book - my whole body held tense, almost literally on the edge of my seat. At times I was laughing out loud, other times open-mouthed speechless, one time bawling like a baby. 
 The writing was excellent - the author kept me guessing through the whole book. Small details slowly revealed, tension building and releasing all the way through until the end. 
 And the end! Holy shit. I didn't realize I was holding my breath until I let it out in one big gust. The author does such a job of keeping the reader off balance that at least one point I thought it WAS going to turn into a bent version of 50 Shades. 
 Thank God it didn't, but the way the author confirms it is with one word near the end of the book that sent my stomach dropping all the way to my toes. 
 If you can stomach the subject matter and the violence this is one of the best books I've read this year.
